======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Carbon offsets and credits
======================================================================

{{Short description|Carbon dioxide reduction scheme}}
{{About|the use of carbon offsets and carbon credits for countries, corporations, and, in some cases, individuals|more information on carbon credits for individuals|personal carbon trading}}
[[File:Turbine aalborg.jpg|thumb|right|[[Renewable energy]] projects, such as these [[wind turbine]]s near [[Aalborg]], Denmark, constitute one common type of carbon offset project.<ref name=":2">{{cite web |last1=Hamrick |first1=Kelley |last2=Gallant |first2=Melissa |date=May 2017 |title=Unlocking Potential: State of the Voluntary Carbon Markets 2017 |url=https://www.forest-trends.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/doc_5591.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814171921/https://www.forest-trends.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/doc_5591.pdf |archive-date=2020-08-14 |access-date=2019-01-29 |publisher=Forest Trends' Ecosystem Marketplace |page=10}}</ref>]]
{{Climate change and society}}
{{Climate change mitigation}}
{{Green economics sidebar}}

A '''carbon credit''' is a tradable instrument (typically a virtual certificate) that conveys a claim to have avoided [[greenhouse gas]] (GHG) emissions or to have enhanced removal of GHG from the atmosphere.<ref name="OffsetGuide.org">{{cite web |author1=Broekhoff, D. |author2=Gillenwater, M. |author3=Colbert-Sangree, T. |year=2024 |title=Offset Guide |url=https://offsetguide.org/what-are-carbon-credits/ |website=Carbon Offset Guide |access-date=July 28, 2025}}</ref><ref name="wri">{{cite web |last1=Goodward |first1=Jenna |last2=Kelly |first2=Alexia |date=August 2010 |title=Bottom Line on Offsets |url=http://www.wri.org/publication/bottom-line-offsets |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190117153158/https://www.wri.org/publication/bottom-line-offsets |archive-date=2019-01-17 |access-date=2010-09-08 |publisher=World Resources Institute |journal=}}</ref><ref name="ced">{{cite web |title=Carbon offset |url=http://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/carbon-offset |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181004185918/https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/carbon-offset |archive-date=October 4, 2018 |access-date=September 24, 2012 |publisher=Collins English Dictionary - Complete & Unabridged 11th Edition. Retrieved September 21, 2012 from CollinsDictionary.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=What are Offsets? |url=http://www.co2offsetresearch.org/consumer/index.html |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191121173536/http://www.co2offsetresearch.org/consumer/index.html |archive-date=2019-11-21 |access-date=2018-10-23 |publisher=Carbon Offset Research & Education}}</ref> One carbon credit represents the avoided or enhanced removal of one metric ton of [[carbon dioxide]] or its [[Global Warming Potential|carbon dioxide-equivalent]] (CO<sub>2</sub>e).<ref name="OffsetGuide.org"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=What is a Carbon Offset? |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/what-is-a-carbon-offset/ |access-date=2023-04-06 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Courtnell |first=Jane |date=2023-02-01 |title=Carbon Offsets vs Carbon Credits: What's the Difference? |url=https://greenbusinessbureau.com/topics/carbon-accounting/carbon-offsets-vs-carbon-credits/ |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=Green Business Bureau |language=en}}</ref>

'''Carbon offsetting''' is the practice of using carbon credits to offset or counter an entity's greenhouse gas inventory emissions in line with reporting programs or institutional emissions targets/goals. [[Carbon emission trading|Carbon credit trading]] mechanisms (''i.e.'', crediting programs), enable project developers to implement projects that mitigate GHGs and receive carbon credits which can be sold to interested buyers who may use the credits to claim they have offset their inventory [[GHG emissions]]. Similar to "offsetting", carbon credits that are permitted as compliance instruments within regulatory compliance markets (e.g., [[European_Union_Emissions_Trading_System|The European Union Emission Trading Scheme]] or the [[Climate_change_policy_of_California#Cap_and_trade|California Cap-n-Trade program]]) can be used by regulated entities to report lower emissions and achieve compliance status (with limitations around their use that vary by compliance program). Aside from "offsetting", carbon credits can also be used to make contributions toward global net zero GHG-level targets. It is an individual buyer's choice how to use, or "retire", the carbon credit.

Projects entail mitigation actions that avoid or enhance the removal of GHG emissions. Projects are implemented in line with the standards of crediting programs, including their methodologies, rules, and requirements. Methodologies are approved for each specific project type (e.g., tree planting, mangrove restoration, early retirement of coal powerplants). Provided a project fulfills all of the requirements and provisions of a crediting program, it will be issued credits that can be sold to buyers. Each crediting program typically has its own carbon credit 'label' such as CDM's Certified Emission Reductions (CERs), Article 6.4 Mechanism Emission Reductions (A6.4ERs), VCS' Verified Emission Reductions (VERs), ACR's Emission Reduction Tonnes, Climate Action Reserves' Climate Reserve Tonnes (CRTs), etc.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbon Offset Programs |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/carbon-offset-programs/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref>

Hundreds of GHG mitigation project types exist and have approved methodologies with established crediting programs. But each crediting program has its own list of approved methodologies, for example unless explicitly stated, an ACR approved methodology could not be used by someone trying to work through [[Verra (organization)|Verra]]'s [[Verified Carbon Standard]]. Carbon credits are a form of [[Carbon price|carbon pricing]], along with [[carbon tax]]es, and [[EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism|Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAM)]]. Carbon credits are intended to be fungible across different markets, but some compliance markets and reporting programs limit eligibility to specified carbon credit types or characteristics (e.g., vintage, project origin, project type).<ref name="OffsetGuide.org Crediting Programs">{{cite web |author1=Broekhoff, D. |author2=Gillenwater, M. |author3=Colbert-Sangree, T. |year=2024 |title=Offset Guide |url=https://offsetguide.org/what-are-carbon-crediting-programs/ |website=Carbon Offset Guide |access-date=July 28, 2025}}</ref><ref name="Cadman-2022">{{Cite journal |last1=Cadman |first1=Tim |last2=Hales |first2=Robert |date=2022-06-01 |title=COP26 and a Framework for Future Global Agreements on Carbon Market Integrity |url=https://www.berghahnjournals.com/view/journals/ijsq/12/1/ijsq120105.xml |journal=The International Journal of Social Quality |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=79–80 |doi=10.3167/IJSQ.2022.120105 |issn=1757-0344 |s2cid=256659556 |hdl-access=free |hdl=10072/422013}}</ref><ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.spglobal.com/commodityinsights/PlattsContent/_assets/_files/en/our-methodology/methodology-specifications/et_carbon-credit-faq.pdf |title=What is a Voluntary Carbon Market Credit? |publisher=[[S&P Global Commodity Insights]] |access-date=May 4, 2023 |year=2021 |archive-date=June 29, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220629132311/https://www.spglobal.com/commodityinsights/PlattsContent/_assets/_files/en/our-methodology/methodology-specifications/et_carbon-credit-faq.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.americanprogress.org/article/the-cftc-should-raise-standards-and-mitigate-fraud-in-the-carbon-offsets-market/ |title=The CFTC Should Raise Standards and Mitigate Fraud in the Carbon Offsets Market |last1=Fredman |first1=Alex |last2=Phillips |first2=Todd |date=October 7, 2022 |publisher=[[Center for American Progress]] |access-date=May 4, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Emissions Trading – UNFCCC |url=https://unfccc.int/process/the-kyoto-protocol/mechanisms/emissions-trading |access-date=May 4, 2023 |publisher=[[United Nations]]}}</ref>

==Credit quality==

"The originating idea behind a carbon credit is that it can substitute for reductions that a buyer could have made to their own emissions (i.e., compensation use). For this to be true, the world must be at least as well off when a carbon credit is used as it would have been if the buyer had reduced their own carbon footprint. The "quality" of a carbon credit refers to the level of confidence that the use of the credit will fulfill this basic principle."<ref name="OffsetGuide.org Credit Quality">{{cite web |last1=Broekhoff |first1=D. |last2=Gillenwater |first2=M. |last3=Colbert-Sangree |first3=T.|date=2024 |title=Offset Guide |url=https://offsetguide.org/what-makes-high-quality-carbon-credits/ |website=Carbon Offset Guide |access-date=July 28, 2025}}</ref>
Carbon credits and crediting programs have come under increased scrutiny following the rigorous assessment of credit quality and many investigative journalism articles, which have identified significant quality, or environmental integrity, concerns related to credit's avoided emissions or enhanced removals claims.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Goldman School of Public Policy |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |url=https://gspp.berkeley.edu/research-and-impact/centers/cepp/projects/berkeley-carbon-trading-project/developing-UCs-offset-strategy |access-date=2023-12-28 |website=gspp.berkeley.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Probst |first1=Benedict S. |last2=Toetzke |first2=Malte |last3=Kontoleon |first3=Andreas |last4=Díaz Anadón |first4=Laura |last5=Minx |first5=Jan C. |last6=Haya |first6=Barbara K. |last7=Schneider |first7=Lambert |last8=Trotter |first8=Philipp A. |last9=West |first9=Thales A. P. |last10=Gill-Wiehl |first10=Annelise |last11=Hoffmann |first11=Volker H. |title=Systematic assessment of the achieved emission reductions of carbon crediting projects |journal=Nature Communications |date=2024 |volume=15 |issue=1 |article-number=9562 |doi=10.1038/s41467-024-53645-z |pmid=39543137 |pmc=11564741 |bibcode=2024NatCo..15.9562P |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":1">Periodicals that have covered this issue include:<br />''[[Christian Science Monitor]]'' [https://www.csmonitor.com/2007/0110/p13s02-sten.html] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170524201318/http://www.csmonitor.com/2007/0110/p13s02-sten.html|date=2017-05-24}}<br />''The Guardian'' [https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/jan/18/revealed-forest-carbon-offsets-biggest-provider-worthless-verra-aoe], {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230120031935/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/jan/18/revealed-forest-carbon-offsets-biggest-provider-worthless-verra-aoe}}<br />''Mother Jones'' [https://www.motherjones.com/commentary/columns/2007/05/practical_values.html] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081217094425/http://www.motherjones.com/commentary/columns/2007/05/practical_values.html|date=2008-12-17}}<br />''The New York Times'' [https://www.nytimes.com/2007/04/29/weekinreview/29revkin.html?ex=1335499200&en=d9e2407e4f1a20f0&ei=5124] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170625031730/http://www.nytimes.com/2007/04/29/weekinreview/29revkin.html?ex=1335499200&en=d9e2407e4f1a20f0&ei=5124|date=2017-06-25}}.</ref> [[The Australia Institute]] highlights 23 instances where carbon crediting programs were found to have significant shortcomings.<ref>{{Cite news |date=23 January 2024 |title=Here are 23 Times Carbon Offsets Were Found to be Dodgy |url=https://australiainstitute.org.au/post/here-are-23-times-carbon-offsets-were-found-to-be-dodgy-2/ |publisher=The Australia Institute}}</ref> These include claims of overestimated [[carbon sequestration]], double-counting of credits, and the failure of projects to provide "additional" environmental benefits beyond what would have occurred in the absence of the project. Many enhanced removal projects have received criticism as [[greenwashing]] because they overstated their ability to sequester carbon, with some projects being shown to actually increase overall emissions.<ref name=":7">{{Cite news |last=Greenfield |first=Patrick |date=2023-01-18 |title=Revealed: more than 90% of rainforest carbon offsets by biggest certifier are worthless, analysis shows |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/jan/18/revealed-forest-carbon-offsets-biggest-provider-worthless-verra-aoe |access-date=2024-07-30 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite magazine |last=Blake |first=Heidi |date=2023-10-16 |title=The Great Cash-for-Carbon Hustle |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2023/10/23/the-great-cash-for-carbon-hustle |access-date=2024-07-30 |magazine=The New Yorker |language=en-US |issn=0028-792X}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite news |last=Greenfield |first=Patrick |date=2023-08-24 |title=Carbon credit speculators could lose billions as offsets deemed worthless |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/aug/24/carbon-credit-speculators-could-lose-billions-as-offsets-deemed-worthless-aoe |access-date=2024-07-30 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Masie |first=Desné |date=2023-08-03 |title=Are carbon offsets all they're cracked up to be? We tracked one from Kenya to England to find out. |url=https://www.vox.com/23817575/carbon-offsets-credits-financialization-ecologi-solutions-scam |access-date=2024-07-30 |website=Vox |language=en-US}}</ref>

The essential elements of carbon credit quality can be distilled to five criteria. Higher-quality carbon credits are those associated with avoided emissions or enhanced removals that are:<ref name="OffsetGuide.org Credit Quality"/><ref name=":5">{{Cite book |title=Regeneration: ending the climate crisis in one generation |date=2021 |publisher=Penguin Books |isbn=978-0-14-313697-2 |editor-last=Hawken |editor-first=Paul |location=New York}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Batjes|first1=N.H.| last2=Ceschia |first2= E. | last3=Heuvelink |first3= G.B.M. |last4=Demenois |first4= J. |last5=le Maire |first5= G. |last6=Cardinael |first6= R. | last7=Arias-Navarro |first7= C. | last8=von Egmond |first8= F. |date=October 2024 |title=Towards a modular, multi-ecosystem monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) framework for soil organic carbon stock change assessment|journal=Carbon Management|volume=15|issue=1|article-number=2410812|doi= 10.1080/17583004.2024.2410812 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2024CarM...1510812B }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-05-15 |title=Mass Audubon 'Followed The Rules' And Earned Millions From Carbon Offsets. But Was It 'Real'? |url=https://www.wbur.org/news/2021/05/15/mass-audubon-followed-rules-earned-millions-from-carbon-offsets-but-was-it-real |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=www.wbur.org |language=en}}</ref>
* Additional
* Robustly quantified
* Permanent
* Not claimed by another entity
*Not associated with significant social or environmental harms

Carbon credit quality is possible to assess and in response to the growing concerns related to credit quality, many credit ratings initiatives began to form around 2020 to aid buyers and crediting programs in discerning high-quality from low-quality projects and to make improvements to crediting methodologies so that future credits will only be issued if they meet more rigorous requirements.<ref name="OffsetGuide.org Credit Quality"/> These credit ratings initiatives have taken the form of open access resources like OffsetGuide.org, labeling initiatives like the [[Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market]] that works to assess methodologies and determine if they meet the threshold of quality (determined by applying an assessment framework) to receive the Core Carbon Principle (CCP) label or not, or the Carbon Credit Quality Initiative which conducts deep analysis (an exhaustive assessment framework) and assigns a score of 1-5 representing the holistic quality of a methodology. For profit credit ratings companies have also sprung up that provide quality ratings for individual projects by reviewing their project documents.

== The Paris Agreement crediting mechanism ==

Through international climate negotiations led by the UNFCCC, [[Cooperative_mechanisms_under_Article_6_of_the_Paris_Agreement|the Paris Agreement was agreed to in 2015 and included provisions for carbon crediting]] to be a mechanism that could be used to aid countries in meeting their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). At [[2022 United Nations Climate Change Conference|COP27]], negotiators agreed to define credits issued under [[Cooperative Mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement|Article 6 of the Paris Agreement]] as "[[Climate change mitigation|mitigation contributions]]" toward a country's NDC fulfillment.<ref name="Crook-2022">{{Cite web |last=Crook |first=Jonathan |date=December 7, 2022 |title=Was COP27 the beginning of the end for corporate offsetting? |url=https://carbonmarketwatch.org/2022/12/07/was-cop27-the-beginning-of-the-end-for-corporate-offsetting/ |access-date=March 26, 2023 |website=Carbon Watch}}</ref> [[Cooperative Mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement|Article 6 of the Paris Agreement]] includes three mechanisms for "voluntary cooperation" between countries toward climate goals, including carbon credit markets. Article 6.2 enabled countries to directly trade carbon credits through the development of bilateral crediting mechanisms (i.e., bilateral crediting programs). Article 6.4 established a new international crediting program that supplants the CDM program. The third option is Article 6.8, which enables non-credit generating cooperation (and is not relevant to this article). These provisions allow for mechanisms (excluding Article 6.8) to be developed to enable carbon credits to aid countries in meeting their [[Nationally determined contribution|Nationally Determined Contributions]] (NDC) commitments to achieve the goals of the [[Paris Agreement]].<ref name="WorldBankExplainer">{{Cite web |title=Climate Explainer: Article 6 |url=https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/feature/2022/05/17/what-you-need-to-know-about-article-6-of-the-paris-agreement |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=World Bank |language=en}}</ref> Article 6.4, also referred to as the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM), and is supplanting the CDM but seeks to respond to quality concerns raised by researchers and the media by enhancing the quality of credits and raise the standard of rigor for the entire market. CDM projects may transition to become PACM projects if they meet the eligibility requirements and the Article 6.4 Methodology Panel is reviewing CDM (and other submitted methodologies) to determine if they meet the more rigorous standards of the PACM standard documents to be adopted by PACM to guide project development.<ref name="OffsetGuide.org"/>

== Project types ==

Some include forestry projects that avoid logging and plant saplings,<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Haya |first1=Barbara K. |last2=Evans |first2=Samuel |last3=Brown |first3=Letty |last4=Bukoski |first4=Jacob |last5=Butsic |first5=Van |last6=Cabiyo |first6=Bodie |last7=Jacobson |first7=Rory |last8=Kerr |first8=Amber |last9=Potts |first9=Matthew |last10=Sanchez |first10=Daniel L. |date=2023-03-21 |title=Comprehensive review of carbon quantification by improved forest management offset protocols |journal=Frontiers in Forests and Global Change |volume=6 |article-number=958879 |doi=10.3389/ffgc.2023.958879 |bibcode=2023FrFGC...6.8879H |issn=2624-893X |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[renewable energy]] projects such as [[wind farm]]s, [[biomass energy]], [[biogas digesters]], [[Hydroelectric Dams|hydroelectric dams]], as well as [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]] projects. Further projects include [[carbon dioxide removal]] projects, [[carbon capture and storage]] projects<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hou |first1=Jing |last2=Cheng |first2=Yingying |last3=Yan |first3=Tao |last4=Liu |first4=Zhikun |last5=Kang |first5=Peng |title=High-efficiency electrochemical air capture enabled by thiadiazole redox carrier with tunable gas-selective channels |journal=Nature Communications |date=2026-03-07 |volume=17 |issue=1 |article-number=3629 |doi=10.1038/s41467-026-70444-w |doi-access=free |pmid=41794892 |pmc=13096194 |bibcode=2026NatCo..17.3629H }}</ref>, and the elimination of [[methane emissions]] in various settings such as [[landfill]]s.

== Common terms ==

''Forward crediting'', is typically regarded as a risky practice that leads to lower-quality credits. Forward crediting is a process where credits are issued for projected avoided emissions or enhanced removals, which can be claimed by buyers even before the reduction activities have occurred.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Avoiding Overestimation |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/high-quality-offsets/avoiding-overestimation/ |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref>

The ''vintage'' of a carbon credit is the year in which a carbon credit was issued by a crediting program, which usually corresponds to the year in which a third party auditor reviews the project<ref>{{Cite web |title=CDM: Designated Operational Entities (DOE) |url=https://cdm.unfccc.int/DOE/index.html |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=cdm.unfccc.int}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Offset Verification |url=https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/our-work/programs/compliance-offset-program/offset-verification |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=ww2.arb.ca.gov}}</ref> — generates the carbon offset credit is known as the ''vintage''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbon Pricing: Why do prices vary by project type? |url=https://www.goldstandard.org/blog-item/carbon-pricing-why-do-prices-vary-project-type |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=www.goldstandard.org|date=12 June 2016 }}</ref>

A ''registry'' is a core function of a carbon crediting program. Through a typically publicly accessible registry, carbon credits are tracked for their ownership and retirement. Registries may contain project information such as project status, project documents, credits generated, ownership, sale, and retirement.<ref name="OffsetGuide.org Crediting Programs"/><ref name="Michaelowa-2019">{{Cite report |url=https://www.nefco.int/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/NICA-Crediting-Mechanisms-Final-February-2019.pdf |title=Overview and Comparison of Existing Carbon Crediting Schemes |last1=Michaelowa |first1=Axel |last2=Shishlov |first2=Igor |publisher=Nordic Initiative for Cooperative Approaches (NICA) and Perspectives Climate Group Gmbh |location=Helsinki |at=Pages 10-17 |last3=Hoch |first3=Stephan |last4=Bofill |first4=Patricio |last5=Espelage |first5=Aglaja |access-date=December 20, 2022 |ref={{harvid|NICA|2019}} |display-authors=4 |year=2019}}</ref>

== History ==
In 1977, major amendments to the US [[Clean Air Act (United States)|Clean Air Act]] created one of the first [[Emissions trading|tradable emission]] offset mechanisms, allowing permitted facilities to increase emissions in exchange for paying another company to reduce its emissions of the same pollutant by a greater amount.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gillenwater |first=Michael |url=https://ghginstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/AdditionalityPaper_Part-1ver3FINAL.pdf |title=What is Additionality? Part 1: A long standing problem |publisher=Greenhouse Gas Management Institute |year=2012 |edition=3rd |location=Silver Spring, MD |at=Page 10}}</ref> The 1990 amendments to that same law established the [[Acid Rain Program|Acid Rain Trading Program]], which introduced the concept of a cap and trade system, which allowed companies to buy and sell offsets created by other companies that invested in emission reduction projects subject to an overall limit on emissions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Conniff |first=Richard |date=August 2009 |title=The Political History of Cap and Trade |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/the-political-history-of-cap-and-trade-34711212/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}}</ref> In the 1990s, regulatory frameworks for the [[Clean Water Act|US Clean Water Act]] enabled mitigation banking and wetlands offsetting, which set the procedural and conceptual precedent for carbon offsetting.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Martin |first=Laura J. |title=Wild by design: the rise of ecological restoration |date=2022 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-97942-0 |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts}}</ref>

In 1997, the original international compliance carbon markets emerged from the [[Kyoto Protocol]], which established three mechanisms that enable countries or operators in developed countries to acquire offset credits.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Mechanisms under the Kyoto Protocol |url=http://unfccc.int/kyoto_protocol/mechanisms/items/1673.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100211225536/http://unfccc.int/kyoto_protocol/mechanisms/items/1673.php |archive-date=2010-02-11 |access-date=2010-01-27 |publisher=UNFCCC}}</ref> One mechanism was the [[Clean Development Mechanism]] (CDM), which expanded the concept of [[Carbon emission trading|carbon emissions trading]] to a global scale, focusing on the major greenhouse gases that cause [[climate change]]:<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Clean Development Mechanism |url=https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-kyoto-protocol/mechanisms-under-the-kyoto-protocol/the-clean-development-mechanism |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=United Nations - Climate Change}}</ref> [[carbon dioxide]] ({{CO2}}), [[methane]], [[nitrous oxide]] (N<sub>2</sub>O), [[perfluorocarbons]], [[hydrofluorocarbons]], and [[sulfur hexafluoride]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=LoPucki |first=Lynn M. |date=May 20, 2022 |title=Corporate Greenhouse Gas Disclosures |journal=56 UC Davis Law Review, No. 1, UCLA School of Law, Public Law Research Paper No. 22-11 |at=Page 416 |ssrn=4051948 }}</ref> The Kyoto Protocol was to expire in 2020, to be superseded by the Paris Agreement. Countries are still determining the role of carbon offsets in the Paris Agreement through international negotiations on the agreement's Article 6.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbon Offsets after 2020: the World Under Paris |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/the-role-of-offsets-in-carbon-management-strategies/carbon-offsets-after-2020-the-world-under-paris/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121015758/http://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/the-role-of-offsets-in-carbon-management-strategies/carbon-offsets-after-2020-the-world-under-paris/ |archive-date=2021-01-21 |access-date=2020-12-30 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref>

In November 2024, after years of deadlock, governments attending the [[2024 United Nations Climate Change Conference|COP29 conference]] in [[Baku]], [[Azerbaijan]] agreed to rules on creating, trading and registering emission reductions and removals as carbon credits that higher-emission countries can buy, thus providing funding for low-emission technologies.<ref name=Guardian_20241124>{{cite news |last1=Greenfield |first1=Patrick |title=Cop29's new carbon market rules offer hope after scandal and deadlock |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2024/nov/24/cop29s-new-carbon-market-rules-offer-hope-after-scandal-and-deadlock |newspaper=The Guardian |date=24 November 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241124211455/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2024/nov/24/cop29s-new-carbon-market-rules-offer-hope-after-scandal-and-deadlock |archive-date=24 November 2024 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Economics ==
The economics behind programs such as the Kyoto Protocol was that the [[Margin (economics)|marginal]] cost of reducing emissions would differ among countries.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Carraro |first1=C. |title=TAR Climate Change 2001: Mitigation |last2=Christensen |first2=J. |last3=Edmonds |first3=J. |last4=Flannery |first4=B. |last5=Gay-Garcia |first5=C. |last6=Lee |first6=H. |last7=Meyer-Abich |first7=K.M. |last8=Nikitina |first8=E. |last9=Rahman |first9=A. |year=2001 |page=660 |chapter=Chapter 10: Decision Making Frameworks |display-authors=4 |chapter-url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/10.pdf |first10=R. |last10=Richels |first11=Y. |last11=Ruqiu |first12=A. |last12=Villavicencio |first13=Y. |last13=Wake |first14=J. |last14=Weyant}}</ref><ref>{{citation |last1=Bashmakov |first1=I. |title=6.3 International Policies, Measures, and Instruments |df=dmy-all |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090805204450/http://www.grida.no/climate/ipcc_tar///wg3/246.htm |archive-date=5 August 2009 |chapter=6. Policies, Measures, and Instruments |chapter-url=http://www.grida.no/climate/ipcc_tar/wg3/246.htm |display-authors=etal}}, in {{harvnb|IPCC TAR WG3|2001}}</ref> Studies suggested that the flexibility mechanisms could reduce the overall cost of meeting the targets.<ref name="hourcade 2001 economic costs of flexibility mechanisms">{{citation |last1=Hourcade |first1=J.-C. |title=8.3.1 International Emissions Quota Trading Regimes |df=dmy-all |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120111150919/http://www.grida.no/climate/ipcc_tar/wg3/341.htm |archive-date=11 January 2012 |chapter=8. Global, Regional, and National Costs and Ancillary Benefits of Mitigation |chapter-url=http://www.grida.no/climate/ipcc_tar/wg3/341.htm |display-authors=etal}}, in {{harvnb|IPCC TAR WG3|2001}}</ref> Offset and credit programs have been identified as a way for countries to meet their NDC commitments and achieve the goals of the Paris agreement at a lower cost.<ref name="WorldBankExplainer" /> They may also help close the emissions gap identified in annual UNEP reports.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Making Carbon Markets Work for Faster Climate Action |url=https://www.nature.org/en-us/what-we-do/our-insights/perspectives/carbon-markets-for-faster-climate-action/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=The Nature Conservancy |language=en-US}}</ref>

There is a diverse range of sources of supply and demand as well as trading frameworks that drive offset and credit markets.<ref name="WBank-2022">{{harvnb|World Bank|2022|p=35}}</ref> Demand for offsets and credits derives from a range of compliance obligations, arising from international agreements, national laws, as well as voluntary commitments that companies and governments have adopted.<ref name="WBank-2022" /> Voluntary carbon markets usually consist of private entities purchasing carbon offset credits to meet voluntary greenhouse gas reduction commitments. In some cases, non-covered participants in an ETS may purchase credits as an alternative to purchasing offsets in a voluntary market.<ref name="Cadman-2022" />

These programs also have other [[Externality|positive externalities]], or co-benefits, which include better air quality, increased biodiversity, and water and soil protection; community employment opportunities, energy access, and gender equality; and job creation, education opportunities, and technology transfer. Some certification programs have tools and research products to help quantify these benefits.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What's in a carbon credit? New tools help quantify the sustainable development benefits of carbon offset projects |url=https://www.ecosystemmarketplace.com/articles/whats-in-a-carbon-credit-new-tools-help-quantify-the-sustainable-development-benefits-of-carbon-offset-projects/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Ecosystem Marketplace |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=How shared value is calculated for Gold Standard Certified Projects |url=https://www.goldstandard.org/articles/how-shared-value-calculated-gold-standard-certified-projects |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=www.goldstandard.org|date=14 June 2019 }}</ref>

Prices for offsets and credits vary widely,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbon Offsetting Price Survey |url=https://www.ecobusinesslinks.com/surveys/carbon-offsetting-price-survey/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=ecobusinesslinks}}</ref> reflecting the uncertainty associated with verifying the indirect value of carbon offsets.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Böhm |first=Steffen |date=19 January 2022 |title=There's a massive bubble in the price of carbon – and yet it won't bring down emissions any faster |url=http://theconversation.com/theres-a-massive-bubble-in-the-price-of-carbon-and-yet-it-wont-bring-down-emissions-any-faster-174821 |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=The Conversation |language=en}}</ref> At the same time, uncertainty has caused some companies to become more skeptical about buying offsets .<ref>{{Cite news |last=Holger |first=Dieter |date=2023-01-17 |title=Many Companies Are Shying Away From Carbon Credits |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/many-companies-are-shying-away-from-carbon-credits-11673900838 |access-date=2023-03-29 |work=Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-05-04 |title=Carbon offsets used by major airlines based on flawed system, warn experts |url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/may/04/carbon-offsets-used-by-major-airlines-based-on-flawed-system-warn-experts |access-date=2022-12-31 |website=the Guardian |language=en}};{{Cite web |last1=Temple |first1=L. |last2=Song |first2=J. |date=29 April 2021 |title=The Climate Solution Actually Adding Millions of Tons of {{CO2}} Into the Atmosphere |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/the-climate-solution-actually-adding-millions-of-tons-of-co2-into-the-atmosphere |access-date=2022-12-31 |website=ProPublica |language=en}};{{Cite news |last=Astor |first=Maggie |date=2022-05-18 |title=Do Airline Climate Offsets Really Work? Here's the Good News, and the Bad. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/18/climate/offset-carbon-footprint-air-travel.html |access-date=2022-12-31 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}};{{Cite news |last=Greenfield |first=Patrick |date=2023-01-18 |title=Revealed: more than 90% of rainforest carbon offsets by biggest certifier are worthless, analysis shows |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/jan/18/revealed-forest-carbon-offsets-biggest-provider-worthless-verra-aoe |access-date=2023-03-29 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

=== Emissions trading systems ===
{{Main|Carbon emissions trading}}

[[Emissions trading]] are now an important element of regulatory programs to control pollution, including GHG emissions. [[Carbon emission trading|GHG emission trading]] programs exist at the sub-national, national, and international level. Under these programs, there is a cap on emissions. Sources of emissions have the flexibility to find and apply the lowest-cost methods for reducing pollution. A central authority or government body usually allocates or sells a limited number (a "cap") of permits. These permit a discharge of a specific quantity of a specific pollutant over a set time period.<ref name="glossary">{{cite web |date=January 2011 |title=Cap and Trade: Key Terms Glossary |url=http://www.c2es.org/docUploads/climate101-captrade.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171005153958/http://www.c2es.org/docUploads/climate101-captrade.pdf |archive-date=2017-10-05 |access-date=27 October 2014 |work=Climate Change 101 |publisher=Center for Climate and Energy Solutions}}</ref> Polluters are required to hold permits in amounts equal to their emissions. Those that want to increase their emissions must buy permits from others willing to sell them.<ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OAR |date=2016-03-16 |title=How Do Emissions Trading Programs Work? |url=https://www.epa.gov/emissions-trading/how-do-emissions-trading-programs-work |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref> These programs have been applied to greenhouse gases for several reasons. Their warming effects are the same regardless of where they are emitted. The costs of reducing emissions vary widely by source. The cap ensures that the environmental goal is attained.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Emissions Trading in the U.S.: Experience, Lessons, and Considerations for Greenhouse Gases |url=https://www.c2es.org/document/emissions-trading-in-the-u-s-experience-lessons-and-considerations-for-greenhouse-gases/ |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Center for Climate and Energy Solutions}}</ref><ref name="California Cap and Trade">{{Cite web |title=California Cap and Trade |url=https://www.c2es.org/content/california-cap-and-trade/ |access-date=2022-12-15 |website=Center for Climate and Energy Solutions}}</ref>

== Regulations and schemes ==
As of 2022, 68 carbon pricing programs were in place or scheduled to be created globally.<ref name="World Bank 2022 15">{{harvnb|World Bank|2022|p=15}}</ref> International programs include the [[Clean Development Mechanism]], [[Cooperative Mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement|Article 6 of the Paris Agreement]], and [[Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation|CORSIA]]. National programs include ETS systems such as the [[European Union Emissions Trading System]] (EU-ETS) and the California Cap and Trade Program. Eligible credits in these programs may include credits that international or independent crediting systems have issued. There are also standards and crediting mechanisms that independent, nongovernmental entities such as [[Verified Carbon Standard|Verra]] and [[Gold Standard (carbon offset standard)|Gold Standard]] manage.

=== Kyoto Protocol ===
Under the [[Clean Development Mechanism]], a developed country can sponsor a greenhouse gas reduction project in a developing country, where the costs of greenhouse gas reduction activities are usually much lower.<ref name="grubb">{{cite journal |author=Grubb, M. |date=July–September 2003 |title=The Economics of the Kyoto Protocol |url=http://www.econ.cam.ac.uk/rstaff/grubb/publications/J36.pdf |journal=World Economics |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=143–189 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717152152/http://www.econ.cam.ac.uk/rstaff/grubb/publications/J36.pdf |archive-date=2011-07-17 |access-date=2010-03-25}}</ref> The developed country receives credits for meeting its emission reduction targets known as [[Certified Emission Reduction]]s (CERs), while the developing country receives capital investment and [[clean technology]] or beneficial [[Land use, land-use change and forestry|change in land use]]. Under [[Joint Implementation]], a developed country with relatively high domestic costs of emission reduction would set up a project in another developed country. Offset credits under this program are designated as Emission Reduction Units.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joint Implementation |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/carbon-offset-programs/united-nations-offset-mechanisms/joint-implementation/ |access-date=2023-03-25 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref>

The International Emissions Trading program enables countries to trade in the international carbon credit market to cover their shortfall in [[assigned amount units]]. Countries with surplus units can sell them to countries that are exceeding their emission targets under Annex B of the Kyoto Protocol.<ref>{{Cite web |title=International Emissions Trading |url=https://unfccc.int/international-emissions-trading |access-date=2023-03-26 |website=UNFCC}}</ref>

Nuclear energy projects are not eligible for credits under these programs.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/np-market-mechanisms-under-paris-agreement.pdf |title=Nuclear Power and Market Mechanisms Under the Paris Agreement |publisher=International Atomic Energy Agency |year=2017 |access-date=March 26, 2023}}</ref> Country-specific designated national authorities approve projects under the CDM.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Clean Development Mechanism |url=https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-kyoto-protocol/mechanisms-under-the-kyoto-protocol/the-clean-development-mechanism |access-date=2023-03-24 |website=UNFCC}}</ref>

=== Paris Agreement Article 6 mechanisms ===
{{Main|Cooperative Mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement|}}

[[Cooperative Mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement|Article 6 of the Paris Agreement]] continues to support offset and credit programs between countries, including CDM projects from the Kyoto Protocol. Programs now occur to help achieve emission reduction targets set out in each country's [[nationally determined contribution]] (NDC).
{| class="wikitable"
|+
!Article
!Regulation
!Ref
|-
|Art 6
|Allows countries to transfer carbon credits from reducing GHG emissions to help other countries meet their climate targets.
|
|-
|Art 6.2
|Creates a program for trading GHG emission reductions via bilateral agreements between countries using credits known as internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs). ITMOs can be purchased by countries to achieve NDCs, and also be used in market-based schemes such as CORSIA
|<ref name="Bassam-2022">{{Cite report |url=https://a9w7k6q9.stackpathcdn.com/wpcms/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Insight-114-Article-6-and-Voluntary-Carbon-Markets.pdf |title=Article 6 and Voluntary Carbon Markets |last1=Bassam |first1=Fattouh |last2=Maino |first2=Andrea |publisher=Oxford Institute for Energy Studies |at=Pages 1-9 |access-date=March 26, 2023 |year=2022}}</ref>
|-
|Art 6.4
|Similar to the Clean Development Mechanism of the Kyoto Protocol, it establishes a centralized program to trade GHG emission reductions between countries, supervised by a UNFCCC supervisory board. Countries, companies, and individuals can buy Emission Reduction (ER) credits purchased under this program.
|<ref>{{Cite web |last=Crook |first=Jonathan |date=November 2, 2022 |title=COP27 FAQ: Article 6 of the Paris Agreement explained |url=https://carbonmarketwatch.org/2022/11/02/cop27-faq-article-6-of-the-paris-agreement-explained |access-date=March 26, 2023 |website=Carbon Watch}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate Explainer: Article 6 |url=https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/feature/2022/05/17/what-you-need-to-know-about-article-6-of-the-paris-agreement |access-date=2023-03-27 |website=World Bank |language=en}}</ref>
|}
The ITMO system requires "corresponding adjustments" to avoid double counting of emission reductions. Double-counting occurs if both the host country and purchasing country count the reduction towards their target. If the receiving country uses ITMOs towards its NDC, the host country must discount those reductions from its emissions budget by adding and reporting that higher total in its biennial reporting.<ref name="Bassam-2022" /> Otherwise Article 6.2 gives countries a lot of flexibility in how they can create trading agreements.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Minas |first=Stephen |date=2022-07-03 |title=Market making for the planet: the Paris Agreement Article 6 decisions and transnational carbon markets* |journal=Transnational Legal Theory |volume=13 |issue=2–3 |pages=287–320 |doi=10.1080/20414005.2023.2174690 |issn=2041-4005 |s2cid=257001813 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The supervisory board under Article 6.4 is responsible for approving methodologies, setting guidance, and implementing procedures. The preparation work for this is expected to last until the end of 2023. ER credits issued will fall by 2% to ensure that the program as a whole results in an overall Mitigation of Global Emissions. An additional 5% reduction of ERs will go to a fund to finance adaptation. Administrative fees for program management are still under discussion.<ref name="Bassam-2022" />

CDM projects may transition to the Article 6.4 program subject to approval by the country hosting the project, and if the project meets the new rules, with certain exceptions for rules on methodologies. Projects can generally continue to use the same CDM methodologies through 2025. From 2026 on, they must meet all Article 6 requirements. Up to 2.8 billion credits could potentially become eligible for issuance under Article 6.4 if all CDM projects transition.<ref name="Crook-2022" />

Article 6 does not directly regulate the voluntary carbon markets. In principle, it is possible to issue and purchase carbon offsets without reference to Article 6. It is possible that a multi-tier system could emerge with different types of offsets and credits available for investors. Companies may be able to purchase 'adjusted credits' that eliminate the risk of double counting. These may be seen as more valuable if they support science-based targets and net-zero emissions. Other non-adjusted offsets and credits could support claims for other environmental or social indicators. They could also support emission reductions that are seen as less valuable in terms of these goals. Uncertainty remains around Article 6's effects on future voluntary carbon markets. There is also uncertainty about what investors could claim by purchasing various types of carbon credits.<ref name="Bassam-2022" />

=== REDD+ ===
[[REDD and REDD+|REDD+]] is a UNFCCC framework, largely addressed at tropical regions in developing countries, that is designed to compensate countries for not clearing or degrading their forests, or for enhancing forest carbon stocks. It aims to create financial value for carbon stored in forests, using the concept of results-based payments.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is REDD+? |url=https://unfccc.int/topics/land-use/workstreams/redd/what-is-redd |access-date=2025-10-13 |website=unfccc.int}}</ref> REDD+ also promotes [[Co-benefits of climate change mitigation|co-benefits]] from reducing deforestation such as biodiversity. It was introduced in its basic form at COP11 in 2005 and has grown into a broad policy initiative to address deforestation and forest degradation.

In 2015, REDD+ was incorporated into Article 5 of the Paris Agreement. REDD+ initiatives typically compensate developing countries or their regional administrations for reducing their emissions from deforestation and forest degradation. It consists of several stages: One, achieving REDD+ readiness; two, formalizing an agreement for financing; three, measuring, reporting, and verifying results; and four, receiving results-based payments.

Over 50 countries have national REDD+ initiatives. REDD+ is also taking place through provincial and district governments and at the local level through private landowners. As of 2020, there were over 400 ongoing REDD+ projects globally. Brazil and Colombia account for the largest amount of REDD+ project land area.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/R/R46952 |title=Reduction in Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation (REDD+) |last1=Sheikh |first1=P. A. |last2=Procita |first2=Kezee |date=November 2021 |publisher=Congressional Research Service |at=Cover page |last3=Riddle |first3=A.A. |last4=Hoover |first4=Katie |access-date=2023-03-26}}</ref>

=== CORSIA ===
The [[Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation]] (CORSIA) is a global, market-based program to reduce emissions from international aviation. It aims to allow credits and offsets for emissions that cannot be reduced by technology and operational improvements or sustainable aviation fuels.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) |url=https://www.icao.int/environmental-protection/CORSIA/pages/default.aspx |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=www.icao.int}}</ref> To ensure the environmental integrity of these offsets, the program has developed a list of eligible offsets that can be used. Operating principles are similar to those under existing trading mechanisms and carbon offset certification standards. CORSIA was applied to international aviation since January 2019. At that point all airlines had been required to report their CO<sub>2</sub> emissions on an annual basis. International flights must undertake offsetting under CORSIA since January 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Offsetting {{CO2}} Emissions with CORSIA |url=https://www.iata.org/en/programs/environment/corsia/ |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=www.iata.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Markets==
Compliance market credits account for most of the offset and credit market today. Trading on voluntary carbon markets was 300 MtCO<sub>2</sub>e in 2021. By comparison, the compliance carbon market trading volume was 12 GtCO<sub>2</sub>e,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stebbing |first=Jen |date=2022-11-01 |title=Compliance and voluntary carbon markets: What is the difference? |url=https://www.respira-international.com/what-is-the-difference-between-the-compliance-and-voluntary-carbon-market/ |access-date=2023-04-07 |website=Respira International |language=en-US}}</ref> and global [[greenhouse gas emissions]] in 2019 were 59 GtCO<sub>2</sub>e.<ref>{{Cite book |author= |author-link=IPCC |title=Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change |publisher=IPCC |year=2022 |at=Fig.SPM.1, p.7 |chapter=Summary for Policymakers |chapter-url=https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_SummaryForPolicymakers.pdf}}</ref>

Currently several exchanges trade in carbon credits and allowances covering both spot and futures markets. These include the [[Chicago Mercantile Exchange]], CTX Global, the [[European Energy Exchange]], Global Carbon Credit Exchange gCCEx, [[Intercontinental Exchange]], MexiCO<sub>2</sub>, [[NASDAQ OMX Commodities Europe]] and Xpansiv.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wagner |first=Gustav C. |date=2022-06-08 |title=A Guide to Carbon Credit Exchanges |url=https://carbonmarketcap.org/a-guide-to-carbon-credit-exchanges/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230303231010/https://carbonmarketcap.org/a-guide-to-carbon-credit-exchanges/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=March 3, 2023 |access-date=2023-04-06 |website=CarbonMarketCap |language=en-US}}</ref> Many companies now engage in emissions abatement, offsetting, and sequestration programs, which generate credits that can be sold on an exchange.

At the start of 2022 there were 25 operational emissions trading systems around the world. They are in jurisdictions representing 55% of global GDP. These systems cover 17% of global emissions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Emissions Trading Worldwide: 2022 ICAP Status Report |url=https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/publications/emissions-trading-worldwide-2022-icap-status-report |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=International Carbon Action Partnership |date=29 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref> The [[European Union Emissions Trading System]] (EU-ETS) is the second largest trading system in the world after the [[Chinese national carbon trading scheme]]. It covers over 40% of European GHG emissions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lam |first=Austin |date=2022-12-03 |title=What is an Emissions Trading Scheme and How Does It Work? |url=https://earth.org/what-is-emissions-trading-scheme/ |access-date=2022-12-27 |website=Earth.Org |language=en}}</ref> California's cap-and-trade program covers about 85% of statewide GHG emissions.<ref name="California Cap and Trade"/>

=== Voluntary carbon markets and certification programs ===
[[Voluntary compliance|Voluntary]] carbon markets (VCM) are largely [[unregulated market]]s where carbon offsets are traded by corporations, individuals and organizations that are under no legal obligation to make emission cuts. In voluntary carbon markets, companies or individuals use carbon offsets to meet the goals they set themselves for reducing emissions. Credits are issued under independent crediting standards. Some entities also purchase them under international or domestic crediting mechanisms. National and subnational programs have been increasing in popularity.<ref>{{Cite report |ref={{harvid|NICA|2019}}|last1=Michaelowa |first1=Axel|last2=Shishlov |first2=Igor |last3=Hoch |first3=Stephan |last4=Bofill |first4=Patricio |last5=Espelage |first5=Aglaja|display-authors=4
|url=https://www.nefco.int/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/NICA-Crediting-Mechanisms-Final-February-2019.pdf |title=Overview and Comparison of Existing Carbon Crediting Cchemes |at=Page 3|publisher=Nordic Initiative for Cooperative Approaches (NICA) and Perspectives Climate Group Gmbh |year=2019|location=Helsinki|access-date= December 20, 2022}}</ref>

Many different groups exist within the voluntary carbon market,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Offset Project Entities |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/carbon-offset-projects/offset-project-entities/ |access-date=2023-03-24 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref> including developers, brokers, auditors, and buyers.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://wwfint.awsassets.panda.org/downloads/vcm_report_final.pdf |title=A Comparison of Carbon Offset Standards - Making Sense of the Voluntary Carbon Market |last1=Kollmus |first1=Anja |last2=Zink |first2=Helge |publisher=WWF Germany |pages=11–12 |language=en |last3=Polycarp |first3=Clifford |access-date=2022-12-20 |year=2008}}</ref> Certification programs for VCMs establish accounting standards, project eligibility requirements, and monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) procedures for credit and offset projects. They include the [[Verified Carbon Standard]] issued by Verra, the [[Gold Standard (carbon offset standard)|Gold Standard]], the [[Global Carbon Council]] based in Qatar, the Climate Action Reserve, the American Carbon Registry, and Plan Vivo.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lee |first1=Henry |url=https://www.belfercenter.org/sites/default/files/files/publication/The%20Future%20of%20Carbon%20Offset%20Markets.pdf |title=The Future of Carbon Offset Markets: Current Trends and Emerging Challenges |last2=Mayer |first2=Abigail |publisher=Harvard Kennedy School |year=2020 |at=Page 6}}</ref> Puro Standard, the first standard for engineered carbon removal, is verified by DNV GL.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Collins |first=Leigh |title=World's first carbon-removal marketplace offers businesses an easy route to net-zero emissions |work=RECHARGE Global News and Intelligence for the Energy Transition |url=https://www.rechargenews.com/transition/worlds-first-carbon-removal-marketplace-offers-businesses-an-easy-route-to-net-zero-emissions/2-1-835191 |access-date=29 November 2021}}</ref> Isometric was the first carbon registry to issue credits for [[enhanced weathering]] carbon removal.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Fehrenbacher |first=Katie |title=Removing CO2 with rock dust gains backers |work=Axios |url=https://www.axios.com/pro/climate-deals/2025/01/06/erw-carbon-removal-momentum |access-date=6 January 2025}}</ref> There are also some additional standards for validating co-benefits, including the Climate, Community and Biodiversity Standard (CCB Standard), also issued by Verra, and the Social Carbon Standard,<ref name="Social-Carbon-Standard">{{cite web |title=Social Carbon profile on database of market governance mechanisms |url=http://shapingsustainablemarkets.iied.org/socialcarbon |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180907071141/https://shapingsustainablemarkets.iied.org/socialcarbon |archive-date=7 September 2018 |access-date=25 Jan 2019 |location=United Kingdom}}</ref> issued by the Ecologica Institute. The [[Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market]] (ICVCM) publishes the Core Carbon Principles (CCPs) as a benchmark for carbon credit integrity and assesses carbon crediting programs to determine whether they are "CCP-Eligible".<ref name="ICVCM_CCP_S1">{{cite report
 |title=Core Carbon Principles: Section 1 - Introduction
 |publisher=Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM)
 |date=January 2024
 |url=https://icvcm.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/CCP-Section-1-V2-FINAL-6Feb24.pdf
 }}</ref><ref name="ICVCM_HowWeAssess">{{cite web
 |title=How we assess carbon-crediting programs
 |website=Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM)
 |url=https://icvcm.org/how-we-assess-carbon-crediting-programs/
}}</ref>

The voluntary carbon markets currently represent less than 1% of the reductions pledged in country NDCs by 2030. It represents an even smaller portion of the reductions needed to achieve the 1.5&nbsp;°C Paris temperature goal pathway in 2030.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://trove-research.com/wp-content/uploads/_pda/2021/06/Trove-Research-Carbon-Credit-Demand-Supply-and-Prices-1-June-2021.pdf |title=Future Demand, Supply and Prices for Voluntary Carbon Credits – Keeping the Balance |last1=Turner |first1=Guy |last2=Helmke |first2=Elyas |date=June 2021 |publisher=UCL-Trove Research-Liebreich Associates |last3=Tetteh-Wright |first3=Teki Anna |last4=Oraee |first4=Atta |last5=Koch |first5=Alexander |last6=Maslin |first6=Mark |last7=Lewis |first7=Simon L. |last8=Pye |first8=Steven |last9=Liebreich |first9=Michael |at=Page 2 |display-authors=4 |archive-date=2023-04-19 |access-date=2023-04-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230419044918/https://trove-research.com/wp-content/uploads/_pda/2021/06/Trove-Research-Carbon-Credit-Demand-Supply-and-Prices-1-June-2021.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, the VCM is growing significantly. Between 2017 and 2021, both the issuance and retirement of VCM carbon offsets more than tripled.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Voluntary Carbon Market 2022–2023 |url=https://storage.pardot.com/881182/1680172478zgFzdrQY/South_Pole___VCM_Report_2022_2023.pdf |access-date=April 6, 2023 |website=south pole}}</ref> Some predictions call for global VCM demand to increase 15-fold between 2021 and 2030, and 100 times by 2050.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 29, 2021 |title=Carbon credits: Scaling voluntary markets |url=https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/sustainability/our-insights/a-blueprint-for-scaling-voluntary-carbon-markets-to-meet-the-climate-challenge |access-date=2023-01-05 |website=McKinsey |archive-date=2024-01-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240118003139/https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/sustainability/our-insights/a-blueprint-for-scaling-voluntary-carbon-markets-to-meet-the-climate-challenge |url-status=dead }}</ref> Carbon removal projects such as forestry and [[carbon capture and storage]] are expected to have a larger share of this market in the future, compared to renewable energy projects.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=ClimateTrade |date=2022-08-04 |title=Voluntary carbon market value tops US$2B |url=https://climatetrade.com/voluntary-carbon-market-value-tops-us2b/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=ClimateTrade |language=en-US}}</ref> However, there is evidence that large companies are becoming more reluctant to use VCM offsets and credits because of a complex web of standards, despite an increased focus on [[net zero emissions]] goals.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Holger |first=Dieter |date=2023-01-17 |title=Many Companies Are Shying Away From Carbon Credits |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/many-companies-are-shying-away-from-carbon-credits-11673900838 |access-date=2023-04-07 |work=Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref>

==== Determining value ====
In 2022 voluntary carbon market (VCM) prices ranged from $8 to $30 per tonne of CO<sub>2</sub>e for the most common types of offset projects. Several factors can affect these prices. The costs of developing a project are a significant factor. Those tied to projects that can sequester carbon have recently been selling at a premium compared to other projects such as renewable energy or energy efficiency. Projects that sequester carbon are also called Nature-Based Solutions. Projects with additional social and environmental benefits can command a higher price. This reflects the value of the co-benefits and the perceived value of association with these projects. Credits from a reputable organization may command a higher price. Some credits located in developed countries may be priced higher. One reason could be that companies prefer to back projects closer to their business sites. Conversely, carbon credits with older vintages tend to be valued lower on the market.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbon Credits Prices by Project Type · Sep 2022 · Abatable |url=https://www.abatable.com/blog/carbon-credits-pricing |access-date=2023-04-07 |website=www.abatable.com |date=9 September 2022 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Prices on the compliance market are generally higher. They vary based on geography, with EU and UK ETS credits trading at higher prices than those in the US in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-01-17 |title=A Year in Review: Tracking Carbon Price Highs & Lows in 2022 and Major Policy Shifts to Watch for in 2023 |url=https://kraneshares.com/a-year-in-review-tracking-carbon-price-highs-lows-in-2022-and-major-policy-shifts-to-watch-for-in-2023/ |access-date=2023-04-08 |website=KraneShares |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://icapcarbonaction.com/system/files/document/ICAP%20Emissions%20Trading%20Worldwide%202023%20Status%20Report_0.pdf |title=Emissions Trading Worldwide: Status Report 2023 |publisher=International Carbon Action Partnership |year=2023 |location=Berlin |at=Page 34}}</ref> Lower prices on the VCM are in part due to an excess of supply in relation to demand. Some types of offsets are able to be created at very low costs under present standards. Without this surplus, current VCM prices could be at least $10/tCO<sub>2</sub>e higher.<ref name=":0">{{Cite report |url=https://trove-research.com/wp-content/uploads/_pda/2021/06/Trove-Research-Carbon-Credit-Demand-Supply-and-Prices-1-June-2021.pdf |title=Future Demand, Supply and Prices for Voluntary Carbon Credits – Keeping the Balance |last1=Turner |first1=Guy |last2=Helmke |first2=Elyas |date=June 2021 |publisher=UCL-Trove Research-Liebreich Associates |at=Page 3 |last3=Tetteh-Wright |first3=Teki Anna |last4=Oraee |first4=Atta |last5=Koch |first5=Alexander |last6=Maslin |first6=Mark |last7=Lewis |first7=Simon L. |last8=Pye |first8=Steven |last9=Liebreich |first9=Michael |display-authors=4 |archive-date=2023-04-19 |access-date=2023-04-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230419044918/https://trove-research.com/wp-content/uploads/_pda/2021/06/Trove-Research-Carbon-Credit-Demand-Supply-and-Prices-1-June-2021.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Some pricing forecasts predict VCM prices could increase to as much as $47–$210 per tonne by 2050. There could be an even higher spike in the short term in certain scenarios. A major factor in future price models is the extent to which programs that support more permanent removals can influence future global climate policy. This could limit the supply of approvable offsets, and thereby raise prices.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-01-10 |title=Carbon Offset Prices Could Increase Fifty-Fold by 2050 |url=https://about.bnef.com/blog/carbon-offset-prices-could-increase-fifty-fold-by-2050/ |access-date=2023-04-08 |website=BloombergNEF |language=en-US}}</ref>

Demand for VCM offsets is expected to increase five to ten-fold over the next decade as more companies adopt Net Zero climate commitments. This could benefit both markets and progress on reducing GHG emissions. If carbon offset prices remain significantly below these forecast levels, companies could be open to criticisms of [[greenwashing]]. This is because some might claim credit for emission reduction projects that would have been undertaken anyway. At prices of $100/tCO<sub>2</sub>e, a variety of carbon removal technologies could deliver around 2 GtCO<sub>2</sub>e per year of annual emission reductions between now and 2050. These technologies include reducing deforestation, forest restoration, CCS, BECCs and renewables in least developed countries.<ref>{{Cite web |date=4 June 2021 |title=Ten-fold increase in carbon offset cost predicted |url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2021/jun/ten-fold-increase-carbon-offset-cost-predicted |access-date=April 7, 2023 |website=University College London}}</ref> In addition, as the cost of using offsets and credits rises, investments in reducing supply chain emissions will become more attractive.<ref name=":0" />

==== Verified Carbon Standard by Verra ====
{{Main|Verified Carbon Standard}}
Verra was developed in 2005. It is a widely used voluntary carbon standard, which also offers specific methodologies for REDD+ projects.<ref name=":6" /> As of 2020, there had been over 1,500 certified VCS projects covering energy, transport, waste, forestry, and other sectors.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Methodologies |url=https://verra.org/methodologies-main/ |access-date=2023-03-24 |website=Verra |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2021, Verra issued 300 MtCO<sub>2</sub>e worth of offset credits for 110 projects.<ref name="Worldbank">{{Cite book
| publisher= World Bank
| year= 2022
| title=State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2022
| url= https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/a1abead2-de91-5992-bb7a-73d8aaaf767f
| access-date=24 March 2023
|doi= 10.1596/978-1-4648-1895-0
