}}</ref>{{rp|37}} Verra is the program of choice for most of the forest credits in the voluntary market, and almost all REDD+ projects.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Chagas |first1=Thiago |url=https://climatefocus.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/A-close-look-at-the-quality-of-REDD-carbon-credits-2020-V2.0.pdf |title=A close look at the quality of REDD+ carbon credits |last2=Galt |first2=Hilda |last3=Lee |first3=Donna |last4=Neeff |first4=Till |last5=Streck |first5=Charlotte |publisher=Climate Focus |year=2020 |at=Page 5}}</ref>

==== Gold Standard ====
{{Main|Gold Standard (carbon offset standard)}}

The [[Gold Standard (carbon offset standard)|Gold Standard]] was developed in 2003 by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) in consultation with an independent standards advisory board. Projects are open to any non-government, community-based organization. Allowable categories include renewable energy supply, energy efficiency, [[afforestation]], reforestation, and agriculture. The program also promotes the [[Sustainable Development Goals|Sustainable Developments Goals]]. Projects must meet at least three of those goals besides reducing GHG emissions. Projects must make a net-positive contribution to the economic, environmental and social welfare of the local population. Program monitoring requirements help determine this.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Collias |first=Anthony |date=2020-11-17 |title=Gold Standard: Why do we carbon offset with them? |url=https://articles.treepoints.green/gold-standard-what-is-it-and-why-do-we-work-with-them/ |access-date=2022-12-24 |website=The Treepoints Blog |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Michaelowa |first1=Axel |url=https://www.nefco.int/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/NICA-Crediting-Mechanisms-Final-February-2019.pdf |title=Overview and comparison of existing carbon crediting schemes |last2=Shishlov |first2=Igor |last3=Hoch |first3=Stephan |last4=Bofill |first4=Patricio |last5=Espelage |first5=Aglaja |publisher=Nordic Initiative for Cooperative Approaches (NICA) and Perspectives Climate Group Gmbh |year=2019 |location=Helsinki |pages=25–26}}</ref>

==Types of offset projects==
A variety of projects can be used to reduce GHG emissions and thus to generate carbon offsets and credits. These can include land use improvement, methane capture, biomass [[Carbon sequestration|sequestration]], [[renewable energy]], or industrial energy efficiency. They also include reducing methane, reforestation and switching fuel, for example to [[carbon-neutral fuel|carbon-neutral]] and [[carbon-negative fuel]]s.<ref name="Carbon Offset Guide">{{Cite web |title=Carbon Offset Projects |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/carbon-offset-projects/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Second Nature">{{Cite web |title=Primer: Carbon Offset Project Types 101 |url=https://secondnature.org/wp-content/uploads/Primer-Carbon-Offset-Project-Types-101-Second-Nature.pdf |access-date=March 23, 2023 |website=Second Nature}}</ref> The CDM identifies over 200 types of projects suitable for generating carbon offsets and credits.<ref name="CDM projects by type">{{cite web |date=2010-02-01 |title=UNEP Risoe CDM/JI Pipeline Analysis and Database |url=http://cdmpipeline.org/cdm-projects-type.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110725151401/http://cdmpipeline.org/cdm-projects-type.htm |archive-date=2011-07-25 |access-date=2010-02-22 |publisher=UNEP Risoe Centre}}</ref> An example of land use improvement is better forest management.<ref name="Carbon Offset Guide" /><ref name="Regan-2020">{{Cite journal |last1=Regan |first1=Courtney M. |last2=Connor |first2=Jeffery D. |date=2020 |title=The influence of crediting and permanence periods on Australian forest-based carbon offsets supply |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264837719316680 |url-status=live |journal=Land Use Policy |volume=97 |article-number=104800 |doi=10.1016/j.landusepol.2020.104800 |bibcode=2020LUPol..9704800R |s2cid=225204587 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416092435/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264837719316680 |archive-date=2021-04-16 |access-date=2021-04-09 |via=Elsevier Science Direct|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Offset certification and carbon trading programs vary by how much they consider specific projects eligible for offsets or credits.<ref>{{Cite report |ref={{harvid|NICA|2019}}|last1=Michaelowa |first1=Axel|last2=Shishlov |first2=Igor |last3=Hoch |first3=Stephan |last4=Bofill |first4=Patricio |last5=Espelage |first5=Aglaja|display-authors=4
|url=https://www.nefco.int/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/NICA-Crediting-Mechanisms-Final-February-2019.pdf |title=Overview and Comparison of Existing Carbon Crediting Cchemes |at=Pages 23-24|publisher=Nordic Initiative for Cooperative Approaches (NICA) and Perspectives Climate Group Gmbh |year=2019|location=Helsinki|access-date= December 20, 2022}}</ref> The European Union Emission Trading System considers nuclear energy projects, afforestation or reforestation activities, and projects involving destruction of industrial gases ineligible.<ref name="climate.ec.europa.eu">{{Cite web |title=Use of international credits |url=https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/eu-emissions-trading-system-eu-ets/use-international-credits_en |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=climate.ec.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref> Industrial gases include HFC-23 and {{N2O}}.

=== Renewable energy ===
Renewable energy projects can include hydroelectric, wind, photovoltaic solar, solar hot water, biomass power, and heat production. These types of projects help societies move from electricity and heating based on fossil fuels towards forms of energy that are less carbon-intensive. However, they may not qualify as offset projects. This is because it is difficult or impossible to determine their [[additionality]]. They usually generate revenue. And they usually involve subsidies or other complex financial arrangements. This can make them ineligible under many offset and credit programs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Renewable Energy |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/avoiding-low-quality-offsets/vetting-offset-projects/renewable-energy/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref>

===Methane collection and combustion===
Methane is a potent greenhouse gas. It is most often emitted from landfills, livestock, and from coal mining.<ref name="Second Nature" /> Methane projects can produce carbon offsets through the capture of methane for energy production. Examples include the combustion or containment of [[methane]] generated by farm animals by use of an [[anaerobic digester]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mnproject.org/e-haubenschildfarm.html|title=Haubenschild Dairy Farm Digester|access-date=6 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150730030658/http://www.mnproject.org/e-haubenschildfarm.html|archive-date=2015-07-30}}</ref> in landfills,<ref>{{cite web |title=State of the Voluntary Carbon Markets 2017 |url=https://www.forest-trends.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/doc_5591.pdf |website=Forest Trends |publisher=Ecosystem Marketplace |access-date=January 25, 2019 |archive-date=August 14, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814171921/https://www.forest-trends.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/doc_5591.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> or from other [[industrial waste]].

===Energy efficiency===
[[File:2009-11-30 - Chicago Climate Justice activists in Chicago - Cap'n'Trade protest 011.jpg|thumb|right|Chicago Climate Justice activists protesting cap and trade legislation in front of [[Chicago Climate Exchange]] building in Chicago Loop]]

Carbon offsets that fund renewable energy projects help lower the [[carbon intensity]] of energy ''supply.'' Energy conservation projects seek to reduce the overall ''demand'' for energy. Carbon offsets in this category fund projects of three main types.

[[Cogeneration]] plants generate both electricity and heat from the same power source. This improves upon the energy efficiency of most power plants. That is because these plants waste the energy generated as heat.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Does Cogeneration Provide Heat and Power? |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-does-cogeneration-provide-heat-power/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191127205316/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-does-cogeneration-provide-heat-power/ |archive-date=2019-11-27 |access-date=2019-11-27 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref> [[Fuel efficiency]] projects replace a combustion device with one using less fuel per unit of energy provided. They can do this by optimizing [[industrial processes]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/26623958|title=(PDF) Analysis and Optimization of Carbon Dioxide Emission Mitigation Options in the Cement Industry<!-- Bot generated title -->|access-date=2020-03-28|archive-date=2020-05-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200515015540/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/26623958_Analysis_and_Optimization_of_Carbon_Dioxide_Emission_Mitigation_Options_in_the_Cement_Industry|url-status=live}}</ref> reducing energy costs per unit. They can also optimize [[Individual action on climate change|individual action]], for example making it easier to cycle to work instead of driving.<ref>{{Cite web|title=CODEX|url=https://carboncodex.app/?utm=wikipedia|access-date=2020-10-05|website=carboncodex.app|language=en|archive-date=2020-05-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200514203048/https://carboncodex.app/?utm=wikipedia|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Destruction of industrial pollutants===
Industrial pollutants such as [[hydrofluorocarbons]] (HFCs) and [[perfluorocarbons]] (PFCs) have a [[Global-warming potential|much greater potential for global warming]] than carbon dioxide by volume.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.epa.gov/highgwp/scientific.html |title=F-gases Emissions – Climate Change – US EPA |date=October 2009 |access-date=6 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121018211612/http://www.epa.gov/highgwp/scientific.html |archive-date=18 October 2012 }}</ref> It is easy to capture and destroy these pollutants at their source. So they present a large low-cost source of carbon offsets. As a category, HFCs, PFCs, and N<sub>2</sub>O reductions represent 71 percent of offsets issued under the CDM.<ref name="CDM projects by type"/> Since many of these are now banned by an amendment to the Montreal Protocol, they are often no longer eligible for offsets or credits.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Industrial Gases |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/avoiding-low-quality-offsets/vetting-offset-projects/industrial-gases/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref><ref name="climate.ec.europa.eu" />

===Land use, land-use change and forestry===
[[Land use, land-use change, and forestry|Land use, land-use change and forestry]] have the collective label LULUCF. LULUCF projects focus on natural [[carbon sink]]s such as forests and soil. There are a number of different types of LULUCF projects. Forestry-related projects focus on avoiding deforestation. They do this by protecting existing forests, restoring forests on land that was once forested, and creating forests<ref>{{Cite book |last=Facility |first=Global Environment |url=https://4irelabs.com/articles/carbon-credit-market-overview/ |title=Land Use, Land-Use Change, and Forestry (LULUCF) Activities |date=2012-11-15 |publisher=Global Environment Facility |isbn=978-1-939339-47-8 |language=en}}</ref> on land that previously had no forests, typically for more than a generation. [[Soil management]] projects attempt to preserve or increase the amount of carbon sequestered in soil.

Deforestation is particularly significant in Brazil, Indonesia, and parts of Africa, accounting for about 20 percent of greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://rainforests.mongabay.com/0801.htm|last1=Butler|first1=Rhett|website=Mongabay|title=Deforestation|date=2012-07-27|access-date=2019-01-28|archive-date=2019-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129123031/https://rainforests.mongabay.com/0801.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> Carbon offsets allow firms to avoid deforestation by paying directly for forest preservation or providing substitutes for forest-based products. Offset schemes using reforestation, such as REDD, are available in developing countries, and are becoming increasingly available in developed countries including the US and the UK.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.reforestaction.com/en/our-reforestation-projects|website=Reforestaction|title=Our reforestation projects|date=14 May 2019 |access-date=2020-04-19|archive-date=2020-05-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200515033140/https://www.reforestaction.com/en/our-reforestation-projects|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mycarbonplan.org/our-carbon-offset-projects|website=My Carbon Plan|title=Tree planting projects for carbon offsetting in the UK|access-date=2020-04-19|archive-date=2020-05-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200515051427/https://www.mycarbonplan.org/our-carbon-offset-projects|url-status=live}}</ref>

China has a [[Climate policy of China|policy]] of forestry carbon credits.<ref name=":023">{{Cite book |last1=Bachulska |first1=Alicja |url=https://ecfr.eu/publication/idea-of-china/ |title=The Idea of China: Chinese Thinkers on Power, Progress, and People |last2=Leonard |first2=Mark |last3=Oertel |first3=Janka |date=2 July 2024 |publisher=[[European Council on Foreign Relations]] |isbn=978-1-916682-42-9 |location=Berlin, Germany |page=124 |format=EPUB |access-date=22 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240717120845/https://ecfr.eu/publication/idea-of-china/ |archive-date=17 July 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Forestry carbon credits are based on the measurement of forest growth, which is converted into carbon emission reduction measurements by government ecological and forestry offices.<ref name=":023" /> Owners of forests (who are typically rural families or [[Rural society in China|rural villages]]) receive carbon tickets (碳票; ''tan piao'') which are tradeable securities.<ref name=":023" />

==Processes==
=== Creation ===
An offset project is designed by project developers, financed by investors, validated by an independent verifier, and registered with a carbon offset program. Official registration indicates that a program has approved the project and that the project is eligible to start generating carbon offset credits once it starts.<ref name="Broekhoff-2019">{{Cite report |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Carbon-Offset-Guide_3122020.pdf |title=Securing Climate Benefit: A Guide to Using Carbon Offsets |last1=Broekhoff |first1=Derik |last2=Gillenwater |first2=Michael |publisher=Stockholm Environment Institute & Greenhouse Gas Management Institute |at=Page 10 |last3=Colbert-Sangree |first3=Tani |last4=Cage |first4=Patrick |access-date=December 17, 2022 |year=2019}}</ref> Most carbon offset programs have a library of approved methodologies covering a range of project types. After a project has begun, programs will often verify it periodically to determine the quantity of emission reductions generated. The length of time between verifications can vary, but is typically one year. After a program approves verification reports, it issues carbon offset credits, which are deposited in the project developer's account in a registry system administered by the offset program.<ref name="Broekhoff-2019" />

=== Criteria for assessing quality ===
Criteria for assessing the quality of offsets and credits usually cover the following areas:
* Baseline and Measurement
* [[Additionality]]
* [[Carbon leakage|Leakage]]
* Permanence
* [[Double counting (accounting)|Double counting]]
* [[Co-benefits of climate change mitigation|Co-benefits]]<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Carbon-Offset-Guide_3122020.pdf |title=Securing Climate Benefit: A Guide to Using Carbon Offsets |last1=Broekhoff |first1=Derik |last2=Gillenwater |first2=Michael |publisher=Stockholm Environment Institute & Greenhouse Gas Management Institute |last3=Colbert-Sangree |first3=Tani |last4=Cage |first4=Patrick |access-date=December 17, 2022 |at=Pages 18-31 |year=2019}}</ref>

=== Approaches for increasing integrity ===
Besides the certification programs mentioned above, industry groups have been working since the 2000s to promote the quality of these projects. The [[International Carbon Reduction and Offset Alliance]] (ICROA) was founded in 2008. It promotes [[best practice]] across the voluntary [[Personal carbon trading|carbon market]].<ref name="TheAge">{{cite news|url=http://www.lexisnexis.com/uk/nexis/results/docview/docview.do?docLinkInd=true&risb=21_T7195727016&format=GNBFI&sort=BOOLEAN&startDocNo=1&resultsUrlKey=29_T7195727021&cisb=22_T7195727020&treeMax=true&treeWidth=0&csi=314239&docNo=12|title=New international standards organisation hopes for plenty of carbon copies|last=Murphy|first=Mathew|format=fee required|date=9 June 2008|work=The Age|publisher=The Age Company|access-date=2009-08-24}}</ref> ICROA's membership consists of carbon offset providers based in the United States, European and [[Asia-Pacific]] markets who commit to the ICROA Code of Best Practice.<ref name="TheAge"/>

Other groups are now advocating for new approaches to ensure that offsets and credits have integrity. The Oxford Offsetting Principles state that traditional carbon offsetting schemes are "unlikely to deliver the types of offsetting needed to ultimately reach net zero emissions."<ref name="Oxford2">{{Cite web |last=Myles |first=Allen |date=September 2020 |title=The Oxford Principles for Net Zero Aligned Carbon Offsetting |url=https://www.smithschool.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-01/Oxford-Offsetting-Principles-2020.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201002083510/https://www.smithschool.ox.ac.uk/publications/reports/Oxford-Offsetting-Principles-2020.pdf |archive-date=2020-10-02 |access-date=24 November 2021}}</ref> These principles focus instead on cutting emissions as a first priority. In terms of offsets, they advocate for shifting to carbon removal offset projects that involve long-term storage. The principles also support the development of offsetting aligned with [[Net zero emissions|net zero]].<ref name="Oxford2" /> The [[Science Based Targets initiative]]'s net-zero criteria argue that it is important to move beyond offsets based on reduced or avoided emissions. Instead projects should base offsets on carbon that has been sequestered from the atmosphere, such as CO<sub>2</sub> Removal Certificates.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The SBTi Net Zero Criteria |url=https://sciencebasedtargets.org/resources/files/SBTi-Net-Zero-Criteria-for-Road-Test.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210726093833/https://sciencebasedtargets.org/resources/files/SBTi-Net-Zero-Criteria-for-Road-Test.pdf |archive-date=2021-07-26 |access-date=29 November 2021}}</ref>

Some initiatives focus on improving the quality of current carbon offset and credit projects. The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market has published a draft set of principles for determining a high integrity carbon credit. These are known as the Core Carbon Principles. Final guidelines for this program are expected in late 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Integrity Of The Voluntary Carbon Market: Draft 'Core Carbon Principles' |url=https://www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/integrity-voluntary-carbon-market-draft-core-carbon-principles |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=www.whitecase.com |date=26 September 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Harvey |first=Fiona |author-link=Fiona Harvey |date=2023-01-20 |title=New carbon offset standards 'should bring greater scrutiny' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/jan/20/new-carbon-offset-standards-should-bring-greater-scrutiny |access-date=2023-03-29 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> The Voluntary Carbon Markets Integrity Initiative has developed a code of practice that was published in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Peters |first=Adele |date=June 8, 2022 |title=This new 'integrity initiative' is designed to fight corporate greenwashing |url=https://www.fastcompany.com/90759104/this-new-integrity-initiative-is-designed-to-fight-corporate-greenwashing |access-date=March 28, 2023 |website=Fast Company}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=VCMI Claims Code of Practice |url=https://vcmintegrity.org/vcmi-claims-code-of-practice/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=VCMI |language=en-GB}}</ref> The UK government partly funds this initiative.

== Limitations and drawbacks ==
The use of offsets and credits faces a variety of criticisms. Some argue that they promote a "business-as-usual" mindset, allowing companies to use carbon offsetting to avoid making larger changes to reduce carbon emissions at source.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Kevin |title=The carbon neutral myth: offset indulgences for your climate sins |date=2007 |publisher=Transnational Institute |others=Oscar Reyes, Timothy Byakola, Carbon Trade Watch |isbn=978-90-71007-18-7 |location=Amsterdam |oclc=778008109}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbon offsets prove risky business for net zero targets |url=https://www.spglobal.com/esg/insights/carbon-offsets-prove-risky-business-for-net-zero-targets |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=www.spglobal.com |language=en-us}}</ref>

Research from [[The Australia Institute]] has suggested that at least 25% of carbon offsets may lack integrity, describing them as "hot air."<ref>{{Cite news |date=23 February 2023 |title=The Problem with Carbon Credits and Offsets Explained |url=https://australiainstitute.org.au/post/carbon-credits-and-offsets-explained/ |access-date=9 January 2025 |work=The Australia Institute}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Hemming |first1=Polly |last2=Merzian |first2=Richie |last3=Schoo |first3=Annica |date=22 September 2021 |title=Questionable integrity: Non-additionality in the Emissions Reduction Fund's Avoided Deforestation Method |url=https://australiainstitute.org.au/report/questionable-integrity-non-additionality-in-the-emissions-reduction-funds-avoided-deforestation-method/ |access-date=9 January 2025}}</ref> Additionally, some reports have raised concerns that carbon offsets could be used to justify the continuation or expansion of fossil fuel projects, potentially delaying direct efforts to reduce emissions.<ref>Carbon credit trickery: more credits will lead to more emissions — and more climate damage - The Australia Institute</ref>

Using projects in this way is called "[[greenwashing]]".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Andreoni |first=Manuela |date=2022-05-20 |title=Spot the greenwashing |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/20/climate/climate-change-greenwashing.html |access-date=2023-03-29 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> [[Pope Francis]] noted in his 2015 [[encyclical letter]] ''[[Laudato si']]'' the risk that countries and sectors may use carbon credits as "a ploy which permits maintaining [their] excessive consumption".<ref>Pope Francis, [https://www.vatican.va/content/dam/francesco/pdf/encyclicals/documents/papa-francesco_20150524_enciclica-laudato-si_en.pdf Laudato si'], paragraph 171, published 24 May 2015, accessed 21 April 2024</ref>

Many projects that give credits for [[carbon sequestration]] have received criticism as greenwashing because they overstated their ability to sequester carbon, with some projects being shown to actually increase overall emissions.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" /><ref name=":9" /><ref name=":10" />

In 2023, a civil suit was brought against [[Delta Air Lines]] based on its use of carbon credits to support claims of carbon neutrality.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Greenfield |first=Patrick |date=2023-05-30 |title=Delta Air Lines faces lawsuit over $1bn carbon neutrality claim |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/may/30/delta-air-lines-lawsuit-carbon-neutrality-aoe |access-date=2023-06-06 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> In 2016 the [[Öko-Institut]] analyzed a series of CDM projects. It found that 85% had a low likelihood of being truly additional or were likely to over-estimate emission reductions.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cames |first1=Martin |url=https://climate.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2017-04/clean_dev_mechanism_en.pdf |title=How additional is the Clean Development Mechanism? |last2=Harthan |first2=Ralph O. |last3=Füssler |first3=Jürg |last4=Lee |first4=Carrie M. |last5=Lazarus |first5=Michael |last6=Erickson |first6=Pete |last7=Spalding-Fecher |first7=Randall |publisher=Öko-Institut |year=2016 |location=Berlin |at=Page 11 |display-authors=4}}</ref> In 2023, the University of California all but dropped the purchase of offsets in favor of direct reductions in emissions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The University of California has all but dropped carbon offsets—and thinks you should, too |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2023/11/30/1084104/the-university-of-california-has-all-but-dropped-carbon-offsets-and-thinks-you-should-too/ |access-date=2023-12-14 |website=MIT Technology Review |language=en}}</ref> An additional challenge is that carbon pricing and existing policies are still inadequate to meet Paris goals.<ref name="World Bank 2022 15"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=COP26 climate pledges could help limit global warming to 1.8 °C, but implementing them will be the key – Analysis |url=https://www.iea.org/commentaries/cop26-climate-pledges-could-help-limit-global-warming-to-1-8-c-but-implementing-them-will-be-the-key |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=IEA |date=4 November 2021 |language=en-GB}}</ref> However, there is evidence that companies that invest in offsets and credits tend to make more ambitious emissions cuts compared with companies that do not.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Why we can't afford to dismiss carbon offsetting in a climate crisis |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2021/04/carbon-offsetting-climate-crisis/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=World Economic Forum |date=22 April 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

Researchers have raised the concern that the use of carbon offsets – such as by maintaining forests, [[reforestation]] or [[carbon capture and storage|carbon capture]] – as well as [[renewable energy]] certificates<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bjørn |first1=Anders |last2=Lloyd |first2=Shannon M. |last3=Brander |first3=Matthew |last4=Matthews |first4=H. Damon |date=9 June 2022 |title=Renewable energy certificates threaten the integrity of corporate science-based targets |journal=Nature Climate Change |language=en |volume=12 |issue=6 |pages=539–546 |bibcode=2022NatCC..12..539B |doi=10.1038/s41558-022-01379-5 |issn=1758-6798 |s2cid=249524667 |doi-access=free|hdl=20.500.11820/fd48d7fc-d354-4ed6-bc99-70e515a7b189 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> allow polluting companies a business-as-usual approach to continue releasing greenhouse gases<ref name="greenw">{{cite news |last1=Meredith |first1=Sam |date=7 February 2022 |title=World's biggest companies accused of exaggerating their climate actions |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/02/07/study-worlds-biggest-firms-seen-exaggerating-their-climate-actions.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221114011055/https://www.cnbc.com/2022/02/07/study-worlds-biggest-firms-seen-exaggerating-their-climate-actions.html |archive-date=November 14, 2022 |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=CNBC |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=13 April 2022 |title=Battle over carbon capture as tool to fight climate change |url=https://apnews.com/article/climate-technology-science-business-louisiana-8e41ce52bcb66117ad97b58dffe3b607 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221109231518/https://apnews.com/article/climate-technology-science-business-louisiana-8e41ce52bcb66117ad97b58dffe3b607 |archive-date=November 9, 2022 |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=The Associated Press |language=en}}</ref> and for being, inappropriately trusted, untried [[Technological fix|techno-fixes]].<ref>{{cite news |date=3 April 2022 |title=Scientists urge end to fossil fuel use as landmark IPCC report readied |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/apr/03/scientists-urge-end-to-fossil-fuel-use-as-landmark-ippc-report-readied |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221122132257/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/apr/03/scientists-urge-end-to-fossil-fuel-use-as-landmark-ippc-report-readied |archive-date=November 22, 2022 |access-date=11 June 2022 |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en}}</ref>

=== Oversight issues ===
Several certification standards exist, with different ways of measuring emissions baseline, reductions, [[additionality]], and other key criteria. However, no single standard governs the industry. Some offset providers have faced criticism that their carbon reduction claims are exaggerated or misleading.<ref name=":1"/> For example, carbon credits issued by the [[California Air Resources Board]] were found to use a formula that established fixed boundaries around forest regions. This created simplified, regional averages for the carbon stored in a wide mix of tree species.

Some experts have estimated that California's cap and trade program has generated between 20 million and 39 million forestry credits that do not achieve real climate benefits. This amounts to nearly one in three credits issued through that program.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Song |first1=Lisa |last2=Temple |first2=James |date=29 April 2021 |title=The Climate Solution Actually Adding Millions of Tons of {{CO2}} Into the Atmosphere |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/the-climate-solution-actually-adding-millions-of-tons-of-co2-into-the-atmosphere |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210526165520/https://www.propublica.org/article/the-climate-solution-actually-adding-millions-of-tons-of-co2-into-the-atmosphere |archive-date=26 May 2021 |access-date=28 May 2021 |website=ProPublica}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author1=Lisa Song |author2=James Temple |date=10 May 2021 |title=Mass Audubon promised to preserve wildlife. Then it made millions claiming it could cut down trees |newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2021/05/10/metro/mass-audubon-promised-preserve-wildlife-then-it-made-millions-claiming-it-could-cut-down-trees/ |url-status=live |access-date=14 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210514191838/https://www.bostonglobe.com/2021/05/10/metro/mass-audubon-promised-preserve-wildlife-then-it-made-millions-claiming-it-could-cut-down-trees/ |archive-date=14 May 2021}}</ref> [[The Australia Institute]] shares that while [[Australia]]'s carbon offset system appears to be regulated, it lacks independent verification and transparency. The government doesn't release the data that would allow independent scrutiny of offset projects.Without reliable data or oversight, there is no way to verify the effectiveness of these projects, which can lead to misleading claims and potentially increase emissions, especially when offsets are used to justify new fossil fuel projects.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hemming |first=Polly |date=26 April 2023 |title=Can carbon offsets save the environment? |url=https://australiainstitute.org.au/post/can-carbon-offsets-save-the-environment/ |access-date=10 January 2025 |website=The Australia Institute}}</ref>

Determining additionality can be difficult. This may present risks for buyers of offsets or credits.<ref name="SEI report">{{cite web |last1=Broekhoff
|first1=Derik
|last2=Gillenwater
|first2=Michael
|last3=Colbert-Sangree
|first3=Tani
|last4=Cage
|first4=Patrick
|url=https://www.offsetguide.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Carbon-Offset-Guide_3122020.pdf |title=Securing Climate Benefit: A Guide to Using Carbon Offsets
|publisher=Stockholm Environment Institute & Greenhouse Gas Management Institute
|year=2019
|access-date=December 17, 2022
}}</ref> Carbon projects that yield strong financial returns even in the absence of revenue from carbon credits are usually not considered additional. Another example is projects that are compelled by regulations. Projects representing common practice in an industry are also usually not considered additional. A full determination of additionality requires a careful investigation of proposed carbon offset projects.<ref>{{Cite web |title=FAQs {{!}} The Gold Standard |url=https://www.goldstandard.org/resources/faqs#faqs_display-page_1-21 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140216121417/http://www.cdmgoldstandard.org/frequently-asked-questions/carbon-market#faqs_display-page_1-21 |archive-date=2014-02-16 |access-date=2020-03-24 |website=www.goldstandard.org}}</ref>

Offsets provide a revenue stream for the reduction of some types of emissions, so they can lead to [[perverse incentive]]s. They may provide incentives to emit more, so that emitting entities can get credit for reducing emissions from an artificially high baseline. Regulatory agencies could address these situations. This could involve setting specific standards for verifiability, uniqueness, and transparency.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The CFTC Should Raise Standards and Mitigate Fraud in the Carbon Offsets Market |url=https://www.americanprogress.org/article/the-cftc-should-raise-standards-and-mitigate-fraud-in-the-carbon-offsets-market/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Center for American Progress |date=7 October 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Concerns with forestry projects ===
Forestry projects have faced increasing criticism over their integrity as offset or credit programs. A number of news stories from 2021 to 2023 criticized nature-based carbon offsets, the REDD+ program, and certification organizations.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-05-04 |title=Carbon offsets used by major airlines based on flawed system, warn experts |url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/may/04/carbon-offsets-used-by-major-airlines-based-on-flawed-system-warn-experts |access-date=2022-12-31 |website=the Guardian |language=en}}<br /></ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Temple |first1=L. |last2=Song |first2=J. |date=29 April 2021 |title=The Climate Solution Actually Adding Millions of Tons of {{CO2}} Into the Atmosphere |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/the-climate-solution-actually-adding-millions-of-tons-of-co2-into-the-atmosphere |access-date=2022-12-31 |website=ProPublica |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Astor |first=Maggie |date=2022-05-18 |title=Do Airline Climate Offsets Really Work? Here's the Good News, and the Bad. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/18/climate/offset-carbon-footprint-air-travel.html |access-date=2022-12-31 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> In one case it was estimated that around 90% of [[Deforestation#Control|rainforest offset]] credits of the [[Verified Carbon Standard]] are likely to be "phantom credits".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Greenfield |first1=Patrick |date=18 January 2023 |title=Revealed: more than 90% of rainforest carbon offsets by biggest certifier are worthless, analysis shows |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/jan/18/revealed-forest-carbon-offsets-biggest-provider-worthless-verra-aoe |url-status=live |access-date=15 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230214230413/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/jan/18/revealed-forest-carbon-offsets-biggest-provider-worthless-verra-aoe |archive-date=14 February 2023}}</ref>

Tree planting projects in particular have been problematic. Critics point to a number of concerns. Trees reach maturity over a course of many decades. It is difficult to guarantee how long the forest will last. It may suffer clearing, [[forest fire|burning]], or mismanagement.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Do You Guarantee Land-Based Offsets Are Permanent? |url=https://www.greenbiz.com/article/how-do-you-guarantee-land-based-offsets-are-permanent |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=www.greenbiz.com |date=19 June 2009 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-07-05 |title=Planting trees "doesn't make any sense" in the fight against climate change say experts |url=https://www.dezeen.com/2021/07/05/carbon-climate-change-trees-afforestation/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Dezeen |language=en}}</ref> Some tree-planting projects introduce fast-growing [[invasive species]]. These end up damaging native forests and reducing biodiversity.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-05-29 |title=Planting invasive species could make our carbon problem worse |url=https://www.popsci.com/story/environment/invasive-plants-change-carbon-cycle/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Popular Science |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Veldman |first1=Joseph W. |last2=Overbeck |first2=Gerhard E. |last3=Negreiros |first3=Daniel |last4=Mahy |first4=Gregory |last5=Le Stradic |first5=Soizig |last6=Fernandes |first6=G. Wilson |last7=Durigan |first7=Giselda |last8=Buisson |first8=Elise |last9=Putz |first9=Francis E. |last10=Bond |first10=William J. |title=Where Tree Planting and Forest Expansion are Bad for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services |journal=[[BioScience]] |date=2015 |volume=65 |issue=10 |pages=1011–1018 |doi=10.1093/biosci/biv118 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aguirre-Gutiérrez |first1=Jesús |last2=Stevens |first2=Nicola |last3=Berenguer |first3=Erika |title=Valuing the functionality of tropical ecosystems beyond carbon |journal=[[Trends in Ecology & Evolution]] |date=2023 |volume=38 |issue=12 |pages=1109–1111 |doi=10.1016/j.tree.2023.08.012 |pmid=37798181 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2023TEcoE..38.1109A }}</ref> In response, some certification standards such as the ''Climate Community and Biodiversity Standard'' require multiple species plantings.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate, Community & Biodiversity Standards |url=https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/carbon-offset-programs/add-on-standards/climate-community-biodiversity-standards/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Carbon Offset Guide |language=en}}</ref> Tree planting in high latitude forests may have a net warming effect on the Earth's climate because tree cover absorbs sunlight thus creating a warming effect that balances out their absorption of carbon dioxide.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate change could expand forests. But will they cool the planet? |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/trees-help-curb-climate-change-can-also-contribute-warming-reducing-earths-reflectivity |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=www.science.org |language=en}}</ref> Tree-planting projects can also cause conflicts with local communities and Indigenous people if the project displaces or otherwise curtails their use of forest resources.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bourke |first=India |date=2021-11-18 |title="A further act of colonisation": why indigenous peoples fear carbon offsetting |url=https://www.newstatesman.com/environment/climate/2021/11/a-further-act-of-colonisation-why-indigenous-peoples-fear-carbon-offsetting |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=New Statesman |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fleischman |first1=Forrest |last2=Basant |first2=Shishir |last3=Chhatre |first3=Ashwini |last4=Coleman |first4=Eric A |last5=Fischer |first5=Harry W |last6=Gupta |first6=Divya |last7=Güneralp |first7=Burak |last8=Kashwan |first8=Prakash |last9=Khatri |first9=Dil |last10=Muscarella |first10=Robert |last11=Powers |first11=Jennifer S|author11-link=Jennifer Sarah Powers |last12=Ramprasad |first12=Vijay |last13=Rana |first13=Pushpendra |last14=Solorzano |first14=Claudia Rodriguez |last15=Veldman |first15=Joseph W |date=2020-09-16 |title=Pitfalls of Tree Planting Show Why We Need People-Centered Natural Climate Solutions |url=https://academic.oup.com/bioscience/advance-article/doi/10.1093/biosci/biaa094/5903754 |journal=BioScience |article-number=biaa094 |language=en |doi=10.1093/biosci/biaa094 |issn=0006-3568|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cadman |first1=Tim |last2=Hales |first2=Robert |date=2022-06-01 |title=COP26 and a Framework for Future Global Agreements on Carbon Market Integrity |url=http://berghahnjournals.com/view/journals/ijsq/12/1/ijsq120105.xml |journal=The International Journal of Social Quality |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=85 |doi=10.3167/IJSQ.2022.120105 |issn=1757-0344|doi-access=free |hdl=10072/422013 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Lack of impact on the company's own operations ===
Offsetting, while a widely used tool for addressing greenhouse gas emissions, has inherent limitations in directly reducing carbon emissions at the source.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is Insetting? |url=https://climateseed.com/blog/what-is-insetting |access-date=2025-01-10 |website=climateseed.com |language=en}}</ref> By purchasing carbon credits from external projects, companies invest in external projects to counterbalance emissions, often through reforestation or renewable energy initiatives. However, offsetting has faced significant scrutiny and exploitation. There have been many cases of large companies purchasing carbon credits to offset their emissions without taking meaningful action to reduce their own emissions directly.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-08-16 |title=Carbon Insetting: A necessary step towards Net Zero? |url=https://proba.earth/probas-blog/insetting |access-date=2025-01-10 |website=proba.earth |language=en}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change in Austria
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
[[File:Austria-TAVG-Trend.svg|thumb|Land-surface temperature in Austria 1743–2013 as 12-month and 10-year moving averages.|368x368px]] 
[[Global warming]] is affecting [[Austria]]n temperatures, [[weather]], [[ecosystem]]s and [[biodiversity]]. Since 1950 temperatures have risen by 1.8&nbsp;°C, and in the past 150 years [[Retreat of glaciers since 1850|glaciers have melted]], losing a significant amount of their volume.<ref name="The Climate in Austria">{{cite web |title=The Climate in Austria |url=https://www.worlddata.info/europe/austria/climate.php |website=WorldData |access-date=25 April 2022 |archive-date=25 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220525101001/https://www.worlddata.info/europe/austria/climate.php |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>[https://www.umweltbundesamt.at/fileadmin/site/publikationen/rep1000.pdf ''14. UMWELTKONTROLLBERICHT''] (pdf, 336 p., June 2025) </ref>
Changed precipitation patterns, increased temperatures, reduced snowfall, melting glaciers and more frequent extreme weather phenomenons, such as droughts, are expected effects from climate change. Ecosystems and biodiversity in Austria are facing changes due to increasing temperatures and the spread of thermophile species, heat and drought stress on animals and plants, an increase in alien and invasive species and an increase in pathogenic organisms and the spread of disease.

The [[Economy of Austria|Austrian economy]] is expected to be significantly affected by the effects of global warming, leading to costs of 4.2 to 5.2 billion Euros per year by the middle of the century. More frequent and intense weather events cause increasing costs for reconstruction and maintenance of infrastructure, fewer days with snow lead to a decline of overnight tourists in the winter, and a higher number of heat related health issues challenge the Austrian healthcare system.<ref name=":4" />

To deal with the effects of global warming, mitigation efforts are being implemented from various directions. Politicians are planning to achieve climate neutrality by 2040 at the latest, as stated in the coalition agreement. As part of the [[European Union]], Austria has to pursue efforts to reach the emission goals of the [[European Green Deal]].<ref name=":5" /> Activists try to speed mitigation efforts up using petitions, campaigns and protests.

== Greenhouse gas emissions ==
According to Austria's national energy and climate strategy to reach the demands of the [[Paris Agreement]], Austria has planned a reduction of [[greenhouse gas emissions]] of 36% by 2030 in relation to 2005 levels. As part of the [[European Union]], Austria is obliged to contribute to the EU's climate targets of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 55% until 2030 in comparison to 1990 levels, determined in the [[European Green Deal]]. In order to reach this goal, it has been proposed that Austria should increase its target to cut down emissions by 48% by 2030. Additionally, the [[Nehammer government]] (2021-2025) planned to bring Austria to [[carbon neutrality]] by 2040.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Die österreichische Klimaschutzstrategie/Politik |url=https://www.oesterreich.gv.at/themen/bauen_wohnen_und_umwelt/klimaschutz/1/Seite.1000310.html |access-date=2022-04-27 |website=oesterreich.gv.at - Österreichs digitales Amt |language=de |archive-date=2022-05-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220531131408/https://www.oesterreich.gv.at/themen/bauen_wohnen_und_umwelt/klimaschutz/1/Seite.1000310.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Austria has historically emitted 5.51 billion tons of CO<sub>2</sub> as a result of burning of fossil fuels and cement production, contributing to a share of 0.32% of cumulative global CO<sub>2</sub> emissions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ritchie |first1=Hannah |author1-link=Hannah Ritchie |last2=Roser |first2=Max |author2-link=Max Roser |last3=Rosado |first3=Pablo |date=2020-05-11 |title=CO₂ and Greenhouse Gas Emissions |url=https://ourworldindata.org/co2/country/austria |journal=Our World in Data |access-date=2022-05-21 |archive-date=2022-05-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220528035223/https://ourworldindata.org/co2/country/austria |url-status=live }}</ref>

The following table shows Austria's greenhouse gas emissions in megatons of [[CO2 equivalent|{{CO2}} equivalents]] in past years, compared to the total [[Member state of the European Union|EU27]] and world emissions.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=EDGAR - The Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research |url=https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/report_2021 |access-date=2022-04-27 |website=edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu|archive-date=2022-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220504140935/https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/report_2021 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Energy consumption ===
[[File:Austria_electricity_production.svg|thumb|Austria electricity supply by source]]
As of 2020, increased energy demand in transportation and construction have contributed to emission growth in the years before. 28% of Austria's energy came from [[renewable energy|renewables]], making Austria a top player in the field, with [[biofuel]]s and [[hydropower]] being the most important [[Renewable energy in Austria|renewable energy sources in Austria]]. [[Nuclear power|Nuclear energy]] is not present in Austria, due to it being banned in the Austrian Constitution. In accordance with its goal to be carbon neutral in 2040, Austria is working to be completely dependent<!--negative wording---> on [[renewable energy]] sources by 2030 – in 2018 this share had already been 77%. Austria closed its last [[Coal power|coal power plant]] in 2020 and targets ending coal and oil-fired heating by 2035.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Austria 2020 – Analysis |url=https://www.iea.org/reports/austria-2020 |access-date=2022-04-27 |website=IEA|archive-date=2022-04-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220427155643/https://www.iea.org/reports/austria-2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Measures contained in Austria's 'National Energy and Climate Plan' to achieve the energy targets include an end of oil and coal heating in buildings, a prohibition of heating new buildings with natural gas, a large increase in the target for [[photovoltaic installation]]s and extending [[Carbon price|carbon pricing]] to more sectors.<ref name=":1" />

[[File:Greenhouse gas emissions by sector, Austria, 2018.png|thumb|349x349px|Greenhouse gas emissions in tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalents (CO₂e) in Austria by sector until 2018.]]

=== Transportation ===
Making up 30% of emissions in 2019, the transportation sector then was Austria's largest contributing sector to global warming.<ref name=":2">Jensen, Liselotte; Carvalho Fachada, João (2021). [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/BRIE/2021/696186/EPRS_BRI(2021)696186_EN.pdf Climate action in Austria: Latest state of play.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220622140739/https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/BRIE/2021/696186/EPRS_BRI(2021)696186_EN.pdf |date=2022-06-22 }} European Parliamentary Research Service.</ref> Since 1990, emissions in the transportation sector have increased by 52% and there has been no significant reduction in [[Greenhouse gas emissions|CO<sub>2</sub> emission]] since 2005.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Verkehr beeinflusst das Klima |url=https://www.umweltbundesamt.at/umweltthemen/mobilitaet/mobilitaetsdaten/verkehr-treibhausgase |access-date=2022-04-28 |website=umweltbundesamt.at |language=de-DE |archive-date=2022-04-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220401085301/https://www.umweltbundesamt.at/umweltthemen/mobilitaet/mobilitaetsdaten/verkehr-treibhausgase |url-status=live }}</ref> 
The largest amount of emissions is connected to road traffic and specifically passenger cars.<ref name=":3" />

With October 26, 2021, the [[Ministry of Climate Action and Energy (Austria)|Federal Ministry for Climate Action, Environment, Energy, Mobility, Innovation and Technology]] introduced the so-called climate ticket. Purchasing this ticket allows using all means of public transport in the whole country for one year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate Ticket |url=https://www.bmk.gv.at/en/topics/mobility/1-2-3-klimaticket.html |access-date=2022-05-09 |website=bmk.gv.at|archive-date=2022-06-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220625134138/https://www.bmk.gv.at/en/topics/mobility/1-2-3-klimaticket.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Largest emitters ===
