======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change in Florida
======================================================================

{{short description|Climate change in the U.S. state of Florida}}
The effects of '''climate change in Florida''' are attributable to man-made increases in [[Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of Earth|atmospheric carbon dioxide]]. Floridians are experiencing increased flooding due to [[sea level rise]], and are concerned about the possibility of more [[Tropical cyclones and climate change|frequent or more intense hurricanes]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=The Palm Beach Post Editorial Board |date=2017-09-08 |title=Editorial: Gov. Scott's Irma leadership undercut by his climate denial |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/opinion/editorial-gov-scott-irma-leadership-undercut-his-climate-denial/44qVCYgU4Wg6kWlwzVpW1J/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170910075113/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/opinion/editorial-gov-scott-irma-leadership-undercut-his-climate-denial/44qVCYgU4Wg6kWlwzVpW1J/ |archive-date=September 10, 2017 |access-date=2020-02-15 |website=The Palm Beach Post |language=en}}</ref>

The state has been described as America's "ground zero" for [[climate change]], [[global warming]] and sea level rise, because "the majority of its population and economy is concentrated along low-elevation oceanfront."<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Bagley |first=Katharine |date=2014-03-13 |title=Climate Change Showdown in Florida Governor's Race |url=http://insideclimatenews.org/news/20140313/climate-change-showdown-florida-governors-race |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140319000109/http://insideclimatenews.org/news/20140313/climate-change-showdown-florida-governors-race |archive-date=March 19, 2014 |access-date=2020-02-15 |website=InsideClimate News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Grunwald |first=Michael |title=Spending Earth Day at Ground Zero for Climate Change In America |url=https://time.com/72821/climate-change-earth-day-ground-zero/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250206233153/https://time.com/72821/climate-change-earth-day-ground-zero/ |archive-date=2025-02-06 |access-date=2025-09-03 |magazine=TIME |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Editorials |date=August 1, 2015 |title=Ground Zero for climate change |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/opinion/editorials/article29609719.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906042355/https://www.miamiherald.com/opinion/editorials/article29609719.html |archive-date=September 6, 2015 |access-date=2020-02-26 |website=[[Miami Herald]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Urdaneta |first=Diego |date=April 22, 2014 |title=Florida is 'Ground Zero' for sea level rise |url=https://phys.org/news/2014-04-florida-ground-sea.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140427002943/https://phys.org/news/2014-04-florida-ground-sea.html |archive-date=April 27, 2014 |access-date=2020-02-26 |website=phys.org |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Morse |first=Hannah |title=Florida is climate change 'ground zero.' But it lacks buzz ahead of presidential debate |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/20190623/florida-is-climate-change-ground-zero-but-it-lacks-buzz-ahead-of-presidential-debate |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624064512/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/20190623/florida-is-climate-change-ground-zero-but-it-lacks-buzz-ahead-of-presidential-debate |archive-date=June 24, 2019 |access-date=2020-02-26 |website=The Palm Beach Post |language=en}}</ref>

Florida residents think climate change is happening at higher rates than the national average. As of March 2025, 88% of Floridians believe climate change is happening, with 55% believing it to be attributable to human activities. However, the state remains politically divided, with 74% of [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] and 40% of [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] agreeing with the [[Scientific consensus on climate change|scientific consensus]] that climate change is anthropogenic. Some communities in Florida have begun implementing [[climate change mitigation]] approaches; however, statewide initiatives have been hampered by the [[Politics of climate change|politicization of climate change]] in the United States, focusing on [[Climate resilience|resilience]] rather than full scale [[Climate change mitigation|mitigation]] and [[Climate change adaptation|adaptation]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Harris |first=Alex |date=March 12, 2022 |title=Florida's statewide climate change response ignores cause |url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/2022/03/12/floridas-statewide-climate-change-response-ignores-cause/ |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230617234315/https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/2022/03/12/floridas-statewide-climate-change-response-ignores-cause/ |archive-date=June 17, 2023 |access-date=2023-06-17 |website=Tampa Bay Times |language=en}}</ref>

== Impacts on the natural environment ==

=== Sea level rise ===
[[File:Koppen-Geiger Map v2 USA Florida 2071–2099 SSP585.svg|thumb|A predicted [[Köppen climate classification]] map for Florida in 2071-2099 using the SSP585 scenario (assuming highest possible greenhouse gas emissions.) The tropical region could hypothetically spread to regions as far north as [[Tampa, Florida|Tampa]] on the Gulf Coast and [[Cape Canaveral]] on the Atlantic coast.]]
[[File:Southeastern United States of America Population Density and Low Elevation Coastal Zones (5457914012).jpg|thumb|South eastern USA population density and [[Low Elevation Coastal Zone|low elevation coastal zones]].]]
Since the early 1990s, [[sea level]]s in the Southeast U.S. have risen 0.12 inches (3.0 mm) per year on average. This rate is accelerating and it is projected to continue accelerating. [[Sea level rise]] is already making [[saltwater intrusion]] worse in Florida which impacts [[groundwater]] supplies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sea Level Rise - Florida Climate Center |url=https://climatecenter.fsu.edu/topics/sea-level-rise |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250812163713/https://climatecenter.fsu.edu/topics/sea-level-rise |archive-date=August 12, 2025 |access-date=2025-09-08 |website=FSU Florida Climate Center}}</ref> A natural phenomenon known as [[king tide]] flooding is also being exacerbated by sea level rise. This is when high tides at certain times of year are so high that they result in saltwater flooding in the absence of any precipitation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pitts |first=Zulekha |date=November 12, 2024 |title=Miami, Brace for November King Tides: Flooding Expected With Full Moon |url=https://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/miami-florida-king-tides-explained-how-they-work-timing-and-more-21330441 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241004013826/https://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/miami-florida-king-tides-explained-how-they-work-timing-and-more-21330441 |archive-date=October 4, 2024 |access-date=2025-09-08 |website=Miami New Times |language=en}}</ref> Salt water rises up through the porous [[limestone]] that Florida sits on.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |last=Ruggeri |first=Amanda |date=3 April 2017 |title=Miami's fight against rising seas |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20170403-miamis-fight-against-sea-level-rise |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250804063454/https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20170403-miamis-fight-against-sea-level-rise |archive-date=August 4, 2025 |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en}}</ref>

A 2018 report by the [[Union of Concerned Scientists]] (UCS) found that by the year 2100, more than 1 million Florida homes would be at risk of flooding according to their high scenario projection.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |year=2018 |title=Underwater: Rising Seas, Chronic Floods, and the Implications for US Coastal Real Estate |url=https://www.ucs.org/sites/default/files/attach/2018/06/underwater-analysis-full-report.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250628134235/https://www.ucs.org/sites/default/files/attach/2018/06/underwater-analysis-full-report.pdf |archive-date=June 28, 2025 |website=Union of Concerned Scientists}}</ref>[[File:Zuid-Florida reliëf.jpg|thumb|color-coded shaded relief map generated with data from the [[Shuttle Radar Topography Mission]]. For the view on the right, elevations below 5 meters (16 feet) above sea level have been colored dark blue, and lighter blue indicates elevations below 10 meters (33 feet).]]A 2018 [[Florida International University]] study says that sea level rise will inundate the [[mangrove]]s of the [[Everglades|Florida Everglades]].<ref name=":18" /> As the ocean rises, it will flood the Everglades and the [[Biscayne Aquifer]], impacting the water supply of [[Miami]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=http://www.miamidade.gov/environment/climate-change-impact.asp|title=Miami-Dade County - Environment - Impact on South Florida|date=Aug 9, 2013|website=www.miamidade.gov|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite web|url=https://www.gsd.harvard.edu/project/the-vulnerability-of-potable-water-with-climate-change-in-miami-dade/|title=The Vulnerability of Potable Water with Climate Change in Miami-Dade|last=Cabrera|first=Pamela|date=2018|website=Harvard Graduate School of Design|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2018-08-29/miami-s-other-water-problem|title=Miami Will Be Underwater Soon. Its Drinking Water Could Go First. The city has another serious water problem.|date=August 29, 2018|website=www.bloomberg.com|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

=== Mangroves ===
Due to climate change, the range of mangroves worldwide is extending. This is due to a combination of fewer hard freezes and more intense storms. Warmer weather prevents mangroves from dying during winter months and stronger storms spread the propagules of mangroves further.<ref name=":19" /> However, sea level rise places certain populations of mangroves, such as those in the Everglades, at risk.<ref name=":18">{{Cite news |last=Milman |first=Oliver |date=2018-05-02 |title=Everglades under threat as Florida's mangroves face death by rising sea level |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2018/may/02/mangroves-everglades-florida-rising-sea-level |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200222185610/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2018/may/02/mangroves-everglades-florida-rising-sea-level |archive-date=2020-02-22 |access-date=2020-02-15 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

Mangroves, as well as other organisms in coastal and ocean ecosystems are referred to as [[blue carbon]], acting as [[Carbon sink|carbon sinks]] in the process of [[carbon sequestration]]. Carbon in blue carbon areas is stored at a faster rate than in other ecosystems, such as forests, and can remain sequestered for millions of years.<ref name=":20">{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=What is Blue Carbon? |url=https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/bluecarbon.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250731131845/https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/bluecarbon.html |archive-date=2025-07-31 |access-date=2025-09-19 |website=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration |language=EN-US}}</ref> The stored carbon in the mangroves of the Everglades has been estimated to be worth between $2 billion and $3.4 billion.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gonzalez |first=Evelyn |date=November 15, 2016 |title=Everglades mangroves worth billions in fight against climate change |url=https://phys.org/news/2016-11-everglades-mangroves-worth-billions-climate.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200928201344/https://phys.org/news/2016-11-everglades-mangroves-worth-billions-climate.html |archive-date=2020-09-28 |access-date=2020-02-15 |website=phys.org |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jerath |first1=Meenakshi |last2=Bhat |first2=Mahadev |last3=Rivera-Monroy |first3=Victor H. |last4=Castañeda-Moya |first4=Edward |last5=Simard |first5=Marc |last6=Twilley |first6=Robert R. |date=2016-12-01 |title=The role of economic, policy, and ecological factors in estimating the value of carbon stocks in Everglades mangrove forests, South Florida, USA |journal=Environmental Science & Policy |language=en |volume=66 |pages=160–169 |bibcode=2016ESPol..66..160J |doi=10.1016/j.envsci.2016.09.005 |issn=1462-9011 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=14 November 2016 |title=Everglades mangroves' carbon storage capacity worth billions |url=https://www.nsf.gov/discoveries/disc_summ.jsp?cntn_id=190254 |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=www.nsf.gov |language=en}}</ref> When damaged, these ecosystems release very large amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.<ref name=":20" />

Mangroves also act as habitat for many species of juvenile fish and shellfish, provide protection from storm surge and strong winds,<ref name=":21">{{Cite news |last=Weinhofer |first=Carter |date=2025-08-11 |title=New report shines light on how Manatee development, hurricanes impact mangroves |url=https://www.bradenton.com/news/local/article311578219.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250919144103/https://www.bradenton.com/news/local/article311578219.html |archive-date=2025-09-19 |access-date=2025-09-19 |work=[[Bradenton Herald]]}}</ref> and produce soil which helps maintain the height of the coastline.<ref name=":19">{{Cite web |last=Rivers |first=Brendan |date=2019-08-29 |title=Mangroves, Climate Change And Hurricanes |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/08/29/755322980/mangroves-climate-change-and-hurricanes |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200215094637/https://www.npr.org/2019/08/29/755322980/mangroves-climate-change-and-hurricanes |archive-date=2020-02-15 |access-date=2020-02-15 |website=NPR |language=en}}</ref> The loss of mangroves and [[wetland]]s would cause [[commercial fisheries]] to decline and negatively impact the ability of coastal areas to resist damage from storms.<ref name=":21" />

=== Red tide ===
[[Harmful algal bloom|Red tide]], or harmful [[algal bloom]], is a naturally occurring overgrowth of microscopic algae that originates in high salinity bodies of water.<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Red Tides in Florida |url=https://myfwc.com/research/redtide/general/about/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250712080703/https://myfwc.com/research/redtide/general/about/ |archive-date=2025-07-12 |access-date=2025-09-24 |website=Florida Fish And Wildlife Conservation Commission |language=en}}</ref> These blooms can cost millions of dollars in fisheries closures, lost tourism dollars, hospital visits, and cleanup efforts.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2024-09-25 |title=Hitting Us Where it Hurts: The Untold Story of Harmful Algal Blooms |url=https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/west-coast/science-data/hitting-us-where-it-hurts-untold-story-harmful-algal-blooms |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250831193741/https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/west-coast/science-data/hitting-us-where-it-hurts-untold-story-harmful-algal-blooms |archive-date=2025-08-31 |access-date=2025-09-24 |website=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries |language=en}}</ref> Economically destructive red tides are expected to be exacerbated by pollution and warming water.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Harris |first=Alex |date=November 27, 2018 |title=Federal report says what Florida already knows — climate change is affecting us now |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/environment/article222086110.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200519234321/https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/environment/article222086110.html |archive-date=2020-05-19 |access-date=2020-02-17 |website=[[Miami Herald]]}}</ref>

=== Hurricanes ===
[[File:Thank you linemen, Chattahoochee (cropped).jpg|thumb|left|Sign thanking [[lineworker]]s and [[first responders]] after [[Hurricane Michael]], Chattahoochee 2019|180x180px]]
A change in [[hurricane]] frequency or intensity is of concern for Floridians. The Climate Change Center at [[Florida State University]] and Climate.gov say the science is inconclusive regarding an increase in hurricane frequency and the limited historical data makes it difficult to find any long term patterns that differentiate from natural variability. However, rainfall rates and hurricane intensity are expected to increase according to most [[climate model]]s and it has been established that the warming of the ocean is partly due to anthropogenic climate change. The storm surge associated with hurricanes will also pose a greater threat due to rising sea levels.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://climatecenter.fsu.edu/topics/climate-change|title=Climate Change Basics for the Southeast USA (from AgroClimate)|website=Florida Climate Center, Florida State University|access-date=2020-02-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/climate-qa/could-climate-change-make-atlantic-hurricanes-worse|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190619202545/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/climate-qa/could-climate-change-make-atlantic-hurricanes-worse|archive-date=June 19, 2019|title=Could climate change make Atlantic hurricanes worse?|date=May 29, 2019|website=NOAA Climate.gov|access-date=2020-02-15}}</ref>

[[File:170914-H-OD937-209 (37474487341) (cropped).jpg|thumb|left|President [[Donald Trump]] viewing [[Hurricane Irma]] damage, [[Naples, Florida|Naples]]|184x184px]]
After [[Hurricane Irma]] in 2017, which occurred just weeks after [[Hurricane Harvey]], Governor [[Rick Scott]] did not attribute the possible changes in hurricane patterns to climate change.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/florida/story/2017/09/14/florida-governor-remains-unsure-about-climate-change-after-hurricane-irma-114498|title=Florida governor remains unsure about climate change after Hurricane Irma|last=Caputo|first=Marc|date=2017-09-14|website=Politico - Politico Florida|language=en|access-date=2020-02-15}}</ref>

There is some evidence that hurricanes may slow down their rate of forward advance, like [[Hurricane Dorian]], which spent a day and a half over [[Grand Bahama Island]] on its way to Florida.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wusfnews.wusf.usf.edu/post/climate-change-fueling-more-intense-stalling-hurricanes|title=Is Climate Change Fueling More Intense, Stalling Hurricanes?|date=September 6, 2019|website=WUSF News|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/145559/a-devastating-stall-by-hurricane-dorian|title=A Devastating Stall by Hurricane Dorian|date=2019-09-04|website=earthobservatory.nasa.gov|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/20190906/hurricane-dorian-why-warming-planet-may-mean-more-dorian-like-storms|title=Hurricane Dorian: Why a warming planet may mean more Dorian-like storms|last=Miller|first=Kimberly|website=The Palm Beach Post|language=en|archive-date=September 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190907065900/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/20190906/hurricane-dorian-why-warming-planet-may-mean-more-dorian-like-storms|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

A category 5 hurricane is of most concern in the [[Tampa Bay]] area, and climate related sea level rise of as little as six inches would exacerbate its impact.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/energy-and-environment/2019/9/11/18485563/hurricane-florida-climate-change-tampa|title=26 feet of water: What the worst-case hurricane scenario looks like for Tampa Bay|last=Resnick|first=Brian|date=2019-09-11|website=Vox|language=en|access-date=2020-02-15}}</ref>

According to the [[Fifth National Climate Assessment]] published in 2023, coastal states including California, Florida, Louisiana, and Texas are experiencing "more significant storms and extreme swings in precipitation".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/11/14/us/national-climate-assessment-extreme-weather-costs/index.html |title=No place in the US is safe from the climate crisis, but a new report shows where it's most severe|first1=Ella|last1=Nilsen|work=CNN|date=November 14, 2023}}</ref>

== Impacts on People ==

=== Transportation ===
The [[Florida Department of Transportation]] (FDOT) has studied how to use [[Greenhouse gas emissions by the United States|greenhouse gas]] calculation tools as part of the [[transportation planning]] processes, and analyzes [[transportation infrastructure]] for impacts of sea level rise.<ref>{{Cite web |last=University of South Florida |first=Florida Department of Transportation |date=November 2010 |title=Developing a Framework for a Toolkit for Carbon Footprint That Integrates Transit (CFIT): Final Report |url=https://fdotwww.blob.core.windows.net/sitefinity/docs/default-source/research/reports/fdot-bdk85-977-10-rpt.pdf?sfvrsn=1a849b1e_2 |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=Florida Department of Transportation}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last= |title=Development of Geospatial Framework to Support Robust Analysis of Transportation Infrastructure to Climate Impacts |url=https://fdotwww.blob.core.windows.net/sitefinity/docs/default-source/research/program_information/contract.development/ballot/opp-21-02.pdf?sfvrsn=52aee1ee_2 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250826115105/https://fdotwww.blob.core.windows.net/sitefinity/docs/default-source/research/program_information/contract.development/ballot/opp-21-02.pdf?sfvrsn=52aee1ee_2 |archive-date=August 26, 2025 |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=Florida Department of Transportation. Planning–Office of Policy Planning}}</ref>[[File:Charging station MIA 09 2017 5955.jpg|thumb|left|Electric vehicle charging station, Miami|202x202px]]To aid in assessing the potential impact of sea level rise on transportation facilities, the [[University of Florida]] (UF) developed a [[geospatial]] tool called the Sea Level Scenario Sketch Planning Tool. This is used by the FDOT, local governments, and other agencies to identify transportation infrastructure that may be vulnerable to flooding from sea level rise.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=The University of Florida GeoPlan Center |title=About – Sea Level Scenario Sketch Planning Tool |url=https://sls.geoplan.ufl.edu/about/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250814024124/https://sls.geoplan.ufl.edu/about/ |archive-date=August 14, 2025 |access-date=2025-09-03 |language=en-US|website=sls.geoplan.ufl.edu}}</ref>

=== Real estate ===
The UCS reported in 2018 that Florida was the state with the most homes at risk from sea level rise.<ref name=":15" />

In 2017, the [[real estate]] website [[Zillow]] wrote that if climate predictions were correct, by 2100 "One in eight Florida homes would be under water, accounting for nearly half of the lost housing value nationwide." This calculation was based on comparing [[NOAA]] maps for a 6-foot sea level rise with the Zillow database of homes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-06-02 |title=Climate Change and Housing: Will a Rising Tide Sink All Homes? |url=https://www.zillow.com/research/climate-change-underwater-homes-12890/ |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=Zillow Research |language=en-US}}</ref>

Real estate website [[Curbed]] has presented a table with impacted cities in Florida, homes at risk, and dollar estimates. Curbed has estimated that "Roughly 64,000 homes—including 12,000 in Miami Beach, a nexus of real estate investment—will face chronic flooding," and has described how changes are needed in National Flood Insurance Program.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sisson |first=Patrick |date=2018-10-16 |title=Climate change and the coming coastal real estate crash |url=https://www.curbed.com/2018/10/16/17981244/real-estate-climate-change-infrastructure |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181016195217/https://www.curbed.com/2018/10/16/17981244/real-estate-climate-change-infrastructure |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 16, 2018 |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=Curbed |language=en}}</ref> AP cites data from climate risk analytics firm Jupiter Intelligence indicating that "extreme flooding could go from affecting 5% to 86% of Miami-Dade's residential real estate supply by 2030."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nelson |first=Tim |date=January 23, 2020 |title=Two New Reports Explain Just How Susceptible Florida Real Estate Will Be to Climate Change |url=https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/two-new-reports-explain-just-how-susceptible-florida-real-estate-will-be-to-climate-change |access-date=2020-02-25 |website=[[Architectural Digest]] |language=en}}</ref>

Officials in the [[Florida Keys]] found that it would take 75 million dollars to save three miles of road serving about two dozen homes. A December 2019 New York Times article describing the decisions facing [[Monroe County, Florida|Monroe County]] was titled, "Florida Keys Deliver a Hard Message: As Seas Rise, Some Places Can't Be Saved."<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Flavelle |first1=Christopher |last2=Mazzei |first2=Patricia |date=2019-12-04 |title=Florida Keys Deliver a Hard Message: As Seas Rise, Some Places Can't Be Saved |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/04/climate/florida-keys-climate-change.html |access-date=2020-02-25 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Some small islands in the Keys may disappear altogether.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-02-25 |title=Global Warming Impact Zones {{!}} U.S. Florida |url=https://www.markey.senate.gov/GlobalWarming/impactzones/florida.html |access-date=2020-02-25 |website=Select Committee on Energy Independence and Global Warming, US Senate}}</ref>

[[Climate gentrification]] is increasing real estate values in parts of Miami that are at higher elevation, and decreasing values in lower-elevation areas.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Olick |first=Diana |date=August 29, 2019 |title=Rising Risks: 'Climate gentrification' is changing Miami real estate values – for better and worse |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/08/29/climate-gentrification-is-changing-miami-real-estate-values.html |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=CNBC}}</ref> By 2017, two poor black neighborhoods of Miami which are located on higher ground, [[Little Haiti]] and [[Liberty City (Miami)|Liberty City]], started becoming more attractive to investors.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Luscombe |first=Richard |date=2017-08-29 |title=How climate change could turn US real estate prices upside down |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2017/aug/29/hurricane-harvey-climate-change-real-estate-florida |access-date=2020-02-16 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref name=":12" /><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Stewart |first1=Ian |last2=Garcia-Navarro |first2=Lulu |date=March 31, 2019 |title=Building For An Uncertain Future: Miami Residents Adapt To The Changing Climate |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/03/31/706940085/building-for-an-uncertain-future-miami-residents-adapt-to-the-changing-climate |access-date=2020-02-26 |website=NPR.org |language=en}}</ref> Home prices appreciated more slowly in 2018 in Miami Beach and lower-lying areas of Miami-Dade County.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Morris |first=David Z |date=April 21, 2018 |title=Climate Change Is Already Depressing the Price of Flood-Prone Real Estate |url=https://fortune.com/2018/04/21/climate-change-is-already-depressing-the-price-of-flood-prone-real-estate/ |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=Fortune |language=en-US}}</ref>

One flood assessment company describes the South Florida housing market as being kept afloat by "systemic fraudulent nondisclosure" of flood risks to property.<ref name=":13">{{Cite news |last=Bergman |first=Megan Mayhew |date=2019-02-15 |title=Florida is drowning. Condos are still being built. Can't humans see the writing on the wall? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2019/feb/15/florida-climate-change-coastal-real-estate-rising-seas |access-date=2020-02-16 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Flavelle |first=Christopher |date=December 29, 2017 |title=South Florida's Real Estate Reckoning Could Be Closer Than You Think. Hurricane Irma showed just how vulnerable South Florida—and some of the nation's most expensive real estate—is to climate change. |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2017-12-29/south-florida-s-real-estate-reckoning-could-be-closer-than-you-think |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=Bloomberg}}</ref> A bill passed by the [[United States House of Representatives|US House of Representatives]] to require real estate agents to disclose flood risks had not made it through the Senate as of February 2019.<ref name=":13" />

=== Agriculture ===
The [[Agriculture in Florida|agriculture industry in Florida]] provides over two million jobs and generates over $120 billion in revenue each year. Agriculture in Florida has historically had to adapt to natural climate variations, but modern climate change is occurring at a faster and greater rate. Rising temperatures are already linked to lower [[crop yield]]s and higher atmospheric CO2 can reduce the nutritional value of many crops despite stimulating growth. Intensified extreme weather events and sea level rise also pose a threat to Florida agriculture, having the potential to impact [[irrigation]] water and increase pressure from [[Pest (organism)|pest]]s and disease.<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |last1=Her |first1=Young Gu |last2=Boote |first2=Kenneth J. |last3=Migliaccio |first3=Kati W. |last4=Fraisse |first4=Clyde |last5=Letson |first5=David |last6=Mbuya |first6=Odemari |last7=Anandhi |first7=Aavudai |last8=Chi |first8=Hongmei |last9=Ngatia |first9=Lucy |last10=Asseng |first10=Senthold |date=November 29, 2017 |title=Climate Book: Chapter 8 Climate Change Impacts and Adaptation in Florida's Agriculture |url=https://floridaclimateinstitute.org/docs/climatebook/Ch08-Her.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220408162542/https://floridaclimateinstitute.org/docs/climatebook/Ch08-Her.pdf |archive-date=April 8, 2022 |website=Florida Climate Institute}}</ref>

Strategies for dealing with climate change challenges include, developing more efficient technologies for irrigation and nutrient use, breeding crops and [[livestock]] that are resistant to heat and disease, and further research to better understand the impact of climate change on Florida agriculture and close any current knowledge gaps.<ref name=":16" />

=== Human health ===
Florida and the [[Southeastern United States|U.S. Southeast]] region face many health-related threats due to tropical storms, sea level rise, extreme heat, and drought.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://health2016.globalchange.gov/downloads#climate-change-and-human-health |title=Ch. 1: Introduction: Climate Change and Human Health. The Impacts of Climate Change on Human Health in the United States: A Scientific Assessment |last1=Balbus |first1=J. |last2=Crimmins |first2=A. |last3=Gamble |first3=J.L. |last4=Easterling |first4=D.R. |last5=Kunkel |first5=K.E. |last6=Saha |first6=S. |last7=Sarofim |first7=M.C. |date=2016 |publisher=U.S. Global Change Research Program |doi=10.7930/j0vx0dfw |doi-broken-date=4 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160922212358/https://health2016.globalchange.gov/downloads#climate-change-and-human-health |archive-date=September 22, 2016 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==== Population vulnerability ====
A considerable proportion of Florida's population has characteristics that may make them more vulnerable to health impacts or that may pose barriers to accessing healthcare; approximately 21.6% of Florida's population is over the age of 65, 21.0% are foreign born, 12.7% live below the federal poverty level, and approximately 13.9% of the population does not have health insurance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts: Florida |url=https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/FL/PST045222 |access-date=2023-12-18 |website=www.census.gov |language=en}}</ref>

==== Flooding and hurricanes ====
Due to its low elevation and the fact that it is the U.S. state with the largest number and percentage of its population living in coastal areas, Florida is at significant risk from flooding.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tagtachian |first1=Daniela |last2=Balk |first2=Deborah |date=2023-08-11 |title=Uneven vulnerability: characterizing population composition and change in the low elevation coastal zone in the United States with a climate justice lens, 1990–2020 |journal=Frontiers in Environmental Science |volume=11 |bibcode=2023FrEnS..1111856T |doi=10.3389/fenvs.2023.1111856 |issn=2296-665X |doi-access=free |article-number=1111856}}</ref> South Florida is especially vulnerable to sea level rise, with 590,000 people facing high or extreme risk from flooding. Of those, it is estimated that 55,000 are medically vulnerable and 125,000 are [[Social vulnerability|socially vulnerable]].<ref name=":32">{{Cite report |url=https://nca2018.globalchange.gov/chapter/19/ |title=Chapter 19: Southeast. Impacts, Risks, and Adaptation in the United States: The Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II |last1=Carter |first1=Lynne M. |last2=Terando |first2=Adam |last3=Dow |first3=Kirstin |last4=Hiers |first4=Kevin |last5=Kunkel |first5=Kenneth E. |last6=Lascurain |first6=Aranzazu |last7=Marcy |first7=Douglas C. |last8=Osland |first8=Michael J. |last9=Schramm |first9=Paul J. |date=2018 |publisher=U.S. Global Change Research Program |doi=10.7930/nca4.2018.ch19 |doi-broken-date=4 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181123190907/https://nca2018.globalchange.gov/chapter/19/ |archive-date=November 23, 2018 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In a 2025 report assessing the people and places in the U.S. most at risk for severe flooding by 2050, [[St. Petersburg, Florida|Saint Petersburg]] and Miami Beach were listed as the cities having the third and fourth largest number of people at risk, with 46,000 and 45,000 respectively.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 2, 2025 |title=Coastal Flood Risks Across the US |url=https://assets.ctfassets.net/cxgxgstp8r5d/1MbLA4rrFhhrlE8WLUG6JG/2e41d8695ee76f6a2a600adb312a1e86/FINAL__Exposure_Analysis_Report.docx.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250722042347/https://assets.ctfassets.net/cxgxgstp8r5d/1MbLA4rrFhhrlE8WLUG6JG/2e41d8695ee76f6a2a600adb312a1e86/FINAL__Exposure_Analysis_Report.docx.pdf |archive-date=July 22, 2025 |access-date=September 4, 2025 |website=Climate Central}}</ref>

Hurricanes can threaten health in a variety of direct and indirect ways.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Waddell |first1=Samantha L. |last2=Jayaweera |first2=Dushyantha T. |last3=Mirsaeidi |first3=Mehdi |last4=Beier |first4=John C. |last5=Kumar |first5=Naresh |date=2021-03-09 |title=Perspectives on the Health Effects of Hurricanes: A Review and Challenges |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |volume=18 |issue=5 |page=2756 |doi=10.3390/ijerph18052756 |issn=1660-4601 |pmc=7967478 |pmid=33803162 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In the United States, [[drowning]] is the leading cause of flooding-related death, particularly due to powerful [[Storm surge|storm surges]].<ref name=":22">{{Cite report |url=https://health2016.globalchange.gov/downloads#extreme-events |title=Ch. 4: Impacts of Extreme Events on Human Health. The Impacts of Climate Change on Human Health in the United States: A Scientific Assessment |last1=Bell |first1=J.E. |last2=Herring |first2=S.C. |last3=Jantarasami |first3=L. |last4=Adrianopoli |first4=C. |last5=Benedict |first5=K. |last6=Conlon |first6=K. |last7=Escobar |first7=V. |last8=Hess |first8=J. |last9=Luvall |first9=J. |date=2016 |publisher=U.S. Global Change Research Program |doi=10.7930/j0bz63zv |doi-broken-date=4 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160922212358/https://health2016.globalchange.gov/downloads#extreme-events |archive-date=September 22, 2016 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Although the U.S. is not considered to be at high risk for post flood related gastrointestinal illness, there is an increased risk among populations facing displacement due to poor sanitation and crowding in shelters. Food spoilage due to power outages have also been shown to cause outbreaks of these types of illnesses.<ref name=":22" /> In Florida, power outages after [[Hurricane Irma]] were associated with higher mortality in nursing home residents.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Skarha |first1=Julianne |last2=Gordon |first2=Lily |last3=Sakib |first3=Nazmus |last4=June |first4=Joseph |last5=Jester |first5=Dylan J. |last6=Peterson |first6=Lindsay J. |last7=Andel |first7=Ross |last8=Dosa |first8=David M. |date=2021-11-24 |title=Association of Power Outage With Mortality and Hospitalizations Among Florida Nursing Home Residents After Hurricane Irma |journal=JAMA Health Forum |language=en |volume=2 |issue=11 |pages=e213900 |doi=10.1001/jamahealthforum.2021.3900  |doi-access=free|issn=2689-0186 |pmc=8796882 |pmid=35977265}}</ref> During the evacuation process, people can lose or forget medication and devices such as hearing aids or dentures and may have difficulty filling prescriptions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ochi |first1=Sae |last2=Hodgson |first2=Susan |last3=Landeg |first3=Owen |last4=Mayner |first4=Lidia |last5=Murray |first5=Virginia |date=2014 |title=Disaster-Driven Evacuation and Medication Loss: a Systematic Literature Review |journal=PLOS Currents |language=en |volume=6 |doi=10.1371/currents.dis.fa417630b566a0c7dfdbf945910edd96 |issn=2157-3999 |pmc=4169391 |pmid=25642363 |doi-access=free}}</ref> A 2004 study of [[Hurricane Charley]] found a link between exposure to high wind speeds and an increased risk of [[preterm birth]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Grabich |first1=Shannon C. |last2=Robinson |first2=Whitney R. |last3=Engel |first3=Stephanie M. |last4=Konrad |first4=Charles E. |last5=Richardson |first5=David B. |last6=Horney |first6=Jennifer A. |date=2016 |title=Hurricane Charley Exposure and Hazard of Preterm Delivery, Florida 2004 |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10995-016-2069-y |journal=Maternal and Child Health Journal |language=en |volume=20 |issue=12 |pages=2474–2482 |doi=10.1007/s10995-016-2069-y |issn=1092-7875 |pmid=27485492 |s2cid=23967536 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> A retrospective analysis from 2020 shows further evidence of this association.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sun |first1=Shengzhi |last2=Weinberger |first2=Kate R. |last3=Yan |first3=Meilin |last4=Brooke Anderson |first4=G. |last5=Wellenius |first5=Gregory A. |date=2020-07-01 |title=Tropical cyclones and risk of preterm birth: A retrospective analysis of 20 million births across 378 US counties |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0160412020317803 |journal=Environment International |volume=140 |bibcode=2020EnInt.14005825S |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2020.105825 |issn=0160-4120 |pmid=32485474 |doi-access=free |article-number=105825}}</ref>

Longer-term impacts include those on mental and respiratory health, as well as exposure to harmful substances. Flooding puts people at higher risk of mental health challenges such as [[post-traumatic stress disorder]] (PTSD), anxiety, and depression.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fernandez |first1=Ana |last2=Black |first2=John |last3=Jones |first3=Mairwen |last4=Wilson |first4=Leigh |last5=Salvador-Carulla |first5=Luis |last6=Astell-Burt |first6=Thomas |last7=Black |first7=Deborah |date=2015-04-10 |editor-last=Ebi |editor-first=Kristie L |title=Flooding and Mental Health: A Systematic Mapping Review |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=10 |issue=4 |article-number=e0119929 |bibcode=2015PLoSO..1019929F |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0119929 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=4393088 |pmid=25860572 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Recovery after a major storm can involve heavy construction and exposure to hazardous materials in floodwaters such as sewage, chemicals, and sharp or broken objects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Johanning |first1=Eckardt |last2=Auger |first2=Pierre |last3=Morey |first3=Philip R. |last4=Yang |first4=Chin S. |last5=Olmsted |first5=Ed |date=2014 |title=Review of health hazards and prevention measures for response and recovery workers and volunteers after natural disasters, flooding, and water damage: mold and dampness |journal=Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine |language=en |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=93–99 |bibcode=2014EHPM...19...93J |doi=10.1007/s12199-013-0368-0 |issn=1342-078X |pmc=3944034 |pmid=24254802}}</ref> Florida's hot and humid climate creates favorable conditions for mold growth, these conditions are exacerbated after flooding and result in an increased exposure to mold spores which can cause worsened asthma, throat irritation, and wheezing.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Choi-Schagrin |first=Winston |date=October 4, 2022 |title=After the Storm, the Mold: Warming Is Worsening Another Costly Disaster |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/04/climate/hurricane-ian-mold-home-remediation.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221004220123/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/04/climate/hurricane-ian-mold-home-remediation.html |archive-date=October 4, 2022 |access-date=December 18, 2023 |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

==== Extreme heat ====
The impacts on health of climate change fueled [[extreme heat]] are anticipated to be minimal due to Florida's already warm climate that means that much of the population is [[Acclimatization|acclimatized]], or adjusted, to heat and most buildings have [[air conditioning]] installed.<ref name=":42">Emrich CT, Morath DP, Bowser GC, Reeves R. ''Climate-Sensitive Hazards in Florida: Identifying and Prioritizing Threats to Build Resilience against Climate Effects''. Hazards and Vulnerability Research Institute under contract for the Florida Department of Health; 2017. https://www.floridahealth.gov/environmental-health/climate-and-health/_documents/climate-sensitive-hazards-in-florida-final-report.pdf </ref> However, extreme heat may still be a threat to older adults, [[Homelessness|homeless]] populations, and people who spend time outdoors such as workers in industries such as [[Agriculture in the United States|agriculture]] and tourism, as well as tourists themselves.<ref name=":42" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Occupational Safety and Health Administration, U.S. Department of Labor |title=Heat: Overview: Working in Outdoor and Indoor Heat Environments |url=https://www.osha.gov/heat-exposure |access-date=December 18, 2023}}</ref> In summer 2023, [[Orlando, Florida|Orlando]], which contains theme parks such as [[Walt Disney World|Disney World]], saw its first-ever heat warning from the [[National Weather Service]] and saw more than double the number of heat-related distress calls compared to five years prior.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Russon |first=Gabrielle |date=2023-11-27 |title=Disney World visitors felt the heat as medical calls spiked this Summer |url=https://floridapolitics.com/archives/645728-disney-world-visitors-felt-the-heat-as-medical-calls-spiked-this-summer/ |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=[[Florida Politics]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Mosquito-borne diseases ====
[[File:Aedes aegypti on leaf.jpg|alt=A closeup of a black and white Aedes aegypti mosquito on a green leaf|thumb|An ''[[Aedes aegypti]]'' mosquito on a leaf. [[CC BY-SA 4.0]] by Wee Hong]]
Because it is habitable for ''[[Aedes aegypti]]'' mosquitoes, Southern Florida has a high suitability for [[Mosquito-borne disease|mosquito-borne diseases]] like [[Zika fever|Zika]], [[Dengue fever|dengue]], [[chikungunya]] and [[yellow fever]].<ref name=":32" /> Climate change is expected to make much of the Southeastern U.S. more vulnerable to mosquito-borne diseases.<ref name=":32" /> As temperatures increase due to climate change, the mosquito breeding season becomes longer and mosquitoes are able to spread further north. A longer breeding season increases the overall number of mosquitoes and with it, the risk of being bitten.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Florida's mosquitoes can make you sick: Here's how to protect yourself » Emerging Pathogens Institute » University of Florida |url=https://epi.ufl.edu/2024/05/01/floridas-mosquitoes-can-make-you-sick-heres-how-to-protect-yourself/ |access-date=2025-09-09 |language=en|date=May 1, 2024|website=epi.ufl.edu}}</ref> In addition to higher temperatures, precipitation during storms is expected to increase due to climate change. This can cause flooding which would exacerbate mosquito issues by providing more standing water for the insects to breed in.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Miami's Fight Against Mosquito-Borne Diseases |url=https://publichealth.med.miami.edu/news/news-releases/2024/miamis-fight-against-mosquito-borne-diseases/index.html |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=publichealth.med.miami.edu |language=en}}</ref>

=== Wildfires ===
[[File:Fox lake fire (5241798112).jpg|thumb|Fox lake wildfire]]
[[File:Wildfire @ Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge; February 2009.jpg|thumb|Wildfire, [[Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge]], 2009]]
While Florida doesn't make headlines like [[California]] and [[Colorado]], it too is vulnerable to wildfires, which can have impacts on respiratory and cardiovascular health.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Reid |first1=Colleen E. |last2=Brauer |first2=Michael |last3=Johnston |first3=Fay H. |last4=Jerrett |first4=Michael |last5=Balmes |first5=John R. |last6=Elliott |first6=Catherine T. |date=September 1, 2016 |title=Critical Review of Health Impacts of Wildfire Smoke Exposure |journal=Environmental Health Perspectives |language=en |volume=124 |issue=9 |pages=1334–1343 |bibcode=2016EnvHP.124.1334R |doi=10.1289/ehp.1409277 |issn=0091-6765 |pmc=5010409 |pmid=27082891}}</ref> Fire is a natural part of many Florida ecosystems and previous attempts at full scale fire suppression have not been successful.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fire Ecology :: Local History :: Living in Harmony |url=https://wec.ifas.ufl.edu/extension/gc/madera/history/fire.htm |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=wec.ifas.ufl.edu}}</ref> After the 1998 fire that burned 500,000 acres, Florida moved away from fire suppression and implemented regular prescribed burns to prevent such a large accumulation of fuel on forest floors.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-06-26 |title=The 1998 Florida Firestorm and NASA's Kennedy Space Center |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/the-1998-florida-firestorm-and-nasas-kennedy-space-center/ |access-date=2025-09-09 |language=en-US|website=NASA}}</ref> The Florida wildfire season is year round, but peaks during the driest months from April to June.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Services |first=Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer |title=Florida Department of Agriculture & Consumer Services |url=https://www.fdacs.gov/News-Events/Press-Releases/2024-Press-Releases/Commissioner-Wilton-Simpson-Florida-Forest-Service-Highlight-Current-Wildfire-Conditions-Urge-Residents-to-Be-Wildfire-Ready |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=www.fdacs.gov |language=en}}</ref> As temperatures increase and droughts become more common due to climate change, so too does the likelihood of more destructive wild fires. Larger areas are drying out to a greater extent and becoming more susceptible to large, destructive fires, as can be seen in the August 2025 wildfire in the Everglades which consumed 48,000 acres.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-26 |title=Everglades wildfire in Broward fully contained after burning nearly 50,000 acres - CBS Miami |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/miami/news/everglades-broward-fire-that-burned-nearly-50000-acres-fully-contained/ |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Herald |first=Miami |date=2025-08-20 |title=Smell that smoke from the Everglades fire? Climate change making it more common |url=https://www.evergladesfoundation.org/post/smell-that-smoke-from-the-everglades-fire-climate-change-making-it-more-common |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=EF Everglades |language=en}}</ref>

== Mitigation and adaptation ==

=== State climate change policy ===
[[File:Köppen Climate Types Florida.png|thumb|[[Köppen climate classification|Köppen climate types]] of Florida, using 1991–2020 [[Climatological normal|climate normals]].]]
[[File:Krashefski 000384 172797 517878 4578 (36776409046).jpg|thumb|Solar array on parking area rooftop, Broward County]]
The [[Florida Climate Protection Act of 2008]] created the [[Florida Energy and Climate Commission]]. It also urged the [[List of environmental agencies in the United States|Department of Environmental Protection]] to develop a [[greenhouse gas reduction]] strategy. However, the bill was never ratified and The Climate Protection Act was repealed in 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ritchie |first=Bruce |date=2024-06-15 |title=Florida has unraveled climate goals for years. DeSantis struck the latest blow. |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/06/15/ron-desantis-florida-climate-change-00163504 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250702023420/https://www.politico.com/news/2024/06/15/ron-desantis-florida-climate-change-00163504 |archive-date=2025-07-02 |access-date=2025-10-21 |website=POLITICO |language=en}}</ref>

Governor [[Charlie Crist]] signed several executive orders related to climate change upon taking office. These executive orders included tailpipe emission limits for cars sold in Florida, called for reductions in the state's greenhouse gas emissions, and mandated a minimum of 20 percent renewable energy by 2020 for Florida's electric utilities. The Public Service Commission rejected six new coal-fired power plants under Crist.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.georgetownclimate.org/adaptation/state-information/florida/overview.html|title=Overview of Florida's Climate Change Preparations|website=Georgetown Climate Center|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

Governor [[Rick Scott]] "denied the idea of anthropogenic global warming" during his first election in 2010.<ref name=":2" /> Use of the term "climate change" was discouraged during his administration. He also eliminated mandates to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and appointed climate skeptics to posts such as the Public Service Commission.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/florida-republicans-demand-climate-change-solutions/|title=Florida Republicans Demand Climate Change Solutions|last=Bolstad|first=Erika|date=March 15, 2016|website=Scientific American|language=en|access-date=2020-02-15}}</ref> Scott vetoed $750,000 budgeted for pumping water out of Miami Beach, on the grounds that the money didn't provide "a clear statewide return for the investment,"<ref name=":3" /> and did not reply directly when asked if he would support efforts to protect Miami's water supply.<ref name=":8" /> Scott was sued by a group of children aged 10–20 for his positions on climate.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://weather.com/science/environment/news/2018-04-17-florida-kids-governor-rick-scott-climate-change|title=Florida Kids Sue Gov. Rick Scott For Not Doing More to Stop Climate Change|last=Wright|first=Pam|date=2018-04-17|website=The Weather Channel|access-date=2020-02-15|archive-date=2023-04-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230404064338/https://weather.com/science/environment/news/2018-04-17-florida-kids-governor-rick-scott-climate-change}}</ref>

Governor [[Ron DeSantis]] established an Office of Resiliency and Coastal Protection.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|url=https://www.wlrn.org/post/florida-new-governor-speaks-words-climate-change|title=In Florida, A New Governor Speaks The Words, 'Climate Change'|last=Green|first=Amy|date=April 30, 2019|website=www.wlrn.org|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref> DeSantis was noted for actually speaking the word "climate change" in his statement: "This idea of – quote – 'climate change' has become politicized. My environmental policy is just to try to do things that benefit Floridians."<ref name=":9" /> However, DeSantis has not made climate mitigation, renewable energy, or greenhouse gas reduction a policy priority.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://insideclimatenews.org/news/28012019/florida-governor-desantis-environment-directives-sea-level-rise-climate-change-republican|title=In Florida, a New Governor Shifts Gears on Environment, and Maybe Climate Change|last=Bruggers|first=James|date=2019-01-28|website=InsideClimate News|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite web|url=https://www.floridaphoenix.com/2020/01/15/greener-gop-still-stalling-on-clean-energy-and-climate-change-in-fl/|title='Greener' GOP still stalling on clean energy and climate change in FL|last=Cassels|first=Laura|date=2020-01-15|website=Florida Phoenix|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref> In January 2020, DeSantis was given a D grade by the Sierra Club of Florida "for his work on environmental protection and sustainability."<ref name=":10" />

Florida's Republican candidates in local, state, and national office have emphasized risk mitigation and resilience for dealing with climate-related impacts, rather than climate mitigation efforts to prevent climate change.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":10" />

By contrast, South Florida Republicans, such as Miami-Dade County Mayor Carlos Giménez, Representative [[Carlos Curbelo]], and former Representative [[Ileana Ros-Lehtinen]], have said that "man-made climate change is real and needs to be taken seriously."<ref name=":2" />

Florida State Senator [[José Javier Rodríguez (Florida politician)|José Javier Rodriguez]] has attempted to draw attention to the problem of [[tidal flooding|sunny day flooding]] by wearing black rainboots during legislative sessions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://health.wusf.usf.edu/post/florida-s-gop-has-change-heart-about-climate-change|title=Florida's GOP Has A Change Of Heart About Climate Change|date=Oct 21, 2019|website=Health News Florida, WUSF|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

In May 2024, Republican governor [[Ron DeSantis]] signed into law, removal of eight of fifteen references to climate change from state laws, removing [[greenhouse gas emissions]] reduction as a priority for energy policy, banning construction of offshore wind turbines off Florida's coasts, weakening regulations on natural gas pipelines, and preventing cities from banning appliances like gas stoves.<ref name="Grist_20240516">{{cite magazine |last1=Yoder |first1=Kate |title=DeSantis says he's 'restoring sanity by erasing climate change from Florida laws |url=https://grist.org/politics/desantis-signs-florida-law-removing-climate-change/ |magazine=Grist |date=May 16, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240516211108/https://grist.org/politics/desantis-signs-florida-law-removing-climate-change/ |archive-date=May 16, 2024 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Coastal management|Coastal protection]], including [[Beach nourishment|beach renourishment]], has been a focus of state government.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Turner |first=Jim |date=2019-10-15 |title=Florida Republican lawmakers focus on climate change |url=https://www.wptv.com/news/protecting-paradise/florida-republican-lawmakers-focus-on-climate-change |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=WPTV |language=en}}</ref>

=== Public opinion ===
The "Energy Poll", conducted by researchers at the [[University of Texas at Austin]], found that 63% of Floridians in March 2012 believed climate change occurs. The same survey conducted in 2016 saw the number rise to 81%.<ref name=":3" /> An October 2020 survey conducted by [[Florida Atlantic University]] (FAU) found that over two-thirds of Florida residents expressed concerns about the impact of climate change on the state's future.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |last=Ritchie |first=Bruce |date=January 23, 2020 |title=As Trump heads to Doral, Florida Republicans send a message on climate change |url=https://politi.co/2tKkrKg |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=Politico |language=en}}</ref> In 2023, the FAU's "Florida Climate Resilience Survey" found that 65% of respondents, including 49% of Republicans, believe that climate change is predominantly the result of human activity.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Perry |first=Mitch |date=2023-05-11 |title=Poll: More Florida Republicans accept that human actions cause climate change |url=https://floridaphoenix.com/2023/05/11/poll-more-florida-republicans-accept-that-human-actions-cause-climate-change/ |access-date=2023-11-21 |website=Florida Phoenix |language=en-US}}</ref> 

As of March 2025, the FAU survey found that 88% of Floridians believe climate change is happening, with 55% believing it to be attributable to human activities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=March 2025 Results : Florida Atlantic University - Center for Environmental Studies |url=https://www.ces.fau.edu/ces-bepi/march-2025.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250914105403/https://www.ces.fau.edu/ces-bepi/march-2025.php |archive-date=2025-09-14 |access-date=2025-10-20 |website=www.ces.fau.edu}}</ref> However, the state remains politically divided, with 74% of [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] and 40% of [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] agreeing with the [[Scientific consensus on climate change|scientific consensus]] that climate change is anthropogenic.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fins |first=Antonio |date=2024-05-16 |title=FAU survey finds political, generational differences on human impact of climate change |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/politics/2024/05/16/fau-survey-shows-90-of-floridians-believe-states-climate-is-changing/73683948007/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251020150532/https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/politics/2024/05/16/fau-survey-shows-90-of-floridians-believe-states-climate-is-changing/73683948007/ |archive-date=2025-10-20 |access-date=2025-10-20 |website=The Palm Beach Post |language=en-US}}</ref> 

=== Education ===
[[File:Flickr - DVIDSHUB - National Guardsmen Evacuate Florida Residents in Wake of Fay.jpg|thumb|Flooding evacuation, [[Melbourne, Florida|Melbourne]]]]
Florida's [[climate change education]] standard states: "Identify, analyze, and relate the internal (earth system) and external (astronomical) conditions that contribute to global climate change."  The standard falls short of the [[Next Generation Science Standards]], which have been adopted by 20 states and the District of Columbia. The human-caused elements of climate change and role of human activity are treated "as an aside," according to a leader with the [[Alliance for Climate Education]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bradenton.com/news/local/education/article236866263.html#storylink=cpy|title=Climate change puts Florida at risk. Public schools not teaching it the right way, experts say|last=Sabella|first=Giuseppe|date=November 2, 2019|website=Bradenton Herald|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

=== Local climate mitigation efforts ===
The city of [[Miami Beach, Florida|Miami Beach]] is spending $500M on elevated roadways, seawalls, and pumping systems, as part of its Sea Level Rise Strategy.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":172">{{Cite web |last=Ruggeri |first=Amanda |date=3 April 2017 |title=Miami's fight against rising seas |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20170403-miamis-fight-against-sea-level-rise |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250804063454/https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20170403-miamis-fight-against-sea-level-rise |archive-date=August 4, 2025 |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=Sea Level Rise Strategy |url=https://www8.miamidade.gov/global/economy/resilience-sea-level-rise-strategy.page |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230404064338/https://www8.miamidade.gov/global/economy/resilience-sea-level-rise-strategy.page |archive-date=2023-04-04 |access-date=2020-02-17 |website=Miami Dade County Office of Resilience}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Ariza |first=Mario Alejandro |title=Disposable city: Miami's future on the shores of climate catastrophe |date=2020 |publisher=[[Type Media Center|Bold Type Books]] |isbn=978-1-5417-8846-6 |edition=First |location=New York, NY |page=4 |oclc=1123233347}}</ref> GIS mapping of areas subject to flooding during high tides, storm surges, and major storm events is available.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Miami-Dade County Flood Zones GIS Tool |url=https://mdc.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=685a1c5e03c947d9a786df7b4ddb79d3}}</ref>

In [[Key Largo]] and [[Big Pine Key]], $517,000 is being spent to raise one mile of roads, as a "Sea Level Rise Pilot Project".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Filosa |first=Gwen |date=November 27, 2018 |title=The latest battle against sea level rise? Raising one mile of road |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/community/florida-keys/article221958885.html |access-date=2020-02-15 |website=[[Miami Herald]]}}</ref>

Miami-Dade County has built [[seawall]]s,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2019/03/24/706295320/adapting-to-climate-change-in-miami|title=Adapting To Climate Change In Miami|last=Garcia-Navarro|first=Lulu|date=March 24, 2019|website=NPR.org|language=en|access-date=2020-02-26}}</ref> implemented an Urban {{CO2}} Reduction Plan,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.miamidade.gov/environment/co2-reduction.asp|title=Urban {{CO2}} Reduction Plan|last=Miami-Dade County - Environment|date=2020|website=www.miamidade.gov|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref> and participates in the South Florida Regional Climate Compact.<ref name=":14" /> Miami Mayor Francis Suarez has pledged to make the city [[Carbon neutrality|carbon neutral]] by 2050.<ref name=":11" />

Pensacola has formed a Climate Mitigation and Adaptation Task Force which meets monthly.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cityofpensacola.com/2900/Climate-Mitigation-and-Adaptation-Task-F|title=Climate Mitigation and Adaptation Task Force|website=City of Pensacola, Florida Official Website|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pnj.com/story/news/2017/01/16/city-task-force-tackling-climate-change/96538896/|title=City task force tackling climate change|last=Robinson|first=Kevin|date=January 17, 2017|website=Pensacola News Journal|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pnj.com/story/news/politics/2017/06/02/pensacola-climate-change-task-force-trump-paris-accord/362602001/|title=Pensacola climate change task force meets to curb local global warming impact|last=Baucum|first=Joseph|date=June 1, 2017|website=Pensacola News Journal|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

[[Orlando, Florida|Orlando]] Mayor Buddy Dyer was "one of the nation's first mayors to sign onto the Climate Mayors' Pledge." Orlando plans to convert its city vehicle fleet to alternative fuels by 2030.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.orlandoweekly.com/orlando/so-why-do-so-many-of-its-residents-keep-voting-for-lawmakers-opposed-to-climate-policy/Content?oid=23804474|title=Florida will bear the brunt of climate change. Why do we keep voting for lawmakers without a plan?|last=Peters|first=Xander|website=Orlando Weekly|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

Sarasota's Climate Adaption and Mitigation Center has been funded to work on "a curated database of peer-reviewed science to inform decision-making in academia, government and the private sector."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sarasotamagazine.com/news-and-profiles/2020/01/climate-adaption-and-mitigation-center-receives-tax-exempt-status|title=Climate Adaption and Mitigation Center Receives Tax-Exempt Status|website=Sarasota Magazine|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

In North Central Florida, where [[climate change denial]] is stronger, climate change efforts were starting to be visible in 2020 in Gainesville, Alachua County, St. Augustine and Jacksonville.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gainesville.com/opinion/20200117/chris-bird-living-with-climate-change-in-north-central-florida|title=Chris Bird: Living with climate change in North Central Florida|last=Bird|first=Chris|date=January 17, 2020|website=Gainesville Sun|language=en|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

In Broward County's Oakland Park, drainage installed with a [[Federal Emergency Management Agency]] (FEMA) Hazard Mitigation Grant prevented damage to 400 homes during Hurricane Irma.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fema.gov/news-release/2018/03/14/florida-mitigation-projects-prove-successful|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180417212632/https://www.fema.gov/news-release/2018/03/14/florida-mitigation-projects-prove-successful|archive-date=April 17, 2018|title=Florida Mitigation Projects Prove Successful|date=March 14, 2018|website=FEMA.gov|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

[[Coral Gables, Florida|Coral Gables]] Mayor Jim Cason has said, "We're working hard to create solutions until we inevitably must [[Managed retreat|retreat]]."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://climate.miami.edu/politics-of-climate-change/the-city-beautiful-confronts-climate-change/|title=The City Beautiful Confronts Climate Change {{!}} Climate Change - a special report from the University of Miami|last=Castillo|first=Jessica M|date=2020|website=University of Miami|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-26}}</ref>

==== Climate journalism ====
The [[Sun-Sentinel|South Florida Sun Sentinel]], [[Miami Herald]] and [[Palm Beach Post]], along with [[WLRN-TV|WLRN]] [[WLRN-FM|Public Media]], have formed a collaboration to cover climate change issues. The collaboration provides news and feature coverage, and a website created by its editorial boards titled: ''The Invading Sea, Florida and the Climate Crisis''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theinvadingsea.com/about-us/|title=About Us|date=2019|website=The Invading Sea|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.niemanlab.org/2019/06/its-just-become-daily-news-six-florida-newsrooms-are-teaming-up-to-cover-climate-change/|title="It's just become daily news": Six Florida newsrooms are teaming up to cover climate change|website=Nieman Lab|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

==== Southeast Florida Regional Climate Compact ====
The [[Southeast Florida Regional Climate Compact]] is a partnership between Broward, Miami-Dade, Monroe, and Palm Beach counties. Formed in 2009, its goal is "to work collaboratively to reduce regional greenhouse gas emissions, implement adaptation strategies, and build climate resilience".<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |title=Southeast Florida Regional Climate Compact |url=https://southeastfloridaclimatecompact.org/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200221081627/https://southeastfloridaclimatecompact.org/ |archive-date=February 21, 2020 |access-date=2020-02-16 |website=Southeast Florida Regional Climate Compact |language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Integrative Collaborative on Climate and Energy (ICCE) ====
The Florida Center for Environmental Studies at [[Florida Atlantic University]] has formed an Integrative Collaborative on Climate and Energy (ICCE) focused on issues of climate adaptation in Florida's urban and natural systems. Partners include the Florida Climate Initiative, the University of South Florida, and various government agencies.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ces.fau.edu/climate_change/|title=CES - Climate Change in South Florida|website=www.ces.fau.edu|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

==== Miami-Dade County Climate Programs ====
Miami has been described as "ground zero" for climate change and sea level rise."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://climate.miami.edu/|title=Climate Change - a special report from the University of Miami|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref> The Miami-Dade County Office of Resilience has implemented climate programs and a Climate Action Plan,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www8.miamidade.gov/global/economy/resilience/county-climate-programs.page|title=Miami-Dade County Climate Programs|website=www8.miamidade.gov|access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.miamidade.gov/greenprint/pdf/climate_action_plan.pdf|title=Climate Action Plan|website=Miami Dade County}}</ref> and there is a Sea Level Rise Committee.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Ariza|first=Mario Alejandro|title=Disposable city: Miami's future on the shores of climate catastrophe|date=2020|publisher=[[Type Media Center|Bold Type Books]]|isbn=978-1-5417-8846-6|edition=First|location=New York, NY|pages=255–260|oclc=1123233347}}</ref> Protecting the water supply and the Biscayne Aquifer is a priority.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" />

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change in Japan
======================================================================

{{Short description|Emissions, impacts and responses of Japan related to climate change}}
[[File:Carbon emissions among selected G7 economies and East Asian economies.png|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|300x300px|Japan and other countries' carbon emissions between 2000 and 2023: Japan has reduced its emissions by 22% since 2000.]]
[[Climate change]] is impacting the human population and environment of Japan. In recent years, the country has observed notable changes in its climate patterns, with rising temperatures serving as a prominent indicator of this phenomenon.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |title=CP - Home |url=https://www.climate-of-the-past.net/index.html |access-date=2023-05-16 |website=www.climate-of-the-past.net |language=en}}</ref> The nation experiences a broad range of climates, spanning from the frigid winters of Hokkaido to the subtropical climates of Okinawa.<ref name=":15" /> Changes in temperature patterns have the potential to disrupt ecosystems, impact agricultural productivity, modify water resources, and pose significant challenges to infrastructure and human settlements.<ref name=":15" />

[[Government of Japan|Japanese government]] is increasingly enacting [[Politics of climate change|climate change policy]] to respond. The government has been criticised for lacking a credible plan to get to its pledged net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Japan has a chequered record on climate change |newspaper=The Economist |url=https://www.economist.com/special-report/2021/12/07/japan-has-a-chequered-record-on-climate-change |access-date=2023-05-16 |issn=0013-0613}}</ref> As a signatory of the [[Kyoto Protocol]], and host of the 1997 conference which created it, Japan is under treaty obligations to reduce its carbon dioxide emissions and to take other steps related to curbing climate change.

==Greenhouse gas emissions==
Out of the global GHG emissions, [[Japan]] is responsible for 2.6%. The average rate of {{CO2}} [[Greenhouse gas emissions|emissions]] per person in Japan is almost double the global average.<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |date=2021-10-19 |title=Japan |url=https://www.g20climaterisks.org/japan/ |access-date=2023-05-17 |website=G20 Climate Risk Atlas |language=en-US}}</ref> Emissions have been slightly reduced since 2013 and the net zero emissions are set by 2050.<ref name=":16" /> 
[[File:20210703 Variwide chart of greenhouse gas emissions per capita by country (includes OTHER).svg|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|Japan is one of the largest greenhouse gas emitters, both nationally and per person.<ref name=GHGemissionsByCountry>● Emissions data source: {{cite web |title=Territorial (MtCO<sub>2</sub>) / 1) Emissions / Carbon emissions / Chart View |url=https://globalcarbonatlas.org/emissions/carbon-emissions/ |date=2024 |publisher=Global Carbon Atlas }} ([https://web.archive.org/web/20250113130608/https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/annual-co2-emissions-per-country archive on Our World in Data])<br />● Country population data source: {{cite web |title=Population, total / All Countries and Economies / Most Recent Value (Thousands) |url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?end=2023&most_recent_value_desc=true&start=1960&view=chart |publisher=World Bank |date=2024 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250122171803/https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?end=2023&most_recent_value_desc=true&start=1960&view=chart |archive-date=22 January 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]
Japan has pledged to become carbon neutral by 2050.<ref>{{Cite news|last=McCurry|first=Justin|date=2020-10-26|title=Japan will become carbon neutral by 2050, PM pledges|language=en-GB|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/oct/26/japan-will-become-carbon-neutral-by-2050-pm-pledges|access-date=2020-10-26|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> In 2019 Japan emitted 1212 Mt CO<sub>2eq</sub>,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Japan documents|url=https://unfccc.int/documents?f%5B0%5D=country:940&f%5B1%5D=country:1489|url-status=live|access-date=2021-05-12|website=unfccc.int|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191114070742/https://unfccc.int/documents?f%5B0%5D=country%3A940&f%5B1%5D=country%3A1489 |archive-date=2019-11-14 }}</ref> The per capita {{CO2}} emissions were 9.31 tonnes in 2017<ref>{{Cite web|title=Per capita CO<sub>2</sub> emissions|url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/co-emissions-per-capita|access-date=2021-08-24|website=Our World in Data}}</ref> and was the 5th largest [[List of countries by carbon dioxide emissions|producer of carbon emissions]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Annual CO<sub>2</sub> emissions|url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/annual-co2-emissions-per-country|access-date=2021-03-12|website=Our World in Data}}</ref> {{As of|2019}} [[greenhouse gas emissions]] by Japan are over 2% of the annual world total,<ref>{{Cite news|date=2021-05-07|title=Report: China emissions exceed all developed nations combined|language=en-GB|work=BBC can China and Japan quit the coal?|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/climate-change-carbon-dioxide-emissions-surge-china-japan-coal-biden/|access-date=2021-05-12|website=www.cbsnews.com|language=en-US}}</ref> [[Coal-fired power Calculations in 2021 show that to give the world a 50% chance of avoiding a temperature rise of 2 degrees or more, Japan should increase its climate commitments by 49%.<ref name=":17">{{Cite journal |last1=R. Liu |first1=Peiran |last2=E. Raftery |first2=Adrian |date=9 February 2021 |title=Country-based rate of emissions reductions should increase by 80% beyond nationally determined contributions to meet the 2 °C target |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |volume=2 |issue=1 |page=29 |bibcode=2021ComEE...2...29L |doi=10.1038/s43247-021-00097-8 |pmc=8064561 |pmid=33899003 |doi-access=free}}</ref> For a 95% chance, it should increase the commitments by 151%. For a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 degrees, Japan should increase its commitments by 229%.<ref name=":17" />{{rp|Table 1}} A March 2021 analysis by [[Climate Action Tracker]] said that Japan should reduce greenhouse gas emissions so that by 2030 the emissions are 60% below 2013 levels; this would support a goal of limiting warming to 1.5&nbsp;°C.<ref>{{Cite web|date=4 March 2021|title=1.5°C-consistent benchmarks for enhancing Japan's 2030 climate target {{!}} Climate Action Tracker|url=https://climateactiontracker.org/publications/1o5C-consistent-benchmarks-for-enhancing-Japans-2030-climate-target/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-03-10|website=climateactiontracker.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304225937/https://climateactiontracker.org/publications/1o5C-consistent-benchmarks-for-enhancing-Japans-2030-climate-target/ |archive-date=2021-03-04 }}</ref>
