|}Furthermore, Japan has witnessed a decrease in its annual emissions, with a 5.3% reduction in industrial emissions due to decreased steel production. Residential emissions fell by 1.4%, while vehicle emissions rose by 3.9%. Despite these changes, Japan still heavily relies on fossil fuels, which constitute about 70% of its power generation. In terms of renewable energy, Japan aims for 10 gigawatts of offshore wind capacity by 2030 but is currently projected to only reach 4.4 gigawatts.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-04-11 |title=Japan's Annual Emissions Drop as Industrial Pollution Shrinks |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-04-11/japan-s-annual-emissions-drop-as-industrial-pollution-shrinks |access-date=2024-04-13 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref>

On 18 February 2025, Japan has set new targets to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 60% by 2035 and 73% by 2040, while aiming for renewables to provide 50% of its electricity by 2040. The revised energy and industrial policies focus on decarbonization, energy security, and economic growth, despite challenges in offshore wind energy and nuclear power.<ref>{{cite news|last=Obayashi|first=Yuka|title=Japan approves new climate, energy and industry policies through 2040|date=17 February 2025|work=Reuters|url= https://www.reuters.com/world/japan/japan-approves-new-climate-energy-industry-policies-through-2040-2025-02-17/|access-date=18 February 2025}}</ref>

=== Transportation ===
The transportation sector accounts for 20% out of the total emission of Japan.<ref name=":1">Kii, M., Isikawa, R., & Komeani, Y. (2023). Toward a carbon neutral urban transportation system in Japan. ''Urban Forestry & Urban Greening,'' Volume 62, 2021, 127171</ref> Within the transportation sector, it is mainly oil that is being used.<ref name=":16" /> This particular sector currently relies on [[fossil fuel]]s and is projected to continue doing so for a while.<ref name=":1" /> One challenge to decarbonize the transportation sector is the cost of such technologies required for the transformation.<ref name=":1" /> Emissions have been decreasing within the sector since 2001 due to fuel efficiency of cars and population decline.<ref name=":1" />

=== Energy supply and fossil fuels ===
The energy supply is mainly made out of fossil fuels, reaching up to 88% of the total primary energy supply in 2019. The fossil fuels are composed of a combination of oil (38%), coal (27%) and gas (23%).<ref name=":16" /> In 2012, the [[Fukushima nuclear accident|Fukushima disaster]] led to an increase in Japan's dependence on fossil fuels. The country's energy supply has been impacted by the phasing out of [[nuclear power]],<ref name=":16" /> with only 4% of the supply coming from nuclear sources in 2019 compared to 15% in 2010.<ref name=":16" /> Fossil fuel is mainly imported and the high dependence on the [[Non-renewable resource|non-renewable]] sources is making it difficult to reach a carbon-neutral society.<ref name=":16" /> Out of Japan's total primary energy supply, only 8% is made out of renewable sources; however, this has been doubled since 1990.<ref name=":16" />

=== Industrial emissions ===
Although Japan is a developed country, it still has a large presence of energy-intensive industries (such as the production of steel and cement) compared to other developed economies.<ref name=":7" /> The country has a high energy consumption that can be compared to emerging countries like China, India, and Brazil.<ref name=":7">Ju, Y., Sugiyama, M., Kato, E. et al. (2021). Industrial decarbonization under Japan's national mitigation scenarios: a multi-model analysis. ''Sustain Sci'' 16, pp. 411 – pp. 427</ref> In Japan, the overall industrial emissions domestically account for approximately 967.4 million tons of {{CO2}} annually.<ref name=":8" /> Among the industries the iron and steel sector has the highest emission rate, accounting for around 111.9 million tons of {{CO2}}.<ref name=":8">Statista. 2020. Carbon dioxide emissions from the manufacturing sector in Japan in 2020, by industry. Available at, https://www.statista.com/statistics/1305632/japan-carbon-dioxide-emissions-manufacturing-sector-by-industry Accessed: 2023-04-10</ref>

=== Current Emissions Overview ===
According to data released by the [[Ministry of the Environment (Japan)|Ministry of Environment]], Japan's total greenhouse gas emissions for the fiscal year ending in March 2023 declined by 2.3%, amounting to 1.085 billion metric tons of CO<sub>2</sub> equivalent. This reduction marks a 23% decrease compared to the levels recorded in 2013. Despite this progress, Japan is yet to meet its ambitious target of a 46% reduction by 2030. The primary contributor to this decrease was the industrial sector, which saw a 5.3% drop in emissions, largely due to a decrease in steel production and a corresponding reduction in power demand. In addition, residential emissions decreased by 1.4%. However, not all sectors showed a decline; emissions from the transportation sector, for example, increased by 3.9%.<ref name=":18">{{Cite news |date=2024-04-11 |title=Japan's Annual Emissions Drop as Industrial Pollution Shrinks |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-04-11/japan-s-annual-emissions-drop-as-industrial-pollution-shrinks |access-date=2024-04-12 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref>

On the renewable energy front, Japan has set a target to achieve 10 gigawatts of offshore wind power by 2030. Yet, projections suggest that Japan is on pace to reach only 4.4 gigawatts by the end of the decade, indicating significant challenges ahead in meeting its renewable energy goals.<ref name=":18" />

== Impacts on the natural environment==

=== Temperature and weather changes ===
[[File:Temperature Bar Chart Asia-Japan--1901-2020--2021-07-13.png|thumb|Average annual [[temperature anomaly]] in Japan, 1901 to 2020]]

}}
Climate change has affected Japan drastically. The temperature and rainfall have increased rapidly in the years leading up to 2020. This has resulted in immature rice grains and also oranges that automatically get separated from their skin due to immature growth by inappropriate weather. Many corals in the Japanese seas and oceans have died due to rising sea temperatures and ocean acidification. Tiger mosquitoes, which transmit [[dengue fever]], were found further north than before.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Japan 2030: Tackling climate issues is key to the next decade |url=https://features.japantimes.co.jp/climate-crisis-2030/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200125204252/https://features.japantimes.co.jp/climate-crisis-2030/ |archive-date=2020-01-25 |access-date=2020-11-08 |website=Deep reads from The Japan Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[Earth Simulator]] calculations reveal the daily increase in mean temperature in Japan during the period 2071 to 2100. The temperature will increase by 3.0&nbsp;°C in Scenario B1 and 4.2&nbsp;°C in A1B compared to that of 1971 to 2000. Similarly, the daily maximum temperature in Japan will increase by 3.1&nbsp;°C in B1 and 4.4&nbsp;°C in A1B. The precipitation in summer in Japan will increase steadily due to [[global warming]] (annual average precipitation will increase by 17% in Scenario B1 and by 19% in Scenario A1B during the period 2071–2100 compared to that of 1971–2000).<ref>[http://www.jamstec.go.jp/frcgc/eng/press/040916/ The latest global warming projection by using the Earth Simulator has been completed] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090226185921/http://www.jamstec.go.jp/frcgc/eng/press/040916/|date=2009-02-26}}, Center for Climate System Research, [[University of Tokyo]]</ref>

Considering the projections in temperature for Japan, depending on the scenario there are different outcomes. In a worst-case scenario for 2100, where [[Greenhouse gas|GHG]] emissions are not declining, an increase of almost 6&nbsp;°C is expected during winter and almost 5&nbsp;°C for summer in comparison to the annual in 1900.<ref name=":9" /> If  a drastic reduction in emissions occurs then the increases will be almost 2&nbsp;°C and 1,5&nbsp;°C respectively by 2100.<ref name=":9">BBC Visual and Data Journalism team (2019) ''How much warmer is your city? - BBC News'', ''News''. Available at: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/resources/idt-985b9374-596e-4ae6-aa04-7fbcae4cb7ee Accessed: 2023-04-10</ref>

==== Precipitation ====
Precipitation in Japan varies between 1000mm to 2,500mm annually, causing various events depending on the year, either flooding or lack of water availability for sectors such as agriculture.<ref name=":16" /> It is also more complex to predict in any case scenario the effects of climate change, easily, for precipitation.<ref name=":16" /> Extreme rainfall events are more frequent the total annual precipitation seems to decrease.<ref name=":16" />

==== Extreme weather events ====
[[File:The wind whips through palm trees as Typhoon Chaba blows ashore at U.S. Marine Corps Base Smedley D. Butler, Okinawa, Japan, Oct. 28, 2010 101028-M-VG363-103.jpg|thumb|Typhoon, Okinawa, Japan 2010]]
Climate change will not only affect parameters such as temperature and precipitation.<ref name=":16" /> Extreme events seem to have increased as well such as heat waves, droughts, tsunamis, storm surges, and typhoons.<ref name=":16" /> An increased frequency and prolonged duration of such natural disasters are likely to impact upon the energy, agricultural and tourism sector of Japan.<ref name=":16" />

==== Sea level rise ====
[[Global warming (disambiguation)|Global warming]] has led to an increase in worldwide sea level rise due to the melting to glaciers and ice sheets.<ref name=":10" />

Southern and eastern coastal parts of Japan, have a high probability to be affected by phenomena such as tsunamis and storms.<ref name=":10">Lindsey, R. (2022) ''Climate Change: Global Sea Level | NOAA Climate.gov''. Available at: {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20190810001842/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-global-sea-level}} Accessed: 2023-04-26</ref>

=== Water resources ===
Water resources are highly dependent on the country's rates of precipitation and [[evapotranspiration]].<ref name=":11" /> Temperature projections in Japan are increasingly affecting both water cycle processes, hurting the availability of water resources for Japan.<ref name=":11">Kim, S., Tachikawa, Y., Nakakita, E., & Takara, K. (2009). Climate change impact on water resources management in the Tone River Basin, Japan. ''Kyoto University Disaster Prevention Research Institute Annual Report.'' no. ''52''B, pp. 587-606</ref> The effect of climate change upon water availability in Japan includes:

* Less snow and ice coverage eventually will mean an increase in droughts. Japan is a country that has experienced droughts before. In areas depending on the snow melting for water availability, a decrease in river discharges is expected.<ref name=":16" />
* Runoffs which are expected based on low and medium emission scenarios to be increased, causing soil erosion, transport of pollutants, and flood risks.<ref name=":16" />
* Alteration in groundwater storage, affects its infrastructure, causing [[contamination]], and even increasing salination due to sea level rise.<ref name=":16" />

A decrease in water resources could potentially cause problems for Japanese sectors like [[Agriculture, forestry, and fishing in Japan|agriculture]] which will have to find different cultivation methods to manage water waste, especially in the scenario of severe droughts.<ref name=":16" />

=== Ecosystems ===
Changes in temperature, precipitation patterns and sea level rise are some potential effects of climate change, which are leading to changes in the distribution and abundance of plant and animal species.<ref name=":16" /> Listed below, are ecosystems that will potentially get affected by climate change in Japan:

* Changes in species distribution: As temperatures increase, species are shifting their ranges to higher latitudes or elevations in search of cooler conditions.<ref name=":2" /> This can disrupt the balance of ecosystems and lead to the loss of species that are unable to adapt.<ref name=":2">Ogawa-Onishi, Y. and Berry, P.M. (2013) 'Ecological impacts of climate change in Japan: The importance of integrating local and international publications', ''Biological Conservation'', 157, pp. 361–371. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2012.06.024</ref>
* Changes in [[phenology]]: Climate change is causing shifts in the timing of seasonal events such as flowering, migration, and hibernation.<ref name=":2" /> These changes can affect the timing of interactions between species, such as pollination or predator-prey relationships.<ref name=":2" />
* Changes in forest ecosystems: Climate change is leading to changes in the growth, productivity, and composition of forests in Japan, depending on the tree species.<ref name=":12" /> For example, primeval forest ecosystems are already affected because of climate change.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Hiura |first1=Tsutom |last2=Go |first2=Sato |last3=Iijima |first3=Hayato |date=2019-10-01 |title=Long-term forest dynamics in response to climate change in northern mixed forests in Japan: A 38-year individual-based approach |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378112719304785 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |language=en |volume=449 |article-number=117469 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2019.117469 |issn=0378-1127|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Changes in temperature and precipitation patterns can affect the timing and intensity of forest fires which eventually could lead to a loss of biodiversity and an increase in emissions.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2021-10-19 |title=Japan |url=https://www.g20climaterisks.org/japan/ |access-date=2023-04-29 |website=G20 Climate Risk Atlas |language=en-US}}</ref>
* Impacts on marine ecosystems: Rising [[Sea surface temperature|sea temperatures]] and ocean acidification are affecting marine ecosystems in Japan, leading to changes in the distribution and abundance of species and altering food webs.<ref name=":13" /> This can have an impact on the fishing industry, which is an important source of livelihood for Japanese communities.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Komatsu |first1=Masayuki |last2=Nakamura |first2=Tomoko |date=2021-10-01 |title=Ecosystem management for protection of Japanese ocean and fishery resources |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0308597X21002931 |journal=Marine Policy |language=en |volume=132 |article-number=104682 |doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2021.104682 |issn=0308-597X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Overall, climate change is having significant impacts on Japan's ecosystems, and these impacts are likely to continue and even accelerate in the future.<ref name=":16" /> Japan must take steps to mitigate and adapt to these impacts to protect its biodiversity and the services that ecosystems provide.<ref name=":16" />

=== Biodiversity ===
Japan is a biodiverse region with over 90,000 recognized species, of which more than 30% of amphibians, reptiles, and freshwater and marine species, and more than 20% of mammals and plants are threatened with extinction.<ref name=":2" /> Ecological changes are increasingly reported, and climate change is recognized as a major threat to biodiversity.<ref name=":2" /> Phenological and distributional records show that ecological changes are occurring in response to climate change in Japan.<ref name=":2" />

On average, the phenology of numerous animal species has been delayed, leading to shifts in species interactions.<ref name=":2" /> Rapid range expansions have been observed for insects and corals, while future projections indicate rapid shifts of plants toward higher elevations and significant losses of climatically suitable areas for high-altitude species.<ref name=":2" /> The impacts of climate change on Japanese species are not always consistent with the observations and projections previously reported in other regions.<ref name=":2" /> There is a need for further investigations in other less-known regions to improve understanding of regional impacts, which can be facilitated by utilizing locally available data and publications, especially in non-English speaking countries.<ref name=":2" />

=== Coral reefs ===
[[File:ISS005-E-10686 Sekisei Lagoon.jpg|thumb|Sekisei Lagoon in [[Okinawa Prefecture|Okinawa]] has suffered [[coral bleaching]].]]
The warming of the world's oceans over the past few decades has had a significant impact on coastal ecosystems, particularly on coral reefs found in tropical and subtropical regions.<ref name=":3" /> The potential future outcome of global warming in Sekisei Lagoon could lead to extreme heating and mass [[Coral bleaching|bleaching]], which would have synergistic effects with local stressors.<ref name=":3">Sato, M. ''et al.'' (2020) 'Changes in the potential stocks of coral reef ecosystem services following coral bleaching in Sekisei Lagoon, southern Japan: implications for the future under global warming', ''Sustainability Science'', 15(3), pp. 863–883. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11625-019-00778-6</ref>

In 2015–2016, [[coral bleaching]] occurred on a large scale due to elevated sea temperatures, and the Ryukyu Islands' coral reefs experienced extreme thermal stress and extensive bleaching in the summer of 2016.<ref name=":3" /> This bleaching affected about 90% of the coral in Sekisei Lagoon.<ref name=":3" /> Analysis indicated that the decline in [[corallivore]]s and [[herbivore]]s' density matched the decrease in coral cover after mass bleaching, while changes in species richness were not correlated with coral cover change.<ref name=":3" /> Short-term declines in corallivores were common in the [[Great Barrier Reef]] after the 2016 mass bleaching, and at Ishigaki Island and other sites during the 1998 bleaching event.<ref name=":3" /> The response of herbivores varied from place to place. All potential stocks, including fisheries production, aquarium fish production, recreational diving, and seaweed control by herbivores, decreased following the bleaching.<ref name=":3" /> In January 2017 the Japanese environment ministry said that 70% of the Sekisei lagoon in Okinawa, Japan's biggest coral reef, had been killed by coral bleaching.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McCurry |first=Justin |date=2017-01-12 |title=Almost 75% of Japan's biggest coral reef has died from bleaching, says report |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/jan/12/almost-75-of-japans-biggest-coral-reef-has-died-from-bleaching-says-report |access-date=2023-05-16 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

These findings suggest that severe bleaching and extreme heating were the main causes of the loss of fish diversity and associated potential stocks of [[ecosystem service]]s in Sekisei Lagoon.<ref name=":3" />

== Impacts on people ==
Climate change is expected to have an impact on various sectors of Japan's population. In the economic sector, it will affect agriculture, [[urbanization]], and energy, while in the health sector, it will affect people in terms of [[Mortality rate|mortality]] and increased exposure to heatwaves, among other impacts

=== Agriculture ===
Changing climatic conditions, with increasing temperature trends, decreasing rainfall and intensifying heat waves, droughts and other external phenomena, affect food production.<ref name=":16" /> These conditions tend to decrease crop yields and quality.<ref name=":16" /> Responses to the increase in temperature may be directed to the displacement of crop zones to higher elevations where ideal climatic conditions for growth can be found.<ref name=":16" /> With the increase in temperature, there may be changes in the length of the vegetative period and the early appearance of phenological phases.<ref name=":16" />

Studies have shown that climate change is already having a significant impact on rice agriculture with the increase of extreme events such as heat or dry spells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hasegawa |first1=T. |last2=Kuwagata |first2=T. |last3=Nishimori |first3=M. |last4=Ishigooka |first4=M. |last5=Murakami |first5=M. |last6=Yoshimoto |first6=M. |last7=Matsuzaki |first7=H. |date=2009 |title=Recent warming trends and rice growth and yield in Japan. In MARCO Symposium on Crop Production under Heat Stress: Monitoring, Impact Assessment and Adaptation. |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/267961860 |journal=National Institute for Agro-Environmental Studies, Tsukuba, Japan}}</ref> These changes represent a serious concern for growers and may become a source of the vulnerability of the crop production system and pose a threat to national food security.<ref>Ishigooka, Y., Nishimori, M., Kuwagata, T., & Hasegawa, T. (2019). Impact of Climate Change on Rice Productivity and Adaptation Strategy in Japan. ''Climate Smart Agriculture for the Small-Scale Farmers in the Asian and Pacific Region'', vol 177</ref> It has been shown that there is a direct relationship between rice production and temperature, when the degree of climate change is large, production decreases.<ref>Matsumoto, K., & Takagi, M. (2017). Climate Change Impact and Adaptation on Rice Production in Japan. ''Environmental Science'', vol ''30, no.'' 6, pp. 346–356</ref> Yield reductions have been reported in specific areas or in extremely hot years.<ref>.Ishigooka, Y., Fukui, S., Hasegawa, T., Kuwagata, T., Nishimori, M., & Kondo, M. (2017). Large-scale evaluation of the effects of adaptation to climate change by shifting transplanting date on rice production and quality in Japan. ''Journal of Agricultural Meteorology'', ''73''(4), 156-173</ref>

Irrigation demand could be increased by higher temperatures due to higher plant evapotranspiration.<ref name=":16" /> The expansion of irrigated areas could become a threat to water resources, in terms of quantity and quality, if demand and cereal production increase.<ref name=":16" />

=== Urbanization ===
Japan is one of the most urbanized countries in the world, with 91.8% of its population concentrated in urban areas by 2020.<ref name=":4" /> This trend will continue and increase.<ref name=":4" /> By 2050 the urbanization rate is expected to be almost 95%.<ref name=":4">Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) (2019), Population Division. United Nations, 2018 Revision of World Urbanization Prospects</ref>

The elderly are especially vulnerable to the impacts of heat waves and according to data from the [[Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change]],<ref name=":16" /> by 2035, approximately 38% of the population will be over the age of 65. High levels of air pollution have been found to increase the effects of urban heat.<ref name=":16" /> In 2017, nearly 77% of the total population was exposed to air pollution levels above [[World Health Organization|WHO]] thresholds.<ref name=":0" />

=== Coastal flooding ===
According to the Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change,<ref name=":16" /> due to its geography, high rates of soil sealing and dense urbanization along the Japanese coastline, the country is vulnerable to extreme rainfall and coastal flooding, particularly on the more populated island of [[Honshu]].<ref name=":16" /> Japan is subject to the regular arrival of typhoons.<ref name=":16" />

In 2018, torrential rains caused flash floods and landslides, resulting in more than 200 deaths the evacuation of 2.3 million people and more than US$7 billion in damages.<ref>Japanese Red Cross Society (JRC) (2018). Japan Floods and Landslides 2018. Available at: https://www.jrc.or.jp/english/relief/180719_005356.html Accessed: 2023-04-28</ref> The Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change refers, that rising sea levels, wave heights and the frequency of typhoons are expected to increase damage to human settlements.<ref name=":16" /> The risk of flooding will increase in the future, with the depth of flooding in [[Tokyo]] increasing by 170% by 2050.<ref name=":16" /> This would result in damages to real estate and infrastructure of 220% to 240%.<ref name=":16" />

=== Energy ===
According to the Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change,<ref name=":16" /> the Japanese energy system has been significantly impacted by severe flooding resulting from heavy precipitation and typhoons.<ref name=":16" /> In September and October 2020, the [[Typhoon Faxai|Faxai]] and Hagibis typhoons caused power outages that affected 10 million households in Japan.<ref name=":16" /> Due to the faster-than-global-average temperature increases and the rising frequency of heat waves, the demand for cooling has been increasing in the country.<ref name=":16" />

The trend for heating needs is somewhat opposite to that of cooling needs.<ref name=":16" /> There will be significant decreases in heating needs across the country, with the largest decrease in [[Hokkaido]] and a moderate decrease in the southern islands.<ref name=":16" /> On the other hand, cooling needs will increase considerably in the southern islands of [[Shikoku]] and [[Kyushu]], while only a slight increase is expected in Hokkaido and elevated areas of [[Honshu]].<ref name=":16" />

=== Health ===
The climate and weather patterns in Japan have undergone changes that have led to an increase in mean temperature.<ref name=":4" /> As a result, vulnerable populations such as the elderly are at high risk due to the intensity of heat waves and heat stress.<ref name=":5" /> The rise in temperatures is anticipated to enable the transmission of diseases throughout Japan, including vector-borne illnesses like [[Dengue virus|dengue]], which tend to thrive in warmer climates.<ref name=":14" />

=== Heatwaves and heat stress ===
Mortality and [[morbidity]] would increase in the country and may even double in eastern and northern Japan due to higher average temperatures and an increase in the frequency and duration of heat waves.<ref name=":4" />  

Japan is experiencing an increasing trend in deaths from heat-related illnesses.<ref name=":4" /> Between 1968 and 1994, 2,326 deaths from heat stroke were recorded, 589 of them in 1994 alone, when a severe heat wave caused temperatures to exceed 38&nbsp;°C.<ref name=":4" /> In the abnormally hot summer of 2018, there were 95,137 emergency patients with heat stroke symptoms of which 160 died, 50% were over 65 years of age.<ref name=":5" /> That trend could continue to increase in the absence of adaptation measures to address climate change.<ref name=":5">Nakamura, S., Kusaka, H., Sato, R., & Sato, T. (2022). Heatstroke Risk Projection in Japan under Current and Near Future Climates. ''Journal of the Meteorological Society of Japan.Ser. II'', ''100''(4), 597-615</ref>

=== Labor ===
The impact of global warming is twofold as it affects both labor supply and productivity.<ref name=":6" /> As climate change progresses, a reduction in both labor supply and productivity is expected to occur in most regions of the world, particularly in tropical areas.<ref name=":6">Dasgupta, S., van Maanen, N., Gosling, S. N., Piontek, F., Otto, C., & Schleussner, C. F. (2021). Effects of climate change on combined labour productivity and supply: an empirical, multi-model study. ''The Lancet Planetary Health'', vol. ''5, no.'' 7, pp.455-465</ref> According to the study by Dasgupta et al. (2021),<ref name=":6" /> under a 3.0&nbsp;°C warming scenario, it is projected that future climate change will lead to a reduction of 18 percentage points in global total labor for low-exposure sectors and a reduction of 24.8 percentage points for high-exposure sectors. In Japan, under a low emissions scenario, the total labor force is estimated to decrease by 0.88%, whereas, under a medium emissions scenario, it is expected to decline by 2.2%.<ref name=":6" />

=== Disease ===
The effects of climate change are expected to widen the geographic range and environmental conditions suitable for various vector-borne infectious diseases, including dengue.<ref name=":14" /> The likelihood of dengue transmission is amplified by rising temperatures, as the development and proliferation of mosquitoes are substantially impacted by factors such as temperature, precipitation, and humidity.<ref name=":14">Ryan, S. J., Carlson, C. J., Mordecai, E. A., & Johnson, L. R. (2019). Global expansion and redistribution of Aedes-borne virus transmission risk with climate change. ''PLoS neglected tropical diseases'', ''13''(3), e0007213</ref> The risks associated with transmission suitability due to climate change have intensified over time, and if the planet continues to warm, more than 1.3 billion individuals could face temperatures conducive to Zika transmission by the year 2050.<ref name=":16" />

The dengue outbreak that occurred in Japan in 2014 suggests that the environmental conditions necessary for its transmission may be increasing.<ref>Quam, M. B., Sessions, O., Kamaraj, U. S., Rocklöv, J., & Wilder-Smith, A. (2016). Dissecting Japan's dengue outbreak in 2014. ''The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene'', ''94''(2), 409</ref> The [[Aedes albopictus|Asian tiger mosquito]], which has adapted well to urban environments, is a significant factor in these changing dynamics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate change brings more risk of diseases from mosquitoes {{!}} The Asahi Shimbun: Breaking News, Japan News and Analysis |url=https://www.asahi.com/ajw/articles/13730306 |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=The Asahi Shimbun |language=en}}</ref> According to the CMCC (2022),<ref name=":16" /> if emissions continue at a moderate level, 84.7% of the population could face transmission-suitable mean temperatures for dengue by 2050, and under a high emissions scenario, 81.8% could be at risk. In the case of Zika, 80.7% of the population could be at risk by 2050 under a medium emissions scenario, while 82.7% could be at risk under a high emissions scenario.<ref name=":16" />

Japan was previously affected by [[malaria]], and although it is no longer considered endemic, the mosquitoes responsible for its transmission still exist.<ref>Macnee, R., Tokai, A., & Kim, O. Y. (2016). A Comparative Analysis of Malaria Risk in Japan and the Republic of Korea: Current Trends and Future Risk in the Context of Climate Change. Journal of the Japan Society for Risk Research, 25(4), 189-198</ref> According to projections, by 2050, 40.4% of the Japanese population could be at risk of malaria under a low-emissions scenario, while 42.5% could be at risk under a high-emissions scenario.<ref name=":16" />

Research suggests that a general rise of 10 μg/m3 in daily PM2.5 concentrations in Japan is linked to a 1.3% increase in total non-accidental mortality.<ref>Michikawa, T., Ueda, K., Takami, A., Sugata, S., Yoshino, A., Nitta, H., & Yamazaki, S. (2019). Japanese nationwide study on the association between short-term exposure to particulate matter and mortality. Journal of epidemiology, 29(12), 471-477</ref> Projections indicate that by 2060, there could be 779 deaths per year per million people in Japan due to outdoor air pollution, which is an increase from 468 deaths in 2010.<ref name=":16" />

== Mitigation and adaptation ==

=== Adaptation ===
In terms of [[adaptation]] measures for agriculture and water resources, efforts should focus on the management and renovation of irrigation facilities, as well as anticipating the transplanting of crops in the hottest periods and developing crop varieties resistant to projected increases in temperatures.<ref name=":16" />

In terms of adaptation measures for mortality and morbidity due to higher average temperatures and the increase in the frequency and duration of heat waves, different studies have suggested that lifestyle changes such as the widespread use of air conditioners may represent an important adaptation to the risk of heat stress emergencies.<ref name=":5" />

Japan adopted its National Plan for Adaptation to the Impacts of Climate Change in 2015, which contains specific measures for various sectors such as Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries, Water Resources, Natural Ecosystems, Natural Disasters and Coastal Areas, Human Health, Industrial and Economic Activity, as well as the Life of Citizenry and Urban Life.<ref>Climate Policy Radar (2015), National Plan for Adaptation to the Impacts of Climate Change. Available at: https://climate-laws.org/document/national-plan-for-adaptation-to-the-impacts-of-climate-change_7186 Accessed at: 2023-04-28</ref>

=== Energy transition ===
In terms of energy, in 2020, Japan made a commitment to achieve full [[decarbonization]] by 2050, but it is still dedicated to reducing emissions by 26% by 2030.<ref name=":16" /> As a result, fossil fuels will continue to be relevant and potentially vulnerable for the next few years, while carbon-free sources such as renewables and residual nuclear energy are expected to become more dominant and potentially face their own vulnerabilities in the second half of the century.<ref name=":16" />
[[File:G20 map.png|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|G20 Countries members in map]]
Japan's overall performance in the Energy Transition indicator is in line with the G20 country average.<ref name=":16" /> The country has shown high performance in the Efficiency and Electrification domains, which has been driving the transformation of the energy sector.<ref name=":16" /> There is still room for improvement in terms of increasing the installed capacity of renewables and reducing the use of fossil fuels.<ref name=":16" /> By making progress in these areas, Japan could also decrease the level of urban air pollution and reduce {{CO2}} emissions per capita, leading to further improvements in the emissions indicator.<ref name=":16" />

Building upon its existing environmental initiatives, Japan is considering a revised climate target aimed at further reducing its [[greenhouse gas emissions]]. The government plans to achieve a reduction of 66% in emissions from 2013 levels by the fiscal year 2035. This ambitious target is part of a comprehensive strategy intended to adjust the country's energy mix by 2040, designed to provide businesses with a predictable framework for future investment and to ensure compliance with international environmental standards set by the [[Paris Agreement]]. The intermediate target for 2030 has been established at a 46% reduction in emissions. Additionally, the strategy includes a significant enhancement of [[Nuclear power|nuclear power's]] role in the national energy portfolio, aiming to increase its share from less than 10% currently to up to 22%. This shift is seen as a key component in accelerating Japan's transition towards more [[sustainable energy]] sources.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-04-15 |title=Japan Considers Emissions Cuts in New Energy Plan, Says Nikkei |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-04-15/japan-considers-emissions-cuts-in-new-energy-plan-says-nikkei |access-date=2024-04-15 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref>

In the light of Japan's climate targets, its energy sector has experienced significant expansion in renewable energy capacity, growing by over 30% in the past five years and driving demand for battery energy storage systems (BESS). More than half of the 2.4 gigawatts of capacity awarded in recent long-term low-carbon power auctions was thereby allocated to foreign companies or consortia. Major projects approved for 2024 include over 1.37 GW of new BESS capacity and more than 6.7 GWh of energy capacity.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.occto.or.jp/market-board/market/oshirase/2025/files/250428_longauction_youryouyakujokekka_kouhyou_besshi_ousatsu2024.pdf |title=Japan BESS Auction Results 2024 |publisher=Organization for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO) |date=2024-04-28 |access-date=2025-06-01}}</ref> Japan's Long Term Decarbonization Power Source Auction incentivizes BESS deployment by guaranteeing fixed cost recovery for 20 years. However, limited price volatility and a market price floor may constrain returns for BESS operators, highlighting the need for further reform.<ref>{{cite news |last=Tani |first=Shotaro |title=Foreign companies bet on Japan's battery storage market |work=Nikkei Asia |date=2025-05-29 |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Energy/Foreign-companies-bet-on-Japan-s-battery-storage-market |access-date=2025-06-01}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Empresas estrangeiras apostam no mercado de armazenamento de energia em baterias no Japão |work=Valor Econômico |date=2025-05-29 |url=https://valor.globo.com/mundo/noticia/2025/05/29/empresas-estrangeiras-apostam-no-mercado-de-armazenamento-de-energia-em-baterias-no-japao.ghtml |access-date=2025-06-01 |language=pt}}</ref>

=== Policies and legislation ===
As a member in the [[Paris Agreement]], Japan was the first nation to release a new national climate plan by 2020 as required in the 2015 agreement. However, this new plan included no major changes from the 2013 national climate plan, which aimed to reduce emissions by 26% from 2013 rates. This lack of aggressive action as the fifth largest polluter in the world led the [[World Resources Institute]] to describe the plan as "putting the world on a more dangerous trajectory." Similarly, the head of the World Wildlife Fund Japan climate and energy group, Naoyuki Yamagishi, described the plan as "completely the wrong signal."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sengupta |first1=Somini |title=Japan's climate plan sends 'wrong signal' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/01/climate/japans-climate-plan-sends-wrong-signal.html |access-date=1 April 2020 |work=The New York Times |date=1 April 2020}}</ref>

In 2018, Japan established its Strategic Energy Plan, with goals set for 2030. The plan aimed to reduce coal use from 32 to 26 percent, to increase renewables from 17 to 22–24 percent, and to increase nuclear from 6 to 20–22 percent of the energy production mix. As part of this goal, Japan announced a goal of shutting down 100 old, low-efficiency coal-fired plants out of its 140 coal fired power plants. As of 2020, 114 of Japan's 140 coal-fired plants are deemed old and inefficient. Twenty-six are considered high-efficiency, and 16 new high-efficiency plants are currently under construction.<ref>{{cite news |title=Japan aims to shut down 100 inefficient coal plants within decade |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2020/07/02/business/japan-shut-100-coal-plants/ |access-date=3 July 2020 |agency=The Japan Times| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200703122814/https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2020/07/02/business/japan-shut-100-coal-plants/ |archive-date=3 July 2020}}</ref> Funding of overseas coal power ended in 2021.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2021-12-27|title=2021 in coal: China's dirty recovery mars international finance crackdown|url=https://www.climatechangenews.com/2021/12/27/2021-in-coal-chinas-dirty-recovery-mars-international-finance-crackdown/|access-date=2021-12-28|website=Climate Home News|language=en|last1=Farand |first1=Chloé }}</ref> The [[Government of Japan|Japanese government]] said that they would try to be carbon neutral as soon as possible in the second half of the century. The official goal of the Japanese government is to be net zero in 2050.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Japan 2030: Tackling climate issues is key to the next decade|url=https://features.japantimes.co.jp/climate-crisis-2030/|access-date=2020-09-24|website=Deep reads from The Japan Times|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Japan's New Climate Pledge Faces a Massive Hurdle|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/japan-e2-80-99s-new-climate-pledge-faces-a-massive-hurdle/ar-BB1aqfEl|access-date=2020-11-08|website=www.msn.com}}</ref>

The [[Cool Biz campaign]] introduced under former [[Prime Minister of Japan]] [[Junichiro Koizumi]] was targeted at reducing energy use through the reduction of [[air conditioning]] use in [[government of Japan|government]] offices.<ref>{{Cite news |date=May 1, 2020 |title='Cool Biz' energy-saving campaign begins in Japan |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2020/05/01/business/cool-biz-energy-campaign/ |work=The Japan Times}}</ref>

=== Carbon price ===
Since 2012 the country has levied a "Tax for Climate Change Mitigation" on [[petroleum]], [[coal]] and [[natural gas]] at {{JPYConvert|289}} per nominal tonne of carbon they emit when burned.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Taxing Energy Use 2019: Country Note – Japan |url=https://www.oecd.org/tax/tax-policy/taxing-energy-use-japan.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210904225018/https://www.oecd.org/tax/tax-policy/taxing-energy-use-japan.pdf |archive-date=4 September 2021 |access-date=2021-07-06 |website=oecd.org}}</ref> In addition, [[Tokyo]] has had a local carbon [[Carbon emission trading|emissions trading]] system since 2010 in which carbon permits are valued at approximately US$50.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arimura |first1=Toshi H. |last2=Abe |first2=Tatsuya |date=2021-03-18 |title=The impact of the Tokyo emissions trading scheme on office buildings: what factor contributed to the emission reduction? |journal=Environmental Economics and Policy Studies |language=en |volume=23 |issue=3 |pages=517–533 |doi=10.1007/s10018-020-00271-w |issn=1432-847X |s2cid=216294026 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In December 2009, nine industry groupings opposed a carbon tax at the opening day of the [[2009 United Nations Climate Change Conference|COP-15 Copenhagen climate conference]] stating, "Japan should not consider a carbon tax as it would damage the economy which is already among the world's most energy-efficient." The industry groupings represented the oil, cement, paper, chemical, gas, electric power, auto manufacturing and electronics, and information technology sectors.<ref>{{cite news |date=7 December 2009 |title=Japan industry unites against carbon tax |work=Reuters |url=http://uk.reuters.com/article/idUKTOE5B609U20091207 |access-date=9 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211119230033/https://www.reuters.com/article/idUKTOE5B609U20091207?edition-redirect=uk |archive-date=19 November 2021}}</ref>

Japan launched a carbon credit market on Oct. 11, 2023, with a carbon levy expected in 2028.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Obayashi |first1=Yuka |last2=Golubkova |first2=Katya |last3=Obayashi |first3=Yuka |date=2023-10-11 |title=Explainer: Japan's carbon pricing scheme kicks off at Tokyo Stock Exchange |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/japans-carbon-pricing-scheme-kicks-off-tokyo-stock-exchange-2023-10-11/ |access-date=2023-11-12}}</ref>

=== Municipality level ===
Local governments, both prefectures and municipalities, are responsible for creating their own [[climate change adaptation]] plans under the Climate Change Adaptation Act, which came into force in December 2018. They are also tasked with creating Local Climate Change Adaptation Centers to study climate change adaptation, which can be established in partnership with research institutes, universities, or other appropriate local institutions. By 2021, 22 of the 47 prefectures and 30 of the 1,741 municipalities had established plans, while 23 prefectures and 2 municipalities had established research centers. While local governments can create joint plans and centers under the legislation, by 2021 none had done so.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.iges.or.jp/en/publication_documents/pub/fact/en/11075/FS_Local_Adaptation_Japan_210128_final.pdf |title=Progress of Local Adaptation in Japan |author1=Yuki Ohashi |author2=Takuya Hattori |author3=Yoshifumi Masago |publisher=Institute for Global Environmental Strategies |date=January 2021 |access-date=2 April 2021}}</ref>

Japan's capital [[Tokyo]] is preparing to force industry to make big cuts in [[greenhouse gas]]es, taking the lead in a country struggling to meet its [[Kyoto Protocol]] obligations. Tokyo's outspoken governor, [[Shintaro Ishihara]], decided to go it alone and create Japan's first [[emissions cap system]], reducing greenhouse gas emission by a total of 25% by 2020 from the 2000 level.<ref>[http://www.wbcsd.org/plugins/DocSearch/details.asp?type=DocDet&ObjectId=MzAyNzQ World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD)<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090104200639/http://www.wbcsd.org/plugins/DocSearch/details.asp?type=DocDet&ObjectId=MzAyNzQ|date=January 4, 2009}}</ref>

=== International cooperation ===
[[File:Special Fossil of the Day Message to Japan (30948154581).jpg|thumb|Protesters opposing Japan's climate change mitigation policies at the [[2016 United Nations Climate Change Conference]]]]
Japan created the Kyoto Protocol Target Achievement Plan to lay out the necessary measures required to meet their 6% reduction commitment under the [[Kyoto Protocol]]. It was first established as an outcome of the evaluation of the Climate Change Policy Program carried out in 2004. The main branches of the plan are ensuring the pursuit of environment and economy, promoting of technology, raising public awareness, utilizing of policy measures, and ensuring international collaboration.<ref>"[http://unfccc.int/files/meetings/seminar/application/pdf/sem_sup1_japan.pdf Gist of the Kyoto Protocol Target Achievement Plan]" United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and then they beat each other up</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change in the United Arab Emirates
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
[[File:Tc-map.png|thumb|420x420px|Map of United Arab Emirates]]
The [[United Arab Emirates]] (UAE) faces the impacts of [[climate change]] such as water stress, rising sea levels, dust storms, [[desertification]] and extreme heat.<ref name=":0">National Climate Change Plan of the United Arab Emirates 2017-2050. (2017). ''UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment.''</ref> Climate change threatens the country's water resources, wetland ecosystems, human health, economic stability, and international affairs.<ref name=":0" /> The UAE has a hot desert climate and is located on the coast of the [[Persian Gulf]] and the [[Gulf of Oman]].<ref name=":1">World Bank. (2024). ''World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal - United Arab Emirates''. Climate Change Knowledge Portal. <nowiki>https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/country/united-arab-emirates</nowiki></ref> Decreasing annual precipitation levels and increased desertification make the country's rural and urban populations vulnerable. Climate change is projected to increase national vulnerabilities in the United Arab Emirates.<ref name=":0" /> [[Sea level rise]] is expected to impact the UAE's urban infrastructure and marine and wetland ecosystems.<ref name=":1" /> The agricultural, fishery, and tourism sectors in the UAE are at risk due to the negative effects of climate change.<ref name=":0" />

UAE has signed and ratified the Paris Treaty. It has revised its third Nationally Determined Contributions, submitted in 2023, focus on both mitigation and adaptation strategies. The UAE intends to reduce its greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions for the year 2030 by 40%.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |last=UNFCCC United Arab Emirates |date=2023 |title=Third Update of Second Nationally Determined Contributions |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/NDC/2023-07/Third%20Update%20of%20Second%20NDC%20for%20the%20UAE_v15.pdf}}</ref>

== Greenhouse gas emissions ==
The UAE's total greenhouse gas emissions in 2005 were approximately 161.134 Mt [[CO2 equivalent|CO<sub>2</sub> equivalent]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Khondaker |first1=A. N. |last2=Hasan |first2=Md. Arif |last3=Rahman |first3=Syed Masiur |last4=Malik |first4=Karim |last5=Shafiullah |first5=Md |last6=Muhyedeen |first6=Musah A |date=2016-06-01 |title=Greenhouse gas emissions from energy sector in the United Arab Emirates – An overview |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1364032116000575 |journal=Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews |volume=59 |pages=1317–1325 |doi=10.1016/j.rser.2016.01.027 |bibcode=2016RSERv..59.1317K |issn=1364-0321|url-access=subscription }}</ref> As of 2021, the country had one of the world's top 10 highest per capita CO<sub>2</sub> emission rates, at 21.8 tons per capita.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Hummieda |first1=Ammar |last2=Bouabid |first2=Ali |last3=Moawad |first3=Karim |last4=Mayyas |first4=Ahmad |date=2023-10-01 |title=The UAE's energy system and GHG emissions: pathways to achieving national goals by 2050 |url=https://academic.oup.com/ce/article/7/5/962/7273027 |journal=Clean Energy |volume=7 |issue=5 |pages=962–980 |doi=10.1093/ce/zkad040 |issn=2515-4230|doi-access=free }}</ref> As part of the energy sector, the oil and gas industry is a significant driver of the economy along with greenhouse gas emissions. The UAE is one of the highest producers and exporters of oil and gas globally<ref name=":6" /> and relies on fossil fuels for the country's electric power.<ref name=":7" /> In 2012, the country supplied 3.2 million barrels of oil per day in production. The UAE's rapid urbanization and population increase have contributed to the country's high per capita energy consumption, one of the highest in the world as of 2016.<ref name=":6" /> The UAE's energy sector contributes 90% of the country's GHG emissions.<ref name=":6"/> The sector for road operations and construction contributes anywhere from 76 to 1100&nbsp;kg CO<sub>2</sub>e/m<sup>2</sup> per year, depending on the road networks analyzed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alzard |first1=Mohammed H. |last2=Maraqa |first2=Munjed A. |last3=Chowdhury |first3=Rezaul |last4=Khan |first4=Qasim |last5=Albuquerque |first5=Francisco D. B. |last6=Mauga |first6=Timur Ibrahim |last7=Aljunadi |first7=Khaled Nazmi |date=2019-04-20 |title=Estimation of Greenhouse Gas Emissions Produced by Road Projects in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=11 |issue=8 |page=2367 |doi=10.3390/su11082367 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019Sust...11.2367A |issn=2071-1050}}</ref>

Energy efficiency and renewable energy efforts allow for the reduction of GHG emissions for the UAE. The work towards lower GHG emissions could lower the health risks for the country's already vulnerable population.<ref name=":5" /> The UAE's Energy Strategy 2050 plan includes adjustments in the country's reliance on fossil fuels in the energy sector, using "clean coal" in the transition to clean energy.<ref name=":7" /> The Energy Strategy 2050 aims to focus on solar energy to diversify the energy sector along with nuclear power.

== Impacts on the natural environment ==
[[File:Temperature Bar Chart Middle East-United Arab Emirates--1901-2020--2021-07-13.png|thumb|Temperature change in United Arab Emirates (1901–2021)]]

=== Temperature and weather changes ===
The UAE faces increased temperatures and a drier climate due to climate change. Using Standardized Temperature Index modeling, Abu Dhabi is expected to have the highest mean temperature when compared with Al-Ain, Dubai and Sharjah.<ref name=":8">{{Citation |last1=Ksiksi |first1=Taoufik Saleh |title=Climate change in the UAE: Modeling air temperature using ARIMA and STI across four bio-climatic zones |date=2019-06-26 |url=https://f1000research.com/articles/8-973/v1 |access-date=2024-11-03 |language=en |doi=10.12688/f1000research.19557.1 |last2=Al-Blooshi |first2=Latifa Saeed|journal=F1000Research |volume=8 |page=973 |doi-access=free }}</ref> All major cities in the country are expected to have increased annual temperatures, and Al-Ain is predicted to have severe heat events in models until 2030.<ref name=":8" /> Between 1975 and 2013 Dubai saw a 2.7&nbsp;°C increase in temperature.<ref name=":8" /> The Arabian Gulf's ocean surface temperature has increased in the last 50 years by 0.2&nbsp;°C to 0.6&nbsp;°C every 10 years.<ref name=":8" /> Sea temperatures are rising, along with ocean acidification, leading to high vulnerabilities for marine life and coastal ecosystems in the area and globally.<ref name=":9">Mfarrej, M. F. B. (2019). Climate change patterns in the UAE: A qualitative research and review. ''Nature Environment and Pollution Technology'', ''18''(1), 261-268</ref> The industries of fishing and agriculture are vulnerable due to increasing temperatures and weather changes such as drought and extreme heat waves, suggesting populations are at risk to food insecurity and regional food shortages.<ref name=":9" />

=== Water resources ===
[[File:Jebel Hafeet Al Ain 3.jpg|thumb|Hafeet Mountain, Al Ain, UAE]]
Water quality, quantity and availability will be effected due to climate change in the Middle East region.<ref name=":9" /> Salinity, extreme heat, drought, and overuse of water resources are factors that impact the population's water resources. Agricultural and industrial use of water resources increases annually while population and [[population density]] increases in the UAE. Each emirate in the country has differing household water consumption data depending on economic growth and population. Rapid growth in population throughout the country will increase the strain on irrigation resources, as the UAE has focused water resources on agriculture.{{Cn|date=April 2025}} The city of Al Ain has at high risk of water scarcity, due to lack of water management and consumption by economic development and agriculture.<ref name=":9" /> It is the only city in the UAE with a known source of renewable groundwater. The UAE is at high risk of water scarcity due to the limited sources of groundwater available.<ref name=":12">Alsharhan, A. S., & Rizk, Z. E. (2020). ''Water resources and integrated management of the United Arab Emirates'' (Vol. 3). Springer Nature.</ref> The current depletion rate of groundwater could lead to stopped groundwater supply to croplands in 2030, as the demand for water resources for food growth grows with the population.{{cn|date=April 2025}} Groundwater sources where available have high salinity and sea level rise will increase salinity, decreasing the quality of the water source in the region.<ref name=":12" /> Increasing temperatures and the decrease in annual rainfall will lead to increased consumption in the industrial and agricultural sectors as well as individual consumption for human health needs and the production of food crops.<ref name=":12" />
[[File:Mangrove National Park, Abu Dhabi city, UAE.jpg|thumb|Mangrove National Park, Abu Dhabi city.]]

=== Ecosystems ===
Marine ecosystems and habitats are threatened by climate change. Mangrove forests, coral reefs, salt marshes and grasses are at risk due to salinization, sea level rise, increased air and ocean temperatures, and changes in precipitation patterns.<ref name=":9" /> Damage to such ecosystems will decrease biodiversity in the Arab region and UAE's coastline. The extreme weather events, desertification and flooding are expected to decrease biodiversity and threaten habitat.<ref name=":9" /> Mangrove forests are important carbon sequestration ecosystems and support regional biodiversity. There are regional efforts to protect wetland habitats including mangroves with initiatives such as the UAE Annual Mangrove Soil Carbon Sequestration Project which provides data on climate change's effects on carbon sequestration and habitat loss.<ref name=":3" /> These projects allow for mitigation and the conservation of vulnerable habitat.

=== Sea level rise ===
The population of Arabian Gulf countries is concentrated near the coast, with 26 million people living in areas concierge{{clarify|date=October 2026}} coastal zones. However, the UAE is particularly vulnerable, because the low-lying coastline is shallow sloping, which makes the country highly susceptible to flooding. The countries have also built 90% of the infrastructure within several meters of sea level and 85% of their population lives within several meters of sea level, including the coastal city of Dubai.<ref>Subraelu, P., et al. "Global warming climate change and sea level rise: Impact on land use land cover features along UAE coast through remote sensing and GIS." ''J. Ecosyst. Ecography'' 12 (2022): 1-8</ref> The 1300-kilometer coastline<ref name=":10">Ali, T., Mortula, M. M., & Gawai, R. (2022, November). Coastal Vulnerability Analysis of the UAE Coast Due to Sea Level Rise. In ''Euro-Mediterranean Conference for Environmental Integration'' (pp. 749-752). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland.</ref> hosts tourism, ports, residential housing, and ongoing construction for development.<ref name=":11">Subraelu, P., Yagoub, M. M., Sefelnasr, A., Rao, K. N., Allamsatti, R. S., Sherif, M., & Ebraheem, A. A. (2021). Sea-level rise and coastal vulnerability: A preliminary assessment of UAE coast through remote sensing and GIS. ''J. Coast. Zone Mang'', ''24'', 477-480</ref> 13.8% of the total UAE coastline has very high coastal vulnerability to sea level rise. Sea level is predicted to rise between 42 and 98&nbsp;cm by the year 2100.<ref name=":11" /> By 2100, Six percent of the UAE coastline is predicted to be under water.<ref name=":9" /> Sea level rise is expected to increase environmental disaster risk, including coastal flooding, increased erosion, storm surge, salination of groundwater (a source of drinking water for UAE), and environmental damage to ecosystems.<ref name=":10" /> The most vulnerable areas in the UAE span from the middle of Dubai city's coast to [[Umm Al Quwain]] to [[Ras Al-Khaimah]].<ref name=":10" /> UAE coastal areas on the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf are at high risk of sea level rise. The eastern coast in the Gulf of Oman has a high vulnerability to sea level rise, while the western side of the UAE coast is less vulnerable but still at risk.<ref name=":10" />

== Impacts on People ==

=== Economic impacts ===
Climate change and sea level rise are expected to have a severe impact on the UAE's coastline, where the country holds its tourism and development for revenue.<ref name=":11" /> The country's coastal cities hold large populations of people, where large areas of its built environment are at high risk of sea level rise and other environmental hazards from climate change.<ref name=":10" /> The UAE's agriculture, fisheries and aquaculture, tourism, and health are vulnerable to the effects of climate change. Strains on water resources and food production will increase UAE's reliance on food imports and economic development to protect the country's people and natural environment. Sustainable development is an economic route that will strengthen the UAE's continuing development while limiting the country's emissions and outputs to worsen the impacts of climate change.<ref>Mazumder, L. K. (2016). ''Restructuring the economy through sustainability initiatives in UAE- a case study analysis''. London: Centre for Business & Economic Research. Retrieved from <nowiki>https://lib-proxy01.skidmore.edu/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/conference-papers-proceedings/restructuring-economy-through-sustainability/docview/1817996106/se-2</nowiki></ref> As part of the UAE's mitigation plans, the country is implementing economic diversification to support its economy to address the strains from climate change.<ref>Al-Sarihi, A. (2018). Prospects for climate change integration into GCC economic diversification strategies.</ref>
[[File:Farms and terraces in the Wadi Litibah.jpg|thumb|Farms and terraces in the Wadi Litibah region of UAE.]]

=== Agriculture ===
The Arid climate and poor soil health make it difficult to form a robust agriculture sector, however, they have still made developments. The UAE's lack of rainfall and natural waterways has led to many of the farms, drawing from underground aquifers for water. There are 160,000 hectares of cultivable land being used in the UAE, with the majority of that land being taken up by date palms. In total, there are around 30,000 farms within the UAE, and the government grants 50% subsidies on seeds, fertilizers, and pesticides.<ref>{{cite web |title=All about the agricultural sector in the UAE |url=https://www.bayut.com/mybayut/all-about-agriculture-uae/ |website=Bayut.com |access-date=18 November 2024}}</ref>

The UAE has looked to develop urban farms that implement rooftop farming, hydroponics, aquaponics, vertical farming, and aeroponics. As there is a high demand to eat local produce over imports.<ref name="agri">{{cite journal |last1=Sharma |first1=Rohit |title=Enhancing domestic food supply in the UAE: A framework for technology-driven urban farming systems |journal=Journal of Cleaner Production |date=January 2024 |volume=434 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2023.139823 |bibcode=2024JCPro.43439823S |doi-access=free }}</ref> In more conventional farms the UAE has looked to replace outdated flood irrigation systems with more modern water-conserving irrigation. There has also been an increased transition, from more traditional farms to organic farms, which have a more sustainable approach, there are approximately 50 organic farms in the UAE. The Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority (ADAFSA) launched a program to establish a gene bank, to ensure that certain crop genes are saved and can be drawn upon in the future. The UAE has also planned to include agriculture in their tourism sector, as they feel there is interest in their organic farms and camel milk industry.<ref name="Ag conference">{{cite web |last1=Sadiku |first1=Matthew NO |date=April 18, 2024 |title=Agriculture in United Arab Emirates |url=https://www.conferenceseries.info/index.php/morocco |access-date=18 November 2024 |publisher=International Conference on Agriculture Sciences, Environment, Urban and Rural Development}}</ref> Overall the UAE has used innovative solutions to try and maximize food production in their climate, by modernizing their farms to be in a controlled environment and bolstering their traditional farms to be water efficient.

People's reliance on the coastal and marine environment centers most of the income for large populations in UAE.<ref name=":3">Crooks, S., Poppe, K., Rubilla, A., Rybczyk J., (2019). ''Mangrove Soil Carbon Accumulation of the United Arab Emirates: Trial Application'', Report by and AGEDI/Environment Agency Abu Dhabi, Silvestrum Climate Associates and Western Washington University.</ref> The impacts of climate change threaten the population's income, livelihood, and health.
[[File:Dubai Tourism.jpg|thumb|Tourism in Dubai, UAE.]]

=== Tourism ===
Tourism in the UAE has been one of the fastest-growing sectors of the country's economy, as in the last year{{when|date=October 2026}} the sector grew by 26%, making up 11% of the country's overall GDP. The country's unique climate, state-of-the-art buildings, and many hotels make it an ideal destination for visitors. However, climate change can potentially deter future visitors, as tourist infrastructure (hotels, housing, and restaurants) is built in areas vulnerable to rising sea levels.<ref>{{cite web |date=April 18, 2024 |title=Travel & Tourism in the UAE reaches new heights, reveals WTTC |url=https://wttc.org/news-article/travel-and-tourism-in-the-uae-reaches-new-heights-reveals-wttc |website=wttc.org}}</ref> In particular, Palm Island, three artificially made islands off the coast of Dubai, had the goal of accommodating luxury housing and around 80 hotels. This project has been deemed a failure as it has eroded the natural coastline, as 5.5 million cubic meters of rock were quarried with an astronomical carbon footprint. Therefore, the project is already being built on top of their natural shoreline, so as climate change raises the sea level in Dubai, Palm Island will be the most vulnerable location.<ref name=":18" /> The rising temperatures will shorten the tourist season in the UAE, as many visitors will avoid Dubai during the shoulder months—those transitional periods between the intense summer heat and the peak winter season when temperatures are more comfortable for outdoor activities.<ref name=":18">{{cite web |url=https://www.responsibletravel.com/holidays/united-arab-emirates/travel-guide/responsible-tourism |website=Responsible Travel |title=Responsible tourism in the United Arab Emirates }}</ref> There are also popular tourist areas that will be damaged because of the effects of climate change: in particular, coral bleaching will occur, as the sea temperature rises. There are also predictions that the cost of visiting the UAE will increase, as the emirates rely so much on air conditioning in their shopping centers and restaurants; when temperature rises, it will only increase the cost of air conditioning, which will in turn raise the price of goods and services.<ref name=":18" />

=== Health ===
As climate change is expected to increase the average annual temperature, that will increase the likelihood of UAE being exposed to some type of heat stress. Particularly during times of heat waves (Prolonged periods of extreme heat) vulnerable populations; people over the age of 65 or people working outside, can die or face heat exhaustion (WHO, 2024).
Many of the drivers of climate change, energy production, transportation, and pollution, can decrease the overall air quality in the UAE. In the U.S., dust is the main contributor to deteriorating air quality as in all UAE cities,  Annual mean PM2.5 levels were significantly higher than the global mean (WHO, 2024).

== Mitigation ==
The UAE has developed [[Climate change mitigation|mitigation]] practices to equip the country for increased sea level rise, salinization of freshwater, and decarbonization. Tools and technologies used to project future precipitation, weather, and storm patterns are crucial to future climate change mitigation, adaptation, and resource management for the UAE. With prediction tools such as statistical downscaling, precipitation and temperature patterns are localized to meet the needs of specific regions of the UAE.<ref>Elhakeem, A., Elshorbagy, W. E., AlNaser, H., & Dominguez, F. (2015). Downscaling global circulation model projections of climate change for the United Arab Emirates. ''Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management'', ''141''(9), 04015007.</ref>

Previous UAE projects focused on regional and international mitigation efforts include the Abu Dhabi Blue Carbon Demonstration Project, prior to the UAE's mangrove sequestration project.<ref name=":3" /> The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE) and the Abu Dhabi Global Environmental Data Initiative (AGEDI) partnered in 2019 to understand the benefits of 'Blue Carbon' ecosystems, including mangroves and other coastal environments, for the nation of UAE.<ref name=":3" /> Commissioned by AGEDI, the UAE Annual Mangrove Soil Carbon Sequestration Project is a continued study conducted in UAE measuring the rate of carbon sequestration, or removal of carbon from the atmosphere, through mangroves.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">Dougherty, B. (2020, July 27). ''First round of results of the UAE Mangroves Annual Carbon Sequestration Project''. Abu Dhabi Global Environmental Data Initiative. <nowiki>https://agedi.org/first-round-of-results-of-the-uae-mangroves-annual-carbon-sequestration-project/</nowiki></ref>

The UAE's mangrove ecosystems provide high levels of carbon sequestration, storage in its biomass in an arid region, and overall climate mitigation.<ref name=":4" /> Mangroves at Khor Kalba were shown to sequester 0.5 tons of carbon per hectare per year.<ref name=":3" /> This study provides data to manage coastal planning and continue conservation efforts for mangrove ecosystems. The use of the term 'Blue Carbon' indicates ecosystems that have the ability to sequester or store carbon and include wetlands: mangrove forests, seagrasses, and salt marshes.<ref name=":3" /> The mangrove study provided localized data collection at multiple locations.

Decarbonization efforts and goals including the Net Zero 2050 Strategic Initiative expect to align with social and economic goals for UAE's people, and increased opportunities while the country divests in its fossil fuel economy.<ref name=":14" /> In the delivery of the UAE Consensus at COP28, plans suggested a full transition from fossil fuels in the energy sector to support the net zero goal by 2050.<ref name=":14" />
[[File:Noor Abu Dhabi 2020.jpg|thumb|Noor Abu Dhabi Solar Power Plant]]

== Adaptation ==
The country's national climate adaptation policy was developed beginning in 2017, as part of the UAE's Climate Plan. Current warming patterns and the effects of climate change are present today, and the UAE is adapting ongoing initiatives to incorporate a climate change lens.<ref name=":0" /> Adaptation and resilience measures are expected to include localized plans for the country, focusing on the improvement of climate change data, health and education, financial well-being, and healthy ecosystems. As part of the Local, National, and Regional Climate Change Program (LNRCCP) of AGEDI, regional climate change modeling addressed the future impacts of greenhouse gas emissions and linked the energy, water, and health sectors together in potential climate change initiatives for societal improvement for vulnerable populations within UAE.<ref name=":5">Dougherty, W. W., Yates, D. N., Pereira, J. E., Monaghan, A., Steinhoff, D., Ferrero, B., ... & Glavan, J. (2019). The energy-water-health nexus under climate change in the United Arab Emirates: impacts and implications. ''Climate Change and Energy Dynamics in the Middle East: Modeling and Simulation-Based Solutions'', 131-180</ref>

The UAE's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) include a transition to greener energy that is affordable, citing solar cells, enhanced wind turbines, and bioenergy conversion processes as energy sources for the country as it divests from fossil fuels and acts to diversify its energy sector.<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last1=Bojarajan |first1=Arjun Kumar |last2=Al Omari |first2=Salah Addin Burhan |last3=Al-Marzouqi |first3=Ali H. |last4=Alshamsi |first4=Dalal |last5=Sherif |first5=Mohsen |last6=Kabeer |first6=Saifudeen |last7=Sangaraju |first7=Sambasivam |date=2024-08-01 |title=A holistic overview of sustainable energy technologies and thermal management in UAE: the path to net zero emissions |journal=International Journal of Thermofluids |volume=23 |article-number=100758 |doi=10.1016/j.ijft.2024.100758 |bibcode=2024IJTf...2300758B |issn=2666-2027|doi-access=free }}</ref> There is high potential for solar as a main energy source for the UAE, as the country yields high photovoltaic potential with solar power systems in place. The expansion of solar power sites around the country has increased this potential use for the energy sector with sites in place.<ref name=":15" />

The UAE's Net Zero by 2050 Strategic Initiative upholds the Paris Agreement's goals and is the first country in the Middle East to implement a carbon-neutral plan.<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |title=UAE Energy Diversification {{!}} UAE Embassy in Washington, DC |url=https://www.uae-embassy.org/discover-uae/climate-and-energy/uae-energy-diversification |access-date=2024-11-15 |website=UAE Energy Diversification {{!}} UAE Embassy in Washington, DC |language=en}}</ref> Expansion of renewable green energy has occurred during the 2020 decade, as the UAE began the country's first program for wind power in October 2023.<ref name=":16" /> The renewable energy capacity of the country increased by nearly 70% between 2022 and 2023.<ref name=":16" /> The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment is working with government bodies at all levels to ensure the reduction of total carbon emissions, the sectors of power/energy, agriculture, transportation, and infrastructure being the top priorities.<ref>Lintang, F. A., Ramadhan, I. A., Lathifa, M. N., & Satria, R. (2024). UNITED ARAB EMIRATES'INTERESTS ON NET ZERO 2050 INITIATIVE. ''Jurnal Pena Wimaya'', ''4''(2).</ref> As part of Dubai's contribution to the UAE's energy transition efforts, the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park is being constructed to have a capacity of 5,000 MW by 2030.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |title=Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park |url=https://www.mbrsic.ae/en/about/mohammed-bin-rashid-al-maktoum-solar-park/ |website=Government of Dubai}}</ref> It is the largest solar power park in the world and it is expected to save 6.5 million tons carbon emissions each year once completed.<ref name=":17" />

The UAE government initiated the [[Masdar City]] project in 2006, with the [[state-owned enterprise]] Mubadala Development Company beginning development with a US$22 billion budget.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Lin |first=Zhongjie |title=Constructing Utopias: China's New Town Movement in the 21st Century |date=2025 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-779330-5 |location=New York, NY}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=197}} Masdar City is intended to be a zero-carbon, zero-waste community with no negative environmental impact.<ref name=":2" />{{Reference page|page=197}}

== Society and culture ==

=== Public Perception and Activism ===
Youth empowerment efforts have been made by university groups in the UAE, including the Mohamed Bin Zayed University for Humanities.<ref name=":13">Aboukhousa, H. (2024). Promoting climate action through youth empowerment and environmental education: Insights from Mohamed Bin Zayed University for Humanities. ''Journal of Infrastructure, Policy and Development'', ''8''(11), 8636.</ref> Environmental education is a form of activism implemented in schools globally, which instills environmental consciousness and promotes participation in national and regional discussions around climate change and solutions to address it.<ref name=":13" /> One hundred and fifty youth participated in programming at COP28 in Dubai, engaging in international environmental advocacy.<ref name=":13" /> The UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment has partnered with universities to support youth environmental education and activism. Environmental journalism supports activism in the UAE, while press and media coverage of environmental projects are maintained by the governing body and monarchy of the UAE, as most news organizations are state owned.<ref>Reinisch, L. (2010). Environmental journalism in UAE. ''Arab Media & Society'', ''11'', 1-19.</ref>

=== International cooperation ===
[[File:Net Zero Nuclear Event, at COP 28, the United Nations Climate Change Conference UNCCC held at the Expo City Dubai, United Arab Emirates on 2 December 2023 - 8.jpg|thumb|Net Zero Nuclear Event at COP 28, the United Nations Climate Change Conference 2023.]]
In 1975, the UAE Supreme Committee of Environment (SCE) was formed, marking the beginning of UAE environmental policy.<ref name=":0" /> The UAE hosted the Conference of the Parties for its 28th year, COP28, in 2023. Dr. Sultan Al Jaber stood as COP28 president, making welcoming and closing remarks at the conference.<ref>{{Cite web |title=COP28 President Delivers Remarks at Closing Plenary |url=https://www.cop28.com/en/news/2023/12/COP28-President-Delivers-Remarks-at-Closing-Plenary |access-date=October 31, 2024 |website=COP28 UAE Consensus}}</ref> He is head of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company and minister of industry and advanced technology of the United Arab Emirates.
[[File:20211104-OSEC-UNC-0004 (51656493911).jpg|thumb|Hunger and climate change discussions at COP 26.]]
The UAE has supported the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) from the 2015 United Nations Sustainable Development Summit. Starting in 2020 the Paris Agreement began overseeing climate commitments and actions made by the UAE as part of the growing international commitment to lowering the impacts of climate change and greenhouse gas emissions.<ref name=":0" /> The Mohamed Bin Zayed Water Initiative serves as a group focused on the issue of water scarcity for global populations. The UAE has called for international cooperation to improve water accessibility with the Mohamed Min Zayed Water Initiative. This initiative supports desalination efforts to increase water access, affordability, and reliability while being sustainable.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Mohamed bin Zayed Water Initiative |url=https://www.mohamedbinzayedwi.ae/ |website=The Mohamed bin Zayed Water Initiative}}</ref>
