======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change in the United Kingdom
======================================================================

{{short description|Emissions, effects, and responses of the United Kingdom related to climate change}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2023}}

[[File:River Teme floods at Leintwardine, February 2020 (geograph 6393207).jpg|thumb|Climate change has increased the risk of flooding, as with [[Storm Dennis]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 February 2020 |title=Heavier rainfall from storms '100% for certain' linked to climate crisis, experts warn |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/climate-change/news/storm-dennis-flooding-climate-change-crisis-extreme-weather-rainfall-a9341201.html |access-date=2 February 2021 |website=The Independent |language=en |archive-date=8 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220708110152/http://www.independent.co.uk/climate-change/news/storm-dennis-flooding-climate-change-crisis-extreme-weather-rainfall-a9341201.html |url-status=live}}</ref>]]

The [[Climate of the United Kingdom|United Kingdom's climate]] is [[Climate change|changing]], with hotter drier summers and warmer wetter winters. Storms, floods, droughts and [[Heat wave|heatwaves]] are becoming more frequent and intense, and [[sea level rise]] is affecting coastal areas. The UK is also a contributor to climate change, having [[greenhouse gas emissions by the United Kingdom|emitted more greenhouse gas]] per person than the world average. Climate change is having [[Economic analysis of climate change|economic effects]] on the UK and presents risks to human health and ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=UK Climate Change Risk Assessment 2022 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-climate-change-risk-assessment-2022 |access-date=28 August 2022 |website=GOV.UK |language=en |archive-date=28 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220828074756/https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-climate-change-risk-assessment-2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The UK has more than halved its greenhouse gas emissions since 1990, and under the [[Paris Agreement]] has [[Nationally determined contribution|committed]] to [[net zero|net zero emissions]] by 2050, via a series of [[Carbon budget|carbon budgets]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The UK’s plans and progress to reach net zero by 2050 |url=https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-9888/}}</ref> [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Parliament]] passed Acts related to climate change in [[Climate Change and Sustainable Energy Act 2006|2006]] and [[Climate Change Act 2008|2008]], the latter being the first time a government legally mandated a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. The [[United Kingdom Climate Change Programme|UK Climate Change Programme]] was established in 2000 and the [[Climate Change Committee]] provides policy advice towards mitigation targets. In 2019, [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Parliament]] declared a '[[Climate emergency declarations in the United Kingdom|climate change emergency]]'.<ref name="bbc.com">{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-48126677|title=UK Parliament declares climate emergency|date=1 May 2019|access-date=2 May 2019|archive-date=4 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204175849/https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-48126677|url-status=live}}</ref> The country [[Coal phase-out|phased out coal power]] in 2024. The UK has been prominent in international cooperation on climate change, including through [[United Nations Climate Change conference|UN conferences]] and during its [[United Kingdom membership of the European Union|European Union membership]].

Climate change has been discussed by British politicians since the late 20th century, but it has attracted greater political, public and [[Mass media in the United Kingdom|media]] attention in the UK from the 2000s, with the commitment to net zero now opposed by some political parties.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Net zero isn’t conservatism. It has more in common with communism |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2026/07/13/net-zero-not-conservatism-more-common-communism/}}</ref> [[Public opinion on climate change|Public opinion]] polls show concern amongst the majority of Britons. Various [[Environmental direct action in the United Kingdom|climate change activism]] initiatives have taken place in the UK.

== Effects on the natural environment ==
=== Temperature and weather changes ===
[[File:20190731 Central England Temperature (CET) (annual mean, beginning in 1659).png|thumb|300x300px|[[Central England temperature]] dataset, 1659 to 2019.]]
{{multiple image

| image1 = Koppen-Geiger Map GBR present.svg

| image2 = Koppen-Geiger Map GBR future.svg
| caption2 = 2071–2100 map under [[Representative Concentration Pathway|the most intense climate change scenario]]. Mid-range scenarios are currently considered more likely<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hausfather|first1=Zeke|last2=Peters|first2=Glen|title=Emissions – the 'business as usual' story is misleading|journal=Nature|date=29 January 2020|volume=577|issue=7792|pages=618–20|doi=10.1038/d41586-020-00177-3|pmid=31996825|bibcode=2020Natur.577..618H|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schuur |first1=Edward A.G. |last2=Abbott |first2=Benjamin W. |last3=Commane |first3=Roisin |last4=Ernakovich |first4=Jessica |last5=Euskirchen |first5=Eugenie |last6=Hugelius |first6=Gustaf |last7=Grosse |first7=Guido |last8=Jones |first8=Miriam |last9=Koven |first9=Charlie |last10=Leshyk |first10=Victor |last11=Lawrence |first11=David |last12=Loranty |first12=Michael M. |last13=Mauritz |first13=Marguerite |last14=Olefeldt |first14=David |last15=Natali |first15=Susan |last16=Rodenhizer |first16=Heidi |last17=Salmon |first17=Verity |last18=Schädel |first18=Christina |last19=Strauss |first19=Jens |last20=Treat |first20=Claire |last21=Turetsky |first21=Merritt |year=2022 |title=Permafrost and Climate Change: Carbon Cycle Feedbacks From the Warming Arctic |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |volume=47 |pages=343–371 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-012220-011847 |quote="Medium-range estimates of Arctic carbon emissions could result from moderate climate emission mitigation policies that keep global warming below 3°C (e.g., RCP4.5). This global warming level most closely matches country emissions reduction pledges made for the Paris Climate Agreement..." |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Phiddian |first=Ellen |date=5 April 2022 |title=Explainer: IPCC Scenarios |url=https://cosmosmagazine.com/earth/climate/explainer-ipcc-scenarios/ |website=[[Cosmos (magazine)|Cosmos]] |access-date=30 September 2023 |quote="The IPCC doesn't make projections about which of these scenarios is more likely, but other researchers and modellers can. [[The Australian Academy of Science]], for instance, released a report last year stating that our current emissions trajectory had us headed for a 3°C warmer world, roughly in line with the middle scenario. [[Climate Action Tracker]] predicts 2.5 to 2.9°C of warming based on current policies and action, with pledges and government agreements taking this to 2.1°C. |archive-date=20 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230920224129/https://cosmosmagazine.com/earth/climate/explainer-ipcc-scenarios/ |url-status=live}}</ref>
}}

The [[Central England temperature]] series, recorded since 1659 in the [[Midlands]], shows an observed increase in temperature, consistent with anthropogenic climate change rather than natural [[climate variability and change]].<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Karoly, D. J. and P. A. Stott |title=Anthropogenic warming of central England temperature |year=2006 |journal=Atmospheric Science Letters |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=81–85 |doi=10.1002/asl.136 |bibcode=2006AtScL...7...81K |s2cid=121456744 |doi-access=free}}</ref> According to the [[Met Office]], climate change will affect the [[climate of the United Kingdom]] with warmer and wetter winters and hotter and drier summers. [[Spanish plume]]s will continue but bring more intense weather conditions such as hotter summer weather and summer [[thunderstorm]]s.<ref name="CC">{{Cite web |title=Climate change in the UK |url=https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/weather/climate-change/climate-change-in-the-uk |access-date=22 August 2022 |website=Met Office |language=en |archive-date=22 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822104716/https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/weather/climate-change/climate-change-in-the-uk |url-status=live}}</ref>

By 2014, the United Kingdom's seven warmest and 4 out of its 5 wettest years had occurred between the years of 2000–2014. Higher temperatures increase evaporation and consequently rainfall. In 2014, England recorded its wettest winter in over 250 years with [[2013–14 United Kingdom winter floods|widespread flooding]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=3 December 2014 |title=2014 on track to be England's hottest year in over three centuries |url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/dec/03/2014-on-track-to-be-englands-hottest-year-in-over-three-centuries |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827212440/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/dec/03/2014-on-track-to-be-englands-hottest-year-in-over-three-centuries |url-status=live}}</ref>

In parts of the south east of the UK, the temperature in the hottest days of the year increased by 1&nbsp;°C per decade in the years 1960–2019. The [[United Kingdom weather records|highest ever recorded temperature]] in the United Kingdom was recorded in [[2022 United Kingdom heat wave|2022]] in [[Coningsby]] at {{convert|40.3|C}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Heatwave latest: Major incident declared as London hits 40C and fires burn |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/live/uk-62184978 |access-date=20 July 2022 |website=BBC News |language=en-gb |archive-date=20 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220720193641/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/live/uk-62184978 |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2020, the chances of reaching a temperature above {{convert|40|C}} were low, but they are 10 times higher than in a climate without human presence. In modest emissions scenario, by the end of the century, it will happen every 15 years and in high emissions scenario every 3–4 years. Summers with temperatures above {{convert|35|C}} occur in the UK every 5 years, but will occur almost every other year in the high emission scenario by 2100.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chances of 40°C days in the UK increasing|url=https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/about-us/press-office/news/weather-and-climate/2020/chances-of-40c-days-in-the-uk-increasing-due-to-human-influence|access-date=2 July 2020|website=Met Office|archive-date=22 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422112444/https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/about-us/press-office/news/weather-and-climate/2020/chances-of-40c-days-in-the-uk-increasing-due-to-human-influence|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Extreme weather events ===
The [[Met Office]] outlines that more frequent and intense [[extreme weather]] events will affect the UK due to climate change.<ref name="CC" />

====Floods====
{{Further| List of floods#United Kingdom}}

Due to increased rainfall from warmer and wetter winters, increased [[flood]]ing is expected.<ref name="CC" /> An interactive map from the UK government shows areas at risk of flooding.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Flood map for planning - GOV.UK|url=https://flood-map-for-planning.service.gov.uk/|access-date=8 February 2021|website=flood-map-for-planning.service.gov.uk|language=en|archive-date=21 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210521214115/https://flood-map-for-planning.service.gov.uk/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==== Heat waves ====
[[File:Wennington wildfire 57.jpg|thumb|Houses burned down in the [[Wennington wildfire]] of July 2022]]
[[Heat wave]]s are becoming more intense and more likely in the UK due to climate change.<ref name="CC" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Vaughan |first=Adam |date=19 July 2022 |title=Temperature hits 40°C on the UK's hottest day on record |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2329138-temperature-hits-40c-on-the-uks-hottest-day-on-record/ |access-date=19 July 2022 |website=New Scientist |language=en-US |archive-date=19 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220719122614/https://www.newscientist.com/article/2329138-temperature-hits-40c-on-the-uks-hottest-day-on-record/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Of the [[United Kingdom weather records|UK's top ten hottest days on record]], nine have been recorded between 1990 and 2022.<ref>{{Cite news |date=19 July 2022 |title=Heatwave: The UK and Europe's record temperatures in maps and charts |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-62224157 |access-date=20 July 2022 |archive-date=19 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220719234656/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-62224157 |url-status=live}}</ref> The [[2022 United Kingdom heat wave|2022 heatwave]] resulted in the first code red extreme heat warning in the country, instigating a declaration of national emergency, and causing wildfires and widespread infrastructure damage.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Faulkner |first1=Doug |last2=Adams |first2=Charley |date=15 July 2022 |title=Heatwave: National emergency declared after UK's first red extreme heat warning |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-62177458 |work=BBC News |access-date=15 July 2022 |archive-date=15 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220715093251/https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-62177458 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=20 July 2022 |title=Britain counts cost of historic heatwave as 13 die |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/britain-counts-cost-hottest-day-ever-2022-07-20/ |access-date=22 July 2022 |website=Reuters |archive-date=31 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220731100926/https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/britain-counts-cost-hottest-day-ever-2022-07-20/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Sea level rise ===
Between 1900 and 2022, the UK's [[Sea level rise|sea level rose]] by {{Convert|16.5|cm|in}}. The rate of rise more than doubled between the early 20th and early 21st century to a rate of 3–5.2 millimetres per year.<ref name="MO">{{Cite news |date=28 July 2022 |title=Climate change: UK sea level rise speeding up - Met Office |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-62322574 |access-date=27 August 2022 |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827140920/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-62322574 |url-status=live}}</ref> By 2050, it is predicted that around a third of [[England]]'s coast will be affected, leading to almost 200,000 homes needing to be abandoned. The most affected regions will be the [[South West England|South West]], [[North West England|North West]] and [[East Anglia]].<ref name="RS">{{Cite news |date=15 June 2022 |title=Climate change: Rising sea levels threaten 200,000 England properties |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-61795783 |access-date=27 August 2022 |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827140918/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-61795783 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Water and drought ===
[[Drought in the United Kingdom|Droughts in the United Kingdom]] are expected to become more severe.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hanlon |first1=Helen M. |last2=Bernie |first2=Dan |last3=Carigi |first3=Giulia |last4=Lowe |first4=Jason A. |date=30 June 2021 |title=Future changes to high impact weather in the UK |journal=Climatic Change |language=en |volume=166 |issue=3 |page=50 |doi=10.1007/s10584-021-03100-5 |bibcode=2021ClCh..166...50H |s2cid=235690689 |issn=1573-1480 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate change will intensify UK droughts so we must take action now |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg25533992-800-climate-change-will-intensify-uk-droughts-so-we-must-take-action-now/ |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=New Scientist |language=en-US |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827150757/https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg25533992-800-climate-change-will-intensify-uk-droughts-so-we-must-take-action-now/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=UK and Global extreme events – Drought |url=https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/research/climate/understanding-climate/uk-and-global-extreme-events-drought |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=Met Office |language=en |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827151301/https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/research/climate/understanding-climate/uk-and-global-extreme-events-drought |url-status=live}}</ref> Water quality in rivers and lakes may decline due to higher temperatures, reduced river flows and increased [[algal bloom]]s in summer, and increased river flows in winter.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Watts |first1=Glenn |last2=Battarbee |first2=Richard W. |last3=Bloomfield |first3=John P. |last4=Crossman |first4=Jill |last5=Daccache |first5=Andre |last6=Durance |first6=Isabelle |last7=Elliott |first7=J. Alex |last8=Garner |first8=Grace |last9=Hannaford |first9=Jamie |last10=Hannah |first10=David M. |last11=Hess |first11=Tim |last12=Jackson |first12=Christopher R. |last13=Kay |first13=Alison L. |last14=Kernan |first14=Martin |last15=Knox |first15=Jerry |date=February 2015 |title=Climate change and water in the UK – past changes and future prospects |journal=Progress in Physical Geography: Earth and Environment |language=en |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=6–28 |doi=10.1177/0309133314542957 |s2cid=26176502 |issn=0309-1333 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Effects on ecosystems ===
[[File:Western Cattle Egret (Bubulcus ibis) (8079752404).jpg|thumb|Climate change has led to an increase of warmer-weather adapted species in the UK, such as the [[cattle egret]].]]
Warming temperatures are affecting [[Fauna of Great Britain|wildlife]] and [[Flora of Great Britain and Ireland|plant]] life. Some [[Species distribution|species' ranges]] are shifting north, and Scottish [[alpine plant]]s have declined.<ref name="IR">{{Cite web |date=16 November 2015 |title=Climate change putting UK wildlife 'increasingly at risk' |url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2015/nov/16/climate-change-putting-uk-wildlife-increasingly-at-risk |access-date=26 August 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en |archive-date=26 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220826183930/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2015/nov/16/climate-change-putting-uk-wildlife-increasingly-at-risk |url-status=live}}</ref> With [[Spring (season)|spring]] coming earlier each year, many plant and animal species are unable to adapt quickly enough.<ref name="MO" /> [[Climate change and birds|Birds are affected by climate change]], with warm weather species like [[cattle egret]]s and [[purple heron]]s observed breeding in the UK for the first time in the 2010s, while cold-adapted birds like [[Northern lapwing|lapwings]] have declined.<ref name="IR" /> More regular [[Drought in the United Kingdom|droughts]] also have cumulative implications for many British species and ecosystems.<ref name="BW">{{Cite web |date=3 August 2022 |title=From badgers to bumblebees: how drought is affecting Britain's wildlife |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2022/aug/03/from-badgers-to-bumblebees-how-drought-is-affecting-britains-wildlife |access-date=26 August 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en |archive-date=26 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220826184703/https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2022/aug/03/from-badgers-to-bumblebees-how-drought-is-affecting-britains-wildlife |url-status=live}}</ref> For example, in 2022, [[Ouse Washes]] wetlands was at risk of drying out.<ref name="BW" />

Climate change will also affect [[Climate change and marine life|marine life]] around the British Isles, including some commercially valuable fish species. The distributions of many fish species are expected to shift, with cold adapted species declining and warm adapted species becoming established.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Graham |first1=C. T. |last2=Harrod |first2=C. |date=April 2009 |title=Implications of climate change for the fishes of the British Isles |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1095-8649.2009.02180.x |journal=Journal of Fish Biology |language=en |volume=74 |issue=6 |pages=1143–1205 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8649.2009.02180.x |pmid=20735625 |access-date=29 August 2022 |archive-date=29 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220829141015/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1095-8649.2009.02180.x |url-status=live|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Effects on people ==

=== Health effects ===
<!-- BEWARE! this section is transcluded into [[Health in the United Kingdom]] -->
[[File:Sadleworth Moor - NASA Landsat - 2018-06-27.jpg|thumb|Wildfire on [[Saddleworth Moor]], 2018]]{{Main|Effects of climate change on health in the United Kingdom}}

The [[National Health Service (England)|National Health Service]] describes climate change as a "health emergency", citing the effects of heat waves, floods, and storms on health, as well as the increased spread of [[Climate change and infectious diseases|infectious diseases]] such as [[tick-borne encephalitis]] and [[vibriosis]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Greener NHS » Health and climate change |url=https://www.england.nhs.uk/greenernhs/national-ambition/national-commitments/ |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=www.england.nhs.uk |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827200116/https://www.england.nhs.uk/greenernhs/national-ambition/national-commitments/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

Due to climate change, the UK has experienced a significant increase in severe [[heat wave]]s which have dire health consequences.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Heat mortality monitoring report: 2022 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-mortality-monitoring-reports/heat-mortality-monitoring-report-2022 |access-date=2024-12-16 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bunn |first1=Sarah |url=https://researchbriefings.files.parliament.uk/documents/POST-PN-0723/POST-PN-0723.pdf |title=Public health impacts of heat |last2=Mehrhof |first2=Sara |date=23 May 2024 |publisher=UK Parliament POST |doi=10.58248/PN723}}</ref> The [[2022 United Kingdom heatwaves|2022 heatwaves]] contributed to nearly 3000 [[Excess mortality|excess deaths]] – meaning people who are not expected to die during this period.<ref name="HM">{{Cite web |title=Heat mortality monitoring report: 2022 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-mortality-monitoring-reports/heat-mortality-monitoring-report-2022 |access-date=2024-12-16 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Health Effects of Climate Change (HECC) in the UK: 2023 report |publisher=UK Health Security Agency |publication-date=11 December 2023 |chapter=State of the past and future UK climate |chapter-url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/657043059462260721c569a6/HECC-report-2023-chapter-1-climate-projections.pdf}}</ref> This represents the highest number of deaths during heatwaves since 2004. Most of the extra deaths occurred in those aged over 65.<ref>{{cite web |date=7 October 2022 |title=Record excess deaths in UK's heatwave summer |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/health-63171417 |access-date=7 October 2022 |publisher=BBC News}}</ref><ref name="HM" /> Without [[climate change mitigation]] or [[Climate change adaptation|adaptation]] measures, heat-related deaths could increase sixfold by the 2050s, particularly affecting children, the elderly and people with pre-existing conditions.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Health Effects of Climate Change (HECC) in the UK: 2023 report |date=11 December 2023 |publisher=UK Health Security Agency |chapter=Temperature effects on mortality in a changing climate |chapter-url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/659ff712e96df5000df844bf/HECC-report-2023-chapter-2-temperature.pdf}}</ref>

Flooding in the UK presents another major threat, currently affecting over six million people. This number expected to rise significantly as temperatures increase.<ref name="HE">{{Cite book |title=Health Effects of Climate Change (HECC) in the UK: 2023 report |date=11 December 2023 |publisher=UK Health Security Agency |chapter=Climate change, flooding, coastal change and public health |chapter-url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/657086ad746930000d488919/HECC-report-2023-chapter-3-flooding.pdf}}</ref> Beyond physical risks, floods have severe long-lasting mental health consequences for survivors, including [[post-traumatic stress disorder]] (PTSD).<ref name="HE" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Waite |first1=Thomas David |last2=Chaintarli |first2=Katerina |last3=Beck |first3=Charles R. |last4=Bone |first4=Angie |last5=Amlôt |first5=Richard |last6=Kovats |first6=Sari |last7=Reacher |first7=Mark |last8=Armstrong |first8=Ben |last9=Leonardi |first9=Giovanni |last10=Rubin |first10=G. James |last11=Oliver |first11=Isabel |date=28 January 2017 |title=The English national cohort study of flooding and health: cross-sectional analysis of mental health outcomes at year one |journal=BMC Public Health |language=en |volume=17 |issue=1 |page=129 |doi=10.1186/s12889-016-4000-2 |issn=1471-2458 |pmc=5273816 |pmid=28129752 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mulchandani |first1=Ranya |last2=Armstrong |first2=Ben |last3=Beck |first3=Charles R. |last4=Waite |first4=Thomas David |last5=Amlôt |first5=Richard |last6=Kovats |first6=Sari |last7=Leonardi |first7=Giovanni |last8=Rubin |first8=G. James |last9=Oliver |first9=Isabel |date=30 March 2020 |title=The English National Cohort Study of Flooding & Health: psychological morbidity at three years of follow up |journal=BMC Public Health |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |page=321 |doi=10.1186/s12889-020-8424-3 |issn=1471-2458 |pmc=7104503 |pmid=32223747 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Economic effects ===
According to the Government, the number of households in flood risk will be up to 970,000 homes in the 2020s, up from around 370,000 in January 2012.<ref>[http://www.foe.co.uk/blog/government-gambles-excluding-climate-change-flood-insurance-deal Government gambles by excluding climate change from flood insurance deal] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161019142829/https://www.foe.co.uk/blog/government-gambles-excluding-climate-change-flood-insurance-deal|date=19 October 2016}} FOE 6 December 2013</ref> The effects of flooding and managing flood risk cost the country about £2.2bn a year, compared with the less than £1bn spent on flood protection and management.<ref>[https://www.wwf.org.uk/sites/default/files/2017-09/Developing%20%26%20Piloting%20a%20Natural%20Capital%20Stress%20Test_AECOM-WWF%20Sept2017.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210314191757/https://www.wwf.org.uk/sites/default/files/2017-09/Developing%20%26%20Piloting%20a%20Natural%20Capital%20Stress%20Test_AECOM-WWF%20Sept2017.pdf|date=14 March 2021}} ''[[WWF-UK]]'' May 2017</ref> [[Agriculture in the United Kingdom|UK agriculture]] is also being affected by drought and weather changes.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Taylor |first=Chloe |title=Britain's economy is already seeing a rapid shift due to climate change |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/08/31/britains-economy-is-already-seeing-rapid-change-due-to-climate-change.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823133418/https://www.cnbc.com/2021/08/31/britains-economy-is-already-seeing-rapid-change-due-to-climate-change.html |archive-date=23 August 2022 |access-date=23 August 2022 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref>

In 2020 [[PricewaterhouseCoopers]] estimated that [[Storm Dennis]] damage to homes, businesses and cars could be between £175m and £225m and [[Storm Ciara]] cost up to £200m.<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/feb/20/storm-dennis-damage-could-cost-insurance-companies-225m Storm Dennis damage could cost insurance companies £225m] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420221752/https://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/feb/20/storm-dennis-damage-could-cost-insurance-companies-225m|date=20 April 2021}} ''The Guardian''. 20 February 2020</ref><ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2020/feb/14/storm-ciara-expected-to-cost-up-to-200m-in-insurance-claims-storm-dennis Storm Ciara expected to cost up to £200m in insurance claims] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200806164829/https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2020/feb/14/storm-ciara-expected-to-cost-up-to-200m-in-insurance-claims-storm-dennis|date=6 August 2020}} Guardian 14 February 2020</ref> [[Friends of the Earth]] criticised British government of the intended cuts to [[flood defence]] spending. The protection against increasing flood risk as a result of climate change requires rising investment. In 2009, the [[Environment Agency]] calculated that the UK needs to be spending £20m more compared to 2010 to 2011 as the baseline, each and every year out to 2035, just to keep pace with climate change.<ref>[http://www.foe.co.uk/blog/camerons-claims-flood-defences-dont-stack Cameron's claims on flood defences don't stack up] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171023044516/https://www.foe.co.uk/blog/camerons-claims-flood-defences-dont-stack|date=23 October 2017}} FOE 6 January 2014</ref>

The British government and the economist [[Nicholas Stern]] published the [[Stern Review]] on the Economics of Climate Change in 2006. The report states that climate change is the greatest and widest-ranging [[market failure]] ever seen, presenting a unique challenge for economics. The Review provides prescriptions including [[ecotax|environmental taxes]] to minimise economic and social disruptions. The Stern Review's main conclusion is that the benefits of strong, early action on climate change far outweigh the costs of not acting.<ref>{{cite book |author=Stern, N. |url=http://www.hm-treasury.gov.uk/d/CLOSED_SHORT_executive_summary.pdf |title=Executive summary (short) |publisher=[[HM Treasury]] |year=2006 |series=Stern Review Report on the Economics of Climate Change (pre-publication edition) |contribution=Summary of Conclusions |access-date=28 April 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190701152335/http://www.hm-treasury.gov.uk/d/CLOSED_SHORT_executive_summary.pdf |archive-date=1 July 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref> The Review points to the potential [[effects of climate change]] on water resources, food production, health, and the environment. According to the Review, without action, the overall costs of climate change will be equivalent to losing at least 5% of global gross domestic product (GDP) each year, now and forever. Including a wider range of risks and costs could increase this to 20% of GDP or more. The review leads to a simple conclusion: the benefits of strong, early action considerably outweigh the costs.<ref>{{Cite web |date=22 November 2023 |title=HM Treasury |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/hm-treasury |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080920174308/http://www.hm-treasury.gov.uk/media/4/3/Executive_Summary.pdf |archive-date=20 September 2008 |website=GOV.UK}}</ref>

Climate change made the unusual rainfall in autumn and winter 2023–2024, 10 times more probable and 20% stronger. The rainfall led to "severe damage to homes and infrastructure, power blackouts, travel cancellations, and heavy losses of crops and livestock". The damage to arable crops alone is £1.2 billion, without counting vegetables. Claims for house insurance from weather related disasters increased by more than a third.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Carrington |first1=Damian |date=22 May 2024 |title='Never-ending' UK rain made 10 times more likely by climate crisis, study says |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/may/22/never-ending-uk-rain-10-times-more-likely-climate-crisis-study |access-date=23 May 2024 |work=The Guardian}}</ref> Policies to address climate change can also reduce poverty according to some experts.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Barnard |first1=Helen |last2=Childs |first2=Mike |title=Taking action against climate change could also help end the need for food banks. Here's how |url=https://www.bigissue.com/opinion/tackling-climate-change-food-banks-trussell-friends-earth/ |website=Big Issue |access-date=25 February 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Gadd |first1=Liz |title=Environmental change, hunger and hardship in the UK |date=February 2026 |publisher=Trussell |url=https://cms.trussell.org.uk/sites/default/files/2026-02/External_Environmental_Evidence_Review-Executive_Summary.pdf}}</ref>

== Mitigation ==
{{See also|Greenhouse gas emissions by the United Kingdom#Mitigation}}[[File:Solar panel installation at Grange farm.jpg|thumb|Solar panel installation, Balcombe]]
In 2019, Prime Minister [[Theresa May]] announced the UK would strive to reach [[carbon neutrality]] by 2050, making the country the first major economy to do so.<ref name="LP">{{Cite news |last=Landler |first=Mark |date=1 November 2021 |title=Once a Leading Polluter, the U.K. Is Now Trying to Lead on Climate Change |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/01/world/europe/britain-climate-change.html |access-date=23 August 2022 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=23 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823135033/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/01/world/europe/britain-climate-change.html |url-status=live}}</ref> Prime Minister [[Boris Johnson]] announced in 2020 that UK would set a target of 68% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and include this target in its [[Nationally determined contribution|commitments]] in the [[Paris Agreement]].<ref name="OO">{{cite news |last1=Harvey |first1=Fiona |author-link=Fiona Harvey |date=4 December 2020 |title=UK vows to outdo other economies with 68% emissions cuts by 2030 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/dec/03/uk-vows-outdo-other-major-economies-emissions-cuts-by-2030 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210521184248/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/dec/03/uk-vows-outdo-other-major-economies-emissions-cuts-by-2030 |archive-date=21 May 2021 |access-date=27 December 2020 |work=The Guardian}}</ref>

Calculations in 2021 indicated that, to give the world a 50% chance of avoiding a temperature rise of 2 degrees or more, the United Kingdom should increase its climate commitments by 17%.<ref name="CB">{{cite journal |last1=R. Liu |first1=Peiran |last2=E. Raftery |first2=Adrian |date=9 February 2021 |title=Country-based rate of emissions reductions should increase by 80% beyond nationally determined contributions to meet the 2 °C target |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |volume=2 |issue=1 |page=29 |bibcode=2021ComEE...2...29L |doi=10.1038/s43247-021-00097-8 |pmc=8064561 |pmid=33899003 |doi-access=free}}</ref>{{rp|Table 1}} For a 95% chance, it should increase the commitments by 58%. To give a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 degrees, the UK should increase its commitments by 97%.<ref name="CB" />

=== Energy ===
{{Further|Green electricity in the United Kingdom|Energy Company Obligation}}
[[File:Curious cows - geograph.org.uk - 185448.jpg|thumb|Electricity generated from [[Wind power in the United Kingdom|wind power in the UK]] increased by 715% between 2009 and 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wind energy in the UK - Office for National Statistics |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/articles/windenergyintheuk/june2021 |access-date=23 August 2022 |website=www.ons.gov.uk |archive-date=23 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823101007/https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/articles/windenergyintheuk/june2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]
Under [[Margaret Thatcher]], the [[Coal mining in the United Kingdom|UK's coal industry]] was reduced, with subsidies cut and coal miners' union weakened following a [[UK miners' strike (1984–85)|significant miners' strike in 1984]].<ref name="LP" /> In 2015, the government announced all [[List of coal-fired power stations in the United Kingdom|coal-fired power stations]] would be closed by 2025.<ref>{{cite news |last=Gosden |first=Emily |date=18 November 2015 |title=UK coal plants must close by 2025, Amber Rudd announces |work=[[The Independent]] |location=London |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/energy/12001752/UK-coal-plants-must-close-by-2025-Amber-Rudd-to-announce.html |access-date=7 March 2016 |archive-date=8 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200108215931/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/energy/12001752/UK-coal-plants-must-close-by-2025-Amber-Rudd-to-announce.html |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2021, it brought forward this [[coal phase-out]] target to 2024.<ref>{{cite web |title=End to coal power brought forward to October 2024 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/end-to-coal-power-brought-forward-to-october-2024 |access-date=7 March 2022 |website=gov.uk |archive-date=7 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220307212422/https://www.gov.uk/government/news/end-to-coal-power-brought-forward-to-october-2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Policies and legislation ===
{{See also|Energy policy of the United Kingdom|}}

The [[Climate Change Programme]] was launched in 2000 by the Government in response to the United Kingdom's commitments under the [[Earth Summit|1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development]] and subsequent international climate agreements.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jordan |first1=Andrew |last2=Rayner |first2=Tim |last3=Schout |first3=Adriaan |title=The Europeanization of Britain's Climate Change Policy: A Study in Multi-Level Governance |journal=Political Studies |volume=51 |issue=3 |year=2003 |pages=545–568 |doi=10.1111/1467-9248.00444}}</ref>

There are in place national legislation, international agreements and the [[Directive (European Union)|EU directives]]. The [[Climate Change and Sustainable Energy Act 2006]] aimed to boost heat and electricity micro-generation installations in the UK, helping to cut emissions and reduce fuel poverty. The [[Climate Change Act 2008]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Averchenkova |first1=Alina |last2=Fankhauser |first2=Sam |last3=Finnegan |first3=Jared J. |date=7 February 2021 |title=The impact of strategic climate legislation: evidence from expert interviews on the UK Climate Change Act |journal=Climate Policy |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=251–263 |doi=10.1080/14693062.2020.1819190 |s2cid=222114592 |issn=1469-3062 |doi-access=free}}</ref> makes it the duty of the Secretary of State to ensure the net UK carbon account for all six [[Kyoto Protocol|Kyoto]] greenhouse gases for 2050 is at least 80% lower than 1990. It also created the independent [[Climate Change Committee]] to advise the government on policies to reach its goals. The Act made the UK the first country to legally mandate reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.<ref name="LP" />

These targets have since been expanded on in the UK's Sixth Carbon Budget of 2021, which set the targets of reducing carbon emissions by 78% in relation to 1990 levels by 2035, and reaching net zero emissions by 2050.<ref>{{Cite web |title=UK enshrines new target in law to slash emissions by 78% by 2035 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-enshrines-new-target-in-law-to-slash-emissions-by-78-by-2035 |access-date=2024-02-16 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref> The [[Health and Care Act 2022]] includes a target of carbon neutrality for the [[National Health Service (England)|National Health Service]] by 2040, and an 80% reduction in emissions by 2028–32.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Greener NHS » Delivering a net zero NHS |url=https://www.england.nhs.uk/greenernhs/a-net-zero-nhs/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220814072545/https://www.england.nhs.uk/greenernhs/a-net-zero-nhs/ |archive-date=14 August 2022 |access-date=26 August 2022 |website=www.england.nhs.uk}}</ref>

In May 2019, Parliament approved a motion declaring a [[Climate emergency declarations in the United Kingdom|national climate change emergency]]. This does not legally compel the government to act, however.<ref name="bbc.com"/> The [[Climate and Ecological Emergency Bill]] was tabled as an [[early day motion]] in September 2020 and received its [[first reading]] the same day.<ref>{{cite news|date=2 September 2020|title=Climate emergency bill offers real hope|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/sep/02/climate-emergency-bill-offers-real-hope|access-date=21 January 2021|issn=0261-3077|archive-date=2 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202172109/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/sep/02/climate-emergency-bill-offers-real-hope|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Lock|first1=Helen|date=4 September 2020|title=The New UK Climate Bill: Everything You Need to Know|url=https://www.globalcitizen.org/en/content/uk-climate-bill-explained-extinction-rebellion/|website=Global Citizen|access-date=21 January 2021|archive-date=20 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201220015053/https://www.globalcitizen.org/en/content/uk-climate-bill-explained-extinction-rebellion/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The United Kingdom does not have a [[carbon tax]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Harvey |first=Fiona |author-link=Fiona Harvey |date=2021-02-24 |title=Carbon tax would be popular with UK voters, poll suggests |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/feb/24/carbon-tax-would-be-popular-with-uk-voters-poll-suggests |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428000629/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/feb/24/carbon-tax-would-be-popular-with-uk-voters-poll-suggests |archive-date=28 April 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |work=The Guardian}}</ref> Instead, various [[fuel tax]]es and [[energy tax]]es have been implemented over the years, such as the [[Fuel Price Escalator|fuel duty escalator]] (1993)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fuel duty - All you need to know |url=https://www.politics.co.uk/reference/fuel-duties/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428000630/https://www.politics.co.uk/reference/fuel-duties/ |archive-date=28 April 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=Politics.co.uk |language=en-US}}</ref> and the [[Climate Change Levy]] (2001).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Environmental taxes, reliefs and schemes for businesses |url=https://www.gov.uk/green-taxes-and-reliefs/climate-change-levy |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref> The UK was a member of the [[European Union Emission Trading Scheme]] until it [[Brexit|left the EU]]. It has since implemented its [[UK Emissions Trading Scheme|own carbon trading scheme]].<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Hodgson |first1=Camilla |last2=Sheppard |first2=David |last3=Pickard |first3=Jim |date=2021-02-27 |title=UK carbon trading system to launch in May |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/1157028b-d074-476b-862c-9eec70010dfc |url-status=live |access-date=2021-04-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428001312/https://www.ft.com/content/1157028b-d074-476b-862c-9eec70010dfc |archive-date=28 April 2021}}</ref>

=== International cooperation ===
[[File:Boris Johnson on the Day 2 of COP26 World Leaders Summit.jpg|thumb|British Prime Minister [[Boris Johnson]] speaking at the [[2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference]] in [[Glasgow]].]]Since the [[premiership of Tony Blair]], climate change has been a high priority issue in the [[Foreign policy of the United Kingdom|UK's foreign policy]].<ref name="PC" /> The UK has raised the issue at meetings of international bodies of which it is a member, including the [[G8]] and [[United Nations Security Council]].<ref name="FP">{{Cite journal |last=Sinha |first=Uttam Kumar |date=17 May 2010 |title=Climate Change and Foreign Policy: The UK Case |journal=Strategic Analysis |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=397–408 |doi=10.1080/09700161003659095 |s2cid=154279944 |issn=0970-0161 }}</ref> The UK was also influential on the climate change policy of the [[European Union]] during [[United Kingdom membership of the European Union|its membership]].<ref name="LP" /><ref name="FP" />

British diplomats have been involved in the negotiation of international agreements in [[United Nations Climate Change conference|United Nations summits]].<ref name="LP" /> Ahead of the [[2009 United Nations Climate Change Conference|2009 conference]] while talks had been stalling, prime minister [[Gordon Brown]] launched a manifesto calling for an international agreement that would bring investment into climate change adaptation in developing countries.<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 June 2009 |title=Gordon Brown puts $100bn price tag on climate adaptation |url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2009/jun/26/gordon-brown-climate-adaptation-cost |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en |archive-date=27 August 2022 |issn=1476-4687 |access-date=27 August 2022 |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827224325/https://www.nature.com/articles/news.2009.604 Climate Pact]] was negotiated and agreed.<ref>{{Cite news |date=24 January 2022 |title=Climate change: 'Fragile win' at COP26 summit under threat |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-60115969 |access-date=27 August 2022 |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827144740/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-60115969 |url-status=live}}</ref> In the lead-up to the conference, [[Richard Moore (diplomat)|Richard Moore]] said the [[Secret Intelligence Service]] had begun monitoring the activities of major polluters to ensure they adhere to their commitments on mitigation<ref>{{Cite web |title=MI6 'green spying' on biggest polluters to ensure nations keep climate change promises |url=https://news.sky.com/story/mi6-green-spying-on-biggest-polluters-to-ensure-nations-keep-climate-change-promises-12286458 |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=Sky News |language=en |archive-date=27 August 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> and the [[Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office]] said it would put £290m towards climate change initiatives in developing countries.<ref>{{Cite news |date=8 November In 2025, the United Kingdom together with [[European Union]] [[China]], [[Brazil]] and others, joined the [[Climate Coalition (COP30 proposal)|Global carbon market coalition]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Global carbon market coalition proposed by Brazil has gained membership in eleven countries |url=https://cop30.br/en/news-about-cop30/global-carbon-market-coalition-proposed-by-brazil-has-gained-membership-in-eleven-countries |website=COP 30 Brazil Amazonia Belem 2025 |access-date=12 November 2025}}</ref> According to some calculations, a global carbon market can speed up emission reduction seven-fold.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-16 |title=Building a Climate Coalition: Aligning Carbon Pricing, Trade, and Development |url=https://salatainstitute.harvard.edu/building-a-climate-coalition-gcpp-flagship-report/ |access-date=2025-10-07 |website=The Salata Institute |language=en}}</ref>

=== Policy Instruments ===

==== Climate Change Levy (CCL) ====
A [[Climate Change Levy]] is a tax on carbon use in industry, commerce and the public sector introduced by the British government in 2001, with the overall aim of promoting carbon efficiency and stimulating investment in low carbon technology.<ref>[http://www.decc.gov.uk/en/content/cms/emissions/ccas/cc_levy/cc_levy.aspx DECC website. ''Climate Change Levy''. Accessed 16/12/2011]</ref> While representing what is classed as a "market-based instrument,"<ref>Jordan, A., Wurzel, R. K. W. & Zito, A. R. Comparative Conclusions-'New' Environmental Policy Instruments: An Evolution or a Revolution in Environmental Policy?. ''Environmental Politics''. Volume 12 2003, p. 201–224 (p. 203)</ref> in that it represents an economic incentive to manage carbon usage more effectively, the CCL is not what is understood as market governance. This is because CCL is not representative of the market steering actors in their carbon behaviour, but the government imposing a sanction<ref>Heritier, A. & Lehmkuhl, D. Introduction: The Shadow of Hierarchy and New Modes of Governance. ''Journal of Public Policy''. Volume 28 2008, pp. 1–17 (p. 13).</ref> to govern behaviour, which is constitutive of hierarchical governance.

==== Climate Change Agreements (CCAs) ====
Introduced at the same time as the CCL, [[Climate Change Agreement]]s are "negotiated agreements between sector industry organisations and the government"<ref>Smith, S. & Swierzbinski, J. Assessing the performance of the UK ETS. ''Environmental Resource Economics''. Volume 37 2007, pp. 131–158 (p. 134)</ref> whereby "energy-intensive industries can obtain a 65% discount from the CCL, provided they meet challenging targets for improving their [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]] or reducing carbon emissions".<ref>DECC website. ''Climate Change Agreements''. Accessed 16/12/2011.[http://www.decc.gov.uk/en/content/cms/emissions/ccas/ccas.aspx].</ref> This is an example of governing carbon behaviour in a more indirect fashion. The DECC is still the authoritative body, but these voluntary agreements represent their attempt to create an atmosphere where it is seen as advantageous to business to manage carbon emissions.<ref>Okereke, C. An Exploration of Motivations, Drivers and Barriers to Carbon Management: The UK FTSE 100. ''European Management Journal''. Volume 25, pp. 475–486.</ref> They have not done this through traditional regulatory controls, in that they have not imposed this rule upon industry. By instead offering businesses incentives to reduce carbon emissions through a tax reduction, they are enhancing the desire of business sectors to make the choice to become more carbon efficient.<ref>Sorensen, E. Metagovernance: The Changing Role of Politicians in Processes of Democratic Governance. ''American Review of Public Administration''. Volume 36 2006, p. 98–114.</ref> The DECC asserts its authority over the process by the imposition of penalties if participating industries do not comply with their agreed targets. It represents the government concerning itself with the outcome of the policy, rather than regulating the entire process.<ref>Bell, S. & Hindmoor, A. ''Rethinking governance: the centrality of the state in modern society''. Cambridge University Press 2009</ref>

==== Enhanced Capital Allowances (ECA) ====
This represents a further example of a government implemented, voluntary scheme that shapes the carbon behaviour of businesses, but the actual management of this scheme is delegated to a specialised body, [[The Carbon Trust]]. The scheme encourages businesses to invest in low-carbon technology by offering a "100% first-year capital allowances on their spending on qualifying plant and machinery".<ref>[http://www.decc.gov.uk/en/content/cms/emissions/ecas/ecas.aspx DECC website. ''Enhanced Capital Allowances''. Accessed 16/12/2011]</ref> Only new equipment is eligible for an ECA – used or second-hand equipment does not qualify. Eligible equipment, and the criteria they have to meet, is published in the Energy Technology List. The criteria are reviewed annually to keep pace with technological progress <ref>[http://www.energy4theplanet.com/what-is-the-enhanced-capital-allowance-scheme "What is the ECA Scheme". Accessed 6/1/2013] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130121081028/http://www.energy4theplanet.com/what-is-the-enhanced-capital-allowance-scheme|date=January 21, 2013}}</ref>

===== The Carbon Trust and the ECA =====
By providing a management service on behalf of the government, [[The Carbon Trust]] is actually helping govern a part of the carbon sector in England. Although created by the government in 2001, they are a private company, which means that, arguably, they represent the diminishment of central capacity to fulfil governing tasks.<ref name="Rhodes">Rhodes, R. A. W. The Hollowing out of the State: The Changing Nature of the Public Service in Britain. ''The Political Quarterly''. Volume 65 1994, p. 138–151 (p. 139).</ref> However, if the workings of the scheme and the part [[The Carbon Trust]] have to play is examined, then the opposite is true. In this instance DECC involved [[The Carbon Trust]], as a body specialised in energy efficiency, and delegated responsibility to them "to ensure sufficient expertise"<ref>Heritier, A. & Lehmkuhl, D. Introduction: The Shadow of Hierarchy and New Modes of Governance. ''Journal of Public Policy''. Volume 28 2008, pp. 1–17 (p. 9)</ref> is brought to the governing process. It is still the government's decision to delegate such responsibility, and it is their policy that is being enacted. They have simply enlisted the help of an expert body to ensure that their desired outcomes are met.

=== Emissions trading ===
The [[Emissions trading|UK Emissions Trading Scheme]] is a massive part of carbon governance. While it has been argued that this is an attempt to allow markets to govern carbon emissions by incentivising their proper management<ref>Anderson, T. & Leal, D. ''Free Market Environmentalism''. Westview Press 1991, p. 7.</ref> Although emissions allowances are traded and priced through market mechanisms, government institutions, the EU, and the Department of Energy and Climate Change (DECC) have continued to play a central role in regulating emissions trading in England. Scholars have therefore described UK carbon governance as combining market-based instruments with hierarchical state regulation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jordan |first1=Andrew |last2=Huitema |first2=Dave |title=Innovations in climate policy: the politics of invention, diffusion, and evaluation |journal=Environmental Politics |volume=23 |issue=5 |year=2014 |pages=715–734 |doi=10.1080/09644016.2014.923614}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Newell |first1=Peter |last2=Paterson |first2=Matthew |title=Climate for Business: Global Warming, the State and Capital |journal=Review of International Political Economy |volume=17 |issue=4 |year=2010 |pages=679–703 |doi=10.1080/09692290903503679}}</ref>

==== The UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) ====
The former [[UK Emissions Trading Scheme]] was a voluntary [[cap-and-trade]] scheme where participants were allocated an allowance of emissions, which included other GHGs as well as carbon, and if a participating company emitted less than their cap for that year they could trade the remaining allowances. It has now closed to new participants but allowances are still traded. While this may appear as recourse to the market to effectively govern carbon emissions, the fact remains "in order to govern through markets, governments must first create those markets through the exercise of a hierarchical authority".<ref>Bell, S. & Hindmoor, A. ''Rethinking governance: the centrality of the state in modern society''. Cambridge University Press 2009, p124.</ref> The UK ETS was created by the [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] (DEFRA), the then responsible government department, and it was the government's ambitious emissions reduction target that "spurred the UK to innovate with"<ref>Jordan, A. et al. Policy Innovation or Muddling Through? New EPIs in the UK. In A. Jordan, R. K. W. Wurzel & A. R. Zito eds. ''New' Instruments of Environmental Governance?: National Experiences and Prospects''. Frank Cass Publishers 2003, p179-199 (p184).</ref> this particular instrument. The Trading Registry for emissions is also run through DECC, exemplifying the government's centralisation of the process and while it was left to businesses to decide how to manage their carbon emissions, and the market to decide the price, it was the governments desire to reach emissions targets and "reduce [the] economic cost"<ref>Smith, S. & Swierzbinski, J. Assessing the performance of the UK ETS. ''Environmental Resource Economics''. Volume 37 2007, pp. 131–158 (p. 135).</ref> of doing so that was being represented.

A new post-Brexit UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) came into operation on 1 January 2021 following the UK's [[Brexit|departure from the European Union]].<ref>Department of Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy, [https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/participating-in-the-uk-ets Participating in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS)], published 17 December 2021, accessed 15 January 2021</ref>

==== EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS) ====
Introduced by the [[European Commission]] (EC) and launched in 2005, the [[EU Emissions Trading Scheme]] is similar to the UK ETS in the sense that it is a cap-and-trade scheme, but it is mandatory and its participants account for 40% of the EU's total GHG emissions.<ref>European Commission website. ''Emissions Trading System''. Accessed 16/12/2011.[http://ec.europa.eu/clima/policies/ets/index_en.htm].</ref> With regard to carbon governance in England, the emissions trading scheme covers energy-intensive industries and the power sector, which together have historically accounted for approximately 48% of the United Kingdom's greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ellerman |first1=A. Denny |last2=Convery |first2=Frank J. |last3=de Perthuis |first3=Christian |title=Pricing Carbon: The European Union Emissions Trading Scheme |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2010 |isbn=9780521196475 |doi=10.1017/CBO9781139042765}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Skjærseth |first1=Jon Birger |last2=Wettestad |first2=Jørgen |title=The EU Emissions Trading System: A Review of the Literature |journal=Climate Policy |volume=9 |issue=1 |year=2009 |pages=101–121 |doi=10.3763/cpol.2008.0485}}</ref> Because the European Commission exercised legislative authority over the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), scholars have argued that its implementation shifted important aspects of carbon market regulation from the United Kingdom to the European Union, creating a multi-level system of climate governance.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jordan |first1=Andrew |last2=Huitema |first2=Dave |title=Innovations in climate policy: the politics of invention, diffusion and evaluation |journal=Environmental Politics |volume=23 |issue=5 |year=2014 |pages=715–734 |doi=10.1080/09644016.2014.923614}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Skjærseth |first1=Jon Birger |last2=Wettestad |first2=Jørgen |title=The Origin, Evolution and Consequences of the EU Emissions Trading System |journal=Global Environmental Politics |volume=9 |issue=2 |year=2009 |pages=101–122 |doi=10.1162/glep.2009.9.2.101}}</ref>Rhodes cited "the loss of functions by British government to EU institutions"<ref>Rhodes, R. A. W. The Hollowing out of the State: The Changing Nature of the Public Service in Britain.''The Political Quarterly''. Volume 65 1994, pp. 138–151 (p. 138).</ref> ...as evidence of the nation state becoming "hollowed out", although scholars have also argued that the British government retained significant authority over the implementation and operation of emissions trading through its role within the broader framework of multi-level climate governance.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jordan |first1=Andrew |last2=Huitema |first2=Dave |title=Innovations in climate policy: the politics of invention, diffusion and evaluation |journal=Environmental Politics |volume=23 |issue=5 |year=2014 |pages=715–734 |doi=10.1080/09644016.2014.923614}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bulkeley |first1=Harriet |title=Reconfiguring environmental governance: Towards a politics of scales and networks |journal=Political Geography |volume=24 |issue=8 |year=2005 |pages=875–902 |doi=10.1016/j.polgeo.2005.07.002}}</ref>}

==== CRC Energy Efficiency Scheme ====
The [[CRC Energy Efficiency Scheme]] is further evidence of the UK government's "recourse to specialised regulatory remits"<ref>Bell, S. & Hindmoor, A. ''Rethinking governance: the centrality of the state in modern society''. Cambridge University Press 2009, p. 88.</ref> in order to effectively govern carbon emissions in England. The CRC scheme is a further mandatory cap-and-trade scheme aimed at large public and private sector organisations who account for 10% of the UK's carbon emissions. It seeks to include organisations not covered by the EU ETS.<ref>DECC website. ''CRC Energy Efficiency Scheme''. Accessed 16 December 2011. [http://www.decc.gov.uk/en/content/cms/emissions/crc_efficiency/crc_efficiency.aspx].</ref> It is again reflective of the UK government's disposition towards employing market mechanisms in order to govern carbon emissions,<ref>Smith, S. & Swierzbinski, J. Assessing the performance of the UK ETS. ''Environmental Resource Economics''. Volume 37 2007, pp. 131–158 (p. 133).</ref> and it is they who have imposed this legislation on businesses, representing an exercise of central power. However, a large bulk of the implementation of the scheme is carried out by [[The Environment Agency]].

===== The Environment Agency and the CRC =====
The Environment Agency has a key role to play in the imposition of the scheme. It is responsible for collecting data regarding participating companies' emissions which it then ranks in a league table "based on participant's changes in energy use against a baseline and not their total emissions"<ref>Environmental Agency website. ''CRC Energy Efficiency Scheme''. Accessed 16/12/2011. [http://www.environment-agency.gov.uk/business/topics/pollution/126698.aspx].</ref> with the hope that carbon efficiency will become a "reputational issue"<ref>[http://www.decc.gov.uk/en/content/cms/emissions/crc_efficiency/crc_efficiency.aspx DECC website. ''CRC Energy Efficiency Scheme''. Accessed 16/12/2011]</ref> for those involved. [[The Environment Agency]] also hosts the CRC Registry where participants can register details and trade their emissions. It is also responsible for administering any sanctions for non-compliance. This is a classic example of the government using the skills of, in this case, a non-governmental public body in order to administer a policy they have established. Again, it is not an example of the power to govern being taken away from central government as the "enactment of legislation is evident as an explicit assertion of hierarchy".<ref>Heritier, A. & Lehmkuhl, D. Introduction: The Shadow of Hierarchy and New Modes of Governance. ''Journal of Public Policy''. Volume 28 2008, pp. 1–17 (p. 8).</ref> It is the government who has delegated this responsibility to [[The Environment Agency]], and they remain the ultimate statutory authority for the scheme.

==Adaptation==
The UK Climate Change Risk Assessment sets out the risks facing the UK. It informs the National Adaptation Programme.<ref name="PI">{{Cite web |title=Climate change adaptation: policy information |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/climate-change-adaptation-policy-information/climate-change-adaptation-policy-information |website=GOV.UK}}</ref>

The [[National Adaptation Programme]] (NAP) seek to create a "climate-ready society" and expects households to adapt to climate change. The NAP outline actions the government and other entities will take to adapt to climate change challenges e.g. in England over a five-year period. They cover aspects such as the natural environment, infrastructure, people and the built environment, business and industry, and local government sectors.<ref name="PI" /> NAP3 explains the government's plans to adapt to climate change between 2023 and 2028.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Understanding climate adaptation and the third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/third-national-adaptation-programme-nap3/understanding-climate-adaptation-and-the-third-national-adaptation-programme-nap3 |website=GOV.UK}}</ref>

A systematic review in [[Climatic Change (journal)|''Climatic Change'']] concluded many [[Housing in the United Kingdom|households in the UK]] struggled to achieve long-term adaptive capacity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Porter |first1=James J. |last2=Dessai |first2=Suraje |last3=Tompkins |first3=Emma L. |date=1 November 2014 |title=What do we know about UK household adaptation to climate change? A systematic review |journal=Climatic Change |language=en |volume=127 |issue=2 |pages=371–379 |bibcode=2014ClCh..127..371P |doi=10.1007/s10584-014-1252-7 |issn=1573-1480 |pmc=4372777 |pmid=25834299 }}</ref> Increased flood risk has implications for the UK's privatised [[insurance]] sector and relevant governance of it.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Keskitalo |first1=E. Carina H. |last2=Vulturius |first2=Gregor |last3=Scholten |first3=Peter |date=1 March 2014 |title=Adaptation to climate change in the insurance sector: examples from the UK, Germany and the Netherlands |journal=Natural Hazards |language=en |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=315–334 |doi=10.1007/s11069-013-0912-7 |issn=1573-0840 |s2cid=113397575 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The [[Bank of England]] has outlined a policy of maintaining financial stability amid climate change effects on the UK.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How is the Bank of England responding to climate change? |url=https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/knowledgebank/how-is-the-bank-of-england-responding-to-climate-change |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823133410/https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/knowledgebank/how-is-the-bank-of-england-responding-to-climate-change |archive-date=23 August 2022 |access-date=23 August 2022 |website=www.bankofengland.co.uk |language=en}}</ref> The town of [[Happisburgh]], where homes are being affected by [[coastal erosion]] and sea level rise, is the location of a "Pathfinder" project where owners of homes about to fall into the sea were offered market prices to [[Managed retreat|relocate inland]].<ref name="RS" />

[[The Wildlife Trusts]] have suggested [[Reintroduction of beavers to Europe|reintroduction]] of [[Eurasian beaver]]s improves resilience of British rivers and wetlands to droughts, create carbon sinks and prevent flooding.<ref>{{Cite web |date=22 August 2022 |title=Drone photos show 'incredible' impact of beavers during drought |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/climate-change/news/drought-heatwave-devon-beavers-photos-b2149993.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827050850/https://www.independent.co.uk/climate-change/news/drought-heatwave-devon-beavers-photos-b2149993.html |archive-date=27 August 2022 |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=21 July 2022 |title=New legal protections for wild beavers in England a 'gamechanger' |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/climate-change/news/wild-beaver-england-government-legislation-b2128333.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827151927/https://www.independent.co.uk/climate-change/news/wild-beaver-england-government-legislation-b2128333.html |archive-date=27 August 2022 |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref>

=== Public opinion ===
{{Further|Public opinion on climate change}}
[[File:2022 Pew survey - is climate change a major threat - 19 nations.svg|alt=Graph comparing agreement with the statement "climate change is a major threat" between countries, showing that 75% of Britons agree.|thumb |In a 2022 [[Pew Research Center]] survey, 75% of UK respondents agreed climate change is a major threat to the country.]]
By 2021, [[YouGov]] recorded that 72% of Britons believe that climate change is caused by human activity, which had increased from 49% in 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |title=72% of Britons think climate change is a result of human activity, up 20pts since 2013 {{!}} YouGov |url=https://yougov.co.uk/topics/politics/articles-reports/2021/11/02/72-britons-think-climate-change-result-human-activ |access-date=23 August 2022 |website=yougov.co.uk |language=en-gb |archive-date=23 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823132427/https://yougov.co.uk/topics/politics/articles-reports/2021/11/02/72-britons-think-climate-change-result-human-activ |url-status=live}}</ref> According to the [[Office for National Statistics]], as of October 2021, 75% of British adults said that they either very or somewhat worried about climate change, whilst 19% were neither worried or unworried. British women were more likely than men to be worried about the effects of climate change, as were younger compared to older age groups.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Three-quarters of adults in Great Britain worry about climate change - Office for National Statistics |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/articles/threequartersofadultsingreatbritainworryaboutclimatechange/2021-11-05#:~:text=In%20October%202021,%20three-quarters,either%20very%20or%20somewhat%20worried. |access-date=18 August 2022 |website=www.ons.gov.uk |archive-date=5 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220805035242/https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/articles/threequartersofadultsingreatbritainworryaboutclimatechange/2021-11-05#:~:text=In%20October%202021,%20three-quarters,either%20very%20or%20somewhat%20worried. |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Politics ===
{{Further|Politics of climate change}}
In 1989, [[Margaret Thatcher]] made two speeches that are considered among the earliest statements by a world leader on climate change.<ref name="LP" />

Climate change has been discussed by members of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom]]; in 2019, [[Carbon Brief]] analysed mention of climate change in the [[Parliamentary records of the United Kingdom|UK parliamentary record]] from [[Hansard]]. It found that mention of the "[[greenhouse effect]]" and "global warming" had appeared in British parliamentary records since the 1980s, with the term "climate change" used more since the late 1990s. The first mention was by [[Jestyn Philipps, 2nd Viscount St Davids|Jestyn Philipps]] in 1969. It concluded that [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] MPs were the most vocal party on the issue, mentioning climate change 8,463 times, compared to 5,860 by [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] MPs and 2,426 by [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrat]] MPs.<ref>{{Cite web |last=harrisson |first=thomas |date=11 September 2019 |title=Analysis: The UK politicians who talk the most about climate change |url=https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-the-uk-politicians-who-talk-the-most-about-climate-change/ |access-date=23 August 2022 |website=Carbon Brief |language=en |archive-date=9 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220709113150/https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-the-uk-politicians-who-talk-the-most-about-climate-change/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

Before 2005 and 2006, climate change received little political attention in the UK.<ref name="PC">{{Cite journal |last=Carter |first=Neil |date=31 January 2014 |title=The politics of climate change in the UK |url=https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/wcc.274 |journal=[[WIREs Climate Change]] |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=423–433 |doi=10.1002/wcc.274 |s2cid=155062628|url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, between 2006 and 2010, campaigns by environmental [[non-governmental organization]] generated attention towards climate change in [[Mass media in the United Kingdom|British media]], and it became a bipartisan issue in [[Politics of the United Kingdom|UK politics]].<ref name="PC" /> The [[Climate Change Act 2008]] passed with the support of 463 MPs from several political parties, and only 5 against.<ref name="LP" /> Under [[David Cameron]], the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] adopted environmental policies as a means to connect with younger voters, with Cameron's support of the [[Big Ask (campaign)|Big Ask campaign]] being a critical turning point.<ref name="LP" /><ref name="PC" /> The [[Cameron–Clegg coalition|Conservative–Liberal Democrat coalition]] maintained political momentum on climate policy, but criticism from the political right later weakened Cameron's international leadership on the issue.<ref name="PC" /> The Conservatives prioritised the issue during the [[premiership of Boris Johnson]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=11 July 2022 |title=Boris Johnson's climate push loses its champion as Tories eye new leader |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/boris-johnson-uk-climate-push-loses-its-champion-as-tories-eye-new-leader/ |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=POLITICO |language=en-US |archive-date=27 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827224325/https://www.politico.eu/article/boris-johnson-uk-climate-push-loses-its-champion-as-tories-eye-new-leader/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[The Global Warming Policy Foundation]] is a [[climate change denial]]ist think tank and [[Lobbying in the United Kingdom|lobby group]] founded by former [[Chancellor of the Exchequer|chancellor]] Lord [[Nigel Lawson]] in 2009.<ref>{{cite news|date=11 May 2014 |title=Nigel Lawson's climate-change denial charity 'intimidated' environmental expert |url=http://www.independent.co.uk/environment/climate-change/nigel-lawsons-climatechange-denial-charity-intimidated-environmental-expert-9350069.html |access-date=9 September 2022 |website= [[Independent.co.uk]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140511082724/http://www.independent.co.uk/environment/climate-change/nigel-lawsons-climatechange-denial-charity-intimidated-environmental-expert-9350069.html |archive-date=11 May 2014 }}</ref> In 2020, some members of the [[UK Independence Party]] were characterised as deniers who had dismissed climate change risks<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cooke |first=Phoebe |date=14 September 2020 |title=New UKIP Leader Neil Hamilton Thinks Climate Change is a 'Hoax' |url=https://www.desmog.com/2020/09/14/new-ukip-leader-neil-hamilton-thinks-climate-change-hoax/ |access-date=9 September 2022 |website=DeSmog |language=en-US |archive-date=9 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220909084058/https://www.desmog.com/2020/09/14/new-ukip-leader-neil-hamilton-thinks-climate-change-hoax/ |url-status=live}}</ref> and the party has opposed climate policies, with some claims within its 2013 energy policy document found to be based on documents from the Global Warming Policy Foundation.<ref>{{Cite web |date=4 March 2013 |title=Ukip's energy and climate policies under the spotlight {{!}} Bob Ward |url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/blog/2013/mar/04/ukip-energy-climate-policies |access-date=9 September 2022 |website=The |url-status=live}}</ref> The Global Warming Policy Foundation and some members of the Conservative Party shifted to opposing the perceived cost of net zero rather than outright denying the occurrence of climate change in the 2020s.<ref>{{Cite web |date=11 October 2021 |title=UK's climate science deniers rebrand |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/climate-change-skeptics-united-kingdom-science-deniers-rebrand/ |access-date=8 September 2022 |website=POLITICO |language=en-US |archive-date=9 September 2022 |website=POLITICO |language=en-US |archive-date=8 September 2022 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/article/2024/jul/01/at-least-30-reform-candidates-have-cast-doubt-on-human-induced-global-heating |newspaper=The Guardian |date=1 July 2024 |archive-date=1 July 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In January 2025, [[Nigel Farage]] was the guest of honour at the launch of a climate denying lobby group, which was also attended by former UK prime minister, [[Liz Truss]] and Conservative Party shadow minister, [[Andrew Griffith]].<ref>{{cite news |last= Cooke |first= Millie |date= 15 January 2025 |title= Nigel Farage and Liz Truss attend launch of climate denial group led by ex-Ukip head |url= https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/farage-truss-climate-denial-heartlands-b2679862.html |work= The Independent |access-date= 26 July 2025}}</ref>
