======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Energiewende
======================================================================

{{short description|Ongoing energy transition in Germany}}
{{Italic title}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2024|cs1-dates=y}}
[[File:Germany electricity generation by source.png|thumb|Share of electricity generation in Germany - percentage share]]
[[File:Schneebergerhof 01.jpg|thumb|Photovoltaic array and wind turbines at the Schneebergerhof wind farm in the German state of [[Rheinland-Pfalz]]]]

The {{langnf|de|'''Energiewende'''|energy turnaround|paren-left}} ({{IPA|de|ʔenɐˈɡiːˌvɛndə|pron|de-Energiewende.ogg}}) is the ongoing [[energy transition]] by [[Germany]]. The new system intends to rely heavily on [[renewable energy]] (particularly [[Wind power|wind]], [[photovoltaics]], and [[hydroelectricity]]), [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]], and [[energy demand management]].

Legislative support for the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} was passed in late 2010 and included [[greenhouse gas]] (GHG) reductions of 80–95% by 2050 (relative to 1990) and a [[renewable energy]] target of 60% by 2050.<ref name="bmwi-2015-b">{{cite report |url=https://www.bmwi.de/Redaktion/EN/Publikationen/vierter-monitoring-bericht-energie-der-zukunft-kurzfassung.pdf |title=Fourth Monitoring Report "The Energy of the Future" 2014 - Summary |date=November 2015 |publisher=Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWi) |location=Berlin, Germany |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref>
Germany had made progress on its GHG emissions reduction target before the introduction of the program, achieving a 27% decrease between 1990 and 2014. The country would need to maintain an average GHG emissions abatement rate of 3.5% per year to reach its {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} goal, equal to the maximum historical value.<ref name="Hillebrandt-et al-2015">{{cite report |url=http://deepdecarbonization.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/DDPP_DEU.pdf |title=Pathways to Deep Decarbonization in Germany |editor-last=Hillebrandt |editor-first=Katharina |date=September 2015 |publisher=Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN) and Institute for Sustainable Development and International Relations (IDDRI) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160909131930/http://deepdecarbonization.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/DDPP_DEU.pdf |archive-date=9 September 2016 |url-status=dead |display-editors=etal |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref>
Germany's [[energy mix]] has a high {{CO2}} intensity due a significant coal and [[fossil gas]] usage.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bmuv.de/themen/atomenergie-strahlenschutz/nukleare-sicherheit/aufsicht-ueber-atomkraftwerke/atomkraftwerke-in-deutschland |title=Atomkraftwerke in Deutschland |website=[[Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation, Nuclear Safety and Consumer Protection]] |language=de |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324193933/https://www.bmuv.de/themen/atomenergie-strahlenschutz/nukleare-sicherheit/aufsicht-ueber-atomkraftwerke/atomkraftwerke-in-deutschland |archive-date=24 March 2022 |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref>

Germany [[Nuclear power phase-out|phased out]] [[Nuclear power in Germany|nuclear power]] in 2023 as part of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}},<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bundesregierung.de/breg-de/themen/energiewende/fragen-und-antworten/kernkraft |title=Kernkraft |website=Press and Information Office of the Federal Government of Germany |language=de |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130142253/https://www.bundesregierung.de/breg-de/themen/energiewende/fragen-und-antworten/kernkraft |archive-date=30 November 2020 |url-status=dead |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> and plans to retire existing [[coal power plant]]s possibly by 2030, and latest by 2038.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bundesregierung.de/breg-de/suche/einigung-zum-kohleausstieg-1712888 |title=Bund-Länder-Einigung: Fahrplan für Kohleausstieg steht|website=Press and Information Office of the Federal Government of Germany |date=16 January 2020 |language=de |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Appunn |first=Kerstine |date=8 December 2021 |title=What does the coalition deal mean for renewables, coal and the power market in Germany? |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/factsheets/what-does-coalition-treaty-mean-renewables-coal-and-power-market-germany |website=Clean Energy Wire |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> By 2023 the early retirement of the country's [[nuclear power plant]]s was no longer supported by the general public<ref>{{cite news |title=Majority of Germans against nuclear phaseout: Survey |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/energy/nuclear/majority-of-germans-against-nuclear-phaseout-survey/37944 |work=[[Anadolu Agency]] |date=12 April 2023 |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> and the plan was controversial among energy experts, fearing that it could have a negative impact on Germany's goals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Reflections on Germany's nuclear phaseout |url=https://www.neimagazine.com/features/featurereflections-on-germanys-nuclear-phaseout-7941915/ |magazine=Nuclear Engineering International |date=28 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200609012940/https://www.neimagazine.com/features/featurereflections-on-germanys-nuclear-phaseout-7941915/ |archive-date=9 June 2020 |url-status=dead |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref>

== Etymology ==
[[File:Biogas Photovoltaik Wind.jpg|thumb|The main renewable energy sources in Germany: [[Biomass (energy)|biomass]], [[wind energy]], and [[photovoltaics]]]]The term {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} is regularly used in [[English language]] publications without being translated (a [[loanword]]).<ref name="jungjohann-and-morris-2014">{{cite report |last1=Jungjohann |first1=Arne |last2=Morris |first2=Craig |date=June 2014 |title=The German Coal Conundrum: The status of coal power in Germany’s energy transition |url=http://www.indiaenvironmentportal.org.in/files/file/German_Coal_Conundrum.pdf |publisher=[[Heinrich Böll Foundation|Heinrich Böll Stiftung]] |location=Washington, DC, USA |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161010055240/http://www.indiaenvironmentportal.org.in/files/file/German_Coal_Conundrum.pdf |archive-date=10 October 2016 |url-status=dead |quote=The term ''Energiewende'', the Country's transition away from nuclear power to renewables with lower energy consumption, is commonly used in English. |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref>

The term {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} was first contained in the title of a 1980 publication by [[Öko-Institut]], calling for the complete abandonment of nuclear and petroleum energy.<ref name="krause-etal-1980">{{cite book |last1=Krause |first1=Florentin |last2=Bossel |first2=Hartmut |last3=Müller-Reißmann |first3=Karl-Friedrich |title=Energie-Wende: Wachstum und Wohlstand ohne Erdöl und Uran |trans-title=Energy transition: growth and prosperity without petroleum and uranium |year=1980 |publisher=S. Fischer Verlag |location=Frankfurt am Main, Germany |isbn=978-3-10-007705-9 |url=http://www2.hu-berlin.de/sachbuchforschung/CONTENT/SBDB/pix/PDF/Krause-Energie-Inhalt.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160914043645/http://www2.hu-berlin.de/sachbuchforschung/CONTENT/SBDB/pix/PDF/Krause-Energie-Inhalt.pdf |archive-date=14 September 2016 |url-status=live |language=de |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="jacobs-2012">
{{cite journal|first=David|journal=Renewable Energy Law and Policy Review|last=Jacobs|number=4|pages=223–233|title=The German ''Energiewende'': history, targets, policies and challenges|volume=3|year=2012}} In support of the claim that Krause et al. (1980) was the first use of the term ''Energiewende''.</ref>{{rp|223}}
The most groundbreaking claim was that economic growth was possible without increased energy consumption.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://book.energytransition.org/origin-term-energiewende |title=Origin of the term "Energiewende" |website=EnergyTransition.org |publisher=[[Heinrich Böll Foundation]] |date=2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181021232116/https://book.energytransition.org/origin-term-energiewende |archive-date=21 October 2018 |url-status=dead |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> On 16{{nbsp}}February 1980, the German Federal Ministry of the Environment hosted a symposium in Berlin called {{Lang|de|Energiewende: Atomausstieg und Klimaschutz}} (Energy Transition: Nuclear Phase-Out and Climate Protection). The Öko-Institut was funded by environmental and religious organizations, and the importance of religious and conservative figures like {{Interlanguage link|Wolf von Fabeck|de}} and Peter Ahmels were crucial. In the following decades, the term {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} expanded in scope; in its present form, it dates back to 2002.<ref>{{cite web |last=Reichert |first=Tobias |date=28 October 2025 |title=Eine kurze Geschichte der deutschen Energiewende |url=https://leibniz-lab-transformationen.de/2025/10/28/eine-kurze-geschichte-der-deutschen-energiewende/ |website=Leibniz-Lab Umbrüche und Transformationen |access-date=14 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref><ref>{{cite report |date=March 2002 |title=Die Zukunft ist Grün: Grundsatzprogramm |url=https://cms.gruene.de/uploads/assets/Grundsatzprogramm-2002.pdf |publisher=[[Alliance 90/The Greens]] |location=Berlin |pages=74–77 |access-date=14 May 2026 |language=de |format=PDF}}</ref>

{{Lang|de|Energiewende}} designated a significant change in [[energy policy]]. The term encompassed a reorientation of policy from demand to supply and a shift from centralized to distributed generation (for example, producing heat and power in small co-generation units), which replace overproduction and avoidable energy consumption with energy-saving measures and increased efficiency.<ref>{{cite report |last=Löschel |first=Andreas |date=2014 |title=Die deutsche Energiewende |url=https://www.bpb.de/system/files/pdf/WLU5B7.pdf |publisher=[[Federal Agency for Civic Education|Bundeszentrale für politische Bildung]] |pages=2–5 |access-date=14 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref>

In a broader sense, the transition also entailed a [[democratization]] of energy.<ref name="paulitz">{{cite web |last=Paulitz |first=Henrik |title=Dezentrale Energiegewinnung — Eine Revolutionierung der gesellschaftlichen Verhältnisse |trans-title=Decentralized energy production — a revolution in social relations |url=http://www.ippnw.de/atomenergie/energiewende/artikel/de/dezentrale-energiegewinnung-eine-r.html |website=[[International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War]] (IPPNW) |language=de |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> In the traditional energy industry, a few companies with large centralized power stations were perceived as dominating the market as an oligopoly and consequently amassing a worrisome level of both economic and political power. Renewable energies can be established in a decentralized manner. Public wind farms and solar parks can involve many citizens directly in energy production.<ref name="dnr-2011">{{cite web |last=Flieger |first=Burghard |date=2011 |title=Mit Bürgerengagement zur Energiewende |trans-title=With citizen involvement for the Energiewende |url=http://www.dnr.de/publikationen/umwelt-aktuell---archiv-2011/102011/mit-buergerengagement-zur-energiewende.html |website=Deutscher Naturschutzring (DNR) |language=de |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160812002056/http://www.dnr.de/publikationen/umwelt-aktuell---archiv-2011/102011/mit-buergerengagement-zur-energiewende.html |archive-date=12 August 2016 |url-status=dead |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> Photovoltaic systems can be set up by individuals. Municipal utilities can also benefit citizens financially, while the conventional energy industry profits from a relatively small number of shareholders. The decentralized structure of renewable energies, enables the creation of value locally and minimizes capital outflows from a region. Renewable energy sources, play an important role in municipal energy policy, and local governments promote the sources.<ref>{{cite report |last1=Sixtus |first1=Frederick |last2=Riesenhuber |first2=Paul |last3=Wazinski |first3=Constantin |last4=Hinz |first4=Catherina |last5=Salecki |first5=Steven |last6=Baerens |first6=Tidian |last7=Hirschl |first7=Bernd |last8=Kempermann |first8=Hanno |last9=Hönig |first9=Tillman |date=September 2013 |title=Stärkung der regionalen Wertschöpfung durch Erneuerbare Energien |url=https://www.bmwi.de/Redaktion/DE/Publikationen/Studien/staerkung-der-regionalen-wertschoepfung-durch-erneuerbare-energien.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&v=2 |publisher=[[Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy]] |location=Berlin |access-date=13 May 2026 |language=de |type=Gemeinschaftsstudie von Berlin-Institut, IÖW und IW Köln}}</ref>

== Status ==
[[File:Ghg-emissionsgrafik-trend-1990-2019-nach-ksg-einteilung.png|400px|right]]
The policy document outlining the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} was published by the German government in September 2010, six months before the [[Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster|Fukushima nuclear accident]].<ref name="bmwi-and-bmu-2010">{{cite report |author1=Federal Ministry of Economics and Technology (BMWi) |author2=Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMU) |date=28 September 2010 |title=Energy Concept for an Environmentally Sound, Reliable and Affordable Energy Supply |publisher=Federal Ministry of Economics and Technology (BMWi) |location=Berlin, Germany |url=http://www.bmwi.de/English/Redaktion/Pdf/energy-concept,property=pdf,bereich=bmwi,sprache=en,rwb=true.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006040920/http://www.bmwi.de/English/Redaktion/Pdf/energy-concept%2Cproperty%3Dpdf%2Cbereich%3Dbmwi%2Csprache%3Den%2Crwb%3Dtrue.pdf |archive-date=6 October 2016 |url-status=dead |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> Legislative support was passed in September 2010. On 6 June 2011, following Fukushima, the government removed the use of nuclear power as a bridging technology as part of their policy.<ref name="bmu-2011">{{cite report |author=BMU |date=October 2011 |title=The Federal Government's energy concept of 2010 and the transformation of the energy system of 2011 |url=http://www.germany.info/contentblob/3043402/Daten/3903429/BMUBMWi_Energy_Concept_DD.pdf |publisher=Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation, and Nuclear Safety |location=Bonn, Germany |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006040646/http://www.germany.info/contentblob/3043402/Daten/3903429/BMUBMWi_Energy_Concept_DD.pdf |archive-date=6 October 2016 |url-status=dead |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> The program was later described as "Germany's vendetta against nuclear" and attributed to the influence of ideologically anti-nuclear green movements in politics.<ref>{{cite web |last=Olson |first=Erik |date=10 September 2019 |title=A Tale of Two Decarbonizations: How the Path of Least Political Resistance Influenced Climate Action in Germany and the United Kingdom |url=https://thebreakthrough.org/issues/energy/tale-of-two-decarbs |website=The Breakthrough Institute |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> In 2014, then-[[Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action|Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy]] [[Sigmar Gabriel]] lobbied Swedish company [[Vattenfall]] to continue investments in brown coal mines in Germany, explaining that "we cannot simultaneously quit nuclear energy and coal-based power generation."<ref>{{cite web |last=Gabriel |first=Sigmar |date=13 October 2014 |title=Letter from Sigmar Gabriel to Stefan Löfven |url=https://www.altinget.se/misc/SigmarGabriel.pdf |website=Altinget.se |publisher=Federal Ministry of Economics and Energy (BMWi) |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref> James Hansen reports that Gabriel argued in June 2008 that "coal use was essential because Germany was going to phase out nuclear power. Period. It was a political decision, and it was non-negotiable".<ref>{{cite book |last=Hansen |first=James |date=21 December 2010 |orig-date=2011 |title=Storms of My Grandchildren: The Truth About the Coming Climate Catastrophe and Our Last Chance to Save Humanity |publisher=Bloomsbury USA |location=New York City |edition=1st U.S. |isbn=978-1-60819-502-2 |language=en |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EZftCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA181 |page=181 |postscript=}}, describing a June 2008 private meeting of Sigmar Gabriel, James Hansen, and [[Stefan Rahmstorf]] at the [[Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research]].</ref>

In 2011, the Ethical Committee on Secure Energy Supply was tasked with assessing the feasibility of the nuclear phase-out and transition to renewable energy, and it concluded:<ref>{{cite report |author=Ethik-Kommission Sichere Energieversorgung |date=30 May 2011 |title=Deutschlands Energiewende – Ein Gemeinschaftswerk für die Zukunft |url=https://www.nachhaltigkeitsrat.de/wp-content/uploads/migration/documents/2011-05-30-abschlussbericht-ethikkommission_property_publicationFile.pdf |publisher=Federal Government of Germany |website=Nachhaltigkeitsrat.de |language=de |format=PDF |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=The Ethics Committee is firmly convinced that the phase-out of nuclear energy can be completed within a decade using the energy transition measures presented here.|title=Deutschlands Energiewende. Ein Gemeinschaftswerk  für die Zukunft|source=Ethik‐Kommission Sichere Energieversorgung}}

In 2019, Germany's [[Bundesrechnungshof|Federal Court of Auditors]] determined the program had cost €160&nbsp;billion over the last 5 years and criticized the expenses for being "in extreme disproportion to the results." Despite widespread initial support, the program is perceived as "expensive, chaotic, and unfair", and a "massive failure" as of 2019.<ref name=":5">{{cite news |last1=Traufetter |first1=Gerald |last2=Schultz |first2=Stefan |last3=Jung |first3=Alexander |last4=Dohmen |first4=Frank |date=13 May 2019 |title=German Failure on the Road to a Renewable Future |url=https://www.spiegel.de/international/germany/german-failure-on-the-road-to-a-renewable-future-a-1266586.html |work=[[Der Spiegel]] International |location=Hamburg, Germany |language=en |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref>

Russian fossil gas was perceived as a "safe, cheap, and temporary" fuel to replace nuclear power in the initial phase of ''Energiewende'' as part of the German policy of integrating Russia with the European Union through mutually beneficial trade relations. German dependency on Russian gas imports was presented as "mutual dependency."<ref>{{cite web |last=Steinmeier |first=Frank-Walter |date=March 2007 |title=Verflechtung und Integration: Die neue Phase der Ostpolitik der EU |url=https://internationalepolitik.de/de/verflechtung-und-integration |website=Internationale Politik |language=de |url-access=subscription |access-date=12 May 2026}}</ref>

{{See also|Ostpolitik|Wandel durch Handel}}

=== Initial phase 2013–2016 ===
[[File:Energy transition scenario in Germany.png|thumb|Energy transition scenario in Germany from 2012]]
After the 2013 federal elections, the new [[Christian Democratic Union of Germany]] (CDU) /[[Christian Social Union in Bavaria]] (CSU) and [[Social Democratic Party of Germany]] (SPD) coalition government continued the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}, with minor modification of its goals in the coalition agreement. The coalition government introduced an intermediate target of a 55–60% share of renewable energy in gross electricity consumption in 2035.<ref name="german-energy-blog-2013">{{cite web |last1=Lang |first1=Matthias |last2=Lang |first2=Annette |title=Overview CDU/CSU and SPD Present Coalition Agreement – 55% to 60% Renewables by 2035 and More |date=27 November 2013 |website=German Energy Blog |url=http://www.germanenergyblog.de/?p=14825 |access-date=13 May 2026 |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305094413/http://www.germanenergyblog.de/?p=14825 |archive-date=5 March 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The targets were described as "ambitious".<ref name="buchan-2012">{{cite book |last=Buchan |first=David |url=https://www.oxfordenergy.org/wpcms/wp-content/uploads/2012/06/SP-261.pdf |title=The Energiewende — Germany's gamble |date=June 2012 |publisher=Oxford Institute for Energy Studies |isbn=978-1-907555-52-7 |location=Oxford, UK |access-date=13 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> The Berlin-based [[Think tank|policy institute]] [[Agora Energiewende]] noted that "while the German approach is not unique worldwide, the speed and scope of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} are exceptional".<ref name="agora-2015-a">{{cite book |author=[[Agora Energiewende]] |title=Understanding the Energiewende: FAQ on the Ongoing Transition of the German Power System |url=http://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2015/Understanding_the_EW/Agora_Understanding_the_Energiewende.pdf |date=2015 |publisher=Agora Energiewende |location=Berlin, Germany |access-date=13 May 2026 |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160602074457/https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2015/Understanding_the_EW/Agora_Understanding_the_Energiewende.pdf |archive-date=2 June 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> A characteristic of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} compared to other planned energy transitions was the expectation that the transition is driven by citizens and not large energy utilities.{{disputed inline|date=March 2019}} Germany's switch to renewable energy was described as "democratization of the energy supply".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Morris |first1=Craig |last2=Jungjohann |first2=Arne |title=Energy Democracy: Germany's Energiewende to Renewables |url=https://link.springer.com/book/9783319318905 |date=2016 |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |isbn=978-3-319-31890-5 |location=Cham, Switzerland |access-date=13 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> The {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} also sought a greater transparency in relation to national [[energy policy]] formation.<ref name="acatech-et al-2016-b">{{cite book |title=Consulting with Energy Scenarios: Requirements for Scientific Policy Advice |url=http://www.akademienunion.de/fileadmin/redaktion/user_upload/Publikationen/Stellungnahmen/Stellungnahme_Energy_scenarios.pdf |date=2016 |publisher=acatech — National Academy of Science and Engineering |isbn=978-3-8047-3550-7 |editor1=acatech |editor2=Leopoldina |editor3=Akademienunion |location=Berlin, Germany |access-date=13 May 2026 |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161109093507/http://www.akademienunion.de/fileadmin/redaktion/user_upload/Publikationen/Stellungnahmen/Stellungnahme_Energy_scenarios.pdf |archive-date=9 November 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

As of 2013, Germany was spending €1.5&nbsp;billion per year on energy research to solve the technical and social issues raised by the transition,<ref name="Schiermeier-2013">{{cite news |last=Schiermeier |first=Quirin |date=10 April 2013 |title=Renewable power: Germany's energy gamble. An ambitious plan to slash greenhouse-gas emissions must clear some highly technical and economic hurdles |work=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/496156a |access-date=13 May 2026 |doi=10.1038/496156a |language=en}}</ref> which are provided by the individual federal states, universities, and the government, which provided €400 million per year.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last=Curry |first=Andrew |date=27 March 2019 |title=Germany faces its future as a pioneer in sustainability and renewable energy |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=567 |issue=7749 |pages=S51–S53 |doi=10.1038/d41586-019-00916-1 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-019-00916-1 |pmid=30918376 |bibcode=2019Natur.567S..51C |doi-access=free |access-date=13 May 2026 |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Government's contribution was increased to €800 million in 2017.<ref name=":0" />

Important aspects included ({{as of|2016|November|lc=yes}}):

In addition, there was an associated [[research and development]] drive. A chart showing German energy [[legislation]] in 2016 is available.<ref name="bmwi-2016a">{{cite book |title=Overview of legislation governing Germany's energy supply system: key strategies, acts, directives, and regulations / ordinances |date=May 2016 |publisher=Federal Ministry of Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWi) |location=Berlin, Germany |url=http://www.bmwi.de/English/Redaktion/Pdf/gesetzeskarte,property=pdf,bereich=bmwi2012,sprache=en,rwb=true.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006040914/http://www.bmwi.de/English/Redaktion/Pdf/gesetzeskarte,property=pdf,bereich=bmwi2012,sprache=en,rwb=true.pdf |archive-date=6 October 2016 |access-date=14 May 2026}}</ref>

The targets went beyond [[European Union]] legislation and the national policies of other European states. The policy objectives have been embraced by the German Federal Government and has resulted in an expansion of renewable energy, particularly wind power. Germany's share of renewables has increased from around 5% in 1999 to 22.9% in 2012, surpassing the [[OECD]] average of 18% usage of renewables.<ref name="economist-2012">{{cite news |title=Germany's energy transformation: Energiewende |date=28 July 2012 |newspaper=The Economist |url=https://www.economist.com/europe/2012/07/28/energiewende |url-access=subscription |access-date=14 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
Producers have been guaranteed a fixed [[feed-in tariff]] for 20 years, guaranteeing a fixed income. Energy co-operatives have been created, and efforts were made to decentralize control and profits. Poor investment designs have caused bankruptcies and low [[Return on investment|returns]], and unrealistic promises have been shown to be far from reality.<ref name="latsch-etal-2014">{{cite news |last1=Latsch |first1=Gunther |last2=Seith |first2=Anne |last3=Traufetter |first3=Gerald |date=30 January 2014 |title=Gone with the wind: weak returns cripple German renewables |url=http://www.spiegel.de/international/business/wind-power-investments-in-germany-proving-riskier-than-thought-a-946367.html |newspaper=[[Der Spiegel]] |access-date=14 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

{{See also|Desertec}}

Nuclear power plants were closed, and the existing nine plants were scheduled to close earlier than planned, in 2022.

A factor that inhibited efficient employment of new renewable energy has been the lack of an accompanying investment in power infrastructure to bring the power to market. It is believed {{convert|8300|km|mi|abbr=on}} of power lines must be built or upgraded.<ref name="economist-2012" /> In 2010 legislation has been passed seeking construction and upgrade of {{convert|7700|km|mi|abbr=on}} of new grid lines, {{convert|950|km|mi|abbr=on}} have been built by 2019—and in 2017, {{convert|30|km|mi|abbr=on}} has been built.<ref name=":5" />

The [[States of Germany|German States]] have varying attitudes to the construction of new power lines. Industry has had their rates frozen and the increased costs of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} had been passed on to consumers, who have had rising electricity bills. Germans in 2013 had the highest electricity [[price]]s (including taxes) in Europe.<ref>{{cite news |title=Germany’s energy reform: Troubled turn |date=7 February 2013 |newspaper=The Economist |url=https://www.economist.com/news/europe/21571440-germanys-national-energy-project-becoming-cause-disunion-troubled-turn |url-access=subscription |access-date=14 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> In comparison, its neighbours (Poland, Sweden, Denmark and nuclear-reliant France) have some of the lowest [[cost]]s (excluding taxes) in the EU.<ref name="esIndu">{{cite web |title=Electricity price statistics: Electricity prices for industrial consumers |url=http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Electricity_price_statistics#Electricity_prices_for_industrial_consumers |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011150523/http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Electricity_price_statistics#Electricity_prices_for_industrial_consumers |archive-date=11 October 2016 |url-status=dead |publisher=[[Eurostat]] |date=October 2015 |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Electricity prices (table): Half-yearly electricity and gas prices (EUR) |url=http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/4/4f/Half-yearly_electricity_and_gas_prices_%28EUR%29.png |format=PNG |publisher=[[Eurostat]] |date=October 2016 |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

On 1 August 2014, a revised [[German Renewable Energy Sources Act|Renewable Energy Sources Act]] entered into force. Deployment corridors stipulated the extent to renewable energy to be expanded in the future and the funding rates ([[feed-in tariff]]s) will no longer be fixed by the government, but will be determined by auction.<ref name="bmwi-2015-a" />

Market redesign was perceived as a key part of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}. The German [[electricity market]] needed to be reworked to suit.<ref name="agora-2013">{{cite book |author=Agora Energiewende |title=12 insights on Germany's Energiewende: a discussion paper exploring key challenges for the power sector |year=2013 |publisher=Agora Energiewende |location=Berlin, Germany |url=https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2012/12-Thesen/Agora_12_Insights_on_Germanys_Energiewende_web.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
Wind and solar power cannot be principally refinanced under the current [[marginal cost]] based market. [[Carbon price|Carbon pricing]] is also central to the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}, and the [[European Union Emissions Trading Scheme]] (EU ETS) needs to be reformed to create a genuine [[scarcity]] of certificates.<ref name="agora-2015-b">{{cite book |author=Agora Energiewende |title=The role of emissions trading in the energy transition: perspectives and limitations on current reform proposals |year=2015 |publisher=Agora Energiewende |location=Berlin, Germany |url=https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2014/Kohledialog/Agora_Background_Roll_of_Emission_Trading_web.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
The German Federal Government is calling for a reform.<ref name="bmwi-2015-a">{{cite book |author=Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy  |title=Making a success of the energy transition: on the road to a secure, clean and affordable energy supply |date=September 2015 |publisher=BMWi |location=Berlin, Germany |url=https://www.bmwi.de/Redaktion/EN/Publikationen/making-a-success-of-the-energy-transition.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&v=8 |format=PDF |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
Most of the computer scenarios used to analyse the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} rely on a substantial carbon price to drive the transition to low-carbon technologies.

Coal-fired generation needs to be retired as part of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}. Some argue for an explicit negotiated phase-out of coal plants, along the lines of the well-publicized nuclear phase-out,<ref name="agora-2016a">{{cite book |author=Agora Energiewende |title=Eleven principles for a consensus on coal: concept for a stepwise decarbonisation of the German power sector (Short version) |year=2016 |publisher=Agora Energiewende |location=Berlin, Germany |url=https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2015/Kohlekonsens/Agora_Kohlekonsens_KF_EN_WEB.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> but as German minister of economy noted, "we cannot shut down both our nuclear and coal-fired power plants".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Traufetter |first1=Gerald |last2=Amann |first2=Melanie |date=19 March 2019 |title=The Climate Activist vs. the Economics Minister: 'My Generation Has Been Fooled' |url=https://www.spiegel.de/international/germany/the-climate-activist-vs-the-economics-minister-my-generation-has-been-fooled-a-1258429.html |newspaper=[[Der Spiegel]] |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> Coal comprised 42% of electricity generation in 2015. A phase-out of [[fossil fuels]] together with a shift to [[100% renewable energy]] is required by about 2040.<ref name="quaschning-2016">{{cite book |last=Quaschning |first=Volker |author-link=Volker Quaschning |title=Sektorkopplung durch die Energiewende: Anforderungen an den Ausbau erneuerbarer Energien zum Erreichen der Pariser Klimaschutzziele unter Berücksichtigung der Sektorkopplung |trans-title=Sector coupling via the Energiewende: requirements for the development of renewable energy to achieve the Paris climate protection goals, taking into account sector coupling |language=de |publisher=[[Hochschule für Technik und Wirtschaft Berlin]] |location=Berlin, Germany |date=20 June 2016 |url=http://pvspeicher.htw-berlin.de/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/HTW-2016-Sektorkopplungsstudie.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160620121706/http://pvspeicher.htw-berlin.de/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/HTW-2016-Sektorkopplungsstudie.pdf |archive-date=20 June 2016 |url-status=dead |format=PDF |access-date=15 May 2026}}</ref>

The {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} is made up of various building blocks and assumptions. [[Electricity storage]] was hoped to become a useful technology in the future.<ref name="agora-2014">{{cite book |author=Agora Energiewende |title=Electricity storage in the German energy transition: analysis of the storage required in the power market, ancillary services market and the distribution grid |year=2014 |publisher=Agora Energiewende |location=Berlin, Germany |url=https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2013/speicher-in-der-energiewende/Agora_Speicherstudie_EN_web.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="schill-etal-2015">{{cite journal |last1=Schill |first1=Wolf-Peter |last2=Diekmann |first2=Jochen |last3=Zerrahn |first3=Alexander |title=Power storage: an important option for the German energy transition |year=2015 |journal=DIW Economic Bulletin |issn=2192-7219 |volume=5 |issue=10 |pages=137–146 |url=https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/108856/1/820492299.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=15 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> As of 2019, a number of potential storage projects (power-to-gas, [[hydrogen storage]] and others) are still in prototype phase with losses up to 40% of the stored energy in the existing small scale installations.<ref>{{cite news |last=Shellenberger |first=Michael |date=6 May 2019 |title=The Reason Renewables Can't Power Modern Civilization Is Because They Were Never Meant To |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaelshellenberger/2019/05/06/the-reason-renewables-cant-power-modern-civilization-is-because-they-were-never-meant-to/ |newspaper=[[Forbes]] |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

[[Efficient energy use|Energy efficiency]] plays a key but under-recognised role.<ref>{{cite report |author=[[Agora Energiewende]] |title=Benefits of energy efficiency on the German power sector: summary of key findings from a study conducted by Prognos AG and IAEW |date=2014 |publisher=Agora Energiewende |location=Berlin, Germany |url=https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2012/positive-effekte-energieeffizienz/Agora_ECF_RAP_System_Benefit_Study_short_version_web.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160602080036/https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2012/positive-effekte-energieeffizienz/Agora_ECF_RAP_System_Benefit_Study_short_version_web.pdf |archive-date=2 June 2016 |format=PDF |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> Energy efficiency is one of Germany's targets. Integration with national [[electricity network]]s can offer benefits. Systems with high shares of renewables can use geographical diversity to offset intermittency.<ref>{{cite report |author=[[Agora Energiewende]] |title=Increased integration of the Nordic and German electricity systems: modelling and assessment of economic and climate effects of enhanced electrical interconnection and the additional deployment of renewable energies |date=2015 |publisher=Agora Energiewende |location=Berlin, Germany |url=http://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2014/nordic-german-integration-project/Agora_Increased_Integration_Nordics_Germany_SHORT_WEB.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

Germany invested €1.5{{nbsp}}billion in energy research in 2013.<ref name="schiermeier2013">{{cite journal |last=Schiermeier |first=Quirin |date=10 April 2013 |title=Renewable power: Germany's energy gamble |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/496156a |journal=[[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=496 |issue=7444 |pages=156–158 |doi=10.1038/496156a |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
The German Federal Government spent €820{{nbsp}}million supporting projects ranging from basic research to applications.<ref name="bmwi-2015-a" /> The federal government also foresees an export role for German expertise in the area.<ref name="bmwi-2015-a" />

The social and political dimensions of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} have been subject to study. Sebastian Strunz argues that the underlying technological, political and economic structures will need to change radically—a process He calls "regime shift".<ref name="strunz-2014">{{cite journal |last=Strunz |first=Sebastian |date=April 2014 |title=The German energy transition as a regime shift |url=https://www.ssoar.info/ssoar/handle/document/34620 |journal=Ecological Economics |volume=100 |pages=150–158 |doi=10.1016/j.ecolecon.2014.01.019 |bibcode=2014EcoEc.100..150S |hdl=10419/76875 |hdl-access=free |language=en}}</ref>
Eva Schmid, [[Brigitte Knopf]], and Anna Pechan analyze the actors and institutions that will be decisive in the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} and how latency in the national electricity [[infrastructure]] may restrict progress.<ref>{{cite chapter |last1=Schmid |first1=Eva |last2=Knopf |first2=Brigitte |author2-link=Brigitte Knopf |last3=Pechan |first3=Anna |chapter=Who puts the German Energiewende into action?: characterizing arenas of change and implications for electricity infrastructure |title=Qualitative Infrastrukturszenarien für die deutsche Energiewende: Integration von Akteuren und Institutionen in langfristige Technologiezukünfte |series=Energie, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft |date=2015 |url=http://www.transformation-des-energiesystems.de/sites/default/files/de_zentral_Schmid_Best_Paper.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160602092917/http://www.transformation-des-energiesystems.de/sites/default/files/de_zentral_Schmid_Best_Paper.pdf |archive-date=2 June 2016 |format=PDF |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

On 3 December 2014, the German Federal Government released its National Action Plan on Energy Efficiency (NAPE) in order to improve the uptake of energy efficiency.<ref name="nape">{{cite report |title=National Action Plan on Energy Efficiency (NAPE): Making more out of energy |publisher=[[Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy]] |date=December 2014 |url=http://www.bmwi.de/EN/Topics/Energy/Energy-Efficiency/nape,did=667778.html |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="bmwi-2014-b">{{cite report |title=Making more out of energy: National Action Plan on Energy Efficiency |date=December 2014 |publisher=[[Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy]] |location=Berlin, Germany |url=http://www.bmwi.de/English/Redaktion/Pdf/nape-national-action-plan-on-energy-efficiency,property=pdf,bereich=bmwi2012,sprache=en,rwb=true.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
The areas covered are the energy efficiency of buildings, energy conservation for companies, consumer energy efficiency, and transport energy efficiency. Under the plan, the Federal Government expects the German industry and business sectors to make a sizeable contribution to these national energy-saving targets.<ref name="bmwi-2014-b" />

An official Federal Government report on progress under the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}, notes:<ref name="bmwi-2015-b" />
* energy consumption fell by 4.7% in 2014 (from 2013) and at {{val|13132}}{{nbsp}}petajoules reached its lowest level since 1990
* renewable generation is the number-one source of electricity
* energy efficiency increased by an average annual 1.6% between 2008 and 2014
* final energy consumption in the transport sector was 1.7% higher in 2014 than in 2005
* for the first time in more than ten years, electricity prices for household customers fell at the beginning of 2015

A commentary on the progress report expands on many of the issues raised.<ref name="loeschel-etal-2015">{{cite report |last1=Löschel |first1=Andreas |last2=Erdmann |first2=Georg |last3=Staiß |first3=Frithjof |last4=Ziesing |first4=Hans-Joachim |title=Statement on the Fourth Monitoring Report of the Federal Government for 2014 |date=November 2015 |publisher=Expert Commission on the "Energy of the Future" Monitoring Process |location=Berlin · Münster · Stuttgart, Germany |url=https://www.bmwi.de/BMWi/Redaktion/PDF/V/vierter-monitoringbericht-energie-der-zukunft-stellungnahme-zusammenfassung-englisch,property=pdf,bereich=bmwi2012,sprache=de,rwb=true.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=19 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Slowdown from 2016 ===
[[File:2018-01-GerPowerData-Changes-01.png|thumb|Electricity generation, demands and exports in Germany, 2003–2017]]
Slow progress on transmission network reinforcement had led to a deferment of new windfarms in northern Germany.<ref name="oltermann-2016">{{cite news |last=Oltermann |first=Philip |date=11 October 2016 |title=Germany takes steps to roll back renewable energy revolution |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2016/oct/11/germany-takes-steps-to-roll-back-renewable-energy-revolution |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> The German cabinet approved costly underground cabling in October 2015 in a bid to dispel local resistance against above-ground pylons and to speed up the expansion process.<ref name="chambers-2015">{{cite news |last=Chambers |first=Madeline |date=7 October 2015 |title=German cabinet agrees to costly underground power lines |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/germany-energy-power-idUSL8N12722320151007 |newspaper=[[Reuters]] |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

[[File:CO2 emissions Germany.svg|thumb|Development of carbon dioxide emissions]]
Analysis by Agora Energiewende in late-2016 suggests that Germany will probably miss several of its key {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} targets, despite recent reforms to the [[German Renewable Energy Sources Act|Renewable Energy Sources Act]] and the wholesale electricity market. The goal to cut emissions by 40% by 2020 "will most likely be missed{{nbsp}}... if no further measures are taken" and the 55–60% share of renewable energy in gross electricity consumption by 2035 is "unachievable" with the current plans for renewables expansion.<ref name="clew-2016a">{{cite news |date=14 October 2016 |title=Energiewende: What do the new laws mean? |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/germany-set-miss-climate-goals-think-tank/energiewende-what-do-new-laws-mean |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161108195921/https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/germany-set-miss-climate-goals-think-tank/energiewende-what-do-new-laws-mean |archive-date=8 November 2016 |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="agora-2016b">{{cite report |date=2016 |title=Energiewende: Was bedeuten die neuen Gesetze? |trans-title=Energiewende: What do the new laws mean? |series=102/06-H-2016/DE |publisher=[[Agora Energiewende]] |location=Berlin, Germany |url=https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2016/EEG-FAQ/Agora_Hintergrund_FAQ-EEG_WEB.pdf |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref> In November 2016, Agora Energiewende reported on the impact of the {{nowrap|EEG (2017)}} and several other related new laws. It concludes that the new legislation will bring "fundamental changes" for large sections of the energy industry, but have limited effect on the economy and on consumers.<ref name="clew-2016b">{{cite news |date=18 November 2016 |title=Energiewende: What do the new laws mean? |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/vw-cuts-23000-german-jobs-putting-jobs-climate/energiewende-what-do-new-laws-mean |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181216121856/https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/vw-cuts-23000-german-jobs-putting-jobs-climate/energiewende-what-do-new-laws-mean |archive-date=16 December 2018 |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="argyropoulos-etal-2016">{{cite report |last1=Argyropoulos |first1=Daniel |last2=Godron |first2=Philipp |last3=Graichen |first3=Patrick |last4=Litz |first4=Philipp |last5=Pescia |first5=Dimitri |last6=Podewils |first6=Christoph |last7=Redl |first7=Christian |last8=Ropenus |first8=Stephanie |last9=Rosenkranz |first9=Gerd |date=November 2016 |title=Energiewende: What do the new laws mean?: Ten questions and answers about EEG 2017, the Electricity Market Act, and the Digitisation Act |series=103/07-H-2016/EN |publisher=[[Agora Energiewende]] |location=Berlin, Germany |url=https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2016/EEG-FAQ/Agora_FAQ-EEG_EN_WEB.pdf |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

The 2016 [[German Climate Action Plan 2050|Climate Action Plan]] for Germany, adopted on 14{{nbsp}}November 2016, introduced sector targets for [[greenhouse gas emissions|greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions]].<ref name="bmub-2016a">{{cite report |date=14 November 2016 |title=Klimaschutzplan 2050: Klimaschutzpolitische Grundsätze und Ziele der Bundesregierung |trans-title=Climate protection plan 2050: Principles and goals of the German government's climate policy |publisher=[[Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety]] |location=Berlin, Germany |url=http://www.bmub.bund.de/fileadmin/Daten_BMU/Download_PDF/Klimaschutz/klimaschutzplan_2050_bf.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170919021410/http://www.bmub.bund.de/fileadmin/Daten_BMU/Download_PDF/Klimaschutz/klimaschutzplan_2050_bf.pdf |archive-date=19 September 2017 |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref><ref name="bmub-2016b">{{cite report |date=14 November 2016 |title=Climate Action Plan 2050: Principles and goals of the German government's climate policy |quote=Note: This document is not an extract translated from the official plan. |publisher=[[Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety]] |location=Berlin, Germany |url=http://www.bmub.bund.de/fileadmin/Daten_BMU/Download_PDF/Klimaschutz/klimaschutzplan_2050_kurzf_en_bf.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171215072622/http://www.bmub.bund.de/fileadmin/Daten_BMU/Download_PDF/Klimaschutz/klimaschutzplan_2050_kurzf_en_bf.pdf |archive-date=15 December 2017 |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> The goal for the energy sector is shown in the [[#table-climate-action-plan-targets|table]]. The plan states that the energy supply must be "almost completely decarbonised" by 2050, with renewable energy as its main source. For the electricity sector, "in the long-term, electricity generation must be based almost entirely on renewable energies" and "the share of wind and solar power in total electricity production will rise significantly". Notwithstanding, during the transition, "less carbon-intensive natural gas power plants and the existing most modern coal power plants play an important role as interim technologies".<ref name="amelang-etal-2016">{{cite news |last1=Amelang |first1=Sören |last2=Wehrmann |first2=Benjamin |last3=Wettengel |first3=Julian |date=17 November 2016 |title=Germany's Climate Action Plan 2050 |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/factsheets/germanys-climate-action-plan-2050/ |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire (CLEW) |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
