The fifth monitoring report on the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} for 2015 was published in December 2016. The expert commission which wrote the report warns that Germany will probably miss its 2020 climate targets and believes that this could threaten the credibility of the entire endeavour. The commission puts forward a number of measures to address the slowdown, including a flat national {{CO2}} price imposed across all sectors, a greater focus on transport, and full market exposure for renewable generation. Regarding the carbon price, the commission thinks that a reformed [[European Union Emission Trading Scheme|EU{{nbsp}}ETS]] would be better, but that achieving agreement across Europe is unlikely.<ref name="egenter-and-wehrmann-2016">{{cite news |last1=Egenter |first1=Sven |last2=Wehrmann |first2=Benjamin |date=15 December 2016 |title=Experts call for CO<sub>2</sub> price to retain Energiewende's credibility |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/experts-call-co2-price-retain-energiewendes-credibility |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire (CLEW) |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="bmwi-2016b">{{cite report |date=December 2016 |title=Die Energie der Zukunft: Fünfter Monitoring-Bericht zur Energiewende: Berichtsjahr 2015 |trans-title=The energy of the future: Fifth monitoring report for the Energiewende: Report year 2015 |publisher=[[Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety]] |location=Berlin, Germany |url=http://bmwi.de/BMWi/Redaktion/PDF/Publikationen/fuenfter-monitoring-bericht-energie-der-zukunft,property=pdf,bereich=bmwi2012,sprache=de,rwb=true.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221062224/http://bmwi.de/BMWi/Redaktion/PDF/Publikationen/fuenfter-monitoring-bericht-energie-der-zukunft,property=pdf,bereich=bmwi2012,sprache=de,rwb=true.pdf |archive-date=21 December 2016 |access-date=20 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref>

=== After 2017 ===
[[File:V4 Web BOeLL-FF Energiewende (page 16 crop) jobs.jpg|thumb|Jobs in the renewable energy sector in Germany in 2018]]
Since 2017, it had become clear that the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} was not progressing at the anticipated speed, with the country's [[Politics of global warming|climate policy]] regarded as "lackluster" and the energy transition "stalling".<ref>{{cite news |last=Thurau |first=Jens |date=11 December 2019 |title=COP25: When it comes to climate protection, Germany still has a lot to do |url=https://www.dw.com/en/cop25-when-it-comes-to-climate-protection-germany-still-has-a-lot-to-do/a-51621620 |newspaper=[[Deutsche Welle]] |access-date=21 May 2026 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=18 September 2017 |title=Urgent rethink required as Germany's energy transition stalls |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/power-levies-big-industry-concern-parties-debate-potential-coalitions/urgent-rethink-required-germanys-energy-transition-stalls |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire |access-date=21 May 2026 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191212091603/https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/power-levies-big-industry-concern-parties-debate-potential-coalitions/urgent-rethink-required-germanys-energy-transition-stalls |archive-date=12 December 2019 |language=en}}</ref> High [[Electricity pricing|electricity prices]], growing resistance against the use of wind turbines over their environmental and potential health impacts, and regulatory hurdles, have been identified as causes for the slowdown.<ref>{{cite news |date=17 November 2019 |title=Germans fall out of love with wind power |url=https://www.ft.com/content/d8b9b0bc-04a6-11ea-a984-fbbacad9e7dd |newspaper=[[Financial Times]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=21 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Hessler |first=Uwe |date=4 September 2019 |title=German wind energy buildup collapsing |url=https://www.dw.com/en/german-wind-energy-stalls-amid-public-resistance-and-regulatory-hurdles/a-50280676 |newspaper=[[Deutsche Welle]] |access-date=21 May 2026 |language=en-GB}}</ref> As of 2017 Germany imported more than half of its energy.<ref>{{cite news |date=21 June 2016 |title=INFOGRAPHIC: Can Germany's Energiewende ensure supply security? |url=http://www.euractiv.com/section/energy/infographic/infographic-can-germany-s-energiewende-ensure-supply-security/ |newspaper=[[EurActiv]] |access-date=21 May 2026 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170505204030/http://www.euractiv.com/section/energy/infographic/infographic-can-germany-s-energiewende-ensure-supply-security/ |archive-date=5 May 2017}}</ref>

A 2018 European Commission case study report on the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} noted 27% decrease in {{CO2}} emissions against the 1990 levels with a slight increase over the few preceding years and concluded achieving of the intended 40% reduction target by 2020 in unfeasible, primarily due to the "simultaneous nuclear phase-out and increased energy consumption". 50% increase of electricity prices was observed (compared to base 2007 prices). Germany's energy sector remains the largest single source of {{CO2}} emissions, contributing over 40%.<ref>{{cite report |title=Mission-oriented R&I policies: In-depth case studies: Energiewende |url=https://ec.europa.eu/info/sites/info/files/mission_oriented_r_and_i_policies_case_study_report_energiewende-de.pdf |publisher=[[European Commission]] |access-date=21 May 2026 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190418141228/https://ec.europa.eu/info/sites/info/files/mission_oriented_r_and_i_policies_case_study_report_energiewende-de.pdf |archive-date=18 April 2019}}</ref>

In 2018 the slow-down of deployment of new renewable energy was partially attributed to high demand for land, which has been highlighted as a potential "downside" by a WWF report.<ref>{{cite news |date=5 October 2021 |title=Land set to become "new currency" of Germany's energy transition – study |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/land-more-precious-money-future-energiewende-audi-fined/land-set-become-new-currency-germanys-energy-transition-study |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire |access-date=21 May 2026 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211005201104/https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/land-more-precious-money-future-energiewende-audi-fined/land-set-become-new-currency-germanys-energy-transition-study |archive-date=5 October 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

{{See also|Surface power density}}

In March 2019, Chancellor Merkel formed a "climate cabinet" to find a consensus on new emissions reduction measures to meet 2030 targets. The result was the Climate Action Program 2030, which Berlin adopted on 9 October 2019.<ref name=":2">{{cite report |title=Germany 2020: Energy Policy Review |date=19 February 2020 |url=https://www.iea.org/reports/germany-2020 |publisher=[[International Energy Agency|IEA]] |access-date=21 May 2026 |language=en-GB}}</ref> The Program contains plans for a carbon pricing system for the heating and transportation sectors, which are not covered by the EU ETS. It includes tax and other incentives to encourage energy-efficient building renovations, higher [[Electric vehicle|EV]] subsidies, and more public transport investments. The IEA report concludes that "[t]he package represents a clear step in the right direction towards Germany meeting its 2030 targets."<ref name=":2" /> The [[Commission on Growth, Structural Change and Employment|German Coal Commission]], composed of 28 industrial, environmental, and regional organizations, voted on the coal phase-out date. 27 members voted in favor of the 2038 coal phase-out date, with only one regional organization from [[Lusatia]] voting against, and [[Greenpeace]] voting in favor and later releasing a non-binding "dissenting opinion".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Egenter |first1=Sven |last2=Wehrmann |first2=Benjamin |date=23 January 2019 |title=German commission proposes coal exit by 2038 |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/factsheets/german-commission-proposes-coal-exit-2038 |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire |access-date=21 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

As result of phasing out nuclear power and, in long term, coal, Germany declared increased reliance on [[fossil gas]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Merkel |first=Angela |title=Speech by Federal Chancellor Angela Merkel at the 49th World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos on 23 January 2019 |url=https://www.bundesregierung.de/breg-en/news/speech-by-federal-chancellor-angela-merkel-at-the-49th-world-economic-forum-annual-meeting-in-davos-on-23-january-2019-1574188 |website=The Federal Government |language=en |date=23 January 2019 |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=We will have phased out nuclear energy by 2022. We have a very difficult problem, namely that almost the only sources of energy that will be able to provide baseload power are coal and lignite. Naturally, we cannot do without baseload energy. Natural gas will therefore play a greater role for another few decades.  I believe we would be well advised to admit that if we phase out coal and nuclear energy then we have to be honest and tell people that we'll need more natural gas.|author=Angela Merkel|title=|source=Speech at 49th World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos on 23 January 2019}}

A similar statement was voiced by SPD MP [[Udo Bullmann]] who explained that Germany has to stick with fossil fuels as it is trying to replace both coal and nuclear "at the same time", while countries that rely on nuclear power have "easier task replacing fossil fuels".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Michalopoulos |first=Sarantis |date=19 March 2021 |title=German MEP: Nord Stream 2 needs a 'European' perspective |url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/politics/short_news/german-mep-nord-stream-2-needs-a-european-perspective/ |website=Euractiv |language=en-GB |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> In 2020 [[Agora Energiewende]] also declared a number of new fossil gas plants will be also required to "guarantee supply security as Germany relies more and more on intermittent renewable electricity".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Amelang |first=Sören |date=22 April 2021 |title=EU indecision over gas as green investment imperils supply security - German utilities |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/eu-indecision-over-gas-green-investment-imperils-supply-security-german-utilities |website=Clean Energy Wire |language=en |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> In January 2019, Germany's Economy Minister [[Peter Altmaier]] did not want to import "cheap nuclear power" from other countries to compensate for planned phase-out of coal.<ref>{{Cite news |date=28 January 2019 |title=German Economy Minister - Do not want imported nuclear power to make up for coal phase-out: ZDF |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/uk-germany-energy-coal-idUKKCN1PM0GW |language=en |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> In 2021 [[European Green Party|Green]] [[Member of the European Parliament|MEP]] [[Sven Giegold]] admitted that Germany may require new fossil gas power plants in order to "stabilise the more fluctuating power supply of renewables".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kurmayer |first=Nikolaus J. |date=1 November 2021 |title=Green MEP: Germany 'may need some additional gas turbines' to stabilise renewables |url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/energy/interview/green-mep-germany-may-need-some-additional-gas-turbines-to-stabilise-renewables/ |website=Euractiv |language=en-GB |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref>

[[File:Energiemix Deutschland.svg|thumb|right|In the late 2010s, there starts to be a significant decline in the use of (brown) coal and therefore in emissions.]]
The 2020 climate goals were successful in the following areas:<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=6 February 2019 |title=Germany to fall short of 2020 climate goals: report |url=https://www.dw.com/en/germany-to-fall-short-of-2020-climate-goals-report/a-47395605 |website=Deutsche Welle |language=en-GB |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wettengel |first=Julian |date=27 June 2018 |title=Climate goal failure warrants high Energiewende priority - gov advisors |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/climate-goal-failure-warrants-high-energiewende-priority-gov-advisors |website=Clean Energy Wire |language=en |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wettengel |first=Julian |date=14 August 2020 |title=Germany set to reach original 2020 climate target due to pandemic - researchers |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/germany-set-reach-original-2020-climate-target-due-pandemic-researchers |website=Clean Energy Wire |language=en |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref>
* closure of nuclear plants
* increasing renewable energy share
* reducing greenhouse gas emissions

The following climate goals failed:
* increasing renewable energy share in the transport sector
* reducing primary energy consumption
* final energy productivity.
In 2020, a number of previously shut down fossil gas plants ([[Irsching Power Station|Irsching]] units 4 and 5) were restarted due to "heavy fluctuations of level of power generated from the wind and sun"<ref>{{Cite web |date=28 May 2020 |title=Uniper and Co-shareholder decide to return Irsching 4 and 5 gas power plants to the market |url=https://www.uniper.energy/news/uniper-and-co-shareholder-decide-to-return-irsching-4-and-5-gas-power-plants-to-the-market/ |website=Uniper |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> and a new fossil gas power plant was announced by RWE near the former [[Biblis Nuclear Power Plant|Biblis nuclear power plant]] shut down in 2017. The project is declared as part of "decarbonization plan" where renewable energy capacity is accompanied by fossil gas plants to cover for intermittency.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nhede |first=Nicholas |date=19 November 2020 |title=RWE gas-fired plant to supply German nuclear decommissioning project |url=https://www.powerengineeringint.com/gas-oil-fired/rwe-gas-fired-plant-to-supply-german-nuclear-decommissioning-project/ |website=Power Engineering International |language=en-US |access-date=22 May 2026}}</ref> In 2020, a new coal power plant unit, [[Datteln Power Station|Datteln]] 4, was also connected to the grid.<ref>{{cite news |last=Proctor |first=Darrell |date=2 June 2020 |title=Germany Brings Last New Coal Plant Online |newspaper=POWER Magazine |url=https://www.powermag.com/germany-brings-last-new-coal-plant-online/ |access-date=23 May 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref> A new fossil gas power plant will be also opened from 2023 in [[Leipheim]], [[Bavaria]] to compensate for loss of power caused by "nuclear exit" in the Region.<ref>{{cite news |last=Appunn |first=Kerstine |date=11 February 2021 |title=Bavaria gets new gas-fired power plant to ensure supply security |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/bavaria-gets-new-gas-fired-power-plant-ensure-supply-security |access-date=23 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> In 2021, the planned decommissioning of [[Heyden Power Station|Heyden]] 4 coal power plant was cancelled and the plant remains online to compensate for shutdown of the [[Grohnde Nuclear Power Plant|Grohnde nuclear power station]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Wettengel |first=Julian |date=2 June 2021 |title=Supply security: Uniper coal plant needs to stay in reserve a while longer |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/supply-security-uniper-coal-plant-needs-stay-reserve-while-longer |access-date=23 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> In 2022, another coal power plant was restarted in [[Schongau, Bavaria]], for the same reasons.<ref>{{cite news |last=Forstner |first=Boris |date=13 February 2022 |title=Zu wenig Strom für die Bürger: Schongauer Reserve-Kraftwerk erstmals im Einsatz |newspaper=[[Münchner Merkur]] |url=https://www.merkur.de/lokales/schongau/schongau-ort29421/zu-wenig-strom-fuer-die-buerger-schongauer-reserve-kraftwerk-erstmals-einsatz-91340483.html |access-date=23 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref>

In June 2021, professor {{Interlanguage link|André Thess|de}} from Stuttgart university published an open letter accusing [[Klaus Töpfer]] and [[Matthias Kleiner]], the authors of the 2011 Ethical Committee for Secure Energy Supply report that served as the scientific background of the "nuclear exit" decision, of disregarding the basic rules of scientific independence. The analysis promised that phase-out of nuclear energy and full transition to renewable energy "can be completed within a decade". Thess highlighted that the authors lacked the expertise necessary to properly understand and "balance between the risk of more rapid climate change without nuclear energy and the risk of slower climate change with nuclear energy".<ref>{{cite web |last=Thess |first=André D. |date=30 May 2021 |title=Unabhängige Wissenschaft? Offener Brief an Matthias Kleiner und die Professoren der Ethikkommission Atomkraft |publisher=[[University of Stuttgart|Universität Stuttgart]] |url=https://www.igte.uni-stuttgart.de/dokumente/dokumente_es/Thess/02_Offener_Brief.html |access-date=23 May 2026 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210601043430/https://www.igte.uni-stuttgart.de/dokumente/dokumente_es/Thess/02_Offener_Brief.html |archive-date=1 June 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Wetzel |first=Daniel |date=31 May 2021 |title=Wegen Zustimmung zum Atomausstieg: Vorwürfe gegen Ethikkommission |newspaper=[[Die Welt]] |url=https://www.welt.de/wirtschaft/article231463371/Wegen-Zustimmung-zum-Atomausstieg-Vorwuerfe-gegen-Ethikkommission.html |access-date=23 May 2026}}</ref>

High average amounts of wind in 2019 and 2020 were presented in Germany as a success of renewable energy, but when the amount of wind was low for the first half of 2021, use of coal rose by 21% as compared to the previous years. In the first half of 2021 coal, gas, and nuclear power delivered 56% of overall electricity in Germany, with proportionally higher {{CO2}} intensity due to high inputs from coal and fossil gas.<ref>{{cite news |date=13 September 2021 |title=Germany: Coal tops wind as primary electricity source |newspaper=[[Deutsche Welle]] |url=https://www.dw.com/en/germany-coal-tops-wind-as-primary-electricity-source/a-59168105 |access-date=23 May 2026 |language=en-GB}}</ref> According to another analysis by Oekomoderne, in 2021, Germany produced nearly 260&nbsp;TWh of electricity from coal in the first half of 2021, making it the single largest source of energy in that period—as it used "one billion tons" of coal.<ref>{{cite web |title=2021: Deutschland brennt |url=https://www.onebilliontons.org/ |website=1 Milliarde Tonnen |language=de |access-date=23 May 2026 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211019063305/https://www.onebilliontons.org/ |archive-date=19 October 2021}}</ref>

The situation once again raised questions about the future of weather-dependent electricity system that is dependent on fossil energy for stability and its contradiction with the initial objectives of decarbonization.<ref name=":6">{{cite web |last=Shellenberger |first=Michael |date=14 September 2021 |title=Skyrocketing Natural Gas Prices Create New Opportunity for Nuclear Energy |publisher=[[Substack]] |url=https://michaelshellenberger.substack.com/p/skyrocketing-natural-gas-prices-create |access-date=23 May 2026}}</ref>

Projections Report published in 2021 predicted that Germany will miss its 2030 target by 16% (49% reduction vs 65% planned) and the 2040 target by 21% (67% vs 88% planned).<ref>{{cite news |last=Wettengel |first=Julian |date=20 August 2021 |title=Germany to widely miss 2030 climate target – draft govt report |newspaper=Clean Energy Wire |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/germany-widely-miss-2030-climate-target-draft-govt-report |access-date=23 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> Reduction of emissions in other sectors of the economy is also expected to miss the original targets.<ref>{{cite news |last=Wehrmann |first=Benjamin |date=19 October 2021 |title=Government projection report confirms Germany clearly off-track from 2030 climate target |work=Clean Energy Wire |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/correction-government-projection-report-confirms-germany-clearly-track-2030-climate-target |access-date=24 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

In October 2021, over 20 climate scientists and activists signed an open letter to the German Government to reconsider the nuclear exit as it will lead to emissions of an extra 60 million tons of {{CO2}} each year and hinder decarbonization efforts even further.<ref>{{cite news |last=Kurmayer |first=Nikolaus J. |date=13 October 2021 |title=Intellectuals urge Germany to keep nuclear plants online |work=Euractiv |url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/electricity/news/german-intellectuals-urge-state-to-keep-nuclear-plants-online/ |access-date=24 May 2026 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=13 October 2021 |title=Dear Germany, please keep your nuclear reactors online |url=https://cleanenergyrevolution.org/publications |website=Clean Energy Revolution |access-date=24 May 2026 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The new coalition formed after the [[2021 German federal election|2021 elections]] proposed earlier phase-out of coal and internal combustion cars by 2035, 65% energy generated from renewables by 2030 and 80% by 2040. In addition, 2% of land surface is to be set aside for on-shore wind power, and off-shore wind capacity is to be increased to 75&nbsp;GW. Fossil gas role was reinforced as "indispensable" [[transition fuel]] with low-carbon nuclear power imported from France to ensure stability of supplies.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mathiesen |first1=Karl |last2=Hernández-Morales |first2=Aitor |date=25 November 2021 |title=The catch with Germany's green transformation |work=[[Politico]] |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/the-catch-with-germanys-green-transition-transformation-coalition/ |access-date=24 May 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Throughout the year 2021, the single largest source of electricity in Germany was coal (30.2%), an increase of 24.9% compared to 2020 due to a significant drop in wind (−13.3%) and solar (−0.5%) power output in that year. Solar power produced 8.7% electricity, while nuclear power produced 12.6% as it was going through the process of decommissioning.<ref>{{cite news |date=17 March 2022 |title=Kohle war 2021 der wichtigste Energieträger in der Stromerzeugung |url=https://www.destatis.de/DE/Presse/Pressemitteilungen/2022/03/PD22_116_43312.html |work=[[Federal Statistical Office of Germany|Destatis]] |access-date=24 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref>

In 2022, Agora Energiewende warned that Germany has missed its 2020 emission targets and is likely going to miss the 2030 targets, and increase of total emissions after 2022 is likely. Previously celebrated 2020 record low emissions were described as one-off effect of favorable weather and lower demand due to COVID-19 pandemics.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hartz |first1=Katharina |last2=Lenck |first2=Thorsten |display-authors=etal |date=November 2022 |title=Die Energiewende in Deutschland: Stand der Dinge 2022 – Rückblick auf die wesentlichen Entwicklungen sowie Ausblick auf 2023 (Analyse) |url=https://www.agora-energiewende.de/fileadmin/Projekte/2022/2022-10_DE_JAW2022/A-EW_283_JAW2022_WEB.pdf |website=Agora Energiewende |publisher=Agora Energiewende |access-date=24 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Wettengel |first=Julian |date=7 January 2022 |title=Germany off course to 2030 climate target – think tank |work=Clean Energy Wire |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/germany-course-2030-climate-target-think-tank |access-date=24 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> Nuclear phase-out, skyrocketing gas prices, and low wind and solar output resulting in increased reliance on coal were also attributed to the increase in emissions.<ref>{{cite news |last=Millard |first=Rachel |date=8 January 2022 |title=Germany’s meltdown over nuclear power risks a costly winter |work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]] |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/2022/01/08/germanys-decision-abandon-nuclear-power-epic-mistake/ |access-date=24 May 2026 |language=en-GB |issn=0307-1235}}</ref>

In January 2022 the new coalition government reiterated its opposition to the inclusion of [[nuclear power]] in the [[Nuclear power debate#EU Taxonomy|EU sustainable taxonomy]], but also requested that fossil gas is instead included as a "transitional" fuel and carbon intensity thresholds for gas are relaxed.<ref>{{cite news |last=Kurmayer |first=Nikolaus J. |date=24 January 2022 |title=Germany takes firm pro-gas stance in green taxonomy feedback to EU |work=[[Euractiv]] |url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/energy-environment/news/germany-takes-firm-pro-gas-stance-in-green-taxonomy-feedback-to-eu/ |access-date=24 May 2026 |language=en-GB}}</ref> As the subsidies for gas were upheld, a number of new fossil gas plants plan to benefit from the subsidies, while expecting increased profits thanks to "rising wholesale electricity prices" as result of "the last nuclear power plants to be removed from the grid" at the same time.<ref>{{cite web |title=STEAG does what it says - Herne energy site: plans for one of the world's most state-of-the-art gas and steam power plants are in full swing |url=https://www.steag.com/en/news/insights/herne-energy-site |publisher=[[STEAG]] |access-date=24 May 2026 |quote=It is also precisely at this point in time that the last nuclear power plants are to be removed from the grid, so that the Herne gas and steam power plant could benefit from rising wholesale electricity prices. |archive-date=2021-04-18  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210418203939/https://www.steag.com/en/news/insights/herne-energy-site |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2023, Germany achieved its lowest [[greenhouse gas emissions]] since the 1950s with a 20% reduction, largely impacted by a decline in industrial production due to economic factors like the [[Russo-Ukrainian War|Ukraine war]] and high energy prices. The Berlin-based think-tank Agora Energiewende attributed approximately half of the reduction to decreased coal-fired power generation, while only 15% resulted from technological improvements such as enhanced renewable energy utilization. Despite these gains, with over 50% of Germany's electricity now derived from renewable energy, concerns persist about the industrial sector's competitiveness and sustainability, as emission levels in construction and transport have not changed, putting Germany at risk of missing its EU emission targets.<ref>{{cite news |date= |title=German emissions fall by a fifth amid stagnant industrial output |url=https://www.ft.com/content/c9aa5a8e-cd6d-4583-b0af-131c8c448913 |work=[[Financial Times]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Post-2022 ===
Following the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]], Germany announced it would re-open 10&nbsp;GW of coal power to allegedly "conserve [[natural gas]]" following the shortage in Europe.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Eddy |first1=Melissa |date=19 June 2022 |title=Germany will fire up coal plants again in an effort to save natural gas |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/06/19/world/europe/germany-russia-gas.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> This led to a subsequent criticism of ''{{Lang|de|Energiewende}}'s'' strategy, and how this impacted different countries in Europe. [[Michael Kretschmer]] (CDU) declared the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} to be a failure, highlighting that renewable generation is insufficient and baseload capabilities have reached their limits. He called for nuclear power phase-out to be cancelled and remaining reactors restarted, until a new feasible strategy is created.<ref>{{cite news |date=1 August 2022 |title="Braunkohlekraftwerke anzuwerfen, ist Wahnsinn" - CDU-Vize Kretschmer hält Energiewende für gescheitert |url=https://www.spiegel.de/wirtschaft/unternehmen/michael-kretschmer-sachsens-ministerpraesident-haelt-energiewende-fuer-gescheitert-und-fordert-akws-statt-kohle-zum-gas-ersatz-a-daeb7d0e-dad5-458e-adae-ec424a5fb1d1 |work=[[Der Spiegel]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=de |issn=2195-1349}}</ref>

From February 2022, there was a heated debate about pausing the nuclear phase-out and restarting still operational reactors in order to better cope with the [[2021–present global energy crisis|energy crisis]] caused by the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine|Russian invasion of Ukraine]].<ref>{{cite news |date=26 July 2022 |title=Germany rethinks nuclear power exit due to threat of winter energy crunch |url=https://www.ft.com/content/cc422ece-92b3-41fa-a05c-900270bfe824 |work=[[Financial Times]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> In August 2022, German counter-intelligence started an investigation into two high-ranked officials at German ministry of energy suspected of representing interests of Russia.<ref>{{cite news |last=Stark |first=Holger |date=31 August 2022 |title=Russische Spionage im BMWi? |url=https://www.zeit.de/2022/36/russland-spionage-bmwi-robert-habeck-verfassungsschutz |work=[[Die Zeit]] |issue=36/2022 |url-access=subscription |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref>

In October 2022, Germany ministry of energy approved extension of RWE [[brown coal]] [[open pit mine]] in [[Lutzerath]], claiming it is "necessary for energy security".<ref>{{cite news |last=Urbach |first=Job |date=14 October 2022 |title=Duits dorp bij Roermond verliest strijd tegen bruinkoolmijn |url=https://nos.nl/artikel/2448356-duits-dorp-bij-roermond-verliest-strijd-tegen-bruinkoolmijn |work=[[Nederlandse Omroep Stichting|NOS]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=nl}}</ref> In October 2022, the Government also declared the operational nuclear power plants will not be shut down by end of 2022, but will instead operate until 15 April {{Clarify|date=May 2024}} to help cope with the electricity demand through the winter.<ref>{{cite news |last1=von der Burchard |first1=Hans |last2=Fiedler |first2=Tristan |date=17 October 2022 |title=Germany extends lifespan of all three nuclear power plants |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-olaf-scholz-extends-lifespan-of-all-three-nuclear-power-plants/ |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref>
[[File:Kernkraftwerk Isar 01.jpg|thumb|The [[Isar Nuclear Power Plant]] was taken out of service on 15 April 2023.]]
In 2023, the Government declared its plans to remove a key clause from the law that binds all ministries to reduce carbon emissions within their areas of responsibility. The binding target will be the overall 2030 emissions reduction target. The largest {{CO2}} emissions source in Germany is its electricity production, and in that sector, emissions have roughly halved from its peak in 2007 until 2023.<ref name=":7">{{cite web |date=28 March 2022 |title=Germany {{!}} Electricity Trends |url=https://ember-climate.org/countries-and-regions/countries/germany/ |website=Ember |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802231036/https://ember-climate.org/countries-and-regions/countries/germany/ |archive-date=2 August 2022 |access-date=25 May 2026}}</ref> 2020 already saw a similar decline as 2023, as electricity demand dropped massively due to COVID-19 lockdowns, leading to an annual average {{CO2}} intensity of German electricity production of 364 gCO<sub>2</sub>/kWh (2023: 380 gCO<sub>2</sub>/kWh).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Icha |first1=Petra |last2=Lauf |first2=Thomas |date=27 June 2024 |title=Entwicklung der spezifischen Treibhausgas-Emissionen des deutschen Strommix in den Jahren 1990 - 2023 |url=https://www.umweltbundesamt.de/en/publikationen/entwicklung-der-spezifischen-treibhausgas-10 |publisher=[[Umweltbundesamt]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> In 2022, the cut-off from Russian gas led to a brief restarting of coal power plants, meaning the share of coal in electricity production increased from 24% in 2020 to 32% in 2022, before going down to 27% in 2023.<ref name=":7" />

In 2023 Energy Economics Institute (EWI) warned that around 50 new fossil gas powered plants need to be built to "compensate for the weather-dependent production of wind and solar power" with the overall cost reaching €60&nbsp;billion. The budget is not secured by the Government nor available from the electricity sales.<ref>{{cite news |last=Wetzel |first=Daniel |date=17 January 2024 |title=Energiewende: Die nächsten 60 Milliarden fehlen – Habeck braucht Geld für Back-up-Kraftwerke |url=https://www.welt.de/wirtschaft/plus249357496/Habeck-braucht-Geld-fuer-Kraftwerke-Die-naechsten-60-Milliarden-fehlen.html |work=[[Die Welt]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Wallenhauer |first=Robert |date=4 January 2024 |title=Übergang zu erneuerbaren Energien: Deutschland braucht 60 Milliarden Euro für Reservekraftwerke |url=https://www.merkur.de/wirtschaft/uebergang-zu-erneuerbaren-energien-energiewende-deutschland-braucht-60-milliarden-reservekraftwerke-zr-92757679.html |work=[[Münchner Merkur|Merkur.de]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref> To move away from coal, in February 2024, the Federal Government agreed to subsidize 10&nbsp;GW of [[Hydrogen economy|hydrogen-ready]] gas plants. In the first years{{Clarify|date=May 2024}}, the plants will use fossil gas and are expected to be switched over to hydrogen between 2035 and 2040.<ref>{{cite news |last=Alkousaa |first=Riham |date=5 February 2024 |title=Germany outlines $17 bln plan to subsidise gas-to-hydrogen shift |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/germany-agrees-subsidy-plans-hydrogen-ready-gas-power-plants-2024-02-05/ |work=[[Reuters]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref> The plants will mainly provide backup capacity in times where solar and wind power are low. As running plants this way is not economically feasible, utilities will be paid for maintaining the baseload capacity.<ref>{{cite news |date=5 February 2024 |title=Förderung für Gaskraftwerke: Ampel einigt sich auf Kraftwerksstrategie |url=https://www.tagesschau.de/inland/kraftwerksstrategie-regierung-100.html |work=[[Tagesschau (German TV programme)|tagesschau.de]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref>

The last three nuclear power plants in Germany—[[Emsland Nuclear Power Plant|Emsland]], [[Isar Nuclear Power Plant|Isar II]] and [[Neckarwestheim Nuclear Power Plant|Neckarwestheim II]]—were shut down on 15 April 2023.<ref>{{cite news |last=Gavin |first=Gabriel |date=5 February 2024 |title=After scrapping nuclear reactors, Germany to spend billions on new gas power plants |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/nuclear-reactors-germany-invest-gas-power-plants-energy/ |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

In March 2024, Federal Audit Office published a report in which it assessed the policy as not meeting goals on a number of points: the planned 80% share of renewable energy requires [[Dispatchable generation|dispatchable sources]] but the assumed 10&nbsp;GW in fossil gas generation is neither sufficient nor on schedule; extension of electric grid is behind the schedule by {{Convert|6000|km|mi|abbr=on}} and 7 years; security of the supply chain is not sufficiently assessed; system costs to ensure 24/7 generation are underestimated and based on "best-case" scenarios; capacity installed in renewables is behind the schedule by 30%, whereas demand is expected to grow by 30% as result of electrification of heating and transport.<ref>{{cite report |date=7 March 2024 |title=Bericht nach § 99 BHO zur Umsetzung der Energiewende im Hinblick auf die Versorgungssicherheit, Bezahlbarkeit und Umweltverträglichkeit der Stromversorgung |url=https://www.bundesrechnungshof.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/DE/Berichte/2024/energiewende-volltext.pdf |publisher=[[Bundesrechnungshof]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=de}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Dierks |first=Stefanie |date=7 March 2024 |title=Special report: Court of Auditors considers power supply jeopardised |url=https://www.energate-messenger.com/news/242052/court-of-auditors-considers-power-supply-jeopardised |work=energate messenger |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=en |archive-date=2024-04-03  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240403111433/https://www.energate-messenger.com/news/242052/court-of-auditors-considers-power-supply-jeopardised |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On 1 January 2025 Germany produced 120% of its electricity demand with renewables.<ref name="Sorge">{{cite news |last=Sorge |first=Nils-Viktor |date=2 January 2025 |title=Stürmischer Neujahrstag: Deutschland deckt Stromverbrauch zu 125 Prozent aus erneuerbaren Energien |url=https://www.spiegel.de/wirtschaft/stuermisches-wetter-an-neujahr-deutschland-deckt-strombedarf-zu-125-prozent-aus-erneuerbaren-energien-a-5642a01e-9447-4749-9372-ad6b21341a49 |work=[[Der Spiegel]] |access-date=25 May 2026 |language=de |issn=2195-1349}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=SMARD Marktdaten visualisieren |url=https://www.smard.de/home/marktdaten |website=www.smard.de |publisher=[[Federal Network Agency]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250119220540/https://www.smard.de/home/marktdaten |archive-date=19 January 2025 |access-date=25 May 2026}}</ref> During 2024 Germany added 3&nbsp;GW of wind energy and 15&nbsp;GW of solar. In 2024, 54% of Germany's electricity demand was produced by renewables.<ref name="Sorge"/>

On 7 April 2026 Germany minister of energy [[Katherina Reiche]] published an article in which she admitted that German society has "calmed itself down with ambitious goals" of the Energiewende while energy prices exploded, which led to deindustrialisation and highlighted that while electricity generation from renewables "does not issue bills [for fuel]" it results in massive grid balancing costs - "ETS costs, capacity reserve, grid reserve, redispatch costs, grid subsidies, subsidies for reducing energy prices", which total of 36 billion euros per year. She also criticized the phase-out of low-carbon and dispatchable nuclear generation.<ref>{{cite news |last=Reiche |first=Katherina |date=7 April 2026 |title=Schluss mit der Selbsttäuschung in der Energiepolitik |url=https://www.faz.net/aktuell/wirtschaft/katherina-reiche-in-der-f-a-z-schluss-mit-der-selbsttaeuschung-in-der-energiepolitik-accg-200707552.html |website=[[Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung|FAZ.NET]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=25 May 2026}}</ref>

== Criticism ==
[[File:Electricity prices for EU household consumers, second half 2024.png|thumb|right|2024 Electricity prices for EU household consumers]][[File:Electricity-price-germany-components.png|alt= Components electricity price Germany|thumb|Components of the German electricity price for households in 2016<ref>{{cite web |title=Electricity Prices in Europe – Who Pays the Most? |url=https://1-stromvergleich.com/electricity-prices-europe/ |website=Stromvergleich |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160818121615/https://1-stromvergleich.com/electricity-prices-europe/ |archive-date=18 August 2016 |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>]]

The {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} has been criticized for the high costs, the early nuclear phase-out which increased carbon emissions, continuation or increase in use of fossil fuels,<ref name="cleanenergywire.org">{{cite news |last=Amelang |first=Sören |date=26 February 2020 |title=Gas-fired power generation reaches record high in Germany |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/news/gas-fired-power-generation-reaches-record-high-germany |work=Clean Energy Wire |language=en |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> risks to power supply stability and the [[environmental damage of biomass]].<ref name=":6" />

German association of local utilities VKU said "the strategy creates significant risks to the stability of power supply in case of 'lengthy periods' of weather unsuitable for wind and solar generation since energy storage in Germany is 'largely non-existent{{' "}}.<ref>{{cite news |last=Eckert |first=Vera |date=19 July 2019 |title=Does renewables pioneer Germany risk running out of power? |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-europe-power-supply-insight-idUSKCN1UD0GZ |work=[[Reuters]] |language=en |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

After introduction of the original [[German Renewable Energy Act|Renewable Energy Act]] in 2000, there was a focus on long term costs, while in later years this has shifted to a focus on short term costs and the "financial burden" of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} while ignoring environmental externalities of fossil fuels.<ref name="lauber-and-jacobsson-2016">{{cite journal |last1=Lauber |first1=Volkmar |last2=Jacobsson |first2=Staffan |date=2016 |title=The politics and economics of constructing, contesting and restricting socio-political space for renewables – The German Renewable Energy Act |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eist.2015.06.005 |journal=Environmental Innovation and Societal Transitions |volume=18 |pages=147–163 |doi=10.1016/j.eist.2015.06.005 |access-date=26 May 2026|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Electricity prices for household customers in Germany have been generally increasing in the last decade.{{Clarify|date=May 2024}}<ref name="bmwi-2015-b" /> The renewable energy levy to finance green power investment is added to Germans' electricity unit price. The surcharge (22.1% in 2016) pays the state-guaranteed price for renewable energy to producers and is 6.35 cents per kWh in 2016.<ref>{{cite web |date=2016 |title=Annual Report 2015 |url=https://www.amprion.net/Dokumente/Amprion/Gesch%C3%A4ftsberichte/2015/Amprion-Annual-Report-2015.pdf |publisher=[[Amprion]] |page=15 |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

A comprehensive study, published in ''Energy Policy'' in 2013, reported that Germany's [[nuclear power phase-out]], to be complete by 2022, is contradictory to the goal of the climate portion of the program.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bruninx |first1=Kenneth |last2=Madzharov |first2=Darin |last3=Delarue |first3=Erik |last4=D'haeseleer |first4=William |date=2013 |title=Impact of the German nuclear phase-out on Europe's electricity generation — a comprehensive study |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301421513003583 |journal=[[Energy Policy]] |volume=60 |pages=251–261 |doi=10.1016/j.enpol.2013.05.026 |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

In June 2019, an open letter to "the leadership and people of Germany", written by almost 100 Polish environmentalists and scientist, urged Germany to "reconsider the decision on the final decommissioning of fully functional nuclear power plants" for the benefit of the fight against global warming.<ref>{{cite news |date=14 May 2019 |title=Polish academics urge end to Germany's nuclear phaseout |url=https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/Articles/Polish-academics-urge-end-to-Germany-s-nuclear-pha |work=World Nuclear News |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

German Economy and Energy Minister [[Sigmar Gabriel]] said in 2014 "For a country like Germany with a strong industrial base, exiting nuclear and coal-fired power generation at the same time would not be possible."<ref name="severin-and-bryan-2014">{{cite news |last1=Severin |first1=Thorsten |last2=Bryan |first2=Victoria |date=12 October 2014 |title=Germany says can't exit coal-fired energy at same time as nuclear |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/germany-energy-idUSL6N0S70W720141012 |work=[[Reuters]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="Letter to Swedish Prime Minister">{{cite news |last=Gabriel |first=Sigmar |author-link=Sigmar Gabriel |date=13 October 2014 |title=Dear Stefan Löfven – Letter to Swedish Prime Minister from Sigmar Gabriel |url=http://www.altinget.se/misc/SigmarGabriel.pdf |work=[[Altinget]] |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

As nuclear and coal power plants are being phased out, the Government had begun to promote the use of fossil gas in order to [[Bridge fuel|bridge the gap]] between other [[fossil fuel]]s and low-carbon energy sources.<ref>{{cite news |last=Stam |first=Claire |date=9 April 2019 |title=Gas, a prominent guest at German energy transition event |url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/energy-environment/news/gas-a-prominent-guest-at-german-energy-transition-event/ |work=[[Euractiv]] |language=en-GB |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Wettengel |first=Julian |date=13 April 2026 |title=Germany, EU remain heavily dependent on imported fossil fuels |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/factsheets/germanys-dependence-imported-fossil-fuels |work=Clean Energy Wire |language=en |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> The move had been criticized by international observers, who argue that fossil fuel gas is "essentially [[methane]], which constitutes at least one-third of global warming and is leaking into the [[Atmosphere of Earth|atmosphere]] all across the gas production and delivery chain." It is also a more potent greenhouse gas than carbon-dioxide.<ref>{{cite news |last=Buchsbaum |first=L. Michael |date=19 March 2019 |title=Gas wars part one: let’s be honest about Germany’s growing dependence on fossil gas |url=https://energytransition.org/2019/03/gas-wars-part-one-lets-be-honest-about-germanys-growing-dependence-on-fossil-gas/ |work=Energy Transition |language=en-US |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> It is also feared that the [[European Union]], but particularly Germany, is making itself overly dependent on [[Russia]] for gas supplies via [[Nord Stream 2]], thereby undermining its [[energy security]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hasselbach |first1=Christoph |last2=Romaniec |first2=Rosalia |last3=Soric |first3=Miodrag |last4=von Nahmen |first4=Alexandra |last5=Sheiko |first5=Iurii |date=4 February 2019 |title=Nord Stream 2 pipeline row highlights Germany's energy dependence on Russia |url=https://www.dw.com/en/nord-stream-2-pipeline-row-highlights-germanys-energy-dependence-on-russia/a-47344788 |work=[[Deutsche Welle]] |language=en-GB |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> In light of the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]] the Nord Stream 2 project was first postponed indefinitely and ultimately cancelled. The [[Scholz cabinet]] has spent considerable efforts since February 2022 to find replacements for Russian fossil gas both in the near and the long term, particularly [[Liquefied natural gas terminal#Germany|LNG import terminals]] in [[Lubmin LNG terminals|Lubmin]] and [[Wilhelmshaven LNG terminal|Wilhelmshaven]].

Germany's [[electrical grid|electricity transmission network]] is currently inadequately developed, therefore lacking the capability of delivering offshore wind energy produced on the Northern coast to industrial regions in southern Germany. The [[transmission system operator]]s are planning to build an additional {{Convert|4000|km|mi|abbr=off}} of [[Electric power transmission|transmission lines]] until 2030.<ref>{{cite news |last=Oroschakoff |first=Kalina |date=23 March 2018 |title=Germany's green energy shift is more fizzle than sizzle |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-climate-change-green-energy-shift-is-more-fizzle-than-sizzle/ |work=[[Politico]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

Slow reduction of {{CO2}} emissions in Germany, had been contrasted with France's successful [[Low-carbon economy|decarbonization]] of its energy sector under the [[Messmer Plan#Messmer Plan|Messmer plan]] (from 1973) and the United Kingdom's carbon tax, which saw a drastic reduction of coal-powered energy from 88% in 1973 to below 1% in 2019.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hook |first1=Leslie |last2=Thomas |first2=Nathalie |last3=Tighe |first3=Chris |date=1 October 2019 |title=How Britain ended its coal addiction |url=https://www.ft.com/content/a05d1dd4-dddd-11e9-9743-db5a370481bc |work=[[Financial Times]] |language=en-GB |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref><ref name=":6" />

German federal audit office report published in March 2021 highlighted the very high costs of {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} for the household users, where taxes and fees account for 50% of the bills, and the energy price is 43% higher than the EU average. It noted predicted shortage of 4.5&nbsp;GW between 2022 and 2025 as result of the planned shutdown of nuclear power plants.<ref>{{cite news |last=Wacket |first=Markus |date=30 March 2021 |title=Germany's energy drive criticised over expense, risks |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/germany-energy-audit-idUSL8N2LS2RC |work=[[Reuters]] |language=en |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

A study found that if Germany had postponed the nuclear phase out and phased out coal first, it could have saved 1,100 lives and €3 to €8&nbsp;billion in social costs per year. The study concludes that policymakers would have to overestimate the risk or cost of a nuclear accident to conclude that the benefits of the phase-out exceed its social costs.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jarvis |first1=S |last2=Deschenes |first2=O |last3=Jha |first3=A |date=June 2022 |title=The Private and External Costs of Germany's Nuclear Phase-Out |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/jeea/jvac007 |journal=[[Journal of the European Economic Association]] |volume=20 |issue=3 |pages=1311–1346 |doi=10.1093/jeea/jvac007 |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> An open letter by a number of climate scientists published in 2021 calls against the shut-down of the remaining nuclear reactors in Germany, that would lead to 5% increase in {{CO2}} emissions from the electricity sector.<ref>{{cite news |date=27 September 2021 |title=Letter: Germany should postpone nuclear exit to help climate |url=https://www.ft.com/content/e7e08182-6749-44df-9594-23ba84ba6dd5 |work=[[Financial Times]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> According to a 2024 study, by keeping nuclear power Germany could have achieved 73% drop in {{CO2}} emissions instead of 25% in the study period (2002–2022).<ref>{{cite journal |last=Emblemsvåg |first=Jan |date=31 December 2024 |title=What if Germany had invested in nuclear power? A comparison between the German energy policy the last 20 years and an alternative policy of investing in nuclear power |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14786451.2024.2355642 |journal=International Journal of Sustainable Energy |volume=43 |issue=1 |article-number=2355642 |doi=10.1080/14786451.2024.2355642 |doi-access=free |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

The Renewable Energy Act had a significant impact on businesses and industries and had been met with criticism, resulting in increased costs and slowed-down growth.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Eddy |first1=Melissa |date=9 April 2024 |title=German Business Is Tangled in Red Tape |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/04/09/world/europe/german-business-bureaucracy.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

During the 2024 presidential debate between the Republican nominee, Donald Trump, and the Democratic nominee, Kamala Harris, Trump criticized Germany's energy transition efforts.

=== Biomass ===
[[Biomass]] made up 7.0% of Germany's power generation mix in 2017.<ref>{{cite news |last=Morris |first=Craig |date=11 January 2018 |title=Germany’s energy consumption in 2017 |url=https://energytransition.org/2018/01/german-energy-consumption-2017/ |work=Energy Transition |language=en-US |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> Biomass has the potential to be a [[carbon-neutral]] fuel because growing biomass absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and a portion of the carbon absorbed remains in the ground after harvest.<ref>{{cite report |last=Bracmort |first=Kelsi |date=4 February 2016 |title=Is Biopower Carbon Neutral? |url=https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R41603/R41603.22.pdf |work=[[Congressional Research Service]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251002104947/https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R41603/R41603.22.pdf |archive-date=2 October 2025 |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> However, using Biomass as a fuel produces [[air pollution]] in the form of [[carbon monoxide]], [[carbon dioxide]], [[NOx|{{NOx}}]] (nitrogen oxides), VOCs ([[volatile organic compound]]s), particulates and other pollutants, although biomass produces less [[sulfur dioxide]] than coal.<ref>{{cite web |date=17 March 2011 |title=Air pollution from biomass energy |url=http://www.pfpi.net/air-pollution-2 |work=Partnership for Policy Integrity |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Melzer |first=Eartha Jane |date=26 January 2010 |title=Proposed biomass plant: Better than coal? |url=http://michiganmessenger.com/33868/proposed-biomass-plant-better-than-coal |work=The Michigan Messenger |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100205080916/http://michiganmessenger.com/33868/proposed-biomass-plant-better-than-coal |archive-date=5 February 2010 |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

Between 2004 and 2011 policies lead to around {{convert|7000|sqkm|mi2|abbr=on}} new maize-fields for biomass-energy by ploughing-up of at least {{convert|2700|sqkm|mi2|abbr=on}} of grassland. This released large amounts of climate active gases, [[loss of biodiversity]], and potential of groundwater recharge.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ukhanova |first1=Mariya |last2=Schoof |first2=Nicolas |last3=Neher |first3=Lucas |last4=Luick |first4=Rainer |date=2018 |title=Balancing energy transition in Germany: how will it influence permanent grassland? A Delphi-study |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/331922425 |journal=Grassland Science in Europe |volume=23 |pages=679–681 |url-access=subscription |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

There are attempts to use [[biogas]] as partially renewable fuel with [[Green Planet Energy]] selling gas containing 10% of biogas, 1% hydrogen and 90% imported fossil gas.<ref>{{cite news |date=11 March 2021 |title=Is Germany’s Greenpeace Energy at peace selling natural gas? |url=https://www.climateandcapitalmedia.com/is-germanys-greenpeace-energy-at-peace-with-selling-mostly-natural-gas/ |work=Climate & Capital Media |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210916102512/https://www.climateandcapitalmedia.com/is-germanys-greenpeace-energy-at-peace-with-selling-mostly-natural-gas/ |archive-date=16 September 2021 |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

== Citizen support and participation ==

{{as of|2016}}, citizen support for the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} remained high, with surveys indicating that about 80–90% of the public are in favor.<ref name="amelang-and-wettengel-2016">{{cite news |last1=Amelang |first1=Sören |last2=Wettengel |first2=Julian |date=4 May 2016 |title=Polls reveal citizen support for climate action and energy transition |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/factsheets/polls-reveal-citizens-support-energiewende |work=Clean Energy Wire |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>
One reason for the high acceptance was the substantial participation of German citizens in the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}, as private households, land owners, or members of energy cooperatives (''Genossenschaft'').<ref name="borchert-2015">{{cite news |last1=Borchert |first1=Lars |last2=Sutton |first2=Isabel |date=10 March 2015 |title=Germany between citizens’ energy and Nimbyism |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/dossiers/peoples-energiewende |work=Clean Energy Wire |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>
A 2016 survey showed that roughly one in two Germans would consider investing in community renewable energy projects.<ref name="st-gallen-2016">{{cite web |date=8 September 2016 |title=About one in two Germans is willing to financially participate in solar photovoltaic or wind power capacity |url=https://www.unisg.ch/en/wissen/newsroom/aktuell/rssnews/forschung-lehre/2016/september/energiewende-deutschland-investoren-umfrage-08september2016 |work=[[University of St. Gallen]] |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>
Manfred Fischedick, Director of the [[Wuppertal Institute for Climate, Environment and Energy]] has commented that "if people participate with their own money, for example in a wind or solar power plant in their area, they will also support [the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}]."<ref name="borchert-2015" /> A 2010 study shows the benefits to [[Municipality|municipalities]] of community ownership of renewable generation in their locality.<ref name="muehlenhoff-2010">{{cite journal |last=Mühlenhoff |first=Jörg |translator-last=Hill |translator-first=Phil |date=December 2010 |title=Value creation for local communities through renewable energies: results of the study by the Institute for Ecological Economy Research (IÖW) |journal=Renews Special |number=46 |issn=2190-3581 |url=https://www.germany.info/contentblob/3097466/Daten/1196468/RenewsSpecial_DD.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120523000452/http://www.germany.info/contentblob/3097466/Daten/1196468/RenewsSpecial_DD.pdf |archive-date=23 May 2012 |access-date=26 May 2026}} See also [[:de:Institut für ökologische Wirtschaftsforschung|Institut für ökologische Wirtschaftsforschung]].{{Circular reference|date=September 2021}}</ref>
[[File:Investments in renewable energy 2016.png|left|thumb|The share of renewable energy owned by citizens has decreased since the beginning of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}.<ref>[https://energytransition.org/2018/02/share-of-german-citizen-renewable-energy-shrinking/ Share of German citizen renewable energy shrinking]</ref>]] [[File:Power-plant-acceptance.jpg|thumbnail|right|Acceptance of power plants in the neighborhood (Germany 2014)<ref>{{cite web |date=22 May 2026 |title=Power Plants and Neighboring Communities |url=https://www.epa.gov/power-sector/power-plants-and-neighboring-communities |work=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>]]Estimates for 2012 suggested that almost half the renewable energy capacity in Germany was owned by citizens through energy cooperatives and private initiatives.<ref name="amelang-2016">{{cite news |last=Amelang |first=Sören |date=29 June 2016 |title=Germany's energy transition revamp stirs controversy over speed, participation |url=https://www.cleanenergywire.org/dossiers/reform-renewable-energy-act |work=Clean Energy Wire |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref> Citizens accounted for nearly half of all installed biogas and solar capacity and half of the installed onshore wind capacity.<ref name="borchert-2015" /><ref name="luenburg-and-nestle-2014">{{cite book |last1=Lüneburg |first1=University |last2=Nestle |first2=Uwe |date=April 2014 |title=Marktrealität von Bürgerenergie und mögliche Auswirkungen von regulatorischen Eingriffen — Eine Studie für das Bündnis Bürgerenergie e.V. (BBEn) und dem Bund für Umwelt und Naturschutz Deutschland e.V. (BUND) |url=http://www.leuphana.de/fileadmin/user_upload/Forschungseinrichtungen/professuren/finanzierung-finanzwirtschaft/files/Studie_Marktrealitaet_von_Buergerenergie_Leuphana_FINAL_23042014.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160914160153/http://www.leuphana.de/fileadmin/user_upload/Forschungseinrichtungen/professuren/finanzierung-finanzwirtschaft/files/Studie_Marktrealitaet_von_Buergerenergie_Leuphana_FINAL_23042014.pdf |archive-date=14 September 2016 |access-date=26 May 2026}}</ref>

According to a 2014 survey conducted by TNS Emnid for the German Renewable Energies Agency among 1015 respondents, 94 percent of the Germans supported the enforced expansion of Renewable Energies. More than two-thirds of the interviewees agreed to renewable power plants close to their homes.<ref name="aee-2014">{{cite web |title=Akzeptanzumfrage 2014: 92 Prozent der Deutschen unterstützen den Ausbau Erneuerbarer Energien |trans-title=Acceptance survey 2014: 92 percent of Germans support the development of renewable energy |url=http://www.unendlich-viel-energie.de/themen/akzeptanz2/akzeptanz-umfrage/akzeptanzumfrage-2014 |website=Agentur für Erneuerbare Energien |place=Berlin |date=2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160809082233/https://www.unendlich-viel-energie.de/themen/akzeptanz2/akzeptanz-umfrage/akzeptanzumfrage-2014 |archive-date=9 August 2016 |access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref>
The share of total energy from renewables was 11% in 2014.<ref>{{cite book |title=Renewables 2015: Global Status Report |url=http://www.ren21.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/REN12-GSR2015_Onlinebook_low1.pdf |publisher=[[REN21]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-3-9815934-6-4 |place=Paris, France |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924090105/http://www.ren21.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/REN12-GSR2015_Onlinebook_low1.pdf |archive-date=24 September 2015 |access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref>{{rp|137}}

Changes in energy policy, with the [[German Renewable Energy Sources Act#Renewable Energy Sources Act (2014)|Renewable Energy Sources Act]] in 2014, have jeopardized the efforts of citizens to participate.<ref name="borchert-2015" /><ref name="morris-2015">{{cite web |last=Morris |first=Craig |date=24 February 2015 |title=Few new German energy co-ops in 2014 |url=http://energytransition.de/2015/02/few-new-german-energy-coops-in-2014/ |website=Energy Transition: The German Energiewende |location=Berlin |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160911152246/http://energytransition.de/2015/02/few-new-german-energy-coops-in-2014/ |archive-date=11 September 2016 |access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref> The share of citizen-owned renewable energy has since dropped to 42.5% as of 2016.<ref>{{cite news |last=Morris |first=Craig |date=7 February 2018 |title=Share of German citizen renewable energy shrinking |url=https://energytransition.org/2018/02/share-of-german-citizen-renewable-energy-shrinking/ |work=Energy Transition |language=en-US |access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref>

The Renewable Energy Sources Act provides compensation to wind turbine operators for every kilowatt-hour of electricity not produced if wind power surpasses peak grid capacity, while grid operators must splice electricity from renewable sources into the grid in times of low or no demand for it.<ref name=":3">{{cite news |last=Harper |first=Jo |date=11 March 2020 |title=Winds of change push German power grid to brink |url=https://www.dw.com/en/winds-of-change-push-german-power-grid-to-brink/a-52701005 |work=[[Deutsche Welle]] |language=en-GB |access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref> This can lead to a [[negative price]] of electricity, and grid operators may pass associated costs on to customers, estimated to be costing them an extra €4&nbsp;billion in 2020. This has resulted in greater resistance to certain {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} policies, specifically wind power.<ref name=":3" />

By 2019, Germany also saws a significant increase of organized opposition against on-shore wind farms,<ref name=":5" /> especially in [[Bavaria]]<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gehrke |first1=Laurenz |last2=Oroschakoff |first2=Kalina |date=20 August 2019 |title=An ill wind blows for the onshore power industry |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/an-ill-wind-blows-for-the-onshore-power-industry/ |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref> and [[Baden-Württemberg]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/305518625|title=Against the wind: Local opposition to the German 'Energiewende'|date=2015}}</ref>

== Computer studies ==

Much of the policy development for the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}} is underpinned by [[computer simulation|computer models]], run mostly by universities and research institutes. The models are usually based on [[scenario analysis]] and are used to investigate different assumptions regarding the stability, sustainability, cost, efficiency, and public acceptability of various sets of technologies. Some models cover the entire [[energy sector]], while others are confined to [[electricity generation]] and consumption. A 2016 book investigates the usefulness and limitations of energy scenarios and energy models within the context of the {{Lang|de|Energiewende}}.<ref name="dieckhoff-and-leuschner-2016"><!-- publishers url: www.transcript-verlag.de/978-3-8376-3171-5 -->
{{cite book|title=Die Energiewende und ihre Modelle: Was uns Energieszenarien sagen können – und was nicht|date=November 2016|publisher=transcript Verlag|isbn=978-3-8376-3171-5|editor1-last=Dieckhoff|editor1-first=Christian|location=Bielefeld, Germany|language=de|trans-title=The Energiewende and its models: What energy scenarios can tell us – and what not|editor2-last=Leuschner|editor2-first=Anna}}
</ref>

A number of computer studies confirm the feasibility of the German electricity system being 100% renewable in 2050. Some investigate the prospect of the entire energy system (all energy carriers) being fully renewable.

=== 2009 WWF study ===

In 2009 [[World Wide Fund for Nature]] (WWF) Germany published a study prepared by the [[Öko-Institut]], Prognos, and Hans-Joachim Ziesing.<ref name="wwf-germany-2009">{{cite book |author=WWF Germany |title=Blueprint Germany: a strategy for a climate safe 2050 |date=2009 |publisher=[[World Wildlife Fund]] |location=Berlin |url=http://www.wwf.de/fileadmin/fm-wwf/Publikationen-PDF/blueprint_germany_wwf.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006042621/http://www.wwf.de/fileadmin/fm-wwf/Publikationen-PDF/blueprint_germany_wwf.pdf |archive-date=6 October 2016 |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref>
The study presumes a 95% reduction in greenhouse gases by the year 2050 and covers all sectors. The study shows that the transformation from a high-carbon to a low-carbon economy is possible and affordable. It notes that by committing to this transformation path, Germany could become a model for other countries.

=== 2011 German Advisory Council on the Environment study ===

A 2011 report from the {{ill|German Advisory Council on the Environment|de|Sachverständigenrat für Umweltfragen}} (SRU) concludes that Germany can attain 100% renewable electricity generation by 2050.<ref name="sru-2010">{{cite press release |title=Climate-friendly, reliable, affordable: 100% renewable electricity supply by 2050 |date=5 May 2010 |publisher=German Advisory Council on the Environment |location=Berlin |url=https://www.umweltrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/EN/CurrentPressReleases/2010/2010_05_PressRelease_100percent_renewable_electricity_supply.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161112040406/http://www.umweltrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/EN/CurrentPressReleases/2010/2010_05_PressRelease_100percent_renewable_electricity_%20supply.html |archive-date=12 November 2016 |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="sru-2011">{{cite book |title=Pathways towards a 100 % renewable electricity system — Special report |date=October 2011 |publisher=German Advisory Council on the Environment |location=Berlin |url=https://www.umweltrat.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/02_Special_Reports/2011_10_Special_Report_Pathways_renewables.pdf |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref> The [[German Aerospace Center]] (DLR) REMix high-resolution energy model was used for the analysis. A range of scenarios were investigated and a cost-competitive transition with good security of supply is possible.

The authors presume that the transmission network will continue to be reinforced and that cooperation with Norway and Sweden would allow their hydro generation to be used for storage. The transition does not require Germany's [[Nuclear power phase-out#Germany|nuclear phase-out]] (''{{lang|de|Atomausstieg}}'') to be extended nor the construction of coal-fired plants with [[carbon capture and storage]] (CCS). Conventional generation assets need not be stranded and an orderly transition should prevail. Stringent energy efficiency and energy saving programs can bring down the future costs of electricity.

=== 2015 Deep Decarbonization Pathways Project study ===

The [[Deep Decarbonization Pathways Project]] (DDPP) aims to demonstrate how countries can transform their energy systems by 2050 in order to achieve a [[low-carbon economy]].
The 2015 German country report, produced in association with the [[Wuppertal Institute]], examines the official target of reducing domestic GHG emissions by 80% to 95% by 2050 (compared with 1990).<ref name="hillebrandt-2015">{{cite book |editor1-last=Hillebrandt |editor1-first=Katharina |editor2-last=Samadi |editor2-first=Sascha |editor3-last=Fischedick |editor3-first=Manfred |display-editors=etal |title=Pathways to deep decarbonization in Germany |date=2015 |publisher=[[Sustainable Development Solutions Network|SDSN]] |url=http://deepdecarbonization.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/DDPP_DEU.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160909131930/http://deepdecarbonization.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/DDPP_DEU.pdf |archive-date=9 September 2016 |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref> Decarbonization pathways for Germany are illustrated by means of three scenarios with energy-related emission reductions between 1990 and 2050 varying between 80% and more than 90%. The three strategies strongly contribute to GHG emission reduction:
* energy efficiency improvements (in all sectors, especially in buildings)
* increased use of domestic renewables (with a focus on electricity generation)
* electrification and (in two of the scenarios) use of renewable electricity-based synthetic fuels (especially in the transport and industry sector)
In addition, some scenarios use controversially:
* final energy demand reductions through behavioral changes ([[mode of transport|modal shift]] in transport, changes in eating and heating habits)
* net imports of electricity from renewable sources or of [[bioenergy]]
* use of [[carbon capture and storage]] (CCS) technology to reduce industry sector GHG emissions (including cement production)
Potential co-benefits for Germany include increased energy security, higher competitiveness of and global business opportunities for companies, job creation, stronger GDP growth, smaller energy bills for households, and less air pollution.

=== 2015 Fraunhofer ISE study ===

Using the model REMod-D (Renewable Energy Model – Germany),<ref name="henning-and-palzer-2014">{{cite journal |last1=Henning |first1=Hans-Martin |last2=Palzer |first2=Andreas |title=A comprehensive model for the German electricity and heat sector in a future energy system with a dominant contribution from renewable energy technologies — Part I: Methodology |journal=[[Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews]] |date=2014 |volume=30 |pages=1003–1018 |doi=10.1016/j.rser.2013.09.012 |bibcode=2014RSERv..30.1003H}}</ref> this 2015 [[Fraunhofer ISE]] study investigates several system transformation scenarios and their related costs.<ref name="henning-and-palzer-2015">{{cite book |last1=Henning |first1=Hans-Martin |last2=Palzer |first2=Andreas |title=What will the energy transformation cost?: pathways for transforming the German energy system by 2050 |date=2015 |publisher=[[Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems|Fraunhofer ISE]] |location=Freiburg |url=https://www.ise.fraunhofer.de/en/publications/veroeffentlichungen-pdf-dateien-en/studien-und-konzeptpapiere/study-what-will-the-energy-transformation-cost.pdf |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref> The guiding question of the study is: "how can a cost-optimised transformation of the German energy system—with consideration of all [[energy carrier]]s and consumer sectors—be achieved while meeting the declared [[climate protection]] targets and ensuring a secure energy supply at all times." [[Carbon capture and storage]] (CCS) is excluded from the scenarios. An energy scenario emitting 85% less {{CO2}} emissions than 1990 levels is compared with a reference scenario, assumes that the German energy system operates in 2050 the same way as it does today. Primary energy supply drops 42%. The total costs depend on the future prices for carbon and oil. If the penalty for {{CO2}} emissions increases to €100/tonne by 2030 and thereafter remains constant and fossil fuel prices increase annually by 2%, then the total cumulative costs of today's energy system are 8% higher than the costs required for the minus 85% scenario up to 2050. The report notes:

{{blockquote|From the macroeconomic perspective, the transformation of Germany's energy system demands a significant shift in cash flow, moving the cash spent on energy imports today to spend it instead on new investments in systems, their operation and maintenance. In this respect a transformed energy system requires a large expenditure for local added value, a factor which also does not appear in the shown cost analysis.<ref name="henning-and-palzer-2015"/>{{rp|8}}}}

=== 2015 DIW study ===

A 2015 study uses DIETER or Dispatch and Investment Evaluation Tool with Endogenous Renewables, developed by the [[German Institute for Economic Research]] (DIW), Berlin, Germany. The study examines the power storage requirements for renewables uptake ranging from 60% to 100%. Under the scenario of 80% (the German government target for 2050), [[Grid energy storage|grid storage]] requirements remain moderate and other options on both the supply side and demand side offer flexibility at low cost. Storage plays a role in the provision of reserves. Storage becomes more pronounced under higher shares of renewables, but strongly depends on the costs and availability of other flexibility options, particularly on biomass availability. The model is fully described in the study report.<ref name="zerrahn-and-schill-2015">{{cite book |last1=Zerrahn |first1=Alexander |last2=Schill |first2=Wolf-Peter |title=A greenfield model to evaluate long-run power storage requirements for high shares of renewables — DIW discussion paper 1457 |date=2015 |publisher=[[German Institute for Economic Research|DIW]] |location=Berlin |issn=1619-4535 |url=https://www.diw.de/documents/publikationen/73/diw_01.c.498475.de/dp1457.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160822184000/http://www.diw.de/documents/publikationen/73/diw_01.c.498475.de/dp1457.pdf |archive-date=22 August 2016 |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref>

=== 2016 acatech study ===

A 2016 [[acatech]]-lead study focused on "flexibility technologies" used to balance the fluctuations inherent in power generation from wind and photovoltaics.<ref name="acatech-2016">{{cite book |editor1=acatech |editor2=Leopoldina |editor3=Akademienunion |date=2016 |title=Flexibility concepts for the German power supply in 2050: ensuring stability in the age of renewable energies |publisher=[[acatech]] |location=Berlin |isbn=978-3-8047-3549-1 |url=http://www.acatech.de/fileadmin/user_upload/Baumstruktur_nach_Website/Acatech/root/de/Publikationen/Kooperationspublikationen/ESYS_Position_Paper_Flexibility_concepts.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006041130/http://www.acatech.de/fileadmin/user_upload/Baumstruktur_nach_Website/Acatech/root/de/Publikationen/Kooperationspublikationen/ESYS_Position_Paper_Flexibility_concepts.pdf |archive-date=6 October 2016 |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="lunz-etal-2016">{{cite journal |last1=Lunz |first1=Benedikt |last2=Stöcker |first2=Philipp |last3=Eckstein |first3=Sascha |last4=Nebel |first4=Arjuna |last5=Samadi |first5=Sascha |last6=Erlach |first6=Berit |last7=Fischedick |first7=Manfred |last8=Elsner |first8=Peter |last9=Sauer |first9=Dirk Uwe |title=Scenario-based comparative assessment of potential future electricity systems — A new methodological approach using Germany in 2050 as an example |journal=[[Applied Energy]] |date=2016 |volume=171 |pages=555–580 |doi=10.1016/j.apenergy.2016.03.087 |bibcode=2016ApEn..171..555L |url=https://nbn-resolving.org/urn:nbn:de:bsz:wup4-opus-62770}}</ref> Set in 2050, several scenarios use [[Gas-fired power plant|gas power plants]] to stabilise the energy system, ensuring supply security during several weeks of low wind and solar radiation. Other scenarios investigate a 100% renewable system and show these to be possible but costly. Flexible consumption and storage control ([[energy demand management|demand-side management]]) in households and the industrial sector is the cost-efficient means of balancing short-term power fluctuations. Long-term storage systems, based on [[power-to-X]], are only viable if carbon emissions are to be reduced by more than 80%. The study notes:

{{blockquote|Assuming that the price of emissions allowances in 2050 will significantly surpass its current level, a power generation system boasting a high percentage of wind and photovoltaics will, as a rule, come cheaper than a system dominated by fossil fuel power plants.<ref name="acatech-2016"/>{{rp|7}}}}

=== 2016 Stanford University study ===

The Atmosphere/Energy Program at [[Stanford University]] has developed roadmaps for 139 countries to achieve energy systems powered only by wind, water, and sunlight (WWS) by 2050.<ref name="jacobson-etal-2016">{{cite book |last1=Jacobson |first1=Mark Z |last2=Delucchi |first2=Mark A |last3=Bauer |first3=Zack AF |last4=Goodman |first4=Savannah C |last5=Chapman |first5=William E |last6=Cameron |first6=Mary A |last7=Bozonnat |first7=Cedric |last8=Chobadi |first8=Liat |last9=Clonts |first9=Hailey A |last10=Enevoldsen |first10=P |last11=Erwin |first11=Jenny R |last12=Fobi |first12=Simone N |last13=Goldstrom |first13=Owen K |last14=Hennessy |first14=Eleanor M |last15=Liu |first15=Jingyi |last16=Lo |first16=Jonathan |last17=Meyer |first17=Clayton B |last18=Morris |first18=Sean B |last19=Moy |first19=Kevin R |last20=O'Neill |first20=Patrick L |last21=Petkov |first21=Ivalin |last22=Redfern |first22=Stephanie |last23=Schucker |first23=Robin |last24=Sontag |first24=Michael A |last25=Wang |first25=Jingfan |last26=Weiner |first26=Eric |last27=Yachanin |first27=Alexander S |author1-link=Mark Z. Jacobson |title=100% clean and renewable wind, water, and sunlight (WWS) all-sector energy roadmaps for 139 countries of the world |date=24 October 2016 |url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/efmh/jacobson/Articles/I/CountriesWWS.pdf |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref><ref name="delucchi-etal-2016">{{cite book |last1=Delucchi |first1=Mark A |last2=Jacobson |first2=Mark Z |last3=Bauer |first3=Zack AF |last4=Goodman |first4=Savannah C |last5=Chapman |first5=William E |author2-link=Mark Z. Jacobson |title=Spreadsheets for 139-country 100% wind, water, and solar roadmaps |date=2016 |url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/efmh/jacobson/Articles/I/AllCountries.xlsx |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref> Total end-use energy drops from 375.8&nbsp;GW for business-as-usual to 260.9&nbsp;GW under a fully renewable transition. Load shares in 2050 would be: on-shore wind 35%, off-shore wind 17%, wave 0.08%, geothermal 0.01%, hydro-electric 0.87%, tidal 0%, residential PV 6.75%, commercial PV 6.48%, utility PV 33.8%, and [[concentrating solar power]] 0%. The study also assess avoided air pollution, eliminated global climate change costs, and net job creation.

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Energy in Taiwan
