{{Short description|none}} {{Multiple issues|
{{update|date=November 2010}}
{{Lead too short|date=March 2026}}
}}
<!-- "none" is preferred when the title is already sufficiently detailed; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:Taiwan CIA map updated.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|alt=Political map of Taiwan|Map of Taiwan]]
[[File:Electricity production by source, Taiwan 1985-2024.png|thumb|2024 TWh: Gas 124, Coal 115, Solar 15, Nuclear 12]]
[[File:Energy consumption by source, Taiwan.svg|thumb|Energy consumption by source, Taiwan]]

In 2024, 83.2% of [[Taiwan]]'s 288 TWh electricity generation came from fossil fuels (42.4% natural gas, 39.3% coal), 4.2% from nuclear, 11.6% from renewables, and 1.1% from [[Pumped-storage hydroelectricity|pumped-storage]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kuo |first=Chien-shen |last2=Wang |first2=Yang-yu |last3=Chao |first3=Yen-hsiang |date=2025-04-29 |title=Taiwan nuclear power phaseout to push fossil fuel use higher: MOEA |url=https://focustaiwan.tw/politics/202504290021 |access-date=2025-05-01 |work=[[Focus Taiwan]]}}</ref> [[Taiwan]] relies on imports for almost 98% of its energy,<ref name="pge">{{cite web |title=【綠能知識庫】台灣能源情勢懶人包｜認識台灣能源政策、能源比例與再生能源現況 |url=https://blog.pgesolar.com.tw/2021/02/25/%E5%8F%B0%E7%81%A3%E8%83%BD%E6%BA%90 |website=PGE Solar|date=25 February 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eia.gov/international/overview/country/TWN |title=International - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)|website=www.eia.gov}}</ref> which leaves the island's energy supply vulnerable to external disruption. In order to reduce this dependence, the [[Ministry of Economic Affairs (Republic of China)|Ministry of Economic Affairs]]' Bureau of Energy has been actively promoting energy research at [[List of universities in Taiwan|several universities]] since the 1990s.

==Nuclear energy==
[[File:台湾第四原子力発電所.jpg|thumb|[[Longmen Nuclear Power Plant]] in [[Gongliao District]], Taiwan.]]
{{excerpt|Nuclear power in Taiwan}}

Taiwan’s energy transition has caused concern about the country's long-term energy security. As of 2024, imports make up over 97% of Taiwan’s energy needs.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-10 |title=Taiwan - Electric Power Equipment (ELP) and Energy |url=https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/taiwan-electric-power-equipment-elp-and-energy |access-date=2025-06-12 |website=www.trade.gov |language=en}}</ref> Public opinion on nuclear energy in Taiwan remains relatively divided. In 2021, a [[Referendum|national referendum]] rejected a proposal to restart construction at the [[Lungmen Nuclear Power Plant|Lungmen (Fourth Nuclear) plant]]. In 2025, polling from the Taiwanese Public Opinion Foundation found that 73.6 percent of respondents supported the extension of nuclear power plant operations, reflecting changing attitudes amid energy concerns.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-18 |title=Poll shows 73% support nuclear plant extension: KMT - Taipei Times |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2025/02/18/2003832075 |access-date=2025-06-12 |website=www.taipeitimes.com}}</ref>

Taiwan has taken a significant step towards restarting its [[Maanshan Nuclear Power Plant|Maanshan nuclear power plant]] after the Nuclear Safety Commission  completed its review of Taiwan Power Company’s restart plan, submitted in March 2026. However, the completion of the review does not constitute final authorization to resume operations as further inspections, technical assessments and regulatory approvals are still required.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-28 |title=Taiwan regulator completes review of restart plan |url=https://world-nuclear-news.org/articles/taiwan-regulator-completes-review-of-restart-plan |access-date=2026-10-16 |website=World Nuclear News |language=en}}</ref> Ultimately, the decision will also depend on the outcome of a referendum scheduled for later in 2026 on abolishing Taiwan’s “nuclear-free homeland” policy. The move marks a renewed effort to reintroduce nuclear power into Taiwan’s energy mix.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2026-08-14 |title=Taiwan parliament approves holding of three referendums, including on caning sex criminals |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/taiwan-parliament-approves-holding-three-referendums-including-caning-sex-2026-08-14/ |access-date=2026-10-16 |work=Reuters |language=en}}</ref>

==Liquefied natural gas==
The annual output of [[liquefied natural gas]] (LNG) from exploration and production within Taiwan is 350-400 million m<sup>3</sup>. While on the other hand, Taiwan imported 18.4 billion m<sup>3</sup> of LNG, the fifth largest LNG importer in the world, primarily from [[Qatar]], [[Malaysia]] and [[Indonesia]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://focustaiwan.tw/news/aeco/201510250017.aspx|title=Oil expected from Chad as Taiwan strives for energy self-sufficiency - Economics - FOCUS TAIWAN - CNA ENGLISH NEWS|date=25 October 2015 }}</ref> LNG-fired power plants in Taiwan produce electricity at a cost of NT$3.91/kWh, more than the electricity cost charged to the customers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://topics.amcham.com.tw/2015/09/is-renewable-energy-the-way-forward-for-taiwan/|title=Is Renewable Energy the Way Forward for Taiwan? - Taiwan Business TOPICS|date=15 September 2015}}</ref>

The [[Democratic Progressive Party]] Government of the [[Republic of China]] under [[Chen Shui-bian]] was elected in early 2000 promising to approve only [[liquefied natural gas]] power projects in the future, and to increase the share of liquefied natural gas of Taiwan's power generation to roughly one-third by 2010. President Chen's administration tried to stop the 2,600 MW [[Longmen Nuclear Power Plant]], currently under construction, but a court has ruled the construction could not be aborted.

In January 2013, [[China National Offshore Oil Corporation]] (CNOOC) and [[Shinfox]] signed an agreement to supply Kinmen with [[liquefied natural gas]] (LNG) from [[Mainland China]]. The delivery of LNG is expected to be started in early 2015 to industrial companies. At a later stage, the supply will be increased up to 100,000 tonnes per year to include power plants and households. The agreement was witnessed by [[Environmental Protection Administration (Republic of China)|Minister of Environmental Protection Administration]] [[Stephen Shen]]. Shen said that the cooperation is helpful to help Taiwan in realizing Kinmen to be a tourism-focused low-carbon county.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wantchinatimes.com/news-subclass-cnt.aspx?id=20140118000077&cid=1102|title=Kinmen to receive LNG from mainland|access-date=20 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140410193937/http://www.wantchinatimes.com/news-subclass-cnt.aspx?id=20140118000077&cid=1102|archive-date=2014-04-10|url-status=dead}}</ref> During the third Cross-Strait Entrepreneurs Summit in [[Nanjing]] on 2–3 November 2015, executives from CNOOC and Shinfox gave a briefing on the joint venture project. Under the cooperation framework, CNOOC facilities in Fujian will also supply compressed natural gas, along with production technology.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://focustaiwan.tw/news/acs/201511050038.aspx|title=Kinmen expected to get natural gas supply from China's Fujian - Cross-Strait Affairs - FOCUS TAIWAN - CNA ENGLISH NEWS|work=Focus Taiwan - CNA English News |date=5 November 2015 }}</ref>

As of 2017, the [[safety stock]] of LNG imported to Taiwan is seven days.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://focustaiwan.tw/news/aeco/201708150032.aspx|date=15 August 2017|first1=Yi-chu|last1=Tsai|first2=Cheng-wei|last2=Chen|first3=S.C.|last3=Chang|title=Taiwan's power supply system unable to withstand minor errors: expert|publisher=Focus Taiwan|access-date=16 August 2017}}</ref> In 2017 Taiwan was the world's fifth largest importer of LNG accounting for 6% of global market share.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Julie Gordon and Henning Gloystein |first1=Jess Macy Yu |title=Cheniere signs 25-year LNG sales deal with Taiwan's CPC |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-cheniere-energy-taiwan/cheniere-signs-25-year-lng-sales-deal-with-taiwans-cpc-idUSKBN1KW03E |website=www.reuters.com |agency=Reuters |access-date=23 June 2019|date=2018-08-11 }}</ref>

A case study related to LNG in Taiwan occurred in 2021 when a proposed LNG receiving station was planned to be built on Taoyuan’s Datan algal reef. The project to build this station was backed up by the DPP, despite typically siding with environmentalists, while the oppositional party (KMT) worked with environmental groups to protest this construction. In December 2021, the proposed referendum to relocate the receiving station failed, but the DPP maintains that the station has avoided impacts on the algae reef habitat. The DPP supported LNG because their energy plan includes more LNG to substitute their zero nuclear energy plan.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tsai |first=Chia-Shen |date=2021-06-05 |title=How the Datan Algal Reef Became a Wedge Issue |url=https://newbloommag.net/2021/06/05/datan-reef-wedge-issue/ |access-date=2025-06-12 |website=New Bloom Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Renewable energy==
{{main|Renewable energy in Taiwan}}
[[File:Wind power.JPG|thumb|Wind farms in [[Qingshui District|Qingshui]], [[Taichung]].]]

In June 2009, the [[Legislative Yuan]] passed a renewable energy act aimed at promoting the use of [[renewable energy]], boosting energy diversification and helping reduce [[greenhouse gas]]es. The new law authorizes the government to enhance incentives for the development of renewable energy via a variety of methods, including the acquisition mechanism, incentives for demonstration projects, and the loosening of regulatory restrictions in order to increase Taiwan's renewable energy generation capacity by 6.5 gigawatts to 10 gigawatts within 20 years.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ey.gov.tw/ct.asp?xItem=56485&ctNode=1335&mp=22|title=行政院整合服務管理平台}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.google.com/hostednews/afp/article/ALeqM5jZDv-rs004rLknGtTYRzA8j21vNw |title=AFP: Taiwan passes major green energy bill |website=[[Google News]] |access-date=17 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110312105514/http://www.google.com/hostednews/afp/article/ALeqM5jZDv-rs004rLknGtTYRzA8j21vNw |archive-date=12 March 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In July 2009,  the [[Executive Yuan]] approved a proposal consisting of 16 measures to transform Taiwan into a “[[low carbon]]” country by 2020. The  [[Ministry of Economic Affairs (Republic of China)|Ministry of Economic Affairs]]’ (MOEA) proposal set a long-term goal of cutting total annual greenhouse gas emissions to 2000 levels by the year 2025. The Executive Yuan also requested the [[legislature]] to complete a bill on reducing [[carbon emissions]] and another bill on developing renewable energy. NT$226 million will be used to promote renewable energy and facilities in homes and public buildings. Over the next five years NT$20 billion would be invested into advanced technologies in seven industries: [[solar energy]], [[LED lighting]], [[wind power]], [[hydrogen energy]] and [[fuel cell]]s, [[biofuel]], energy [[information and communications technology]] and [[electric vehicle]]s. Cooperation between local governments and the central government will be enhanced by providing incentives for conserving energy and cutting emissions. Two pilot communities will be created per county or city over 2009-2011, with 50 percent of the energy supply in those areas coming from renewable sources.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2009/07/30/2003449934|title=Cabinet plans 'low carbon' Taiwan|date=30 July 2009|access-date=20 August 2015}}</ref>

In August 2009, Taiwan's government has announced that it will invest T$45 billion ($1.4 billion) in the island's domestic renewable energy sector in an attempt to help the sector grow nearly eight-fold by 2015 thereby increasing industry production value to T$1.158 trillion in 2015 compared to T$160.3 billion in mid-2009. Proponents hope that "the green energy sector will help Taiwan become a major power in energy technology and production, as well as provide the creation of green jobs."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.renewableenergymagazine.com/paginas/Contenidosecciones.asp?ID=14&Cod=3925&Tipo=&Nombre=Latest%20news|title=Renewable Energy Magazine, at the heart of clean energy journalism|access-date=20 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100202204404/http://www.renewableenergymagazine.com/paginas/Contenidosecciones.asp?ID=14&Cod=3925&Tipo=&Nombre=Latest%20news|archive-date=2 February 2010|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

In May 2016 Economics Minister Lee Shih-guang stated that the government expects renewable energy to account for 20% of electricity generation by 2025, to support the government's ambition to phase out nuclear power generation.<ref name=chinapost-20160526>{{cite news |url=http://www.chinapost.com.tw/taiwan/national/national-news/2016/05/26/467321/Govt-to.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160526115839/http://www.chinapost.com.tw/taiwan/national/national-news/2016/05/26/467321/Govt-to.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 26, 2016 |title=Gov't to end nuclear power in 2025: MOEA |newspaper=The China Post |date=26 May 2016 |access-date=1 November 2016}}</ref>

== Emissions==
[[File:Taichung Thermal Power Plant.JPG|thumb|[[Taichung Power Plant]], world's fourth largest coal-fired power plant.]]
Total carbon dioxide emissions nationwide were 277.645 million tonnes in 2006, representing 124.68 percent growth over 1990's 123.574 million tonnes, according to the [[Environmental Protection Administration (Republic of China)|Environmental Protection Administration]] (EPA). [[Energy conversion]] industry contributed to 6.9 percent of emissions in 2006, while [[heavy industry]] contributed 52.5 percent, the [[transportation]] sector contributed 14.3 percent, the commercial sector 6.3 percent and private households 12.1 percent.

Taiwan ranked third in Asia and 32nd worldwide in the 2009 Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI) for carbon dioxide emissions, published by Climate Action Network Europe (CAN-Europe) and Germanwatch.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2009/05/30/2003444911|title=Taiwan places third in region in climate report|date=30 May 2009|access-date=20 August 2015}}</ref> In 2025, Taiwan ranked 60th in the CCPI and received a “very low” rating in Energy Use and GHG emissions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weinreich |first=Lydia |date=2024-11-20 |title=Chinese Taipei – Climate Performance Ranking 2025 {{!}} Climate Change Performance Index |url=https://ccpi.org/country/twn/ |access-date=2025-06-12 |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2022, Taiwan officially announced their plan to have [[net-zero emissions]] by 2050, including a plan to get there. The four transition strategies Taiwan has included in their plan are transitions in the energy, industrial, lifestyle, and social sectors. In February 2023, Taiwan’s president [[Tsai Ing-wen]] announced the revision of the Greenhouse Gas Management Act as the Climate Change Response Act, incorporating net-zero by 2050 sentiments.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Net Zero Roadmap｜Taiwan 2050 Net-zero |url=https://www.cca.gov.tw/en/climatetalks/net-zero-roadmap/1891.html |access-date=2025-06-12 |website=www.cca.gov.tw |language=en}}</ref>

==Historical energy consumption==
[[File:2010 07 15500 5504, Chintsun, LPG tankers, Taiwan.JPG|thumb|LPG tanker off of Pingtung coast]]
Taiwan produces electricity from fossil fuels, wind, nuclear and hydro power. Taiwan's energy consumption is the equivalent of 10.5 million kiloliters of oil, or about 2.2 million barrels a day.

Consumption of petroleum products account for about half of Taiwan's energy supply equivalent of 4.5 million kiloliters of oil. Demand for diesel declined 21 percent, while that for gasoline dropped 8.7 percent. Monthly Power consumption is around  20.9 billion kilowatt-hours. [[Formosa Plastics Group|Formosa Petrochemical Corp]]. and [[CPC Corp]] are Taiwan's only oil refiners.

Energy use in the first six months of the year rose 6.7 percent to the equivalent of 61.6 million kiloliters of oil, the energy bureau said.

Crude oil processing: 4.59 million kiloliters in June.

Coal imports: 5.23 million metric tons

Imports of crude oil: 26.9 million kiloliters

[LNG] purchases: 5.58 billion cubic meters. Purchases of liquefied natural gas increased 13 percent to 1.06 billion cubic meters. LNG accounted for 97 percent of gas supply.

In 2013, coal imports to Taiwan amounted 65.96 million tons, which consists of 58.96 million tons of steam coal and 7.02 million tons of coking coal. The largest coal exporter country to Taiwan is [[Indonesia]] (41.64%) and [[Australia]] (40.20%).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web3.moeaboe.gov.tw/ECW/english/content/ContentLink.aspx?menu_id=1540|title=Energy Statistical annual Reports - Energy Statistics - Bureau of Energy, Ministry of Economic Affairs, R.O.C.|access-date=20 August 2015|archive-date=19 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171119222336/http://web3.moeaboe.gov.tw/ecw/english/content/contentlink.aspx?menu_id=1540|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2018, [[Petroleum|oil]] accounted for 48.28% of the total energy consumption. [[Coal]] comes next with 29.38%, followed by [[natural gas]] (indigenous and liquefied) with 15.18%, [[nuclear power|nuclear energy]] with 5.38%, [[biomass]] and [[Waste-to-energy|waste]] with 1.13%, and energy from other renewable sources (plus hydroelectric power) with 0.64%.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.moeaboe.gov.tw/ECW/english/content/ContentLink.aspx?menu_id=1540 |title=Energy Statistical annual Reports |date=2019-08-01 |website=Bureau of Energy, Ministry of Economic Affairs |access-date=2019-09-10 |archive-date=2019-10-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191029060155/https://www.moeaboe.gov.tw/ECW/english/content/ContentLink.aspx?menu_id=1540 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2020, 45% of Taiwan's electricity generation came from coal, 35.7% from natural gas, 11.2% from nuclear, and 5.4% from renewables.<ref>{{cite web |author1=孫文臨 |title=2020年用電創歷史新高 水情不佳影響再生能源成績 |url=https://e-info.org.tw/node/229789 |website=Environmental Information Center |access-date=3 May 2021}}</ref>

In 2024, about 12% of Taiwan’s power came from renewable energy, 47% from natural gas, 4.7% from nuclear, and 31% from coal.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-02-21 |title=History of Net Power Generated and Purchased by Energy Type |url=https://www.taipower.com.tw/2764/2826/2828/25340/ |access-date=2025-06-12 |website=Taiwan Power Company}}</ref>

== Energy efficiency ==
[[File:Rational-use-of-electricity logo on Taipower Taipei North Branch 20100923.jpg|thumb|Efficient-Usage of Electricity Logo by Taipower]]
The Taiwan government has been active in promoting [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]], and set a target of energy efficiency of 33% by 2025. This target is higher than Japan's commitment to APEC with the target of 25%-26% efficiency. The government is currently assisting 200 major energy users (companies and organizations) in implementing energy-saving measures.

Taiwan is preparing for the age of high oil prices, and is proactively developing clean energy, such as solar and wind power and biofuels. The efforts would help reduce Taiwan's reliance on imported oil, while contributing to the reduction of greenhouse gases.

The government aims for renewable energy to account for 15% of the nation's energy by 2025. It would amount to 8.45 million kilowatts, capable of producing 28.7 billion kilowatt hours of electricity. Wind-generated power could create as much as 8.9 billion kilowatt hours of electricity by 2025, comparable to 2.3 times the capacity of [[Linkou, Taipei|Linkou]]'s thermal power plants. Many domestic companies are now beginning to work on the development of solar energy, and conservative estimates are projecting that 1.2 billion kilowatt hours of electricity will be produced through solar power by 2025.

Under the Energy Management Law and the underlying Implementing Regulations and related measures, companies are encouraged to improve the energy efficiency of their operations and products. Mandatory programs have been established for the purpose of [[energy conservation]], including [[energy audit]] and energy efficiency standards for certain electrical and electronic products.

The Energy Commission under the [[Ministry of Economic Affairs (Republic of China)|Ministry of Economic Affairs]] is responsible for formulating and implementing [[energy policy]] and laws, including the programs instituted under the Energy Management Law. The principal responsibilities of the Energy Commission include:

# supervising general affairs related to energy management to assure the stability of energy supply;
# accelerating the rationalization of energy pricing;
# promoting the effectiveness of energy utilization;
# preventing energy-related environmental pollution; and
# enhancing energy research and development.

The day-to-day work of the Energy Commission involves activities such as the development of policies and regulations, planning and conservation, research and development of technology, and data collection, processing, and publication.

Through the [[Greenmark]] program set up by the Fundamentals for Promoting the Use of the Taiwan Ecolabel, a number of energy-using appliances have been granted [[Ecolabel]]s. For the electronic products, energy efficiency is one of the most important criteria for granting Green Marks. For further details, refer to the section on packaging and labeling. The Statute for Upgrading Industries also provides incentives for the improvement of energy efficiency.

== Energy research ==

The Center for Energy Research (CER) at [[National Central University]] has initiated a plan to educate energy professionals. It would coordinate professors from related disciplines and attempt to build a diversified teaching platform to recruit young students and researchers. The center focuses on training students in [[GREEN TECHNOLOGY|green technology]] and supporting research into new product development.

*Energy Technology and Management Research Center at [[National Chiao Tung University]]
*CER at [[National Central University]] [http://www.cc.ncu.edu.tw/~w3energy/EnergyCenter/English/intro_en.htm] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111008140941/http://www.cc.ncu.edu.tw/~w3energy/EnergyCenter/English/intro_en.htm |date=2011-10-08 }}
*New Energy Research Center at [[National Taiwan University]]

Currently there are four nuclear research centers in Taiwan ranging up to 2.8 MW.<ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=http://www.world-nuclear.org/info/Country-Profiles/Others/Nuclear-Power-in-Taiwan/|title=Taiwan Nuclear Power|access-date=20 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150323131343/http://www.world-nuclear.org/info/Country-Profiles/Others/Nuclear-Power-in-Taiwan/|archive-date=23 March 2015}}</ref>

According to reports by National Cheng Kung University, Taiwan is in need of stepping up its pace in [[Fusion power#2000s|fusion power research]] if it wishes to develop more sources of "clean" energy.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news-en.secr.ncku.edu.tw/files/14-1083-32424,r614-1.php |title=NCKU Nears Step in Nuclear Fusion Power - NCKU, National Cheng Kung University-News Center |access-date=2016-03-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160328095908/http://news-en.secr.ncku.edu.tw/files/14-1083-32424,r614-1.php |archive-date=2016-03-28 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Energy in the United States
======================================================================

{{Short description|None}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2023}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2023}}
[[File:Tree Chart of U.S. Energy Consumption by Energy Type in 2025 created from data listed on the EIA website.png|thumb|298x298px|US energy consumption in 2025<ref name="EIA 1.3">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 1.3 Primary energy consumption by source |date = 26 Nov 2024 |website = EIA |access-date = 11 Aug 2026}}</ref>]]
[[File:In 2024, wind and solar together overtook coal in a historic first for the United States.png|thumb|In 2024, wind and solar together overtook coal for the first time in the US. Natural gas remains the largest energy source in the US at 43%.<ref>{{Cite news |last=EMBER Energy |date=8 April 2025 |title=United States of America |url=https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/united-states-of-america/#:~:text=Wind%20and%20solar%20played%20a,43%25%20of%20generation%20in%202024. |access-date=2025-05-14 |work=Ember Energy |language=en-US}}</ref>]]
'''Energy in the United States''' is obtained from a variety of sources, although the majority came from [[fossil fuel]]s in 2025: 37% of the nation's [[Energy development|energy]] originated from [[petroleum]], 36% from [[natural gas]], and 9% from [[coal]]. Electricity from [[nuclear power]] supplied 9% and [[renewable energy]] supplied 9%, which includes [[Biomass (energy)|biomass]], [[Wind power|wind]], [[Hydroelectricity|hydro]], [[Solar power|solar]] and [[Geothermal energy|geothermal]].<ref name="EIA Facts">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/us-energy-facts/ |title = U.S. energy facts explained |date = 28 July 2026 |website = EIA |access-date = 11 Aug 2026}}</ref><ref name="EIA 1.3"/> Energy consumption in 2025 was mostly for industry (35%) and transportation (37%), with use in homes (15%) and commercial buildings (13%) making up the remainder.<ref name="EIA 2.1a"/><ref name="EIA 2.1b"/> The United States' portion of the [[electrical grid in North America]] had a [[nameplate capacity]] of 1,281 [[Watt#Gigawatt|GW]]<ref name="EIA Electric 4.3">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/ |title = Electric Power Annual |at = 4.3. Existing capacity by energy source |date = 26 Nov 2024 |website = EIA |access-date = 12 Dec 2024}}</ref> and produced 4,429 [[TWh]]<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2b">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 7.2b Electric power sector |date = 26 Nov 2024 |website = EIA |access-date = 12 Dec 2024}}</ref> in 2025, using 32% of primary energy to do so.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 2.1b Energy consumption: Transportation sector, total end-use sectors, and electric power sector |date = 26 Nov 2024 |website = EIA |access-date = 12 Dec 2024}}</ref>

Natural gas overtook coal as the dominant source for electric generation in 2016. Coal was overtaken by nuclear for the first time in 2020 and by renewables in 2023.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2b"/>

Energy figures are measured in [[BTU]], with 1 BTU equal to 1.055 [[joule#Multiples|kJ]] and 1 quadrillion BTU (1 [[quad (unit)|quad]]) equal to 1.055 EJ. Because BTU is a unit of [[heat]], sources that generate electricity directly are multiplied by a conversion factor to equate them with sources that use a [[heat engine]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = Appendix A6 |date = November 26, 2024 |website = EIA |access-date = December 12, 2024}}</ref>

The United States was the second-largest energy producer and consumer in 2024 after [[Energy policy of China|China]].<ref name="EIA World">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/international/data/world |title = International - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) |website = EIA |access-date = 11 Aug 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260809195008/https://www.eia.gov/international/data/world|archive-date=2026-08-09}}</ref> The United States had a per capita energy consumption of {{convert|277|e6BTU|abbr=unit}}, ranking it tenth in the world behind [[Energy in Canada|Canada]], [[Energy in Iceland|Iceland]], and several [[Arab world|Arab nations]].<ref name="EIA World"/>

== History ==
{{Further|Environmental history of the United States#History of energy}}
[[File:US Energy Consumption historical percap.png|thumb|upright=1.6|Per capita energy use by source]]

[[File:US Energy Consumption historical percent.png|thumb|upright=1.6|The percentage of energy use by source]]

[[File:Energy consumption by source, United States.svg|thumb|upright=1.6| Energy consumption by source]]

From its founding until the late 19th century, population and energy use in the United States both increased by about 3% per year,<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.census.gov/library/publications/1975/compendia/hist_stats_colonial-1970.html |title = Bicentennial Edition: Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970 |at = p8 |date = September 1975 |website = US Census |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref><ref name="EIA Monthly D1">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = Appendix D1 Estimated primary energy consumption in the United States, selected years, 1635–1945 |date = March 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref> resulting in a relatively constant per capita energy use of 100 million BTU. [[Wood fuel|Wood]] made up the majority of this until near the end of the 1800s, meaning the average American burned eight tons of wood each year.<ref>{{cite web |last=Stelzer |first=Hank |title=Wood Fuel for Heating |url=https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g5450 |access-date=2023-04-13 |website=extension.missouri.edu |language=en}}</ref>

The [[Industrial Revolution in the United States]] saw an increased use of [[coal]]. By the late 1800s, it had surpassed wood as the major source of energy, as it was cheaper for those living in cities. Lighting, heating and transportation could all be fueled by coal.<ref>{{cite web |last=Adams |first=Sean Patrick |title=The US Coal Industry in the Nineteenth Century |url=https://eh.net/encyclopedia/the-us-coal-industry-in-the-nineteenth-century-2/ |access-date=2023-04-13 |website=EH.net}}</ref> Between 1925 and 1975, coal use was more stagnant, although it dominated the growing electricity sector.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2a"/> [[Petroleum]] and [[natural gas]] took its place, as car ownership doubled in the two decades [[Economic history of the United States#Post-World War II prosperity: 1945–1973|after the war]],<ref>{{cite web |url = https://tedb.ornl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/TEDB_Ed_40.pdf#page=85 |title = Transportation Energy Data Book |at = p85 |date = June 2022 |website = ORNL |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref> and as [[Natural gas pipeline system in the United States|the number of pipelines]] rose dramatically.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://pstrust.org/about-pipelines/stats/age-of-natural-gas-pipelines/ |title = Age of Natural Gas Pipelines |website = Pipeline Safety Trust |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref>

During the first half of the 20th century, per capita energy use doubled to 200 million BTU, and reached 300 million BTU by the late 60s. After a peak of 360 million BTU in 1979, per capita consumption generally declined, and dipped below 300 million BTU in 2020.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.7">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 1.7 Primary energy consumption, energy expenditures, and carbon dioxide emissions indicators |date = March 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref> In comparison, the world average increased from {{convert|68|to|74|e6BTU|abbr=unit}} per person between 1980 and 2020.<ref name="EIA World"/>

Domestic oil production peaked in 1970 and did not recover for 40 years. However, [[oil]] imports allowed consumption to double. Oil represented the vast majority of net imports during this time.<ref name="EIA Imports"/> Increased reliance on imported oil coincided with the [[1973 oil crisis]].

Total imports peaked in 2005, when they represented 30% of total consumption. A consistent decline occurred over the next 15 years, as oil production doubled and domestic use receded. This allowed the United States to be a net exporter of energy for the first time in 70 years. As of 2021, the US net exports 3.9% of energy production.<ref name="EIA Imports">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/us-energy-facts/imports-and-exports.php |title = U.S. energy facts explained  |at = Imports & Exports |date = June 10, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref>

Around 2010, many other trends began to reverse. By 2020, improvements in [[fracking]] had allowed [[natural gas]] production to increase by more than half,<ref>{{cite news |last=Kemp |first=John |date=2022-11-23 |title=Column: Is the U.S. shale oil revolution over? |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/commodities/is-us-shale-oil-revolution-over-kemp-2022-11-22/ |access-date=2023-04-13}}</ref> while coal decreased by half.

[[Renewable energy|Renewables]] in the 20th century consisted mainly of [[Hydroelectricity|hydro]] and wood. Hydro power had been relatively constant since 1970, while wood saw a bump in 1980. Between 2000 and 2020, wind, solar and biofuels increased by a factor of ten. By 2020, wind had surpassed hydro, and biofuels had surpassed wood.<ref name="EIA Renewable">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 10.1 Production and consumption by source |date = March 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref>

===2026 Iran war===
Instability in the Middle East has driven a push for oil and gas production in the Americas as nations seek reliable supply sources. Across the region—from Canada to Brazil—production is projected to rise by 10 percent by December 2026. Meanwhile, Venezuela and Suriname are ramping up their output, supported by investments from Western oil companies.<ref name="FT">{{cite web |last1=Smyth |first1=Jamie |last2=Nugent |first2=Ciara |title=Iran war tilts balance of global oil power towards Americas |url=https://www.ft.com/content/cfa976d5-e320-4ee8-8c86-84733471a4a1?syn-25a6b1a6=1 |website=Financial Times}}</ref>

== Primary energy production ==

{{Chart|align=center|caption=[[U.S. Energy Information Administration]].<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Table 1.2 Primary Energy Production by Source
 |url=https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T01.02
 |website=U.S. Energy Information Administration
 |access-date=29 October 2025
}}</ref>|chart=US Primary Energy Production by Source.Line.chart|data=US Primary Energy Production by Source.tab|source=US Primary Energy Production by Source.tab|border=1}}

The United States is the world's second-largest producer of energy. It produces 16% of the world's energy, about three-fourths as much as China.<ref name="EIA World" /> Since 2019, the country has been a net exporter of energy. In 2023, 102.8 quads were produced and net exports were 7.6% of production.<ref name="EIA Imports" />

[[File:US energy production 2023.png |thumb|upright=1.2| US energy production in 2023<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2">{{cite web |date=26 Nov 2024 |title=Monthly Energy Review |url=https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |access-date=12 Dec 2024 |website=EIA |at=1.3 Primary energy production by source}}</ref>]]

=== Fossil fuels ===

[[Fossil fuels]] have long produced most energy in the US, accounting for 84% of total production<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/> and 60% of electric generation as of 2023.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2a"/> Although costs for some fossil fuels are declining, renewables are becoming cheaper faster.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://ourworldindata.org/cheap-renewables-growth |title = Why did renewables become so cheap so fast? |date = December 1, 2020 |website = EIA |access-date = June 30, 2023}}</ref> Despite this, use of fossil fuels has remained near 80% for the past 30 years.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/>

The vast majority of [[Greenhouse gas emissions|carbon emissions]] in the US came from fossil fuels.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.epa.gov/ghgemissions/sources-greenhouse-gas-emissions |title = Sources of Greenhouse Gas Emissions |date = April 28, 2023 |website = EPA |access-date = June 30, 2023}}</ref> The largest sources for carbon pollution from energy were petroleum (46%), natural gas (35%) and coal (19%),<ref name="EIA Monthly 11.1">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 11.1 By source |date = April 25, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = June 30, 2023}}</ref> and of petroleum, motor gasoline (21%) and diesel (12%) were the largest contributors. As gas has been replacing coal, emissions from the two combined have declined from a peak in 2008, down 25% as of 2021. During the same time frame, petroleum declined by only 17%.<ref name="EIA Monthly 11.1"/> Fossil fuels in the United States produced 8% more carbon dioxide in 2022 compared to 2020.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sources of Greenhouse Gas Emissions |url=https://www.epa.gov/ghgemissions/sources-greenhouse-gas-emissions#:~:text=In%202022%2C%20CO2%20emissions,decreased%20by%206%25%20from%202021. |website=EPA | date=December 29, 2015 }}</ref>

In 2023, fossil fuels generated 2,509 TWh of electricity, accounting for 60 percent of all electricity generation.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2a"/>

==== Coal ====

{{main|Coal power in the United States}}

{{see also|List of coal-fired power stations in the United States}}

[[Coal]] made up 11% of production in 2021,<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/> 90% of which went to producing electricity.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2a"/> Coal [[Electrification|electrified]] rapidly throughout the 50s, 60s and 70s and half of annual electricity was from coal until the 2010s. Coal peaked in 2006, when it represented a third of total energy production. During the 2010s it underwent a steady decline, mostly being replaced by natural gas. In contrast, net exports have remained near 2 quads in the same time period, but this now amounts to 17% of total production.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.4c">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 1.4c Primary energy net imports by source |date = June 27, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref>

The decline of coal has many factors, including the aforementioned rise of natural gas, the closing of old plants, and environmental regulations.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://siepr.stanford.edu/publications/policy-brief/what-killing-us-coal-industry |title = What Is Killing the US Coal Industry? |date = March 1, 2017 |website = SIEPR |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref> Coal supply has not become an issue, as the US has the largest coal reserve in the world, 40% larger than Russia.<ref name="EIA World"/>

The first DC plant in the US was a coal plant in [[New York City]], opened in 1882. The first AC plant was a coal plant in [[Ehrenfeld, Pennsylvania]], opened in 1902.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://energybc.ca/cache/historyofenergyuse/www.netl.doe.gov/KeyIssues/historyofcoaluse.html |title = History of U.S. Coal Use |website = energybc.ca |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref> Among the largest plants still operating is the [[James H. Miller Jr. Electric Generating Plant]] in [[West Jefferson, Alabama]]<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.al.com/news/2022/12/alabama-coal-plant-still-the-largest-greenhouse-gas-emitter-in-united-states.html |title = Alabama coal plant still the largest greenhouse gas emitter in United States  |date = December 6, 2022 |website = al.com |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref> and among the oldest is the James E. Rogers Energy Complex in [[Mooresboro, North Carolina]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.duke-energy.com/our-company/about-us/power-plants/rogers-energy-complex |title = Rogers Energy Complex |website = Duke Energy |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref>

==== Natural gas ====

{{main|Natural gas in the United States}}
{{see also|List of natural gas-fired power stations in the United States}}

[[File:US Natural Gas.webp|thumb|US natural gas production, imports, and exports]]
[[File:Natural gas production and price.webp|thumb|Natural gas production by field]]

In 2025, dry [[natural gas]] production reached a record 39 trillion cubic feet. Natural gas remained the largest source of US domestic energy production.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The United States set record energy production in 2025, again - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) |url=https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67684 |access-date=2026-10-27 |website=www.eia.gov}}</ref> Natural gas surpassed coal for production in 2011 and for generation in 2016. Between 2006 and 2022, the US has gone from net importing 4 quads of natural gas to exporting 4 quads.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.4c"/>

The United States has been the world's largest producer of natural gas since 2011, when it surpassed [[Russia]]. However, the US ranks 7th in proven reserves.<ref name="EIA World"/> Differences in supply explain why gas is cheaper in the US than it is in Europe.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=3310 |title = Global natural gas prices vary considerably |date = September 30, 2011 |website = EIA |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref>

Among the largest natural gas power plants in the US is [[West County Energy Center]] in [[Palm Beach County, Florida]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.arnolditkin.com/blog/plant-accidents/the-10-biggest-power-plants-in-the-u-s-/ |title = The 10 Biggest Power Plants in the U.S. |date = September 9, 2022 |website = arnolditkin.com |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref> [[Philadelphia]] had the first natural gas distributor in the US.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.apga.org/apgamainsite/aboutus/facts/history-of-natural-gas|title = A Brief History of Natural Gas |website = arnolditkin.com |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref>

[[Natural gas liquids]] are liquid hydrocarbons obtained from natural gas fields. Production has tripled from 2000 to 2022, now making up 9% of fossil fuels.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/> The US leads the world in NGL production, ahead of Saudi Arabia.<ref name="EIA World"/>

During the 2023-24 winter heating season in the United States, natural gas inventories ended at 2,290 billion cubic feet (Bcf), 39% above the five-year average, due to mild weather resulting in reduced consumption. Withdrawals from storage were approximately 1,500 Bcf, lower than the usual 2,000 Bcf. By March 2024, the [[Henry Hub]] spot price had decreased to $1.50 per million British thermal units (MMBtu), significantly below the forecasted $3.10/MMBtu, with expectations of prices staying below $2.00/MMBtu until the second half of 2024, averaging $2.20/MMBtu for the year<ref>{{Cite web |last=EIA |first=U.S. Energy Information Administration |date=2024-04-11 |title=Mild winter weather may lead to persistently high natural gas inventories through 2025 |url=https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=61803 |access-date=14 April 2024 |website=www.eia.gov}}</ref>

==== Petroleum ====

{{main|Petroleum in the United States}}

[[File:US oil production, imports, & exports.webp|thumb|US oil production, imports, and exports]]

[[Crude oil]] made up 24% of production in 2021.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/> Oil has more than doubled from a slump in the early 2000s, even surpassing its previous peak in 1970. Imports have declined during the same time period, but the US still net imports 20% of consumption.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.4c"/>

The US has been the largest producer of crude oil since 2018, ahead of Saudi Arabia.<ref name="EIA World"/> Texas produces far more oil than any other state.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/oil-and-petroleum-products/where-our-oil-comes-from.php |title = Oil and petroleum products explained  |date = September 16, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = June 29, 2023}}</ref>

U.S. oil and gas production was higher at the end of both the [[Donald Trump|Trump]] and [[Joe Biden|Biden]] administrations compared to the beginning of their terms. Oil and gas constitute the majority of energy consumption in the United States. This production not only enhances energy security but also helps maintain lower prices. However, the combustion of oil and gas significantly contributes to climate change.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Thomas |first1=Valerie |editor-first1=Stacy |editor-last1=Morford |title=Under both Trump and Biden-Harris, US oil and gas production surged to record highs, despite very different energy goals |url=https://theconversation.com/under-both-trump-and-biden-harris-us-oil-and-gas-production-surged-to-record-highs-despite-very-different-energy-goals-236859 |website=the conversation |date=September 9, 2024 |doi=10.64628/AAI.4v6cwc5ku |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Nuclear ===

[[File:WSUReactorCore.JPG | thumb|Cherenkov radiation]]

{{main|Nuclear power in the United States}}

[[Nuclear power]] was 8.3% of total production<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/> and 18.8% of electric generation<ref name="Electric 3.1.A"/> in 2021. Seven states made up half the total: [[Illinois]] (12%), [[Pennsylvania]] (10%), [[South Carolina]] (7%), [[Alabama]] (6%), [[North Carolina]] (6%), [[Texas]] (5%) and [[Tennessee]] (5%).

The US generated 772 TWh of nuclear power in 2022, surpassing [[Nuclear power in China|China]] (395 TWh) and [[Nuclear power in France|France]] (282 TWh). However, nuclear power constitutes a much smaller percentage of total power generation (18%) when compared to France (63%).<ref>{{cite web |url = https://pris.iaea.org/pris/worldstatistics/nuclearshareofelectricitygeneration.aspx |title = Nuclear Share of Electricity Generation in 2021  |date = May 14, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref>

Nuclear had significant growth from the 70s through the 90s, but has stagnated since.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/> A cessation of new nuclear plant construction coincided with the [[Three Mile Island accident|accident at Three Mile Island]].<ref>{{cite news |url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/three-mile-island-represented-the-power-and-peril-of-nuclear-energy-now-its-closed/2019/09/26/513a430c-dfcd-11e9-be96-6adb81821e90_story.html |title = Three Mile Island represented the power and peril of nuclear energy. Now it's closed. |date = September 26, 2019 |newspaper = Washington Post |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref> Future growth may come from smaller reactors.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://apnews.com/article/technology-politics-utilities-nuclear-power-climate-and-environment-23357f4087988a9d21fe714e5660838b |title = Nuclear industry hopes to expand output with new reactors |date = June 21, 2022 |website = AP News |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref>

Among the largest nuclear plants in the US are [[Grand Gulf Nuclear Station|Grand Gulf]] in [[Claiborne County, Mississippi]] and [[Peach Bottom Nuclear Generating Station|Peach Bottom]] in [[York County, Pennsylvania]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.statista.com/statistics/273111/largest-nuclear-power-reactors-worldwide-by-capacity/ |title = Leading nuclear power reactors in operation worldwide as of December 2021, by gross capacity  |date = August 1, 2022  |website = Statista |access-date = June 30, 2023}}</ref> The oldest reactor still in commercial operation is [[Nine Mile Point]] in [[Scriba, New York]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=228&t=21 |title = How old are U.S. nuclear power plants, and when was the newest one built? |date = March 7, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = June 30, 2023}}</ref>

=== Renewables ===

[[File:US Energy Production 2021 Renewable.png|thumb|Renewable energy sources, 2021.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/>]]

{{Main|Renewable energy in the United States}}

[[Renewable energy]] in the United States accounted for 12.5% of the total production in 2021,<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/> and 20.7% of electric generation.<ref name="Electric 3.1.A"/> The category has seen rapid growth, doubling in total output between 2000 and 2020. They have exceeded nuclear since 2011 and surpassed coal in 2020 for the first time since wood fuel fell out of use.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/>

Renewables are expected to continue growing.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=51698 |title = EIA projects that renewable generation will supply 44% of U.S. electricity by 2050 |date = December 8, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref> Because many of these are [[variable renewable energy]], there are plans for considerable growth in [[Battery storage power station|battery storage]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=54939 |title = U.S. battery storage capacity will increase significantly by 2025 |date = March 18, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref> As of 2025, 755 counties have bans on wind or solar energy production.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tilton |first=Julia |date=September 20, 2026 |title=An Idaho county banned wind and solar projects. Some locals are having regrets. |url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/09/bannock-county-idaho-solar-wind-renewables-development-projects-ban-referendum-farming-regrets/ |access-date=2026-10-07 |website=Mother Jones |language=en-US}}</ref>

{{Clear}}

==== Biomass ====
{{see also|Biofuel in the United States}}

[[File:Lincolnway Energy ethanol plant.jpg | thumb | An ethanol plant in [[Nevada, Iowa]]]]
[[File:WOOD CHIP BURNER AT NIGHT - NARA - 543002.jpg | thumb | Wood burner in [[Scotia, California]] ]]

[[Biomass (energy)|Biomass]] made up 5% of total production and 38% of renewables in 2022.<ref name="EIA Monthly 1.2"/> About 49% of this was [[biofuels]], 43% was [[wood fuel|wood]], and 8% was [[Municipal solid waste#Energy generation|waste]] and other biomass.

[[Ethanol]] made up the majority of biofuels in 2022, while [[biodiesel]] and renewable diesel made up about 16%. For ethanol, about 40% of the available energy is lost or diverted to co-products during the manufacturing process,<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 10.3 Fuel ethanol overview |date = March 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 15, 2023}}</ref> and the equivalent of 20% is used to power and run the equipment.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/manufacturing/data/2018/ |title = 2018 MECS Survey Data |at = 5.2 By Manufacturing Industry with Net Electricity p64 |date = February 23, 2021 |website = EIA |access-date = April 15, 2023}}</ref> About 45% of domestic corn output goes toward producing ethanol.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/crops/corn-and-other-feed-grains/feed-grains-sector-at-a-glance |title = Feed Grains Sector at a Glance |date = January 27, 2023 |website = USDA ERS |access-date = April 29, 2023}}</ref> The US led the world in ethanol production in 2021, producing more than half of the total.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://ethanolrfa.org/markets-and-statistics/annual-ethanol-production |title = World Fuel Ethanol Production by Region |website = RFA |access-date = April 15, 2023}}</ref> The US is a net exporter of biofuels.

Use of biofuels increased by a factor of 10 between 2000 and 2020, eventually exceeding wood.<ref name="EIA Renewable"/> The desire for ethanol originated from the need to replace [[methyl tert-butyl ether]], which was contaminating groundwater.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/supplements.php |title = Short-Term Energy Outlook  |at = 2001: MTBE Production Economics |date = April 2001 |website = EIA |access-date = April 15, 2023}}</ref> The [[Energy Policy Act of 2005]] mandated an increased use of ethanol.<ref>
{{cite web |url = https://www.ag.ndsu.edu/energy/biofuels/energy-briefs/history-of-ethanol-production-and-policy |title = History of Ethanol Production and Policy |website = ag.ndsu.edu |access-date = April 15, 2023}}</ref> Most [[gasoline]] sold in the US contains up to 10% ethanol.<ref>
{{cite web |url = https://afdc.energy.gov/fuels/ethanol_blends.html |title = Ethanol Blends
|website = AFDC |access-date = April 15, 2023}}</ref>

Industry uses two-thirds of the wood fuel in the US, while the residential sector uses about a quarter. [[History of the lumber industry in the United States|Wood]] and [[Pulp and paper industry|paper]] factories use wood waste on-site to reduce their energy costs. About 9% of homes used [[firewood]] in 2020.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/biomass/wood-and-wood-waste.php |title = Biomass explained
|at = Wood and wood waste |date = June 2, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 15, 2023}}</ref>

Wood made up the majority of energy consumption until near the end of the 1800s, after which it declined in total use for several decades, to about half its peak.<ref name="EIA Monthly D1"/> The 80s saw the first significant increase in over a century, of about 65%, before declining again by the 2010s.<ref name="EIA Renewable"/>

{{Clear}}

==== Geothermal ====

[[File:McGinness Hills 1&2 Snow.jpg | thumb | [[McGinness Hills Geothermal Complex|McGinness Hills]] in Nevada]]

{{main|Geothermal energy in the United States}}

Two-thirds of the [[geothermal energy]] in the US in 2021 was electric, with the remainder being direct use and heat pumps.<ref name="EIA Renewable"/><ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 10.2c Consumption: transportation and electric power sectors |date = April 25, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 12, 2023}}</ref> [[Geothermal power]] made up 2% of renewable generation,<ref name="Electric 3.1.A"/> 70% of which came from California.<ref name="State Electric"/> [[The Geysers]] is the largest complex of geothermal energy production in the world.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/largest-geothermal-power-plants-in-the-world.html |title = Largest Geothermal Power Plants In The World |date = April 25, 2017 |website = World Atlas |access-date = May 12, 2023}}</ref> The US ranks first in geothermal capacity, ahead of [[Indonesia]] and the [[Philippines]].<ref name="IRENA"/>

{{Clear}}

==== Hydro ====

[[File:Grand Coulee Dam.jpg | thumb | [[Grand Coulee Dam]] in Washington]]

{{main|Hydroelectricity in the United States}}

[[Hydroelectricity|Hydro]] made up 6% of electric generation and 29% of renewable generation in 2021.<ref name="Electric 3.1.A"/> Three states made up over half of the total: [[Washington (State)|Washington]] (29%), [[New York (State)|New York]] (12%) and [[Oregon]] (11%).<ref name="State Electric"/> Overall 246 TWh were generated across 1,449 conventional plants and 40 [[Pumped-storage hydroelectricity|pumped storage]] plants.<ref name="EIA Electric 4.1">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/ |title = Electric Power Annual |at = 4.1. Count of electric power industry power plants, by sector, by predominant energy sources within plant |date = November 7, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 29, 2023}}</ref> As of 2021, the US was fourth in the world in total hydroelectric generation behind Canada and Brazil, each generating over 350 TWh. China produced the most, with an estimated 1,300 TWh.<ref name="IRENA">{{cite web |url = https://www.irena.org/Data/View-data-by-topic/Capacity-and-Generation/Country-Rankings |title = Country Rankings |date = March 25, 2023 |website = IRENA |access-date = April 29, 2023}}</ref>

Hydro has been used in the US since 1880 when it powered the Wolverine Chair factory in [[Grand Rapids, Michigan]].<ref name="Hydro explained">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/hydropower/ |title = Hydropower explained |at = Hydropower has a long history |date = April 20, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = April 29, 2023}}</ref> Additionally electricity from hydropower has been sold in the U.S. since 1882 with a plant in [[Appleton, Wisconsin]] being the first to sell it.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hydropower explained - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) |url=https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/hydropower/ |access-date=2026-08-12 |website=www.eia.gov}}</ref>By 1950, 29% of total electricity production came from hydro, as it produced 96 TWh.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2b"/> Hydro generation had tripled by the 70s, but has not consistently grown since. Hydro has had large fluctuations from year to year: for example in 2010, generation jumped from 253 to 311 TWh the next year, before dropping to 269 TWh the year after that. While hydro has maintained generation in the 200 to 350 TWh range for the past few decades, its share of the total has declined as other sources have risen. Since 2019, wind power has exceeded hydro as the largest renewable electricity source.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2b"/>

At 132 years old, the plant in [[Whiting, Wisconsin]] is the oldest power plant still running in the US.<ref name="Hydro explained"/> The [[Grand Coulee Dam]] is the largest plant [[List of hydroelectric power stations in the United States|for hydro]] and [[List of largest power stations in the United States|in general]] in the US, and the fifth-largest hydro plant [[List of largest hydroelectric power stations|in the world]]. Built in Washington in 1942, it continues to operate with a capacity of 6,765 MW.<ref name="Hydro explained"/> The [[Bath County Pumped Storage Station]] is the second-largest such facility in the world, with a capacity of 3,003 MW.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.nsenergybusiness.com/features/largest-pumped-storage-plants/ |title = Largest pumped storage plants in operation and development |date = May 13, 2020 |website = NS Energy |access-date = April 29, 2023}}</ref>

==== Solar ====

[[File:Ivanpah Solar Electric Generating System Tower.jpg | thumb | [[Concentrated solar power|Concentrated solar thermal]] plant ([[Ivanpah Solar Power Facility|Ivanpah Solar]])]]

{{main|Solar power in the United States}}

[[Solar power|Solar]] made up 4% of electric generation and 19% of renewable generation in 2021. Of the 164 TWh generated, 70% was by utilities and an estimated 30% was small-scale such as rooftop solar.<ref name="Electric 3.1.A">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/ |title = Electric Power Annual |at = 3.1.A. Net generation by energy source: Total (all sectors) |date = November 7, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = May 5, 2023}}</ref> Three states made up over half of total grid generation: [[California]] (30%), [[Texas]] (13%) and [[North Carolina]] (9%).<ref name="State Electric"/> In 2021, the US grid produced the second most solar power in the world, behind China's 328 GWh.<ref name="IRENA"/>

Since 2006, solar has been the fastest growing energy source in the US, expanding 50% per year on average.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2a"/> The largest solar farms in the US include [[Solar Star]] in [[Rosamond, California]], [[Desert Sunlight Solar Farm|Desert Sunlight]] in [[Desert Center, California]] and [[Copper Mountain Solar Facility|Copper Mountain]] in [[Boulder City, Nevada]].<ref name="EIA Plants">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia923/ |title = Form EIA-923 detailed data |date = April 27, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 12, 2023}}</ref> The [[Bureau of Land Management]] leases federal land to be used for solar farms.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://blmsolar.anl.gov/competitive/other-procedures/sez/ |title = Solar Energy Zones |website = BLM |access-date = May 12, 2023}}</ref>

Almost all states employ [[net metering]] to compensate owners of small-scale solar, although [[Net metering in the United States|policies by state]] vary considerably.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.solarpowerworldonline.com/2020/03/which-states-offer-net-metering/ |title = 2022 UPDATE: Which states offer net metering? |date = April 1, 2022 |website = Solar Power World |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref>

==== Wind ====

[[File:Spruce Mt Wind in Fall.jpg | thumb | Wind turbines in [[Maine]]]]

{{main|Wind power in the United States}}

[[Wind power|Wind]] made up 9% of electric generation and 44% of renewable generation in 2021.<ref name="Electric 3.1.A"/> Four states made up over half of the total: [[Texas]] (26%), [[Iowa]] (10%), [[California]] (9%) and [[Kansas]] (7%).<ref name="State Electric"/> The US grid produces significantly more wind power than Germany or India, but less than half of China.<ref name="IRENA"/>

Since 1998, wind power has grown 23% per year on average in the US.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2a"/> Prominent areas for wind turbines include [[Alta Wind Energy Center|Alta Wind]] in [[Kern County, California]], [[Shepherds Flat Wind Farm|Shepherds Flat]] in [[Gilliam County, Oregon]] and [[Roscoe Wind Farm]] in [[Nolan County, Texas]].<ref name="EIA Plants"/>

{{Clear}}

== Final energy consumption ==

[[File:Consumption sector treemap.png | thumb|Consumption by sector, 2021]]

{{Image frame|width=300|content=[[File:Oil refinery in Houston 2018a.jpg|150px]][[File:Minneapolis neighborhood Near North (52247881193).jpg|150px]][[File:2007 Toyota RAV4 V6 AWD.jpg|150px]][[File:Federal Office Building Oak Ridge (7071647423).jpg|150px]]
|caption=An example of each consumption sector: a refinery, a house, a car and an office|align=right}}

[[Industry (economics)|Industry]] has long been the country's largest energy sector.<ref name="EIA 2.1a">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 2.1a Energy consumption: Residential, commercial, and industrial sectors |date = April 25, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 2, 2023}}</ref><ref name="EIA 2.1b">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 2.1b Energy consumption: Transportation sector, total end-use sectors, and electric power sector |date = April 25, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 2, 2023}}</ref> It used 33% of total energy in 2021, most of which was divided evenly between natural gas, electricity and petroleum. A survey from 2018 estimated that the largest energy users were the [[chemical industry]] (30%), [[Petroleum refining processes|petroleum]] and [[Coal preparation plant|coal]] processing (18%), [[Mining in the United States|mining]] (9%) and [[Pulp and paper industry|paper]] (9%).<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/use-of-energy/industry.php |title = Energy use in industry |date = June 13, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref>

The most energy-intensive industry was by far petroleum and coal, at over 30 billion BTU per employee. The paper industry was second at 6.5 billion BTU per employee. Each of these handles energy sources as part of their raw materials (fossil fuels and wood).<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/manufacturing/data/2018/ |title = 2018 MECS Survey Data |at = Table 6.1 By Manufacturing Industry and Region |date = August 27, 2021 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref> The same survey found that half of the electric use was to drive machines and about 10% each for heating, cooling and electro-chemical processes. Most of the remainder was for factory lighting and [[HVAC]]. About half of the natural gas was for process heating, and most of the rest was for [[boilers]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/manufacturing/data/2018/ |title = 2018 MECS Survey Data |at = Table 5.4 By Manufacturing Industry with Total Consumption of Electricity |date = August 27, 2021 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref>

[[Transportation]] used 28% of energy, almost all of which was petroleum and other fuels. Half of the combustible fuels that make up the transportation sector were [[gasoline]], and half of the vehicle usage was for [[cars]] and small trucks.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/use-of-energy/transportation.php |title = Energy use for transportation |at = 1.1 Primary energy overview |date = June 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref> [[Diesel fuel|Diesel]] and [[List of truck types|heavier trucks]] each made up about a quarter of their respective categories; [[jet fuel]] and [[Air travel|aircraft]] were about a tenth each. Biofuels such as ethanol and biodiesel made up 5%, while natural gas was 4%. Electricity from [[mass transit]] was 0.2%; electricity for light passenger vehicles is counted in other sectors, but figures from the US Department of Energy estimate that 2.1 million electric vehicles used 6.1 TWh to travel 19 billion miles, indicating an average fuel efficiency of 3.1 miles per kWh.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://insideevs.com/news/623977/us-2021-plugins-traveled-19billion-miles-electricity/ |title = US: In 2021, Plug-Ins Traveled 19 Billion Miles On Electricity |date = November 29, 2022 |website = InsideEVs |access-date = August 6, 2023}}</ref>

Over two-thirds of the energy used by homes, offices, and other commercial businesses is electric, including [[Energy conversion efficiency|electric losses]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 2.2 Residential sector energy consumption |date = April 25, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 2.3 Commercial sector energy consumption |date = April 25, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref> Most of the energy used in homes was for space heating (34%) and [[water heating]] (19%), much more than the amount used for space cooling (16%) and [[Refrigerator|refrigeration]] (7%).<ref>Assuming electric losses of about 65%. {{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/use-of-energy/homes.php |title = Energy use in homes |date = June 14, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref> Businesses use similar percentages for space cooling and refrigeration. They use less for space and water heating but more for [[lighting]] and cooking.<ref>Assuming ventilation is roughly proportional for heating and cooling. {{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/commercial/data/2018/index.php?view=consumption |title = 
2018 CBECS Survey Data |at = End-use consumption |date = December 21, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref>

Most homes in the US are [[House|single-family detached]],<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2015/hc/php/hc9.1.php |title = Table HC9.1 Household demographics of U.S. homes by housing unit type, 2015 |date = May 2018 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref> which on average use almost triple the energy of [[apartments]] in larger buildings.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2015/index.php?view=consumption |title = 2015 RECS Survey Data  |at = CE1.1 Summary consumption and expenditures in the U.S. - totals and intensities |date = May 2018 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref> However, single family households have 50% more persons and triple the floor space. Usage per square foot of living space is roughly equal for most housing types except small apartment buildings and [[mobile homes]]. Small apartments are more likely to be older than other housing types,<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2015/hc/php/hc2.3.php |title = Table HC2.3 Structural and geographic characteristics of U.S. homes by year of construction, 2015 |date = May 2018 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref> while mobile homes tend to have poor [[Building insulation|insulation]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2015/hc/php/hc2.1.php |title = Table HC2.1 Structural and geographic characteristics of U.S. homes by housing unit type, 2015 |date = May 2018 |website = EIA |access-date = May 3, 2023}}</ref>

=== Regional variation ===

The state with the lowest per capita energy use is [[Rhode Island]], at 161 million BTU per year, and the highest is [[Louisiana]], at 908 million BTU per year. Energy use and prices often have an inverse relationship; [[Hawaii]] uses some of the least energy per capita but pays the highest price on average, while Louisiana pays the least on average.<ref name="SEDS">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/state/seds/seds-data-complete.php |title = State Energy Data System |at = Consumption: Total energy consumption per capita by end-use sector |date = June 24, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref>

Residential prices follow a similar trend, but the differences between states are usually less drastic. The exception is Hawaii, which pays 84 cents per million BTU, more than double the next largest state of [[Florida]], which pays 33 cents.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/state/seds/seds-data-complete.php |title = State Energy Data System |at = Prices and Expenditures: Prices Total End-use |date = June 24, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref>

Household energy use varies by home type and by region. Although single-family detached homes are less common in the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast]], the average house there uses 60% more energy than one in the [[Western United States|West]]. Some of the regional differences can be explained by climate, as two-thirds of northeastern homes are in cold regions, while less than a third of western homes are.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2015/index.php?view=consumption |title = 2015 RECS Survey Data  |at = CE1.2 Summary consumption and expenditures in the Northeast - totals and intensities |date = May 2018 |website = EIA |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2015/index.php?view=consumption |title = 2015 RECS Survey Data  |at = CE1.5 Summary consumption and expenditures in the West - totals and intensities |date = May 2018 |website = EIA |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref>

<gallery mode=packed>
File:Average energy percap.png | Overall use per capita
File:Residential Energy Consumption per Capita.png | Home use per capita
File:Overall energy price.png | Overall price per million BTU
File:Residential Energy Price.png | Home price per million BTU
</gallery>

The land-use decisions of cities and towns also explain some of the regional differences in energy use. [[Townhouses]] are more energy efficient than single-family homes because less heat, for example, is used per person. Similarly, areas with more homes in a compact neighborhood encourage walking, biking and transit, thereby reducing transportation energy use. A 2011 U.S. EPA study found that multi-family homes in urban neighborhoods, with well-insulated buildings and fuel-efficient cars, use less than two-thirds of the energy used by conventionally built single-family houses in suburban areas (with standard cars).<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.epa.gov/smartgrowth/location-efficiency-and-housing-type |title = Location Efficiency and Housing Type: Boiling It Down to BTUs |date = April 18, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref>

== Electricity ==
{{main|Electricity sector of the United States}}
[[File:United States power plants by type and nameplate capacity.webp|thumb|United States power stations by type and nameplate capacity]]
[[File:US Electricity treemap.png | thumb|Generation by source<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2a"/>]]
[[File:Electricity prices by sector.webp|thumb|Electricity prices by sector in the United States]]

The United States is the world's second-largest producer and consumer of electricity. It generates 15% of the world's electricity supply, about half as much as China.<ref name="EIA World Electric">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/international/data/world |title = International |at = Electricity |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref>

The United States produced 3,988 TWh in 2021. Total generation has been flat since 2010. Net electricity imports were 39 TWh, or about 1% of sales. Historically, net imports have been between just under 0% to just over 1.5%.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2b"/>

[[Fossil fuel]]s made up the majority of generation, with natural gas providing 38% and coal 23%. Petroleum provided less than 1%. Natural gas as a proportion of fossil fuels has been increasing since the 90's, with coal peaking around 2008 and natural gas becoming the top fossil fuel in 2016.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.2a">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 7.2a Total (all sectors) |date = March 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref>

Nuclear provided 20%, a level consistent since about 1990. Nuclear surpassed coal in 2020 for the first time, as coal dipped to its lowest proportion in over 70 years.

Among renewables, wind and solar continued to expand, with wind exceeding hydro since 2019. Renewable use has doubled from 2010 to 2020, reaching 21% of total generation.

=== Grid capacity ===

{{see also|North American power transmission grid}}

The United States had a [[Nameplate capacity|nameplate generation capacity]] of 1,213 GW  in 2021.<ref name="EIA Electric 4.3"/> The following table summarizes the electrical energy generated by fuel source for the United States grid in 2021. Figures account for generation losses, but not transmission losses. Fission had the highest [[capacity factor]], while petroleum had the lowest.

The US grid first connected East and West in 1967.<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Cohn |first1 = Julie  |title = When the grid was the grid: The history of north america's brief coast-to-coast interconnected machine &#91;scanning our past&#93; |journal = Proceedings of the IEEE |date = January 1, 2019    |volume = 107 |issue = 1 |pages = 232–243 |doi = 10.1109/JPROC.2018.2880938 |bibcode = 2019IEEEP.107..232C }}</ref> There are over 7,300 power plants and almost 160,000 miles of high voltage lines.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.epa.gov/green-power-markets/us-electricity-grid-markets |title = U.S. Electricity Grid & Markets  |date = April 18, 2023 |website = EPA |access-date = June 30, 2023}}</ref>

=== Generation by state ===

[[File:State generation treemap.png | upright=1.1|thumb | Generation by state and source]]

The following figures offer detail into the sources of generation used in each state.<ref name="State Electric">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/state/ |title = Historical State Data |at = Net Generation by State by Type of Producer by Energy Source |date = March 8, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref> Most often, natural gas is the largest source in a given state, with 22 states using it more than any other. Among renewable sources, 18 states use wind power more than any other.

Though not always the most prominent source, each state will use at least one source at a rate above the national average. Twelve states use nuclear power more than average, and California and Hawaii each use more solar and petroleum, respectively.

Texas contributes more to the grid than any other state, followed by Florida, Pennsylvania and California. On net, Pennsylvania exports the most power, while California imports the most.

=== Electric consumption ===

[[File:Electric pct Resid.png|thumb|Home electrification]]

[[Electric energy consumption|Electric grid consumption]] in the US was 3,806 TWh in 2021. Since 2010, total consumption has remained within 2% of this figure. Per capita consumption was 11.5 MWh in 2021, down 8% from its peak in 2007.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.6">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 7.6 Electricity end use |date = March 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref><ref name="US Stats">{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = Appendix C1 Population, U.S. gross domestic product, and U.S. gross output |date = March 28, 2022
|website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref>

Residential customers used 39% of total electricity.<ref name="EIA Monthly 7.6"/> Each month, the average customer used 886 kWh and paid $121 at an average rate of 13.7 cents/kWh.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 9.8 Average prices of electricity to ultimate customers |date = March 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref> The commercial sector used 35% and industrial used 26%. Transportation used less than half of one percent.

System loss within the grid includes use in the generation process and transmission losses, as well as unaccounted loads. For 2021, this amounted to 203 TWh, or 5.3% of grid generation. Electricity used directly at the commercial or industrial level added 139 TWh, so total consumption was 3,945 TWh.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/ |title = Monthly Energy Review |at = 7.1 Overview |date = March 28, 2022 |website = EIA |access-date = April 14, 2023}}</ref>

The northeastern US has long paid the highest electricity prices, while simultaneously using it the least per capita.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/state/ |title = Historical State Data |at = EIA-861 Annual Electric Power Industry Report |date = April 27, 2023 |website = EIA |access-date = May 15, 2023}}</ref> [[California]] is an outlier in the west region; its neighbors tend to pay some of the lowest rates in the country, while California is second only to [[Hawaii]] and [[Alaska]].

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Energy policy of the United States

{{Short description|none}}
{{see also|United States energy law}}
