<!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:Hoover dam from air.jpg|thumb|[[Hoover Dam]]]]
[[File:US oil production, imports, & exports.webp|thumb|300px|US oil production, imports, & exports]]

The '''energy policy of the United States''' is determined by federal, state, and local entities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fowler |first=Luke |last2=Johnson |first2=Autumn |date=2017-11-01 |title=Overlapping Authorities in U.S. Energy Policy |url=https://scholarworks.boisestate.edu/pubadmin_facpubs/76 |journal=The Electricity Journal |doi=10.1016/j.tej.2017.09.014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fowler |first=Luke |date=2018-09-01 |title=Intergovernmental Relations and Energy Policy: What We Know and What We Still Need to Learn |url=https://experts.boisestate.edu/en/publications/intergovernmental-relations-and-energy-policy-what-we-know-and-wh/ |journal=State and Local Government Review |issn=0160-323X}}</ref> Federal Energy policy is principally led by the [[United States Department of Energy|U.S. Department of Energy]]. Energy policy intersects closely with [[decarbonization]], [[Climate change|climate]] policy, and [[environmental policy]]. 

Energy policy spans issues of decarbonization, energy production, distribution, consumption, and modes of use, such as building codes, mileage standards, and commuting policies. U.S. [[energy policy]] may be addressed via [[legislation]], regulation, court decisions, public participation, and other techniques.

Major federal [[List of United States energy acts|energy policy acts]] were passed in 1974, 1992, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2009,<ref name="EISA">{{cite web
 |url          = http://www.thomas.gov/cgi-bin/query/z?c110:H.R.6.ENR:
 |title        = Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (Enrolled as Agreed to or Passed by Both House and Senate)
 |access-date  = 2008-01-18
 |url-status   = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20160115001453/http://www.thomas.gov/cgi-bin/query/z?c110%3AH.R.6.ENR%3A
 |archive-date = January 15, 2016
 |df           = mdy
}}</ref> 2020, 2021, and 2022, although energy-related policies have appeared in many other bills. The most significant recent bills include the [[Presidency of Joe Biden|Biden Administration]] [[Inflation Reduction Act]] as well as the [[Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act|Bipartisan Infrastructure Law]]. 

State and local energy policies typically relate to efficiency standards and/or transportation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency |url=http://www.dsireusa.org/ |access-date=2012-03-30 |publisher=Dsireusa.org}}</ref>

Federal energy policies since the [[1973 oil crisis]] have been criticized for having an alleged crisis-mentality, promoting expensive quick fixes and single-shot solutions that ignore market and technology realities.<ref>{{cite book| last =Grossman| first =Peter| title =U.S. Energy Policy and the Pursuit of Failure| publisher =Cambridge University Press| year =2013| page =416| url =http://www.cambridge.org/us/knowledge/isbn/item7078295/U-S--Energy-Policy-and-the-Pursuit-of-Failure/?site_locale=en_US| isbn =978-1107005174}}</ref><ref>Hamilton, Michael S. 2013. ''Energy Policy Analysis: A Conceptual Framework''. Armonk, NY: M.E. Sharpe, Inc.</ref>

[[United States#Demographics|Americans]] constitute less than 4% of the [[world population|world's population]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is the United States’ share of world energy consumption?  - Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) |url=https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?t=1&id=87 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261011181901/https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?t=1&id=87 |archive-date=2026-10-11 |access-date=2026-10-14 |website=www.eia.gov}}</ref> but consume 16% of the [[Energy use in the United States|world's energy]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=U.S. Energy System Factsheet {{!}} Center for Sustainable Systems |url=https://css.umich.edu/publications/factsheets/energy/us-energy-system-factsheet |access-date=2026-10-14 |website=css.umich.edu |language=en}}</ref> to produce 15.1% of the world's industrial output<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://itif.org/publications/2025/02/18/new-study-finds-us-share-of-global-manufacturing-fall-to-11-percent-by-2030/ |title=Fact of the Week: A New Study Finds the US Share of Global Manufacturing Will Fall to 11 Percent by 2030 |last=Ostertag |first=Meghan |date=2025-02-18 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=2020-01-24 |title=U.S. Manufacturing Economy |url=https://www.nist.gov/el/applied-economics-office/manufacturing/manufacturing-economy/total-us-manufacturing |journal=NIST |language=en}}</ref>. Technologies such as [[Hydraulic fracturing|fracking]] and [[Directional drilling|horizontal drilling]] allowed the United States to become the world's top oil fossil fuel producer in 2014.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=Grant |date=4 July 2014 |title=U.S. is now world's biggest oil producer |website=www.chicagotribune.com |publisher=Bloomberg News |url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/chi-us-is-now-worlds-biggest-oil-producer-20140704,0,1536194.story |access-date=4 July 2014}}</ref> In 2018, US exports of coal, natural gas, crude oil and petroleum products exceeded imports, achieving a degree of [[energy independence]] for the first time in decades.<ref name="oil">{{cite web|url=https://www.usnews.com/news/national-news/articles/2018-07-10/eia-us-net-oil-imports-to-drop-to-lowest-levels-in-60-years |title=EIA: U.S. Net Oil Imports to Drop to Lowest Levels in 60 Years |access-date=13 July 2018}}</ref><ref name="gas">{{cite web |title=BP Statistical Review 2018 |url=https://www.bp.com/content/dam/bp/en/corporate/pdf/energy-economics/statistical-review/bp-stats-review-2018-full-report.pdf |access-date=15 June 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://oilprice.com/Energy/Crude-Oil/US-Will-Soon-Export-More-Oil-Liquids-Than-Saudi-Arabia.html |title=U.S. Will Soon Export More Oil, Liquids Than Saudi Arabia |access-date=9 March 2019}}</ref> In the second half of 2019, the US was the world's top producer of oil and gas.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://oilprice.com/Energy/Energy-General/US-Is-Now-Largest-Oil-And-Gas-Producer-In-The-World.html |title=U.S. Is Now Largest Oil... And Gas Producer In The World |access-date=24 August 2019}}</ref> This energy surplus ended in 2020.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://oilprice.com/Energy/Crude-Oil/Is-US-Energy-Dominance-Coming-To-An-End.html |title=Is U.S. Energy Dominance Coming To An End? |access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-52226236 |title=Oil producers agree to cut production by a tenth |work=BBC News |date=April 9, 2020 |access-date=10 April 2020}}</ref>

Various multinational groups have attempted to establish goals and timetables for energy and other climate-related policies, such as the 1997 [[Kyoto Protocol]] and the [[Paris Agreement|2015 Paris Agreement]]. {{Toclimit}}

==History==
{{See also|History of the petroleum industry in the United States|History of coal mining in the United States|Category:United States federal energy legislation}}
[[File:US historical energy consumption 1776-2024.svg|thumb|US energy use (values in [[Quad (unit)|quad]]/year, each equal to {{Convert|1|quad|TWh|abbr=on|disp=out|lk=on}}/year)]]
[[File:US Proven Oil Reserves 1900 to 2005.png|thumb|US oil reserves increased until 1970, then began to decline.]]
[[File:Grand Coulee Dam.jpg|thumb|[[Grand Coulee Dam]] in Washington State.]]

In the early days of the Republic, energy policy allowed free use of standing [[timber]] for heating and industry. Wind and water provided energy for tasks such as milling grain. In the 19th century, coal became widely used. Whales were rendered into [[whale oil|lamp oil]].<ref name=HistElect>{{cite web | url=http://www.eia.doe.gov/emeu/aer/eh/elec.html | title=Energy in the United States: 1635–2000 – Electricity | publisher=[[United States Department of Energy]] | access-date=2007-07-04 }}</ref> [[Coal gas]] was [[Fractionation|fractionated]] for use as lighting and [[town gas]]. Natural gas was first used in America for lighting in 1816.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://lsa.colorado.edu/summarystreet/texts/naturalgas.htm |title=Natural Gas |access-date=2008-01-18 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080108155406/http://lsa.colorado.edu/summarystreet/texts/naturalgas.htm |archive-date=January 8, 2008 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> Since then, natural gas has grown in importance, especially for electricity generation. US natural gas production peaked in 1973,<ref>{{cite web |title=Oil and natural gas depletion and our future |url=http://www.energybulletin.net/32146.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080209195939/http://www.energybulletin.net/32146.html|archive-date=February 9, 2008}}</ref> and the price has risen significantly since then.

[[Coal]] provided the bulk of US energy needs well into the 20th century. Most urban homes had a coal bin and a coal-fired furnace. Over the years these were replaced with oil furnaces that were easier and safer to operate.<ref>{{cite web|last=Vivian |first=John |url=http://www.motherearthnews.com/Homesteading-and-Self-Reliance/1992-12-01/Mothers-1993-Wood-and-Coal-Stove-Advisory.aspx |title=Wood and Coal Stove Advisory |publisher=Motherearthnews.com |access-date=2012-03-30}}</ref>

From the early 1940s, the [[US government]] and the oil industry entered into a mutually beneficial collaboration to control global oil resources.<ref>{{Cite book |last= Painter |first= David S. |author-link= David S. Painter |year= 1986 |title= Oil and the American Century: The Political Economy of US Foreign Oil Policy, 1941–1954 |location= Baltimore,&nbsp;MD |publisher= [[Johns Hopkins University Press]] |isbn= 978-0-801-82693-1 |url= https://archive.org/details/oilamericancent00pain }}</ref> By 1950, [[oil consumption]] exceeded that of coal.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.eia.doe.gov/kids/history/timelines/petroleum.html | title=Petroleum Timeline | publisher=United States Department of Energy | access-date=2007-07-04 }}</ref><ref name=HistCoal>{{cite web | url=http://www.eia.doe.gov/emeu/aer/eh/coal.html | title=Energy in the United States: 1635–2000 – Coal | publisher=United States Department of Energy| access-date=2007-07-04 }}</ref> Abundant oil in California, Texas, Oklahoma, as well as in Canada and Mexico, coupled with its low cost, ease of transportation, high [[energy density]], and use in [[internal combustion engine]]s, led to its increasing use.<ref name=HistTotal/>

Following [[World War II]], oil heating boilers replaced coal burners along the Eastern Seaboard; [[diesel locomotives]] replaced coal-fired [[steam engines]]; oil-fired power plants dominated; petroleum-burning buses replaced electric [[streetcars]], and citizens bought gasoline-powered cars. [[Interstate Highways]] helped make cars the major means of personal transportation.<ref name=HistTotal>{{cite web | url=http://www.eia.doe.gov/emeu/aer/eh/total.html | title=Energy in the United States: 1635–2000 – Total Energy |  publisher=United States Department of Energy | access-date=2007-07-04 }}</ref> As oil imports increased, [[Foreign policy of the United States|US foreign policy]] was drawn into [[Middle East]]ern politics, seeking to maintain a steady supply via actions such as protecting [[Persian Gulf]] sea lanes.<ref name=HistPetro>{{cite web | url=http://www.eia.doe.gov/emeu/aer/eh/petro.html | title=Energy in the United States: 1635–2000 – Petroleum | publisher=United States Department of Energy | access-date=2007-07-04 }}</ref>

[[Hydroelectricity]] was the basis of [[Nikola Tesla]]'s introduction of the US electricity grid, which started at [[Niagara Falls, New York]], in 1883.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.niagarafrontier.com/power.html |title=Niagara Falls History of Power |publisher=Niagarafrontier.com |access-date=2012-03-30}}</ref> Electricity generated by major dams, such as the [[Tennessee Valley Authority|TVA Project]], [[Grand Coulee Dam]] and [[Hoover Dam]], still produce some of the cheapest ($0.08/kWh) electricity. Rural electrification strung [[Electric power transmission|power lines]] to many more areas.<ref name=HistElect /><ref name=HistRenew>{{cite web | url=http://www.eia.doe.gov/emeu/aer/eh/renew.html | title=Energy in the United States: 1635–2000 – Renewable | publisher=United States Department of Energy | access-date=2007-07-04 }}</ref>

A [[National Maximum Speed Law|National Maximum Speed Limit]] of 55&nbsp;mph (88&nbsp;km/h) was imposed in 1974 (and repealed in 1995) to help reduce energy consumption. With the [[Energy Policy and Conservation Act]], [[Corporate Average Fuel Economy]] (aka CAFE) standards were enacted in 1975 and progressively tightened over time to compel manufacturers to improve vehicle mileage.<ref>{{cite web |title=Performance Profiles of Major Energy Producers 1993 |url=http://tonto.eia.doe.gov/FTPROOT/financial/020693.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011127094625/http://tonto.eia.doe.gov/FTPROOT/financial/020693.pdf |archive-date=2001-11-27 |access-date=2007-07-04 |publisher=United States Department of Energy |quote=See page 48.}}</ref> Year-round [[Daylight Saving Time]] was imposed in 1974 and repealed in 1975. The EPCA also created the [[Strategic Petroleum Reserve (United States)|Strategic Petroleum Reserve]] and banned exports of American-made oil from 1977 until a repeal effort in 2015.

The [[Weatherization Assistance Program]]<ref>{{cite web |date=2012-01-30 |title=Weatherization Assistance Program |url=http://www.eere.energy.gov/weatherization/ |access-date=2012-03-30 |publisher=Eere.energy.gov}}</ref> was enacted in 1977. On average, low-cost [[weatherization]] reduces heating bills by 31% and overall energy bills by $358 per year at 2012 prices. Increased energy efficiency and weatherization spending has a high [[return on investment]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Communities of the Future |url=http://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy99osti/26318.pdf |access-date=2012-03-30}}</ref>

On August 4, 1977, President [[Jimmy Carter]] signed into law the ''Department of Energy Organization Act of 1977'' ({{USStatute|95|91|91|565|1977|08|04}}), which created the [[United States Department of Energy]] (DOE).<ref name=Relyea2003>{{cite book |last1=Relyea |first1=Harold |last2=Carr |first2=Thomas P. |title=The Executive Branch, Creation and Reorganization |year=2003 |publisher=Nova Publishers |page=29}}</ref> The new agency, which began operations on October 1, 1977, consolidated the [[Federal Energy Administration]], the [[Energy Research and Development Administration]], the [[Federal Power Commission]], and programs of various other agencies. Former Secretary of Defense [[James Schlesinger]], who served under Presidents Nixon and Ford during the [[Vietnam War]], was appointed as its first secretary.

On June 30, 1980, Congress passed the [[Energy Security Act]], which reauthorized the [[Defense Production Act of 1950]] and enabled it to cover domestic energy supplies. It also obligated the federal government to promote and reform the [[Strategic Petroleum Reserve (United States)|Strategic Petroleum Reserve]], [[biofuel]]s, [[geothermal power]], [[acid rain]] prevention, [[solar power]], and [[synthetic fuel commercialization]].<ref>{{USPL|96|294}}</ref> The Defense Production Act was further reauthorized in 2009, with modifications requiring the federal government to promote renewable energy, energy efficiency, and improved grid and grid storage installations with its defense procurements.<ref>{{USPL|111|67}}</ref><ref>{{USC|50|4502}}</ref>

The [[Federal government of the United States|federal government]] provided substantially larger [[fossil fuel subsidies|subsidies to fossil fuel]]s than to renewables in the 2002–2008 period. Subsidies to [[fossil fuels]] totaled approximately $72 billion, a direct cost to taxpayers, over the study period. Subsidies for renewable fuels totaled $29 billion over the same period, this was also a direct cost to taxpayers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.elistore.org/Data/products/d19_07.pdf |title=Estimating U.S. Government Subsidies to Energy Sources: 2002–2008|publisher= [[Environmental Law Institute]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130117072837/http://www.elistore.org/Data/products/d19_07.pdf |archive-date=January 17, 2013 }}</ref>

In some cases, the US used energy policy to pursue other international goals. [[Richard Heinberg]] claimed that a declassified [[CIA]] document showed that, during the [[Presidency of Ronald Reagan|Reagan administration]], the US used oil prices as leverage against the [[Soviet Union]] economy by working with Saudi Arabia to keep oil prices low, thus decreasing the value of the USSR's petroleum export industry.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.portlandpeakoil.org/node/1116|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304103830/http://www.portlandpeakoil.org/node/1116|url-status=dead|archive-date=2016-03-04|title=The Challenges Facing the Intelligence Community Regarding Global Oil Depletion|last=Erwin|first=Jerry|date=2006-10-09|publisher=Portland Peak Oil|access-date=2009-04-29}}</ref>

The 2005 [[Energy Policy Act of 2005|Energy Policy Act]] (EPA) addressed (1) energy efficiency; (2) renewable energy; (3) oil and gas; (4) coal; (5) tribal energy; (6) nuclear matters; (7) vehicles and motor fuels, including ethanol; (8) hydrogen; (9) electricity; (10) energy tax incentives; (11) hydropower and geothermal energy; and (12) climate change technology.<ref>{{cite web |date=22 February 2013 |title=Summary of the Energy Policy Act |url=https://www.epa.gov/laws-regulations/summary-energy-policy-act |access-date=16 April 2020 |website=EPA.gov}}</ref> The Act also started the Department of Energy's [[Loan Guarantee]] Program.<ref name=":0" /> It represented an overhaul of the [[Energy Policy Act of 1992]] and previous Acts.

The [[Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007]] provided funding to help improve building codes and outlawed the sale of [[incandescent light bulbs]] in favor of fluorescents and [[Light-emitting diode|LEDs]].<ref name="EISA" /> The act included a [[solar air conditioning]] program and funding to increase [[photovoltaics]]. The act also created the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Block Grant and set the CAFE standard to 35 mpg by 2020.

In February 2009, the [[American Recovery and Reinvestment Act]] was passed, with an initial projection of $45 billion in funding levels going to energy. $11 billion went to the Weatherization Assistance Program, the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Block Grant, and the State Energy Program; $11 billion went to federal buildings and vehicles; $8 billion went to research and development programs; $2.4 billion went to new technology and facility development projects; $14 billion went to the electric grid; and $21 billion was projected to go to tax credits for renewable energy and electric vehicles, among other things.<ref>{{Cite report|url=https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/R/R40412|title=Energy Provisions in the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act|date=March 12, 2009|publisher=Congressional Research Service|number=R40412|access-date=October 25, 2019|author=Fred Sissine, Anthony Andrews, Peter Folger, Stan Mark Kaplan, Daniel Morgan, Brent D. Yacobucci}}</ref> Due in part to the design of the tax credits, the final amount of energy spending and incentives reached over $90 billion, leveraged $150 billion in private investment, funded 180 advanced manufacturing projects, and created more than 900,000 job-years.<ref name="whitehouse.gov 2016">{{cite web | title=FACT SHEET: The Recovery Act Made The Largest Single Investment In Clean Energy In History, Driving The Deployment Of Clean Energy, Promoting Energy Efficiency, And Supporting Manufacturing | website=[[White House]] | date=February 25, 2016 | url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/02/25/fact-sheet-recovery-act-made-largest-single-investment-clean-energy| access-date=October 25, 2023}}</ref>

In December 2009, the [[United States Patent and Trademark Office]] announced the Green Patent Pilot Program.<ref>{{cite web |date=2010-05-21 |title=USPTO Expands Green Technology Pilot Program to More Inventions |url=http://www.uspto.gov/news/pr/2010/10_21.jsp |access-date=2012-07-12 |publisher=[[United States Patent and Trademark Office]]}}</ref> The program was initiated to accelerate the examination of patent applications relating to certain green technologies, including the energy sector.<ref>{{cite web |date=2012-05-22 |title=Emerging Energy and Intellectual Property – The Often Unappreciated Risks and Hurdles of Government Regulations and Standard Setting Organizations |url=http://www.natlawreview.com/article/emerging-energy-and-intellectual-property-often-unappreciated-risks-and-hurdles-gove |access-date=2012-07-10 |work=The National Law Review |publisher=[[Husch Blackwell]]}}</ref> The pilot program was initially designed to accommodate 3,000 applications related to certain green technology categories, and the program was originally set to expire on December 8, 2010. In May 2010, the USPTO announced that it would expand the pilot program.<ref>{{cite web |date=2010-11-10 |title=USPTO Extends Deadline to Participate in Green Technology Pilot Program by One Year |url=http://www.uspto.gov/news/pr/2010/10_55.jsp. |access-date=2012-07-12 |publisher=[[United States Patent and Trademark Office]]}}</ref>

In 2016, federal government energy-specific subsidies and support for renewables, fossil fuels, and nuclear energy amounted to $6,682 million, $489 million and $365 million, respectively.<ref>{{DoE|article=Direct Federal Financial Interventions and Subsidies in Energy in Fiscal Year 2016|url=https://www.eia.gov/analysis/requests/subsidy/}}</ref>

On June 1, 2017, then-President [[Donald Trump]] announced that the U.S. would cease participation in the [[Paris Agreement|2015 Paris Agreement]] on [[climate change mitigation]], agreed to under the President [[Barack Obama]] administration.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/336011-pro-paris-agreement-protesters-arrive-outside-white-house|title=Pro-Paris agreement protesters flock to White House|last=Beavers|first=Olivia|date=2017-06-01|website=The Hill|language=en|access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref> On November 3, 2020, incoming President [[Joe Biden]] announced that the U.S. would resume its participation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://metro.co.uk/2021/01/21/us-re-joins-paris-climate-agreement-as-biden-signs-executive-order-13941697/|title=United States rejoins Paris climate agreement as Biden signs executive order|last=Parsons|first=Jeff|date=2020-01-21|website=Metro|language=en|access-date=2020-01-28}}</ref>

The [[Energy Information Administration]] (EIA) predicted that the reduction in energy consumption in 2020 due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|COVID-19 pandemic]] would take many years to recover.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/aeo/pdf/AEO_Narrative_2021.pdf|title=Annual Energy Outlook 2021|access-date=21 February 2021}}</ref> For many decades, the US imported much of its oil, but in 2020 it became a net exporter.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oil imports and exports - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) |url=https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/oil-and-petroleum-products/imports-and-exports.php |access-date=2022-11-10 |website=www.eia.gov}}</ref>

In December 2020, Trump signed the [[Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021]], which contained the Energy Act of 2020 and was the first major revision package to U.S. energy policy in over a decade. The bill contains increased incentives for energy efficiency (particularly in federal government buildings), improved funding for weatherization assistance, standards to phase out the use of [[hydrofluorocarbons]], plans to rebuild the nation's energy research sector including fossil fuel research, and $7 billion in demonstration projects for [[carbon capture and storage]].<ref name="U.S. Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources 2020">{{cite web | title=ICYMI: What They're Saying About the Energy Act of 2020 | website=U.S. Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources | date=December 29, 2020 | url=https://www.energy.senate.gov/2020/12/icymi-what-they-re-saying-about-the-energy-act-of-2020 | access-date=April 14, 2023}}</ref><ref name="EESI 2020">{{cite web | last=Bresette | first=Daniel | title=The Energy Act of 2020 is a Step in the Right Direction, But More Comprehensive Climate Action is Still Needed - Press Release | website=EESI | date=December 22, 2020 | url=https://www.eesi.org/press-releases/view/the-energy-act-of-2020-is-a-step-in-the-right-direction-but-more-comprehensive-climate-action-is-still-needed | access-date=April 14, 2023}}</ref><ref name="IEA 2022">{{cite web | title=Energy Act of 2020 (CCUS provisions) – Policies | website=IEA | date=March 10, 2022 | url=https://www.iea.org/policies/13192-energy-act-of-2020-ccus-provisions | access-date=April 14, 2023}}</ref>

Under President Joe Biden, one-third of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve was tapped to reduce energy prices during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=DOE Announces Notice of Sale of Additional Crude Oil From the Strategic Petroleum Reserve |url=https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-announces-notice-sale-additional-crude-oil-strategic-petroleum-reserve |access-date=2022-11-09 |website=Energy.gov |date=September 20, 2022 |language=en}}</ref> He also invoked the Defense Production Act to boost manufacturing of [[solar cell]]s, renewable energy generators, [[fuel cell]]s, electricity-dependent clean fuel equipment, [[building insulation]], [[heat pump]]s, critical [[power grid]] infrastructure, and [[electric vehicle]] [[Electric battery|batteries]].<ref name="Energy.gov DPA announcement 2022">{{cite web | title=President Biden Invokes Defense Production Act to Accelerate Domestic Manufacturing of Clean Energy | website=Energy.gov | date=June 6, 2022 | url=https://www.energy.gov/articles/president-biden-invokes-defense-production-act-accelerate-domestic-manufacturing-clean | access-date=November 24, 2022}}</ref><ref name="The White House DPA 2022">{{cite web | author=The White House | title=FACT SHEET: President Biden Takes Bold Executive Action to Spur Domestic Clean Energy Manufacturing | website=The White House | date=June 6, 2022 | url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/06/06/fact-sheet-president-biden-takes-bold-executive-action-to-spur-domestic-clean-energy-manufacturing/ | access-date=November 24, 2022}}</ref>

Biden also signed the [[Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act]] to invest $73 billion in the energy sector.<ref name="npr.org">{{cite news |last1=Sprunt |first1=Barbara |title=Here's What's Included In The Bipartisan Infrastructure Bill |url=https://www.npr.org/2021/06/24/1009923468/heres-whats-included-in-the-infrastructure-deal-that-biden-struck-with-senators |access-date=25 March 2023|agency=NPR |date=10 August 2021}}</ref> $11 billion of that amount will be invested in power grid infrastructure, with the first selected recipients for $3.46 billion announced in October 2023. This is the largest investment in the grid since the [[Recovery Act]].<ref name="GRIP 2023">{{cite web | title=Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) Program | website=Energy.gov | date=October 24, 2023 | url=https://www.energy.gov/gdo/grid-resilience-and-innovation-partnerships-grip-program | access-date=October 25, 2023}}</ref> $6 billion will go to [[nuclear power in the United States|domestic nuclear power]]. From the $73 billion, the IIJA will invest $45 billion in [[innovation]] and [[industrial policy]] for key emerging technologies in energy; $430 million<ref name="Energy.gov IDP announcement 2023">{{cite web | title=Biden-Harris Administration Announces $6 Billion To Drastically Reduce Industrial Emissions and Create Healthier Communities | website=Energy.gov | date=March 8, 2023 | projects at the DOE; and nearly $24 billion in onshoring, [[supply chain resilience]], and bolstering competitive advantages in energy, divided into an $8.6 billion investment in [[carbon capture and storage]], $3 billion in battery material reprocessing, $3 billion in [[battery recycling]], $1 billion in [[rare-earth mineral]]s stockpiling, and $8 billion in new research hubs for [[green hydrogen]].<ref name="Higman 2021">{{cite journal | last=Higman | first=Morgan | title=The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act Will Do More to Reach 2050 Climate Targets than Those of 2030 | website=Center for Strategic and International Studies | date=August 18, 2021 | url=https://www.csis.org/analysis/infrastructure-investment-and-jobs-act-will-do-more-reach-2050-climate-targets-those-2030 | access-date=November 24, 2022}}</ref> $4.7 billion will go to plugging [[orphan well]]s abandoned by oil and gas companies.<ref name="Interior Department press release 2021">{{cite web | title=Interior Department Releases Implementation Guidance to States on Infrastructure Law Efforts to Address Legacy Pollution | website=U.S. Department of the Interior | date=December 17, 2021 | }}</ref><ref name="EESI 2021">{{cite web | last=Bertrand | first=Savannah | title=Plugging Orphaned Oil and Gas Wells Provides Climate and Jobs Benefits - Article | website=EESI | date=August 12, 2021 | url=https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/plugging-orphaned-oil-and-gas-wells-provides-climate-and-jobs-benefits | access-date=December 30, 2022 | archive-date=December 30, 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221230095139/https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/plugging-orphaned-oil-and-gas-wells-provides-climate-and-jobs-benefits | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Center for American Progress 2022">{{cite In August 2022, Biden signed the [[CHIPS and Science Act]] to boost DOE and [[National Science Foundation]] research activities by $174 billion.<ref name="CSIS Science Act 2022">{{cite journal | last1=Shivakumar | first1=Sujai | last2=Arcuri | first2=Gregory|last3=Uno|first3=Hideki|last4=Glanz|first4=Benjamin | title=A Look at the Science-Related Portions of CHIPS+ | website=Center for Strategic and International Studies | date=August 11, 2022 | url=https://www.csis.org/analysis/look-science-related-portions-chips | access-date=November 24, 2022}}</ref> He also signed the [[Inflation Reduction Act]] to create assistance programs for [[utility cooperative]]s<ref name="Lechleitner 2022">{{cite web | last=Lechleitner | first=Liz | title=Electric and agricultural co-op |title=CBO Scores IRA with $238 Billion of Deficit Reduction |url=https://www.crfb.org/blogs/cbo-scores-ira-238-billion-deficit-reduction |access-date=2022-09-21 |website=Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget |date=September 7, 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Tax Foundation">{{Cite web |last1=McBride|first1=William|last2=Bunn|first2=Daniel|date=2023-06-07 |title=Repealing Inflation billion in electric vehicles and batteries, $215 billion in clean power, $93 billion in clean energy tech manufacturing and infrastructure, and $51 billion in heavy industry) and over $756.2 billion Even so, the Biden administration also presided over record high oil and gas production, reaching averages of 12.9 million barrels per day nationwide in 2023,<ref name="EIA 2024">{{cite web | title=United States produces more crude oil than any country, ever | website=Homepage - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) | date=May 13, 2024 | url=https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=61545 | access-date=May 16, 2024}}</ref> and 530,000 barrels per day from public lands since 2020 (despite a campaign pledge to halt drilling on said lands). However, growth has been driven more by [[Permian Basin (North America)|Permian Basin]] drilling than by the administration's policies.<ref name="Richards 2024">{{cite web | last=Richards | first=Heather | title=What Biden's oil record means for the industry's future | website=E&E News by POLITICO | date=May 13, 2024 | url=https://www.eenews.net/articles/what-bidens-oil-record-means-for-the-industrys-future/ | access-date=May 16, 2024}}</ref>

Around spring 2024, the Biden administration announced several changes to its energy policy approach. First, the EPA issued new tailpipe emissions limits that it projected would cut emissions by 7 billion metric tons, or 56% of 2026 levels, by 2032.<ref name="Daly Krisher 2024">{{cite web | last1=Daly | first1=Matthew | last2=Krisher | first2=Tom | title=EPA issues new auto rules aimed at cutting carbon emissions, boosting electric vehicles and hybrids | website=AP News | date=March 20, 2024 | url=https://apnews.com/article/epa-electric-vehicles-emissions-limits-climate-biden-e6d581324af51294048df24269b5d20a | access-date=May 16, 2024}}</ref> Second, it raised royalty rates from 12.5% to 16.7%, doubled rents and increased lease bond minimums by a factor of 15 on federal lands for oil and gas companies.<ref name="Groom 2024">{{cite web | last=Groom | first=Nichola | title=US finalizes higher fees for oil and gas companies on federal lands | website=Reuters | date=April 12, 2024 | url=https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/us-finalizes-big-reforms-federal-oil-gas-drilling-2024-04-12/ | access-date=May 16, 2024}}</ref> Third, the EPA finalized new standards for power plant carbon emissions, projecting cuts of 65,000 tons by 2028 and 1.38 billion tons by 2047.<ref name="EPA power plant rules 2024">{{cite web | title=Biden-Harris Administration Finalizes Suite of Standards to Reduce Pollution from Fossil Fuel-Fired Power Plants | website=US EPA | date=April 24, 2024 | url=https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/biden-harris-administration-finalizes-suite-standards-reduce-pollution-fossil-fuel | access-date=May 16, 2024}}</ref> Fourth, the DOE announced that it would assume the role of default lead agency on permitting approvals for most new power transmission projects, as well as enact a two-year deadline, require only one environmental impact statement per project, and increase transparency around the permitting process.<ref name="DOE CITAP 2024">{{cite web | title=Biden-Harris Administration Announces Final Transmission Permitting Rule and Latest Investments To Accelerate the Build Out of a Resilient, Reliable, Modernized Electric Grid | website=Energy.gov | date=April 25, 2024 | url=https://www.energy.gov/articles/biden-harris-administration-announces-final-transmission-permitting-rule-and-latest | access-date=May 16, 2024}}</ref> Lastly, it issued a new rule to make large water heaters  much more energy-efficient by 2029, cutting carbon emissions by a projected 332 million tons over 30 years, as part of the DOE's overall effort since 2020 to drive 2.5 billion tons in 30-year appliance emissions cuts.<ref>{{CodeFedReg|89|37778}}</ref><ref name="DOE water heater announcement">{{cite web | title=DOE Finalizes Efficiency Standards for Water Heaters to Save Americans Over $7 Billion on Household Utility Bills Annually | website=Energy.gov | date=April 30, 2024 | url=https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-finalizes-efficiency-standards-water-heaters-save-americans-over-7-billion-household | access-date=May 17, 2024}}</ref>

On January 22, 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump declared a national energy emergency, stating that increased drilling and expedited pipeline construction would necessitate court orders. However, legal experts indicated that oil and gas producers would not be permitted to bypass all environmental laws. The national emergency law could grant the president extensive powers across 150 different pieces of legislation, yet limitations on environmental laws and regulations would still apply. “It could accelerate energy projects, but it would compromise water standards, jeopardize endangered species, and create significant gaps,” remarked Mark Novitt, a professor at Emory University School of Law. “There’s a reason those emergency regulations aren’t invoked on a daily basis.”<ref>{{cite web |last1=Queen |first1=Jack |title=Trump US energy emergency order should withstand court challenges |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/trump-us-energy-emergency-order-should-withstand-court-challenges-2025-01-22/ |website=reuters}}</ref>

== Department of Energy ==
{{Main|21st-century fossil fuel regulations in the United States|United States Department of Energy}}

The Energy Department's mission statement is "to ensure America's security and prosperity by addressing its energy, environmental and nuclear challenges through transformative science and technology solutions."<ref name="Energy.gov">{{cite web |title=Mission |url=https://www.energy.gov/mission |access-date=April 25, 2026 |website=Energy.gov}}</ref>

{{As of|2026|04}}, its elaboration of the mission statement is as follows:
* "Catalyze timely, material, and efficient transformation of the nation's energy system and secure US leadership in energy technologies.
* "Maintain a vibrant US effort in science and engineering as a cornerstone of our economic prosperity with clear leadership in strategic areas.
* "Enhance nuclear security through defense, nonproliferation, and environmental efforts.
* "Build the world's most powerful scientific platform [the [[Genesis Mission]]] to accelerate discovery science, strengthen national security, and drive energy innovation."<ref name="Energy.gov" />

===Petroleum===
[[File:Oil imports by country.webp|thumb|300px|United States oil product imports by country]]
The US bans energy imports from countries such as Russia (because of the [[Russo-Ukrainian War]])<ref>{{Cite web |last=House |first=The White |date=2022-03-08 |title=FACT SHEET: United States Bans Imports of Russian Oil, Liquefied Natural Gas, and Coal |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/03/08/fact-sheet-united-states-bans-imports-of-russian-oil-liquefied-natural-gas-and-coal/ |access-date=2022-11-10 |website=The White House |language=en-US}}</ref> and [[Venezuela]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Weekly U.S. Imports from Venezuela of Crude Oil (Thousand Barrels per Day) |url=https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=W_EPC0_IM0_NUS-NVE_MBBLD&f=W |access-date=2022-11-10 |website=www.eia.gov}}</ref> The US also limits exports of oil from [[Iran]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wallace |first=Paul |date=June 5, 2022 |title=US May Allow More Iran Oil to Flow Even Without Deal, Says Vitol |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-06-05/us-may-allow-more-iran-oil-to-flow-even-without-deal-says-vitol |access-date=2022-11-10 |website=Bloomberg}}</ref>  Although it is a net exporter, the US imports energy from multiple countries, led by Canada.

=== Clean technology ===
{{expand section|with=a comprehensive history of clean technology import policy in the US|date=May 2024}}
In May 2024, the Biden administration doubled [[tariff]]s on [[solar cell]]s imported from China and more than tripled tariffs on [[Lithium-ion battery|lithium-ion electric vehicle batteries]] imported from China.<ref name="tariff report">{{Cite web |last1=Boak |first1=Josh |last2=Hussein |first2=Fatima |last3=Wiseman |first3=Paul |last4=Tang |first4=Didi |date=2024-05-14 |title=Biden hikes tariffs on Chinese EVs, solar cells, steel, aluminum — and snipes at Trump |url=https://apnews.com/article/biden-china-tariffs-electric-vehicles-evs-solar-2024ba735c47e04a50898a88425c5e2c |access-date=2024-05-16 |website=[[AP News]] |language=en}}</ref> The increased tariffs will be phased in over a period of three years.<ref name="tariff report" />

== Export ==
{{expand section|date=November 2022}}
In 1975, the United States implemented a crude oil export ban, which limited most exports to other countries. It came two years after an [[OPEC]] oil embargo banned oil sales to the U.S. and sent gas prices skyrocketing. Newspaper photographs of long car lines outside of gas stations became a common and worrisome image.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Egan |first=Matt |date=2016-01-29 |title=After 40-year ban, U.S. starts exporting crude oil |url=https://money.cnn.com/2016/01/29/investing/us-oil-exports-begin/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129215633/http://money.cnn.com/2016/01/29/investing/us-oil-exports-begin/index.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 29, 2016 |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=CNNMoney}}</ref> Forty years later in 2015, [[United States Congress|Congress]] voted to repeal its ban on exporting U.S. crude oil. Since that year, crude exports have skyrocketed nearly 600% to 3.2 million barrels per day in 2020, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Kelly |first1=Stephanie |last2=Renshaw |first2=Jarrett |last3=Kelly |first3=Stephanie |date=2021-12-09 |title=White House not weighing oil export ban, source says, as lawmakers urge higher domestic {{as written|oup|ut [sic]}} |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/bipartisan-group-warns-biden-not-halt-us-oil-exports-letter-2021-12-09/ |access-date=2023-03-19}}</ref>

Under President Biden, the pattern continued, as hundreds of other new oil and gas projects, many of them marked for boosting exports to counter China and Russia's influence, were approved.<ref name="Bearak 2023">{{cite web | last=Bearak | first=Max | title=It's Not Just Willow: Oil and Gas Projects Are Back in a Big Way | website=The New York Times | date=April 6, 2023 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/06/climate/oil-gas-drilling-investment-worldwide-willow.html| access-date=May 16, 2024}}</ref><ref name="WaPo 2024">{{cite news | author=Editorial Board | title=Biden's LNG decision is a win for political symbolism, not the climate | newspaper=The Washington Post | date=January 29, 2024 | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2024/01/29/biden-lng-natural-gas-exports-europe/ | access-date=May 17, 2024}}</ref> In response to criticism from environmentalists, Biden temporarily suspended regulatory approvals for new natural gas export terminals in January 2024,<ref name="McKibben 2024">{{cite web | last=McKibben | first=Bill | title=Joe Biden just did the rarest thing in US politics: he stood up to the oil industry | website=the Guardian | date=February 7, 2024 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2024/feb/07/joe-biden-big-oil-lng-permits | access-date=May 16, 2024}}</ref> but in July, Louisiana federal judge [[James D. Cain Jr.]] halted the suspension temporarily amid a lawsuit from 16 Republican-governed states.<ref name="Cain ruling 2024">{{cite web | author=The Associated Press | title=A judge sides with states over Biden and allows gas export projects to move forward | website=NPR | date=July 2, 2024 | url=https://www.npr.org/2024/07/02/g-s1-7645/judge-sides-with-16-states-putting-on-pause-bidens-delay-of-consideration-of-gas-export-projects | access-date=July 3, 2024}}</ref>

== Utilities ==
{{expand section|date=November 2022}}
In the U.S., utilities are regulated at the federal level by the [[Federal Energy Regulatory Commission]]. In each state, a [[Public utilities commission|public utility commission]] (PUC) regulates electricity, gas, and other forms of power.<ref>[https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-03/documents/background_paper.pdf An Overview of PUC s for State Environment and Energy Officials]. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.</ref>

States began deregulating electricity systems in the 1990s as a way to promote competition and lower costs. While transmission lines and distribution services are still provided by local utility companies, wholesale markets were created to enable power plant investments and allow utilities to acquire power for customers. Those wholesale markets are operated by regional transmission organizations (RTOs).<ref>{{Cite web |title=US Electricity Markets 101 |url=https://www.rff.org/publications/explainers/us-electricity-markets-101/ |access-date=2024-02-28 |website=Resources for the Future |language=en-US}}</ref>

Deregulation led to the creation of independent energy suppliers and allowed customers to choose their electric supplier.

==Energy efficiency==
{{Main|Efficient energy use}}
Opportunities for increased energy efficiency are available across the economy, including buildings/appliances, transportation, and manufacturing. Some opportunities require new technology. Others require behavioral change by individuals or at the community level or above.

The U.S. federal government has initiated various energy-efficiency policies, programs and legislation, including the [[Weatherization Assistance Program]] (WAP), [[CAFE standards]] for vehicle fuel efficiency, and the [[Energy Star]] program for promoting efficiency in [[household appliances]]. American governments, at all levels, have implemented various building standards to improve energy efficiency.<ref name="study">Doris, Elizabeth; Jaquelin Cochran; and Martin Vorum: [https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc935377/m2/1/high_res_d/970345.pdf ''Energy Efficiency Policy in the United States: Overview of Trends at Different Levels of Government''] Technical Report NREL/TP-6A2-46532, December 2009, [[National Renewable Energy Laboratory]], U.S. Dept. of Energy, retrieved August 18, 2024</ref>

Building-related [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency innovation]] takes many forms, including improvements in water heaters; refrigerators and freezers; building control technologies for heating, ventilation, and cooling (HVAC); adaptive windows; building codes; and lighting.<ref name="kam">{{cite web|url=http://rael.berkeley.edu/files/2007/Kammen_House-GovReform-11-8-07.pdf |title=Opportunities for Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reductions |access-date=2012-03-30}}</ref>

Energy-efficient technologies can enable superior performance. For example, this could include higher quality lighting, heating and cooling with greater controls, or improved reliability of service through greater ability of utilities to respond to time of peak demand.<ref name="kam" />

More efficient vehicles save on fuel purchases, emit fewer pollutants, improve health and save on medical costs.<ref name=kam/>

Heat engines are only 20% efficient at converting oil into work.<ref>{{cite web |title=Improving IC Engine Efficiency |url=http://courses.washington.edu/me341/oct22v2.htm |access-date=2012-03-30 |publisher=Courses.washington.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Carnot Cycle |url=http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/thermo/carnot.html |access-date=2012-03-30 |publisher=Hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu}}</ref> However, heat pumps are highly efficient, up to 300% in some cases, at moving heat to and from outside air.<ref name="Heat pump physics 2024">{{cite web | title=In-depth guide to heat pumps | website=Energy Saving Trust | date=June 4, 2024 | url=https://energysavingtrust.org.uk/advice/in-depth-guide-to-heat-pumps/ | access-date=July 24, 2024}}</ref>

==Energy budget, initiatives and incentives==
{{Main|List of United States Energy Acts}}

{{See also|Energy subsidies in the United States}}
Most energy policy incentives are financial. Examples of these include tax breaks, tax reductions, tax exemptions, rebates, loans and subsidies.

The [[Energy Policy Act of 2005]], the [[Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007]], the [[Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008]], and the [[Inflation Reduction Act]] all provided such incentives.

===Tax incentives===
{{See also|Tax credit#Renewable Energy/Investment Tax Credit (ITC)}}
The US [[Tax credit|Production Tax Credit]] (PTC) reduces the [[Income tax in the United States|federal income taxes]] of qualified owners of renewable energy projects based on grid-connected output. The Investment Tax Credit (ITC) reduces federal income taxes for qualified tax-payers based on capital investment in renewable energy projects. The Advanced Energy Manufacturing Tax Credit (MTC) awards tax credits to selected domestic manufacturing facilities that support clean energy development.<ref>[http://pdf.wri.org/bottom_line_renewable_energy_tax_credits_10-2010.pdf The Bottom Line on Renewable Energy Tax Credits.] World Resources Institute</ref>

===Loan guarantees===
The Department of Energy's [[Loan Guarantee]] Program guarantees financing up to 80% of a qualifying project's cost.<ref name=":0">[http://www.acore.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/02/ACORE_USonly_Q_REVIEW_low411.pdf U.S. Renewable Energy Quarterly Report, October 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111001030046/http://www.acore.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/02/ACORE_USonly_Q_REVIEW_low411.pdf |date=October 1, 2011 }} American Council On Renewable Energy</ref>

===Renewable energy===

[[File:TeslaRoadster-front.jpg|thumb|[[Tesla Roadster (2008)]] uses [[Li-Ion|lithium ion]] batteries to achieve {{convert|220|mi|abbr=on}} per charge, while also capable of going 0–60 in under 4 seconds.]]In the United States, the share of renewable energy in electricity generation has grown to 21% by 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Renewables became the second-most prevalent U.S. electricity source in 2020 - Today in Energy - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) |url=https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=48896 |access-date=2021-11-24 |website=www.eia.gov}}</ref> Oil use is expected to decline in the US because of increasing vehicle efficiency and replacement of crude oil by natural gas as a feedstock for the petrochemical sector. One forecast is that the rapid uptake of electric vehicles will reduce oil demand drastically by 80% lower in 2050 compared with today.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DNV GL's Energy Transition Outlook 2018 |url=http://eto.dnvgl.com/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211123224842/https://eto.dnv.com/2021 |archive-date=23 November 2021 |access-date=17 October 2018 |website=eto.dnvgl.com |language=en}}</ref>

A [[Renewable Portfolio Standard]] (RPS) is a state/local mandate that requires electricity providers to supply a minimum amount of power from renewable sources, usually defined as a percentage of total energy production.<ref>[http://www.acore.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/02/ACORE_USonly_Q_REVIEW_low411.pdf U.S. Renewable Energy Quarterly Report] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111001030046/http://www.acore.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/02/ACORE_USonly_Q_REVIEW_low411.pdf|date=October 1, 2011}} American Council on Renewable Energy, October 2010. Retrieved 2011-04-12.</ref>

===Biofuels===
The federal government offers many programs to support the development and implementation of biofuel-based replacements for fossil fuels.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Alternative Fuels Data Center: Ethanol Laws and Incentives in Federal |url=https://afdc.energy.gov/fuels/laws/ETH?state=US |access-date=2022-11-11 |website=afdc.energy.gov |language=en}}</ref>

Landowners and operators who establish, produce, and deliver biofuel crops may qualify for partial reimbursement of startup costs as well as for annual payments.<ref name=":2" /> Loan guarantees help finance development, construction, and retrofitting of commercial-scale biorefineries. Grants help build demonstration-scale biorefineries and also help scale up existing biorefineries. Loan guarantees and grants support the purchase of pumps that dispense ethanol-including fuels.<ref name=":2" />

Production support helps makers expand output.<ref name=":2" /> Tax credits support the purchase of fueling equipment (gas pumps) for specific fuels including some biofuels.<ref name=":2" />

Education grants support training the public about biodiesel.<ref name=":2" /> Research, development, and demonstration grants support feedstock development and biofuel development.<ref name=":2" /> Grants support research, demonstration, and deployment projects to replace buses and other petroleum-fueled vehicles with biofuel or other alternative fuel-based vehicles in addition to necessary fueling infrastructure.<ref name=":2" />

===Producer subsidies===
The 2005 Energy Policy Act offered incentives including billions in tax reductions for nuclear power, fossil fuel production, [[clean coal technology|clean coal technologies]], renewable electricity, and conservation and efficiency improvements.<ref>[[Energy Policy Act of 2005]]</ref>

=== Federal leases ===
The US leases federal land to private firms for energy production. The volume of leases has varied by presidential administration. During the first 19 months of the [[Joe Biden]] administration, 130,000 acres were leased, compared to 4 million under the [[Donald Trump]] administration, 7 million under the [[Barack Obama|Obama]] administration, and 13 million under the [[George W. Bush]] administration.<ref>{{Cite news |last=DeBarros |first=Timothy Puko and Anthony |date=2022-09-04 |title=Federal Oil Leases Slow to a Trickle Under Biden |language=en-US |work=The Wall Street Journal |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/federal-oil-leases-slow-to-a-trickle-under-biden-11662230816 |access-date=2022-11-09 |issn=0099-9660}}</ref>

The Inflation Reduction Act requires that for federal lands, oil and gas auctions be carried out before wind and solar lease consideration, even as the Act brought about royalty rate increases.<ref name="Hart 2023">{{cite web | last=Hart | first=Sarah | title=Potential Impacts of the IRA's Onshore Energy Leasing Provisions | website=Harvard Law School - Environmental & Energy Law Program | date=March 24, 2023 | url=https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/2023/03/ira-onshore-leasing/ | access-date=May 16, 2024 | archive-date=May 16, 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240516055405/https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/2023/03/ira-onshore-leasing/ | url-status=dead }}</ref> Permian Basin drilling activity, some of it on federal lands, also brought about record high oil production even after the Act's signing in 2022.<ref name="Richards 2024"/>

==Electricity transmission and distribution==
{{Main|North American power transmission grid}}

{{transcluded section|source=Federal Energy Regulatory Commission#History|part=yes}}

[[File:High voltage power grid of the United States.webp|thumb|300px|High voltage power grid in [[kilovolts]] (kV)
{{legend-line|#8E0707 solid 3px|500+}}
