A 2-month study about vehicular travel in Massachusetts in 2020 revealed a 71% and 46% reduction in car and truck traffic, respectively. The significant decrease in traffic correlated with a direct reduction in atmospheric levels of harmful particulates, resulting in a decrease in overall air pollution.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-04-22|title=How has COVID-19 influenced the environment?|url=https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/how-covid-19-has-changed-the-face-of-the-natural-world|access-date=2021-11-08|website=www.medicalnewstoday.com|language=en}}</ref> As seen in other instances, the atmospheric particulate reductions led to an improvement in water quality.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-06-08|title=Coronavirus Is Improving Water Quality — For Now, At Least|url=https://news.climate.columbia.edu/2020/06/08/coronavirus-improving-water-quality/|access-date=2021-12-09|website=State of the Planet|language=en}}</ref>

=== Peru ===
The Peruvian jungle experienced 14 oil spills from the beginning of the pandemic through early October 2020. Of these, eight spills were in a single sector (Block 192) operated by [[Frontera Energy|Frontera Energy del Perú S.A.]] which ceased operations during the pandemic and failed to maintain its wells and pipes. The oil seeped into the ground where it contaminated the drinking water of the indigenous people in Quichua territory.<ref name="Zarate-2020">{{Cite news| vauthors = Zárate J |date=2020-10-02|title=Opinion {{!}} The Amazon Was Sick. Now It's Sicker.|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/02/opinion/amazon-pollution-oil.html|access-date=2020-10-04|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Oil spills in the Peruvian Amazon have been a problem for decades, leaking toxic metals and hydrocarbons into the drinking water and surrounding environment.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Righting the many wrongs at Peru's polluted oil Block 192|url=https://politicsofpoverty.oxfamamerica.org/righting-the-many-wrongs-at-perus-polluted-oil-block-192/|access-date=2021-12-04|website=politicsofpoverty.oxfamamerica.org|language=en-US}}</ref> A 2016 study done on 1,168 people living near Block 192 indicated that 50% of those tested had toxic metals (lead, arsenic, mercury, and cadmium) in their blood at levels above WHO acceptable limits. As a result of these oil spills, the Quichua people of Nueva Andoas were at a particularly high risk for diseases before the pandemic. Further compounded by a lack of medicine, lack of doctors, lack of access to vaccines, and poor government response, the Indigenous people of the Peruvian Amazon were in an extremely vulnerable position and at high risk during the pandemic.<ref name="Zarate-2020" />

=== Italy ===
[[File:Deserted Venetian lagoon.jpg|thumb|Images taken from a satellite of Venice's water canals during April 2019 and 2020.]]
In Venice, shortly after quarantine began in March 2020, water in the canals cleared and experienced greater water flow.<ref>{{cite news|date=23 April 2020|title=Jellyfish seen swimming in Venice's canals|publisher=[[CNN]] |url=https://www.cnn.com/travel/article/jellyfish-venice/index.html|access-date=25 April 2020}}</ref> The increase in water clarity was primarily caused by a decrease in boat traffic, which in turn, allowed the normally stirred up sediment to instead remain at the floor of the canals.<ref name="63GlJ">{{cite web |url=https://thehill.com/changing-america/sustainability/environment/488286-italys-coronavirus-lockdown-shows-what-nature |title=As Italy quarantines over coronavirus, swans appear in Venice canals, dolphins swim up playfully | vauthors = Srikanth A |work=The Hill |date=18 March 2020 |access-date=20 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200319215915/https://thehill.com/changing-america/sustainability/environment/488286-italys-coronavirus-lockdown-shows-what-nature |archive-date=19 March 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref> In the year prior, during the initial onset of the coronavirus, organizations such as the European Space Agency detected the striking change between the water in the Venetian canals as the country became more and more contaminated.<ref>{{Cite web|author=Sara Spary|title=Space images of Venice show how coronavirus has changed the city's iconic canals|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/04/16/europe/venice-space-satellite-images-canals-scli-intl-scn/index.html|access-date=2021-11-01|website=[[CNN]] |date=16 April 2020 }}</ref> Two satellite images, one taken on 19 April 2019, and the other on 13 April 2020, showed the water in the canals transitions from a paler, teal coloration to a deeper blue. This showed the increase in the health of the water as the coronavirus set in across the country.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Deserted Venetian lagoon|url=https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Images/2020/04/Deserted_Venetian_lagoon|access-date=2021-11-01|website=www.esa.int|language=en}}</ref> Through this Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, the space agency's images captured the benefit of less transportive travel on Venice's waterways and highlighted that, despite the decline in tourists as the city shut down, the canals contained water far cleaner and safer for organisms and consumption than was the case previously.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Sentinel-2|url=https://www.esa.int/Applications/Observing_the_Earth/Copernicus/Sentinel-2|access-date=2021-11-01|website=www.esa.int|language=en}}</ref> While the water in the Venetian canals cleared up due to the decrease in boat transportation and pollution, marine life returned to the area in far less numbers than previously believed. Although numerous social media posts depicted dolphins and other oceanic creatures venturing back to Venice's shores, National Geographic exposed the falsities behind these rumors, showing images captured in different places and debunking the hopes circulating around that the impact of COVID-19 contributed to healthier waters and a re-emergence of wildlife.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-03-20|title=Fake animal news abounds on social media as coronavirus upends life|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/coronavirus-pandemic-fake-animal-viral-social-media-posts|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210218044430/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/coronavirus-pandemic-fake-animal-viral-social-media-posts|url-status=dead|archive-date=18 February 2021|access-date=2021-11-28|website=Animals|language=en}}</ref> Misinformation such as the claims made about animals infiltrating Venice's waterways have given people a distorted image of both the ongoing pandemic and climate change crises, concealing growing problems such as the city's current low tides.

=== India ===
In [[COVID-19 pandemic in India|India]], more than 28 million people were affected by the rapid transmission of the COVID-19 virus. As a result, the Government of India put the whole country on a [[COVID-19 pandemic in India|full lockdown]]. While many suffered under these circumstances, both socially and financially, environmental researchers discovered significant improvements to environmental quality during the slow in human activity and travel. A metadata analysis of river water quality (RWQ) indicated that the rivers in Damodar, an urban-industrial area, had improved in quality. There was a reduction in pollution that led to this improvement in water quality.<ref name="Chakraborty-2021b">{{cite journal | vauthors = Chakraborty B, Bera B, Adhikary PP, Bhattacharjee S, Roy S, Saha S, Ghosh A, Sengupta D, Shit PK | display-authors = 6 | title = Positive effects of COVID-19 lockdown on river water quality: evidence from River Damodar, India | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 11 | issue = 1 | article-number = 20140 | date = October 2021 | pmid = 34635728 | doi = 10.1038/s41598-021-99689-9  | doi-access = free| pmc = 8505400 | bibcode = 2021NatSR..1120140C }}</ref> A second study conducted on the Damodar in January 2021 revealed a significant change of the water quality during the pandemic. In the pre-lockdown period, the Water Pollution Index (WPI) of samples from the river fell between 1.59 and 2.46, indicating a high level of pollution. In contrast, during the lockdown, the WPI for water samples ranged from 0.52 to 0.78, indicating that samples were either 'good' or 'moderately polluted' water. The significant improvement in the WPI suggested that the shutdowns of heavy industries and subsequent reduction of toxic pollutants led to an increase in water quality.<ref name="Chakraborty-2021a">{{cite journal | vauthors = Chakraborty B, Roy S, Bera A, Adhikary PP, Bera B, Sengupta D, Bhunia GS, Shit PK | display-authors = 6 | title = Cleaning the river Damodar (India): impact of COVID-19 lockdown on water quality and future rejuvenation strategies | journal = Environment, Development and Sustainability | volume = 23 | issue = 8 | pages = 11975–11989 | date = January 2021 | pmid = 33424426 | pmc = 7779165 | doi = 10.1007/s10668-020-01152-8| bibcode = 2021EDSus..2311975C | issn=1387-585X }}</ref>

Similar to the river Damodar, the Ganga experienced significant improvements with regards to water quality. Specifically, DO levels increased, while BOD and nitrate concentrations decreased. The nationwide lockdown and subsequent shutdown of major industries not only increased river quality, but the quality of polluted creeks. In some regions, waste inflow was reduced up to 50%.<ref name="Balamurugan-2021">{{Cite journal| vauthors = Balamurugan M, Kasiviswanathan KS, Ilampooranan I, Soundharajan B |date=2021|title=COVID-19 Lockdown Disruptions on Water Resources, Wastewater, and Agriculture in India|journal=Frontiers in Water|volume=3|page=24|article-number=603531 |doi=10.3389/frwa.2021.603531|issn=2624-9375|doi-access=free|bibcode=2021FrWat...3.3531B }}</ref> Both studies point to a significant improvement in water quality as a result of India's complete lockdown. The changes were a result of a decrease in sewage and wastewater being discharged into the rivers. This was most likely because of Damodar's specific location in an industrial area.<ref name="Chakraborty-2021b" /> The industrial areas experienced extremely different levels of activity as a result of the lockdown, so the results of the water quality tests from before the pandemic and after were affected by the different levels of activity.<ref name="Balamurugan-2021" />

In addition to the above studies, research on India's longest lake, Vembanad Lake, in April 2020, showed that suspended particulate matter concentration decreased by 16% during early lockdowns.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yunus AP, Masago Y, Hijioka Y | title = COVID-19 and surface water quality: Improved lake water quality during the lockdown | journal = The Science of the Total Environment | volume = 731 | article-number = 139012 | date = August 2020 | pmid = 32388159 | doi = 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.139012| pmc=7185006 | bibcode = 2020ScTEn.73139012Y }}</ref>

=== China ===
As the first country affected by the pandemic, China had to quickly adapt new health and safety restrictions before any other nation in January 2020.<ref name="Liu-2022" /> Similar to other countries, numerous large industries in China shutdown during the COVID-19 lockdown. As a result, the water quality significantly improved. Results from monthly field measurements on river water quality in China showed improvements for several different indicators. Ammonia nitrogen (NH<sub>3</sub>-N) was the first indicator to rapidly reduce after the lockdown, while dissolved oxygen (DO) and chemical oxygen demand (COD) started to show improvements in early-February 2020. The pH levels of the river water started to increase in late-March 2020. After the lockdown was lifted, a study conducted by scientists, Dong Liua, Hong Yang, and Julian R. Thompson, found that all water quality parameters returned to normal conditions. Because the conditions improved during a temporary lockdown period, this study suggested that future pollutant reduction strategies should be location-specific and sustained in order to maintain progress to protect the environment.<ref name="Liu-2022">{{cite journal | vauthors = Liu D, Yang H, Thompson JR, Li J, Loiselle S, Duan H | title = COVID-19 lockdown improved river water quality in China | journal = The Science of the Total Environment | volume = 802 | article-number = 149585 | date = January 2022 | pmid = 34454149 | pmc = 8526986 | doi = 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.149585 | bibcode = 2022ScTEn.80249585L |issn=0048-9697 }}</ref>

'''<big>South Africa</big>'''

During the pandemic, developing countries in Africa didn't have the infrastructure, equipment, facilities, and trained staff to do widespread tests for COVID-19, so they used [[wastewater surveillance]] as a way to highlight hotspot areas, especially in the country of South Africa. This allowed them to discover where SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA existed in different wastewater after testing municipal wastewater (industrial wastewater), surface water (rivers, canals, dams), and drinking water. Traces of SARS-CoV-2 RNA were found in wastewater treatment facilities in the first phases of treatment, but once the water was treated there was no RNA detected. While the treated water was safe for drinking and other uses, the wastewater from the treatment facilities that drained into rivers or seas could still have some SARS-CoV-2 RNA, but it was too low to be detected which proved it to be unlikely. No other water source had detected SARS-CoV-2 RNA which led scientists of this experiment to see no prominent harm done from the pandemic on the water quality in South Africa.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Masindi V, Foteinis S, Nduli K, Akinwekomi V | title = Systematic assessment of SARS-CoV-2 virus in wastewater, rivers and drinking water - A catchment-wide appraisal | journal = The Science of the Total Environment | volume = 800 | article-number = 149298 | date = December 2021 | pmid = 34388648 | pmc = 8319043 | doi = 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.149298 | bibcode = 2021ScTEn.80049298M }}</ref>

=== Morocco ===
The COVID-19 lockdown had a positive effect for the water quality of the Boukhalef River in northern Morocco. Researchers used Sentinel 3 water surface temperature (WST) values to test several locations along the Boukhalef River before and after the lockdown. Before the lockdown there were high WST values indicating poor water quality at these sites. However, after the lockdown, industrial activities greatly reduced their production and subsequent polluting of the water. As a result, there were normal WST values indicating normal water quality in the same sites.<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Cherif EK, Vodopivec M, Mejjad N, Esteves da Silva JC, Simonovič S, Boulaassal H |date= September 2020 |title= COVID-19 Pandemic Consequences on Coastal Water Quality Using WST Sentinel-3 Data: Case of Tangier, Morocco |journal=Water|language=en|volume=12|issue=9|page=2638|doi=10.3390/w12092638|doi-access= free |bibcode= 2020Water..12.2638C }}</ref>

=== England ===
A study of water use using the CityWat-SemiDistributed (CWSD) system analyzed how the lockdown during COVID-19 affected the water supply in England. Increases in household water consumption were attributed to increased use of appliances and preventative measures such as hand washing during lockdowns.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Menneer T, Qi Z, Taylor T, Paterson C, Tu G, Elliott LR, Morrissey K, Mueller M | display-authors = 6 | title = Changes in Domestic Energy and Water Usage during the UK COVID-19 Lockdown Using High-Resolution Temporal Data | journal = International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health | volume = 18 | issue = 13 | page = 6818 | date = June 2021 | pmid = 34202018 | pmc = 8297134 | doi = 10.3390/ijerph18136818 | doi-access = free }}</ref> A decrease in activity outside of the home was associated with a 35% increase in water use.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Abu-Bakar H, Williams L, Hallett SH |date=December 2021|title=Quantifying the impact of the COVID-19 lockdown on household water consumption patterns in England|journal=npj Clean Water|language=en|volume=4|issue=1|article-number=13|doi=10.1038/s41545-021-00103-8|bibcode=2021npjCW...4...13A |s2cid=231948492|issn=2059-7037|doi-access=free}}</ref> As in other countries, England saw a decrease in transportation, such as daily commuting, in large cities, the result of which was a change in pollution concentration zones. Additionally, the rivers in London became less polluted, but water quality became worse near peoples' households. This minimized the continued pollution of larger rivers, but instead increased the pollution in smaller ones in suburban areas.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Dobson B, Jovanovic T, Chen Y, Paschalis A, Butler A, Mijic A |date=2021|title=Integrated Modelling to Support Analysis of COVID-19 Impacts on London's Water System and In-river Water Quality |journal=Frontiers in Water|volume=3|page=26|article-number=641462 |doi=10.3389/frwa.2021.641462 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2021FrWat...3.1462D |hdl=10044/1/86568|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

=== Ecuador ===
During the pandemic, surveys were distributed and data was collected in Ecuador to study the water quality of the ocean. Preliminary data suggested that the water appeared clearer and cleaner because of the lack of people swimming and visiting the beaches. Residents of the Salinas beach were surveyed on the quality of the water twice, 10 weeks apart, during quarantine. Using a 1-5 scale, with 1 being the worst quality and 5 being the best, participants said that during the 10 weeks, the quality went from a 2.83 to a 4.33. Off the coast of Ecuador, the Galapagos Islands also saw improvements in water quality during the pandemic. Researchers noticed the presence of more turtles, sea lions and sharks in the water because of the lack of pollution.<ref>{{Cite journal|vauthors=Ormaza-Gonzaìlez FI, Castro-Rodas D, Statham PJ|date=2021|title=COVID-19 Impacts on Beaches and Coastal Water Pollution at Selected Sites in Ecuador, and Management Proposals Post-pandemic|journal=Frontiers in Marine Science|volume=8|page=710|article-number=669374 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2021.669374|issn=2296-7745|doi-access=free|bibcode=2021FrMaS...869374O }}</ref>

Unfortunately, sanitary water conditions became a concern in Ecuador during the COVID-19 pandemic. It was suggested that SARS-CoV-2 could be contracted through fecal matter from wastewater treatment plants. In Ecuador, only 20% of wastewater was treated before being discharged back into the water. The urban area of Quito, Ecuador was particularly affected by the lack of wastewater treatment. Its population of 3 million citizens represented an under-diagnosed demographic. At the time of testing, reports claimed that only 750 citizens were infected with COVID-19, but actual wastewater contamination showed a larger percentage of the population infected. Improper wastewater management during the COVID-19 pandemic may have infected Ecuador's citizens through water contamination.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Guerrero-Latorre L, Ballesteros I, Villacrés-Granda I, Granda MG, Freire-Paspuel B, Ríos-Touma B | title = SARS-CoV-2 in river water: Implications in low sanitation countries | journal = The Science of the Total Environment | volume = 743 | article-number = 140832 | date = November 2020 | pmid = 32679506 | doi = 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.140832 |pmc=7343659 | bibcode = 2020ScTEn.74340832G }}</ref>

=== Nepal ===
The [[Bagmati River]] passes through the Nepalese capital of [[Kathmandu]], and with its tributaries, comprises a water basin that spans the Kathmandu valley. A July 2021 study revealed the Bagmati River basin saw considerable improvements in water quality during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reduced human activity caused a decrease in [[Biochemical oxygen demand|biological oxygen demand]], an important indicator of bacteria levels in water, by 1.5 times the level before lockdowns were implemented.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Pant RR, Bishwakarma K, Rehman Qaiser FU, Pathak L, Jayaswal G, Sapkota B, Pal KB, Thapa LB, Koirala M, Rijal K, Maskey R | display-authors = 6 | title = Imprints of COVID-19 lockdown on the surface water quality of Bagmati river basin, Nepal | journal = Journal of Environmental Management | volume = 289 | article-number = 112522 | date = July 2021 | pmid = 33848878 | doi = 10.1016/j.jenvman.2021.112522 | pmc = 9626473 | bibcode = 2021JEnvM.28912522P | s2cid = 233233194 }}</ref>

=== Egypt ===
A reduction in human activities due to COVID-19 mitigation measures resulted in less industrial wastewater dumping in the [[Nile|Nile River]], the Nile's canals and tributaries, the [[Nile Delta]], and several lakes in Egypt. Additionally, fewer tourist ships sailed the Nile, thereby minimizing the frequency of oil and gas spills. A decrease in shipping traffic through the [[Suez Canal]] also helped improve its water quality. Similar reductions in wastewater dumping and shipping traffic contributed to improving the quality of Egypt's coastal Mediterranean waters as well.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mostafa MK, Gamal G, Wafiq A | title = The impact of COVID 19 on air pollution levels and other environmental indicators - A case study of Egypt | journal = Journal of Environmental Management | volume = 277 | article-number = 111496 | date = January 2021 | pmid = 33069147 | doi = 10.1016/j.jenvman.2020.111496 | pmc = 7547608 | bibcode = 2021JEnvM.27711496M }}</ref> After the onset of the pandemic, residents in Egyptian villages needed to purify their own water. The Zawyat Al-Na'ura village, for example, used ultraviolet rays as a water purification technique.<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors = Al-Masry R |date=1 September 2020|title=Egyptian villagers purify their drinking water|url=https://www.infonile.org/en/2020/09/egyptian-villagers-purify-their-drinking-water/|access-date=3 December 2021|website=InfoNile}}</ref>

== Water demand ==
Water demand was impacted by the pandemic in a myriad of ways. Practicing good hygiene was one of the main protocols done to combat the pandemic. Frequent hand washing with soap and water for 20 seconds, disinfecting surfaces, and cleaning food containers as they came into the home, increased the demand for water.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Campos MA, Carvalho SL, Melo SK, Gonçalves GB, dos Santos JR, Barros RL, Morgado UT, da Silva Lopes E, Abreu Reis RP | display-authors = 6 |date=2021-06-03|title=Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on water consumption behaviour|journal=Water Supply| volume = 21 |issue=ws2021160| pages = 4058–4067 |doi=10.2166/ws.2021.160| bibcode = 2021WatSu..21.4058C | s2cid = 236225945 |issn=1606-9749|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Residential areas ===
Water demand increased in residential areas due to mandated lockdowns that kept people home. For example, home water use in Portsmouth, England increased by 15%, while non-residential use decreased by 17%. The increased water usage at home led to higher residential water bills, exacerbating financial stress to those impacted by the stay-at-home lockdowns mandated by the pandemic.<ref name="Cooley-2020"/>

=== Desert-like areas ===
While some regions benefitted from lockdowns, water scarce regions suffered severely. For example, in Nevada, there was a 13.1% water usage increase within the first month of quarantine; businesses used substantially less water. Furthermore, water usage at academic institutions declined by 66.2%. Cumulatively in all water sectors, during the first month of quarantine, there was a 3.3% uptick in overall water usage. Consequently, there were efforts to restrict household water usage because of the region's already scarce water supply. These measures included water rations and other limitations put on citizens for their water use, such as watering the grass.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Irwin NB, McCoy SJ, McDonough IK | title = Water in the time of corona(virus): The effect of stay-at-home orders on water demand in the desert | journal = Journal of Environmental Economics and Management | volume = 109 | article-number = 102491 | date = September 2021 | pmid = 34176994 | pmc = 8220444 | doi = 10.1016/j.jeem.2021.102491 | bibcode = 2021JEEM..10902491I }}</ref>

=== Industrial sector ===
Numerous public buildings were shut down for significant amounts of time during the pandemic. The results of these shutdowns were water quality issues such as mold in standing water in pipes and leaching. These became of concern as non-residential demand increased back to normal levels when the shutdowns ended. The effects varied depending on the makeup of the non-residential sectors however, as a whole changes in water demand were seen. The changes in water demand also had notable impacts on water utilities. Utilities experienced significant revenue losses as total water usage dropped in many areas, and simultaneously multitudes of water bills went unpaid while businesses and non-commercial customers struggled financially. Some companies offered overtime and hazard pay to their employees as their work became increasingly essential, which led to increased operational costs.<ref name="Cooley-2020" /> Industries that were part of the water supply chain experienced revenue losses as the industrial water demand declined.<ref name="IFC-2021">{{Cite web|title=The Impact of COVID-19 on Water and Sanitation|url=https://www.ifc.org/wps/wcm/connect/Industry_EXT_Content/IFC_External_Corporate_Site/Infrastructure/Resources/The+Impact+of+COVID-19+on+Water+and+Sanitation|access-date=2021-11-08|website=www.ifc.org|language=en}}</ref>

=== Underdeveloped countries ===
In regions already facing barriers to water access across the globe, such as [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|the Democratic Republic of the Congo]] and [[Yemen]], the pandemic exacerbated challenges.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2020-09-15|title=Democratic Republic of the Congo: Caught between COVID-19 and water shortages in Kinshasa|url=https://www.icrc.org/en/document/drcongo-caught-between-covid-19-and-water-shortages-kinshasa|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=COVID-19 Exacerbates the Effects of Water Shortages on Women in Yemen|url=https://www.wilsoncenter.org/blog-post/covid-19-exacerbates-effects-water-shortages-women-yemen|access-date=2021-09-25|website=www.wilsoncenter.org|date=20 August 2020 |language=en}}</ref> These preexisting inequalities relating to infrastructure and water access were likely a factor contributing to disparate impacts of the pandemic.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ezell JM, Griswold D, Chase EC, Carver E | title = The blueprint of disaster: COVID-19, the Flint water crisis, and unequal ecological impacts | language = English | journal = The Lancet. Planetary Health | volume = 5 | issue = 5 | pages = e309–e315 | date = May 2021 | pmid = 33964240 | doi = 10.1016/S2542-5196(21)00076-0 | pmc = 9709384 | s2cid = 234344645 }}</ref> The [[World Health Organization]] and [[UNICEF]] strongly recommended sanitary hand washing facilities to be the bare minimum for fighting COVID-19 and suggested that lack of access to these necessary facilities (for over 74 million people in the Arab regions) was responsible for putting people at very high risk of contracting COVID-19.<ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Escwa U |date=2020|title=The impact of COVID-19 on the water-scarce Arab region|url=https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3873924|language=en}}</ref>

In some undeveloped countries, water utilities have worked with governments to temporarily suspend billing for vulnerable groups. This was an effort to mitigate the impact of using extra water during the pandemic while people were out of work. The implementation of this process caused a huge loss in revenue for water companies.<ref name="IFC-2021" />

==Wildlife==
[[File:The effects of COVID-19 litter on animal life - 10.1163 - 15707563-bja10052 - Fig. 2.jpg|thumb|upright|A littered medical glove trapped a [[Perca fluviatilis|perch]] to death]]
Fish prices and demand for fish decreased due to the pandemic in early 2020, and fishing fleets around the world sat mostly idle.<ref name="smithsonian">{{cite news|date=8 April 2020|title=With Boats Stuck in Harbor Because of COVID-19, Will Fish Bounce Back?|publisher=Smithsonian Magazine|url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/fish-stop-covid-19-180974623/|access-date=24 April 2020|vauthors=Korten T}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Reiley L |title=Commercial fishing industry in free fall as restaurants close, consumers hunker down and vessels tie up |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2020/04/08/commercial-fishing-coronavirus/ |access-date=25 April 2020 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=8 April 2020}}</ref> German scientist [[Rainer Froese]] has said the fish [[Biomass (ecology)|biomass]] will increase due to the sharp decline in fishing, and projected that in European waters, some fish, such as [[herring]], could double their biomass.<ref name=smithsonian/> As of April 2020, signs of aquatic recovery remain mostly anecdotal.<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Lombrana LM |title=With Fishing Fleets Tied Up, Marine Life Has a Chance to Recover |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-04-17/with-fishing-fleets-tied-up-marine-life-has-a-chance-to-recover |access-date=25 April 2020 |publisher=Bloomberg Green |date=17 April 2020}}</ref>
As people stayed at home due to lockdown and travel restrictions, many types of animals have been spotted roaming freely in cities. [[Sea turtles]] were spotted laying eggs on beaches they once avoided (such as the coast of the [[Bay of Bengal]]), due to lower levels of human interference and light pollution.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.euronews.com/living/2020/04/25/while-you-stay-home-animals-roam-free-in-our-towns-and-cities|title=While you stay home, animals roam free in our towns and cities|date=25 April 2020|website=living}}</ref> In the United States, [[Roadkill|fatal vehicle collisions with animals]] such as deer, elk, moose, bears, mountain lions fell by 58% during March and April 2020.<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Katz C |date=26 June 2020 |title=Roadkill rates fall dramatically as lockdown keeps drivers at home |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/2020/06/decline-road-kill-pandemic-lockdown-traffic/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200628175206/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/2020/06/decline-road-kill-pandemic-lockdown-traffic/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=28 June 2020 |work=[[National Geographic]] |access-date=5 July 2020 }}</ref> In [[Glacier National Park (U.S.)|Glacier National Park]] scientists noted considerable changes in wildlife behavior due to the massive decline in the presence of humans (in effect an [[involuntary park]] within a [[national park]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.wsu.edu/press-release/2023/01/19/low-impact-human-recreation-changes-wildlife-behavior/|title=Low-impact human recreation changes wildlife behavior}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Partial COVID-19 closure of a national park reveals negative influence of low-impact recreation on wildlife spatiotemporal ecology|first1=Alissa K.|last1=Anderson|first2=John S.|last2=Waller|first3=Daniel H.|last3=Thornton|date=13 January 2023|journal=Scientific Reports|volume=13|issue=1|page=687|doi=10.1038/s41598-023-27670-9|doi-access=free|pmid=36639399 |pmc=9839714 |bibcode=2023NatSR..13..687A }}</ref> In Poland, scientists saw a decrease in the occurrence of granivorous and waste-feeding birds in urban areas during the lockdowns, but the presence of other birds remained unchanged.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Woszczyło |first1=Patrycja K. |last2=Mikula |first2=Peter |last3=Jankowiak |first3=Łukasz |last4=Ondrejková |first4=Anna |last5=Tryjanowski |first5=Piotr |date=2024-10-24 |title=A diet perspective on the impact of the COVID -19 lockdown on urban bird assemblages |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ibi.13372 |journal=Ibis |volume=167 |issue=2 |pages=397–406 |language=en |doi=10.1111/ibi.13372 |issn=0019-1019|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Conservationists expected that [[Africa]]n countries would experience a massive surge in [[bush meat]] [[poaching]]. Matt Brown of the [[The Nature Conservancy|Nature Conservancy]] said that "When people don't have any other alternative for income, our prediction -- and we're seeing this in South Africa -- is that poaching will go up for high-value products like [[rhino horn]] and [[ivory]]."<ref name=" Poaching1"/><ref name=" Poaching2"/> On the other hand, [[Gabon]] decided to ban the human consumption of [[bat]]s and [[pangolin]]s, to stem the spread of zoonotic diseases, as [[SARS-CoV-2]] was thought to have transmitted itself to humans through these animals.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Eating bats and pangolins banned in Gabon as a result of coronavirus pandemic|url=https://www.newsweek.com/eating-bats-pangolins-gabon-coronavirus-pandemic-1496329 | vauthors = McCall R |date=6 April 2020|website=Newsweek|language=en|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> Pangolins are no longer thought to have transmitted SARS-CoV-2.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Frutos R, Serra-Cobo J, Chen T, Devaux CA | title = COVID-19: Time to exonerate the pangolin from the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 to humans | journal = Infection, Genetics and Evolution | volume = 84 | article-number = 104493 | date = October 2020 | pmid = 32768565 | pmc = 7405773 | doi = 10.1016/j.meegid.2020.104493 | bibcode = 2020InfGE..8404493F }}</ref> In June 2020, [[Myanmar]] allowed breeding of endangered animals such as [[tiger]]s, pangolins, and [[elephant]]s. Experts fear that the Southeast Asian country's attempts to deregulate wildlife hunting and breeding may create "a New Covid-19."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tiger, pangolin farming in Myanmar risks 'boosting demand'|url=https://phys.org/news/2020-07-tiger-pangolin-farming-myanmar-boosting.html|access-date=2020-07-17|website=phys.org|language=en}}</ref>

In 2020, a worldwide study on mammalian wildlife responses to human presence during COVID lockdowns found complex patterns of animal behavior. Carnivores were generally less active when humans were around, while herbivores in developed areas were more active. Among other findings, this suggested that herbivores may view humans as a shield against predators, highlighting the importance of location and human presence history in understanding wildlife responses to changes in human activity in a given area.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Main |first1=Douglas |title=How Wild Animals Actually Responded to Our COVID Lockdowns |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-wild-animals-actually-responded-to-our-covid-lockdowns/ |access-date=20 March 2024 |publisher=Scientific American |date=18 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319030256/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-wild-animals-actually-responded-to-our-covid-lockdowns/ |archive-date=19 March 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

===Infections===
A [[List of animals that can get SARS-CoV-2|wide variety]] of largely mammalian species, both captive and wild, have been shown to be susceptible to SARS-CoV-2, with some encountering particularly fatal outcomes.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Pappas |first1=Georgios |last2=Vokou |first2=Despoina |last3=Sainis |first3=Ioannis |last4=Halley |first4=John M. |title=SARS-CoV-2 as a Zooanthroponotic Infection: Spillbacks, Secondary Spillovers, and Their Importance |journal=Microorganisms |date=31 October 2022 |volume=10 |issue=11 |page=2166 |doi=10.3390/microorganisms10112166 |pmid=36363758 |pmc=9696655 |issn=2076-2607 |doi-access=free }}</ref> In particular, both [[SARS-CoV-2 in mink|farmed and wild mink]] have developed highly symptomatic and severe COVID-19 infections, with a mortality rate as high as 35–55% according to one study.<ref name="Frontiers Spread">{{cite journal|last1=Devaux |first1=Christian |last2=Pinault |first2=Lucile |last3=Delerce |first3=Jérémy |last4=Raoult |first4=Didier |last5=Levasseur |first5=Anthony |last6=Frutos |first6=Roger |title=Spread of Mink SARS-CoV-2 Variants in Humans: A Model of Sarbecovirus Interspecies Evolution |journal=Frontiers in Microbiology |date=20 September 2021 |volume=12 |article-number=675528 |doi=10.3389/fmicb.2021.675528 |pmid=34616371 |pmc=8488371 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Eckstrand |first1=Chrissy |last2=Baldwin |first2=Thomas |last3=Rood |first3=Kerry |last4=Clayton |first4=Michael |last5=Lott |first5=Jason |last6=Wolking |first6=Rebecca |last7=Bradway |first7=Daniel |last8=Baszler |first8=Timothy |title=An outbreak of SARS-CoV-2 with high mortality in mink (Neovison vison) on multiple Utah farms |journal=PLOS Pathogens |date=12 November 2021 |volume=17 |issue=11 |article-number=e1009952 |doi=10.1371/journal.ppat.1009952 |pmid=34767598 |pmc=8589170 |doi-access=free}}</ref> [[SARS-CoV-2 in white-tailed deer|White-tailed deer]], on the other hand, have largely avoided severe outcomes but have effectively become [[natural reservoir]]s of the virus, with large numbers of free-ranging deer infected throughout the US and Canada, including approximately 80% of [[Iowa]]'s wild deer herd.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Jacobs |first1=Andrew |title=Widespread Coronavirus Infection Found in Iowa Deer, New Study Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/02/science/deer-covid-infection.html |access-date=5 November 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=2 November 2021 ==Deforestation and reforestation==
{{See also|#Retail and food production}}
Due to the sharp decrease in job opportunities during the pandemic, many unemployed individuals were hired to help illegal deforestation operations throughout the world, specifically in the tropics. According to the deforestation alerts from Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD), a total of 9583&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup> of deforested lands were detected across the global tropics during the first month following the establishment of COVID-19 precautions, which was approximately two times that seen the year before, in 2019 (4732&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brancalion PH, Broadbent EN, de-Miguel S, Cardil A, Rosa MR, Almeida CT, Almeida DR, Chakravarty S, Zhou M, Gamarra JG, Liang J, Crouzeilles R, Hérault B, Aragão LE, Silva CA, Almeyda-Zambrano AM | display-authors = 6 | title = Emerging threats linking tropical deforestation and the COVID-19 pandemic | journal = Perspectives in Ecology and Conservation | volume = 18 | issue = 4 | pages = 243–246 | date = 2020-10-01 | pmid = 33020748 | pmc = 7526655 | doi = 10.1016/j.pecon.2020.09.006 | bibcode = 2020PEcoC..18..243B }}</ref> The disruption from the pandemic provided cover for illegal [[deforestation]] operations in [[COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil|Brazil]], which were at a 9-year high.<ref name="conservation-2021" /> Satellite imagery showed [[deforestation of the Amazon rainforest]] surging by over 50% compared to baseline levels.<ref name="Amazon1" /><ref name="Amazon2" /> Conversely, [[unemployment]] caused by the COVID-19 pandemic facilitated the recruitment of laborers for [[Pakistan]]'s [[Plant for Pakistan|10 Billion Tree Tsunami]] campaign [[reforestation|to plant]] 10 billion trees – the estimated global annual net loss of trees – over the span of 5 years.<ref>{{cite web|date=2 September 2015|title=Earth has 3 trillion trees but they're falling at alarming rate|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-science-trees-idUSKCN0R21Z620150902|access-date=26 May 2020|website=Reuters|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=As a 'green stimulus' Pakistan sets virus-idled to work planting trees |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-health-coronavirus-pakistan-trees-fea/as-a-green-stimulus-pakistan-sets-virus-idled-to-work-planting-trees-idUSKCN22A369 |access-date=30 May 2020 |work=Reuters |date=28 April 2020 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Pakistan Hires Thousands of Newly-Unemployed Laborers for Ambitious 10 Billion Tree-Planting Initiative|url=https://www.goodnewsnetwork.org/pakistan-hires-laborers-for-planting-10-billion-tree/|agency=thegoodnewsnetwork|website=Good News Network|language=en|date=30 April 2020|access-date=2 May 2020}}</ref> Because the pandemic saw many authorities unemployed, [[poaching]] became much more popular during 2020 and 2021. In Columbia, illegal activities and wildfires were the two biggest factors contributing to the further destruction of the rainforests.<ref name="conservation-2021">{{Cite web|title=Poaching, deforestation reportedly on the rise since COVID-19 lockdowns|url=https://www.conservation.org/blog/poaching-deforestation-reportedly-on-the-rise-since-covid-19-lockdowns|access-date=2021-11-18|website=www.conservation.org}}</ref>

Deforestation has an impact on clean drinking water. One study showed that a 1% increase in deforestation decreases access to clean drinking water by 0.93%. Deforestation lowers water quality because it lowers the soil infiltration of water which causes a higher level of turbidity in the water. In countries that are not able to pay for drinking water treatment this poses a significant issue.<ref name="Mapulanga-2019">{{cite journal | vauthors = Mapulanga AM, Naito H | title = Effect of deforestation on access to clean drinking water | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 116 | issue = 17 | pages = 8249–8254 | date = April 2019 | pmid = 30910966 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1814970116|pmc=6486726 | bibcode = 2019PNAS..116.8249M | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Climate change==
{{See also|Climate crisis|Travel restrictions related to the COVID-19 pandemic|#Retail and food production|#Investments and other economic measures}}
{{Update section|reason=most studies during 2020 - need later studies to measure whole of 2020|date=December 2021}}
[[File:Change in global daily fossil CO₂ emissions, % during the COVID-19 pandemic.jpg|thumb|400px|Change in global daily fossil CO<sub>2</sub> emissions, % during the COVID-19 pandemic.]]

[[File:Daily CO2 emissions for countries.webp|thumb|300px|Effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on daily CO<sub>2</sub> emissions globally and in 11 nations<ref name="the-immediate-co2effects"/>]]
Societal shifts caused by the COVID-19 lockdowns – such as adoption of [[remote work]] policies,<ref name="C3vSo">{{Cite news |url=https://fortune.com/2020/03/10/coronavirus-remote-flexible-work-from-home/ |title=Commentary: Coronavirus may finally force businesses to adopt workplaces of the future |website=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]] |access-date=9 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200405200635/https://fortune.com/2020/03/10/coronavirus-remote-flexible-work-from-home/ |archive-date=5 April 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Foevb">{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/26/business/coronavirus-businesses.html |title=1,000 Workers, Go Home: Companies Act to Ward Off Coronavirus | vauthors = Yaffe-Bellany D |date=26 February 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=9 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200304092105/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/26/business/coronavirus-businesses.html |archive-date=4 March 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref> and [[virtual event]]s – may have a more sustained impact beyond the short-term reduction of transportation usage.<ref name="nationalgeographic1">{{cite news|date=3 April 2020|title=Carbon emissions are falling sharply due to coronavirus. But not for long.|language=en|work=Science|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/2020/04/coronavirus-causing-carbon-emissions-to-fall-but-not-for-long/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200405204814/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/2020/04/coronavirus-causing-carbon-emissions-to-fall-but-not-for-long/|url-status=dead|archive-date=5 April 2020|access-date=30 May 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Viglione G | title = How scientific conferences will survive the coronavirus shock | journal = Nature | volume = 582 | issue = 7811 | pages = 166–167 | date = June 2020 | pmid = 32488188 | doi = 10.1038/d41586-020-01521-3 | s2cid = 219284783 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2020Natur.582..166V }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tao |first1=Yanqiu |last2=Steckel |first2=Debbie |last3=Klemeš |first3=Jiří Jaromír |last4=You |first4=Fengqi |title=Trend towards virtual and hybrid conferences may be an effective climate change mitigation strategy |journal=Nature Communications |date=16 December 2021 |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=7324 |doi=10.1038/s41467-021-27251-2  |doi-access=free|pmid=34916499 |pmc=8677730 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12.7324T |language=en |issn=2041-1723}}</ref> In a study published in September 2020, scientists estimate that such behavioral changes developed during confinement may reduce 15% of all transportation CO<sub>2</sub> emissions permanently.<ref name="Stoll-2020">{{cite journal | vauthors = Stoll C, Mehling MA | title = COVID-19: Clinching the Climate Opportunity | journal = One Earth | volume = 3 | issue = 4 | pages = 400–404 | date = October 2020 | pmid = 34173539 | pmc = 7508545 | doi = 10.1016/j.oneear.2020.09.003 | bibcode = 2020OEart...3..400S | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Despite this, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere was the highest ever recorded in human history in May 2020.<ref name="nationalgeographic-plunge">{{cite news |title=Plunge in carbon emissions from lockdowns will not slow climate change |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.co.uk/environment-and-conservation/2020/05/plunge-in-carbon-emissions-from-lockdowns-will-not-slow |access-date=7 June 2020 |work=National Geographic |date=29 May 2020 |language=en-gb}}</ref> Energy and climate expert Constantine Samaras states that "a pandemic is the worst possible way to reduce emissions" and that "technological, behavioral, and structural change is the best and only way to reduce emissions".<ref name="nationalgeographic-plunge"/> Tsinghua University's Zhu Liu clarifies that "only when we would reduce our emissions even more than this for longer would we be able to see the decline in concentrations in the atmosphere".<ref name="nationalgeographic-plunge"/> The world's demand for fossil fuels decreased by almost 10% amid COVID-19 measures and reportedly many energy economists believe it may not recover from the crisis.<ref name="guardian-fossilfuels"/>

===Impact on climate===
In a study published in August 2020, scientists estimated that global NO<sub>x</sub> emissions declined by as much as 30% in April but were offset by ~20% reduction in global SO<sub>2</sub> emissions that weakens the cooling effect and conclude that the direct effect of the response to the pandemic on global warming will likely be negligible, with an estimated cooling of around 0.01 ± 0.005&nbsp;°C by 2030 compared to a baseline scenario but that indirect effects due to an economic recovery tailored towards stimulating a [[green economy]], such as by reducing fossil fuel investments, could avoid future warming of 0.3&nbsp;°C by 2050.<ref name="PhysPaper">{{cite news |title=Lockdown emissions fall will have 'no effect' on climate |url=https://phys.org/news/2020-08-lockdown-emissions-fall-effect-climate.html |access-date=31 August 2020 |work=phys.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name="effectspaper">{{cite journal | vauthors = Forster PM, Forster HI, Evans MJ, Gidden MJ, Jones CD, Keller CA, Lamboll RD, Le Quéré C, Rogelj J, Rosen D, Schleussner CF | display-authors = 6 |title=Current and future global climate impacts resulting from COVID-19 |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=7 August 2020 |volume=10 |issue=10 |pages=913–919 |doi=10.1038/s41558-020-0883-0 |bibcode=2020NatCC..10..913F |language=en |issn=1758-6798|doi-access=free |hdl=10044/1/84662 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The study indicates that [[systemic change]] in how humanity powers and feeds itself is required for a substantial impact on global warming.<ref name="PhysPaper"/>

In October 2020 scientists reported, based on near-real-time activity data, an 'unprecedented' abrupt 8.8% decrease in global CO<sub>2</sub> emissions in the first half of 2020 compared to the same period in 2019, larger than during previous economic downturns and World War II. Authors note that such decreases of human activities "cannot be the answer" and that [[structural change|structural]] and [[Transformation in economics|transformational]] changes in human [[economy|economic management]] and [[Behavioral economics|behaviour]] systems are needed.<ref>{{cite news |title=Pandemic caused 'unprecedented' emissions drop: study |url=https://phys.org/news/2020-10-pandemic-unprecedented-emissions.html |access-date=9 November 2020 |work=phys.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name="the-immediate-co2effects">{{cite journal | vauthors = Liu Z, Ciais P, Deng Z, Lei R, Davis SJ, Feng S, Zheng B, Cui D, Dou X, Zhu B, Guo R, Ke P, Sun T, Lu C, He P, Wang Y, Yue X, Wang Y, Lei Y, Zhou H, Cai Z, Wu Y, Guo R, Han T, Xue J, Boucher O, Boucher E, Chevallier F, Tanaka K, Wei Y, Zhong H, Kang C, Zhang N, Chen B, Xi F, Liu M, Bréon FM, Lu Y, Zhang Q, Guan D, Gong P, Kammen DM, He K, Schellnhuber HJ | display-authors = 6 | title = Near-real-time monitoring of global CO<sub>2</sub> emissions reveals the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic | journal = Nature Communications | volume = 11 | issue = 1 | article-number = 5172 | date = October 2020 | pmid = 33057164 | pmc = 7560733 | doi = 10.1038/s41467-020-18922-7  | doi-access = free| arxiv = 2004.13614 | bibcode = 2020NatCo..11.5172L }} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Available under [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ CC BY 4.0].</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ibn-Mohammed |first1=T. |last2=Mustapha |first2=K. B. |last3=Godsell |first3=J. |last4=Adamu |first4=Z. |last5=Babatunde |first5=K. A. |last6=Akintade |first6=D. D. |last7=Acquaye |first7=A. |last8=Fujii |first8=H. |last9=Ndiaye |first9=M. M. |last10=Yamoah |first10=F. A. |last11=Koh |first11=S. C. L. |title=A critical analysis of the impacts of COVID-19 on the global economy and ecosystems and opportunities for circular economy strategies |journal=Resources, Conservation and Recycling |date=1 January 2021 |volume=164 |article-number=105169 |doi=10.1016/j.resconrec.2020.105169 |pmid=32982059 |pmc=7505605 |bibcode=2021RCR...16405169I |s2cid=221858124 |language=en |issn=0921-3449|quote=The paper diagnosed the danger of relying on pandemic-driven benefits to achieving sustainable development goals and emphasizes a need for a decisive, fundamental structural change to the dynamics of how we live. It argues for a rethink of the present global economic growth model, shaped by a linear economy system and sustained by profiteering and energy-gulping manufacturing processes, in favour of a more sustainable model recalibrated on circular economy (CE) framework.}}</ref>

In January 2021 scientists reported that reductions in air pollution due to worldwide COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020 were larger than previously estimated. It was concluded that, because of the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the climate during that year, a slight warming of Earth's climate during the year was seen instead of a slight cooling. Climate models were used to identify small impacts that could not be discerned with observations. The study's lead author noted that aerosol emissions into the lower atmosphere have major health ramifications and can't be part of a viable approach for mitigating global warming.<ref name="Heidari 1–1">{{Cite journal|vauthors=Heidari H, Grigg N|date=August 2021|title=Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on the Urban Water Cycle|url=http://www.lidsen.com/journals/aeer/aeer-02-03-021|journal=Advances in Environmental and Engineering Research|language=en|volume=2|issue=3|page=1|doi=10.21926/aeer.2103021|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=COVID-19 lockdowns temporarily raised global temperatures |url=https://phys.org/news/2021-02-covid-lockdowns-temporarily-global-temperatures.html |access-date=13 February 2021 |work=phys.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gettelman A, Lamboll R, Bardeen CG, Forster PM, Watson-Parris D |title=Climate Impacts of COVID-19 Induced Emission Changes |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=2021 |volume=48 |issue=3 |article-number=e2020GL091805 |doi=10.1029/2020GL091805 |bibcode=2021GeoRL..4891805G |language=en |issn=1944-8007|doi-access=free }} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Available under [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ CC BY 4.0].</ref> In contrast [[Stratospheric aerosol injection|aerosol emissions into the upper atmosphere]] are not thought to be a health risk, but their environmental impact has not yet been properly researched.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Give research into solar geoengineering a chance | journal = Nature | volume = 593 | issue = 7858 | page = 167 | date = May 2021 | pmid = 33981056 | doi = 10.1038/d41586-021-01243-0 | bibcode = 2021Natur.593..167. | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Despite a decrease in anthropogenic methane emissions, methane levels in the atmosphere increased. Researchers have attributed this increase in methane despite a reduction of human emissions of methane to an increase in wetland methane emissions facilitated by a reduction of nitrous oxide emissions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Peng |first1=Shushi |last2=Lin |first2=Xin |last3=Thompson |first3=Rona L. |last4=Xi |first4=Yi |last5=Liu |first5=Gang |last6=Hauglustaine |first6=Didier |last7=Lan |first7=Xin |last8=Poulter |first8=Benjamin |last9=Ramonet |first9=Michel |last10=Saunois |first10=Marielle |last11=Yin |first11=Yi |last12=Zhang |first12=Zhen |last13=Zheng |first13=Bo |last14=Ciais |first14=Philippe |date=14 December 2022 |title=Wetland emission and atmospheric sink changes explain methane growth in 2020 |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=612 |issue=7940 |pages=477–482 |doi=10.1038/s41586-022-05447-w |pmid=36517714 |bibcode=2022Natur.612..477P |s2cid=254710988 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Fossil fuel industry ===
A report by the London-based think tank [[Carbon Tracker]] concludes that the COVID-19 pandemic may have pushed the fossil fuel industry into "terminal decline" as demand for oil and gas decreases while governments aim to accelerate the clean energy transition. It predicts that an annual 2% decline in demand for fossil fuels could cause the future profits of oil, gas and coal companies to collapse from an estimated $39tn to $14tn.<ref>{{cite news |title=Pandemic is triggering 'terminal decline' of fossil fuel industry, says report |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/independentpremium/world/coronavirus-climate-change-fossil-fuel-oil-gas-a9547301.html |access-date=6 June 2020 |work=The Independent |date=3 June 2020 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="guardian-fossilfuels">{{cite news | vauthors = Ambrose J |title=Coronavirus crisis could cause $25tn fossil fuel industry collapse |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/jun/04/coronavirus-crisis-collapse-fossil-fuels-demand |access-date=6 June 2020 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=3 June 2020}}</ref> However, according to Bloomberg New Energy Finance more than half a trillion dollars worldwide are currently intended to be poured into high-carbon industries.<ref name="guardian-recovery">{{cite news |title=Covid-19 relief for fossil fuel industries risks green recovery plans |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/jun/06/covid-19-relief-for-fossil-fuel-industries-risks-green-recovery-plans |access-date=6 June 2020 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=6 June 2020 |language=en}}</ref> Preliminary disclosures from the [[Bank of England]]'s Covid Corporate Financing Facility indicate that billions of pounds of taxpayer support are intended to be funneled to fossil fuel companies.<ref name="guardian-recovery"/> According to Reclaim Finance the [[European Central Bank]] intends to allocate as much as €220bn (£193bn) to fossil fuel industries.<ref name="guardian-recovery"/> An assessment by [[Ernst & Young]] finds that a stimulus program that focuses on renewable energy and climate-friendly projects could create more than 100,000 direct jobs across Australia and estimates that every $1m spent on renewable energy and exports creates 4.8 full-time jobs in renewable infrastructure while $1m on fossil fuel projects would only create 1.7 full-time jobs.<ref>{{cite news |title=Renewable energy stimulus can create three times as many Australian jobs as fossil fuels |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2020/jun/07/renewable-energy-stimulus-three-times-as-many-australia-jobs-fossil-fuels-coronavirus-economic-recovery |access-date=7 June 2020 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=7 June 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

In addition, due to the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic [[Financial market impact of the COVID-19 pandemic|on the fossil fuel and petrochemical industry]], natural gas prices dropped so low for a short time that gas producers were [[Flaring|burning it off on-site]] (not being worth the cost to transport it to [[Ethane#Uses|cracking facilities]]). Bans on single-use consumer plastic (in China, the European Union, Canada, and many countries in Africa), and bans on plastic bags (in several states in the USA) have also reduced demand for plastics considerably. Many cracking facilities in the USA were suspended. The petrochemical industry has been trying to save itself by attempting to rapidly expand demand for plastic products worldwide (i.e. through pushbacks on plastic bans and by increasing the number of products wrapped in plastic in countries where plastic use is not already as widespread (i.e. developing nations)).<ref>{{Cite magazine |url=https://time.com/5831005/coronavirus-plastic-industry/ |title=Will Coronavirus Be the Death or Salvation of Big Plastic? |magazine=Time |access-date=19 January 2021 }}</ref>

===Cycling===
During the pandemic, many people started [[cycling]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Richard Smith: How can we achieve a healthy recovery from the pandemic? |url=https://blogs.bmj.com/bmj/2020/06/08/richard-smith-how-can-we-achieve-a-healthy-recovery-from-the-pandemic/ |website=The BMJ |access-date=8 June 2020 |date=8 June 2020}}</ref> causing bike sales to surge.<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Villafranca O |title=Americans turn to cycling during the coronavirus pandemic |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/americans-turn-to-cycling-coronavirus-pandemic-2020-05-20/ |access-date=8 June 2020 |work=www.cbsnews.com |date=20 May 2020 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Winkelmann S |title=Bike shops see surge in sales during pandemic |url=https://www.weau.com/content/news/Bike-shops-see-surge-in-sales-during-pandemic-570947211.html |access-date=8 June 2020 |work=www.weau.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Earls S |title=Bike sales boom during the pandemic as more kids pedal as a pastime |url=https://gazette.com/news/bike-sales-boom-during-the-pandemic-as-more-kids-pedal-as-a-pastime/article_a30bf14a-a80d-11ea-b3a0-1f59e4c3e6a7.html |access-date=8 June 2020 |work=Colorado Springs Gazette |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=On your bike! Coronavirus prompts cycling frenzy in Germany |url=https://www.dw.com/en/on-your-bike-coronavirus-prompts-cycling-frenzy-in-germany/a-53462018 |access-date=8 June 2020 |work=DW.COM}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Lee E |title=Bike shops shift into higher gear as Marylanders become more active outdoors during coronavirus pandemic |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/05/29/bike-shops-shift-into-higher-gear-as-marylanders-become-more-active-outdoors-during-coronavirus-pandemic/ |access-date=8 June 2020 |work=baltimoresun.com}}</ref> Many cities set up semi-permanent "[[pop-up bike lanes]]" to provide people who switched from public transit to bicycles with more room. Many individuals chose cycling due to a heightened anxiety over public transportation. This was because public transportation could be crowded at times, raising the fear that one may catch COVID-19. Additionally, exercise became more popular during the pandemic, since lockdowns led to mass unemployment.
