Third, they protected the domestic economy by raising tariffs on imported goods. Fourth, they slashed taxes: the top rate fell from 73 per cent in 1919 to 24 per cent in 1929. What all this adds up to isn’t strictly laissez-faire - a state that does almost nothing - but rather a state that rigorously enforces American independence by building a protective wall around the country within which capitalism is unleashed to work its wonders. This is Business Nationalism, and it goes back far.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2016-03-09 |title=Donald Trump's Mexican Imports |url=http://www.wsj.com/articles/donald-trumps-mexican-imports-1457481637 |access-date=2026-04-02 |work=The Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660|quote=Mr. Trump is a business nationalist without a core philosophy of government, so his policy arc is going to be an adventure.}}</ref> and [[Ultraconservatism in the United States|ultraconservative]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-11-13 |title=Maryanne Trump Barry, former federal judge and sister of ex-president, dead at 86 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-sister-maryanne-barry-dead-b2446506.html |access-date=2026-04-24 |website=The Independent |language=en |quote=[Maryanne Barry Trump] was widely respected and well-known in the legal community, and her reputation as a judge stood in stark contrast with the ultraconservative views her [[Donald Trump|brother]] espoused as president. But during his 2016 campaign for the White House, he mused that she would be a “phenomenal” pick for the Supreme Court were he to be elected.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Huntington |first=John S. |title=Far-right Vanguard: The Radical Roots of Modern Conservatism |date=2021 |publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania Press]] |isbn=978-0-8122-5347-4 |series=Politics and culture in modern America |location=Philadelphia|quote=Donald Trump shocked the nation in 2016 by winning the presidency through an ultraconservative, anti-immigrant platform, but, despite the electoral surprise, Trump's far-right views were not an aberration, nor even a recent phenomenon.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Feldenkirchen |first=Markus |last2=Medick |first2=Veit |last3=Stark |first3=Holger |date=2016-02-01 |title=Donald Trump Is the Most Dangerous Man in the World |url=https://www.spiegel.de/international/world/donald-trump-is-the-most-dangerous-man-in-the-world-a-1075060.html |access-date=2026-09-05 |work=Der Spiegel |language=en |issn=2195-1349 |quote=For his part, though, Trump acts as if this past never even existed. He presents his new, ultraconservative positions in the most populist of ways and with even greater determination.}}</ref> Trump has variously described himself as "[[common sense]]" and nationalist.<ref>{{cite news |date=February 27, 2017|title=Trump: I Am a Nationalist in a True Sense|url=https://www.realclearpolitics.com/video/2017/02/27/trump_i_am_a_nationalist_in_a_true_sense.html|work=[[RealClearPolitics]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Young|first=Dannagal G.|date=2025-02-06|title=How populist leaders like Trump use 'common sense' as an ideological weapon to undermine facts|url=http://theconversation.com/how-populist-leaders-like-trump-use-common-sense-as-an-ideological-weapon-to-undermine-facts-248608|access-date=2026-04-01|website=The Conversation|language=en-US}}</ref> Prior to 2016, he at times identified with the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]].<ref name="cnn.com3">{{Cite web |last=Moody |first=Chris |date=2015-07-21 |title=Trump in '04: 'I probably identify more as Democrat' {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2015/07/21/politics/donald-trump-election-democrat |access-date=2026-04-23 |publisher=CNN |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Gillin3">Gillin, Joshua; [http://www.politifact.com/florida/statements/2015/aug/24/jeb-bush/bush-says-trump-was-democrat-longer-republican-las/ "Bush says Trump was a Democrat longer than a Republican 'in the last decade'"], ''[[PolitiFact]]'' (August 24, 2015).</ref> Trump's political beliefs and ideologies are described as [[Trumpism]].

Trump consistently advocates for [[supply-side economics]], [[deregulation]],<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Barstow|first1=David|last2=Craig|first2=Susanne|last3=Buettner|first3=Russ|date=2018-10-02|title=Trump Engaged in Suspect Tax Schemes as He Reaped Riches From His Father|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/10/02/us/politics/donald-trump-tax-schemes-fred-trump.html|access-date=2025-07-29|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|quote=As the chip episode demonstrated, [Fred Trump] and  [Donald Trump] were of one mind about rules and regulations, viewing them as annoyances to be finessed or, when necessary, ignored.}}</ref> achieving [[Energy independence of the United States|energy independence]], and prioritizing the interests of domestic industry, expanding [[school choice]] and adopting a "[[Law and order (politics)|law and order]]" approach to [[Law enforcement in the United States|law enforcement]]. He is also [[Opposition to immigration|anti-immigrant]], wanting to deter [[Illegal immigration to the United States|illegal]] and unskilled migration through stricter [[List of United States immigration and nationality laws|immigration laws]] and [[Immigration Enforcement|enforcement]]. In foreign policy, he is [[Grand strategy#Neo-isolationism|neo-isolationist]] and [[Protectionism|protectionist]], preferring a [[Unilateralism|unilateral]] [[military policy]] to counter "[[Rogue state|rogue states]]" and deter [[China]], eschewing [[collective security]] while diplomatically and militarily supporting [[Israel]], and renegotiating [[Free trade agreements of the United States|free trade agreements]] while levying [[Tariff|import tariffs]] to favor domestic industry.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Matthews|first=Dylan|date=January 19, 2017|title=Trump's books reveal there is so much more beneath the insults he hurls|url=https://www.vox.com/a/donald-trump-books|access-date=2025-07-22|website=Vox.com|quote=On the core issues he cares about the most — international trade, immigration, foreign policy — he’s strikingly consistent. He’s always been anti-immigrant, always been protectionist, always been fiercely nationalistic on matters of war and peace.}}</ref><ref name="at"/><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Trump|first1=Donald|title=[[The America We Deserve]]|last2=Shiflett|first2=Dave|date=2000|publisher=[[Renaissance Books]]|isbn=978-1-58063-131-0|edition=|location=Los Angeles}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Trump|first=Donald|title=[[Time to Get Tough|Time to Get Tough: Making America #1 Again]]|date=2011|publisher=[[Regnery Publishing]]|isbn=978-1-59698-773-9|location=Washington, D.C}}</ref>

He has been variously accused of espousing [[Racism|racist]]<ref name="hr"/> and [[Misogyny|misogynist]] views.<ref name="Shear"/> 

Trump has personally cited [[Roy Cohn]], [[Arthur Laffer]], and [[Norman Vincent Peale]] as influences on his worldview. [[Jerome Corsi]], [[Lee Iacocca]], and [[Roger Stone]] are further purported to be influences on his politics.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=N |last2=P |last3=R |date=2019-02-21 |title=How 2 Conspiracy Theorists Shaped Trump's Worldview |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/02/21/696614139/how-2-conspiracy-theorists-shaped-trumps-worldview |access-date=2026-04-01 |publisher=NPR |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Toobin |first=Jeffrey |date=2019-02-11 |title=Roger Stone's and Jerome Corsi's Time in the Barrel |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2019/02/18/roger-stones-and-jerome-corsis-time-in-the-barrel |access-date=2026-04-01 |magazine=The New Yorker |language=en-US |issn=0028-792X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Schlesinger |first=Jacob M. |date=2018-11-15 |title=Trump Forged His Ideas on Trade in the 1980s—and Never Deviated |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/trump-forged-his-ideas-on-trade-in-the-1980sand-never-deviated-1542304508 |access-date=2026-04-01 |work=The Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref><!--He has also been accused of espousing [[Sexism|sexist]], [[Misogyny|misogynistic]], and [[Antifeminism|anti-feminist]] attitudes towards women, as well as holding [[Racism in the United States|racist]] views toward [[Person of color|individuals of color]] that align with [[White nationalism|white nationalist]] sentiments; however, he has consistently rejected these allegations.-->

==Political affiliation and ideology==
===Self-described===
[[File:Donald Trump by Gage Skidmore 3.jpg|thumb|Trump speaking at CPAC in 2015]]
As a [[New York (state)|New York]] real estate developer and celebrity, Trump often donated to and associated with whichever party held more influence in the jurisdictions where he did business. For example, he typically aligned more with [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] in [[New York City]], as the city was and still is a heavily Democratic jurisdiction. He frequently donated to candidates from both parties in order to "curry favor" and gain access to the political elite.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hall |first1=Amy |title="Donald Trump was once a registered Democrat and party donor. So why did he jump ship?" |url=https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/donald-trump-was-once-a-registered-democrat-and-party-donor-why-did-he-jump-ship/wj85mj5yq#:~:text=%22I%20think%20those%20political%20donations,he%20was%2C%22%20he%20said. |website=[[Special Broadcasting Service|SBS Australia]] |date=July 25, 2024 |access-date=25 July 2024}}</ref> Trump initially registered as a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] in [[Manhattan]], New York City, in 1987; since that time, he has changed his party affiliation five times. In 1999, he changed his party affiliation to the [[Reform Party of the United States of America|Reform Party]] and had even considered running a [[Donald Trump 2000 presidential campaign|presidential campaign in 2000]] as a [[Reform Party of the United States of America|Reformist]] before ultimately withdrawing from the race due to becoming disillusioned with the party and not wanting to become associated with certain members that had differing views, such as [[David Duke]], [[Pat Buchanan]] and [[Lenora Fulani]], whom he referred to as a [[Ku Klux Klan|Klansman]], a [[Neo-Nazism|Neo-Nazi]], and a [[Communism|Communist]] respectively.<ref name="ducks">{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=VvBHAAAAIBAJ&pg=2376,6423681|title=The Donald ducks out on presidential run, blames party fighting|date=February 14, 2000|work=Deseret News|access-date=July 28, 2011}}</ref> In August 2001, Trump changed his party affiliation to [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]]. In September 2009, he changed his party affiliation back to the Republican Party. In December 2011, Trump changed his party affiliation to "no party affiliation" ([[Independent (voter)|independent]]) to preserve his right to run as an independent if he was dissatisfied with the Republican nominee. In April 2012, he again returned to the Republican Party and has remained a Republican since then.<ref name="Gillin3"/>

In a 2004 interview, Trump told [[CNN]]'s [[Wolf Blitzer]]: "In many cases, I probably identify more as Democrat", explaining: "It just seems that the economy does better under the Democrats than the Republicans. Now, it shouldn't be that way. But if you go back, I mean it just seems that the economy does better under the Democrats...But certainly we had some very good economies under Democrats, as well as Republicans. But we've had some pretty bad disaster under the Republicans."<ref name="cnn.com">Moody, Chris; [http://www.cnn.com/2015/07/21/politics/donald-trump-election-democrat/ "Trump in '04: 'I probably identify more as Democrat'"], CNN (July 21, 2015).</ref> In a July 2015 interview, Trump said that he has a broad range of political positions and that "I identify with some things as a Democrat."<ref name="Gillin3"/>

During [[2016 Donald Trump Presidential campaign|his 2016 presidential campaign]], Trump consistently described the state of the United States in bleak terms, referring to it as a nation in dire peril that is plagued by lawlessness, poverty, and violence, constantly under threat, and at risk of having "nothing, absolutely nothing, left".<ref>Johnson, Jenna; [https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/donald-trumps-message-of-doom-and-despair-in-america/2016/07/21/8afe4cae-3f22-11e6-80bc-d06711fd2125_story.html "Donald Trump's vision of doom and despair in America"], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (July 21, 2016).</ref><ref name="Flores">Reena Flores, [https://www.cbsnews.com/news/donald-trump-gop-convention-speech/ "Donald Trump offers dark vision of America in GOP convention speech"], ''[[CBS News]]'' (July 22, 2016).</ref> In accepting the Republican nomination for president, Trump said that "I alone can fix" the system,<ref>Jackson, David; [https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2016/07/21/donald-trump-republican-convention-acceptance-speech/87385658/ "Donald Trump accepts GOP nomination, says 'I alone can fix' system"], ''[[USA Today]]'' (July 22, 2016).</ref> and pledged that if elected, "[[Americanism (ideology)|Americanism]], not globalism, will be our credo."<ref name="Flores"/> He described himself as a "law and order" candidate and "the voice" of "the forgotten men and women".<ref>Rucker, Philip; Fahrenthold, David A.; [https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/in-speech-at-republican-national-convention-trump-to-paint-dire-picture-of-america/2016/07/21/418f9ae6-4fad-11e6-aa14-e0c1087f7583_story.html "Donald Trump positions himself as the voice of 'the forgotten men and women'"], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (July 21, 2016).</ref> Trump's inaugural address on January 20, 2017, focused on his campaign theme of America in crisis and decline.<ref name="Page">Page, Susan; [https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2017/01/20/donald-trump-president-inauguration-speech-analysis-defiant-address-and-political-revolt/96836152/ "Analysis: Trump's short, dark and defiant inaugural address"] {{webarchive |url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170717043705/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2017/01/20/donald-trump-president-inauguration-speech-analysis-defiant-address-and-political-revolt/96836152/ |date=July 17, 2017}}, ''[[USA Today]]'' (January 20, 2017).</ref> He pledged to end what he referred to as "American carnage",<ref>{{cite news |url= http://globalnews.ca/news/3194820/donald-trump-inauguration-speech-and-transcript/ |title=Donald Trump's full inauguration speech and transcript |publisher=[[Global News]] |date=January 20, 2017 |access-date=January 28, 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170128155656/http://globalnews.ca/news/3194820/donald-trump-inauguration-speech-and-transcript/ |archive-date=January 28, 2017}}</ref><ref name="WaPo">{{cite news |url= https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/trump-to-be-sworn-in-marking-a-transformative-shift-in-the-countrys-leadership/2017/01/20/954b9cac-de7d-11e6-ad42-f3375f271c9c_story.html |title=Donald Trump is sworn in as president, vows to end 'American carnage' |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=January 22, 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170122040205/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/trump-to-be-sworn-in-marking-a-transformative-shift-in-the-countrys-leadership/2017/01/20/954b9cac-de7d-11e6-ad42-f3375f271c9c_story.html |archive-date=January 22, 2017}}</ref> depicting the United States in a [[dystopia]]n light—as a "land of abandoned factories, economic angst, rising crime"—while pledging "a new era in American politics".<ref name="Page" />

Although Trump was the Republican nominee, he has signaled that the official [[party platform]], adopted at the [[2016 Republican National Convention]], diverges from his own views.<ref>O'Keefe, Ed; Balz Dan; [[David Weigel|Weigel, David]]; [https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/in-gop-platform-fight-donald-trump-is-a-distant-presence/2016/07/11/439abe0e-4780-11e6-bdb9-701687974517_story.html "In GOP platform fight, Donald Trump is a distant presence"], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (July 11, 2016).</ref> According to a ''[[The Washington Post]]'' tally, Trump made some 282 [[campaign promise]]s over the course of his 2016 campaign.<ref>Johnson, Jenna; [https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/i-will-give-you-everything-here-are-282-of-donald-trumps-campaign-promises/2016/11/24/01160678-b0f9-11e6-8616-52b15787add0_story.html "'I will give you everything.' Here are 282 of Donald Trump's campaign promises"], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (November 24, 2016).</ref> In February 2017, Trump stated that he was a "total [[American nationalism|nationalist]]" in a "true sense".<ref>{{cite news |work=[[RealClearPolitics]] |title=Trump: I Am a Nationalist in a True Sense |url= https://www.realclearpolitics.com/video/2017/02/27/trump_i_am_a_nationalist_in_a_true_sense.html |date=February 27, 2017}}</ref> In October 2018, Trump again described himself as a nationalist.<ref>{{Cite news |url= https://www.politico.com/story/2018/10/22/trump-nationalist-926745 |title=Trump: 'I'm a nationalist' |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=2018-10-23}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/23/us/politics/nationalist-president-trump.html |title=Promoting His Agenda, Trump Embraces the 'Nationalist' Label |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 23, 2018 |access-date=2018-10-23|last1=Baker |first1=Peter }}</ref> During the last week of his presidential term in January 2021, Trump reportedly considered founding a new political party called the Patriot Party.<ref>{{Cite web|agency=[[Associated Press]]|date=19 January 2021|title=Trump Has Discussed Starting a New Political Party - WSJ.com|url=https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/trump-impeachment-biden-inauguration/card/90pPMzFPqr5fMzg1Bkbs|access-date=19 January 2021|website=[[The Wall Street Journal]]}}</ref>

===As described by others===
Observers and analysts often attribute Donald Trump's constant shifts to pragmatism, political expediency, and a desire for influence rather than a rigid adherence to a specific ideology or party loyalty. Trump's political positions are [[Populism|populist]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ross |first1=Bertrall L. |date=October 2024 |title=Polarization, Populism, and the Crisis of American Democracy |journal=Annual Review of Law and Social Science |volume=20 |pages=293–308 |issn=1550-3631 |doi=10.1146/annurev-lawsocsci-041922-035113 |quote-page=298|quote=In 2016, a populist won the presidential election in the United States.|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Urbinati |first=Nadia |date=May 2019 |title=Political Theory of Populism |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-polisci-050317-070753 |journal=Annual Review of Political Science |volume=22 |access-date=December 20, 2024 |pages=111–127 |issn=1094-2939 |doi=10.1146/annurev-polisci-050317-070753|url-access=subscription }}</ref> more specifically described as [[right-wing populist]].<ref>

Liberal economist and columnist [[Paul Krugman]] disputes that Trump is a populist, arguing that his policies favor the rich over those less well off.<ref>Krugman, Paul. [https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/20/opinion/obamas-war-on-inequality.html Obama's War on Inequality], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (May 20, 2016): "Just for the record, while Mr. Trump is sometimes described as a 'populist,' almost every substantive policy he has announced would make the rich richer at workers' expense".</ref> [[John F. Kennedy School of Government|Harvard Kennedy School]] political scientist [[Pippa Norris]] has described Trump as a "populist authoritarian" analogous to European parties such as the [[Swiss People's Party]], [[Austrian Freedom Party]], [[Swedish Democrats]], and [[Danish People's Party]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/monkey-cage/wp/2016/03/11/its-not-just-trump-authoritarian-populism-is-rising-across-the-west-heres-why/ |title=It's not just Trump. Authoritarian populism is rising across the West. Here's why|last=Norris|first=Pippa|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=March 11, 2016}}</ref> Columnist [[Walter Shapiro]] and political commentator [[Jonathan Chait]] describe Trump as [[Authoritarianism|authoritarian]].<ref name="WShapiro">{{cite web|url=http://www.rollcall.com/opinion-analysis/319/?dcz=|title=Dear Republican Sirs: It's Up to You to Save the Republic|last=Shapiro|first=Walter|magazine=[[Roll Call]]|date=February 23, 2016|quote=He is the embodiment of the authoritarian temptation that has imperiled liberty since the days of the Roman Republic.|access-date=May 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200123144034/http://www.rollcall.com/opinion-analysis/319/?dcz=|archive-date=January 23, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="ChaitClassify">{{cite web|url=https://nymag.com/daihly/intelligencer/2016/05/heres-how-trumps-authoritarianism-would-work.html|title=Here's How Donald Trump's Authoritarianism Would Actually Work|last=Chait|first=Jonathan|magazine=[[New York (magazine)|New York]]|date=May 13, 2016|access-date=February 20, 2020|archive-date=March 23, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200323175144/https://nymag.com/daihly/intelligencer/2016/05/heres-how-trumps-authoritarianism-would-work.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Conservative commentator [[Mary Katharine Ham]] characterized Trump as a "casual authoritarian," saying "he is a candidate who has happily and proudly spurned the entire idea of limits on his power as an executive and doesn't have any interest in the Constitution and what it allows him to do and what [it] does not allow him to do. That is concerning for people who are interested in limited government."<ref>[http://www.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/1605/11/cnr.03.html Transcript: Donald Trump Sweeps Nebraska and West Virginia Primaries; Bernie Sanders Wins West Virginia But Gains Little], CNN (May 11, 2016).</ref> [[Charles C. W. Cooke]] of the ''[[National Review]]'' has expressed similar views, terming Trump an "anti-constitutional authoritarian."<ref name="Cooke">{{cite web|author=Charles C. W. Cooke|url=http://www.nationalreview.com/article/428208/trump-anti-constitutional-authoritarian|title=Here's How Donald Trump's Authoritarianism Would Actually Work|magazine=National Review|date=December 8, 2015}}</ref> [[Libertarianism in the United States|Libertarian]] journalist [[Nick Gillespie]], by contrast, calls Trump "populist rather than an authoritarian".<ref>Gillespie, Nick. [http://reason.com/blog/2016/03/14/donald-trump-supporters-are-less-authori Donald Trump Supporters Are Less Authoritarian Than Ted Cruz Voters], ''[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]]'' (March 14, 2016): "Understanding Trump as a populist rather than an authoritarian helps explain why he can get away with sloppy, inconsistent thinking."</ref> In an article for [[Newsweek]], political theorist [[Rafael Holmberg]] described Trump's politics as even more unsettling than populism, and as a new type of political discourse.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Holmberg |first1=Rafael |title=Donald Trump is No Populist |url=https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trump-no-populist-opinion-2023522 |work=Newsweek |date=4 February 2025}}</ref> [[Rich Benjamin]] refers to Trump and his ideology as [[fascist]] and a form of [[totalitarian capitalism|inverted totalitarianism]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://theintercept.com/2020/09/27/trump-supporters-fascism-election/|title=Democrats Need to Wake Up: The Trump Movement Is Shot Through With Fascism|first1=Rich |last1=Benjamin|website=[[The Intercept]]|date=September 27, 2020}}</ref>

Legal experts spanning the political spectrum, including many conservative and libertarian scholars, have suggested that "Trump's blustery attacks on the press, complaints about the judicial system and bold claims of presidential power collectively sketch out a constitutional worldview that shows contempt for the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]], the [[Separation of powers under the United States Constitution|separation of powers]] and the [[rule of law]]."<ref name="LiptakRuleofLaw">{{Cite news |last=Liptak |first=Adam |author-link=Adam Liptak |date=2016-06-03 |title=Donald Trump Could Threaten U.S. Rule of Law, Scholars Say |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/06/04/us/politics/donald-trump-constitution-power.html |access-date=2025-03-01 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Law professors [[Randy E. Barnett]], [[Richard Epstein]], and [[David G. Post]], for example, suggest that Trump has little or no awareness of, or commitment to, the constitutional principles of separation of powers and [[Federalism in the United States|federalism]].<ref name="LiptakRuleofLaw"/> Law professor [[Ilya Somin]] believes that Trump "poses a serious threat to the press and the First Amendment," citing Trump's proposal to expand defamation laws to make it easier to sue journalists and his remark that the owner of ''[[The Washington Post]]'', [[Jeff Bezos]], would "have problems" if Trump was elected president.<ref name="LiptakRuleofLaw"/> [[Anthony D. Romero]], the executive director of the [[American Civil Liberties Union]], wrote in an op-ed published in ''The Washington Post'' in July 2016 that "Trump's proposed policies, if carried out, would trigger a constitutional crisis. By our reckoning, a Trump administration would violate the First, Fourth, Fifth and Eighth amendments if it tried to implement his most controversial plans."<ref name="RomeroACLU">Anthony D. Romero, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/a-president-trump-would-threaten-our-constitutional-freedoms/2016/07/13/42b41048-4876-11e6-bdb9-701687974517_story.html ACLU Director: We will defend the constitution against a President Trump], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (July 13, 2016).</ref>

Prior to his election as president, his views on social issues were often described as centrist or moderate. Political commentator [[Josh Barro]] termed Trump a "moderate Republican," saying that except on immigration, his views are "anything but ideologically rigid, and he certainly does not equate deal making with surrender."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/18/upshot/donald-trump-moderate-republican.html|title=Donald Trump, Moderate Republican|last=Barro|first=Josh|publisher=The Upshot, [[The New York Times]]|date=August 14, 2015|access-date=March 5, 2016}}</ref> [[MSNBC]] host [[Joe Scarborough]] said Trump is essentially more like a "centrist Democrat" on [[social issue]]s.<ref>Hains, Tim. [http://www.realclearpolitics.com/video/2016/04/22/joe_scarborough_donald_trump_is_a_centrist_democrat_its_not_been_a_secret.html "Joe Scarborough: Donald Trump Is A Centrist Democrat On Social Issue, 'It's Not Been A Secret'"], [[Real Clear Politics]] (April 22, 2016).</ref> Journalist and political analyst [[John Heilemann]] characterized Trump as [[Modern liberalism in the United States|liberal]] on social issues,<ref>[[With All Due Respect (TV series)]] (April 21, 2016).</ref> while conservative talk radio host and political commentator [[Rush Limbaugh]] said that Heilemann is seeing in Trump what he wants to see.<ref>Limbaugh, Rush. [http://www.rushlimbaugh.com/daily/2016/04/25/trump_walks_it_back_on_bathrooms Trump Walks It Back on Bathrooms] (April 25, 2016): "[P]eople make Trump into what they want him to be. So here you have these two guys Heilemann and Halperin, who are liberals, and they want to like Trump, I think."</ref> Since he became president, commentators have generally characterized his policy agenda as [[socially conservative]].<ref>{{cite news|work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/04/04/trump-administration-cuts-funding-un-population-fund-concerns/ |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/04/04/trump-administration-cuts-funding-un-population-fund-concerns/ |archive-date=January 12, 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|date=April 4, 2017|title=Trump administration cuts off funding to UN Population Fund over concerns about abortion}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|work=[[Fortune magazine|Fortune]]|url=http://fortune.com/2017/03/13/mark-cuban-president-trump-sxsw/|title=Mark Cuban Calls Trump the 'Zoolander President.' He's Also Not Ruling Out a White House Bid|date=March 12, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|work=[[Politico]]|title=Social Conservatives Are 'Over the Moon' About Trump|url=https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2017/04/26/donald-trump-social-conservatives-215073/|date=April 26, 2017}}</ref>

Trump and his political views have often been described as [[American nationalism|nationalist]].<ref name="fp"/><ref name="tv"/> [[John Cassidy (journalist)|John Cassidy]] of ''[[The New Yorker]]'' writes that Trump seeks to make the Republican Party "into a more populist, nativist, avowedly protectionist, and semi-isolationist party that is skeptical of immigration, free trade, and military interventionism."<ref>John Cassidy, [https://www.newyorker.com/news/john-cassidy/donald-trump-is-transforming-the-g-o-p-into-a-populist-nativist-party Donald Trump Is Transforming the G.O.P. into a Populist, Nativist Party], ''[[The New Yorker]]'' (February 29, 2016).</ref> ''[[The Washington Post]]'' editorial page editor [[Fred Hiatt]] and [[College of the Holy Cross]] political scientist Donald Brand describe Trump as a [[Nativism (politics)|nativist]].<ref name="Hiatt">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/in-america-citizenship-trumps-tribe/2015/08/23/51be75da-481b-11e5-846d-02792f854297_story.html|title=Donald Trump's nativist bandwagon |last=Hiatt|first=Fred|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=August 23, 2015|access-date=March 5, 2016}}</ref><ref>Donald Brand, [http://fortune.com/2016/06/21/donald-trump-nativism-gop/ How Donald Trump's Nativism Ruined the GOP], ''[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]'' (June 21, 2016).</ref> [[Rich Lowry]], the editor of ''National Review'', instead calls Trump an "immigration hawk" and supports Trump's effort to return immigration levels to what Trump calls a "historically average level".<ref>Lowry, Rich. [https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2015/08/donald-trump-2016-immigration-pandering-121541/ Yes, Pander to Trump on Immigration], ''[[Politico]]'' (August 19, 2015).</ref> Trump is a [[Protectionism|protectionist]], according to free-market advocate [[Stephen Moore (writer)|Stephen Moore]] and conservative economist [[Larry Kudlow]].<ref name="realclearpolitics.com">{{cite web|url=http://www.realclearpolitics.com/articles/2015/08/26/donald_trump_a_21st_century_protectionist_herbert_hoover_127893.html|title=Donald Trump: A 21st Century Protectionist Herbert Hoover|last1=Kudlow|first1=Lawrence|last2=Moore|first2=Stephen|website=[[Real Clear Politics]] |date=August 26, 2015|access-date=March 5, 2016}}</ref> Historian [[Joshua M. Zeitz]] wrote in 2016 that Trump's appeals to "[[law and order (politics)|law and order]]" and "the [[silent majority]]" were comparable to the [[Dog-whistle politics|dog-whistle]] and racially-coded terminology of [[Richard Nixon]].<ref name="ZeitzPolitico16.1">{{cite news|last1=Zeitz|first1=Josh|title=How Trump Is Recycling Nixon's 'Law and Order' Playbook|url=https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2016/07/donald-trump-law-and-order-richard-nixon-crime-race-214066/|access-date=February 5, 2017|work=[[Politico]] Magazine|date=July 18, 2016}}</ref>

According to a 2020 study, voters had the most difficulty assessing the ideology of Trump in the 2016 election out of all presidential candidates since 1972 and all contemporary legislators.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Eady|first1=Gregory|last2=Loewen|first2=Peter|date=2020-07-28|title=Measuring Public Uncertainty about Candidate Ideology: An Application to US Presidential Elections|url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/710147|journal=The Journal of Politics|volume=83|issue=2|pages=794–799|doi=10.1086/710147|s2cid=225466445|issn=0022-3816|url-access=subscription}}</ref> As of 2021, the [[Southern Poverty Law Center]] identifies Trump as a leader of the [[Radical right (United States)|radical right]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-02-05 |title=The Year in Hate and Extremism: Far-right extremists coalescing in broad-based, loosely affiliated movement |url=https://www.splcenter.org/resources/stories/year-hate-and-extremism-far-right-extremists-coalescing-broad-based-loosely-affiliated/ |access-date=2026-04-03 |website=[[Southern Poverty Law Center]] |language=en-US}}</ref> 

===Trump's views of the presidency===

{{Quote box
|width = 33%
| quote = "I have the right to do anything I want to do. I'm the president of the United States."
| author = Donald Trump, during a cabinet meeting on August 26, 2025.<ref name="absolute"/>
| align = right
}}
In 2019, Trump said that Article 2 of the [[United States Constitution|Constitution]] gave him "the right to do whatever I want as president".<ref>{{cite news |last=Wofford |first=Claire B. |url=https://theconversation.com/trumps-claims-of-vast-presidential-powers-run-up-against-article-2-of-the-constitution-and-exceed-previous-presidents-power-grabs-249662 |title=Trump's claims of vast presidential powers run up against Article 2 of the Constitution and exceed previous presidents' power grabs |work=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]] |date=February 25, 2025 |access-date=May 23, 2026}}</ref> In February 2025, Trump wrote and pinned a comment on [[Truth Social]] and [[Twitter|X]]: "He who saves his Country does not violate any Law", which the [[White House]] later reposted on X that day. The phrase itself is a variation of one attributed to [[Napoleon Bonaparte]], and was noted to be in line with his administration's aggressive push for expanding presidential power under the [[unitary executive theory]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chiacu |first1=Doina |title=Trump: If it saves the country, it's not illegal |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-if-it-saves-country-its-not-illegal-2025-02-16/ |access-date=February 17, 2025 |work=[[Reuters]] |date=February 16, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Haberman |first1=Maggie |last2=Savage |first2=Charlie |last3=Swan |first3=Jonathan |title=Trump Suggests No Laws Are Broken if He's 'Saving His Country' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/15/us/politics/trump-saves-country-quote.html |access-date=February 17, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 15, 2025}}</ref> In May 2025, when asked by ''[[Meet the Press]]'' moderator [[Kristen Welker]] if he has "to uphold the Constitution of the United States as president", Trump responded "I don't know".<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Terkel|first1=Amanda|last2=Hurley|first2=Lawrence|date=May 4, 2025|title=Trump, asked if he has to 'uphold the Constitution,' says, 'I don't know'|work=NBC News|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/trump-asked-uphold-constitution-says-dont-know-rcna204580|access-date=May 26, 2026}}</ref> During a cabinet meeting on August 26, 2025, Trump repeated his claim that he has "the right to do anything I want to do" as president. This rhetoric and his actions led to [[Donald Trump and fascism|allegations of ruling like a dictator or fascist]] by opponents.<ref name="absolute">{{Cite news|last=Bennett|first=John T.|date=August 27, 2025|title=The US system always had loopholes. Trump 2.0 exploits what others resisted |work=Roll Call|url=https://rollcall.com/2025/08/27/the-u-s-system-always-had-loopholes-trump-2-0-exploits-what-others-resisted/|access-date=May 21, 2026}}</ref> In January 2026, when asked if there were limits to his power as commander in chief, Trump said the only limit was "my own morality" and that he didn't need international law because "I'm not looking to hurt people". When asked if he needed to abide by international law, Trump said "I do", but that it "depends what your definition of international law is".<ref name="NYTimes_20260108">{{cite news |last1=Sanger |first1=David E. |last2=Pager |first2=Tyler |last3=Rogers |first3=Katie |last4=Kanno-Youngs |first4=Zolan |title=Trump Lays Out a Vision of Power Restrained Only by 'My Own Morality' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/08/us/politics/trump-interview-power-morality.html |work=The New York Times |date=January 8, 2026 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Scales and rankings===
====''Crowdpac''====
In 2015, [[Crowdpac]] gave Trump a ranking of 0.4[[Modern liberalism in the United States|L]] out of 10, indicating moderate positions. In 2016, the ranking was changed to 5.1[[Conservatism in the United States|C]] out of 10, shifting him more to the conservative spectrum.<ref name="Scorecards and rankings">{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/2016_presidential_candidate_ratings_and_scorecards |title=2016 presidential candidate ratings and scorecards |publisher=Ballotpedia.org |access-date=July 27, 2016}}</ref>

====''On the Issues''====
The organization and website [[On the Issues]] has classified Trump in a variety of ways over time:
* "Moderate populist" (2003)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |title=Donald Trump On the Issues August 16, 2003 |date=August 16, 2003 |access-date=July 27, 2016 |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030816141728/http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |archive-date=August 16, 2003}}</ref>
* "[[Modern liberalism in the United States|Liberal]]-leaning populist" (2003–2011)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |title=Donald Trump On the Issues December 5, 2003 |date=December 5, 2003 |access-date=July 27, 2016 |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031205131757/http://ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |archive-date=December 5, 2003}}</ref>
* "Moderate populist [[Conservatism in the United States|conservative]]" (2011–2012)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ontheissues.org/donald_trump.htm |title=Donald Trump On the Issues May 7, 2011 |access-date=July 27, 2016 |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110507083640/http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm|archive-date=May 7, 2011}}</ref>

* "Moderate conservative" (2013–2014)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ontheissues.org/donald_trump.htm |title=Donald Trump On the Issues May 27, 2013 |access-date=July 27, 2016 |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131213224859/http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |archive-date=December 13, 2013}}</ref>
* "Libertarian-leaning conservative" (2014–2015)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |title=Donald Trump On the Issues September 24, 2014 |access-date=July 27, 2016 |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141003004540/http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm|archive-date=October 3, 2014}}</ref>
* "Hard-core conservative" (2015)<ref name="web.archive.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |title=Donald Trump On the Issues July 19, 2015 |access-date=July 27, 2016 |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150719083750/http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |archive-date=July 19, 2015}}</ref>

* "Moderate conservative" (2016–2017)<ref>{{cite web|title=Donald Trump On the issues August 1, 2016 |url=http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm|publisher=Ontheissues.org|access-date=August 1, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160801221604/http://www.ontheissues.org/Donald_Trump.htm |archive-date=August 1, 2016 |url-status=deviated}}</ref>

==Politics and policies during presidency==
As president, Trump has pursued sizable income tax cuts, deregulation, increased military spending, rollbacks of federal health-care protections, and the appointment of conservative judges consistent with conservative ([[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]]) policies.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/where-president-trump-stands-on-the-issues-in-2020|title=Where President Trump stands on the issues in 2020|date=2019-06-19|website=[[PBS NewsHour]]|access-date=2019-08-09}}</ref> However, his [[anti-globalization]] policies of trade [[protectionism]] cross party lines.<ref name="Amber Phillips">{{cite news|author=Amber Phillips|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2016/08/08/a-shortlist-of-economic-issues-on-which-donald-trump-sounds-more-like-a-democrat-than-a-republican/|title=A shortlist of economic issues on which Donald Trump sounds more like a Democrat than a Republican|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=August 8, 2016}}</ref> In foreign affairs he has described himself as a [[Nationalism|nationalist]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/23/us/politics/nationalist-president-trump.html|title='Use That Word!': Trump Embraces the 'Nationalist' Label|last=Baker|first=Peter|date=2018-10-23|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2019-08-09|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Trump has said that he is "totally flexible on very, very many issues."<ref name="Jenna Johnson">{{cite news|author=Jenna Johnson|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2016/05/13/trump-all-policy-proposals-are-just-flexible-suggestions/|title=Trump: All policy proposals are just flexible suggestions|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=May 13, 2016}}</ref>

Trump's signature issue is [[Immigration policy of the first Donald Trump administration|immigration]], especially [[Illegal immigration to the United States|illegal immigration]],<ref name="CFR">{{cite web |url=http://www.cfr.org/campaign2016/donald-trump/on-immigration |title=Campaign 2015: The Candidates & the World: Donald Trump on Immigration |publisher=[[Council on Foreign Relations]] |access-date=May 15, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170205113607/http://www.cfr.org/campaign2016/donald-trump/on-immigration |archive-date=February 5, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and in particular building or expanding a [[Mexico–United States border wall|border wall between the U.S. and Mexico]].<ref name="boston.cbslocal.com">Keller, Jon. [http://boston.cbslocal.com/2016/02/02/donald-trump-immigration-mexico-wall-ted-cruz-marco-rubio-hillary-clinton-bernie-sanders-wbz-jon-keller-at-large/ "On The Issues: Building A Wall Along The Mexican Border"], ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' (February 2, 2016): "It has become Donald Trump's signature issue: his vow to wall off the Mexican border..."</ref>

In his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump promised significant infrastructure investment and protection for entitlements for the elderly, typically considered liberal ([[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]]) policies. In October 2016, Trump's campaign posted fourteen categories of policy proposals on his website, which have been since removed.<ref name="DTCampaign1">{{cite web|url=https://www.donaldjtrump.com/policies/|title=Trump Pence Campaign Policies|date=October 16, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161101083734/http://www.donaldjtrump.com/policies/|archive-date=2016-11-01}}</ref> During October 2016, Trump outlined a series of steps for [[First 100 days of the first Donald Trump presidency|his first 100 days in office]].<ref name="DT100days">{{cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/2016/11/10/501597652/fact-check-donald-trumps-first-100-days-action-plan|title=Fact Check: Donald Trump's First 100 Days Action Plan|publisher=[[NPR]]|date=November 10, 2016}}</ref>

Trump's political positions, and his descriptions of his beliefs, have often been inconsistent.{{refn|<ref name="davida.fahrenthold">{{cite web |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2015/08/17/20-times-donald-trump-has-changed-his-mind-since-june/ |title=20 times Donald Trump has changed his mind since June|author=David A. Fahrenthold |date=August 17, 2015|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref><ref name="TimmTracks">{{cite web|author=Jane C. Timm|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2016-election/full-list-donald-trump-s-rapidly-changing-policy-positions-n547801|title='Meet the Press' tracks Trump's flip-flops|publisher=[[NBC News]]|date=March 30, 2016}}</ref><ref name="real Donald">{{cite web |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2015/07/will-the-real-donald-trump-please-stand-up-120607|author=Timothy Noah|title=Will the real Donald Trump please stand up? |newspaper=[[Politico]]|date=July 26, 2015}}</ref><ref>[[Chris Cillizza]], [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2015/07/12/the-massive-flip-floppery-of-donald-trump-explained-in-238-seconds/ The massive flip-floppery of Donald Trump, explained in 113 seconds], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (July 12, 2015).</ref><ref>Michelle Ye Hee, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/fact-checker/wp/2016/08/03/a-guide-to-all-of-donald-trumps-flip-flops-on-the-minimum-wage/ A guide to all of Donald Trump's flip-flops on the minimum wage], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (August 3, 2016).</ref><ref name="JacobsonPinDown">Louis Jacobson, [http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/article/2016/may/11/trying-pin-down-what-donald-trump-thinks-about-abo/ Trying to pin down what Donald Trump thinks about abortion, the minimum wage, taxes, and U.S. debt], ''[[PolitiFact]]'' (May 11, 2016). "But how much of this stems from actual changes in position from one day to the next, and how much stems from his penchant for using confusing, vague and even contradictory language?"</ref>}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2016/05/donald-trump-2016-contradictions-213869/|title=Donald Trump's Greatest Self-Contradictions|last1=Kruse|first1=Michael|last2=Weil|first2=Noah|website=[[Politico]] Magazine|date=May 5, 2016 |access-date=2019-07-15}}</ref> ''[[Politico]]'' has described his positions as "eclectic, improvisational and often contradictory."<ref name="real Donald2">{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2015/07/will-the-real-donald-trump-please-stand-up-120607|title=Will the real Donald Trump please stand up?|date=July 26, 2015|newspaper=[[Politico]]|author=Timothy Noah}}</ref> According to an [[NBC News]] count, over the course of his campaign Trump made "141 distinct shifts on 23 major issues."<ref name="AFullList">{{Cite web|author=Jane C. Timm|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2016-election/full-list-donald-trump-s-rapidly-changing-policy-positions-n547801|title=The 141 Stances Donald Trump Took During His White House Bid (alt. headline: A Full List of Donald Trump's Rapidly Changing Policy Positions)|publisher=[[NBC News]]|date=November 7, 2016}}</ref> [[Fact-checking]] organizations reported that during the campaign, [[False or misleading statements by Donald Trump|Trump made a record number of false statements and lies]] compared to other candidates,{{refn|<ref name = "whoppers">{{cite web |url=http://www.factcheck.org/2015/12/the-king-of-whoppers-donald-trump/ |title=The 'King of Whoppers': Donald Trump |publisher=[[FactCheck.org]] |date=December 21, 2015}}</ref><ref name = "year">{{cite news |url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/article/2015/dec/21/2015-lie-year-donald-trump-campaign-misstatements/ |title=2015 Lie of the Year: the campaign misstatements of Donald Trump |work=[[PolitiFact]] |date=December 21, 2015 |first1=Angie Drobnic |last1=Holan |first2=Linda |last2=Qiu}}</ref><ref name="wapo-false">{{cite news |first=Paul |last=Farhi |title=Think Trump's wrong? Fact checkers can tell you how often. (Hint: A lot.) |date=February 26, 2016 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/the-existential-crisis-of-professional-factcheckers-in-the-year-of-trump/2016/02/25/e994f210-db3e-11e5-81ae-7491b9b9e7df_story.html}}</ref>}} a pattern that has continued{{Snd}}and further increased{{Snd}}in office.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2018/09/13/president-trump-has-made-more-than-false-or-misleading-claims/|title=President Trump has made more than 5,000 false or misleading claims|last1=Kelly|first1=Meg|last2=Rizzo|first2=Salvador|date=September 13, 2018|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=February 19, 2019|last3=Kessler|first3=Glenn}}</ref><ref>[Trump's Lies vs. Obama's {{cite news| url = https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2017/12/14/opinion/sunday/trump-lies-obama-who-is-worse.html| title = Opinion {{!}} Trump's Lies vs. Obama's - The New York Times| newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| date = December 14, 2017| last1 = Leonhardt| first1 = David| last2 = Philbrick| first2 = Ian Prasad| last3 = Thompson| first3 = Stuart A.}} NYT-Trump's Lies Vs. Obama's-December 14, 2017]</ref>

==Domestic policy==
{{Main|Domestic policy of the first Trump administration|Domestic policy of the second Trump administration}}

[[File:Donald_Trump_Signs_The_Pledge_25.jpg|thumb|Trump signs the Republican loyalty pledge: had Trump not [[2016 Republican National Convention|become the Republican Party nominee]] for the [[United States presidential election, 2016 timeline#July 2|2016 general election]], he pledged to support whoever the nominee may have been, and to not run as a [[Third party (United States)|third-party candidate]].]]

[[File:Trump_with_supporters_in_Iowa,_January_2016_(2).jpg|thumb|Trump and supporters at a rally in [[Muscatine, Iowa]], January 2016. Multiple supporters hold up signs stating "The [[silent majority]] stands with Trump."]]

===Campaign finance===
{{See also|Campaign finance reform in the United States}}
While Trump has repeatedly expressed support for "the idea of [[Campaign finance reform in the United States|campaign finance reform]]",<ref name="Pildes" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/politics/articles/2015-08-14/trump-i-love-the-idea-of-campaign-finance-reform-|title=Trump: 'I Love the Idea of Campaign Finance Reform'|date=August 14, 2016|publisher=[[Bloomberg Politics]]}}</ref> he has not outlined specifics of his actual views on campaign-finance regulation.<ref name="Pildes" /><ref>Peter Overby, [https://www.npr.org/2016/02/14/466668949/presidential-candidates-pledge-to-undo-citizens-united-but-can-they Presidential Candidates Pledge To Undo 'Citizens United.' But Can They?], ''Morning Edition'' NPR (February 14, 2016) ("Trump says he supports campaign finance reform, though a specific plan is not available on his website.").</ref><ref>Charles Borden, Claire Rajan & Daniel Holman, [http://www.corpcounsel.com/id=1202752884135/The-Presidential-Candidates-on-Campaign-Finance-Reform?slreturn=20160518165911 The Presidential Candidates on Campaign Finance Reform], ''Corporate Counsel'' (March 23, 2016) ("While saying he is open to reform, however, Trump has refrained from detailing specific policies and focused instead on accusing fellow candidates of being bought while arguing that his personal wealth guarantees his political independence.").</ref> For example, Trump has not said whether he favors [[Publicly funded elections|public financing of elections]] or caps on expenditures of campaigns, outside groups, and individuals.<ref name="Pildes" />

During the Republican primary race, Trump on several occasions accused his Republican opponents of being bound to their campaign financiers, and asserted that anyone (including Trump himself) could buy their policies with donations.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/2016/01/17/politics/donald-trump-public-financing/index.html|title=Trump on public financing: 'I don't know yet'|author=Eugene Scott|publisher=[[CNN]]|access-date=June 15, 2016}}</ref> He called [[super PAC]]s a "scam" and "a horrible thing".<ref name="Pildes">[[Richard Pildes]], [https://electionlawblog.org/?p=81159 What are Donald Trump's Views on Campaign Finance Regulation?], ''Election Law Blog'' (ed. [[Richard L. Hasen]]) (March 23, 2016).</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://thehill.com/blogs/ballot-box/presidential-races/266189-trump-open-to-campaign-finance-reform/|title=Trump open to campaign finance reform|last=Richardson|first=Bradford|date=January 17, 2016|newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref> In October 2015, he said, "All Presidential candidates should immediately disavow their Super PACs. They're not only breaking the spirit of the law but the law itself."<ref name="ed">{{Cite magazine|url=https://time.com/4373124/donald-trump-donors-super-pacs/|title=Trump Embraces Donors, Super PACs He Once Decried|last=Levinthal|first=Dave|magazine=Time|access-date=July 29, 2016}}</ref>

Having previously touted the self-funding of his campaign as a sign of his independence from the political establishment and big donors, Trump reversed course and started to fundraise in early May 2016.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/self-financing-campaign-all-the-way-would-have-been-a-stretch-for-trump-1463341722|title=Donald Trump Wouldn't Have Had the Ready Cash to Self-Finance Entire Campaign – Analysis|last1=Grant|first1=Peter|date=May 16, 2016|last2=Mullins|first2=Brody|newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|issn=0099-9660|access-date=June 15, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/donald-trump-wont-self-fund-general-election-campaign-1462399502|title=Donald Trump Won't Self-Fund General-Election Campaign|last1=Langley|first1=Monica|date=May 5, 2016|last2=Ballhaus|first2=Rebecca|newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|issn=0099-9660|access-date=June 15, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/2016/05/18/politics/trump-big-donors/index.html|title=How Donald Trump won over big donors|author1=Sara Murray|author2=Theodore Schleifer|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=May 18, 2016}}</ref> While Trump systematically disavowed pro-Trump super PACs earlier in the race, he stopped doing so from early May 2016.<ref name="ed"/>

===Civil servants===
According to [[Chris Christie]] (who served briefly as leader of Trump's [[United States presidential transition|White House transition]] team), Trump will seek to [[purge]] the federal government of officials appointed by Obama and will ask Congress to pass legislation making it easier to fire public workers.<ref>{{Cite news|author=Emily Flitter|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-election-trump-purge-exclusive-idUSKCN10003A|title=Exclusive: Trump could seek new law to purge government of Obama appointees|date=July 20, 2016|work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref>

Trump's former Chief Strategist, [[Steve Bannon]], stated in February 2017 that Trump's goal is to "deconstruct the administrative state".<ref>Philip Rucker and Robert Costa, ''[[The Washington Post]]'' [https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/top-wh-strategist-vows-a-daily-fight-for-deconstruction-of-the-administrative-state/2017/02/23/03f6b8da-f9ea-11e6-bf01-d47f8cf9b643_story.html Bannon Vows a Daily Fight For "Deconstruction of the Administrative State"] February 23, 2017</ref>

===Disabled people===
Trump has provided "little detail regarding his positions on disability-related policies," and his campaign website made no mention of [[disability|disabled people]].<ref name="Carmon">Irin Carmon, [https://www.msnbc.com/msnbc/disability-rights-have-long-been-bipartisan-will-trump-end Disability rights have long been bipartisan. Will Trump end that?], MSNBC (June 1, 2016).</ref><ref>[https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/candidates-offer-americans-disabilities-growing-voting-bloc What the candidates offer to Americans with disabilities, a growing voting bloc], ''[[PBS NewsHour]]'', PBS (November 2, 2016): "[[Judy Woodruff]]: Trump doesn't address disability issues in detail on his Web site."</ref><ref>Jacqueline Alemany, [https://www.cbsnews.com/news/the-election-that-forgot-americas-disabled/ The election that forgot America's disabled], CBS News (November 4, 2016): "Trump has not mentioned a plan for research or improved care for the disabled, and there is nothing on his website on this issue."</ref> As of June 1, 2016, Trump had not responded to the issue questionnaire of the nonpartisan disability group [[RespectAbility]].<ref name="Carmon"/>

===District of Columbia statehood===
{{Main|Statehood movement in the District of Columbia}}

Trump is opposed to [[District of Columbia statehood movement|D.C. statehood]]. In 2020, Donald Trump indicated that if the statehood legislation for Washington, D.C. passes both houses of Congress, he would veto the admission legislation.<ref>{{cite news| url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/dc-politics/white-house-opposes-dc-statehood/2020/06/24/d74a2b24-b597-11ea-aca5-ebb63d27e1ff_story.html| title = Before historic D.C. statehood vote, Trump White House states opposition| newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref>

===Education===
{{Main|Education in the United States}}

====2016 campaign====
Trump has stated his support for [[school choice]] and local control for primary and secondary schools. On school choice he's commented, "Our public schools are capable of providing a more competitive product than they do today. Look at some of the high school tests from earlier in this century and you'll wonder if they weren't college-level tests. And we've got to bring on the competition—open the schoolhouse doors and let parents choose the best school for their children. Education reformers call this school choice, charter schools, vouchers, even opportunity scholarships. I call it competition—the American way."<ref>{{cite web|title=Donald Trump on School Choice |url=http://www.americanprinciplesinaction.org/apia-education/education/school-choice/donald-trump-on-school-choice/ |website=American Principles in Action |access-date=November 25, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151125105242/http://www.americanprinciplesinaction.org/apia-education/education/school-choice/donald-trump-on-school-choice/ |archive-date=November 25, 2015 }}</ref>

Trump has blasted the [[Common Core State Standards Initiative]], calling it a "total disaster".<ref name="GillinCCSSI">Joshua Gillin, [http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2016/mar/10/donald-trump/common-core-education-through-washington-dc-trump-/ Common Core is 'education through Washington, D.C.,' Trump says], ''[[PolitiFact]]'' (March 10, 2016).</ref><ref name="StraussCCSSI">Valerie Strauss, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/answer-sheet/wp/2016/03/04/donald-trump-is-wrong-about-common-core-but-hes-not-the-only-candidate-who-is/ Donald Trump is wrong about Common Core — but he's not the only candidate who is], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (March 4, 2016).</ref> Trump has asserted that Common Core is "education through Washington, D.C.", a claim which [[PolitiFact]] and other journalists have rated "false", since the adoption and implementation of Common Core is a state choice, not a federal one.<ref name="GillinCCSSI"/><ref name="StraussCCSSI"/>

Trump has stated that [[Ben Carson]] will be "very much involved in education" under a Trump presidency.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://theweek.com/speedreads/612056/donald-trump-promised-education-secretary-ben-carson|title=Has Donald Trump promised education secretary to Ben Carson?|website=[[The Week]] |date=March 11, 2016|access-date=July 15, 2016}}</ref> Carson rejects the [[theory of evolution]] and believes that "[[Homeschooling in the United States|home-schoolers]] do the best, [[private school]]ers next best, [[Charter schools in the United States|charter schoolers]] next best, and [[Public school (United States)|public schoolers]] worst"; he said that he wanted to "take the federal bureaucracy out of education."<ref>{{cite news|author=Valerie Strauss|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/answer-sheet/wp/2016/03/11/donald-trump-thinks-ben-carson-is-an-education-expert-oy-vey/|title=Donald Trump thinks Ben Carson is an education expert. Oy vey|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=March 11, 2016}}</ref>

Trump has proposed redirecting $20 billion in existing federal spending to [[block grant]]s to states to give poor children vouchers to attend a school of their family's choice (including a charter school, private school, or [[online school]]).<ref name="ParkerVoucher">{{cite web|author=Ashley Parker|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/09/us/politics/donald-trump-education.html|title=Donald Trump Releases Education Proposal, Promoting School Choice|website=[[The New York Times]]|date=September 8, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Abby Jackson|url=http://www.businessinsider.com/donald-trump-pledges-20-billion-to-school-choice-education-agenda-2016-9|title=Donald Trump just provided the first detailed education proposal of his campaign|website=[[Business Insider]]|date=September 8, 2016}}</ref> Trump did not explain where the $20 billion in the federal budget would come from.<ref name="ParkerVoucher"/> Trump stated that "Distribution of this grant will favor states that have private school choice and charter laws."<ref name="ParkerVoucher"/>

====Presidency====
As president, Trump chose Republican financier [[Betsy DeVos]], a prominent Michigan [[charter school]] advocate, as Secretary of Education.<ref name="HuettemanAlcindor">Emmarie Huetteman & Yamiche Alcindor, [https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/07/us/politics/betsy-devos-education-secretary-confirmed.html Betsy DeVos Confirmed as Education Secretary; Pence Breaks Tie], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (February 7, 2017).</ref> The nomination was highly controversial;<ref>Greg Toppo, [https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2017/01/30/trump-education-nominee-opposition/97260878/ Trump education nominee opposed by special ed advocates], ''[[USA Today]]'' (January 31, 2017).</ref> ''[[The Washington Post]]'' education writer Valerie Strauss wrote that "DeVos was considered the most controversial education nominee in the history of the nearly 40-year-old Education Department."<ref>Valerie Strauss, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/answer-sheet/wp/2017/01/31/why-betsy-devos-is-the-most-polarizing-education-secretary-nominee-ever/ Why Betsy DeVos is the most polarizing education secretary nominee ever], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (January 31, 2017).</ref> On the confirmation vote the Senate split 50/50 (along party lines, with two Republican senators joining all Democratic senators to vote against confirmation). Vice President [[Mike Pence]] used his [[List of tie-breaking votes cast by vice presidents of the United States|tie-breaking vote]] to confirm the nomination, the first time in U.S. history that occurred.<ref name="HuettemanAlcindor"/>

==== 2024 campaign ====
During his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump expressed opposition to the use of [[academic tenure]] and [[diversity, equity, and inclusion]] programs in U.S. educational institutions.<ref name="vr"/>

===Eminent domain===
{{See also|Eminent domain in the United States}}
In 2015 Trump called [[eminent domain]] "wonderful". He repeatedly asked the government to invoke it on his behalf during past development projects.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.realclearpolitics.com/video/2015/10/06/trump_eminent_domain_wonderful.html |title=Trump: Eminent Domain "Wonderful" |work=[[RealClearPolitics]] |date=October 6, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/volokh-conspiracy/wp/2015/08/19/donald-trumps-abuse-of-eminent-domain/ |title=Donald Trump's history of eminent domain abuse |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=August 19, 2015}}</ref>

===Food safety===
{{Main|Food safety in the United States}}

In September 2016, Trump posted a list on his website of regulations that he would eliminate. The list included what it called the "FDA Food Police" and mentioned the [[Food and Drug Administration]]'s rules governing "farm and food production hygiene" and "food temperatures".<ref name="we">{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/regulation/healthcare/296152-trump-says-he-would-eliminate-food-safety-regulations/|title=Trump floats rolling back food safety regulations|last=Wheeler|first=Lydia|work=The Hill |date=September 15, 2016|access-date=September 16, 2016}}</ref> The factsheet provided by Trump mirrored a May report by the conservative [[The Heritage Foundation|Heritage Foundation]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/aponline/2016/09/15/us/politics/ap-us-campaign-2016-trump-food-rules.html|title=Trump Campaign Pushes Food Safety Rollbacks, Then Deletes|agency=[[Associated Press]]|date=September 15, 2016|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|issn=0362-4331|access-date=September 16, 2016|archive-date=September 16, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160916042004/http://www.nytimes.com/aponline/2016/09/15/us/politics/ap-us-campaign-2016-trump-food-rules.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> It was replaced later that month and the new factsheet did not mention the FDA.<ref name="we"/>

===Native Americans===
{{Further|Native Americans in the United States}}
[[Colman McCarthy]] of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' wrote in 1993 that in testimony given that year to the [[United States House Natural Resources Subcommittee on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs|House Natural Resources subcommittee on Native American Affairs]], Trump "devoted much of his testimony to bad-mouthing Indians and their casinos," asserted that "organized crime is rampant on [[Indian reservation]]s" and that "if it continues it will be the biggest scandal ever." Trump offered no evidence in support of his claim, and testimony from the FBI's organized crime division, the [[United States Department of Justice Criminal Division|Justice Department's criminal division]], and the [[IRS Criminal Investigation Division|IRS's criminal investigation division]] did not support Trump's assertion.<ref name="McCarthy">[[Colman McCarthy]], [https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1993/10/26/trumped-up-assault-on-indian-gambling/beece94f-3c59-481d-9174-84808b288fa1/ Trumped Up Assault on Indian Gambling], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (October 26, 1993).</ref> Representative [[George Miller (California politician)|George Miller]], a Democrat who was the chairman of the [[United States House Committee on Natural Resources|Natural Resources Committee]] at the time, stated: "In my 19 years in Congress, I've never heard more irresponsible testimony."<ref name="McCarthy"/>

Trump bankrolled in 2000 a set of anti-[[Native American gaming|Indian gaming]] ads in [[upstate New York]] that featured "a dark photograph showing hypodermic needles and drug paraphernalia," a warning that "violent criminals were coming to town," and an accusation that the [[St. Regis Mohawk Reservation|St. Regis Mohawks]] had a "record of criminal activity."<ref name="BurnsInstinct">Alexander Burns, [https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/01/nyregion/trumps-instinct-for-racially-charged-rhetoric-before-his-presidential-bid.html Donald Trump's Instinct for Racially Charged Rhetoric, Before His Presidential Bid], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (July 31, 2015).</ref> The ad—aimed at stopping the construction of a casino in the [[Catskills]] that might hurt Trump's own Atlantic City casinos<ref name="MahoneyCasino">Joe Mahoney, [http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/news/trump-fined-attack-indian-casino-article-1.888723 Trump is Fines in Attack on Indian Casino], ''[[New York Daily News]]'' (November 14, 2000).</ref>—was viewed as "incendiary" and racially charged, and at the time local tribal leaders, in response, bought a newspaper ad of their own to denounce the "smear" and "racist and inflammatory rhetoric" of the earlier ad.<ref name="BurnsInstinct"/> The ads attracted the attention of the New York Temporary State Commission on Lobbying because they failed to disclose Trump's sponsorship as required by state [[lobbying]] rules.<ref name="BurnsInstinct"/><ref name="MahoneyCasino"/><ref name="BagliCasinos">Charles V. Bagli, [https://www.nytimes.com/2000/10/06/nyregion/trump-and-others-accept-fines-for-ads-in-opposition-to-casinos.html Trump and Others Accept Fines For Ads in Opposition to Casinos], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (October 6, 2000).</ref> Trump acknowledged that he sponsored the ads and reached a settlement with the state in which he and his associates agreed to issue a public apology and pay $250,000 (the largest civil penalty ever levied by the commission) for evading state disclosure rules.<ref name="BurnsInstinct"/><ref name="MahoneyCasino"/><ref name="BagliCasinos"/>

In 2015, Trump defended the [[Washington Redskins name controversy|controversial team name and mascot]] of the [[Washington Redskins]], saying that the [[National Football League|NFL]] team should not change its name and he did not find [[Redskin|the term]] to be offensive.<ref>Scott Allen, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/dc-sports-bog/wp/2015/10/05/donald-trump-doesnt-think-the-redskins-should-change-their-name/ Donald Trump doesn't think the Redskins should change their name], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (October 5, 2015).</ref><ref>John Keim, [https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/13814698/donald-trump-says-nfl-washington-redskins-change-name Donald Trump: Redskins a 'positive' name, Washington shouldn't change], ESPN (October 5, 2015).</ref> The "Change the Mascot" campaign, led by the [[Oneida Indian Nation]] and [[National Congress of American Indians]], condemned Trump's stance.<ref>Mark Weiner, [http://www.syracuse.com/politics/index.ssf/2015/10/oneida_indian_nation_blasts_donald_trump_for_defending_washington_redskins.html Oneida Indian Nation blasts Donald Trump for defending Washington Redskins], [[Syracuse.com]] (October 5, 2015).</ref>

===Questioning Obama's citizenship===
{{Main|Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories}}

[[File:Donald Trump by Gage Skidmore 12.jpg|thumb|Trump speaking at a rally in Phoenix, Arizona, August 2016]]
For several years, Trump promoted false [[Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories|"birther" conspiracy theories]] about Barack Obama's citizenship.<ref name="Gass_1/12/2012">{{cite web | last=Gass | first=Nick | title=Trump: I'm still a birther | website=[[Politico]] | date=January 12, 2012 | url=https://www.politico.com/story/2015/07/donald-trump-birther-obama-119945.html | access-date=October 27, 2018}}</ref><ref name="Keneally_9/18/2015">{{cite web | last=Keneally | first=Meghan | title=Trump's History of Raising Birther Questions About Obama | website=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] | date=September 18, 2015 | url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/donald-trumps-history-raising-birther-questions-president-obama/story?id=33861832 | access-date=October 27, 2018}}</ref><ref name="Epps_2/26/2016">{{cite web | last=Epps | first=Garrett | title=Trump's Birther Libel | website=[[The Atlantic]] | date=February 26, 2016 | url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2016/02/trump-birther-rubio-cruz/471015/ | access-date=October 27, 2018}}</ref>

In March 2011, during an interview on ''[[Good Morning America]]'', Trump said he was seriously considering running for president, that he was a "little" skeptical of Obama's citizenship and that someone who shares this view should not be so quickly dismissed as an "idiot". Trump added: "Growing up no one knew him"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2011/03/donald-trump-birther-051473|title=Donald Trump, birther?|magazine=[[Politico]]|date=March 17, 2011 |access-date=May 16, 2016}}</ref>—a claim ranked "Pants on Fire" by [[PolitiFact]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2011/feb/14/donald-trump/donald-trump-says-people-who-went-school-obama-nev/|title=Donald Trump says people who went to school with Obama never saw him|website=[[PolitiFact]]|date=February 14, 2011}}</ref> Later, Trump appeared on ''[[The View (U.S. TV series)|The View]]'' repeating several times that "I want him (Obama) to show his birth certificate" and speculating that "there's something on that birth certificate that he doesn't like."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blogs.wsj.com/speakeasy/2011/03/24/donald-trump-discusses-president-obama-on-the-view/|title=Donald Trump, Whoopi Goldberg, Spar Over Obama on 'The View'|newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|date=March 24, 2011}}</ref> Although officials in [[Hawaii]] certified Obama's citizenship, Trump said in April 2011 he would not let go of the issue, because he was not satisfied that Obama had proven his citizenship.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www2.readingeagle.com/article.aspx?id=299949|title=Trump hammers away at Obama's citizenship question|date=April 7, 2011|agency=[[Associated Press]]|access-date=May 18, 2016|archive-date=January 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220119173254/http://www2.readingeagle.com/article.aspx?id=299949 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

After Obama released his long-form birth certificate on April 27, 2011, Trump said: "I am really honored and I am really proud, that I was able to do something that nobody else could do."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://swampland.time.com/2011/04/27/birtherism-is-dead-but-the-birther-industry-continues/|title=Birtherism Is Dead, But the Birther Industry Continues|last=Scherer|first=Michael|magazine=Time|issn=0040-781X|date=April 27, 2011}}</ref> Trump continued to falsely question Obama's birth certificate in the following years, as late as 2015.<ref name="wa">{{Cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/2016/09/16/494231757/without-apology-trump-now-says-obama-was-born-in-the-u-s|title=Without Apology, Trump Now Says: 'Obama Was Born In' The U.S.|publisher=[[NPR]]|date=September 16, 2016|access-date=September 16, 2016|last1=Montanaro|first1=Domenico}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/video/long-strange-trip-trump-s-birther-claims-through-the-years-766964803832|title=Long, Strange Trip: Trump's Birther Claims Through the Years |publisher=[[NBC News]]|access-date=September 18, 2016}}</ref> In May 2012, Trump suggested that Obama might have been born in Kenya.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/blogs/burns-haberman/2012/05/trump-obama-born-in-kenya-124569|title=Trump: Obama born in Kenya|website=[[Politico]]|date=May 25, 2012 |access-date=May 16, 2016}}</ref> In October 2012, Trump offered to donate five million dollars to the charity of Obama's choice in return for the publication of his college and passport applications before the end of the month.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/OTUS/donald-trump-fails-drop-bombshell-offers-cash-obama/story?id=17553670|title=Donald Trump's Obama 'Bombshell' Falls Short|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|date=October 24, 2012}}</ref> In a 2014 interview, Trump questioned whether Obama had produced his long-form birth certificate.<ref name="wa"/> When asked in December 2015 if he still questioned Obama's legitimacy, Trump said that "I don't talk about that anymore."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.realclearpolitics.com/video/2015/12/16/trump_post-debate_interview_with_chris_matthews_goes_off_the_rails.html|title=Trump Post-Debate Interview With Chris Matthews Goes Off The Rails: Won't Put "Birth Certificate" Talk To Bed|website=RealClearPolitics.com|date=December 16, 2015}}</ref>

On September 14, 2016, Trump declined to acknowledge whether he believed Obama was born in the United States.<ref name="no">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/17/us/politics/donald-trump-birther-obama.html|title=Trump Drops False 'Birther' Theory, but Floats a New One: Clinton Started It|last1=Haberman|first1=Maggie|date=September 16, 2016|last2=Rappeport|first2=Alan|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|issn=0362-4331|access-date=September 16, 2016}}</ref> On September 15, 2016, Trump for the first time acknowledged that Obama was born in the United States.<ref name="no"/> He gave a terse statement, saying, "President Barack Obama was born in the United States, period."<ref name="no"/> He falsely accused Hillary Clinton of having started the "Birther" movement.<ref name="no"/><ref name="ww">{{Cite web|url=http://www.factcheck.org/2016/09/trump-on-birtherism-wrong-and-wrong/|title=Trump on Birtherism: Wrong, and Wrong|website=factcheck.org|date=September 16, 2016|access-date=September 16, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-election-idUSKCN11M1F3|title=Trump finally backs off Obama birth claim, falsely accuses Clinton of starting it|date=September 16, 2016|work=[[Reuters]]|access-date=September 16, 2016}}</ref> He also asserted that he "finished" the birther controversy, apparently referring to Obama's 2011 release of his long-form birth certificate, despite the fact that he continued to question Obama's citizenship in the years that followed.<ref name="wa"/><ref name="ww"/><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-37382612|title=US election: Donald Trump keeping fact-checkers busy|date=September 16, 2016|newspaper=[[BBC News]]|access-date=September 16, 2016}}</ref> The next day, Trump tweeted a story in ''[[The Washington Post]]'' with the headline "Donald Trump's birther event is the greatest trick he's ever pulled".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.motherjones.com/kevin-drum/2016/09/ap-jumps-lie-bandwagon|title=AP jumps on the "lie" bandwagon|access-date=September 17, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://twitter.com/SopanDeb/status/777023971959058432?lang=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308121711/https://twitter.com/SopanDeb/status/777023971959058432?lang=en|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 8, 2021|title=Sopan Deb on Twitter|access-date=September 17, 2016}}</ref> The "greatest trick" of the headline referred to the fact that cable networks aired the event live, waiting for a "birther" statement, while Trump touted his new hotel and supporters gave testimonials.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2016/09/16/donald-trumps-birther-event-is-the-greatest-trick-hes-ever-pulled/|title=Donald Trump's birther event is the greatest trick he's ever pulled|last=Cillizza|first=Chris|date=September 16, 2016|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=September 19, 2016}}</ref> In October 2016, Trump appeared to falsely question the legitimacy of Barack Obama's presidency, referring to him at a rally as the "quote 'president'⁠ ⁠".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2016/10/donald-trump-obama-legitimacy-229842|title=Trump air-quotes Obama's presidency|newspaper=[[Politico]]|access-date=October 15, 2016}}</ref>

===Social Security and Medicare===
{{Main|Social Security (United States)|Medicare (United States)|Medicaid}}

====2016 presidential campaign====
During his campaign Trump repeatedly promised "I'm not going to cut [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]] like every other Republican and I'm not going to cut [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]] or [[Medicaid]]."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/promises/trumpometer/subjects/medicare/|title=Promises about Medicare on Trump-O-Meter|work=[[PolitiFact]]|access-date=11 August 2020}}</ref>

====Presidency====
For the first three years of his presidency he said nothing about cutting Social Security or Medicare. In a January 2020 interview he said he planned to "take a look" at entitlement programs like Medicare,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://slate.com/business/2020/01/trump-entitlements-social-security-medicare-davos.html|title=Donald Trump Says He's Willing to "Look" at Entitlements "Toward The End of This Year"|last=Weissman|first=Jordan|date=January 22, 2020|work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|access-date=11 August 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/22/us/politics/medicare-trump.html |title=Trump Opens Door to Cuts to Medicare and Other Entitlement Programs |first1=Alan |last1=Rappeport |author-link1=Alan Rappeport |first2=Maggie |last2=Haberman |author-link2=Maggie Haberman |date=January 22, 2020 |access-date=January 24, 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=limited}}</ref> but he then said
