== Health care ==
In 1999, during his [[Donald Trump presidential campaign, 2000|abortive 2000 Reform Party presidential campaign]], Trump told TV interviewer [[Larry King]], "I believe in [[universal health care]]."<ref name="PastHealthCare" /> In his 2000 book, ''The America We Deserve'', Trump reiterated his call for universal health care and focused on a Canadian-style [[single-payer health care]] system as a means to achieve it.<ref name="PastHealthCare" />

===2016 campaign===
[[File:U.S. Mortality - Premature Death Rates by County.png|thumb|right|450px|The map illustrates the frequency of premature deaths (those under age 75) adjusted for the age of persons in the county.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fredblog.stlouisfed.org/2017/11/theres-death-and-then-theres-death/|title=There’s death and then there’s death &#124; FRED Blog}}</ref> Nobel laureate economist [[Angus Deaton]] stated in January 2017 that: "If you take county by county in the US, and you look at what we call deaths of despair{{Snd}}suicides, opioids and liver disease{{Snd}}that it correlates by .4 with votes for Trump. That's a big correlation...a very strong relationship."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/angus-deaton-white-deaths-trump-2017-1|title=There is a correlation between 'deaths of despair' among white people and voters for Trump|first=Jim|last=Edwards|website=[[Business Insider]]}}</ref>]]
According to a report by the [[RAND Corporation]], Trump's proposed health-care policy proposals, depending on specific elements implemented, would result in between 15 and 25 million fewer people with health insurance and increase the federal deficit in a range from zero to $41 billion (~${{Format price|{{Inflation|index=US-GDP|value=41000000000|start_year=2018}}}} in {{Inflation/year|US-GDP}}) in 2018. This was in contrast to Clinton's proposals, which would expand health insurance coverage for between zero and 10 million people while increasing the deficit in a range from zero to $90 billion (~${{Format price|{{Inflation|index=US-GDP|value=90000000000|start_year=2018}}}} in {{Inflation/year|US-GDP}}) in 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/politics/articles/2016-09-23/the-numbers-behind-trump-versus-clinton-health-reform-proposals|title=The Numbers Behind Trump Versus Clinton Health-Reform Proposals|date=September 23, 2016|publisher=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]] Politics}}</ref><ref name="hp">{{Cite web|url=http://www.rand.org/blog/2016/09/estimating-the-impacts-of-the-trump-and-clinton-health.html|title=Estimating the Impacts of the Trump and Clinton Health Plans|last=Christine|first=Eibner|publisher=[[RAND Corporation]]|date=September 23, 2016}}</ref> According to the report, low-income individuals and sicker people would be most adversely affected by his proposed policies, although it was pointed out that not all policy proposals have been modeled.<ref name="hp"/>

=== Actions while in office (2017–2021) ===
{{See also|Economic policy of the first Trump administration#Health care}}
[[File:CBO AHCA Health Insurance Coverage Impact.png|thumb|450px|CBO estimated in May 2017 that under the Republican [[American Healthcare Act]] or AHCA, about 23 million fewer people would have health insurance in 2026, compared with current law.<ref name="CBO_Score1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/52752|title=H.R. 1628, American Health Care Act of 2017 &#124; Congressional Budget Office|date=May 24, 2017|website=cbo.gov}}</ref>]]

====Legislation====
{{Further|American Health Care Act|2017 Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act replacement proposals}}
President Trump advocated repealing and replacing the [[Affordable Care Act]] (ACA or "Obamacare"). Trump celebrated the Republican-controlled House passing the [[American Health Care Act]] (AHCA) in May 2017. The Senate decided to write its own version of the bill rather than voting on the AHCA.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/senate-plan-for-healthcare-bill-ahca-2017-5|title=Senate Republicans signal they plan to scrap bill the House just passed and write their own|first=Bob|last=Bryan|website=[[Business Insider]]}}</ref> One Senate bill, called the "Better Care Reconciliation Act of 2017" (BCRA), failed on a vote of 45–55 in the Senate during July 2017. [[Health Care Freedom Act|One variation]] fell one vote short amid opposition from all Democrats as well as John McCain, [[Lisa Murkowski]] and Susan Collins.<ref name="mh">{{Citation |last=Klein |first=Ezra | author-link = Ezra Klein |title=The GOP's massive health care failures, explained |publisher=[[Vox (website)|Vox]] |date=July 28, 2017 |url=https://www.vox.com/health-care/2017/7/28/16055284/gop-massive-health-care-failures-explained | access-date = 2017-08-03}}</ref> In all, the Senate rejected five bills to repeal and/or replace Obamacare.<ref name="mh"/> The [[Congressional Budget Office]] estimated that the bills would increase the number of uninsured by over 20 million persons, while reducing the budget deficit marginally.<ref name="CBO_Score1"/>

====Actions to hinder the implementation of ACA====
{{See also|Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act}}
President Trump continued Republican attacks on the ACA while in office,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/27/opinion/health-care-obamacare.html|title=Opinion &#124; Killing Obamacare Softly|first=Thomas B.|last=Edsall|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=July 27, 2017}}</ref> including steps such as:
* Weakening the individual mandate through his first executive order, which resulted in limiting enforcement of mandate penalties by the IRS. For example, tax returns without indications of health insurance ("silent returns") will still be processed, overriding instructions from the Obama administration to the IRS to reject them.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2017/05/03/trump-obamacare-mandate-enforcement-237937|title=Trump still enforcing Obamacare mandate|first1=Brianna|last1=Ehley|first2=Aaron|last2=Lorenzo|website=[[Politico]]|date=May 3, 2017 }}</ref>
* Reducing funding for advertising for the 2017 and 2018 exchange enrollment periods by up to 90%, with other reductions to support resources used to answer questions and help people sign-up for coverage. Some attributed the reduction in ACA enrollment in 2018 to these cuts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/2017/8/31/16236280/trump-obamacare-outreach-ads|title=Trump is slashing Obamacare's advertising budget by 90%|first=Sarah|last=Kliff|date=August 31, 2017|website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-09-16 |title=Donald Trump misrepresents his push to repeal the Affordable Care Act |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/donald-trump-misrepresents-repeal-affordable-care-act-obamacare-rcna171293 |access-date=2024-10-10 |publisher=NBC News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Galewitz |first=Phil |date=November 28, 2018 |title=Obamacare Sign-Ups Lag As Trump Slashes Funds For Enrollment Help |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2018/11/28/671045006/obamacare-sign-ups-lag-as-trump-slashes-funds-for-enrollment-help |publisher=NPR}}</ref>
* Cutting the enrollment period for 2018 by half, to 45 days. The NYT editorial board referred to this as part of a concerted "sabotage" effort.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/04/opinion/obamacare-vs-the-saboteurs.html|title=Opinion &#124; Obamacare vs. the Saboteurs|author=The Editorial Board|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=November 4, 2017}}</ref>
* Issuing public statements that the exchanges are unstable or in a [[death spiral (insurance)|death spiral]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.healthinsurance.org/blog/12-ways-the-gop-sabotaged-obamacare/|title=12 ways the GOP sabotaged Obamacare|date=July 26, 2019}}</ref> CBO reported in May 2017 that the exchanges would remain stable under current law (ACA), but would be less stable if the AHCA were passed.<ref name="CBO_Score1"/>
* Advocating in 2020 for a lawsuit that would have wiped out the ACA entirely (the Supreme Court upheld the law in 2021)<ref name="ac"/>

Several insurers and actuary groups cited uncertainty created by President Trump, specifically non-enforcement of the individual mandate and not funding cost sharing reduction subsidies, as contributing 20-30 percentage points to premium increases for the 2018 plan year on the ACA exchanges. In other words, absent Trump's actions against the ACA, premium increases would have averaged 10% or less, rather than the estimated 28-40% under the uncertainty his actions created.<ref name="VoxDS1">{{Cite web |last=Scott |first=Dylan |date=2017-10-18 |title=Obamacare premiums were stabilizing. Then Trump happened. |url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2017/10/18/16458316/obamacare-premiums-trump |access-date=2024-10-10 |website=Vox |language=en-US}}</ref>

CNN in 2020 described Trump's administration as opting to undermine the Affordable Care Act from within after failing to overturn the law in Congress.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Luhby |first=Tami |date=2020-10-17 |title=Trump keeps chipping away at Obamacare with only weeks until the election – and a Supreme Court hearing {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/17/politics/affordable-care-act-georgia-medicaid/index.html |access-date=2024-10-10 |publisher=CNN |language=en}}</ref> The outlet described in particular approving requests by Georgia that consumer advocates say weakened the law and would reduce coverage and raise premiums.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Luhby |first=Tami |date=2020-11-02 |title=Trump takes last swipe at Affordable Care Act before Election Day {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/11/02/politics/affordable-care-act-georgia-obamacare/index.html |access-date=2024-10-10 |publisher=CNN |language=en}}</ref> His administration had also repeatedly attempted to water down or repeal the ACA's protections for people with preexisting medical conditions, without any proposal on how to restore these protections if the ACA was rendered void.<ref name="Aug19C" />

In February 2021, the [[Center on Budget and Policy Priorities]] (CBPP) published a timeline of "sabotage" efforts to undermine the Affordable Care Act throughout the Trump Administration.<ref>[https://www.cbpp.org/sabotage-watch-tracking-efforts-to-undermine-the-aca "Sabotage Watch: Tracking Efforts to Undermine the ACA"]. [[Center on Budget and Policy Priorities]]. Updated February 2, 2021.</ref>

====Ending cost-sharing reduction (CSR) payments====
{{Main|Cost sharing reductions subsidy}}

President Trump announced in October 2017 he would end the smaller of the two types of subsidies under the ACA, the cost sharing reduction (CSR) subsidies. This controversial decision significantly raised premiums on the ACA exchanges (as much as 20 percentage points) along with the premium tax credit subsidies that rise with them, with the CBO estimating a $200 billion increase in the budget deficit over a decade.<ref name="Vox1SK">{{Cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/health-care/2017/10/18/16499806/trump-insurance-bailouts-completely-incoherent|title=Trump's stance on insurance "bailouts" is completely incoherent|first=Sarah|last=Kliff|date=October 18, 2017|website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref> CBO also estimated that initially up to one million fewer would have [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|health insurance coverage]], although more might have it in the long run as the subsidies expand. CBO expected the exchanges to remain stable (e.g., no "death spiral") as the premiums would increase and prices would stabilize at the higher (non-CSR) level.<ref name="CBO-CSR1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/53009|title=The Effects of Terminating Payments for Cost-Sharing Reductions &#124; Congressional Budget Office|date=August 15, 2017|website=cbo.gov}}</ref>

President Trump's argument that the CSR payments were a "bailout" for [[Insurance|insurance companies]] and therefore should be stopped, actually results in the government paying more to insurance companies ($200B over a decade) due to increases in the premium tax credit subsidies. Journalist Sarah Kliff described Trump's argument as "completely incoherent."<ref name="Vox1SK"/>

====Affordable Care Act and health-care reform====
{{Main|Healthcare reform in the United States|Healthcare reform debate in the United States|Affordable Care Act}}

As the 2016 campaign unfolded, Trump stated that he favors repealing the [[Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act|Affordable Care Act]] (ACA or "Obamacare")—which Trump refers to as a "complete disaster"<ref name="Suderman">Peter Suderman, [https://reason.com/blog/2015/09/29/donald-trump-wants-to-repeal-obamacare-r Donald Trump Wants to Repeal Obamacare, Replace It With Obamacare], ''Reason'' (September 29, 2015).</ref>—and replacing it with a "[[Free market healthcare|free-market system]]".<ref name="PastHealthCare">{{cite web|url=http://www.politifact.com/wisconsin/statements/2015/sep/11/reid-ribble/donald-trump-wants-replace-obamacare-single-payer-/ |title=Donald Trump wants to replace Obamacare with a single-payer health care system, GOP congressman says|date=September 11, 2015|website=[[PolitiFact]]|last1=Kertscher|first1=Tom}}</ref> On his campaign website, Trump said, "on day one of the Trump Administration, we will ask Congress to immediately deliver a full repeal of Obamacare."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.donaldjtrump.com/positions/healthcare-reform|title=Healthcare Reform|publisher=Donald J. Trump for President, Inc.|access-date=May 21, 2016|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170113005945/https://www.donaldjtrump.com/positions/healthcare-reform|archive-date=January 13, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2016/may/05/hillary-clinton/clinton-video-lists-8-promises-trump-presidency/|title=Hillary Clinton video lists 8 promises of Donald Trump presidency. Did he say that?|website=[[PolitiFact]]|date=May 5, 2016}}</ref> Trump's campaign has insisted that the candidate has "never supported [[socialized medicine]]."<ref name="PastHealthCare" />

Trump has cited the rising costs of premiums and deductibles as a motivation to repeal the Affordable Care Act.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.donaldjtrump.com/policies/health-care/|title=Health Care|publisher=donaldjtrump.com|access-date=November 4, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161212080424/https://www.donaldjtrump.com/policies/health-care/|archive-date=December 12, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> However, an estimated 70% of persons on the exchanges could still purchase a plan for $75/month thanks to subsidies.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2016/10/24/499190020/rates-rise-again-for-obamacare-health-plans-but-so-do-subsidies|title=Rates Up 22 Percent For Obamacare Plans, But Subsidies Rise, Too|publisher=[[NPR]]|access-date=November 19, 2016}}</ref> Further, in the employer market, health insurance premium cost increases from 2015 to 2016 were an estimated 3% on average, low by historical standards. While deductibles rose 12% on average from 2015 to 2016, more workers are pairing higher-deductible plans with tax-preferred [[health savings account]]s (HSAs), offsetting some of the deductible increase (i.e., lowering their effective deductible).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://kff.org/health-costs/press-release/average-annual-workplace-family-health-premiums-rise-modest-3-to-18142-in-2016-more-workers-enroll-in-high-deductible-plans-with-savings-option-over-past-two-years/|title=Average Annual Workplace Family Health Premiums Rise Modest 3%|website=Kaiser Family Foundation|date=September 14, 2016|access-date=November 23, 2016}}</ref>

The [[Congressional Budget Office]] reported in March 2016 that there were approximately 23 million people with insurance due to the law, with 12 million people covered by the exchanges (10 million of whom received subsidies to help pay for insurance) and 11 million made eligible for Medicaid.<ref>{{Cite web|url= https://www.cbo.gov/publication/51385|title=Federal Subsidies for Health Insurance Coverage for People Under Age 65:2016 to 2026|website=CBO|date=March 24, 2016|access-date=November 23, 2016}}</ref> The CBO also reported in June 2015 that: "Including the budgetary effects of macroeconomic feedback, repealing the ACA would increase federal budget deficits by $137 billion over the 2016–2025 period."<ref name="CBO_Repeal">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/50252|title=Budgetary and Economic Effects of Repealing the Affordable Care Act|website=CBO|date=June 19, 2015|access-date=December 4, 2016}}</ref> CBO also estimated that excluding the effects of macroeconomic feedback, repeal of the ACA would increase the deficit by $353 billion over that same period.<ref name="CBO_Repeal"/>

In the early part of his campaign, Trump responded to questions about his plan to replace the ACA by saying that it would be "something terrific!"<ref name="Suderman"/><ref name="Ferris">Sarah Ferris, [https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/249697-trump-replace-obamacare-with-something-terrific/ Trump: I'll replace ObamaCare with 'something terrific'], ''[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]'' (July 29, 2015).</ref> Trump subsequently said at various points that he believes that the government should have limited involvement in health care, but has also said that "at the lower end, where people have no money, I want to try and help those people," by "work[ing] out some sort of a really smart deal with hospitals across the country."<ref name="Ferris"/> and has said "everybody's got to be covered."<ref name="Suderman"/> At a February 2016 town hall on CNN, Trump said that he supported the individual [[health insurance mandate]] of the ACA, which requires all Americans to have health insurance, saying "I like the mandate. So here's where I'm a little bit different [from other Republican candidates]."<ref>{{cite web |last=Sullivan |first=Peter |url=https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/270021-gop-senator-hits-trump-over-obamacare-mandate-support/|title=GOP senator hits Trump over ObamaCare mandate support |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |date=February 19, 2016}}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160220091639/http://cnnpressroom.blogs.cnn.com/2016/02/18/rush-transcript-donald-trump-cnn-republican-presidential-town-hall-columbia-sc/ Transcript: Donald Trump: CNN Republican Presidential Town Hall, Columbia, South Carolina], CNN (February 18, 2016).</ref> In March 2016, Trump reversed himself, saying that "Our elected representatives must eliminate the individual mandate. No person should be required to buy insurance unless he or she wants to."<ref name="Vitali">{{cite web |last=Vitali |first=Ali |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2016-election/donald-trump-reveals-details-his-health-care-plan-n530701 |title=Donald Trump Reveals Details of His Health Care Plan |publisher=[[NBC News]] |date=March 3, 2016 |access-date=August 11, 2016}}</ref>

In March 2016, Trump released his health care plan, which called for allowing health insurance companies to compete across state lines and for making Medicaid into a [[block grant]] system for the states. He also called for elimination of the individual mandate for health insurance, for allowing health insurance premiums to be deducted on tax returns, and for international competition in the drug market. In the same document, Trump acknowledged that [[mental health care]] in the U.S. is often inadequate but offered no immediate solution to the problem, instead stating that "there are promising reforms being developed in Congress."<ref name="Vitali" />

Explaining how he would address the problem of ensuring the people that would lose their insurance coverage if Obamacare were repealed, Trump said, "We have to come up, and we can come up with many different plans. In fact, plans you don't even know about will be devised because we're going to come up with plans—health care plans—that will be so good. And so much less expensive both for the country and for the people. And so much better."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2016/09/15/donald-trumps-visit-with-dr-oz-was-just-as-amazing-as-you-though-it-would-be/|title=Donald Trump's interview with Dr. Oz was just as amazingly strange as we thought it would be|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=September 24, 2016}}</ref> His plan has been criticized by Republican health experts as "a jumbled hodgepodge of old Republican ideas, randomly selected, that don't fit together" (Robert Laszewski)<ref>{{cite news |last1=Laughland |first1=Oliver |last2=Ackerman |first2=Spencer |last3=Borger |first3=Julian |last4=Holpuch |first4=Amanda |last5=Redden |first5=Molly |last6=Milman |first6=Oliver |last7=Rushe |first7=Dominic |last8=Lartey |first8=Jamiles |date=9 November 2016 |title=What will President Donald Trump do? Predicting his policy agenda |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/nov/09/donald-trump-president-policy-immigration-agenda-healthcare |access-date=November 9, 2016 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> providing nothing that "would do anything more than cover a couple million people" (Gail R. Wilensky).<ref name="NYT-8-4-16">{{cite news|last1=Pear|first1=Robert|last2=Haberman|first2=Maggie|title=Donald Trump's Health Care Ideas Bewilder Republican Experts|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/09/us/politics/donald-trump-health-care.html|access-date=November 9, 2016|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 8, 2016}}</ref>

He characterized the [[Healthcare in Canada|Canadian healthcare system]] as "catastrophic in certain ways" in October 2016 during the second presidential debate.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/oct/10/canada-healthcare-donald-trump-debate|title=Trump's attack on 'catastrophic' Canadian healthcare system draws ire|last=Kassam|first=Ashifa|date=October 10, 2016|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|issn=0261-3077|access-date=October 10, 2016}}</ref> In 2015, Trump also expressed admiration for the [[NHS Scotland|Scottish health-care system]], which is single payer, but argued it would work well in the US.<ref name="PastHealthCare" />

=== 2024 campaign ===
In November 2023, Trump continued to advocate for repealing and replacing Obamacare.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kapur |first=Sahil |date=2023-11-29 |title=Trump doubles down, saying 'Obamacare Sucks' and must be replaced |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/trump-doubles-saying-obamacare-sucks-must-replaced-rcna126978 |access-date=2024-10-10 |publisher=NBC News |language=en}}</ref>

During a March 11, 2024 interview, Trump suggested he was open to cutting entitlement programs such as [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]] and [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]], which the Trump campaign later claimed was merely referring to "cutting waste" and that he would protect the programs. Trump previously suggested while president in 2020 that he would "at some point" look into cutting entitlement programs, and Trump's previous budget proposals have suggested some cuts to the programs. During the Republican primary, Trump attacked his opponents by suggesting they would cut entitlement benefits.<ref>{{cite news |last=Browning |first=Kellen |date=March 11, 2024 |title=Trump Mentions Cutting Entitlements, and Biden Pounces |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/11/us/politics/trump-mentions-cutting-entitlements-and-biden-pounces.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240311202251/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/11/us/politics/trump-mentions-cutting-entitlements-and-biden-pounces.html |archive-date=March 11, 2024 |access-date=March 11, 2024 |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Cancryn |first=Adam |date=March 11, 2024 |title=Trump tees up a Biden broadside on Social Security |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/03/11/trump-biden-social-security-2024-elections-00146307 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240322002140/https://www.politico.com/news/2024/03/11/trump-biden-social-security-2024-elections-00146307 |archive-date=March 22, 2024 |access-date=March 21, 2024 |work=Politico}}</ref>

Trump admitted in the debate that he did not have a Health Care plan, saying only that he had "concepts of a plan."<ref name="ac">{{Cite web |last=Kapur |first=Sahil |date=2024-09-16 |title=Donald Trump misrepresents his push to repeal the Affordable Care Act |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/donald-trump-misrepresents-repeal-affordable-care-act-obamacare-rcna171293 |access-date=2024-10-10 |publisher=NBC News |language=en}}</ref>

===Public health===
====Ebola====
{{Main|Ebola virus cases in the United States}}

In 2014, after a New York physician returned from treating [[West African Ebola virus epidemic|Ebola patients in West Africa]] and showed symptoms of the disease, Trump tweeted that if the doctor had Ebola, "Obama should apologize to the American people & resign!"<ref>[[Nicholas Kristof]], [https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/12/opinion/congress-to-america-drop-dead.html?_r=0 Congress to America: Drop Dead], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (May 12, 2016),</ref> When the doctor was later confirmed to have [[Ebola virus cases in the United States#Fourth case: Craig Spencer|developed Ebola in New York]], Trump tweeted that it was "Obama's fault" and "I have been saying for weeks for President Obama to stop the flights from [[West Africa]]. So simple, but he refused. A TOTAL incompetent!"<ref>{{cite web|author= Melanie Eversley|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2014/10/23/trump-ebola-twitter-obama/17815841/|title=Trump hits Twitter to blame Obama for Ebola in NYC|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|date=October 23, 2014}}</ref> Trump also criticized President Obama's decision to send 3,000 U.S. troops to affected regions to help combat the outbreak (see [[Operation United Assistance]]).<ref name="ChampionEbola">Matthew Champion, [https://web.archive.org/web/20160818130908/http://indy100.independent.co.uk/article/donald-trump-has-a-novel-approach-to-fighting-ebola-irrationality--gJ2mxU1kLe Donald Trump has a novel approach to fighting Ebola: Irrationality], ''[[The Independent]]'' (2014).</ref>

As doctor [[Kent Brantly]] returned to the U.S. for treatment, Trump tweeted that U.S. doctors who went abroad to treat Ebola were "great" but "must suffer the consequences" if they became infected and insisted that "the U.S. must immediately stop all flights from EBOLA infected countries or the plague will start and spread inside our 'borders.'"<ref>{{cite news|author=Jenn Selby|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/donald-trump-says-ebola-doctors-must-suffer-the-consequences-9646445.html|title=Donald Trump says Ebola doctors 'must suffer the consequences'|date=August 4, 2014|newspaper=[[The Independent]]}}</ref> When an Ebola patient was scheduled to come to the U.S. for treatment, Trump tweeted, "now I know for sure that our leaders are incompetent. KEEP THEM OUT OF HERE!"<ref>{{cite web|author=Sarah Smith|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2014/08/ebola-us-donald-trump-reaction-109636|title=Trump: Keep out Ebola victims|newspaper=[[Politico]]|date=August 8, 2014}}</ref>

Trump's suggestion on the Ebola crisis "would go against all the expert advice being offered". Doctors warned "that isolating West Africa would only make the Ebola outbreak much worse" by "potentially denying help and supplies from getting in", and might destabilize the countries and contribute to the disease's spread outside West Africa.<ref name="ChampionEbola"/>

====Zika====
{{Main|2015–2016 Zika virus epidemic}}

On August 3, 2016, Trump called the Zika virus outbreak in Florida "a big problem".<ref name="tz">{{Cite web|url=http://miamiherald.typepad.com/nakedpolitics/2016/08/trump-on-the-zika-rick-scott-has-it-under-control.html|title=Trump on 'the Zika': Rick Scott has it 'under control' {{!}} Naked Politics|access-date=August 12, 2016}}</ref> He expressed his support for Florida governor [[Rick Scott]]'s handling of the crisis, saying that he's "doing a fantastic job".<ref name="tz"/> When asked if Congress should convene an emergency session to approve Zika funding, Trump answered, "I would say that it's up to Rick Scott."<ref name="tz"/> On August 11, 2016, Trump said that he was in favor of Congress setting aside money to combat the Zika virus.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/election/donald-trump/article95144337.html|title=Trump: Americans could be tried in Guantánamo|website=[[Miami Herald]]|access-date=August 12, 2016}}</ref>

====Vaccines====
Trump suggested that [[MMR vaccine and autism|childhood vaccinations were related to autism]], a hypothesis which has been repeatedly debunked.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://politicalticker.blogs.cnn.com/2014/03/28/trump-weighs-in-on-vaccine-autism-controversy/ |title=Trump weighs in on vaccine-autism controversy |publisher=[[CNN]] |date=March 28, 2014 |access-date=August 24, 2015 |archive-date=February 15, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210215005730/https://politicalticker.blogs.cnn.com/2014/03/28/trump-weighs-in-on-vaccine-autism-controversy/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="EunjungCha">Ariana Eunjung Cha, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/to-your-health/wp/2015/09/17/the-origins-of-donald-trumps-autismvaccine-theory-and-how-it-was-completely-debunked-eons-ago/ The origins of Donald Trump's autism/vaccine theory and how it was completely debunked eons ago], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (September 17, 2015).</ref> The [[American Academy of Pediatrics]] and [[Autism Speaks]] have "decried Trump's remarks as false and potentially dangerous."<ref name="EunjungCha"/>

In 2010, the [[Donald J. Trump Foundation]] donated $10,000 to [[Generation Rescue]], [[Jenny McCarthy]]'s [[nonprofit organization]] that advocates the incorrect view that [[autism]] and related disorders are primarily caused by [[vaccine]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/emilywillingham/2016/10/01/finally-someone-found-a-beneficiary-of-trump-charity-and-its-an-antivaccine-organization/|title=Finally, Someone Found A Beneficiary Of Trump Charity, And It's An Antivaccine Organization|last=Willingham|first=Emily|website=[[Forbes]]|access-date=October 2, 2016}}</ref>

Despite his prior views, however, Trump did drop his false claims of vaccines being [[MMR vaccine and autism|related to autism]] in 2019 after the [[2019 measles outbreaks]], in saying: "They have to get those shots," as well as "...vaccinations are so important".<ref>{{Cite news|last=Sink|first=Justin|date=Apr 26, 2019|title=Trump Backs Vaccines Amid Measles Outbreak, Drops Autism Claims|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-04-26/trump-backs-vaccines-amid-measles-outbreak-drops-autism-claims|access-date=2020-07-29|newspaper=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg L.P.]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Fritze|first1=John|last2=Collins|first2=Michael|title=Donald Trump urges measles shots for children, in shift from prior warnings on vaccines|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2019/04/26/measles-outbreak-trump-says-children-have-get-shots/3560304002/|access-date=2020-07-29|website=[[USA Today]]}}</ref>

==Immigration==
{{Main|Immigration policy of the first Trump administration|Immigration policy of the second Trump administration}}

[[File:Donald Trump by Gage Skidmore 5.jpg|thumb|Donald Trump speaking at a rally in Fountain Hills, Arizona, on March 19, 2016]]

[[Illegal immigration to the United States|Illegal immigration]] was a signature [[Donald Trump presidential campaign, 2016#Temporary Muslim ban proposal|issue of Trump's presidential campaign]], and he proposed reforms and made controversial remarks regarding immigrants.

In August 2019, Trump accused Democrats of supporting "[[open border]]s" by attempting to use their opposition to his immigration priorities as an example despite no explicit evidence to support his claim.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Qiu |first1=Linda |title=No, Democrats Don't Want 'Open Borders' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/27/us/politics/fast-check-donald-trump-democrats-open-borders.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 27, 2018 |access-date=8 July 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Farley |first1=Robert |title=calls to abolish ice not open borders |url=https://www.factcheck.org/2018/07/calls-to-abolish-ice-not-open-borders/ |website=factcheck.org |date=July 3, 2018 |access-date=8 July 2021}}</ref> He also claimed that his administration is "building the wall faster and better than ever", but no new barriers were erected by June 2019 at the [[Mexico–United States border]] unlike what Trump promised during his 2016 campaign. The only installations have been replacement fencing of old barriers. Trump also falsely claimed that only 2% of migrants who were released instead of detained eventually returned for their immigration hearings. The 2017 statistic is 72% for migrants, and 89% of migrants applying for asylum.<ref name="Aug19C"/>

[[File:President Trump Addresses Joint Session of Congress, March 4, 2025.webm|thumb|alt=Trump addresses congress in 2025, "I have sent Congress a detailed funding request laying out exactly how we will (...) complete the largest deportation operation in American history, larger even then current record holder, President Dwight D. Eisenhower" |Trump addresses congress in 2025, "I have sent Congress a detailed funding request laying out exactly how we will (...) complete the largest deportation operation in American history, larger even then current record holder, President Dwight D. Since at least the [[2016 Republican Party presidential debates and forums#November 10, 2015 – Milwaukee, Wisconsin|November 2015 debates]], Trump has expressed support for deportation under President [[Eisenhower]] while not saying [[Operation Wetback]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=ADRIANA GOMEZ LICON |title=Trump's vows to deport millions are undercut by his White House record and one family's story |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-deportations-immigration-gop-147d96fd00aa4c56e2cbe6074eceb874 |work=[[AP News]] |date=January 3, 2024 |language=en |quote=Donald Trump has lauded the Eisenhower-era raids without using their name since he first ran for president and is now promising voters he would begin the largest domestic deportation operation in American history, exceeding the 1950s. Donald Trump did not mention it by name, but he was describing the 1950s program Operation Wetback.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Republican Presidential Candidates Debate : FBC : November 10, 2015 9:00pm-11:01pm EST |url=https://archive.org/details/FBC_20151111_020000_Republican_Presidential_Candidates_Debate |website=[[Archive.org]] |date=November 11, 2015 |quote=let me just tell you that dwight eisenhower, good president, great president, people liked him. i like ike, right? the expression. i like ike. moved a million 1/2 illegal immigrants out of this country, moved them just beyond the border. ==Law and order==
===Capital punishment===
{{See also|Capital punishment in the United States}}
[[File:Trump_Bring_Back_Death_Penalty_ad_1989.jpg|thumb|right|"The full-page advertisement was taken out by Trump in the May 1, 1989, issue of the [[New York Daily News|''Daily News''.]]"<ref name="the Guardian-2016">{{Cite web |date=February 17, 2016 |title=Donald Trump and the Central Park Five: the racially charged rise of a demagogue |url=http://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/feb/17/central-park-five-donald-trump-jogger-rape-case-new-york |access-date=December 7, 2022 |website=The Guardian |language=en}}</ref> Donald Trump spent $85,000 in submitting the ad across four New York City newspapers.<ref name="the Guardian-2016" />]]
Trump has long advocated for [[capital punishment in the United States]].<ref name="Ford">Matt Ford, [https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2015/12/donald-trump-death-penalty/420069/ Donald Trump's Racially Charged Advocacy of the Death Penalty], ''[[The Atlantic]]'' (December 18, 2015).</ref> In May 1989, shortly after the [[Central Park jogger case]] received widespread media attention, Trump purchased a [[Newspaper display advertising|full-page ad]] in four New York City newspapers with the title "BRING BACK THE DEATH PENALTY!" Five defendants (the "Central Park Five") were [[Wrongful conviction|wrongfully convicted]] in the case and were subsequently [[Exoneration|exonerated]].<ref name="Ford"/><ref name="FullPageAd1989">{{cite news|last1=Foderaro|first1=Lisa|title=Angered by Attack, Trump Urges Return Of the Death Penalty|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/05/01/nyregion/angered-by-attack-trump-urges-return-of-the-death-penalty.html|access-date=March 15, 2016|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=May 1, 1989}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Ford|first1=Matt|title=Donald Trump's Racially Charged Advocacy of the Death Penalty|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2015/12/donald-trump-death-penalty/420069/|access-date=March 15, 2016|work=[[The Atlantic]]|date=December 18, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Laughland|first1=Oliver|title=Donald Trump and the Central Park Five: the racially charged rise of a demagogue|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/feb/17/central-park-five-donald-trump-jogger-rape-case-new-york|access-date=March 15, 2016|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=February 17, 2016}}</ref> By October 2016, Trump still maintained that the Central Park Five were guilty.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cnn.com/2016/10/06/politics/reality-check-donald-trump-central-park-5/index.html|title=Reality Check: Donald Trump and the Central Park 5|first=Steven A. |last=Holmes|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=October 6, 2016|access-date=October 7, 2016}}</ref>

In December 2015, in a speech accepting the endorsement of the New England Police Benevolent Association, Trump said that "One of the first things I do [if elected President] in terms of [[Executive order (United States)|executive order]] if I win will be to sign a strong, strong statement that will go out to the country, out to the world, that...anybody killing a police officer—death penalty. It's going to happen, O.K.?"<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/politics/first-draft/2015/12/10/verbatim-donald-trump-promises-death-penalty-in-killings-of-police-officers/ Verbatim: Donald Trump Promises Death Penalty in Killings of Police Officers], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (December 10, 2015).</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mediaite.com/online/trump-tells-police-group-every-single-cop-killer-gets-death-penalty-if-i-win/ |title=Trump Tells Police Group: Every Single Cop-Killer Gets Death Penalty If I Win|date=December 11, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/262897-trump-i-will-mandate-death-penalty-for-killing-police-officers/ |title=Trump: I will mandate death penalty for killing police officers |newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|date=December 10, 2015 }}</ref><ref name="Cop_killers">{{cite news|last1=Diamond|first1=Jeremy|title=Trump: Death penalty for cop killers|url=http://www.cnn.com/2015/12/10/politics/donald-trump-police-officers-death-penalty/|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=December 11, 2015}}</ref> However, the president has no authority over these prosecutions as they usually take place in [[State court (United States)|state court]] under state law,<ref name="Ford"/><ref name="CapitalPunishmentFactchecker">[https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2016/us/elections/fact-check.html#/factcheck-20?smid=tw-share Fact Checks: Donald J. Trump: "One of the first things I do in terms of executive order if I win will be to sign a strong, strong statement" that "anybody killing a police officer—death penalty."], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (December 11, 2016).</ref> and [[Capital punishment in the United States|over one-third of U.S. states have already abolished the death penalty]]. Furthermore, mandatory death sentences are unconstitutional, as held by the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] in ''[[Woodson v. North Carolina]]'' (1976).<ref name="Ford"/><ref name="CapitalPunishmentFactchecker"/>

In the six months between July 2020<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-12-07 |title=Trump ratchets up pace of executions before Biden inaugural |url=https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-death-penalty-legacy-838932ac2b665b42373309336d130f56 |access-date=2024-03-06 |website=AP News |language=en |archive-date=April 21, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240421172426/https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-death-penalty-legacy-838932ac2b665b42373309336d130f56 |url-status=live }}</ref> and the end of Trump's term, the [[Federal death penalty|federal government executed]] thirteen people; the first executions since 2002.<ref name="tarm">{{Cite news|first1=Michael |last1=Tarm |first2=Michael |last2=Kunzelman |url=https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-wildlife-coronavirus-pandemic-crime-terre-haute-28e44cc5c026dc16472751bbde0ead50 |access-date=November 10, 2021 |title=Trump administration carries out 13th and final execution |work=[[Associated Press News]] |date=January 15, 2021}}</ref> In this time period, Trump oversaw more federal executions than any president in the preceding 120 years.<ref name="tarm" />

===Torture===
{{Main|Torture and the United States}}

Trump has said that he believes that "torture absolutely works". During his campaign, Trump said that "I would bring back [[waterboarding]], and I'd bring back a hell of a lot worse than waterboarding".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-38753000|title=Donald Trump says he believes waterboarding works|website=BBC|date=January 27, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=McCarthy |first=Tom |title=Donald Trump: I'd bring back 'a hell of a lot worse than waterboarding' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/feb/06/donald-trump-waterboarding-republican-debate-torture |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=February 7, 2016 |access-date=February 8, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Ted Cruz, Donald Trump Advocate Bringing Back Waterboarding |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/video/ted-cruz-donald-trump-advocate-bringing-back-waterboarding-36764410 |work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] |date=February 6, 2016 |access-date=February 9, 2016}}</ref>

===Criminal justice===
{{Main|Criminal justice reform in the United States}}

As of May 2016, Trump's campaign website made no mention of [[Criminal justice reform in the United States|criminal justice reform]], and Trump rarely talked in specifics.<ref name="GoodwinHardline">{{cite web|author=Liz Goodwin|url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/1990s-mugging-roots-donald-trump-000000780.html|title=A 1990s mugging and the roots of Donald Trump's hardline criminal justice views|publisher=[[Yahoo! News]]|date=May 25, 2016}}</ref><ref name="WisnieskiCrime">{{cite web|author=Adam Wisnieski|url=http://www.thecrimereport.org/news/inside-criminal-justice/2016-03-trump-on-crime-tough-talk-few-specifics|title=Trump On Crime: Tough Talk, Few Specifics|website=The Crime Report|publisher=Center on Media, Crime and Justice, [[John Jay College of Criminal Justice]]|access-date=May 31, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160505060744/http://www.thecrimereport.org/news/inside-criminal-justice/2016-03-trump-on-crime-tough-talk-few-specifics|archive-date=May 5, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> Trump has stated that he would be "tough on crime" and criticized Barack Obama's and Hillary Clinton's criminal justice reform proposals.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2016/may/26/donald-trump/donald-trump-wrong-hillary-clinton-wants-release-a/|title=Donald Trump wrong that Hillary Clinton wants to release all violent criminals from prison|website=[[PolitiFact]]|date=May 26, 2016}}</ref> When asked about specific criminal justice reforms, Trump reportedly often changes the subject back to supporting police or vague answers about needing to be "tough."<ref name="WisnieskiCrime" /> In January 2016, Trump said that along with veterans, "the most mistreated people in this country are police."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.c-span.org/video/?c4577615/trump-mistreated-people-country-police-veterans|title=Trump: The most mistreated people in this country are police and veterans|publisher=[[C-SPAN]]|access-date=June 1, 2016}}</ref>

Trump supports the use of "stop and frisk" tactics, of the kind [[Stop-and-frisk in New York City|once used in New York City]].<ref>Julia Craven, [https://www.huffingtonpost.com/entry/donald-trump-crime-chicago-comments_us_56e1d8d9e4b0860f99d84542 Donald Trump on Crime in Chicago: You Have To Be Tough On 'These People'], ''[[HuffPost]]'' (March 10, 2016).</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-election-trump-idUSKCN11R2NZ|title=Trump praises 'stop-and-frisk' police tactic|date=September 21, 2016|newspaper=[[Reuters]]|access-date=September 21, 2016}}</ref> In 2000, Trump also rejected as elitist and naive the arguments of criminal justice reformers that the U.S. criminal justice system puts too many criminals in jail.<ref name="GoodwinHardline" /> Trump is in favor of at least one mandatory sentence, where using a gun to commit a crime results in a five-year sentence.<ref name="WisnieskiCrime" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.donaldjtrump.com/positions/second-amendment-rights |title=Second Amendment Rights|publisher=Donald J. Trump for President, Inc.|access-date=May 31, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160107050849/https://www.donaldjtrump.com/positions/second-amendment-rights|archive-date=January 7, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Trump on several occasions asserted that crime was rising in the United States.<ref name="GoodwinHardline"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/m/de1817b5-0662-3ac7-bc55-d0e0c7cc0049/donald-trump-actually-read.html|title=Donald Trump actually read his victory speech from a teleprompter. Here's the transcript|website=[[Yahoo News]]|access-date=June 8, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160808150618/https://www.yahoo.com/news/m/de1817b5-0662-3ac7-bc55-d0e0c7cc0049/donald-trump-actually-read.html?nhp=1|archive-date=August 8, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="tw">{{Cite web|url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2016/aug/30/donald-trump/donald-trump-wrong-inner-city-crime-reaching-recor/|title=Trump wrong that inner-city crime is reaching record levels|access-date=August 30, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite tweet |last=Trump |first=Donald J. |author-link= Donald Trump|user=realDonaldTrump |number=752834632907943936 |date= 12 July 2016|title=Crime is out of control, and rapidly getting worse. Look what is going on in Chicago and our inner cities. Not good! |access-date=August 30, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite tweet |last= Trump|first= Donald J.|author-link=Donald Trump |user= realDonaldTrump|number=759450053379579905 |date= July 30, 2016 |title=Violent crime is rising across the United States, yet the DNC convention ignored it. Crime reduction will be one of my top priorities. |access-date=August 30, 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.vox.com/2016/6/7/11880448/donald-trump-victory-speech-transcript|title=Donald Trump actually read his victory speech from a teleprompter. Here's the transcript|last=Golshan|first=Tara|date=June 8, 2016 |website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|access-date=August 30, 2016}}</ref> Trump's assertions that crime was rising were false; in fact, both violent and property crimes [[Crime in the United States|consistently declined in the U.S.]] from the early 1990s until 2014.<ref>Louis Jacobson, [http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2016/jun/09/donald-trump/donald-trump-said-crime-rising-its-not-and-hasnt-b/ Donald Trump said, 'Crime is rising.' It's not (and hasn't been for decades)], ''[[PolitiFact]]'' (June 9, 2016).</ref> Trump's false claim that "inner-city crime is reaching record levels" received a "pants-on-fire" rating from PolitiFact.<ref name="tw"/> As president, Trump reiterated in February 2017 the false claim that crime was rising, saying, "the murder rate in our country is the highest it's been in 47 years."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/true-crime/wp/2017/02/07/trump-makes-false-statement-about-u-s-murder-rate-to-sheriffs-group/|title=Trump makes false statement about U.S. murder rate to sheriffs' group|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=2017-02-07}}</ref>

In May 2016, Trump stated that the cities of [[Oakland, California|Oakland]] and [[Ferguson, Missouri|Ferguson]] are "among the most dangerous in the world".<ref>Draper, Robert. [http://mobile.nytimes.com/2016/05/22/magazine/donald-trump-primary-win.html "Mr. Trump's Wild Ride"], ''[[The New York Times Magazine]]'' (May 18, 2016): "there are places in America that are among the most dangerous in the world. You go to places like Oakland. Or Ferguson. The crime numbers are worse. Seriously."</ref> In response, [[KPIX-TV|CBS News in San Francisco]] reported that the murder rates in Oakland and Baghdad are comparable,<ref>[http://sanfrancisco.cbslocal.com/video/category/news-politics/3402075-trump-gets-flak-for-crack-about-oakland-being-most-dangerous-city/ "Trump Gets Flak For Crack About Oakland Being 'Most Dangerous' City"], [[KPIX-TV]] (May 18, 2016): "In Baghdad it's 32 murders per 100,000 people...In Oakland it's 25 per 100,000, 32 versus 25, so Baghdad/Oakland, not out of the ballparkTrum according to the statistics."</ref> but [[PolitiFact]] rated Trump's claim false given that "homicide rates alone are not enough to gauge whether a city is dangerous or not".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2016/may/25/donald-trump/donald-trumps-false-claim-oakland-ferguson-are-amo/|title=Donald Trump's false claim that Oakland, Ferguson are 'among the most dangerous in the world'|website=[[PolitiFact]]|date=May 30, 2016}}</ref>

On November 22, 2015, Trump retweeted a graphic with purported statistics—cited to a nonexistent "Crime Statistics Bureau"—which falsely claimed that [[African Americans]] were responsible for 81% of the homicides of [[White Americans]] and that police were responsible for 1% of black homicides compared to 4% of white homicides. Trump's retweet earned PolitiFact's "Pants on Fire" rating and was called "grossly inaccurate" by FactCheck.org the next day.<ref name="PolitiFactTweet">{{cite web|url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2015/nov/23/donald-trump/trump-tweet-blacks-white-homicide-victims/|title=Trump's Pants on Fire tweet that blacks killed 81% of white homicide victims|website=[[PolitiFact]]|access-date=May 30, 2016}}</ref><ref name="cg">{{cite web|author=Robert Farley|url=http://www.factcheck.org/2015/11/trump-retweets-bogus-crime-graphic/|title=Trump Retweets Bogus Crime Graphic|website=FactCheck.org|publisher=[[Annenberg Public Policy Center]]|date=November 23, 2015}}</ref> Blacks were actually responsible for only 15% of white homicides according to FBI data for 2014.<ref name="PolitiFactTweet"/> The breakdown of the racial differences in police killings in Trump's retweet was also inaccurate. Based on the percentages, the number of whites killed by police would be almost 4 times greater than the number of blacks. Data from ''The Washington Post'' for 2009 to 2013 showed a ratio of 1.5 white deaths by police for each black death.<ref name="PolitiFactTweet"/> A separate estimate by Peter Moskos, associate professor at the [[John Jay College of Criminal Justice]] attributed 10% of white homicides to police and 4% to police for blacks.<ref name="cg"/> When asked about the statistics, Trump falsely maintained that the statistics came "from sources that are very credible."<ref name="cg"/>

===Drug policy===
{{See also|Federal drug policy of the United States}}
Trump's views on [[drug policy]] have shifted dramatically over time.<ref>Emily Gray Brosious, [http://extract.suntimes.com/news/10/153/6390/dramatic-evolution-donald-trump-marijuana-drug-policy-reform-rhetoric The dramatic evolution of Donald Trump's drug policy rhetoric] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160314103541/http://extract.suntimes.com/news/10/153/6390/dramatic-evolution-donald-trump-marijuana-drug-policy-reform-rhetoric |date=March 14, 2016 }}, ''Chicago Sun-Times'' (October 28, 2015).</ref>

At a luncheon hosted by the ''[[Miami Herald]]'' in April 1990, Trump told a crowd of 700 people that U.S. drug enforcement policy was "a joke," and that: "We're losing badly the [[war on drugs]]. You have to [[Legalization of drugs|legalize drugs]] to win that war. You have to take the profit away from these drug czars."<ref name="SuebsaengDrugs">Asawin Suebsaeng, [http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2015/08/03/donald-trump-legalize-all-the-drugs.html Wayback Machine: Donald Trump: Legalize ALL the Drugs], ''[[The Daily Beast]]'' (August 3, 2015).</ref><ref>[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1755&dat=19900414&id=eUoeAAAAIBAJ&sjid=EHoEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4675,4533445&hl=en Donald Trump: Legalize Drugs], ''Sarasota Herald-Tribune'' (April 14, 1990).</ref>

In his campaign for the presidency in 2015 and 2016, however, Trump adopted "drug warrior" positions<ref name="SuebsaengDrugs"/> and has sought advice on the issue from [[William J. Bennett]], who served as the U.S. first "[[drug czar]]" in the 1980s "and has remained a proponent of harsh 1980s-style drug war tactics."<ref>Christopher Ingraham, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/wonk/wp/2016/03/03/donald-trump-thinks-a-wall-will-solve-the-nations-heroin-problem/ Donald Trump's drug policy is an alarming throwback to the 1980s], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (March 3, 2016).</ref> Trump told [[Sean Hannity]] in June 2015 that he opposes [[Legalization of non-medical cannabis in the United States|marijuana legalization]] and that "I feel strongly about that."<ref name="SuebsaengDrugs"/> Trump also claims to have personally never used [[controlled substance]]s of any kind.<ref name="SuebsaengDrugs"/>

Trump has voiced support for [[Medical cannabis in the United States|medical marijuana]],<ref name="SuebsaengDrugs"/> saying that he is "a hundred percent in favor" because "I know people that have serious problems...and...it really, really does help them."<ref>Jon Gettman, [http://www.hightimes.com/read/pot-matters-trump-marijuana Pot Matters: Trump on Marijuana] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160704065458/http://www.hightimes.com/read/pot-matters-trump-marijuana |date=July 4, 2016 }}, ''[[High Times]]'' (February 12, 2016).</ref> When asked about Colorado (where [[Drug policy of Colorado|recreational use of marijuana is legal]]), Trump softened his previously expressed views and essentially said that states should be able to decide on whether marijuana for recreational purposes should be legal.<ref name="SuebsaengDrugs"/><ref name="JohnsonMarijuana">{{cite web |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2015/10/29/trump-wants-marijuana-legalization-decided-at-the-state-level/ |title=Trump softens position on marijuana legalization |author=Jenna Johnson|date=October 29, 2015|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151030153150/https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2015/10/29/trump-wants-marijuana-legalization-decided-at-the-state-level/|archive-date=October 30, 2015|url-status=live}}</ref>

The administration organized the [[Marijuana Policy Coordination Committee]] in 2018.<ref>{{citation|newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|title=Trump tasked multi-agency committee with countering pro-marijuana message: report|author=Megan Keller|date=August 29, 2018|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/404187-trump-tasked-multi-agency-committee-with-countering-pro-marijuana/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180829193916/https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/404187-trump-tasked-multi-agency-committee-with-countering-pro-marijuana/|archive-date=August 29, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2024, Trump endorsed decriminalization of marijuana in Florida. On full legalization of marijuana, he suggested it would be inevitable in the state regardless of his personal stance on the issue, and instead advocated regulations restricting its use in public spaces.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.firstpost.com/world/trump-backs-marijuana-decriminalisation-opposes-arrests-for-small-amounts-13810240.html | title=Trump backs marijuana decriminalisation, opposes arrests for small amounts | work=Firstpost | date=August 31, 2024 }}</ref>

On Jan. 21, 2025, a day into his second term, Trump pardoned [[Ross Ulbricht]], the founder of the Silk Road [[dark Web]] marketplace for illegal drugs, including [[opioids]], such as [[fentanyl]], [[date rape drug|incapacitating agents]] and other narcotics.<ref>{{cite news |title=Trump pardons Silk Road founder Ross Ulbricht - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-pardons-silk-road-founder-ross-ulbricht/ |access-date=7 February 2025 |publisher=CBS News |agency=Associated Press |date=22 January 2025}}</ref> During a Dec. 2023 meeting at [[Mar-a-Lago]], [[Angela McArdle]], chairwoman of the Libertarian Party, told Trump that "he needed to free Ulbricht if he wanted Libertarian support" for his 2024 campaign.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Collins |first1=Eliza |last2=Viswanatha |first2=Aruna |last3=Gurman |first3=Sadie |title=How Silk Road Founder Ross Ulbricht Got a Pardon From Trump |url=https://www.wsj.com/us-news/law/ross-ulbricht-silk-road-trump-pardon-16f2e7a9 |access-date=7 February 2025 |work=The Wall Street Journal |date=25 January 2025}}</ref>

===Gun regulation===
{{Main|Gun politics in the United States}}

In his 2000 book ''The America We Deserve'', Trump wrote that he generally opposed gun control, but supported the [[Federal Assault Weapons Ban]] and supported a "slightly longer [[waiting period]] to purchase a gun."<ref name="ZezimaGuns"/><ref name="PBSSummary"/><ref>{{cite book | title=The America We Deserve | author=Donald Trump | year=2000 | publisher=Macmillan | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PV6qZU_xev8C&pg=124| isbn=9781580631686 }}</ref><ref name="GabrielGuns">Trip Gabriel, [https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/20/us/politics/hillary-clinton-donald-trump-gun-control.html?_r=0 Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton Set for Clash on Gun Control], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (May 19, 2016).</ref> In his book, Trump also criticized the [[gun lobby]], saying: "The Republicans walk the N.R.A. line and refuse even limited restrictions."<ref name="GabrielGuns"/> In 2008, Trump opposed hunting-education classes in schools and called the "thought of voluntarily putting guns in the classroom...a really bad plan."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/donald-trump-said-hillary-clinton-would-make-a-good-president-in-2008-1468281714|title=Donald Trump Said Hillary Clinton Would 'Make a Good President' in 2008|last1=Rothfeld|first1=Michael|date=July 12, 2016|last2=Maremont|first2=Mark|newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|issn=0099-9660|access-date=July 12, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712012806/https://www.wsj.com/articles/donald-trump-said-hillary-clinton-would-make-a-good-president-in-2008-1468281714|archive-date=July 12, 2016|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

====2016 campaign====
While campaigning for the presidency Trump reversed some of his positions on gun issues, calling for the expansion of gun rights.<ref name="GabrielGuns"/> In 2015 he described himself as a staunch advocate of the [[Second Amendment to the United States Constitution|Second Amendment]]<ref name="PBSSummary">{{cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/donald-trump-believe-candidate-stands-10-issues |author1=Lisa Desjardins |author2=Nathalie Boyd |title=What does Donald Trump believe? Where the candidate stands on 10 issues|work=[[PBS NewsHour]]|date=June 16, 2015}}</ref><ref>Sopan Deb, [https://www.cbsnews.com/news/election-2016-donald-trump-takes-on-gun-control-mass-shootings/ Donald Trump takes on gun control, mass shootings], [[CBS News]] (October 5, 2015).</ref> and said concealed carry "is a right, not a privilege."<ref name="ZezimaGuns"/> He proposed eliminating prohibitions on assault weapons, military-style weapons and [[high-capacity magazine]]s (which Trump described as "scary sounding phrases" used by [[gun control]] advocates "to confuse people"), as well as making [[concealed carry permit]]s valid nationwide, rather than on the current state-to-state basis.<ref name="ZezimaGuns">Katie Zezima, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2015/09/18/trump-plan-calls-for-nationwide-concealed-carry-and-an-end-to-gun-bans/ Trump plan calls for nationwide concealed carry and an end to gun bans], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (September 18, 2015).</ref> At his campaign website he called for an overhaul of the [[National Instant Criminal Background Check System|current federal background check system]], arguing that "Too many states are failing to put criminal and mental health records into the system."<ref name="ZezimaGuns"/><ref>{{cite news |author1=Jon Keller |title=On The Issues: Guns And The Race For President |url=http://boston.cbslocal.com/2016/03/08/gun-control-second-amendment-nra-donald-trump-hillary-clinton-ted-cruz-marco-rubio-bernie-sanders-john-kasich/ |work=CBS Boston |date=March 8, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160310104315/http://boston.cbslocal.com/2016/03/08/gun-control-second-amendment-nra-donald-trump-hillary-clinton-ted-cruz-marco-rubio-bernie-sanders-john-kasich/ |archive-date=March 10, 2016 |language=en-US |url-status=live}}</ref>

On the campaign trail in 2015, Trump praised the [[National Rifle Association of America]] (NRA),<ref name="PfannenstielGuns">{{cite news |author1=Brianne Pfannenstiel |title=Trump in Iowa: More guns could stop mass shootings |url=http://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/news/elections/presidential/caucus/2015/12/05/trump-iowa-more-guns-could-stop-mass-shootings/76838578/ |work=Des Moines Register |date=December 5, 2015 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20210311163100/https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/news/elections/presidential/caucus/2015/12/05/trump-iowa-more-guns-could-stop-mass-shootings/76838578/ |archive-date=March 11, 2021 |language=en-US |url-status=live}}</ref> and received the group's endorsement after becoming the presumptive Republican nominee.<ref>[[Beth Reinhard]], [https://www.wsj.com/articles/donald-trump-expected-to-win-nra-endorsement-1463769758 Donald Trump Wins NRA Endorsement], ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' (May 20, 2016).</ref> He asserted that the presence of more guns in schools and public places could have stopped [[mass shooting]]s such as those in 2015 [[November 2015 Paris attacks|in Paris]]; [[2015 San Bernardino attack|in San Bernardino, California]]; and [[2015 Umpqua Community College shooting|at Umpqua Community College]].<ref name="PfannenstielGuns"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-san-bernardino-victims-couldve-protected-themselves-if-they-had-guns/|title=Trump: San Bernardino victims "could've protected themselves if they had guns"|publisher=[[CBS News]]|date=December 5, 2015}}</ref> Trump supported barring people on the government's [[Terrorist Screening Database|terrorist watch list]] from purchasing weapons, saying in 2015: "If somebody is on a watch list and an [[Enemy of the state|enemy of state]] and we know it's an enemy of state, I would keep them away, absolutely."<ref name="GabrielGuns"/> On this position, Trump departed from the position of gun-rights groups and most of his 2016 Republican rivals for the presidency and supported a stance backed by Senate Democrats.<ref name="GabrielGuns"/> Trump said that he holds a New York concealed carry permit<ref name="ZezimaGuns"/><ref name="BalakrishnanGuns">Anita Balakrishnan, [https://www.cnbc.com/2015/10/28/trump-i-carry-a-gun-on-occasion.html Trump: I carry a gun on occasion], [[CNBC]] (October 28, 2015).</ref> and that "I carry on occasion, sometimes a lot. I like to be unpredictable."<ref name="BalakrishnanGuns"/> A 1987 Associated Press story said that he held a [[handgun]] permit at that time.<ref name="ZezimaGuns"/>

In January 2016, Trump said: "I will get rid of gun-free zones on schools, and—you have to—and on military bases...My first day, it gets signed, okay? My first day. There's no more gun-free zones."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2016/01/08/donald-trump-i-will-get-rid-of-gun-free-zones-on-schools/|title=Donald Trump: 'I will get rid of gun-free zones on schools'|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=May 21, 2016}}</ref> Trump could not eliminate gun-free school zones by executive order, however, since such zones were created by a [[Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990|federal law]] that can only be reversed [[Act of Congress|by Congress]].<ref name="GabrielGuns"/> In May 2016, Trump made ambiguous comments on guns in classrooms, saying: "I don't want to have guns in classrooms. Although, in some cases, teachers should have guns in classrooms."<ref>Janell Ross, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2016/05/22/donald-trumps-stance-on-guns-in-classrooms-yes-no-and-probably/ Donald Trump's stance on guns in classrooms – yes, no and probably], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (May 22, 2016).</ref> In May 2016, Trump accused Hillary Clinton of lying when she claimed that "Donald Trump would force schools to allow guns in classrooms on his first day in office."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/trump-vows-end-gun-free-zones-amid-string/story?id=39305921|title=Trump's Gun Views in Spotlight Amid Accidental Shootings|date=May 24, 2016|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|access-date=May 24, 2016}}</ref> According to ''[[The Washington Post]]'' fact-checker, Clinton's statement was accurate.<ref>{{cite web|author=Michelle Ye Hee Lee|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/fact-checker/wp/2016/05/18/clinton-campaigns-claim-that-trump-would-force-schools-to-allow-guns-in-classrooms/|title=Clinton campaign's claim that Trump would 'force schools to allow guns in classrooms'|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=May 18, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160519080203/https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/fact-checker/wp/2016/05/18/clinton-campaigns-claim-that-trump-would-force-schools-to-allow-guns-in-classrooms/|archive-date=May 19, 2016|url-status=live}}</ref>

In June 2016, Trump said "it would have been a beautiful, beautiful sight" to see [[Omar Mateen]] shot in the head by an armed patron in the [[Orlando nightclub shooting]], reiterating his stance that more people should be armed in public places.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s3FWUoD444o|title=Donald Trump's blistering words toward Orlando shooter|last=Trump|first=Donald J.|date=June 17, 2016|publisher=[[CNN]]|via=YouTube|access-date=June 18, 2016}}</ref> A few days later, after two top officials of the [[National Rifle Association of America|NRA]] challenged the notion that drinking clubgoers should be armed, Trump reversed his position, saying that he "obviously" meant that additional guards or employees should have been armed in the nightclub.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/donald-trump-guards-orlando-club-armed-clubgoers/story?id=39984788|title=Trump Contradicts Previous Stance on Guns at Pulse Nightclub|date=June 20, 2016|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|access-date=June 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160620201202/https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/donald-trump-guards-orlando-club-armed-clubgoers/story?id=39984788|archive-date=June 20, 2016|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2016/06/trump-guns-nra-224533|title=Trump clarifies stance on guns after NRA criticism|website=[[Politico]]|date=June 20, 2016 |access-date=June 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160620132718/http://www.politico.com/story/2016/06/trump-guns-nra-224533|archive-date=June 20, 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> Security personnel and other staffers at a number of Trump's hotels and golf courses told [[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] that patrons are not permitted to carry guns on the property. A Trump spokesman denied this, saying that licensed persons are permitted to carry guns on the premises.<ref>Christopher Good & Candace Smith, [https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/donald-trump-gun-free-zones-guns-allowed-properties/story?id=39266544 Donald Trump Is Against 'Gun-Free Zones' But Guns Aren't Allowed on Many of His Properties, Staff Says], ABC News (May 20, 2016).</ref>

At a rally on August 9, 2016, Trump accused his opponent of wanting to "essentially abolish the Second Amendment", and went on: "By the way, and if she gets to pick her judges, nothing you can do, folks. Although the Second Amendment people, maybe there is, I don't know." These comments were interpreted by critics as suggesting violence against Clinton or her appointees, but Trump's campaign stated that he was referring to gun rights advocates' "great political power" as a voting bloc.<ref>{{cite web | last=Rafferty | first=Andrew | title=Trump '2nd Amendment' Comment Seen as Threat Against Clinton | publisher=[[NBC News]] | date=August 9, 2016 | url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2016-election/trump-campaign-defends-2nd-amendment-comment-n626601 | access-date=August 17, 2016}}</ref>

====First presidency (2017–2021)====
One month after his inauguration, Trump reversed an Obama-era regulation that had been intended to prevent weapons purchases by certain people with mental health problems. Had the regulation been allowed to take effect, it would have added 75,000 names, including the names of those who receive federal financial assistance due to a mental illness or who have financial proxies due to a mental illness, to a background check database.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/trump-signs-bill-revoking-obama-era-gun-checks-people-mental-n727221|title=Trump signs bill revoking Obama-era gun checks for mental illness|last=Vitali|first=Ali|date=28 February 2017|publisher=[[NBC News]]|access-date=2019-08-23}}</ref>

Following the [[Stoneman Douglas High School shooting]] in February 2018, Trump met with students and others at the White House for a "listening session". Trump suggested arming up to 20% of the teachers to stop "maniacs" from attacking students. The following day Trump called a "gun free" school a "magnet" for criminals and tweeted, "Highly trained, gun adept, teachers/coaches would solve the problem instantly, before police arrive. GREAT DETERRENT!"<ref>{{cite web|title='Gun free' schools are magnets for 'bad people': Trump|url=https://nz.news.yahoo.com/apos-gun-free-apos-schools-131408755.html|publisher=[[Yahoo! News]]|access-date=February 22, 2018|archive-date=October 31, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201031094709/https://nz.news.yahoo.com/apos-gun-free-apos-schools-131408755.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Trump suggests arming teachers as a solution to increase school safety|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/02/21/politics/trump-listening-sessions-parkland-students/index.html|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=February 21, 2018|access-date=February 22, 2018}}</ref>

In August 2019, following mass shootings [[2019 El Paso shooting|in El Paso, Texas]], and [[2019 Dayton shooting|in Dayton, Ohio]], Trump declined to support [[universal background check]]s, saying that existing background checks are already "very, very strong," even though "we have sort of missing areas and areas that don't complete the whole circle." He also indicated that he was not interested in working on bipartisan compromises.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/08/20/us/politics/trump-gun-control-nra.html|title=N.R.A. Gets Results on Gun Laws in One Phone Call With Trump|last1=Haberman|first1=Maggie|date=2019-08-20|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2019-08-23|last2=Karni|first2=Annie|issn=0362-4331|last3=Hakim|first3=Danny}}</ref>

In a speech at a 2023 NRA convention, Trump expressed support for national concealed carry reciprocity which would allow a person with a [[concealed carry]] permit in one state to have their permit apply across state lines nationwide.<ref>{{Cite web |first1=Eric |last1=Bradner |first2=Steve |last2=Contorno |first3=Kristen |last3=Holmes |date=2023-04-14 |title=GOP 2024 hopefuls attend NRA convention following mass shootings in Kentucky and Tennessee {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/04/14/politics/nra-convention-republican-2024-presidential-race/index.html |access-date=2023-05-21 |publisher=[[CNN]]|language=en}}</ref>

===Judiciary===
{{further|List of federal judges appointed by Donald Trump}}
According to ''[[The New York Times]]'', many of Trump's statements on legal topics are "extemporaneous and resist conventional legal analysis," with some appearing "to betray ignorance of fundamental legal concepts."<ref name="LiptakRuleofLaw"/>

====Supreme Court====
{{Main|Donald Trump Supreme Court candidates}}

Trump stated he wanted to replace U.S. Supreme Court justice [[Antonin Scalia]], who had died, with "a person of similar views and principles".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2016/07/21/full-text-donald-trumps-prepared-remarks-accepting-the-republican-nomination/|title=Donald Trump's prepared speech to the Republican National convention, annotated|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=July 21, 2016}}</ref> He released a list of eleven potential picks to replace Scalia.<ref name="tu">{{cite web|url=http://bigstory.ap.org/c68d11041efe47cc918fe3d7d2da4edb|title=Trump unveils list of potential picks for Supreme Court seat|website=The Big Story|access-date=May 19, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160602163331/http://bigstory.ap.org/c68d11041efe47cc918fe3d7d2da4edb|archive-date=June 2, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> The jurists were widely considered to be conservative.<ref name="tu"/><ref name="rl">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/19/us/politics/donald-trump-supreme-court-nominees.html|title=Donald Trump Releases List of Possible Supreme Court Picks|last1=Rappeport|first1=Alan|date=May 18, 2016 | last2 = Savage | first2 = Charlie | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |issn=0362-4331|access-date=May 19, 2016 |author-link2=Charlie Savage (author) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160722041723/http://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/19/us/politics/donald-trump-supreme-court-nominees.html |archive-date=July 22, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2016/05/18/478609623/trumps-supreme-court-list-might-reassure-conservatives-but-leaves-off-big-names|title=Trump's Supreme Court List Might Reassure Conservatives, But Leaves Off Big Names|publisher=[[NPR]]|date=May 18, 2016|access-date=May 19, 2016|last1=Totenberg|first1=Nina}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/politics/articles/2016-05-18/trump-lists-11-possible-u-s-supreme-court-successors-to-scalia|title=Trump Goes Conventional With Conservative Supreme Court List|newspaper=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg L.P.]]|date=May 18, 2016 |access-date=May 19, 2016}}</ref> All are white, and eight of the eleven are men.<ref name="rl"/> Trump had previously insisted that he would seek guidance from conservative groups such as the [[Federalist Society]] and the Heritage Foundation when it came to picking Supreme Court candidates.<ref name="rl"/> Several of the judges listed by Trump had questioned [[Abortion rights in the United States|abortion rights]].<ref name="rl"/> Six of the eleven judges had clerked for conservative Supreme Court justices.<ref name="rl"/>

Trump has claimed that he "would probably appoint" justices to the Supreme Court who "would look very seriously" at the [[Hillary Clinton email controversy]] "because it's a criminal activity."<ref>{{cite web|author=Nolan D. McCaskill|url=https://www.politico.com/blogs/2016-gop-primary-live-updates-and-results/2016/03/trump-supreme-court-clinton-email-221377|title=Trump: I'd pick justices who would look at Clinton's email scandal|website=[[Politico]]|date=March 30, 2016}}</ref> However, under the U.S. Constitution, Supreme Court justices "are neither investigators nor prosecutors."<ref name="LiptakRuleofLaw"/>

Trump criticized Chief Justice of the United States [[John Roberts]], a [[List of federal judges appointed by George W. Bush|George W. Bush appointee]], as a "nightmare for conservatives," citing Roberts' vote in the 2015 decision in ''[[King v. Burwell]]'', which upheld provisions of the [[Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act|Affordable Care Act]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/donald-trump-calls-chief-justice-john-roberts-nightmare/story?id=36336627|title=Trump Calls Chief Justice Roberts a 'Nightmare for Conservatives'|date=January 17, 2016|publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|access-date=May 26, 2016}}</ref> He also blamed Roberts for the June 2015 [[Obergefell v. Hodges|Supreme Court ruling legalizing same-sex marriage]], apparently in error, since in that case Roberts actually dissented from the majority opinion.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.factcheck.org/2016/02/cruz-distorts-rubios-stance-on-gay-marriage/|title=Cruz Distorts Rubio's Stance on Gay Marriage|website=[[FactCheck.org]]|date=February 16, 2016|access-date=May 26, 2016}}</ref>

In February 2016, Trump called on the Senate to stop Obama from filling the vacant seat on the Supreme Court.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/live/supreme-court-justice-antonin-scalia-dies-at-79/at-debate-trump-calls-on-republicans-to-delay-delay-delay/|title=At Debate, Donald Trump Calls on Republicans to 'Delay, Delay, Delay'|last=Corasaniti|first=Nick|date=February 13, 2016|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

An analysis by ''[[FiveThirtyEight]]'' predicted that, under the assumption that Scalia's vacant seat on the Court would not be filled before Trump's presidency, and taking account of the advanced age of three of the sitting justices, that a Trump presidency would move the Supreme Court "rightward toward its most conservative position in recent memory".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/clinton-and-trump-are-both-promising-an-extreme-supreme-court/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160802142718/https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/clinton-and-trump-are-both-promising-an-extreme-supreme-court/|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 2, 2016|title=Clinton And Trump Are Both Promising An Extreme Supreme Court|last=Roeder|first=Oliver|date=August 1, 2016|access-date=August 1, 2016}}</ref>

Trump ultimately appointed three justices to the court: [[Neil Gorsuch]] to replace Scalia, [[Brett Kavanaugh]] to replace [[Anthony Kennedy]], and [[Amy Coney Barrett]] to replace [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]]. The appointments of Trump's nominees shifted the court to a strongly conservative position. In the period after Trump left office, the court issued several conservative rulings, including [[Dobbs v.
