Jackson Women's Health Organization|declaring that the constitution does not protect abortion]], in which Trump's appointees contributed to the majority.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Biskupic |first=Joan |author-link=Joan Biskupic |date=July 26, 2021 |title=Trump's appointees are turning the Supreme Court to the right with different tactics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/07/26/politics/trump-kavanaugh-gorsuch-barrett-supreme-court/index.html |access-date=September 3, 2023 |publisher=[[CNN]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Hurley |first1=Lawrence |last2=Chung |first2=Andrew |date=July 1, 2022 |title=Explainer: How the conservative Supreme Court is reshaping U.S. law |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/how-conservative-supreme-court-is-reshaping-us-law-2022-07-01/ |access-date=September 3, 2023 |website=[[Reuters]]}}</ref>

====Comments on judges and judicial decisions====
Since taking office, Trump has made a series of "escalating attacks on the [[United States federal courts|federal judiciary]]" in response to judicial decisions against him.<ref name="Demoralize">Abby Phillip, Robert Barnes & Ed O'Keefe, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/supreme-court-nominee-gorsuch-says-trumps-attacks-on-judiciary-are-demoralizing/2017/02/08/64e03fe2-ee3f-11e6-9662-6eedf1627882_story.html Supreme Court nominee Gorsuch says Trump's attacks on judiciary are 'demoralizing'], ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (February 8, 2017).</ref> After a federal district judge, [[James Robart]], issued a stay of Trump's [[Executive Order 13769|executive order on travel, immigration, and refugees]], Trump disparaged him on Twitter, referring to him as a "the so-called judge" and writing: "[He] put our country in such peril. If something happens blame him and court system. People pouring in. Bad!"<ref name="Demoralize"/><ref>Eric Bradner and Jeff Zeleny, [http://www.cnn.com/2017/02/05/politics/trump-twitter-attacks-judge/ Trump: 'If something happens blame' the judge], [[CNN]] (February 5, 2017).</ref>

While presidents in the past have sometimes offered muted criticism of judicial opinions, Trump's personal attacks on individual judges are seen as unprecedented in American history.<ref>[[Jeffrey Rosen (legal academic)|Jeffrey Rosen]], [https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2017/02/a-historical-precedent-for-trumps-attack-on-judges/516144/ Not Even Andrew Jackson Went as Far as Trump in Attacking the Courts], ''[[The Atlantic]]'' (February 2017).</ref> Trump's remarks prompted criticism from his own nominee, Gorsuch, who told Senator [[Richard Blumenthal]] that Trump's statements were "disheartening" and "demoralizing" to the federal judiciary.<ref name="Demoralize"/> A number of legal scholars feared that Trump's conduct could undermine public confidence in the courts and endanger the [[independence of the judiciary]].<ref>Corky Siemaszko, [https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/experts-trump-undermines-judiciary-twitter-attack-judge-robart-n717626 Experts: Trump Undermines Judiciary With Twitter Attack on Judge Robart], NBC News (February 7, 2017).</ref>

===Term limits and ethics regulations===
{{Main|Term limits in the United States}}

In October 2016, Trump said that he would push for a constitutional amendment to impose [[Term limits in the United States#Congress|term limits on members of Congress]], so that members of the House of Representatives could serve for a maximum of six years and senators for a maximum of twelve years. Trump also pledged to re-institute a ban on executive branch officials from lobbying for five years after leaving government service and said that he supported Congress instituting a similar five-year lobbying ban of its own, applicable to former members and [[Congressional staff|staff]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Vitali|first1=Ali|title=Donald Trump: I Will Push Term Limits to Tell Congress 'You're Fired'|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2016-election/trump-proposes-term-limits-congress-n668466|access-date=October 19, 2016|publisher=[[NBC News]]|date=October 18, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Trump Pledges To Drain The Swamp and Impose Congressional Term Limits|url=https://www.donaldjtrump.com/press-releases/trump-pledges-to-drain-the-swamp|publisher=Donald J. Trump for President, Inc.|access-date=October 19, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161018233021/https://www.donaldjtrump.com/press-releases/trump-pledges-to-drain-the-swamp|archive-date=October 18, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="FoxTerm">{{cite news|title=Trump calls for congressional term limits, lobbyist crackdown|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/trump-calls-for-congressional-term-limits-lobbyist-crackdown|access-date=October 19, 2016|publisher=[[Fox News]]|date=October 18, 2016}}</ref><ref name="WaPoFiveYear">Catherine Ho, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/powerpost/wp/2016/10/17/trump-proposes-five-year-ban-on-executive-branch-officials-and-lawmakers-who-want-to-become-lobbyists/ Trump proposes five-year ban on executive branch officials and lawmakers who want to become lobbyists], ''[[The Washington Post]]t'' (October 17, 2016).</ref> Under current "cooling-off period" regulations, former U.S. representatives are required to wait one year before they can lobby Congress, former U.S. senators are required to two years, and former executive-branch officials "must wait either two years or one year before lobbying their former agency, depending on how senior they were."<ref name="WaPoFiveYear"/>

==== Twenty-second Amendment ====
On multiple occasions since taking office in 2017, Trump has questioned presidential term limits and in public remarks has talked about serving beyond the limits of the [[Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution|Twenty-second Amendment]]. For instance, during an April 2019 White House event for the [[Wounded Warrior Project]], he joked that he would remain president "at least for 10 or 14 years".<ref>{{cite web |last=Einbinder |first=Nicole |title=Trump suggested his supporters want him to serve more than 2 terms as president |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/trump-suggests-supporters-serve-more-two-terms-president-2019-6 |website=[[Business Insider]] |access-date=September 14, 2019 |date=June 17, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Croucher |first=Shane |title=Donald Trump Posts Image on Twitter, Instagram Joking That He'll Stand in 2024 |url=https://www.newsweek.com/trump-twitter-instagram-joke-third-term-2024-1458686 |website=[[Newsweek]]|access-date=September 14, 2019 |date=September 11, 2019}}</ref>

===First Amendment===
====Flag desecration====
During a rally in June 2020, President Trump told supporters that he thinks [[Flag Desecration Amendment|flag burning should be punishable by one year in prison]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2020-06-24/column-trump-revives-banning-flag-burning|title=Trump revives a lower of an issue: banning flag burning|first=Robin|last=Abcarian|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=2020-06-24|access-date=2020-06-26}}</ref>

==== Libel ====
During his [[Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign|2016 presidential campaign]], Trump proposed that the United States should "open up" its [[United States defamation law|libel laws]] to make it easier to sue newspapers that write "purposely negative and horrible and false articles".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gold |first=Hadas |author-link=Hadas Gold |date=2016-02-26 |title=Donald Trump: We're going to 'open up' libel laws |url=https://www.politico.com/blogs/on-media/2016/02/donald-trump-libel-laws-219866 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20160227001333/http://www.politico.com/blogs/on-media/2016/02/donald-trump-libel-laws-219866 |archive-date=2016-02-27 |access-date=2025-03-01 |website=[[Politico]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Official language===
In 2015 during a debate, Trump said, "This is a country where we speak English, not Spanish."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2016/09/donald-trumps-english-only-campaign-228559|first=Shane|last=Goldmacher|date=September 23, 2016|title=Trump's English-only campaign|website=[[Politico]]|access-date=January 27, 2020}}</ref>

In June 2019, Senator [[Steve Daines]] proposed reviving the previously unsuccessful language amendment, and in doing so received the support of the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/06/trump-backs-ban-flag-burning-no-brainer.html|title=Trump Backs Measure to Ban Flag Burning: 'A No Brainer!'|work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|first=Daniel|last=Politi|date=June 15, 2019}}</ref>

On March 1, 2025, Trump signed an [[executive order]] [[English-only movement|designating English as the country's]] [[official language]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/mar/02/trump-signs-executive-order-designating-english-as-official-language-of-us|title=Trump signs executive order designating English as official language of US|work=The Guardian |agency=Associated Press|date=March 2, 2025}}</ref>

===Video game violence===
{{Main|Violence and video games}}

Trump has voiced his opposition to [[video game violence]]. After it was erroneously reported that the [[Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting|Sandy Hook shooter]] frequently played violent video games, Trump tweeted, "Video game violence & glorification must be stopped—it is creating monsters!"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://twitter.com/realDonaldTrump/status/280812064539283457|title=Donald J. Trump on Twitter|website=[[Twitter]]|access-date=May 26, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Chris Morris|url=https://www.yahoo.com/tech/bp/donald-trump--not-so-great-for-gamers-201007482.html|publisher=[[Plugged In (publication)]]/[[Yahoo! Tech]]|title=Donald Trump: Not so great for gamers|date=August 10, 2015}}</ref>

Following the [[Parkland high school shooting|Stoneman Douglas shooting event]], President Trump arranged to meet with several video game industry professionals on March 8, 2018; in attendance beyond Trump and other Congressmen included Mike Gallagher, the president and CEO of the ESA; Pat Vance, the president of the ESRB; Strauss Zelnick, CEO of [[Take Two Interactive]], Robert Altman, CEO of [[ZeniMax Media]]; [[L. Brent Bozell III|Brent Bozell]], founder of the [[Media Research Center]]; and Melissa Hanson, program manager for the [[Parents Television Council]]. The meeting was not designed to come to a solution but only for the invited parties to present their stance on video games and their relationship to violent activity as to try to determine appropriate steps in the future.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://variety.com/2018/politics/news/trump-video-games-2-1202721889/ | title = Trump Meets With Video Game Industry, Watchdog Groups to Talk Gun Violence | first = Ted | last = Johnson | date = March 8, 2018 | access-date = March 12, 2018 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] }}</ref> At the start of the meeting, the President showed the attendees a short 88-second video of numerous violent video game segments put together by his staff, including the infamous "[[No Russian]]" level from ''[[Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2]]'', which featured the player watching and potentially participating in a massacre of civilians in an airport.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gamespot.com/articles/president-trumps-video-games-meeting-included-a-vi/1100-6457255/ | title = President Trump's Video Games Meeting Included A Violent Game Montage |first = Chris | last = Pereira | date = March 10, 2018 | access-date = March 12, 2018 | work = [[GameSpot]] }}</ref>

After the [[2019 El Paso shooting]], Trump said in a speech, "We must stop the glorification of violence in our society. This includes the gruesome and grisly video games that are now commonplace. It is too easy today for troubled youth to surround themselves with a culture that celebrates violence. We must stop or substantially reduce this and it has to begin immediately."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/fact-check-trump-suggests-video-games-blame-mass-shootings-n1039411|title=Fact check: Trump suggests video games to blame for mass shootings|publisher=[[NBC News]]|date=August 5, 2019 |access-date=2019-10-08}}</ref>

===Online gambling===
Trump supports [[online gambling]], based on the following reasoning: "This has to happen because many other countries are doing it and like usual the U.S. is just missing out."<ref>{{cite magazine|author=Nathan Vardi |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/nathanvardi/2011/10/20/donald-trump-internet-gambling-mogul/|magazine=[[Forbes]]|title=Donald Trump: Internet Gambling Mogul|date=October 20, 2011}}</ref>

===Pardons===
{{Main|List of people granted executive clemency in the first Trump presidency|List of people granted executive clemency in the second Trump presidency}}

Trump has said multiple times that if he were [[2024 United States presidential election|reelected in 2024]], he would [[pardon]] participants in the [[January 6 United States Capitol attack]].<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Pager |first1=Tyler |date=January 30, 2022 |title=Trump suggests that if he is reelected, he will pardon Jan. 6 Capitol rioters |language=en-US |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2022/01/29/trump-jan6-protesters/ |access-date=January 30, 2022 |issn=0190-8286 |archive-date=January 31, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220131120245/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2022/01/29/trump-jan6-protesters/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Papenfuss |first1=Mary |date=June 17, 2022 |title=Trump Says He'll 'Look Very Seriously' At Pardoning Jan. 6 Defendants If Reelected |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/trump-nashville-very-very-seriously-pardons-jan-6-insurrection_n_62acecfbe4b0cdccbe5d9bc1 |access-date=June 18, 2022 |website=HuffPost |language=en |archive-date=June 21, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220621022230/https://www.huffpost.com/entry/trump-nashville-very-very-seriously-pardons-jan-6-insurrection_n_62acecfbe4b0cdccbe5d9bc1 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Papenfuss |first1=Mary |date=2022-11-05 |title='Let Them All Go Now': Trump Calls For Release Of Everyone Arrested In Jan. 6 Riot |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/donald-trump-release-jan-6-prisoners-unfair_n_6366cea1e4b05f221e7a9335 |access-date=2022-11-06 |website=HuffPost |language=en |archive-date=November 6, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221106162718/https://www.huffpost.com/entry/donald-trump-release-jan-6-prisoners-unfair_n_6366cea1e4b05f221e7a9335 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On January 20, 2025, Upon assuming the presidency again, Trump issued roughly [[Pardon of January 6 United States Capitol attack defendants|1,500 pardons and 14 commutations to people charged in connection]] to the [[January 6 United States Capitol attack]].<ref>{{cite web |author1=Reilly, Ryan J. |title=Trump pardons roughly 1,500 criminal defendants charged in the Jan. 6 Capitol attack |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/trump-set-pardon-defendants-stormed-capitol-jan-6-2021-rcna187735 |publisher=NBC News |access-date=20 January 2025 |date=20 January 2025}}</ref>

==Science and technology==
:''See also [[#Climate change and pollution|Climate change and pollution]], above.''

A 2016 report in ''[[Scientific American]]'' graded Trump and three other top presidential candidates—Hillary Clinton, Gary Johnson, and Jill Stein—on science policy, based on their responses to a twenty-question [[ScienceDebate.org]] survey. Trump "came in last on all counts" in grading, with scientists and researchers faulting him for a lack of knowledge or appreciation of scientific issues.<ref>Christine Gorman & Ryan F. Mandelbaum, [http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/grading-the-presidential-candidates-on-science/ Grading the Presidential Candidates on Science: Scientific American evaluates responses from Clinton, Trump, Johnson and Stein to 20 questions], ''Scientific American'' (September 26, 2016).</ref>

===Space===
{{Main|Space policy of the first Trump administration|Space policy of the second Trump administration}}

[[File:President Trump Signs NASA Transition Authorization Act of 2017 (33443482781).jpg|thumb|President Trump signing the NASA Transition Authorization Act of 2017]]
As of October 2016, one of Trump's policy advisors declared that, under Trump, [[NASA]] would recreate the [[National Space Council]] and pursue a goal of "[[Exploration of the solar system|human exploration of the solar system]] by the end of the century", to drive technology developments to a stronger degree than a [[Human mission to Mars|crewed mission to Mars]]. Other goals would include shifting budget to deep space exploration from Earth science and climate research, and pursuit of small satellites and hypersonic technology.<ref name="ms">{{Cite news|url=http://spacenews.com/what-a-trump-administration-means-for-space/|title=What a Trump administration means for space |date=2016-11-09|newspaper=SpaceNews.com|access-date=2016-11-11}}</ref> A possibility of China joining the [[International Space Station programme|International Space Station program]] was also considered.<ref name="ms"/> A stronger role of [[Lunar mission|crewed Lunar exploration]] is possible in NASA's quest for a crewed mission to Mars.<ref name="ms"/> Prior to that statement, the Trump campaign appeared to have little to no space policy at all.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2016/08/trump-flip-flops-on-nasa-from-wonderful-to-like-a-third-world-nation/|title=Trump: "Look at your space program… We're like a third world nation"|date=August 8, 2016|website=Ars Technica|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref>

===Technology and net neutrality===
{{Main|Net neutrality in the United States}}

As of June 2016, Trump has published no tech policy proposals.<ref name="SwartzInternet">Jon Swartz, [https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/columnist/2016/06/28/clinton-tech-plan-reads-like-silicon-valley-wish-list/86474144/ Clinton wants high-speed Internet in every U.S. home by 2020], ''[[USA Today]]'' (June 30, 2016).</ref> On the campaign trail, Trump frequently antagonized [[Silicon Valley]] figures,<ref name="ChmielewskiInternet">Dawn Chmielewski, [http://www.recode.net/2016/6/30/12060228/hillary-clinton-donald-trump-tech-policy Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump are worlds apart on tech policy issues], ''[[Recode]]'' (June 30, 2016).</ref> using his Twitter account to lambast tech leaders such as [[Jeff Bezos]] of [[Amazon.com|Amazon]], [[Tim Cook]] of [[Apple Inc.|Apple]], and [[Brian Chesky]] of [[Airbnb]] over a series of months.<ref name="SwartzInternet"/> He is particularly concerned about the social breakdown of American culture caused by technology, and said, "the Internet and the whole computer age is really a mixed bag,"<ref name="Trump On The Record">{{cite web | title = Trump: Sony has 'no courage, no guts...it's extortion' | publisher=[[Fox News]] | url = http://www.foxnews.com/on-air/on-the-record/2014/12/19/trump-sony-has-no-courage-no-guts-its-extortion | access-date=September 20, 2016}}</ref> having "complicated lives very greatly".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/312076-trump-computers-have-complicated-lives-very-greatly/|title=Trump on Russian hacking: 'Computers have complicated lives very greatly'|first=Rebecca|last=Savransky|date=December 29, 2016|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref>

Trump is opposed to [[net neutrality]], asserting that it is "Obama's attack on the internet" and saying that it "will target the conservative media."<ref>Caroline Craig, [http://www.infoworld.com/article/2986220/net-neutrality/where-the-candidates-stand-on-net-neutrality.html Where the candidates stand on Net neutrality], ''InfoWorld'' (September 25, 2015).</ref>

Trump has suggested closing "certain areas" of the Internet. Regarding how this relates to freedom of speech, he added "Somebody will say, 'Oh freedom of speech, freedom of speech.' These are foolish people. We have a lot of foolish people."<ref>David Goldman, [https://web.archive.org/web/20151212192417/http://money.cnn.com/2015/12/08/technology/donald-trump-internet/index.html "Donald Trump wants to 'close up' the Internet"], ''[[CNN]]'' (December 8, 2015).</ref>

The tech publication ''[[Recode]]'' reports that Trump has made no public statements on the issues of [[United States patent law|patent reform]] or [[broadband access]].<ref name="ChmielewskiInternet"/>

The [[Free Press (advocacy group)|Free Press Action Fund]], a group of tech policy activists, rated Trump the worst 2016 presidential candidate for "citizens' digital lives," citing his positions opposing reforming the Patriot Act, favoring [[Internet censorship]], and opposing net neutrality.<ref>Sam Thielman, [https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/mar/14/election-2016-tech-policy-net-neutrality-bernie-sanders-donald-trump "Tech policy activists find Bernie Sanders is best bet – while Trump is the worst"], ''[[The Guardian]]'' (March 14, 2016).</ref>

==Social issues and civil liberties==
{{Main|Social policy of the first Trump administration}}

=== Abortion ===
{{Main|Abortion in the United States}}

[[File:March for Life (49435741078).jpg|thumb|right|President Trump speaks at the 2020 [[March for Life (Washington, D.C.)|March for Life]].]]
Trump describes himself as [[pro-life]] and generally opposes [[abortion]] with some exceptions: rape, incest, and circumstances endangering the health of the mother.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.cnn.com/2016/04/21/politics/donald-trump-republican-platform-abortion/ |title=Trump: I would change GOP platform on abortion |last=Wright |first=David |date=April 21, 2016 |publisher=[[CNN]]}}</ref> As a candidate in 2016, he said he believes the issue of abortion "would have been better if it were up to the states."<ref>{{cite web |via=[[YouTube]] |title=Donald Trump clarifies his stance on abortion |date=2 April 2016 |work=[[Face the Nation]] |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-33wt9KKGxs |language=en |access-date=2022-05-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Donald Trump took 5 different positions on abortion in 3 days |language=en-US |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2016/04/03/donald-trumps-ever-shifting-positions-on-abortion/ |first=Philip |last=Bump |access-date=2022-05-09 |date=3 April 2016 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> He said he was committed to appointing justices who would overturn the ruling in ''[[Roe v. Wade]]''.<ref name="60min">{{cite news|last=de Vogue|first=Ariane|date=November 15, 2016|title=Trump: Same-sex marriage is 'settled,' but Roe v Wade can be changed|work=[[60 Minutes]]|publisher=[[CBS]]|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2016/11/14/politics/trump-gay-marriage-abortion-supreme-court/|access-date=November 30, 2016|via=[[CNN]]}}</ref> 

In October 1999, during Trump's [[Donald Trump 2000 presidential campaign|2000 presidential campaign]], he stated on ''[[Meet the Press]]'' "I am very pro-choice. I hate the concept of abortion. [...] But I am strongly pro-choice."<ref name="many many">{{cite web |publisher=[[NBC News]] |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/trumps-many-abortion-positions-timeline-rcna146601 |title=A timeline of Trump's many, many positions on abortion |date=April 8, 2024 |first=Natasha |last=Korecki |access-date=17 February 2026 }}</ref><ref name="evolving">{{cite news |url=https://abcnews.com/Politics/donald-trumps-evolving-stance-abortion/story?id=38057176 |title=Donald Trump's Evolving Stance on Abortion |first=Meghan |last=Keneally |date=March 31, 2016 |work=ABC News |access-date=17 February 2026 }}</ref> While contemplating a campaign for the [[2012 Republican Party presidential primaries|2012 Republican presidential nomination]], Trump gave a speech at [[Conservative Political Action Conference|CPAC]] in 2011, where he stated he was pro-life,<ref name="many many"/> a stance he reiterated during [[Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign|his 2016 campaign]].<ref name="evolving"/>

After ''Roe v. Wade'' was overturned in ''[[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization]]'' in 2022, Trump took credit for the decision but has not stated whether he supports a federal ban or federal restrictions on abortion.<ref name="vr"/> During the [[2024 United States presidential debates#September 10: Second presidential debate (ABC, Philadelphia)|second presidential debate]] in September 2024, Trump stated he would not sign a federal ban but declined to answer questions about whether he would veto such legislation.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dixon |first1=Matt |title=Trump says he wouldn't sign a federal abortion ban while dodging veto questions |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/trump-says-wont-sign-federal-abortion-ban-dodging-veto-questions-rcna170536 |access-date=10 November 2024 |publisher=[[NBC News]] |date=11 September 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

=== LGBTQ rights ===
{{See also|LGBTQ rights in the United States}}
Despite being the first [[bisexual]] president, Trump has rolled back many existing LGBTQ protections and also introduced new policies that undermine [[LGBTQ rights in the United States|LGBTQ rights]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Donald Trump|url=https://www.glaad.org/tap/donald-trump|date=2016-11-28|website=GLAAD|access-date=2020-05-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title='Whiplash' Of LGBTQ Protections And Rights, From Obama To Trump|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2020/03/02/804873211/whiplash-of-lgbtq-protections-and-rights-from-obama-to-trump|last=Simmons-Duffin|first=Selena|date=2 March 2020|publisher=[[NPR]]|access-date=2020-05-19}}</ref>

==== Workplace discrimination ====
{{Main|Employment discrimination law in the United States}}

In early 2017, Trump reversed an Obama-era directive that had required companies with large federal contracts to prove their compliance with LGBTQ protections.<ref name="Vogue">{{cite magazine|last1=Kutner|first1=Jenny|date=March 29, 2017|title=Trump Rolls Back Protections for LGBTQ Workers, Despite Recent Promises|url=https://www.vogue.com/article/trump-executive-order-rolls-back-lgbtq-protections|magazine=Vogue|access-date=6 December 2018}}</ref>

In 2018, Trump signed the [[United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement|United States–Mexico–Canada trade agreement]] with a footnote exempting the United States from complying with the agreement's call for an end to "sex-based discrimination".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trump agrees to USMCA agreement with LGBT provisions|url=https://www.washingtonblade.com/2018/11/30/trump-agrees-to-nafta-update-with-lgbt-provisions/|date=November 30, 2018}}</ref>

The Trump administration unsuccessfully tried to eliminate nondiscrimination protections at the level of the Supreme Court, where the Justice Department intervened in three employment lawsuits—''[[Bostock v. Clayton County]]''; ''[[Altitude Express, Inc. v. Zarda]]''; and [[R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes Inc. v. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission|''Harris Funeral Homes v. EEOC'']]—arguing that Title VII of the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]] does not prohibit job discrimination based on [[sexual orientation]]<ref>{{cite news|last1=Barbash|first1=Fred|date=July 27, 2017|title=Trump administration, intervening in major LGBTQ case, says job bias law does not cover sexual orientation|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/morning-mix/wp/2017/07/27/trump-administration-intervening-in-major-lgbt-case-says-job-bias-law-does-not-cover-sexual-orientation/|access-date=August 24, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Feuer|first1=Alan|date=July 27, 2017|title=Justice Department Says Rights Law Doesn't Protect Gays|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/27/nyregion/justice-department-gays-workplace.html|access-date=August 25, 2017}}</ref> or "transgender status."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court To Legalize Firing Transgender Workers|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/trump-administration-supreme-court-transgender-workers_n_5d57254be4b056fafd0be1aa|last=Blumberg|first=Antonia|date=2019-08-16|website=[[HuffPost]]|access-date=2019-08-17}}</ref> However, despite the Trump administration's intervention, the Supreme Court ruled on these three cases on June 15, 2020, that [[sexual orientation]] and [[gender identity]] are indeed covered under existing protections for "[[sex discrimination]]".

==== Healthcare discrimination ====
The [[Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act|Affordable Care Act]] included an Obama-era nondiscrimination provision that explicitly entitled people to receive care regardless of sex or gender identity, but the Trump administration reversed it. On June 12, 2020, the Department of Health and Human Services finalized and revealed its replacement rule. Now, healthcare providers and insurers may decide whether to serve transgender people.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Sanger-Katz|first1=Margot|last2=Weiland |first2=Noah|date=2020-06-12|title=Trump Administration Erases Transgender Civil Rights Protections in Health Care |work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/12/us/politics/trump-transgender-rights.html|access-date=2020-06-13|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|publisher=Department of Health and Human Services|title=Nondiscrimination in Health and Health Education Programs or Activities, Delegation of Authority (4153-01-P)|url=https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/1557-final-rule.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200613001752/https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/1557-final-rule.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 13, 2020|access-date=12 June 2020}}</ref>

==== Transgender rights ====
{{Main|Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration|Transgender rights in the United States}}

One month after taking office, Trump reversed a directive from the Obama administration that had allowed [[transgender]] students to use bathrooms that correspond with their [[gender identity]]; this reversal allowed public schools to make their own rules about gendered bathrooms.<ref>{{cite news|author1=Faith Karimi|author2=Emanuella Grinberg|title=Trump's reversal on transgender directive: How we got here|publisher=[[CNN]]|url=http://www.cnn.com/2017/02/23/health/transgender-bathrooms-trump-q-and-a/index.html|access-date=2017-08-03}}</ref> In 2020, the U.S. Department of Education threatened to withhold funding from Connecticut school districts that allow transgender girls to compete on girls' teams, claiming that the transgender students' participation is a violation of [[Title IX]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=US rules against state allowing transgender athletes to compete in women's sports|url=https://thehill.com/changing-america/respect/equality/499960-us-rules-against-state-allowing-transgender-athletes-to/|last=Kelley|first=Alexandra|date=2020-05-28|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|access-date=2020-05-28}}</ref>

Six months into his presidency, Trump tweeted that transgender individuals would not be allowed to serve "in any capacity" in the U.S. military, an order that took Pentagon officials by surprise.<ref>{{cite magazine|last1=Miller|first1=Zeke|date=July 26, 2017|title=President Trump's Tweets Catch D.C. Off Guard|magazine=Time|url=https://time.com/4874245/president-trumps-tweets-catch-d-c-off-guard/|access-date=August 24, 2017}}</ref> Eventually, in 2019, the Supreme Court—without hearing arguments or explaining its own decision—allowed the Trump administration to move ahead with the ban.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Stohr|first=Greg|date=22 January 2019|title=Supreme Court Lets Trump's Transgender Military Ban Take Effect|work=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg L.P.]]|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-01-22/supreme-court-lets-trump-s-transgender-military-ban-take-effect|access-date=22 January 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Jackson|first=Brie|date=22 January 2019|title=President Trump's transgender ban goes into effect|work=ABC4|url=https://www.abc4.com/news/national/president-trump-s-transgender-ban-goes-into-effect/1716979968|access-date=22 January 2019|archive-date=January 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190123121503/https://www.abc4.com/news/national/president-trump-s-transgender-ban-goes-into-effect/1716979968|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2018, the [[Department of Health and Human Services]] wrote a memo planning to establish a definition of gender based on [[Sex assignment|sex assignment at birth]]. The memo argued in favor of a definition of gender "on a biological basis that is clear, grounded in science, objective and administrable" and the government's prerogative to [[Genetic testing|genetically test]] individuals to determine their sex. If approved by the Justice Department, the definition would apply across federal agencies, notably the departments of [[United States Department of Education|Education]], [[United States Department of Justice|Justice]], and [[United States Department of Labor|Labor]], which, along with Health and Human Services, are responsible for enforcing [[Title IX]] nondiscrimination statutes.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Green|first1=Erica L.|last2=Benner|first2=Katie|last3=Pear|first3=Robert|date=21 October 2018|title='Transgender' Could Be Defined Out of Existence Under Trump Administration|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/21/us/politics/transgender-trump-administration-sex-definition.html|access-date=2018-10-27}}</ref>

The Trump administration also reversed Obama-era guidance on [[LGBTQ people in prison|transgender prisoners]], ordering the [[Federal Bureau of Prisons|Bureau of Prisons]] instead to house them according to their "biological sex."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Browning|first1=Bil|date=12 May 2018|title=Trump strips transgender prisoners of protections against rape & abuse|publisher=LGBTQ Nation|url=https://www.lgbtqnation.com/2018/05/trump-strips-transgender-prisoners-protections-rape-abuse/|access-date=9 December 2018}}</ref>

In 2019, HUD proposed a new rule<ref>{{Cite web|title=RIN: 2506-AC53|url=https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eAgendaViewRule?pubId=201904&RIN=2506-AC53|website=reginfo.gov|access-date=2019-05-23}}</ref> to weaken the 2012 Equal Access Rule, which requires equal access to housing regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. This could allow homeless shelters to place transgender women in men's housing or to deny transgender people admission altogether.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Proposed HUD rule would strip transgender protections at homeless shelters|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2019/05/22/proposed-hud-rule-would-strip-transgender-protections-homeless-shelters/|last=Jan|first=Tracy|date=22 May 2019|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=22 May 2019}}</ref>

In a 2021 speech at the [[Conservative Political Action Conference]] in [[Orlando, Florida]], Trump referred to [[transgender women]] who are athletes as "biological males".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trump promises to ban transgender women from sports if re-elected|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/nbc-out/out-politics-and-policy/trump-promises-ban-transgender-women-sports-re-elected-rcna14248|access-date=2022-02-09|publisher=[[NBC News]]|date=February 2022 |language=en}}</ref> During his second presidency Trump signed [[Executive Order 14201]] titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" that attempts to ban [[Trans woman|transgender women athletes]] of all ages from competing on girls and [[women's sports]] teams.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-05 |title=Trump signs executive order that will ban transgender athletes from women's sports - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-executive-order-banning-transgender-athletes-womens-sports/ |access-date=2025-08-31 |publisher=CBS News |language=en-US}}</ref>

In April 2021 Donald Trump attacked Arkansas governor [[Asa Hutchinson]] for vetoing legislation that would have banned gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-04-08|title=Donald Trump attacks GOP Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson over veto of transgender bill: "Bye-Bye!"|url=https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trump-attacks-gop-arkansas-governor-asa-hutchinson-over-veto-transgender-bill-bye-bye-1582142|access-date=2021-04-08|website=[[Newsweek]]}}</ref>

In a video posted on his 2024 and during a Campaign Event in Fort Dodge, Iowa in November 2023 campaign website, Trump called [[Transgender health care|gender-affirming care]] to minors "chemical, physical, sexual and emotional mutilation" and that he would pass a federal law banning it if in office. He also stated that he would have the Department of Justice investigate pharmaceutical companies and hospital networks to determine if they "covered up the long-term side effects of gender transitions" and would remove hospitals who provide gender-affirming care from receiving funds from both Medicare and Medicaid.<ref name="vr">{{Cite news |last=Cai |first=Sophia |date=May 21, 2023 |title=Trump's 2025 vision, revealed |work=[[Axios (website)|Axios]]|url=https://www.axios.com/2023/05/21/trump-2025-vision |access-date=May 21, 2023}}</ref><ref name="gi">{{Cite web |title=President Trump's Plan to Protect Children from Left-Wing Gender Insanity {{!}} Donald J. Trump For President 2024 |url=https://www.donaldjtrump.com/agenda47/president-trumps-plan-to-protect-children-from-left-wing-gender-insanity |access-date=2023-05-21 |website=www.donaldjtrump.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=FiscalNote |first=Roll Call |title=Roll Call Factba.se - Speech: Donald Trump Holds a Campaign Event in Fort Dodge, Iowa - November 18, 2023 |url=https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-campaign-event-fort-dodge-iowa-november-18-2023 |access-date=2025-08-31 |website=Roll Call Factba.se |language=en-US}}</ref> During his second presidency Trump signed [[Executive Order 14187]] which directed federal agencies to withhold funding from institutions that provide gender-affirming care for minors (which the order labeled as "chemical and surgical mutilation") and calls for legal enforcement against such practices.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-03 |title=Protecting Children From Chemical and Surgical Mutilation |url=https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/02/03/2025-02194/protecting-children-from-chemical-and-surgical-mutilation |access-date=2025-08-31 |website=Federal Register |language=en}}</ref>

On his 2024 campaign website Trump states that he would direct Congress to pass a bill that would mandate the United States only recognize the male and female genders and that they are assigned at birth.<ref name="gi"/> During his second presidency Trump signed [[Executive Order 14168]] which removed recognition of gender identity from the U.S. government, defines sex in the eyes of the federal government as a male-female binary biological classification, and attempts to end federal funding for "gender ideology".<ref>{{Cite web |last=House |first=The White |date=2025-01-21 |title=Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism And Restoring Biological Truth To The Federal Government |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/defending-women-from-gender-ideology-extremism-and-restoring-biological-truth-to-the-federal-government/ |access-date=2025-08-31 |website=The White House |language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Same-sex marriage ====
{{Main|Same-sex marriage in the United States}}

After several decades of national debate, the U.S. Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage nationwide in 2015 in the ''[[Obergefell v. Hodges]]'' ruling. After his election, Trump acknowledged that the court had already "settled" the issue.<ref name="MEhren" /><ref name="60min" /><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cnn.com/2016/11/14/politics/trump-gay-marriage-abortion-supreme-court/ |title=Trump: Same-sex marriage is 'settled', but Roe v Wade can be changed |publisher=[[CNN]] |first=Ariane |last=de Vogue |date=November 15, 2016 |access-date=November 30, 2016}}</ref> Trump has not, however, been a personal proponent of same-sex marriage, saying as recently as 2011 that he was "not in favor of gay marriage"<ref>{{Cite news|last=Uy|first=JD|date=15 February 2011|title=Donald Trump says he's against gay marriage|work=Metro Weekly (DC)|url=https://www.metroweekly.com/2011/02/donald-trump-says-hes-against/|access-date=29 March 2020}}</ref> and saying during his 2016 campaign that he would "strongly consider" appointing Supreme Court justices who were inclined to overturn ''Obergefell v. Hodges''.<ref>{{cite news|last=Johnson|first=Chris|date=March 22, 2016|title=Trump's far-fetched plan to undo marriage equality|work=[[Washington Blade]]|url=http://www.washingtonblade.com/2016/03/22/trump-unlikely-to-undo-marriage-equality-before-supreme-court/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Trump attacks Supreme Court decision legalizing same-sex marriage|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2016/01/31/trump-attacks-supreme-court-decision-legalizing-same-sex-marriage/|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=2017-03-24}}</ref><ref name="rl"/> He had previously supported and been a proponent of [[civil union]]s and he included the policy in his [[Donald Trump 2000 presidential campaign|2000 presidential campaign]] as a [[Reform Party of the United States of America|Reform Party]] candidate.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Robert |last2=Johnson |first2=Jenna |date=July 26, 2017 |title='It's not my thing': A history of Trump's shifting relationship with the LGBT community |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/its-not-my-thing-a-history-of-trumps-shifting-relationship-with-the-lgbt-community/2017/07/26/92920302-7220-11e7-8f39-eeb7d3a2d304_story.html |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-09-28 |title=READ: Donald Trump's Advocate Interview Where He Defends Gays, Mexicans |url=http://www.advocate.com/election/2015/9/28/read-donald-trumps-advocate-interview-where-he-defends-gays-mexicans |access-date=2022-04-27 |website=advocate.com |language=en}}</ref> [[Donald Trump 2020 presidential campaign|Donald Trump's 2020 presidential campaign]] launched "Trump Pride", a coalition within the Trump campaign focused on outreach to LGBTQ voters, and stated that Trump now supports same-sex marriage.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Haberman|first=Maggie|date=2020-08-26|title=After Three Years of Attacking L.G.B.T.Q. Rights, Trump Suddenly Tries Outreach|language=en-US|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/08/26/us/politics/trump-lgbtq-rights.html|access-date=2021-12-22|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-10-13|title=Donald Trump just sent invites to a 'Trump Pride' rally with no mention of LGBT+ people – or his 181 attacks on the community|url=https://www.pinknews.co.uk/2020/10/13/donald-trump-pride-rainbow-richard-grenell-lara-eric-pennsylvania-rally-amy-coney-barrett/|access-date=2021-12-22|website=PinkNews }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|author=Kate Bennett|title=Melania Trump posts video that misleads on the President's LGBTQ policies|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/30/politics/melania-trump-lgbtq-donald-trump/index.html|access-date=2021-12-22|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=October 30, 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-08-20|title=Trump Bafflingly Says It's "Great Honor" to Be "Most Pro-Gay President in America"|url=https://www.them.us/story/log-cabin-republicans-trump-tweet|access-date=2021-12-22|website=them.|language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Data collection ====

Lo|date=30 March 2018|title=2020 Census Will Ask About Same-Sex Relationships|publisher=[[NPR]]|url=https://www.npr.org/2018/03/30/598192154/2020-census-will-ask-about-same-sex-relationships|access-date=9 December 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite Community Survey]],<ref>{{cite news|last1=Johnson|first1=Chris|date=28 March 2017|title=Trump's U.S. Census proposes, immediately cuts LGBT survey questions|newspaper=[[Washington patients|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2019/04/24/trump-administration-prepares-rule-that-civil-rights-groups-worry-may-deny-care-transgender-patients/|access-date=22 May 2019}}</ref>

==== HIV/AIDS ====
{{Main|HIV/AIDS in the United States}}

In 2017, Trump dissolved the [[Office of National AIDS Policy]] and the [[Presidential Advisory Council on HIV/AIDS]], both of which had existed since the 1990s. Every year on World AIDS Day—2017, 2018, 2019—Trump's proclamations have omitted mention of LGBTQ people.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Armus|first1=Teo|date=1 December 2017|title=Trump's World AIDS Day proclamation leaves out LGBTQ people|publisher=[[NBC News]]|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/feature/nbc-out/trump-s-world-aids-day-proclamation-leaves-out-lgbtq-people-n825756|url-status=live|access-date=9 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181209165204/https://www.nbcnews.com/feature/nbc-out/trump-s-world-aids-day-proclamation-leaves-out-lgbtq-people-n825756|archive-date=9 December 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=President Donald J. Trump Proclaims December 1, 2017, as World AIDS Day|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-proclaims-december-1-2017-world-aids-day/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120202416/https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-proclaims-december-1-2017-world-aids-day/|archive-date=January 20, 2021|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[White House]]|access-date=2019-12-01}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Presidential Proclamation on World AIDS Day, 2018|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/presidential-proclamation-world-aids-day-2018/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120202326/https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/presidential-proclamation-world-aids-day-2018/|archive-date=2021-01-20|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[White House]]|access-date=2019-12-01}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Presidential Proclamation on World AIDS Day, 2019|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/presidential-proclamation-world-aids-day-2019/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120202040/https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/presidential-proclamation-world-aids-day-2019/|archive-date=2021-01-20|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[White House]]|access-date=2019-12-01}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Herrick|first1=John|date=1 December 2018|title=VP Pence Criticized for Not Mentioning Gay Community in AIDS Speech|publisher=WIBC|url=https://www.wibc.com/news/national/vp-pence-criticized-not-mentioning-gay-community-aids-speech|access-date=9 December 2018|archive-date=March 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190329224106/https://www.wibc.com/news/national/vp-pence-criticized-not-mentioning-gay-community-aids-speech|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==== Religion-based exemptions ====
In 2018, the [[United States Department of Health and Human Services|Department of Health and Human Services]] (HHS) announced the creation of the Conscience and Religious Freedom Division.<ref>{{cite news|date=18 January 2018|title=HHS Announces New Conscience and Religious Freedom Division|publisher=Health and Human Services|url=https://www.hhs.gov/about/news/2018/01/18/hhs-ocr-announces-new-conscience-and-religious-freedom-division.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180118210204/https://www.hhs.gov/about/news/2018/01/18/hhs-ocr-announces-new-conscience-and-religious-freedom-division.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 18, 2018|access-date=21 January 2018}}</ref> Its purpose is to enforce federal laws that related to "conscience and religious freedom"; that is, to enable individuals and businesses to exempt themselves from obeying nondiscrimination laws.

In 2019, HHS granted an exemption from an Obama-era nondiscrimination regulation to a foster care agency in South Carolina. HHS cited the [[Religious Freedom Restoration Act]] (RFRA) as a basis for allowing federally funded Christian groups to discriminate against non-Christians.<ref>{{Cite web|title=S.C. group can reject gays and Jews as foster parents, admin says|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/feature/nbc-out/s-c-group-can-reject-gays-jews-foster-parents-trump-n962306|last=Fitzsimons|first=Tim|date=2019-01-24|publisher=[[NBC News]]|access-date=2019-01-27}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=The Trump Administration Will Let Adoption Agencies Turn Away Jews and Same-Sex Couples. Thank SCOTUS.|url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/01/trump-adoption-same-sex-couples-jews-miracle-mill.html| author-link = Mark Joseph Stern | last = Stern |first=Mark Joseph|date=2019-01-24|website=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|access-date=2020-02-09}}</ref> Later that year, the [[United States Department of Labor|Department of Labor]], also referencing the RFRA, proposed a new rule to exempt "religious organizations" from obeying employment nondiscrimination law if they invoke "sincerely held religious tenets and beliefs" as their reason to discriminate.<ref>{{Cite web|title=U.S. Department of Labor Proposes a Rule Clarifying Civil Rights Protections for Religious Organizations {{!}} U.S. Department of Labor|url=https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/ofccp/ofccp20190814|date=14 August 2019|website=www.dol.gov|access-date=2019-08-14}}</ref> In 2020, the Justice Department filed a brief with the Supreme Court in support of another foster care agency in Pennsylvania, defending the agency's right to turn away same-sex couples as part of its "free exercise of religion".<ref>{{Cite web|last=Kelleher|first=Patrick|date=4 June 2020|title=The Trump administration just asked the Supreme Court to make it legal to ban same-sex couples from adopting|url=https://www.pinknews.co.uk/2020/06/04/donald-trump-department-of-justice-brief-supreme-court-same-sex-parents-adoption-catholic-social-services/|access-date=6 June 2020|website=Pink News}}</ref>

In 2019, the [[United States Department of State|State Department]] created the [[Commission on Unalienable Rights]] to initiate philosophical discussions of human rights that are grounded in the Catholic concept of "[[natural law]]" rather than modern identities based on gender and sexuality. Most of the twelve members of the commission have a history of anti-LGBTQ comments.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Wong|first1=Edward|last2=Sullivan|first2=Eileen|date=2019-07-08|title=New Human Rights Panel Raises Fears of a Narrowing U.S. Advocacy|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/08/us/politics/state-human-rights.html|access-date=2019-07-12|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

==== Education ====
In March 2022 Trump said he approved of Florida's [[Florida Parental Rights in Education Act|Parental Rights in Education bill]], also referred to as the "don't say gay" bill, during an interview with ''[[The Washington Post]]'' that occurred after the bill was signed by Florida governor [[Ron DeSantis]], but did not elaborate as to why he supports it.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brooke Migdon|date=2022-04-08 |title=Trump says DeSantis signing 'Don't Say Gay' was a 'good move' |url=https://thehill.com/changing-america/respect/equality/3262616-trump-says-desantis-signing-dont-say-gay-was-a-good-move/ |access-date=2022-04-10 |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Diplomacy ====
The Trump administration eliminated the State Department's position for a [[United States Special Envoy for the Human Rights of LGBTI Persons|Special Envoy for the Human Rights of LGBTI Persons]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Envoy for the Human Rights of LGBTI Persons: Vacant (Archive)|url=https://2009-2017.state.gov/r/pa/ei/biog/title/as/237773.htm|date=July 27, 2017|publisher=U.S. State Department|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170727032140/https://2009-2017.state.gov/r/pa/ei/biog/title/as/237773.htm|archive-date=July 27, 2017|access-date=October 21, 2018}}</ref>

In 2018, the Trump administration denied visas to the unmarried same-sex partners of foreign diplomats, even if they were from countries that recognize only civil partnership or that ban same-sex marriage.<ref>{{Cite news|title=U.S. Halts Visas For Diplomats' Same-Sex Partners If They're Not Married|url=https://www.npr.org/2018/10/02/653646121/u-s-halts-visas-for-diplomats-same-sex-partners-if-they-re-not-married|publisher=[[NPR]]|date=October 2, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191012194746/https://www.npr.org/2018/10/02/653646121/u-s-halts-visas-for-diplomats-same-sex-partners-if-they-re-not-married|archive-date=2019-10-12|access-date=2019-10-14|last1=Dwyer|first1=Colin}}</ref>

[[Richard Grenell]], nominated by Trump as the U.S. ambassador to Germany, is openly gay. In February 2019, Grenell was announced as the leader of a new campaign to decriminalize homosexuality worldwide, and he hosted a meeting with 11 European activists.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gilchrist|first=Tracy E.|date=19 February 2019|title=Trump Launches Campaign to Decriminalize Homosexuality|work=Advocate|url=https://www.advocate.com/politics/2019/2/19/trumps-campaign-launches-campaign-decriminalize-homosexuality|access-date=23 February 2019}}</ref> Trump seemed unaware of the initiative when he was asked about it the next day.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Fitzsimons|first=Tim|date=21 February 2019|title='I don't know': Trump draws blank on homosexuality decriminalization push|publisher=[[NBC News]]|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/feature/nbc-out/i-don-t-know-trump-draws-blank-homosexuality-decriminalization-push-n974161|access-date=23 February 2019}}</ref> Several months later, Trump tweeted that, "as we celebrate LGBT Pride Month," Americans should "stand in solidarity with the many LGBT people who live in dozens of countries worldwide that punish, imprison, or even execute" people for their sexual orientation. However, that same week, the Trump administration instructed U.S. embassies not to fly the [[pride flag]] during [[Pride Month]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=State Dept denies embassies' requests to fly rainbow pride flag on official flagpoles|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/state-dept-denies-embassies-requests-fly-rainbow-pride/story?id=63566900|last1=Finnegan|first1=Conor|last2=Palmeri|first2=Tara|date=7 June 2019|website=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|access-date=2019-06-10}}</ref>

==== Judicial appointments ====
{{See also|List of federal judges appointed by Donald Trump}}
About one-third of Trump's judicial nominees have anti-LGBTQ records.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Stacking the Courts: The Fight Against Trump's Extremist Judicial Nominees|url=https://www.lambdalegal.org/judicial-nominees|website=Lambda Legal|access-date=2020-05-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=A third of Trump's court nominees have anti-LGBTQ history, report finds|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/feature/nbc-out/third-trump-s-court-nominees-have-anti-lgbtq-history-report-n1106691|last=Sopelsa|first=Brooke|date=23 December 2019|publisher=[[NBC News]]|access-date=2020-05-19}}</ref> The U.S. Senate has, as of May 2020, confirmed nearly 400 of Trump's nominees to their new roles. At least one of the confirmed judges, [[Patrick Bumatay]], is openly gay.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/President-Trump-nominates-3-to-Court-of-Appeals-13300981.php|title=President Trump nominates 3 to Court of Appeals in S.F.|date=2018-10-12|work=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|access-date=2018-10-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/zoetillman/trump-judicial-nominees-dianne-feinstein-kamala-harris-9th-c|title=Trump's Latest Group Of Judicial Nominees Is A Jab At Dianne Feinstein And Kamala Harris|work=[[BuzzFeed News]]|access-date=2018-10-14}}</ref>

=== Marijuana ===
{{See also|Cannabis policy of the first Trump administration}}[[Marijuana]] and the rights of individual states to legalize [[Recreational marijuana|recreational]] and [[Medical cannabis|medical marijuana]] was an issue of Trump's presidential campaign, and he formally stated during his campaign that he believed states should have the right to manage their own policies with regard to medical and recreational marijuana.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hightimes.com/news/politics/pot-matters-trump-on-marijuana/|title=Pot Matters: Trump on Marijuana|date=February 12, 2016|website=High Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://time.com/4594445/legal-marijuana-trump-sessions-policy/|title=7 Reasons Trump Is Unlikely to Fight Legal Marijuana|magazine=Time}}</ref> Following his election, he reversed his position on recreational marijuana and stated he believed medical marijuana should be allowed but stated the Federal Government may seek legal resolutions for those states which regulate the growth and sale of recreational marijuana.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/320902-white-house-hints-at-crackdown-on-recreational-marijuana/|title=White House hints at crackdown on recreational marijuana|first=Meghashyam|last=Mali|work=The Hill |date=February 23, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.marketwatch.com/story/expect-greater-enforcement-of-marijuana-laws-under-trump-spicer-says-2017-02-23|title=Expect 'greater enforcement' of marijuana laws under Trump, Spicer says|first=Trey|last=Williams|newspaper=Marketwatch }}</ref> However, in April 2018, he once again reversed himself, endorsing leaving the issue to the states;<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-04-13/trump-to-give-states-latitude-on-legal-marijuana-senator-says|title = Trump Backs State-Level Marijuana Regulation, Lifting Pot Stocks |newspaper=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg L.P.]] |date=April 13, 2018}}</ref> and in June 2018, Trump backed a bill introduced by Republican senator [[Cory Gardner]] of [[Colorado]] and Democratic senator [[Elizabeth Warren]] of [[Massachusetts]] that would leave the decision to the states.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/08/us/politics/trump-marijuana-bill-states.html|title=Trump Says He's Likely to Back Marijuana Bill, in Apparent Break With Sessions|last=Sullivan |first=Eileen|date=2018-06-08|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2018-12-08|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In September 2024 Trump expressed support for [[2024 Florida Amendment 3]], an amendment that would legalize cannabis in the state.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Suter |first=Tara |date=2024-09-09 |title=Former President Donald Trump endorses Florida marijuana legalization |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/4869303-donald-trump-backs-florida-marijuana/ |access-date=2024-09-09 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Religion in the public square ===
{{Main|Accommodationism in the United States}}

Trump wove [[Christian symbolism|Christian religious imagery]] into his [[Donald Trump 2024 presidential campaign|2024 presidential campaign]], characterizing it as a "righteous crusade" against "atheists, globalists and the Marxists". He stated that his aims included restoring the United States "as one nation under God with liberty and justice for all".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Vakil |first1=Caroline |title=Trump paints 2024 campaign as 'righteous crusade' as he rallies evangelicals |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/trump-paints-2024-campaign-righteous-024641796.html |publisher=[[Yahoo]] |access-date=24 January 2025 |language=en-US|date=25 June 2023}}</ref>

Trump has been critical of what he sees as a [[persecution of Christians]].<ref name="Bose2025"/> On February 6, 2025, following the [[National Prayer Breakfast]], he signed an executive order to create a task force to "immediately halt all forms of anti-Christian targeting and discrimination within the federal government, including at the DOJ, which was absolutely terrible, the IRS, the FBI — terrible — and other agencies".<ref name="MadhaniSmith2025">{{cite web |last1=Madhani |first1=Aamer |last2=Smith |first2=Peter |title=After prayer breakfast, Trump creates task force to root out 'anti-Christian bias' |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-national-prayer-breakfast-30ff6f55a2e3c7b8643a15e7b158537d |work=[[Associated Press News]] |access-date=7 February 2025 |language=en |date=6 February 2025}}</ref><ref name="Lasher2025">{{cite web |last1=Lasher |first1=James |title=President Trump Champions Faith and Freedom at National Prayer Breakfast - Charisma News |url=https://charismanews.com/news/president-trump-champions-faith-and-freedom-at-national-prayer-breakfast/ |work=[[Charisma (magazine)|Charisma News]] |access-date=7 February 2025 |date=6 February 2025}}</ref> Donald Trump appointed Attorney General [[Pam Bondi]] to lead the task force and appointed [[Paula White]] to direct the White House Faith Office.<ref name="Bose2025">{{cite web |last1=Bose |first1=Nandita |last2=Chiacu |first2=Doina |title=Trump to create religious office in White House, target 'anti-Christian bias' |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-says-he-will-sign-order-targeting-anti-christian-bias-2025-02-06/ |publisher=[[Reuters]] |access-date=7 February 2025 |date=6 February 2025}}</ref>

==Political positions and rhetoric==
{{further|Trumpism|Rhetoric of Donald Trump}}
Beginning with his 2016 campaign, Trump's politics and rhetoric led to the creation of a [[political movement]] known as Trumpism.<ref>{{cite news |last=O'Brien |first=Timothy L. |author-link=Timothy L. O'Brien |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2024-11-01/trumpism-has-deep-roots-in-american-history-and-it-will-outlast-trump |title=The Peculiarly American Roots of Trumpism |work=[[Bloomberg News]] |date=November 1, 2024 |access-date=November 26, 2024 |url-access=limited}}</ref> His political positions are [[populist]],{{sfn|Ross|2024|p=298}}{{sfn|Urbinati|2019}} more specifically described as [[right-wing populist]].{{sfn|Campani|Concepción|Soler|Savín|2022}}<ref>{{cite news |last=Chotiner |first=Isaac |url=https://www.newyorker.com/news/q-and-a/redefining-populism |title=Redefining Populism |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |date=July 29, 2021 |access-date=October 14, 2021}}</ref> In 2016, he helped bring far-right fringe ideas and organizations into the mainstream.<ref>{{cite news |last=Bierman |first=Noah |date=August 22, 2016 |title=Donald Trump helps bring far-right media's edgier elements into the mainstream |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-na-pol-trump-media-20160820-snap-story.html |access-date=October 7, 2021}}</ref> Many of his actions and rhetoric have been described as [[authoritarian]] and contributing to [[Democratic backsliding in the United States|democratic backsliding]].{{sfn|Parker|Towler|2019|p=505; 513}} Trump pushed for an expansion of presidential power under a maximalist interpretation of the [[unitary executive theory]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Savage |first=Charlie |author-link=Charlie Savage (journalist) |date=January 22, 2025 |title=Trump Seeks to Paralyze Independent Privacy and Civil Liberties Watchdog |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/22/us/trump-privacy-civil-liberties-oversight-board.html |url-access=limited |access-date=January 25, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Savage |first=Charlie |author-link=Charlie Savage (journalist) |date=January 22, 2025 |title=How Trump Is Pushing at Limits of Presidential Power in Early Orders |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/22/us/politics/trump-executive-orders.html |url-access=limited |access-date=January 28, 2025}}</ref> His political base [[Trumpism#Cult of personality|has been compared]] to a [[cult of personality]].{{sfn|Sundahl|2022}}{{sfn|Franks|Hesami|2021|loc="Results of the current study... may lend credence to accusations that some Trump supporters have a cult-like loyalty to the 45th president"}}{{sfn|Adams|2021|p=256}}{{sfn|Reyes|2020|p=869}}{{sfn|Diamond|2023|p=96}}{{sfn|Hassan|2024|p=xviii}}<ref>{{cite news |last=Ben-Ghiat |first=Ruth |author-link=Ruth Ben-Ghiat |date=December 19, 2020 |title=Op-Ed: Trump's formula for building a lasting personality cult |url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2020-12-09/donald-trump-strongman-personality-cult |access-date=October 4, 2023 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref>

Trump's rhetoric and actions have been accused of creating and exacerbating anger and distrust through the use of an [[In-group and out-group|"us" versus "them" narrative]].{{sfn|Ross|2024|p=299|}} He explicitly and routinely disparages racial, religious, and ethnic minorities,{{sfn|Stephens-Dougan|2021|p=302}} and scholars consistently find that racial animus regarding blacks, immigrants, and Muslims are the best predictors of support for Trump.{{sfn|Berman|2021|p=76}} His rhetoric has been described as using [[fearmongering]] and [[demagogy]] which [[Donald Trump 2024 presidential campaign#Fearmongering|intensified during his 2024 presidential campaign]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Haberman |first=Maggie |author-link=Maggie Haberman |date=September 11, 2024 |title='The End of Our Country': Trump Paints Dark Picture at Debate |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/11/us/politics/trump-debate-dark-picture.html |access-date=September 25, 2024 |url-access=limited}}</ref> He has said that he believes real power comes from fear.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Tackett |first1=Michael |last2=Haberman |first2=Maggie |author-link2=Maggie Haberman |date=February 4, 2019 |title=Trump Once Said Power Was About Instilling Fear. In That Case, He Should Be Worried. |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/02/04/us/politics/fear-trump.html |access-date=March 29, 2025 |url-access=limited}}</ref> The [[alt-right]] movement coalesced around and supported his candidacy, due in part to its [[opposition to multiculturalism]] and [[Opposition to immigration|immigration]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Weigel |first=David |author-link=David Weigel |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/racial-realists-are-cheered-by-trumps-latest-strategy/2016/08/20/cd71e858-6636-11e6-96c0-37533479f3f5_story.html |title='Racialists' are cheered by Trump's latest strategy |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=August 20, 2016 |access-date=June 23, 2018 |url-access=limited}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cnn.com/2016/08/25/politics/alt-right-explained-hillary-clinton-donald-trump/ |title=Clinton is attacking the 'Alt-Right' – What is it? |first=Gregory |last=Krieg |access-date=August 25, 2016 |date=August 25, 2016 |publisher=[[CNN]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Pierce |first=Matt |title=Q&A: What is President Trump's relationship with far-right and white supremacist groups? |url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2020-09-30/la-na-pol-2020-trump-white-supremacy |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=September 20, 2020 |access-date=October 7, 2021}}</ref> He has a strong [[Trumpism#Christian Trumpism|appeal to evangelical Christian voters]] and [[Christian nationalism#United States|Christian nationalists]],{{sfn|Perry|Whitehead|Grubbs|2021|p=229}} and his rallies take on the symbols, rhetoric, and agenda of Christian nationalism.<ref>{{cite news |last=Smith |first=Peter |date=May 18, 2024 |title=Jesus is their savior, Trump is their candidate. Ex-president's backers say he shares faith, values |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-christian-evangelicals-conservatives-2024-election-43f25118c133170c77786daf316821c3 |access-date=November 23, 2024 |work=[[AP News]]}}</ref> Trump has also used [[Anti-communism|anti-communist sentiment]] in his rhetoric, regularly calling his opponents "[[Communism|communists]]" and "[[Marxism|Marxists]]".<ref>{{cite news |last=Sarat |first=Austin |author-link=Austin Sarat |date=June 22, 2023 |title=Why Donald Trump Says His Enemies Are 'Communists' |url=https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2023/06/22/donald-trump-red-scare-communism-00102990 |access-date=March 30, 2025 |work=[[Politico]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Santana |first1=Rebecca |last2=Swenson |first2=Ali |date=June 28, 2023 |title=Trump wants to keep 'communists' and 'Marxists' out of the US. Here's what the law says |url=https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-immigration-marxists-communists-ban-2024-d9a377149926457d1b8b182293d9c86e |access-date=March 30, 2025 |work=[[AP News]]}}</ref>

=== Racial and gender views ===
{{main|Racial views of Donald Trump|Donald Trump sexual misconduct allegations}}

Many of Trump's comments and actions have been characterized as racist.<ref name="hr">*{{cite news |last=Lopez |first=German |date=February 14, 2019 |title=Donald Trump's long history of racism, from the 1970s to 2019 |url=https://www.vox.com/2016/7/25/12270880/donald-trump-racist-racism-history |access-date=June 15, 2019 |work=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}
*{{cite news |last=Desjardins |first=Lisa |author-link=Lisa Desjardins |date=January 12, 2018 |title=Every moment in Trump's charged relationship with race |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/every-moment-donald-trumps-long-complicated-history-race |access-date=January 13, 2018 |work=[[PBS NewsHour]]}}
*{{cite news |last=Dawsey |first=Josh |author-link=Josh Dawsey |date=January 11, 2018 |title=Trump's history of making offensive comments about nonwhite immigrants |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/trump-attacks-protections-for-immigrants-from-shithole-countries-in-oval-office-meeting/2018/01/11/bfc0725c-f711-11e7-91af-31ac729add94_story.html |access-date=January 11, 2018 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url-access=limited}}
*{{cite news |last=Weaver |first=Aubree Eliza |date=January 12, 2018 |title=Trump's 'shithole' comment denounced across the globe |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2018/01/12/trump-shithole-comment-reaction-337926 |access-date=January 13, 2018 |work=[[Politico]] |ref={{harvid|Weaver|2018b}}}}
*{{cite news |last1=Stoddard |first1=Ed |last2=Mfula |first2=Chris |date=January 12, 2018 |title=Africa calls Trump racist after 'shithole' remark |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-trump-immigration-reaction/africa-calls-trump-racist-after-shithole-remark-idUSKBN1F11VC |access-date=October 1, 2019 |work=[[Reuters]] |url-access=limited}}</ref> In a 2018 national poll, about half of respondents said he is racist; a greater proportion believed that he emboldened racists.<ref>{{cite web |date=July 3, 2018 |title=Harsh Words For U.S. Family Separation Policy, Quinnipiac University National Poll Finds; Voters Have Dim View Of Trump, Dems On Immigration |url=https://poll.qu.edu/Poll-Release-Legacy?releaseid=2554 |access-date=July 5, 2018 |publisher=[[Quinnipiac University Polling Institute]]}}</ref> Several studies and surveys found that racist attitudes fueled his political ascent and were more important than economic factors in determining the allegiance of Trump voters.<ref>{{cite news |last=Lopez |first=German |date=December 15, 2017 |title=The past year of research has made it very clear: Trump won because of racial resentment |url=https://www.vox.com/identities/2017/12/15/16781222/trump-racism-economic-anxiety-study |access-date=January 14, 2018 |work=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref> Racist and [[Islamophobic]] attitudes are strong indicators of support for Trump.{{sfn|Lajevardi|Oskooii|2018}} He has been accused of racism for insisting a group of five black and Latino teenagers were guilty of raping a white woman in the 1989 [[Central Park jogger case]], even after they were exonerated in 2002.<ref>{{cite news |last=Diaz |first=Jaclyn |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/09/11/nx-s1-5108632/central-park-five-trump-debate |title=The Central Park 5 are suing Trump over Philly debate comments |work=[[NPR News]] |date=October 21, 2024 |access-date=November 27, 2024}}</ref>

In 2011, Trump became the leading proponent of the racist [[Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories|"birther" conspiracy theory]] that Barack Obama, the first black U.S. president, was not born in the United States.<ref>{{cite news |last=John |first=Arit |date=June 23, 2020 |title=From birtherism to 'treason': Trump's false allegations against Obama |url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2020-06-23/trump-obamagate-birtherism-false-allegations |access-date=February 17, 2023 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref> He claimed credit for pressuring the government to publish Obama's birth certificate, which he falsely considered fraudulent.<ref>{{cite news |last=Keneally |first=Meghan |date=September 18, 2015 |title=Donald Trump's History of Raising Birther Questions About President Obama |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/donald-trumps-history-raising-birther-questions-president-obama/story?id=33861832 |access-date=August 27, 2016 |work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]}}</ref> In September 2016, he acknowledged that Obama was born in the U.S.,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Haberman |first1=Maggie |author-link1=Maggie Haberman |last2=Rappeport |first2=Alan |author-link2=Alan Rappeport |date=September 16, 2016 |title=Trump Drops False 'Birther' Theory, but Floats a New One: Clinton Started It |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/17/us/politics/donald-trump-birther-obama.html |access-date=October 12, 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=limited}}</ref> though he reportedly expressed birther views privately in 2017.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Haberman |first1=Maggie |author-link1=Maggie Haberman |last2=Martin |first2=Jonathan |author-link2=Jonathan Martin (journalist) |date=November 28, 2017 |title=Trump Once Said the 'Access Hollywood' Tape Was Real. Now He's Not Sure. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/28/us/politics/trump-access-hollywood-tape.html |access-date=June 11, 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=limited}}</ref> During the 2024 presidential campaign, he made false attacks against the racial identity of his opponent, Kamala Harris, that were described as reminiscent of the birther conspiracy theory.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Doherty |first1=Erin |last2=Cai |first2=Sophia |title=Trump doubles down after false attack on Kamala Harris |url=https://www.axios.com/2024/08/01/trump-kamala-harris-interview-nabj |newspaper=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |date=July 31, 2024 |access-date=July 31, 2024}}</ref> His 2024 campaign made extensive use of [[Dehumanization|dehumanizing language]] and [[Ethnic stereotype|racial stereotypes]].<ref>
* {{cite news |last1=Shear |first1=Michael D. |author-link1=Michael D. Shear |last2=Aleaziz |first2=Hamed |last3=Ulloa |first3=Jazmine |date=September 11, 2024 |title=How Trump Uses Vitriol for Migrants to Sideline Other Issues |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/11/us/politics/trump-debate-migrants.html |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=limited}}
* {{cite news |last1=Gold |first1=Michael |last2=Huynh |first2=Anjali |date=April 2, 2024 |title=Trump Again Invokes 'Blood Bath' and Dehumanizes Migrants in Border Remarks |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/04/02/us/politics/trump-border-blood-bath.html |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=limited}}
* {{cite news |last=Sullivan |first=Kate |date=October 6, 2023 |title=Trump's anti-immigrant comments draw rebuke |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/10/06/politics/trump-anti-immigrant-comments/ |access-date=July 27, 2025 |publisher=[[CNN]]}}
* {{cite news |last=Ward |first=Myah |date=October 12, 2024 |title=We watched 20 Trump rallies. His racist, anti-immigrant messaging is getting darker. |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/10/12/trump-racist-rhetoric-immigrants-00183537 |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[Politico]]}}
</ref>

Trump's comments on the 2017 [[Unite the Right rally]], condemning "this egregious display of hatred, bigotry and violence on many sides" and stating that there were "very fine people on both sides", were criticized as implying a [[moral equivalence]] between the [[white supremacist]] demonstrators and the counter-protesters.<ref>{{cite news |last=Kessler |first=Glenn |author-link=Glenn Kessler (journalist) |date=May 8, 2020 |title=The 'very fine people' at Charlottesville: Who were they? |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2020/05/08/very-fine-people-charlottesville-who-were-they-2/ |access-date=October 23, 2021 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url-access=limited}}</ref> In a January 2018 discussion of immigration legislation, he reportedly referred to El Salvador, Haiti, Honduras, and African nations as "shithole countries",<ref>{{cite news |last=Beauchamp |first=Zack |date=January 11, 2018 |title=Trump's "shithole countries" comment exposes the core of Trumpism |url=https://www.vox.com/2018/1/11/16880804/trump-shithole-countries-racism |access-date=January 11, 2018 |work=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref> remarks condemned as racist.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wintour |first1=Patrick |author-link1=Patrick Wintour |last2=Burke |first2=Jason |author-link2=Jason Burke |last3=Livsey |first3=Anna |date=January 13, 2018 |title='There's no other word but racist': Trump's global rebuke for 'shithole' remark |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2018/jan/12/unkind-divisive-elitist-international-outcry-over-trumps-shithole-countries-remark |access-date=January 13, 2018 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref>
[[File:President Trump Visits St. John's Episcopal Church (49964153176).jpg|thumb|With a group of officials and advisors walking from the White House to St. John's Church, following the [[Donald Trump photo op at St. John's Church#Clearing Lafayette Square and St. John's|forced removal of protesters at Lafayette Square]]]]
In July 2019, Trump [[Racial views of Donald Trump#Democratic congresswomen should "go back" to their countries|tweeted that four Democratic congresswomen&mdash;three of whom are native-born Americans&mdash;should "go back" to the countries they "came from"]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rogers |first1=Katie |last2=Fandos |first2=Nicholas |author-link2=Nicholas Fandos |date=July 14, 2019 |title=Trump Tells Congresswomen to 'Go Back' to the Countries They Came From |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/14/us/politics/trump-twitter-squad-congress.html |access-date=September 30, 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=limited}}</ref> Two days later, the House of Representatives voted 240&ndash;187 to condemn his "racist comments".<ref>{{cite news |last=Mak |first=Tim |author-link=Tim Mak |date=July 16, 2019 |title=House Votes To Condemn Trump's 'Racist Comments' |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/07/16/742236610/condemnation-of-president-delayed-by-debate-can-lawmakers-call-trump-tweets-raci |access-date=July 17, 2019 |work=[[NPR News]]}}</ref>

In June 2020, during the [[George Floyd protests]], federal law-enforcement officials used tear gas and other crowd control tactics to remove a largely peaceful crowd of lawful protesters from [[Lafayette Square, Washington, D.C.|Lafayette Square]], outside the [[White House]].<ref name="wb">{{cite news |last1=Leonnig |first1=Carol D. |author-link1=Carol D. Shear |last2=Sullivan |first2=Eileen |author-link2=Eileen Sullivan |date=October 16, 2018 |title='Horseface,' 'Lowlife,' 'Fat, Ugly': How the President Demeans Women |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/16/us/politics/trump-women-insults.html |access-date=August 5, 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=limited}}</ref> He made lewd comments, disparaged women's physical appearances, and referred to them using derogatory epithets.<ref name="Shear" /> As of 2020, 26 women have publicly [[Donald Trump sexual misconduct allegations|accused him of sexual misconduct]], including rape, kissing without consent, groping, looking under women's skirts, and walking in on naked teenage pageant contestants.
