Transmission and distribution cables are at medium risk from earthquakes and transformers at high risk whereas solar is low risk:<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |date=2023-03-31 |title=Doğal Afetler Karşısında Elektrik Sisteminin Güçlendirilmesi |trans-title=Strengthening the electricity system against natural disasters |url=https://shura.org.tr/dogal-afetler-karsisinda-elektrik-sisteminin-guclendirilmesi/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |language=tr-TR}}</ref>{{Rp|page=5}} Think tank Shura suggests that microgrids of solar and batteries could increase resilience against earthquakes.<ref name=":17" />{{Rp|page=14}}

==Future==
[[Wind power in Turkey|Wind]], and especially [[Solar power in Turkey|solar]], could supply much more [[energy in Turkey]].<ref name="renewable">{{Cite journal |last1=Dawood |first1=Kamran |year=2016 |title=Hybrid wind-solar reliable solution for Turkey to meet electric demand |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/pub/bajece/issue/36581/415798 |journal=Balkan Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=62–66 |doi=10.17694/bajece.06954|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 }}</ref> It is estimated that over half of [[electricity generation]] could be from renewables by 2026,<ref>{{Cite web |date=9 March 2022 |title=Legislation to promote use of renewable energy |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/legislation-to-promote-use-of-renewable-energy-172057 |access-date=2022-03-23 |website=[[Hürriyet Daily News]] |language=en}}</ref> but Turkey has invested less in solar and wind power than similar Mediterranean countries.<ref name="TCMB">{{cite web |last1=Saygılı |first1=Hülya |title=Renewable Energy use in Turkey |url=http://www.tcmb.gov.tr/wps/wcm/connect/blog/en/main+menu/analyses/renewable_energy_us_+in_turkey |access-date=17 February 2019 |website=[[Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey]] blog|date=June 2018 }}</ref> More renewable energy could be used to reduce [[Greenhouse gas emissions by Turkey|the nation's greenhouse gas emissions]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sahin |first1=Habip |last2=Esen |first2=Hikmet |date=2022-06-01 |title=The usage of renewable energy sources and its effects on GHG emission intensity of electricity generation in Turkey |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960148122004256 |journal=[[Renewable Energy (journal)|Renewable Energy]] |language=en |volume=192 |pages=859–869 |doi=10.1016/j.renene.2022.03.141 |bibcode=2022REne..192..859S |issn=0960-1481 |s2cid=247903903|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and thus avoid paying other countries' [[Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism|carbon tariff]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-20 |title=Domestic share of wind turbine production in Turkey reaches 72% |url=https://balkangreenenergynews.com/domestic-share-of-wind-turbine-production-in-turkey-reaches-72/ |access-date=2022-06-22 |website=Balkan Green Energy News |language=en-US}}</ref> Turkey is a net exporter of wind power equipment, but a net importer of solar power equipment.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Saygin |first1=Deger |last2=Godron |first2=Philipp |last3=Hoffman |first3=Max |date=10 July 2018 |title=How Turkey Can Ensure a Successful Energy Transition |url=https://www.americanprogress.org/issues/security/reports/2018/07/10/453281/turkey-can-ensure-successful-energy-transition/ |access-date=19 February 2019 |publisher=[[Center for American Progress]]}}</ref> Total non-hydro renewables overtook hydro in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |date=22 January 2022 |title=Non-hydro renewables overtake hydro for first time |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/non-hydro-renewables-overtake-hydro-for-first-time-170949 |access-date=2022-04-18 |website=[[Hürriyet Daily News]] |language=en}}</ref> Solar is expected to overtake wind before 2030.<ref name=":10">{{Cite report |url=https://ember-climate.org/insights/research/energy-independence-only-comes-with-clean/ |title=Türkiye energy independence only comes with clean |last=Alparslan |first=Ufuk |date=2022-10-04 |language=en-US |access-date=2022-10-10 |website=[[Ember (non-profit organisation)|Ember]]}}</ref> The Energy Minister said in 2023 that by 2035 renewables would supply almost a quarter of the nation’s energy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Türkiye to increase energy investments with zero emission target |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkiye-to-increase-energy-investments-with-zero-emission-target-180261 |access-date=2023-01-21 |website=[[Hürriyet Daily News]] |date=21 January 2023 |language=en}}</ref> According to one study, by massively increasing [[Solar power in Turkey|solar power]] in the south and [[Wind power in Turkey|wind power]] in the west the country's entire electricity demand could be met from renewable sources.<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal|last1=Kilickaplan|first1=Anil|last2=Bogdanov|first2=Dmitrii|last3=Peker|first3=Onur|last4=Caldera|first4=Upeksha|last5=Aghahosseini|first5=Arman|last6=Breyer|first6=Christian|date=2017-12-01|title=An energy transition pathway for Turkey to achieve 100% renewable energy powered electricity, desalination and non-energetic industrial gas demand sectors by 2050|journal=[[Solar Energy (journal)|Solar Energy]]|volume=158|pages=218–235|doi=10.1016/j.solener.2017.09.030|bibcode=2017SoEn..158..218K|issn=0038-092X}}</ref> 

A 2022 simulation by Shura of typical spring 2030 generation shows that wind and nuclear could provide baseload, and solar much of daytime demand, reserving dammed hydro for evening flexibility.<ref name=":5" />{{Rp|page=17}} Other experts believe that [[Nuclear power in Turkey|nuclear power]] will keep the grid stable from fluctuations in [[variable renewable energy]],<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Matalucci |first=Sergio |date=30 March 2022 |title=Turkey targets Balkans and EU renewables markets |url=https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-targets-balkans-and-eu-renewables-markets/a-61300638 |access-date=2022-04-18 |website=[[Deutsche Welle]] |language=en-GB}}</ref> while some state that more geothermal [[Base load|baseload]] capacity should be added.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chandrasekharam |first1=Dornadula |last2=Baba |first2=Alper |date=2022-04-07 |title=Carbon dioxide emissions mitigation strategy through enhanced geothermal systems: western Anatolia, Turkey |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s12665-022-10345-5 |journal=Environmental Earth Sciences |language=en |volume=81 |issue=8 |pages=235 |doi=10.1007/s12665-022-10345-5 |issn=1866-6299 |pmc=8986971 |pmid=35411211|bibcode=2022EES....81..235C }}</ref> 

Think tank [[Ember (non-profit organisation)|Ember]] said in 2022 that Turkey needs to expand renewables at least twice as fast, to decarbonize the electricity sector and lower import bills.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkey Electricity Review 2022 |url=https://ember-climate.org/project/turkey-electricity-review-2022/ |access-date=2022-01-20 |website=[[Ember (non-profit organisation)|Ember]] |date=20 January 2022 |language=en-GB}}</ref> In 2023 they said that solar power rollout should be accelerated in the sunny south.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-04 |title=The south can unlock Türkiye's solar ambitions |url=https://ember-climate.org/insights/research/the-south-can-unlock-turkiyes-solar-ambitions/ |access-date=2023-04-08 |website=Ember |language=en-US}}</ref> Shura states that renewables could generate 70% of electricity by 2030, with coal reduced to 5%.<ref name=":5">{{Cite report |date=2022-04-28 |title=Integration of Renewable Energy into the Turkish Electricity System |url=https://shura.org.tr/en/integration-of-renewable-energy-into-the-turkish-electricity-system/ |access-date=2022-06-24|publisher=Shura |language=en-US}}</ref>{{Rp|page=13}}  Many new 400kV transmission lines are planned to be built by 2030.<ref name=":5" />{{Rp|page=15}}

The national energy plan published in 2022 expects an increase in the share of renewable energy and intermittent renewable energy sources in electricity generation to 55% and 34% respectively by 2035.<ref name=":12">{{Cite report |year=2022 |title=Türkiye national energy plan |url=https://enerji.gov.tr/Media/Dizin/EIGM/tr/Raporlar/TUEP/T%C3%BCrkiye_National_Energy_Plan.pdf |publisher=[[Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources (Turkey)|Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources]]}}</ref>{{Rp|page=vi}} According to the plan by 2035 installed capacity will increase to: 30 GW (25 GW onshore, 5 GW offshore) of wind power, and 53 GW of solar power. The plan is for installed capacity to increase to 35 GW of hydroelectricity and 5 GW total of geothermal and biomass power.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|page=15}} The plan expects the share of renewable energy in primary energy consumption, which was 16.7% in 2020, to increase to 23.7% by 2035.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|page=19}} The plan expects the share of electricity from [[variable renewable energy]], which was 12% in 2020, to increase gradually to 34% by 2035.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|page=24}}

==Economics==
[[File:Renewable energy increases employment in Turkey.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|According to studies a coal-phase out in favour of renewable energy would increase employment.{{sfnp|DifiglioGürayMerdan|2020|p=37}}{{sfn whitelist|CITEREFDifiglioGürayMerdan2020}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=Coal Phase-out in the Turkish Power Sector towards net-zero emission targets: An Integrated Assessment of Energy-Economy-Environment Modeling |url=https://www.gtap.agecon.purdue.edu/resources/download/11741.pdf}}</ref>]]
The fuel-only cost of fossil gas-fired power in early 2022 was 128 USD/MWh,<ref name=":7">{{Cite report |url=https://irena.org/publications/2022/Jul/Renewable-Power-Generation-Costs-in-2021 |title=Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2021 |date=July 2022 |publisher=[[International Renewable Energy Agency]] |language=en |isbn=978-92-9260-452-3 |access-date= |archive-date=2024-07-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240710162259/https://www.irena.org/publications/2022/Jul/Renewable-Power-Generation-Costs-in-2021 |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{Rp|page=194}} which was more than double that of the [[levelized cost of electricity]] of new [[Utility-scale solar|utility scale solar]] PV and new onshore wind.<ref name=":7" />{{Rp|page=40}} Renewable energy is competitive with domestic coal.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Energy crisis is an opportunity to accelerate Türkiye's energy transition: Op-ed |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/energy-crisis-is-an-opportunity-to-accelerate-turkiyes-energy-transition-op-ed-174938 |access-date=2022-07-26 |website=[[Hürriyet Daily News]] |date=29 June 2022 |language=en}}</ref> However in 2022 wind and solar remained more expensive than [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]] measures, which were estimated at 14 USD/MWh.<ref name=":8" />

There are [[Feed-in tariff|feed-in-tariffs]] in [[Turkish lira|lira]] (but partly adjusted to USD) per kWh depending on the source and there may be extra if local components are used.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Olğun |first=Kinstellar-Şeyma |date=February 2021 |title=New Turkish-Lira tariff scheme for renewable energy projects in Turkey |url=https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=73fa54e4-0571-487b-b532-466c4893c8f6 |access-date=2021-02-03 |website=Lexology |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=April 2022 |title=Doing business in Turkey: Energy |url=https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/ad4409f2/doing-business-in-turkey-energy |access-date=2022-04-18 |website=[[Norton Rose Fulbright]] |language=en}}</ref> Geothermal and pumped storage get 15 years of this YEKDEM.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://balkangreenenergynews.com/turkey-introduces-subsidies-for-wave-tidal-energy-offshore-wind/ | title=Turkey introduces subsidies for wave, tidal energy, offshore wind | date=4 May 2023 }}</ref> Otherwise tariffs apply for 10 years and any local bonus for 5 years, and are revised quarterly.<ref name=":0" /> Although feed-in tariffs continue to 2030 investors are concerned about the [[2018–2023 Turkish currency and debt crisis|volatility of the lira]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Türkiye 2022 Report |url=https://www.avrupa.info.tr/en/news/turkiye-2022-report-10910 |access-date=2023-01-13 |website=EU Delegation to Türkiye |language=en |archive-date=2023-01-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230113174042/https://www.avrupa.info.tr/en/news/turkiye-2022-report-10910 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=":20" />

Following the invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 the cost of imported fuel soared and the [[Energy Market Regulatory Authority]] (EMRA) was empowered to intervene in the electricity market.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last1=Ardiyok |first1=Sahin |last2=Kıl |first2=İlker |date=20 April 2022 |title=(In)Visible Hand Of EMRA: Recent Regulatory Developments In Turkish Electricity Prices - Energy and Natural Resources - Turkey |url=https://www.mondaq.com/turkey/oil-gas-electricity/1184738/invisible-hand-of-emra-recent-regulatory-developments-in-turkish-electricity-prices |access-date=2022-04-20 |website=[[Mondaq]]}}</ref> According to the [[Industrial Development Bank of Turkey]], the support fee based on source model depends on transferring money from low-cost solar, wind and hydroelectric power plants to those with high operating expenses, examples of which include imported coal and natural gas.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=2022 energy outlook |url=https://www.tskb.com.tr/uploads/file/energy-outlook-final.pdf |website=[[Industrial Development Bank of Turkey]]}}</ref>{{Rp|page=9}} Despite some renewables generators calling for it to be scrapped, it was extended into 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 2022 |title=Monthly Energy Bulletin |url=https://www.tskb.com.tr/uploads/file/energy-bulletin-august-20220920.pdf |website=[[Industrial Development Bank of Turkey]]}}</ref><ref name=":11" /> This applies to both the market exchange price and fixed prices determined by bilateral agreements.<ref name=":9" /> EMRA determining such fees has been criticised by some lawyers, who say that the fees are like a tax on low cost generators, and that according to the constitution taxes can only be imposed by parliament.<ref name=":9" />

The [[World Bank]] said in 2022 that "the war in Ukraine and attendant energy supply disruptions and price increases highlight risks for countries like Türkiye that rely on fossil fuel imports, underscoring the urgency of climate action in support of energy security and affordability" and proposed a plan to integrate development with action on climate change.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/37521 |title=Türkiye - Country Climate and Development Report |date=2022-06-13 |publisher=[[World Bank]] |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=6}} 

{{Blockquote|text=Türkiye can achieve energy security through an accelerated pace of least-cost investments in domestic solar and wind—building on its track record of tripling renewable energy capacity in the last decade—and investing in energy efficiency, battery and pumped storage, geothermal, and gas generation with carbon capture and storage (as well as completion of the nuclear plant under construction). This would enable the country to meet a doubling of energy demand by 2053 to fuel its growth ambitions, with the added benefit of lowering emissions and improving energy security by reducing reliance on imported coal, gas, and oil.|author=[[World Bank]]|source=page 8|title=Türkiye - Country Climate and Development Report}}

Earlier reports from other organisations say that such an expansion of renewables benefits employment,<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.undp.org/turkiye/publications/social-and-employment-impacts-climate-change-and-green-economy-policies-turkiye |title=Social and Employment Impacts of Climate Change and Green Economy Policies in Türkiye |last1=Simas |first1=Moana |last2=Wiebe |first2=Kirsten Svenja |date=June 2022 |language=en |last3=Sodersten |first3=Carl Johan |website=[[United Nations Development Programme]]}}</ref> industrial production, and balance of trade.<ref name="coben">{{Cite report |url=https://www.cobenefits.info/country-studies-infographics/studies/turkey/ |title=COBENEFITS Policy Report Turkey |date=December 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref>

A 2022 study by [[Ember (non-profit organisation)|Ember]] in advance of the Energy Ministry long-term plan suggested that dependence on imported energy could be reduced from a half to a quarter by 2030 by energy efficiency and increasing solar capacity to 40 GW and wind to 30 GW: this would mean the increase in wind and solar accelerating from 1 GW a year each to 2.5 and 4 GW respectively. They said that domestic solar manufacturing capacity could achieve 8 GW a year. The report was based on 4 modeling studies by: the Istanbul Policy Center, the World Bank’s Climate and Development report, a report from Europe Beyond Coal and other local environmental organizations, and analysis from Turkish energy transition think tank Shura.<ref name=":10" /> In 2023 Shura estimated that doubling the capacity of wind and solar compared to 2022 would cut the wholesale cost of electricity by a quarter.<ref>{{Cite report |date=2023-05-29 |title=Yenilenebilir Enerji Kaynaklarının Elektrik Piyasasına Etkisi - 2022 Yılı Analizi |trans-title=The Impact of Renewable Energy Resources on the Electricity Market - Analysis for the Year 2022|url=https://shura.org.tr/yenilenebilir-enerji-kaynaklarinin-elektrik-piyasasina-etkisi-2022-yili-analizi-2/ |access-date=2023-08-19 |language=tr-TR|quote=2022 yılı itibarıyla, Rüzgâr ve Güneşin Fazla Olduğu Senaryo’da hesaplanan piyasa maliyetleri aynı dönemde gerçekleşmiş reel maliyetlerin %24,7 altında seyretmiştir.}}</ref>

If more renewable energy is generated it may be possible to export [[green hydrogen]] to the EU.<ref name=":2" /> Another example of such “sector coupling” would be using excess renewable energy for desalination.<ref name=":18" /> Eser Özdil at the [[Atlantic Council]] said in 2022 that interconnectors with the EU need to be greatly increased, and suggested joint electricity projects with [[Balkans|Balkan]] companies.<ref name=":2" /> A green tariff has been offered since 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |date=14 November 2020 |title=Elektri̇k Pi̇yasasinda Yeni̇lenebi̇li̇r Enerji̇ Kaynak Garanti̇ Belgesi̇ Yönetmeli̇ği̇ |trans-title=Renewable Energy Source Guarantee Certificate Regulation in the Electricity Market |url=https://www.resmigazete.gov.tr/eskiler/2020/11/20201114-2.htm |access-date=2021-01-02 |website=[[Official Gazette of the Republic of Turkey]]}}</ref> Companies with a lot of renewables include [[Electricity Generation Company (Turkey)|the state electricity generation company]] (mainly hydro),<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |date=2021-09-02 |title=Turkey's hydropower capacity grows despite drought lowering output |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/hydropower-capacity-grows-despite-drought-lowering-output-167560 |website=[[Hürriyet Daily News]] |language=en}}</ref> [[Aydem Holding|Aydem]],<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |last=Todorović |first=Igor |date=2021-04-20 |title=Five renewable energy firms preparing to enter stock market in Turkey |url=https://balkangreenenergynews.com/five-renewable-energy-firms-preparing-to-enter-stock-market-in-turkey/ |access-date=2022-07-08 |website=Balkan Green Energy News |language=en-US}}</ref> and [[Kalyon Group|Kalyon]].<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |last=Aslanhan |first=Ugur |date=18 April 2022 |title=Europe's biggest solar power plant in Turkiye to meet power needs of 2M |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/economy/europes-biggest-solar-power-plant-in-turkiye-to-meet-power-needs-of-2m/2566386 |access-date=2022-07-08 |website=[[Anadolu Agency]]}}</ref>

Increasing export of electricity to the EU has also been proposed but analyst Kadri Taştan pointed out that this depends on "reliable and solid political relations between the two and an ambitious environmental policy in Turkey".<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Taştan |first=Kadri |date=2022 |title=Decarbonising EU-Turkey Energy Cooperation: Challenges and Prospects |url=https://www.swp-berlin.org/en/publication/decarbonising-eu-turkey-energy-cooperation-challenges-and-prospects |access-date=2022-04-21 |website=[[German Institute for International and Security Affairs]] |language=en-EN}}</ref> Using renewable electricity to produce [[green hydrogen]] for export has also been suggested, but would require substantial investment.<ref name=":4" /> The 60% import tariff on Chinese components has been criticised as favouring large companies over SMEs.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Ergenç |first1=Ceren |last2=Göçer |first2=Derya |date=5 May 2023 |title=China's Response to Türkiye's Volatile Authoritarianism |url=https://carnegieendowment.org/research/2023/05/chinas-response-to-turkiyes-volatile-authoritarianism?lang=en |website=[[Carnegie Endowment for International Peace]]}}</ref> As of 2023 Chinese companies consider Turkey high risk, in part due to unpredictable and changeable regulations.<ref name=":20" /> SMEs buy solar parts from Malaysia due to the trade agreement.<ref name=":20" />

== Regulations ==
Unlicensed (about 2% of supply and over 90% of which is solar)<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Electricity Generation in Turkey |url=https://guleryuz.av.tr/news-publications/detail/electricity-generation-in-turkey |date=2022-10-06|website=Güleryüz Partners |language=en|last1=Keskin |first1=Yasemin |last2=Koç |first2=M. R. Cafer}}</ref> generators must apply to distribution companies or industrial park license holders in their region for technical checks and approval.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> Production could increase far more quickly if [[Coal in Turkey#Subsidies|subsidies for coal]] were abolished<ref name="OECD 2019">{{cite journal |date=February 2019 |title=Turkey 2019 |journal=Environmental Performance Reviews |series=OECD Environmental Performance Reviews |publisher=[[OECD]] |doi=10.1787/9789264309753-en |isbn=9789264309746 |s2cid=242969625}}</ref>{{Rp|page=36}} and the auction system was improved.<ref name="Shura auctions">{{cite report |title=Opportunities to strengthen the YEKA auction model for enhancing the regulatory framework of Turkey's power system transformation |url=https://www.shura.org.tr/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/SHURA_Opportunities-to-strengthen-the-YEKA-auction-model-for-enhancing-the-regulatory-framework-of-Turkeys-power-system.pdf|year=2018 |first1=Ayşe Ceren|last1=Sarı|first2=Değer|last2=Saygın |publisher=Shura}}</ref> In 2022 the Unlicensed Electricity Generation Regulation was amended so that the amount of surplus energy that can be sold may not exceed the total consumption of the consumer the previous year: the excess goes to the Renewable Energy Resources Support Mechanism.<ref name=":1" /> This regulation might be [[unconstitutional]] by being retrospective.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkey Causes A Splash: New Rules For Generating Unlicensed Electricity! |url=https://www.mondaq.com/turkey/renewables/1227758/turkey-causes-a-splash-new-rules-for-generating-unlicensed-electricity |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=[[Mondaq]]}}</ref>

== Politics ==
The Turkish Electricity Industry Association has suggested a taxonomy, including investments in renewable energy, based on the [[EU taxonomy for sustainable activities]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Taksonomi: Avrupa Birliği Taksonomi Mevzuatı Çerçevesinde Türkiye Elektrik Sektörünün Değerlendirilmesi ve Dünyadan Örnekler |trans-title=Analysis of the Turkish Electricity Sector in the Framework of the European Union Taxonomy Legislation and global examples |url=http://www.tesab.org.tr/attachments/article/130/takso~.pdf |website=Türki̇ye Elektri̇k Sanayi̇ Bi̇rli̇ği̇|date=December 2022 |language=tr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-02-03 |title=Turkey's Green Taxonomy explained: read the book! |url=https://www.eurelectric.org/news/turkey_greentaxonomy/ |access-date=2023-03-21 |website=[[Eurelectric]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Some academics say that governments have not allowed civil society enough say on [[energy policy]], leading to protests against building hydropower, geothermal power, and at least one wind farm.<ref name="Tezcür 2022" /> In 2022 the EU complained about local content requirements, saying that they did not meet [[World Trade Organization]] and [[European Union–Turkey Customs Union]] rules.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Türkiye 2022 Report |url=https://www.avrupa.info.tr/en/news/turkiye-2022-report-10910 |access-date=2023-01-13 |website=EU Delegation to Türkiye |language=en |archive-date=2023-01-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230113174042/https://www.avrupa.info.tr/en/news/turkiye-2022-report-10910 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Think tank Shura says that renewables could replace [[Coal power in Turkey|coal power]] by 2035.<ref>{{Cite web |year=2023 |title=Executive Summary: Net Zero 2053: A Roadmap for the Turkish Electricity Sector |url=https://shura.org.tr/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/SHURA-2023-02-Rapor-NetZero-2053_Executive_-Summary.pdf |website=SHURA Energy Transition Center}}</ref> Better co-operation between city government and central government has been suggested.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2025-07-18 |title=Local governments do not utilise their potential in energy transition |url=https://beyondfossilfuels.org/2025/07/18/local-governments-do-not-utilise-their-potential-in-energy-transition/ |access-date=2025-07-20 |website=Beyond Fossil Fuels |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Health ==
{{See also|Coal power in Turkey#Air pollution}}[[File:Renewable_energy_reduces_health_costs_in_Turkey.jpg|thumb|Renewable energy reduces health costs in Turkey.]]
[[Geothermal power in Turkey]] is used mainly for heating, and [[solar water heating]] is also widespread. However, burning wood for home heating (classified as "traditional biomass" within academic reports) has been causing indoor air pollution throughout history,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shillito |first1=Lisa-Marie |last2=Namdeo |first2=Anil |last3=Bapat |first3=Aishwarya Vikram |last4=Mackay |first4=Helen |last5=Haddow |first5=Scott D. |date=2022-03-01 |title=Analysis of fine particulates from fuel burning in a reconstructed building at Çatalhöyük World Heritage Site, Turkey: assessing air pollution in prehistoric settled communities |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10653-021-01000-2 |journal=Environmental Geochemistry and Health |language=en |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=1033–1048 |doi=10.1007/s10653-021-01000-2 |issn=1573-2983 |pmc=8863713 |pmid=34155558|bibcode=2022EnvGH..44.1033S }}</ref> and still poses such problems.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-01-27 |title=Health and Environment Alliance {{!}} Health experts demand more attention and action on the public health threat of wood burning in the Western Balkans |url=https://www.env-health.org/health-experts-demand-more-attention-and-action-on-the-public-health-threat-of-wood-burning-in-the-western-balkans/ |access-date=2023-04-04 |website=Health and Environment Alliance |language=en-GB}}</ref> 

Possible health benefits of expanding modern renewable energy have been estimated at US$800 million a year.<ref name="coben" /> Health benefits could be greater if renewables succeeded in phasing out coal by 2030.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-22 |title=Health and Environment Alliance {{!}} Curing Chronic Coal: The health benefits of a 2030 coal phase out in Turkey |url=https://www.env-health.org/curing-chronic-coal-turkey/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=Health and Environment Alliance |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== History ==
{{See also|Wind power in Turkey#History|Hydroelectricity in Turkey#History|Geothermal energy in Turkey#History}}
[[File:Bodrum windmills 03.JPG|thumb|[[Bodrum]] windmills]]
[[Neolithic Anatolia|Neolithic]] people in the [[Fertile Crescent]] burnt [[Dry dung fuel|dung]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davies |first=Caleb |date=13 August 2019 |title=Neolithic remains help sniff out the earliest human use of dung |url=https://ec.europa.eu/research-and-innovation/en/horizon-magazine/neolithic-remains-help-sniff-out-earliest-human-use-dung |access-date=2023-04-04 |website=[[Horizon (online magazine)]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Allen |first=Susan E. |date=2019-05-01 |title=Context and contents: Distinguishing variation in archaeobotanical assemblage formation processes at Early Halaf Fistıklı Höyük, Turkey |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00334-019-00728-3 |journal=Vegetation History and Archaeobotany |language=en |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=247–262 |doi=10.1007/s00334-019-00728-3 |bibcode=2019VegHA..28..247A |s2cid=134417004 |issn=1617-6278|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The use of wood as "traditional biomass" in pre-republican times particularly affected [[Forest in Turkey|Turkish forests]] in central and southeast Anatolia, whereas forests in coastal regions proved somewhat more renewable because these regions receive more precipitation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gümüşçü |first1=Osman |last2=Uğur |first2=Abdullah |last3=Aygören |first3=Tülay |date=2014 |title=Deforestation in Sixteenth Century Anatolia: The Case of Hüdavendi̇gar (Bursa) Sancak |url=https://belleten.gov.tr/tam-metin/193/eng |journal=Belleten |volume=78 |issue=281 |pages=167–200 |doi=10.37879/belleten.2014.167 |s2cid=245293300 |issn=0041-4255|url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref> Due to deforestation in arid regions, poor communities continued to burn dry dung in some remote villages into the late 20th century.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=Seona |last2=Ertug-Yaras |first2=Fusün |date=1998-06-01 |title=Fuel Fodder and Faeces: An Ethnographic and Botanical Study of Dung Fuel Use in Central Anatolia |url=https://doi.org/10.1179/env.1996.1.1.99 |journal=Environmental Archaeology |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=99–109 |doi=10.1179/env.1996.1.1.99 |bibcode=1998EnvAr...1...99A |issn=1461-4103|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In the early 21st century wood was the major source of energy in rural areas.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Balat |first1=Mustafa |last2=Acici |first2=Neslihan |last3=Ersoy |first3=Gulyeter |date=2005 |title=Turkey's Wood Reserves, Potential Trends and Future Perspectives of Wood Use |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43754661 |journal=Energy Exploration & Exploitation |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=71–80 |doi=10.1260/0144-5987.23.1.71 |jstor=43754661 |bibcode=2005EExEx..23...71B |s2cid=130507400 |issn=0144-5987|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

[[File:Ihlara_(2).jpg|thumb|Many rooftop solar water heaters were installed in the late 20th and early 21st centuries ]]
In late 20th century, biogas became the focus of much research.<ref name=":19">{{Cite journal |last1=Hepbaşlı |first1=Arif |last2=Özgener |first2=Onder |date=2004-08-01 |title=Turkey's Renewable Energy Sources: Part 1. Historical Development |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00908310490473183 |journal=Energy Sources |volume=26 |issue=10 |pages=961–969 |doi=10.1080/00908310490473183 |bibcode=2004EneSA..26..961H |issn=0090-8312 |s2cid=110777951|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The first residential heat pump was installed at the turn of the century.<ref name=":19" /> Geothermal heat and solar heat were developed early.<ref name=":19" /> Hydropower was expanded for many decades with geothermal, wind and solar electricity following.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Şahin |first=Cem |date=August 2021 |title=The Development of Renewable Energy in Turkish Electricity Markets |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/1626665| journal=European Journal of Science and Technology|doi=10.31590/ejosat.893539 |s2cid=237991754 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Although there has been some academic research on [[Passive solar building design|solar houses]] since the 1970s this has been criticised as insufficient given the importance of the [[Turkish construction industry|construction industry]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dikmen |first=Çiğdem Belgin |date=2 December 2021 |title=Comparative Evaluation of Solar Houses Applied in Turkey |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/1916647}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Renewable energy in the Philippines
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is already sufficiently detailed; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2022}}
{{Use Philippine English|date=October 2022}}
[[File:Philippines electricity generation by source.png|thumb|upright=1.5|Electricity generation in the Philippines in terawatt-hours]]
As of 2023, renewable energy sources accounted for about 22% of the Philippines' total installed electricity generation capacity, according to the Department of Energy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Philippines Renewable Energy Statistics 2024 |url=https://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy |website=Department of Energy |access-date=31 August 2025}}</ref> The Philippines remains a net importer of fossil fuels, which underscores the government's push to expand local renewable energy options. Available renewable resources include [[hydropower]], [[geothermal power]], [[wind power]], [[solar power]], and [[biofuel|biomass power]]. The government has implemented a range of policies and targets aimed at increasing the contribution of renewables to the country's overall energy mix.

The Philippine government has committed to increasing the share of renewables to 50% of total installed power capacity by 2030, equivalent to about 15.3 gigawatts (GW).<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://business.inquirer.net/4182/philippines-sets-50-renewables-target-by-2030|title=Philippines sets 50% renewables target by 2030|agency=Agence France-Presse|access-date=31 March 2018|archive-date=31 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180331104541/http://business.inquirer.net/4182/philippines-sets-50-renewables-target-by-2030|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=http://www.climateactionprogramme.org/news/the_philippines_pursues_renewable_energy_expansion|title=The Philippines pursues renewable energy expansion|last=Programme|first=Climate Action|website=Climate Action Programme|language=en|access-date=31 March 2018|archive-date=31 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180331104538/http://www.climateactionprogramme.org/news/the_philippines_pursues_renewable_energy_expansion|url-status=live}}</ref> This target is aligned with the country's nationally determined contribution (NDC) under the Paris Agreement, which aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by up to 75% by 2030.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Philippines |url=https://climatepromise.undp.org/what-we-do/where-we-work/philippines |access-date=2023-05-29 |website=UNDP Climate Promise |archive-date=28 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528023221/https://climatepromise.undp.org/what-we-do/where-we-work/philippines |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Background ==
Philippine energy policy aims to reduce reliance on fossil fuels because of air pollution, climate risks, and exposure to volatile import prices.<ref name=":25">World Journal [https://time.com/4137154/philippines-ground-zero-for-climate-disaster/ "See how climate change affects the Philippines"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241014022716/https://time.com/4137154/philippines-ground-zero-for-climate-disaster/ |date=14 October 2024 }} ''TIME'' Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref><ref name=":26" /> Key statutes supporting renewable energy include the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (Republic Act No. 9136); the Biofuels Act of 2006 (RA 9367); the Renewable Energy Act of 2008 (RA 9513); and the Climate Change Act of 2009 (RA 9729).<ref name=":24" /><ref name=":27" /><ref name=":28" /><ref name=":29" />

Renewable energy implementation is important to the Philippines for several reasons.<ref>[http://www.reurasia.com/single-post/2016/09/13/Latest-Renewable-Energies-Projects-in-the-Philippines Latest renewable energies projects] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180813143653/http://www.reurasia.com/single-post/2016/09/13/Latest-Renewable-Energies-Projects-in-the-Philippines |date=13 August 2018 }} Reurasia.com 13 September 2016.</ref> The [[Geography of the Philippines|geographic characteristics]] of the country make it vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. [[Rising sea levels]] are a threat because the Philippines is an [[archipelago]] with many cities located in coastal areas. As the coastline recedes due to rising seas, coastal cities become vulnerable to flooding. Climate change has also been linked to changing weather patterns and [[extreme weather]] events.<ref name=":6">''Verifying greenhouse gas emissions'' National Research Council [[Washington DC]] 2010 p vii – 36. {{ISBN|978-0-309-15211-2}}.</ref>

Reliance on fossil fuels is detrimental to the [[energy security]] of the Philippines.<ref>[http://www.iea.org/topics/energysecurity/ "Energy security"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130109143354/http://www.iea.org/topics/energysecurity/ |date=9 January 2013 }} International Energy Agency. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> The Philippines is a net importer of fossil fuels. In 2012, the Philippines imported 20 million tons of coal. Eight million tons were produced domestically.<ref>[http://www.doe.gov.ph/exploration-development/coal-statistics/402-production-vs-importation "Coal statistics"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160410232112/http://www.doe.gov.ph/exploration-development/coal-statistics/402-production-vs-importation |date=10 April 2016 }} Department of Energy. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> In 2010, the Philippines imported 54 million barrels of oil and produced 33,000 barrels.<ref>[http://www.indexmundi.com/energy.aspx?country=ph&product=oil&graph=production "Philippines crude oil production by year"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305022922/http://www.indexmundi.com/energy.aspx?country=ph&product=oil&graph=production |date=5 March 2016 }} Index Mundi website. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> Given this dependence on imported coal and oil, the Philippines is vulnerable to price fluctuations and supply constraints.<ref name=":26">Brahim S. "Renewable energy and energy security in the Philippines" in ''Energy Procedia''.</ref>

The Philippine Department of Energy wrote:<blockquote>The harnessing and utilization of renewable energy comprises a critical component of the government's strategy to provide energy supply for the country. This is evident in the power sector where increased generation from geothermal and hydro resources has lessened the country's dependency on imported and polluting fuels. In the government's rural electrification efforts, on the other hand, renewable energy sources such as solar, micro-hydro, wind and biomass resources are seeing wide-scale use.<ref>Membrere L. [http://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy-res "Renewable energy"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160407194449/http://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy-res |date=7 April 2016 }} Department of Energy. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref></blockquote>

== Sources ==
The Philippines utilizes renewable energy sources including hydropower, geothermal and solar energy, wind power and biomass resources.{{citation needed|date=February 2022}} In 2013, these sources contributed 19,903 GWh of electrical energy, representing 26.44 percent of the country's electricity needs.<ref name=":0">Membrere L. [http://www.doe.gov.ph/electric-power-statistics/philippine-power-statistics/2498-2013-philippine-power-statistics "2013 Philippine power statistics"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160410230734/http://www.doe.gov.ph/electric-power-statistics/philippine-power-statistics/2498-2013-philippine-power-statistics |date=10 April 2016 }} Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> Among the renewable energy sources available in the country, geothermal shows to be the cheapest and most (economically) attractive energy source followed by wind, hydropower, and lastly, solar PV.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Agaton|first=Casper Boongaling|date=25 January 2018|title=Use coal or invest in renewables: a real options analysis of energy investments in the Philippines|journal=Renewables: Wind, Water, and Solar|volume=5|issue=1|article-number=1|doi=10.1186/s40807-018-0047-2|bibcode=2018RWWS....5....1A |issn=2198-994X|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Hydroelectric plants ===
[[File:AngatDam.jpg|thumb|right|[[Angat Dam]], a major hydropower facility in the Philippines]]Hydropower is one of the main sources of renewable energy in the Philippines. There are [[hydroelectric]] plants of both the [[Hydroelectricity#Conventional (dams)|conventional dam]] and [[run-of-the-river]] types in the country. Of twenty-nine hydroelectric plants, fourteen are conventional dam and fifteen are run-of-the-river systems.<ref name=":2">[http://www.doe.gov.ph/doe_files/pdf/01_Energy_Situationer/2015_existing_power_plants_luzon_december_2015.pdf "List of existing plants (Luzon)"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160418192407/http://www.doe.gov.ph/doe_files/pdf/01_Energy_Situationer/2015_existing_power_plants_luzon_december_2015.pdf|date=18 April 2016}} Department of Energy</ref><ref name=":3">[http://www.doe.gov.ph/doe_files/pdf/01_Energy_Situationer/2015_existing_power_plants_visayas_december_2015.pdf "List of existing plants (Visayas)"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610233915/http://www.doe.gov.ph/doe_files/pdf/01_energy_Situationer/2015_existing_power_plants_visayas_december_2015.pdf|date=10 June 2016}} Department of Energy</ref><ref name=":4">[http://www.doe.gov.ph/doe_files/pdf/01_Energy_Situationer/2015_existing_power_plants_mindanao_december_2015.pdf "List of existing plants (Mindanao)] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610235053/http://www.doe.gov.ph/doe_files/pdf/01_energy_Situationer/2015_existing_power_plants_mindanao_december_2015.pdf|date=10 June 2016}} Department of Energy</ref> Hydropower accounts for 11.8% of the energy generation and 17-18% of installed capacity in the Philippines.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Erdiwansyah |last2=Mamat |first2=R. |last3=Sani |first3=M. S. M. |last4=Sudhakar |first4=K. |date=20 June 2019 |title=Renewable energy in Southeast Asia: Policies and recommendations |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969719312653 |journal=Science of the Total Environment |language=en |volume=670 |pages=1095–1102 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2019.03.273 |pmid=31018425 |bibcode=2019ScTEn.670.1095E |s2cid=109529680 |issn=0048-9697|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |last1=Guiamel |first1=Ismail Adal |last2=Lee |first2=Han Soo |date=1 November 2020 |title=Potential hydropower estimation for the Mindanao River Basin in the Philippines based on watershed modelling using the soil and water assessment tool |journal=Energy Reports |language=en |volume=6 |pages=1010–1028 |doi=10.1016/j.egyr.2020.04.025 |bibcode=2020EnRep...6.1010G |s2cid=218971298 |issn=2352-4847 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":52">{{Cite journal |last=Delina |first=Laurence L. |date=1 July 2020 |title=Indigenous environmental defenders and the legacy of Macli-ing Dulag: Anti-dam dissent, assassinations, and protests in the making of Philippine energyscape |journal=Energy Research & Social Science |language=en |volume=65 |article-number=101463 |doi=10.1016/j.erss.2020.101463 |bibcode=2020ERSS...6501463D |s2cid=213895250 |issn=2214-6296 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Many areas of the Philippines are suitable for hydroelectricity production.<ref name=":92">[http://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy-res/hydropower "Hydropower"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160430165857/http://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy-res/hydropower|date=30 April 2016}} Department of Energy Accessed 8 April 2016</ref> However, hydroelectricity production in the Philippines can cause upstream and downstream flooding during [[monsoon]]al weather and when excess water is released from dams.<ref name=":92" /><ref name=":02">[http://interaksyon.com/article/121675/release-of-angat-ipo-dam-water-aggravates-bulacan-floods "Release of Angat, Ipo dam water aggravates Bulacan floods"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170221140323/http://interaksyon.com/article/121675/release-of-angat-ipo-dam-water-aggravates-bulacan-floods |date=21 February 2017 }} InterAksyon.com Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> Hydropower integration also has the potential to disturb pre-existing natural ecosystems and cultures as well as cause land dispossession and community resettlement.<ref name=":14" /><ref name=":62">{{Cite web |last=Talamayan |first=Fernan |date=1 May 2020 |title=Mapping Anti-Dam Movements: The Politics of Water Reservoir Construction and Hydropower Development Projects in the Philippines |url=https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=3748391 |language=en |location=Rochester, NY |doi=10.2139/ssrn.3748391|ssrn=3748391 |s2cid=234896254 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The methods of using [[geographic information system]] (GIS) and [[remote sensing]] (RS) to determine suitable sites for constructing hydroelectric plants do not tend to incorporate social or environmental considerations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fesalbon |first1=R. M. A. |last2=Blanco |first2=A. C. |title=Hydropower Dam Site Selection and Visualization Using Gis and Rs Techniques: A Case of Marinduque, Philippines |date=23 December 2019 |url=https://www.int-arch-photogramm-remote-sens-spatial-inf-sci.net/XLII-4-W19/207/2019/ |journal=The International Archives of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences |language=English |publisher=Copernicus GmbH |volume=XLII-4-W19 |pages=207–214 |doi=10.5194/isprs-archives-XLII-4-W19-207-2019 |bibcode=2019ISPAr4219..207F |s2cid=210896283 |doi-access=free |archive-date=15 June 2022 |access-date=8 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220615132954/https://www.int-arch-photogramm-remote-sens-spatial-inf-sci.net/XLII-4-W19/207/2019/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In response to the construction of large scale hydroelectric infrastructure, opposition movements have arisen. Anti-dam organizations and protests may advocate for indigenous peoples, environmental conservation, [[anti-capitalism]], or [[anti-imperialism]].<ref name=":52" /> Vocal environmental human rights defenders have been [[Red-tagging in the Philippines|red-tagged]] by the government or [[extrajudicially killed]] by the military or police.<ref name=":52" /><ref name=":62" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Del Bene |first1=Daniela |last2=Scheidel |first2=Arnim |last3=Temper |first3=Leah |date=1 May 2018 |title=More dams, more violence? A global analysis on resistances and repression around conflictive dams through co-produced knowledge |journal=Sustainability Science |language=en |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=617–633 |doi=10.1007/s11625-018-0558-1 |bibcode=2018SuSc...13..617D |s2cid=158360331 |issn=1862-4057 |url=https://ddd.uab.cat/record/189130 }}</ref> The rights, concerns, and political agency of indigenous peoples trying to protect their villages and sacred sites from being submerged have often been disregarded due to urban-centric economic development.<ref name=":52" /><ref name=":62" />

Incorporating [[Small hydro|small scale]] plants, especially [[Micro hydro|micro-hydroelectric]] plants that have a capacity of less than 0.1 MW (100&nbsp;kW), may mitigate adverse side effects and be a cost-effective way to bring electricity to rural and off-the-grid communities.<ref name=":14" /> Isolated mountain communities have seen improvements in education, community engagement, and economy due to improved lighting provided by micro-hydropower.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arnaiz |first1=M. |last2=Cochrane |first2=T. A. |last3=Hastie |first3=R. |last4=Bellen |first4=C. |date=1 August 2018 |title=Micro-hydropower impact on communities' livelihood analysed with the capability approach |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0973082617308943 |journal=Energy for Sustainable Development |language=en |volume=45 |pages=206–210 |doi=10.1016/j.esd.2018.07.003 |bibcode=2018ESusD..45..206A |hdl=10092/15826 |s2cid=158665491 |issn=0973-0826 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=13 March 2022 |access-date=8 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220313031523/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0973082617308943 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Geothermal power ===
{{main|Geothermal power in the Philippines}}
 
In the Philippines, geothermal energy is used to generate electricity. Two types of technologies are used in the Philippines. These are firstly, the higher temperature [[flash boiler|flash steam method]] and secondly, the lower temperature [[binary cycle]] method.<ref name=":12">[http://www.renewableenergyworld.com/geothermal-energy/tech/geoelectricity.html "Geothermal power and electricity production"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190603092949/http://www.renewableenergyworld.com/geothermal-energy/tech/geoelectricity.html |date=3 June 2019 }} Renewable energy world website. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> In the Philippines, the first is the more common. The second is used only at the MAKBAN plant. Geothermal plants are suitable for areas with low winds, such as [[Mindanao]], and areas that have rainy weather, such as [[Batanes]]. Geothermal energy production can result in the release of toxic substances such as [[Mercury (element)|mercury]], [[hydrogen sulfide]], [[arsenic]] and [[selenium]].<ref name=":13">[http://education.nationalgeographic.org/encyclopedia/geothermal-energy/ "Geothermal energy"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160416041543/http://education.nationalgeographic.org/encyclopedia/geothermal-energy/ |date=16 April 2016 }} National Geographic Society 20 November 2012. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> In 2014, at a geothermal plant in [[Biliran]], eight plant workers were hospitalized with [[hydrogen sulphide]] poisoning.<ref>[http://www.philstar.com/region/2014/06/22/1337741/biliran-geothermal-project-eight-workers-hurt-gas-poisoning "At Biliran geothermal project eight workers hurt in gas poisoning"] philstar.com 22 June 2014. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref>

=== Solar power ===
{{see also|Commercial solar power in the Philippines}}
[[File:Monocrystalline solar panel.png|thumb|Photovoltaic solar cell]]

The Philippines receives some of the highest levels of solar irradiance in Southeast Asia, with average daily values reaching over 7 kWh/m<sup>2</sup> in April and around 3 kWh/m<sup>2</sup> in December, based on measurements in 33 cities nationwide.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Maldicem |first=Ervin |date=2015 |title=Optimal Tilt of Solar Panels in the Philippines |url=https://www.academia.edu/34980472 |journal=Schadow1 Expeditions |page=6 |doi=10.13140/RG.2.2.19886.61764 |access-date=5 November 2017}}</ref>

In 2019, solar power accounted for about 1.2% of the country's total installed generation capacity of 23 GW. Government projections indicate that solar could reach at least 3.5% of a forecast 43 GW by 2040.<ref name="auto">{{cite web |title=Philippines Renewable Energy Statistics 2024 |url=https://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy |website=Department of Energy |access-date=11 August 2025}}</ref> In 2019, a 2.16 MWp commercial rooftop solar project in Calamba, Laguna, developed by PROINSO and Solaren Renewable Energy Solutions, was awarded the Asian Power Awards "Solar Power Project of the Year".<ref>{{cite web |title=PROINSO, SOLAREN Win Asian Power Award for 2.16 MWp Commercial Solar Rooftop Project |url=https://www.saurenergy.com/solar-energy-news/proinso-solaren-win-asian-power-award-for-2-16-mwp-commercial-solar-rooftop-project |website=Saur Energy |date=2019-09-05 |access-date=2025-08-31}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Find out who emerged as the victors in the Asian Power Awards 2019 |url=https://asian-power.com/ipp/news/find-out-who-emerged-victors-in-asian-power-awards-2019 |website=Asian Power |date=2019-09-05 |access-date=2025-08-31}}</ref>

By the end of 2024, Department of Energy data recorded 2,312 MW of installed solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity, driven by both utility-scale facilities and distributed systems in the commercial and residential sectors.<ref name="auto"/> The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) reported 1.7 GW of capacity earlier in the year, reflecting continuing growth in the sector.<ref name="IRENA2024">{{cite web |title=Renewable Capacity Statistics 2024 |url=https://www.irena.org/Statistics/View-Data-by-Topic/Capacity-and-Generation/Technologies |website=IRENA |access-date=11 August 2025}}</ref>

Major planned developments include the Meralco Terra Solar Farm, with a projected capacity of over 700 MW, which will contribute to the expansion of utility-scale solar generation in the country.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guno |first1=Charmaine Samala |last2=Agaton |first2=Casper Boongaling |last3=Villanueva |first3=Resy Ordona |last4=Villanueva |first4=Riza Ordona |date=1 February 2021 |title=Optimal Investment Strategy for Solar PV Integration in Residential Buildings: A Case Study in The Philippines |url=https://ejournal.undip.ac.id/index.php/ijred/article/view/32657 |journal=International Journal of Renewable Energy Development |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=79–89 |doi=10.14710/ijred.2021.32657 |issn=2252-4940 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

As of 2025, commercial PV systems are increasingly adopted by businesses, farms, schools, and local government facilities, contributing to reductions in daytime peak demand and offsetting grid electricity costs.<ref>{{cite web |title=DOE Solar PH Roadmap 2024 |url=https://www.doe.gov.ph/sites/default/files/pdf/renewable_energy/solar-roadmap-2024.pdf |publisher=Department of Energy |access-date=6 August 2025}}</ref>

In the commercial rooftop segment, a 2.16 MWp installation in [[Calamba, Laguna]] received the Asian Power Awards' 2019 "Solar Power Project of the Year – Philippines".<ref>{{cite web |title=Find out who emerged as the victors in the Asian Power Awards 2019 |url=https://asian-power.com/ipp/news/find-out-who-emerged-victors-in-asian-power-awards-2019 |website=Asian Power |date=5 September 2019 |access-date=17 August 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=PROINSO, SOLAREN Win Asian Power Award for 2.16 MWp Commercial Solar Rooftop Project |url=https://www.saurenergy.com/solar-energy-news/proinso-solaren-win-asian-power-award-for-2-16-mwp-commercial-solar-rooftop-project |website=Saur Energy |date=5 September 2019 |access-date=17 August 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250218041858/https://www.saurenergy.com/solar-energy-news/proinso-solaren-win-asian-power-award-for-2-16-mwp-commercial-solar-rooftop-project |archive-date=2025-02-18 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Wind power ===
[[File:Pililla Wind Farm.jpg|thumb|right|Pililla wind farm]]
As of the end of 2023, the Philippines had 427 MW of installed wind power capacity, according to the Department of Energy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Philippines Renewable Energy Statistics 2024 |url=https://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy |website=Department of Energy |access-date=2025-08-31}}</ref> Most wind power sites are onshore facilities, with Ilocos Norte hosting the country's first large-scale wind farms. Other projects, such as the [[Pililla Wind Farm]] in [[Rizal (province)|Rizal]] and the [[Bangui Wind Farm]] in Ilocos Norte, have also become popular tourist destinations.<ref name=":21">[http://www.mb.com.ph/ilocos-n-breaks-tourists-record/ "Ilocos N. breaks tourists record"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160501210739/http://www.mb.com.ph/ilocos-n-breaks-tourists-record/ |date=1 May 2016 }} ''The Manila Bulletin'' Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref><ref name=":22">[http://www.philstar.com/news-feature/2016/01/21/1544770/wind-farm-drawing-tourists-rizal "Wind farm drawing tourists to Rizal"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160326163044/http://www.philstar.com/news-feature/2016/01/21/1544770/wind-farm-drawing-tourists-rizal |date=26 March 2016 }} ''The Philippine Star'' Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref>

On March 13, 2024, German wind and solar developer wpd GmbH announced plans to invest ₱392.4 billion in the Philippines to establish offshore wind farms in Cavite, Negros Occidental, and Guimaras. The undertaking, registered with the Board of Investments (BOI) in 2023, represents the largest renewable energy investment of its kind in the country. According to the BOI, the projects in Cavite and Negros (1 & 2) will have a combined capacity of 3,260 MW and an estimated value of ₱400 billion.<ref>{{cite news |last=Gita-Carlos |first=Ruth Abbey |title=German wind, solar developer commits ₱392.4B for PH renewable energy |url=https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1220770 |work=Philippine News Agency |date=14 March 2024 |access-date=31 August 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240314130119/https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1220770 |archive-date=14 March 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Biomass power ===
[[File:Bagasse baling machine in Hainan - 06.jpg|thumb|right|Bagasse, a kind of biomass fuel]]
[[File:Rice husk.jpg|thumb|right|Rice husks]]

[[Biofuel|Biomass energy]] refers to energy derived from plant and animal sources.<ref>[http://www.biomassenergycentre.org.uk/portal/page?_pageid=76,15049&_dad=portal "What is biomass"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161003092000/http://www.biomassenergycentre.org.uk/portal/page?_pageid=76,15049&_dad=portal |date=3 October 2016 }} Biomass Energy Centre UK Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> Biomass resources are abundant in the Philippines due to its large agricultural industry. [[Bagasse]], [[rice]] husks, and [[coconut]] husks are used to generate power.<ref name=":18">[http://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy-res/biomass-solar-wind-and-ocean "Biomass, solar, wind and ocean"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160323163855/http://www.doe.gov.ph/renewable-energy-res/biomass-solar-wind-and-ocean |date=23 March 2016 }} Department of Energy. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref> The Philippines also uses [[biogas]] from [[landfill]] as a biomass energy source. The availability of biomass can be affected by events such as [[drought]].<ref name="Advantages and Disadvantages">[http://science134.tripod.com/id9.html "Advantages and Disadvantages"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190715165647/http://science134.tripod.com/id9.html |date=15 July 2019 }} Science 134 website. Accessed 8 April 2016.</ref>|

== Legislation ==
The Philippine government has passed four laws that seek to improve the state of renewable energy. These are the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (RA 9136); the Biofuel Act of 2006 (RA 9367); the Renewable Energy Act of 2008 (RA 9513); and the Climate Change Act of 2009 (RA 9729).

The Electric Power Industry Reform Act (2001) (EPIRA) promotes the use of  renewable energy particularly through [[private sector]] investment.<ref name=":24">[{{cite web |url=http://www.doe.gov.ph/issuances/republic-act/609-ra-9136 |title=Republic Act No. 9136 - an Act Ordaining Reforms in the Electric Power Industry, Amending for the Purpose Certain Laws and for Other Purposes |access-date=12 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160421232828/http://www.doe.gov.ph/issuances/republic-act/609-ra-9136 |archive-date=21 April 2016 }} "Republic Act No. 9136" department of Energy. Accessed 12 April 2016.</ref> However, after a decade of EPIRA's enactment, advocacy groups and lawmakers said the law only strengthened monopolies and caused electricity rates to double.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ibon.org/2016/06/repeal-epira-ph-power-rates-double-in-15-years-ibon/|title=Repeal EPIRA: PH power rates double in 15 years–IBON|website=IBON Foundation|language=en-US|access-date=30 March 2018|archive-date=9 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180409093802/http://ibon.org/2016/06/repeal-epira-ph-power-rates-double-in-15-years-ibon/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.sunstar.com.ph/davao/business/2017/04/07/electric-consumer-group-calls-review-epira-535511|title=Electric consumer group calls for review of Epira|last=Arado|first=Jennie P.|date=7 April 2017|work=SunStar|access-date=30 March 2018|language=en|archive-date=31 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180331104243/http://www.sunstar.com.ph/davao/business/2017/04/07/electric-consumer-group-calls-review-epira-535511|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.rappler.com/philippines/46252-drilon-joins-calls-to-review-epira/|title=Drilon: Review EPIRA after 'apparent failure'|work=Rappler|access-date=30 March 2018|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://business.inquirer.net/157645/solon-pines-for-pre-epira-days-in-power-generation|title=Solon pines for pre-Epira days in power generation|last=Cabacungan|first=Gil|access-date=30 March 2018|language=en|archive-date=29 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170629193457/http://business.inquirer.net/157645/solon-pines-for-pre-epira-days-in-power-generation|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Biofuels Act (2006) documents state policy to reduce the Philippines' dependence on imported fossil fuels. It encourages investment in biofuels through incentives including reduced tax on local or imported biofuels; and bank loans for Filipino citizens engaged in biofuel production. The law resulted in the formation of the National Biofuel Board (NBB).<ref name=":27">[http://www.doe.gov.ph/issuances/republic-act/614-ra-9367 "Republic Act No. 9367"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220620184448/http://www.doe.gov.ph/issuances/republic-act/614-ra-9367 |date=20 June 2022 }} Department of Energy Accessed 13 April 2016.</ref>

The Renewable Energy Act (2008) legislates state policy to accelerate the development and use of renewable energy resources.<ref name=":28">[http://www.doe.gov.ph/issuances/republic-act/627-ra-9513 "Republic Act No. 9513"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160331000909/http://www.doe.gov.ph/issuances/republic-act/627-ra-9513 |date=31 March 2016 }} Department of Energy.</ref> Under this act (section 6), mandated a minimum percentage of generation of electricity from renewable sources (a renewable portfolio standard (RPS)). Also under this act (section 7), a [[Feed-in tariff|feed-In tariff]] system was implemented for electricity produced from renewable sources, giving producers the security of long term fixed prices.<ref name=":23">{{cite journal|doi= 10.1016/j.rser.2016.01.084|title= Alternative framework for renewable energy planning in the Philippines|journal= Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews|volume= 59|pages= 1396–1404|year= 2016|last1= Roxas|first1= Fernando|last2= Santiago|first2= Andrea|bibcode= 2016RSERv..59.1396R}}</ref> Electricity utilities make [[net metering]] agreements with qualified end-users of renewable energy systems. A minimum percentage of electricity from renewable sources for the off-grid missionary electrification system was also mandated.

Under the Renewable Energy Act (2008), incentives are available to developers of renewable energy. These incentives include an income tax holiday for the first seven years of the entity's commercial operations; duty-free importation and special realty tax rates on renewable energy machinery, equipment and materials within the first ten years; net operating loss carry-over; zero percent [[Value-Added Tax]] (VAT) rate for the sale of fuel or power generated from renewable sources of energy; and [[Tax Credit]] on domestic capital equipment and services.

The Climate Change Act (2009) legislated state policy to incorporate a gender-sensitive, pro-children and pro-poor perspective in all climate change and renewable energy efforts.<ref name=":29">[https://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/2009/10/23/republic-act-no-9729/ "Republic Act No. 9729"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201031155801/https://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/2009/10/23/republic-act-no-9729/ |date=31 October 2020 }} Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines 23 October 2009. Accessed 13 April 2016</ref>

== Private sector involvement ==
The Renewable Energy Act (2008) encourages the involvement of the private sector in renewable energy production through fiscal and non-fiscal incentives.<ref name=":19">{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.egypro.2014.07.101|title=Renewable Energy and Energy Security in the Philippines|journal=Energy Procedia|volume=52|pages=480–486|year=2014|last1=Brahim|first1=Sahara Piang|bibcode=2014EnPro..52..480B |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Fiscal incentives include tax reductions, as well as funding assistance from both government and third parties. A number of international organizations have expressed willingness to aid Philippine businesses in developing local renewable energy infrastructure including [[Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit|German Technical Cooperation (GTZ)]], [[United States Agency for International Development|United States Agency for International Development (USAID)]], [[Asian Development Bank|Asian Development Bank (ADB)]], [[United Nations Development Programme|United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)]], and [[Japan International Cooperation Agency|Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA)]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.erss.2015.07.013|title=The politics of energy and development: Aid diversification in the Philippines|journal=Energy Research & Social Science|volume=10|pages=259–272|year=2015|last1=Marquardt|first1=Jens |bibcode=2015ERSS...10..259M }}</ref> Impediments to private sector investment include high transaction costs, social engineering costs, lack of suitable local technology, and caps on electricity prices made by the Energy Regulatory Commission.<ref name=":20" /><ref name=":19" />

== Social and environmental issues ==
Renewable energy companies in the Philippines continue to invest in fossil fuel expansion. Environmentalists say these companies are deliberately delaying the development of renewable energy to increase profits.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last=Fonbuena |first=Carmela |date=2025-09-25 |title=The tycoons behind the Philippines' dirty energy |url=https://pcij.org/2025/09/25/tycoons-behind-the-philippines-dirty-energy/ |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism |language=en-US}}</ref> Youth climate activist Jonelle Mitzi Tan said that the energy sector should phase out coal, stop the expansion of liquefied natural gas (LNG), and commit to "retiring fossil fuels on urgent timelines, respecting human rights and Indigenous sovereignty, and protecting workers through job guarantees".<ref name=":7" />

[[Mining in the Philippines]] has expanded to supply nickel, copper, and other transition materials during the Philippines' and the global energy shift. According to [[Global Witness]], this has led to the displacement of indigenous peoples' communities, killings and forced disappearances, militarization in mining areas, damage to forests and rivers, and worsening climate risks such as floods and landslides.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Flores |first=Dominique Nicole |title='A case of greenwashing': How the Philippines' energy transition comes at the cost of lives, biodiversity |url=https://www.philstar.com/headlines/climate-and-environment/2024/12/06/2405457/a-case-greenwashing-how-philippines-energy-transition-comes-cost-lives-biodiversity |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=Philippine Star}}</ref>

'''The''' '''Schmidt Family Foundation''' is a [[private foundation]] created in 2006 by [[Eric Schmidt]], the executive chairman of [[Google]], and his wife [[Wendy Schmidt]], to address issues pertaining to [[sustainability]] and the responsible use of natural resources.<ref>{{cite web |title=Schmidt Family Foundation |url=http://theschmidtfamilyfoundation.org/ |accessdate=April 27, 2013 }}</ref>

== History and assets ==

The foundation was established in 2006 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, with assets valued at over $1 billion,<ref>{{cite web |title = Schmidt Family Foundation 2006 IRS Form 990-PF |url = http://dynamodata.fdncenter.org/990pf_pdf_archive/204/204170342/204170342_200612_990PF.pdf |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref> which included $307 million in Google Class A stock.<ref name="2011-2010">{{cite web|title = Schmidt Family Foundation and Subsidiaries Consolidated Financial Statements Years Ended December 31, 2011 and 2010 | url = http://theschmidt.org/site/grants/media/pdf/2011_audited_financial_statement.pdf | publisher = Schmidt Family Foundation website | accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref>

== Focus area ==

The foundation is focused on  the application of new knowledge and innovation and   advancement original research in science, energy, and [[biosphere]] [[sustainability]], often in collaboration with other organizations. Its initial specific focus areas are [[Environmentalism|environmental]] preservation and education.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://theschmidt.org/site/about/ |title = About |publisher = Schmidt Family Foundation website | accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref>

== Programs and grants ==

Since 2006, the Foundation has made grants to organizations, including the Energy Foundation, the [[California Academy of Sciences]], the Regeneration Project, the [[Columbia University|Columbia]] Center for Children’s Environmental Health, [[Green for All]], [[Grist (magazine)|''Grist'' magazine]], the [[Center for Investigative Reporting]], the [[Environmental Media Association]], and the [[Precourt Institute for Energy]] at [[Stanford University]].<ref>{{cite web |url = http://theschmidtfamilyfoundation.org/site/grants/ |title = Grants |publisher = Schmidt Family Foundation website |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.kcnn.org/toolkit/foundations/C39/ |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110303231341/http://www.kcnn.org/toolkit/foundations/C39 |url-status = usurped |archive-date = March 3, 2011 |title = New Media Makers – Foundations |publisher = Knight Community News Network |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url = http://www.bizjournals.com/sanfrancisco/stories/2009/01/12/daily24.html |title = Stanford plans $100M energy institute |author = Lindsay Riddell |date = January 13, 2009 |work = San Francisco Business Times |accessdate=April 27, 2013 }}</ref>

Between 2006 and 2011, it made a five-year grant of $1 million per year to the [[Natural Resources Defense Council]].

It has supported several Schmidt family projects. In 2010, it made a $1 million grant to the Marine Science and Technology Foundation,<ref name="2011-2010" /> a private operating foundation founded in 2010 by Eric Schmidt.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.guidestar.org/organizations/26-3630378/marine-science-technology-foundation.aspx |title = Marine Science and Technology Foundation |publisher = Guidestar.org |accessdate=April 27, 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://mstfoundation.org |title = Home Page |publisher = Marine Science and Technology Foundation website |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref>

The '''11th Hour Project''' was founded by Wendy Schmidt in 2005, and operates as part of the foundation. It works to raise [[Climate change education|awareness about climate change]] and renewable energy sources, and operates as part of the foundation.<ref name="2011-2010" /> The project awards various grants and helped distribute the documentary film ''[[An Inconvenient Truth]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://foundationcenter.org/focus/gpf/climatechange/03.html |title = 11th Hour Project case study |publisher=Foundationcenter.org |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref> It also provided initial operating budget for the  nonprofit news organization [[Climate Central]].<ref>{{cite news |url = https://www.cjr.org/the_observatory/climate_central.php?page=all |title = A One-Stop Shop for Climate Information? |author = Curtis Brainard |date = December 8, 2008 |work = Columbia Journalism Review. |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.11thhourproject.org/grantees |title = Grantees |publisher = 11th Hour Project website |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref>

'''ReMain Nantucket''', formed in 2007, is a wholly owned subsidiary of the foundation, dedicated to the economic, social, and environmental vitality of downtown [[Nantucket]], [[Massachusetts]].<ref>{{cite news |url = http://www.nantuckettodayonline.com/aprilmay08/wschmidt.html |title = The Philanthropy of Wendy Schmidt |author = Dan Fost |date = April–May 2008 |work = Nantucket Today |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2012/08/30/fashion/nantucket-benefits-from-a-google-long-distance-marriage.html?_r=1& |title = You Could Google Her |author = Laura M. Holson |date = August 28, 2012 |work = The New York Times |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://remainnantucket.org |title = Home Page |publisher = ReMain Nantucket website |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref>

The [[Schmidt Ocean Institute]] founded in 2009, is a separate private foundation<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.11thhourproject.org/about-us/faq |title = FAQ |publisher = 11th Hour Project website |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref> established by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, that has received grants from the Schmidt Family Foundation for acquiring and operating the Institute’s oceanographic [[research vessel]]s, including the ''Falkor''.

The Foundation has provided support for the [[Wendy Schmidt Oil Cleanup X Challenge]]. a challenge award offered by the [[X Prize Foundation]] for efficient capturing of [[crude oil]] from [[ocean water]], inspired by the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill]]. It was announced in July 2010, and $1.3 million in prizes, were awarded in October 2011.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.iprizecleanoceans.org/blog/2011/10/11/and-winners-are |title = And the Winners are… |date = October 11, 2011 |publisher = iprizecleanoceans.org |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url = http://www.popsci.com/technology/article/2011-10/x-prize-challenge-seeks-new-designs-and-inspiration-clean-future-oil-spills |title = Winner of Million-Dollar X Challenge Cleans Up Oil Spills Three Times Better Than Existing Tech |author = Rebecca Boyle |author2 = Clay Dillow |date = October 11, 2011 |work = PopSci.com |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref> It also supports the  $1.5 million Wendy Schmidt Ocean Health X Prize for work on [[ocean acidification]].<ref>{{cite news |url = http://www.xprize.org/blog/2013/01/25/unleashing-innovation-to-save-our-oceans |title = Unleashing Innovation to Save Our Oceans |author = Robert K. Weiss |date = January 25, 2013 |publisher = X PRIZE blog |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url = https://www.forbes.com/sites/lorikozlowski/2012/04/23/attention-heroes-who-will-save-the-worlds-oceans-xprize/ |title = Attention Heroes: Who Will Save The World's Oceans? |author = Lori Kozlowski |date = April 23, 2012 |work = Forbes.com |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref>

In March 2013, the Foundation and the [[Ellen MacArthur Foundation]] launched the Schmidt-MacArthur Fellowship, a global fellowship program for developing the skills and innovative mindset needed for the [[circular economy]].<ref>{{cite news |url = http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/news/schmidt-macarthur-fellowships-launched/2002420.article |title = Schmidt-MacArthur fellowships launched |author = Chris Parr |date = March 10, 2013 |work = Times Higher Education |accessdate=April 27, 2013}}</ref>

In 2020, [[Sophie Schmidt (publisher)|Sophie Schmidt]], daughter of Eric Schmidt and Wendy Schmidt, stated that ''[[Rest of World]]'', a nonprofit news organization, has received 6 million dollars from her family trust. She also indicated that she would spend $60 million on ''Rest of World'' over the next decade to fund its operations. ''Rest of World'' is an American nonprofit publication that covers technology stories from outside [[Western world|Western countries]]. It was launched in 2020 by Sophie Schmidt.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Alpert |first=Lukas |date=2020-09-27 |title=Eric Schmidt’s Daughter Has Tech Ambitions—Just Not in Silicon Valley |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/eric-schmidts-daughter-has-tech-ambitionsjust-not-in-silicon-valley-11601218509 |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]}}</ref>

In 2024, the Foundation provided a founding investment to its former chief innovation officer [[Thomas Kalil|Tom Kalil]] for the founding of [[Renaissance Philanthropy]], a new organization dedicated to increasing philanthropic funding for science and technology.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schultz |first=Abby |title=Science and Tech Ideas Need Philanthropic Support. A New Eric and Wendy Schmidt-Backed Advisory Aims to Help. |url=https://www.barrons.com/articles/science-and-tech-ideas-need-philanthropic-support-a-new-eric-and-wendy-schmidt-backed-advisory-aims-to-help-1bf34e88 |access-date=2026-08-30 |website=www.barrons.com |language=en-US}}</ref>
