{{as of|2012}}, North Texas sponsored fifteen athletic teams that compete at the intercollegiate level of [[Division I (NCAA)|NCAA Division I]]—for men: [[American football|football]]; for men and women: [[basketball]], [[Track and field|track & field]], [[cross country running|cross country]], and golf; for women only: [[Diving (sport)|diving]], soccer, [[softball]], [[Swimming (sport)|swimming]], [[tennis]], and [[volleyball]]. North Texas was a member of [[Conference USA]] until it moved to the [[American Conference (NCAA)|American Conference]] in 2023.{{Sfn|"AAC Commissioner"|2022}} As of April 2021, the Mean Green have won 142 conference championships, including 50 since 2000.{{Sfn|UNT: "Athletic Impact," May|2025}}

===Football===
<!--NOTE EDITORS: If you are making a change to this summary of football, it may be wise to also make similar changes or see if they are needed at the main article, "North Texas Mean Green football".-->
<!--NOTE B TO EDITORS: When using ORDINAL TO WORD TEMPLATE, subtract a year from the start date.-->
In its {{age|1913|09|01}}–year history of intercollegiate athletics, the [[North Texas Mean Green football|North Texas football team]] has won 24 conference championships, with the last four occurring from 2001 to 2004 in the [[Sun Belt Conference]].{{Sfn|DeLassus|Noel}} {{as of|2014}}, the team has appeared in thirteen [[bowl games]], winning three including the 1946 Optimist Bowl, the [[2002 New Orleans Bowl]] and the 2014 [[Heart of Dallas Bowl]]. From 1952 to 2010, home football games were played at [[Fouts Field]]. In 2011, UNT began playing in newly constructed [[DATCU Stadium]].

===Men's basketball===
<!--NOTE EDITORS: If you are making a change to this summary of Men's basketball, it may be wise to also make similar changes or see if they are needed at the main article, "North Texas Mean Green men's basketball".-->
The [[North Texas Mean Green men's basketball|North Texas men's basketball team]] won the [[National Invitation Tournament|NIT]] in 2023,{{Sfn|Piellucci, March 31,|2021}} following Conference USA titles in 2022 (West Division), 2021 (tournament), and 2020 (regular season). Earlier, the team won the [[Sun Belt Conference]] Tournament in 2010 and 2007, earning NCAA Tournament bids in both seasons. The 2006–07 campaign began a four-year run of 20-plus wins. The {{age|0000|10|01}}–{{age|-0001|10|01}} season marks the {{Ordinal to word|{{age|format=raw|1972|10|01}}}} season that the [[UNT Coliseum]] has served as the home for men's basketball.{{Sfn|UNT: Men's Basketball,|2024–25|p=101}}

== Sustainability ==
[[File:UNT wind turbines.jpg|thumb|upright|Wind turbines near [[DATCU Stadium]]]]

In 2008, the university became the first large public university in Texas to sign the "[[American College and University President's Climate Commitment (ACUPCC)|American College and University President's Climate Commitment]]" (ACUPCC). {{as of|2012|September}}, twenty-four of the 658 signatory institutions of higher learning were from Texas. Of those twenty-four, five were full undergraduate-graduate institutions (2 private, 3 public). Of those five, UNT was the largest. The objectives include achieving [[carbon neutrality]] by 2040 and ensuring that all new university buildings and facilities meet a minimum [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design]] (LEED) Silver rating by the [[U.S. Green Building Council]].{{Sfn|"UNT Briefs"|2012}} The university continued to promote sustainability in 2017 when it purchased a year worth of renewable energy credits, to allow the University of North Texas to be powered by renewable energy.{{Sfn|''NT Daily'', Apr. 6,|2017|p=2}}

The Life Science Complex, built in 2011, became UNT's first [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design|LEED]] certified structure, earning a Gold rating. The Complex is a state-of-the-art research facility that houses the university's [[biochemistry]], [[molecular biology]], developmental [[physiology]], [[genetics]] and [[plant sciences]] programs. The building features four climate-controlled rooftop [[greenhouses]] and one of the country's most sophisticated [[Aquatic science|aquatics laboratories]] with more than 2,500 tanks.  Also in 2011, [[DATCU Stadium]], the {{Cardinal to word|{{age|format=raw|2011|09|10}}}}-year-old football stadium, became the first newly built sports stadium in the nation to earn a Platinum [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design|LEED]] certification, the highest of four certifications.{{Sfn|Vito|2011}} The facility features wind turbines, eco-friendly building materials, and native landscape architecture.

The following year, ''The Princeton Review's Guide to 322 Green Colleges, 2012 Edition'', listed UNT for the second consecutive year, citing its top 17-percent ranking among green-compliant universities nationwide under [[American College and University President's Climate Commitment (ACUPCC)|ACUPCC]]. The article stated that forty percent of the energy on campus is derived from renewable sources, and 43 percent of the buildings have undergone energy retrofits. The campus has posted strong numbers in recycling: since 2009, the university has recycled nearly 1,000 tons of waste materials. UNT offers graduate degrees in Environmental Science and Public Administration and Management.{{Sfn|''Princeton Review's Guide'', 2012 ed.||p=164}}{{Sfn|''Princeton Review's Guide'', 2013 ed.||p=154}}

==See also==
* ''[[American Literary Review]]'' is a national magazine of poetry, fiction, and nonfiction by writers at all stages in their careers. It was founded in 1990. The ''Review'' is largely student run, with faculty editorial oversight. In the fall of 2013, the ''Review'' become exclusively an online digital publication. {{ISSN|1051-5062}}
* ''[[Environmental Ethics (journal)|Environmental Ethics]]'' is a peer-reviewed academic journal covering the study of philosophical aspects of environmental problems. It was established in 1979.
* [[University of North Texas Press]], founded in 1987, is a relatively young albeit prolific book publisher with more than 300 titles in print ({{as of|2012|lc=y}}).

{{Short description|Standard for certifying carbon emissions reductions}}

The '''Verified Carbon Standard''' (VCS), formerly the '''Voluntary Carbon Standard''',<ref>{{cite news |last1=Peters-Stanley |first1=Molly |title=Regulators Embrace Voluntary Carbon |url=https://www.forest-trends.org/ecosystem_marketplace/regulators-embrace-voluntary-carbon/ |access-date=2018-09-17 |publisher=Ecosystem Marketplace |date=2011-03-15}}</ref> is a standard for certifying [[Carbon offsets and credits|carbon credits]] to offset emissions.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Patch {{!}} Carbon Offset Verification and Registries, Explained|url=https://www.patch.io/blog/carbon-offset-verification-and-registries-explained|access-date=2021-12-18|website=www.patch.io|language=en}}</ref> VCS is administered by Verra, a certifier of voluntary carbon offsets.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Greenfield |first=Patrick |date=2023-03-10 |title=As carbon offsetting faces 'credibility revolution', shoppers should be wary |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/mar/10/as-carbon-offsetting-faces-credibility-revolution-shoppers-should-be-wary |access-date=2023-09-18 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> As of 2024, more than 2,300 projects were registered under the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), spanning various sectors such as AFOLU (Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use), energy, transport, waste, manufacturing industries, and others. These projects have collectively issued over 1.3 billion credits, with more than 776 million credits retired to date.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Verra Search Page |url=https://registry.verra.org/app/search/VCS |access-date=2025-01-10 |website=registry.verra.org}}</ref>

There are also specific methodologies for [[REDD and REDD+|REDD+ projects]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Methodologies |url=https://verra.org/methodologies-main/ |access-date=2023-03-24 |website=Verra |language=en-US}}</ref> Verra is a program of choice for most of the forest credits in the voluntary market, and almost all REDD+ projects.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Chagas |first1=Thiago |url=https://climatefocus.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/A-close-look-at-the-quality-of-REDD-carbon-credits-2020-V2.0.pdf |title=A close look at the quality of REDD+ carbon credits |last2=Galt |first2=Hilda |last3=Lee |first3=Donna |last4=Neeff |first4=Till |last5=Streck |first5=Charlotte |publisher=Climate Focus |year=2020 |at=Page 5}}</ref> The [[Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market]] lists Verra's Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) as a "CCP-Eligible" program under the Core Carbon Principles benchmark.<ref name="ICVCM_AssessmentStatus">{{cite web
 |title=Assessment Status
 |website=Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM)
 |url=https://icvcm.org/assessment-status/
 |access-date=17 February 2026
}}</ref>

Verra was developed in 2005 when the company Climate Wedge and its partner [[Cheyne Capital Management|Cheyne Capital]] designed and drafted the first version (version 1.0) of the Voluntary Carbon Standard.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-04 |title=India's Voluntary Offset Scheme in Carbon Credit Trading Market |url=https://www.ceew.in/publications/voluntary-carbon-offset-mechanism-and-challenges-in-carbon-credit-trading-scheme-market-for-india |access-date=2025-08-18 |website=CEEW |language=en}}</ref> This standard was intended as a quality standard for transacting and developing [[Kyoto Protocol|"non-Kyoto" Protocol]] carbon credits. Climate Wedge was at the time active as a carbon markets investment advisory firm.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate Wedge Ltd |url=http://www.climatewedge.com/company.html |access-date=2024-04-25 |website=www.climatewedge.com}}</ref>

There are controversies around this standard and how it is implemented. In 2023, an investigation by ''[[The Guardian]]'', ''[[Die Zeit]]'', and SourceMaterial (a non-profit investigative journalism outlet) found that about 94% of the rainforest [[carbon offset]]s certified by Verra are worthless.<ref name="GuardianWorthless">{{Cite news |last=Greenfield |first=Patrick |date=2023-01-18 |title=Revealed: more than 90% of rainforest carbon offsets by biggest certifier are worthless, analysis shows |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/jan/18/revealed-forest-carbon-offsets-biggest-provider-worthless-verra-aoe |access-date=2023-09-16 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> The investigation even found that the standard may in fact worsen [[climate change]]: "Investigation into Verra carbon standard finds most are ‘phantom credits’ and may worsen global heating".<ref name="GuardianWorthless" /> In May 2023, following months of criticism towards Verra in its handling of carbon-offsetting, CEO David Antonioli resigned.<ref name=":0" />

In June 2024, three carbon credit projects were suspended in the [[Amazônia Legal|Brazilian Amazon]] after the police raids targeting Verra certified projects linked to a land-grabbing and illegal logging scam.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wenzel |first=Fernanda |date=2024-06-11 |title=Verra suspends carbon credit projects following police raid in Brazil |url=https://news.mongabay.com/2024/06/verra-suspends-carbon-credit-projects-following-police-raid-in-brazil/ |access-date=2025-06-18 |website=Mongabay Environmental News |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Usage in voluntary carbon markets== 
{{excerpt|Carbon offsets and credits#Verified Carbon Standard by Verra}}

== Development ==
{{climate change mitigation}}
In 2005, carbon markets investment advisory firm Climate Wedge and its partner [[Cheyne Capital Management|Cheyne Capital]] designed and drafted the first version (version 1.0) of the Voluntary Carbon Standard, intended as a quality standard for transacting and developing [[Kyoto Protocol|"non-Kyoto" Protocol]] carbon credits. Those were voluntary carbon emissions reductions from greenhouse gas reduction projects that met the quality and verification standards of the UNFCCC Kyoto Protocol's [[Clean Development Mechanism]] (CDM) carbon offset mechanism, but were not eligible, as the CDM only allows emission-reduction projects in developing countries to earn certified emission reduction (<abbr>CER</abbr>) credits.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CDM: About CDM |url=https://cdm.unfccc.int/about/index.html |access-date=2025-08-18 |website=United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement}}</ref>

In March 2006, Climate Wedge and Cheyne Capital transferred the Voluntary Carbon Standard version 1.0 to [[The Climate Group]], International Emissions Trading Association (IETA) and [[World Economic Forum]]. They also provided the initial sponsor capital for these non-profit organizations to subsequently convene a team of global carbon market experts to further draft the VCS requirements. The [[World Business Council for Sustainable Development]] (WBCSD) joined later on. The team later formed the VCS Steering Committee, which worked to draft the second and subsequent versions of the VCS Standard.{{Citation needed|date=January 2023}}

In 2008, the Board of Directors named David Antonioli the organization's first chief executive officer. In 2009, VCS incorporated in [[Washington D.C.]] as a non-profit non-governmental organization.{{Citation needed|date=January 2023}}

On February 15, 2018, the organization that maintains the Verified Carbon Standard changed its name from Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) to Verra.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Zwick |first1=Steve |title=Verified Carbon Standard Changes Name To Verra |url=https://www.forest-trends.org/ecosystem_marketplace/verified-carbon-standard-changes-name-verra/ |date=2018-02-15}}</ref> The new name was chosen to suggest "‘verification’ and ‘terra’, and reflects the fundamental nature of our work".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-02-15 |title=VCS is now Verra |url=https://verra.org/vcs-is-now-verra/ |access-date=2024-01-15 |website=Verra |language=en-US}}</ref>

In May 2023, following months of criticism towards Verra in its handling of carbon-offsetting, CEO David Antonioli resigned.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Greenfield |first=Patrick |date=2023-05-23 |title=CEO of biggest carbon credit certifier to resign after claims offsets worthless |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/may/23/ceo-of-worlds-biggest-carbon-credit-provider-says-he-is-resigning |access-date=2023-05-24 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

== Controversies ==
A 2021 study by ''[[The Guardian]]'' newspaper and [[Unearthed (publication)|''Unearthed'']] reported that Verra's carbon offsetting standard was flawed. Accredited forest protection projects were using inconsistent predictive methods and overstating their emissions reductions. 11 of the 12 projects studied showed no difference in emissions compared to control groups. The study said the findings raised doubts about the validity of the carbon offsetting market.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Greenfield |first=Patrick |date=2021-05-04 |title=Carbon offsets used by major airlines based on flawed system, warn experts |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/may/04/carbon-offsets-used-by-major-airlines-based-on-flawed-system-warn-experts |access-date=2023-09-16 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

A nine-month investigation published on January 18, 2023, by ''The Guardian'', ''[[Die Zeit]]'', and SourceMaterial, a non-profit investigative journalism organization, found that approximately 94% of the rainforest [[Carbon offset|carbon credits]] certified by Verra  –  which accounted for about 40% of all credits it approved – do not represent a tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. They also found that the credit scheme may worsen global heating and that the deforestation threat for Verra projects was overstated by 400% on average. At one of Verra's project sites in Peru, residents complained about being forcefully evicted from their homes, which were then demolished. The investigation was based on one [[Peer-reviewed journal|peer-reviewed]] study by a group of [[University of Cambridge]] scientists, and another from a team of international researchers that at the time of the Guardian publication was not published or peer-reviewed.<ref name="GuardianWorthless" />

In 2024, a Channel 4 documentary highlighted these concerns alongside claims from [[Human Rights Watch]] that it was investigating a Verra carbon reduction project where Indigenous Cambodians lived in fear of homes and farmland being destroyed by armed rangers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Change Climate Season: Leading carbon offsetting certifier investigated in new Channel 4 documentary The Great Climate Scandal {{!}} Channel 4 |url=https://www.channel4.com/press/news/change-climate-season-leading-carbon-offsetting-certifier-investigated-new-channel-4 |access-date=2024-04-23 |website=www.channel4.com}}</ref>

In May 2024, an investigation report by Brazilian news outlet Mongbay discovered that two carbon credit projects certified by Verra in the Brazilian Amazon has found that they may be connected to illegal timber laundering.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wenzel |first=Fernanda |date=2024-05-21 |title=Top brands buy Amazon carbon credits from suspected timber laundering scam |url=https://news.mongabay.com/2024/05/top-brands-buy-amazon-carbon-credits-from-suspected-timber-laundering-scam/ |access-date=2025-06-18 |website=Mongabay Environmental News |language=en-US}}</ref> Following the report, Brazilian police raided the three carbon credit projects belonging to Ricardo Stoppe, Brazil's top individual seller of carbon credits.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wenzel |first=Fernanda |date=2024-06-07 |title=Brazil police raid Amazon carbon credit projects exposed by Mongabay |url=https://news.mongabay.com/2024/06/brazilian-investigators-raid-amazon-carbon-credit-projects-exposed-by-mongabay/ |access-date=2025-06-18 |website=Mongabay Environmental News |language=en-US}}</ref> Clientele of the projects include major corporations such as GOL Airlines, [[Nestlé]], [[Toshiba]], Spotify, Boeing, and PwC.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Analysis |first=Center for Climate Crime |date=2024-06-25 |title=Top brands buy Amazon carbon credits from suspected timber laundering scam |url=https://climatecrimeanalysis.org/top-brands-buy-amazon-carbon-credits-from-suspected-timber-laundering-scam/ |access-date=2025-06-18 |website=Center for Climate Crime Analysis |language=en-US}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Wendy Schmidt
======================================================================

{{short description|American businesswoman and philanthropist}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=May 2020}}
{{Infobox person
| name               = Wendy Schmidt
| image              = File:Wendy Schmidt.jpg
| birth_name         = Wendy Susan Boyle
| birth_date         = {{Birth date and age|df=y|1955|07|26}}
| birth_place        = [[Orange, New Jersey|Orange]], [[New Jersey]], U.S.
| education          = [[Smith College]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])<br>[[University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Master of Arts|MA]])
| occupation         = Philanthropist and investor
| title              = President and co-founder [[Schmidt Family Foundation]] <br>President and co-founder [[Schmidt Ocean Institute]]<br>Cofounder [[Schmidt Sciences]]<br>Cofounder 11th Hour Racing<br>Cofounder Agog
| spouse             = {{Marriage|[[Eric Schmidt]]|1980}}
| children           = [[Sophie Schmidt (publisher)|Sophie Schmidt]]
| website            = {{URL|https://wendyschmidt.com/}}
}}

'''Wendy Susan Schmidt''' (''[[née]]'' '''Boyle''') is an American philanthropist and investor. She is the president and co-founder of the [[Schmidt Family Foundation]], holding over $2 billion in philanthropic assets, and [[Schmidt Ocean Institute]]. She is married to [[Eric Schmidt]], the former CEO of Google.

==Early life and education==
Wendy Susan Boyle was born on July 26, 1955, in Orange, New Jersey,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2025-02-20 |title=Wendy Schmidt Invests Big in Documentary Film |url=https://www.insidephilanthropy.com/home/wendy-schmidt-invests-big-in-documentary-film |access-date=2026-02-02 |website=www.insidephilanthropy.com |language=en-US}}</ref> the second of five children and the only girl.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2022-08-26 |title=Wendy Schmidt gives big to protect oceans, planet's future |url=https://apnews.com/article/science-technology-climate-and-environment-philanthropy-b31e7f4445a95fc0819e72b81b226a1b |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

She graduated from [[Smith College]] in 1977 with a dual bachelor's degree in anthropology and sociology, before earning a master's degree in journalism from [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name=":1" />

== Career ==
After graduate school, Schmidt worked in marketing at [[Plexus Computers]]. In 1982, she was recruited to join the marketing department of [[Sun Microsystems]], where she was employee #42. Schmidt left Sun Microsystems in 1986 after the company went public.<ref name=":1" />

Schmidt studied interior design at [[Cañada College]]; she later founded and ran an interior design firm for 16 years.<ref>{{Cite web |title=LEADERS Interview with Wendy Schmidt, President, The Schmidt Family Foundation |url=https://www.leadersmag.com/issues/2020.2_Apr/Purpose/LEADERS-Wendy-Schmidt-Schmidt-Family-Foundation.html |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=www.leadersmag.com}}</ref>

In 2025, Schmidt acquired a controlling interest in Jigsaw Productions from its founder and president, [[Alex Gibney]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barnes |first=Brooks |date=2025-02-06 |title=A Top Documentary Director Finds a Billionaire Backer |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/06/business/alex-gibney-wendy-schmidt-jigsaw-documentaries.html |access-date=2026-02-05 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Philanthropy ==
Schmidt is known for her philanthropic work related to clean energy, regenerative agriculture, ocean health, human rights and scientific research.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mento |first=Maria Di |date=2025-03-04 |title=Philanthropy 50 |url=https://www.philanthropy.com/project/the-philanthropy-50/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Chronicle of Philanthropy |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cruz |first=Ryan P. |date=2025-04-21 |title=How Two Santa Barbara Philanthropists Stepped in to Preserve Tri-County Produce |url=https://www.independent.com/2025/04/21/how-two-santa-barbara-philanthropists-stepped-in-to-preserve-tri-county-produce/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=The Santa Barbara Independent |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Moxley |first=Mitch |title=Actor Ted Danson and Philanthropist Wendy Schmidt Are Fighting to Save Our Oceans |url=https://www.barrons.com/articles/actor-ted-danson-and-philanthropist-wendy-schmidt-are-fighting-to-save-our-oceans-01616442211 |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=www.barrons.com |language=en-US}}</ref> She has created multiple philanthropic organizations with the support of her husband, [[Eric Schmidt]]. Wendy has led the [[Schmidt Family Foundation]] and [[Schmidt Ocean Institute]] since their founding.<ref name=":0" />

=== Climate and sustainability ===
{{Main|Schmidt Family Foundation|Schmidt Ocean Institute}}
In 2006, Schmidt and her husband co-founded the [[Schmidt Family Foundation]] to support climate change initiatives.<ref name=":1" /> She serves as president of the foundation and directs its grantmaking and [[impact investing]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wendy Schmidt |url=https://schmidtocean.org/person/wendy-schmidt/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Schmidt Ocean Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> The foundation's main grantmaking program, the 11th Hour Project, supports renewable energy, regenerative agriculture and food systems, ocean health and human rights.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Clarke |first=John |date=2022-08-30 |title=Wendy Schmidt Is No Longer a Rookie at the Maxi Cup |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/30/sports/sailing/wendy-schmidt-maxi-yacht-cup.html |access-date=2026-02-05 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Another grantmaking program, Schmidt Marine Technology Partners, invests in early marine technologies that restore and protect ocean health.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kavate |first=Michael |date=2025-01-21 |title=Green 990s: What Are Four Major Donor Couples Funding? |url=https://www.insidephilanthropy.com/home/green-990s-what-are-donors-like-schmidt-grantham-simons-and-doerr-funding |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=www.insidephilanthropy.com |language=en-US}}</ref> The foundation also supports program-aligned organizations including [[Ecovative Design]], Navajo Power and [[Virunga National Park]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Impact Investing |url=https://11thhourproject.org/impact-investing/ |access-date=2026-08-24 |website=11th Hour Project |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2010, through the Schmidt Family Foundation, she offered the prize purse of the [[Wendy Schmidt Oil Cleanup X Challenge]], a challenge award for the efficient capturing of [[crude oil]] from seawater motivated by the [[Deepwater Horizon oil spill]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Wealthy Activist and X Prize Group Team Up on Oil-Spill Challenge|url=http://philanthropy.com/blogs/philanthropytoday/wealthy-activistx-prize-group-team-up-on-oil-spill-challenge/25885|publisher=Chronicles of Philanthropy|accessdate=September 19, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Schwartz|first=Ariel|title=X Prize Foundation Unveils $1.4 Million Oil Cleanup X Challenge|work=Fast Company |date=July 29, 2010 |url=http://www.fastcompany.com/1675688/x-prize-foundation-unveils-14-million-oil-cleanup-x-challenge|accessdate=September 19, 2013}}</ref>
[[File:Wendy Schmidt at Schmidt Science Fellows Global Meeting 2022.jpg|thumb|Schmidt at the Schmidt Science Fellows Global Meeting in 2022.]]In 2015, Schmidt initiated the 'Wendy Schmidt Ocean Health XPRIZE': a global competition that awarded $2 million to scientists and engineers who demonstrated excellence in the creation of new accurate and affordable [[ocean acidification]] technology.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wendy Schmidt Ocean Health XPRIZE |url=https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/co2/story/Wendy+Schmidt+Ocean+Health+XPRIZE |publisher=NOAA.com website |access-date=March 20, 2022}}</ref> The Schmidt Family Foundation announced a $10 million grant to the [[Monterey Bay Aquarium]] in February 2015. The grant enabled the aquarium to collaborate with industry leaders and address growing challenges in global fisheries.<ref>{{cite web|title=Monterey Bay Aquarium Receives $10 Million From Schmidt Foundation|url=https://philanthropynewsdigest.org/news/monterey-bay-aquarium-receives-10-million-from-schmidt-foundation|publisher=Philanthropy News Digest|access-date=May 13, 2022}}</ref>

Through the foundation, Wendy Schmidt has supported Indigenous causes, contributing a $5 million professorship endowment to [[Princeton University]] in December 2020,<ref>{{cite web |title=Eric and Wendy Schmidt endow new professorship of Indigenous studies at Princeton |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2020/12/03/eric-and-wendy-schmidt-endow-new-professorship-indigenous-studies-princeton |access-date=April 23, 2022 |publisher=Princeton University website}}</ref> and an endowed gift to [[Stanford University]] to expand its [[Native American studies|Native American Studies]] program.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New gift will help Stanford reimagine Native American Studies through a 21st-century Indigenous lens {{!}} Stanford School of Humanities and Sciences |url=https://humsci.stanford.edu/feature/new-gift-will-help-stanford-reimagine-native-american-studies-through-21st-century |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=humsci.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref>

In 2008, Schmidt founded Remain to support the social and environmental sustainability of [[Nantucket]], Massachusetts, including the year-round viability of its downtown.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Percelay |first=Bruce A. |date=2021-06-30 |title=GLOBAL CHANGEMAKERS |url=https://n-magazine-archive.com/global-changemakers/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Nantucket Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=DePace |first=Antonia |last2=Percelay |first2=Bruce A. |date=July 31, 2024 |title="Introducing The Hive" |url=https://www.n-magazine.com/wendy-schmidt-the-hive |work=N-Magazine}}</ref> Schmidt, who is a competitive sailor, also founded 11th Hour Racing to improve sustainability in sailing and the maritime industry.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2023-09-27 |title=Wendy Schmidt |url=https://thesuperyachtlife.com/humansofyachting/wendy-schmidt/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Superyacht Life |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2009, Schmidt and her husband founded [[Schmidt Ocean Institute]].<ref name=":1" /> The virtual institute operates [[RV Falkor Too|R/V Falkor (too)]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=McCarthy |first=Michael |title=Wendy Schmidt: Innovating for Ocean Health and Climate Change |url=https://www.modernluxury.com/wendy-schmidt-ocean-climate-philanthropy/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Modern Luxury |language=en-US}}</ref> and makes it available at no cost to scientists worldwide in exchange for making their science and discoveries publicly available in real-time.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mock-Bunting |first=Logan |date=2021-03-23 |title=Schmidt Ocean Institute Acquires New Research Vessel To Expand Ability To Explore, Research The Ocean |url=https://schmidtocean.org/soi-acquires-new-research-vessel/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Schmidt Ocean Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Science, technology, and education ===
{{Main|Schmidt Sciences}}
In 2009, Wendy and Eric Schmidt created the $25&nbsp;million Schmidt Transformative Technology Fund at [[Princeton University]] to support research and technology in the natural sciences and engineering.<ref>{{cite news |date=October 14, 2009 |title=Eric Schmidt: Princeton Receives $25M From Google CEO For Tech Fund |url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2009/10/14/eric-schmidt-princeton-re_n_321016.html |accessdate=September 19, 2013 |work=HuffPost}}</ref>

In partnership with the Rhodes Trust, Wendy and Eric Schmidt created Schmidt Science Fellows in 2018: a post-doctoral program that advances interdisciplinary scientific research. The Fellowship equips participants with tools and expertise to drive new discoveries to benefit human and planetary health.<ref>{{cite web|title=Inaugural Class of Schmidt Science Fellows announced|url=https://www.rhodeshouse.ox.ac.uk/news-events/latest-news/news/2018/april/inaugural-class-of-schmidt-science-fellows-announced/|publisher=Rhodes Trust|access-date=May 31, 2022}}</ref>

In 2019, Wendy and Eric Schmidt funded the rebuilding and expansion of historic Guyot Hall at [[Princeton University]]’s Department of Computer Science. The new building will be renamed ‘Eric and Wendy Schmidt Hall’, with construction scheduled to be complete in 2026.<ref>{{cite web|title=Gift from Eric and Wendy Schmidt to create a new home for computer science at Princeton University|url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2019/05/29/gift-eric-and-wendy-schmidt-create-new-home-computer-science-princeton-university|publisher=Princeton University website|access-date=March 23, 2022}}</ref>
[[File:Eric and Wendy Schmidt in 2024.jpg|thumb|Wendy and Eric Schmidt in 2024.]]In 2021, the Schmidts gave $150 million to establish the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Center at the [[Broad Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Broad Institute launches $300m initiative to fight diseases with artificial intelligence - The Boston Globe |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2021/03/25/business/broad-institute-names-new-center-ai-medicine-former-google-chief-schmidt/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=BostonGlobe.com |language=en-US}}</ref> The center combines machine learning and biology research on human health.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Broad Institute Launches $150 Million Schmidt Center for Research in Machine Learning, Biology |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2021/3/31/broad-institute-launches-schmidt-center/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Harvard Crimson}}</ref>

In 2022, the Schmidts donated $12.6 million to establish the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Center for Data Science and the Environment at UC Berkeley.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lohwater |first=Tiffany |last2=Gipple |first2=Julie |title=New UC Berkeley center will apply data science to solving environmental challenges |url=https://inspire.berkeley.edu/o/new-uc-berkeley-center-will-apply-data-science-to-solving-environmental-challenges/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=inspire.berkeley.edu |language=en}}</ref>

In 2024, Schmidt and her husband co-founded [[Schmidt Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rose |first=Frank |date=2025-03-26 |title=New A.I. Project Explores Mysteries of Delacroix, Master of Romanticism |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/26/arts/design/digital-delacroix-ai-eric-wendy-schmidt-murals.html |access-date=2026-02-05 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-22 |title=The Schmidt Family Foundation |url=https://www.insidephilanthropy.com/find-a-grant/grants-s/the-schmidt-family-foundation |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=www.insidephilanthropy.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Arts and communications ===
Schmidt and journalist [[Chip Giller]] co-founded Agog: The Immersive Media Institute, a nonprofit organization, in 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stiffman |first=Eden |date=2024-03-19 |title=Wendy Schmidt and Grist Founder Launch Immersive-Media Nonprofit |url=https://www.philanthropy.com/news/wendy-schmidt-and-grist-founder-launch-immersive-media-nonprofit/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Chronicle of Philanthropy |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2025, the Schmidt Family Foundation joined a philanthropic effort to provide emergency funding to support the Public Media Company after the loss of federal funding.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ramirez |first=Martha |date=2025-08-21 |title=Rapid Response: Funders Pool Their Dollars to Protect Public Media |url=https://www.insidephilanthropy.com/home/rapid-response-funders-pool-their-dollars-to-protect-public-media |access-date=2026-08-24 |language=en-US}}</ref> As part of these efforts, the foundation helped to establish the Public Media Bridge Fund, beginning with a planning grant made to the Public Media Company before the federal funding cuts. That fund provides emergency grants to help build sustainability for public media. The Bridge Fund arose from a planning grant from the Schmidt Family Foundation provided to the Public Media Company.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mullin |first=Benjamin |date=2025-08-19 |title=The Race to Rescue PBS and NPR Stations |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/08/19/business/the-race-to-rescue-pbs-and-npr-stations.html |access-date=2026-08-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> 

In 2024, the [[Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles]] announced the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Environment and Art Prize, an unrestricted $100,000 honorarium<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eric and Wendy Schmidt Environment and Art Prize |url=https://www.moca.org/about/schmidt-prize |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=www.moca.org |language=en}}</ref> supporting artists who contribute to the dialogue surrounding climate, conservation and sustainability.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-16 |title=MOCA announces a new $100,000 environment and arts prize |url=https://www.dailynews.com/2024/07/16/moca-announces-a-new-100000-environment-and-arts-prize/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=Daily News |language=en-US}}</ref>

She is a co-founder and board member of [[Climate Central]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Wendy Schmidt, Corporate Secretary, Founding Board Member|url=https://www.climatecentral.org/what-we-do/people/wendy-schmidt-corporate-secretary-founding-board-member|publisher=Climate Central website|accessdate=January 20, 2023}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Schmidt met her future husband, [[Eric Schmidt|Eric]], in 1977 while both were attending graduate school at Berkeley. He is the former CEO of Google. They were married in June 1980 and together they have two children, including [[Sophie Schmidt (publisher)|Sophie Schmidt]].<ref name="Google Her">{{cite news |last=Holson |first=Laura |date=August 29, 2012 |title=You Could Google Her |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/08/30/fashion/nantucket-benefits-from-a-google-long-distance-marriage.html |accessdate=September 19, 2013 |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

Schmidt has been a competitive sailor since 2007,<ref name=":2" /> and is skipper of ''Deep Blue''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kochetkova |first=Maria |date=2024-10-12 |title=Wendy Schmidt Returns to Barcolana: Sailing, Sustainability, and a Deep Connection to the Sea |url=https://www.intrieste.com/2024/10/12/wendy-schmidt-returns-to-barcolana-sailing-sustainability-and-a-deep-connection-to-the-sea/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=InTrieste |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2022, she won the 54th [[Barcolana]] regatta,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-03 |title=Wendy Schmidt Brings Ocean Conservation to Barcolana Regatta |url=https://www.intrieste.com/2024/10/03/wendy-schmidt-brings-ocean-conservation-to-barcolana-regatta/ |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=InTrieste |language=en-US}}</ref> becoming the first American and first woman to win the world's largest sailing race.<ref name=":3" />

Schmidt has supported political causes in California.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Rainmakers: California's top political donors, 2001–2011 |url=http://rainmaker.apps.cironline.org/donors/wendy-schmidt/ |accessdate=September 19, 2013 |publisher=CaliforniaWatch.org website, produced by the Center for Investigative Reporting}}</ref> She funded a campaign to save a [[2024 United States ballot measures#Withdrawn from November ballot|California law]] banning new oil and gas wells within 3,200 feet of schools, parks and other neighborhood locations.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stark |first=Kevin |last2=Lagos |first2=Marisa |date=2024-06-27 |title=Oil Industry's Referendum on California Drilling Law Is Pulled From Ballot {{!}} KQED |url=https://www.kqed.org/science/1993497/oil-industrys-referendum-on-california-drilling-law-is-pulled-from-ballot |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=www.kqed.org |language=en}}</ref>

'''WWF''' is a Swiss-based [[international non-governmental organization]] that works in the field of wilderness preservation and the reduction of [[human impact on the environment]].<ref name=":0" /> It was founded in 1961 as the '''World Wildlife Fund'''. The official name of the Swiss umbrella organization and in some countries is '''World Wide Fund for Nature''' following a renaming (retaining the abbreviation WWF), while World Wildlife Fund remains the official name in other countries, including Canada and the United States. WWF is the world's largest [[List of environmental organizations|conservation organization]], with over 5 million supporters worldwide, working in more than 100 countries and supporting around 3,000 conservation and environmental projects.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.panda.org/about_wwf/where_we_work/project/ |title=WWF conservation projects around the world |access-date=6 February 2009 |archive-date=12 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210212212431/https://wwf.panda.org/404error/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It has invested over $1 billion in more than 12,000 conservation initiatives since 1995.<ref name="WorldWildLife">{{cite web |title=WWF – Endangered Species Conservation |url=https://www.worldwildlife.org |website=World Wildlife Fund |access-date=18 April 2018 |archive-date=17 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180417223651/https://www.worldwildlife.org/ |url-status=live }}</ref> WWF is a [[Foundation (nonprofit)|foundation]] with 65% of funding from individuals and bequests including [[The 1001: A Nature Trust]], 17% from government sources (such as the [[World Bank]], [[Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office|Foreign Office]], and [[United States Agency for International Development|USAID]]) and 8% from corporations in 2020.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://wwf.panda.org/discover/about_wwf/how_were_run/finance/ |title=How is WWF run? |access-date=13 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220613100459/https://wwf.panda.org/discover/about_wwf/how_were_run/finance/ |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-date=13 June 2022 }}</ref><ref name="WWF-INT Annual Review">{{cite book |title=WWFN-International Annual Review |year=2020 |publisher=World Wide Fund for Nature |url=https://wwfint.awsassets.panda.org/downloads/wwfintl_annualreview2020.pdf |access-date=13 June 2022 |page=60 |archive-date=10 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221010020615/https://wwfint.awsassets.panda.org/downloads/wwfintl_annualreview2020.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

WWF aims to "stop the degradation of the planet's natural environment and to build a future in which humans live in harmony with nature."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://wwf.panda.org/mission_principles_goals.cfm |title=WWF's Mission, Guiding Principles and Goals |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=<!--Not stated--> |website=WWF |access-date=13 January 2019 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190113210818/https://wwf.panda.org/mission_principles_goals.cfm| archive-date=13 January 2019}}</ref> ''[[Living Planet Report]]'' has been published every two years by WWF since 1998; it is based on a [[Living Planet Index]] and [[ecological footprint]] calculation.<ref name=":0" /> In addition, WWF has launched several notable worldwide campaigns, including [[Earth Hour]] and the [[debt-for-nature swap]], and its current work is organized around these six areas: food, climate, freshwater, wildlife, forests, and oceans.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="WorldWildLife" />

WWF has faced criticism for its corporate ties<ref name="Corp1"/><ref name="Corp2"/><ref>{{Cite news |last=Paddison |first=Laura |date=15 October 2013 |title=WWF's president on business partnerships and greenwashing |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sustainable-business/wwf-president-business-partnerships-greenwashing |access-date=3 March 2024 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> and for support of conservation measures that have resulted in violent conflict with local people.<ref>{{cite web |title=Green Violence: 'Eco-Guards' Are Abusing Indigenous Groups in Africa |url=https://e360.yale.edu/features/green-violence-eco-guards-are-abusing-indigenous-groups-in-africa |access-date=7 July 2020 |website=Yale E360 |archive-date=19 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200719233424/https://e360.yale.edu/features/green-violence-eco-guards-are-abusing-indigenous-groups-in-africa |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Beaumont |first=Peter |date=25 November 2020 |title=Report clears WWF of complicity in violent abuses by conservation rangers |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/nov/25/report-clears-wwf-of-complicity-in-violent-abuses-by-conservation-rangers |access-date=3 March 2024 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

== History ==

[[File:Prins Bernhard (l) bij de auto, Bestanddeelnr 924-6551.jpg|thumb|upright|left|[[Prince Bernhard of Lippe-Biesterfeld|Prince Bernhard]] with a WWF field vehicle, 1971]]
The idea for a fund on behalf of endangered animals was officially proposed by [[Victor Stolan]] to [[Julian Huxley|Sir Julian Huxley]] in response to articles he published in the British newspaper ''[[The Observer]].'' This proposal led Huxley to put Stolan in contact with [[Edward Max Nicholson]], a person who had had 30 years of experience in linking [[progressivism|progressive]] intellectuals with [[big business]] interests through the [[Political and Economic Planning]] think tank.<ref name="WWF history">{{cite web |url=http://wwf.panda.org/who_we_are/history/sixties/ |title=WWF in the 60s |publisher=World Wide Fund for Nature |access-date=19 August 2012 |archive-date=26 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110126165134/http://wwf.panda.org/who_we_are/history/sixties/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Kellaway">Kate Kellaway (7 November 2010). [https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2010/nov/07/wwf-world-wildlife-fund-huxley How the Observer brought WWF into being] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191209040023/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2010/nov/07/wwf-world-wildlife-fund-huxley |date=9 December 2019 }} The Observer.</ref><ref>Scott, P. (1965). The launching of a new ark: first report of the president and trustees of the World Wildlife Fund, an international foundation for saving the world's wildlife and wild places and countries; 1962–1965 (Collins).</ref> Nicholson thought up the name of the organization and the original panda logo was designed by [[Peter Scott (conservationist)|Sir Peter Scott]]. WWF was conceived on 29 April 1961, under the name of ''World Wildlife Fund''. Its first office was opened on 11 September in [[International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]]'s headquarters at Morges, Switzerland.
 
WWF was conceived to act as an international fundraising organization to support the work of existing conservation groups, primarily the International Union for Conservation of Nature.<ref name="wwfhistory">{{cite web |url=https://www.worldwildlife.org/about/history |title=History – WWF |website=World Wildlife Fund |access-date=27 March 2015 |archive-date=13 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200413065837/https://www.worldwildlife.org/about/history |url-status=live }}</ref> Its establishment was marked with the signing of the '''Morges Manifesto''', the founding document that sets the fund's commitment to assisting worthy organizations struggling to save the world's wildlife:<ref>"[http://wwf.panda.org/who_we_are/history/ History: Fifty Years of Environmental Conservation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130103053944/http://wwf.panda.org/who_we_are/history/ |date=3 January 2013 }}". With link to [http://assets.panda.org/downloads/morgesmanifesto.pdf PDF] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120315050757/http://assets.panda.org/downloads/morgesmanifesto.pdf |date=15 March 2012 }} of "Morges Manisto". World Wide Fund for Nature. wwf.panda.org. Retrieved 20 June 2017.</ref>

{{blockquote|They need above all money, to carry out mercy missions and to meet conservation emergencies by buying land where wildlife treasures are threatened, and in many other ways. Money, for example, to pay guardians of wildlife refuges&nbsp;.... Money for education and propaganda among those who would care and help if only they understood. Money to send out experts to danger spots and to train more local wardens and helpers in Africa and elsewhere. Money to maintain a sort of 'war room' at the international headquarters of conservation, showing where the danger spots are and making it possible to ensure that their needs are met before it is too late.|source=Morges Manifesto}}

[[File:Prinses Beatrix koopt zilveren aap tbv World Wild Life Fund Zeist, Bestanddeelnr 924-9397.jpg|thumb|[[Beatrix of the Netherlands|Princess Beatrix]] visiting the organization, 1971]]
[[Prince Bernhard of Lippe-Biesterfeld]] helped to found WWF, becoming its first president in 1961. In 1963, the Foundation held a conference and published a major report warning of [[Human impact on the environment|anthropogenic]] [[global warming]], written by Noel Eichhorn based on the work of [[Frank Fraser Darling]] (then foundation vice president), [[Edward Deevey]], Erik Eriksson, [[Charles Keeling]], [[Gilbert Plass]], [[Lionel Walford]], and [[William Garnett (photographer)|William Garnett]].<ref>{{cite book |url=http://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/001495147 |title=Implications of Rising Carbon Dioxide Content of the Atmosphere: A statement of trends and implications of carbon dioxide research reviewed at a conference of scientists |last=Eichhorn |first=Noel |date=1963 |publisher=The Conservation Foundation |place=New York |access-date=27 March 2015 |archive-date=6 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906065159/http://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/001495147 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1970, along with [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh]], and a few associates, Bernhard established WWF's financial endowment ''[[The 1001: A Nature Trust]]'' to handle the organization's administration and fundraising. 1001 members each contributed $10,000 to the trust.<ref name="WWF Finland">{{in lang|en}} [https://web.archive.org/web/20100715155311/http://www.wwf.fi/english/international/history WWF Finland – History of WWF International]</ref> Prince Bernhard resigned his post after being involved in the [[Lockheed bribery scandals]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1478171/HRH-Prince-Bernhard-of-the-Netherlands.html |title=Obituary: HRH Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands |date=4 December 2004 |publisher=The Telegraph |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081108050115/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1478171/HRH-Prince-Bernhard-of-the-Netherlands.html |archive-date=8 November 2008 |access-date=30 November 2017}}</ref>

=== Recent developments ===
[[File:WWF Big Ballon 2013.jpg|thumb|A WWF hot air balloon in Mexico, 2013]]
[[File:People's Climate March 2017 20170429 4331 (34351241115).jpg|thumb|WWF at the [[People's Climate March (2017)|People's Climate March]], 2017]]
WWF has set up offices and operations around the world. It originally worked by fundraising and providing grants to existing non-governmental organizations with an initial focus on the protection of [[endangered species]]. As more resources became available, its operations expanded into other areas such as the preservation of [[Extinction|biological diversity]], sustainable use of [[natural resources]], the reduction of [[pollution]], and [[climate change]]. The organization also began to run its own conservation projects and campaigns.{{citation_needed|date=July 2019}} In 1986, the organization changed its name to ''World Wide Fund for Nature'', while retaining the WWF initials. However, it continued at that time to operate under the original name in the United States and Canada.<ref name="history-eighties">{{cite web |url=https://wwf.panda.org/knowledge_hub/history/eighties/ |title=WWF in the 80's |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=<!--Not stated--> |website=WWF |access-date=13 January 2019 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190113210304/https://wwf.panda.org/knowledge_hub/history/eighties/| archive-date=13 January 2019}}</ref>

1986 was the 25th anniversary of WWF's foundation, an event marked by a gathering in Assisi, Italy to which the organization's International President Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, invited religious authorities representing Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, and Judaism. These leaders produced The Assisi Declarations, theological statements showing the spiritual relationship between their followers and nature that triggered a growth in the engagement of these religions with conservation around the world.<ref name="history-eighties" />{{Failed verification|reason=Verification failed, see talk page.|date=March 2026}}

In the 1990s, WWF revised its mission statement to:{{citation_needed|date=July 2019}}

{{blockquote|Stop the degradation of the planet's natural environment and to build a future in which humans live in harmony with nature,
*conserving the world's biological diversity;
*ensuring that the use of renewable natural resources is sustainable; [and]
*promoting the reduction of pollution and wasteful consumption.}}

WWF researchers and many others identified 238 [[ecoregions]] that represent the world's most biologically outstanding terrestrial, freshwater, and marine habitats, based on a worldwide biodiversity analysis which the organization says was the first of its kind.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.panda.org/about_our_earth/ecoregions/about/ |title=About global ecoregions |publisher=World Wide Fund for Nature |access-date=19 August 2012 |archive-date=22 April 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100422143720/http://www.panda.org/about_our_earth/ecoregions/about/ |url-status=dead}}</ref> In the early 2000s (decade), its work was focused on a subset of these ecoregions, in the areas of forest, freshwater and marine [[habitat conservation]], endangered species conservation, climate change, and the elimination of the most toxic chemicals.
{{blockquote|We shan't save all we should like to, but we shall save a great deal more than if we had never tried.|Sir [[Peter Scott]]<ref name="WWF Finland"/>}}

Harvard University published a case study on WWF titled "Negotiating Toward the Paris Accords: WWF & the Role of Forests in the 2015 Climate Agreement":<ref>{{cite web |title=Negotiating Toward the Paris Accords: WWF & the Role of Forests in the 2015 Climate Agreement |url=https://case.hks.harvard.edu/negotiating-toward-the-paris-accords-wwf-the-role-of-forests-in-the-2015-climate-agreement/ |access-date=13 May 2021 |website=HKS Case Program |archive-date=29 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210329181746/https://case.hks.harvard.edu/negotiating-toward-the-paris-accords-wwf-the-role-of-forests-in-the-2015-climate-agreement/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2023, [[Adil Najam]], a globally renowned climate scientist and policy expert from Pakistan, was appointed as the president of WWF International signifying the growing importance on climate change as well as of human well-being in the WWF agenda.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr Adil Najam appointed new President of WWF International|url=https://wwf.panda.org/wwf_news/?8360941/Dr-Adil-Najam-named-as-new-President-of-WWF-Intern/ |date=3 April 2023|publisher=WWF site|access-date=21 January 2024 }}</ref>

==Conservation Foundation==
{{Further|Russell E. Train}}

In 1947, the Conservation Foundation was formed in New York City by [[Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr.|Fairfield Osborn]]. It arranged funding for scientific research into global conservation issues. It did not lobby or engage in politics. In 1985, it became an affiliate of WWF. In 1990, it completely merged into WWF.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://www.worldwildlife.org/about/history|title=History {{!}} WWF|website=World Wildlife Fund|access-date=22 January 2019|archive-date=13 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200413065837/https://www.worldwildlife.org/about/history|url-status=live}}</ref> 

===Conservation Foundation in the United States===
The organization now known as the [[Conservation Foundation in the United States]] is the former Forest Foundation of DuPage County.<ref name="wwfhistory" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://theconservationfoundation.org/page.php?PageID=2 |title=The Conservation Foundation |website=theconservationfoundation.org |access-date=27 March 2015 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402133429/http://theconservationfoundation.org/page.php?PageID=2 |url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1996, the organization obtained general consultative status from [[UNESCO]].<ref>For the Illinois group see [https://theconservationfoundation.org/ About Us]</ref>

== Panda symbol ==
[[File:Grosser Panda.JPG|thumb|The giant panda has become the symbol of WWF.|200x200px]]

WWF's [[giant panda]] logo originated from a panda named [[Chi Chi (giant panda)|Chi Chi]] that had been transferred from the [[Beijing Zoo]] to the [[London Zoo]] in 1958, three years before WWF was established. Being famous as the only panda residing in the Western world at that time, her uniquely recognisable physical features and status as an endangered species were seen as ideal to serve the organization's need for a strong recognisable symbol that would overcome all language barriers.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wwf.panda.org/who_we_are/history/sixties/ |title=WWF – WWF in the 60's |publisher=WWF |access-date=10 August 2014 |archive-date=26 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110126165134/http://wwf.panda.org/who_we_are/history/sixties/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The organization also needed an animal that would have an impact in black and white printing. The logo was then designed by [[Peter Scott (conservationist)|Sir Peter Scott]] from preliminary sketches by Gerald Watterson, a Scottish naturalist.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wwf.panda.org/who_we_are/history/sixties/ |title=WWF in the 60's |access-date=7 November 2010 |archive-date=26 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110126165134/http://wwf.panda.org/who_we_are/history/sixties/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.worldwildlife.org/species/finder/giantpanda/panda.html |title=WWF – Giant Panda – Overview |publisher=Worldwildlife.org |access-date=19 August 2012 |archive-date=9 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120809023057/http://www.worldwildlife.org/species/finder/giantpanda/panda.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The logo, simplified and made geometric in 1978, then was stylized and made less detailed in 1986 at the time that the organization changed its name, with the revised version featuring solid black shapes for eyes.<ref>"[http://www.logodesignlove.com/world-wildlife-fund World Wildlife Fund logo sketches] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190926095736/https://www.logodesignlove.com/world-wildlife-fund |date=26 September 2019 }}". Logo Design Love. 7 June 2011; updated by Jerry Kuyper, 9&nbsp;June 2011. logodesignlove.com. Retrieved 21 June 2017.</ref> In 2000, a change was made to the font used for the initials WWF in the logo.<ref>"[https://www.famouslogos.us/wwf-logo/ WWF Logo] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191014173541/https://www.famouslogos.us/wwf-logo/ |date=14 October 2019 }}". Famous Logos. famouslogos.us. Retrieved 21 June 2017.</ref>

== Organization and operation ==

===Policy-making===
[[File:Oasi WWF Stagni Casale 15 agosto 2012 n11.jpg|thumb|The nature reserve, Oasis of Stagni di Casale, managed by WWF in Vicenza, Italy]]
Policies of WWF are made by board members elected for three-year terms. An executive team guides and develops WWF's strategy. There is also a national council which stands as an advisory group to the board and a team of scientists and experts in conservation who research for WWF.

National and international law plays an important role in determining how habitats and resources are managed and used. Laws and regulations become one of the organization's global priorities.

WWF has been opposed to the extraction of oil from the Canadian [[tar sands]] and has campaigned on this matter. From 2008 to 2010, WWF worked with [[The Co-operative Group]], the UK's largest [[consumer co-operative]] to publish reports which concluded that (1) exploiting the Canadian tar sands to their full potential would be sufficient to bring about what they described as 'runaway climate change';<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.co-operative.coop/upload/ToxicFuels/docs/WWF_CFS_Unconventionals_report.pdf |title=Unconventional Oil |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150708080954/http://www.co-operative.coop/upload/ToxicFuels/docs/WWF_CFS_Unconventionals_report.pdf |archive-date=8 July 2015 |url-status=dead |access-date=5 June 2015}}</ref> (2) [[carbon capture and storage]] (CCS) technology cannot be used to reduce the release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere to a level comparable to that of other methods of oil extraction;<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.co-operative.coop/upload/ToxicFuels/docs/CCS-in-the-Alberta-oil-sands-a-dangerous-myth.pdf |title=Carbon capture and storage in the Alberta oil sands – a dangerous myth |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923205501/http://www.co-operative.coop/upload/ToxicFuels/docs/CCS-in-the-Alberta-oil-sands-a-dangerous-myth.pdf |archive-date=23 September 2015 |url-status=dead |access-date=5 June 2015}}</ref> (3) the $379 billion which is expected to be spent extracting oil from tar sands could be better spent on research and development in renewable energy technology;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.co-operative.coop/upload/ToxicFuels/docs/opportunity-cost-report.pdf |title=Opportunity cost of tar sands development |work=co-operative.coop |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906001129/https://www.co-operative.coop/upload/ToxicFuels/docs/opportunity-cost-report.pdf |archive-date=6 September 2015 |url-status=dead |access-date=25 September 2018}}</ref> and (4) the expansion of tar sands extraction poses a serious threat to the caribou in Alberta .<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.co-operative.coop/upload/ToxicFuels/docs/caribou-report.pdf |title=Save the caribou - stop the tar sands |access-date=5 June 2015 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304100633/http://www.co-operative.coop/upload/ToxicFuels/docs/caribou-report.pdf |url-status=dead}}</ref>

The organization convinces and helps governments and other political bodies to adopt, enforce, strengthen and/or change policies, guidelines, and laws that affect biodiversity and natural resource use. It also ensures consent by governments and/or keeps their commitment to international instruments relating to the protection of biodiversity and natural resources.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wwf.panda.org/what_we_do/how_we_work/tackling_the_causes/ |title=Tackling the Causes |access-date=13 December 2010 |archive-date=2 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110102133022/http://wwf.panda.org/what_we_do/how_we_work/tackling_the_causes/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://wwf.panda.org/what_we_do/how_we_work/policy/ |title=Advocacy & policy |access-date=13 December 2010 |archive-date=28 December 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101228074857/http://wwf.panda.org/what_we_do/how_we_work/policy/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2012, David Nussbaum, chief executive of WWF-UK, spoke out against the way [[shale gas]] is used in the UK, saying: "...{{nbsp}}the Government must reaffirm its commitment to tackling climate change and prioritise renewables and energy efficiency."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.securingthefuture.co.uk/energy/12572-take-foot-off-the-pedal-on-shale-gas-charities-warn-government |title='Take foot off the pedal on shale gas', charities warn Government |last=Buckler |first=Scott |website=www.securingthefuture.co.uk |access-date=10 September 2012 |archive-date=1 January 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130101124059/http://www.securingthefuture.co.uk/energy/12572-take-foot-off-the-pedal-on-shale-gas-charities-warn-government |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Collaboration ===
[[File:Oasi naturale wwf Le Cesine.jpg|thumb|[[Cesine|Le Cesine]], a natural wetlands in Italy, managed by WWF since 1979]]
The organization works on a number of [[list of global issues|global issues]] driving [[biodiversity loss]] and unsustainable use of natural resources, including species conservation, finance, business practices, laws, and consumption choices. Local offices also work on national or regional issues.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.panda.org/what_we_do/ |title=What does the World Wild Life Fund do? |publisher=World Wide Fund for Nature |access-date=19 August 2012 |archive-date=19 April 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100419175316/http://www.panda.org/what_we_do/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

WWF works with a large number of different groups to achieve its goals, including other NGOs, governments, business, investment banks, scientists, fishermen, farmers and local communities. It also undertakes public campaigns to influence decision makers, and seeks to educate people on how to live in a more environmentally friendly manner. It urges people to donate funds to protect the environment. The donors can also choose to receive gifts in return.{{citation needed|date=May 2016}}

In October 2020, WWF was named as one of the alliance partner's of [[Prince William, Duke of Cambridge|Prince William]]'s Earthshot Prize to find solutions to environmental issues.<ref>{{cite web |last=Frangoul |first=Anmar |date=8 October 2020 |title=Prince William launches £50 million Earthshot Prize, with a nod to John F. Kennedy |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/10/08/prince-william-launches-50-million-earthshot-prize.html |access-date=14 October 2020 |website=CNBC |archive-date=14 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201014182852/https://www.cnbc.com/2020/10/08/prince-william-launches-50-million-earthshot-prize.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In March 2021, WWF announced an extension of its partnership with [[H&M]] to address sustainable supply chain practices.<ref>{{cite web |last=Glover |first=Simon |title=H&M extends partnership with WWF |url=https://www.ecotextile.com/2021032627584/fashion-retail-news/h-m-extends-partnership-with-wwf.html |access-date=26 March 2021 |website=Ecotextile News |date=26 March 2021 |archive-date=30 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210330100034/https://www.ecotextile.com/2021032627584/fashion-retail-news/h-m-extends-partnership-with-wwf.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Publications ===
WWF publishes the ''[[Living Planet Index]]'' in collaboration with the [[Zoological Society of London]]. Along with [[ecological footprint]] calculations, the ''Index'' is used to produce a biennial ''[[Living Planet Report]]'' giving an overview of the impact of human activity on the world.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.panda.org/about_our_earth/all_publications/living_planet_report/ |title=Living Planet Report |publisher=World Wide Fund for Nature |access-date=19 August 2012 |archive-date=19 April 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100419173713/http://www.panda.org/about_our_earth/all_publications/living_planet_report/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2019, WWF and [[Knorr (brand)|Knorr]] jointly published the [[Future 50 Foods report]] identifying "50 Foods for Healthier People and a Healthier Planet".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.wwf.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-02/Knorr_Future_50_Report_FINAL_Online.pdf |title=Future 50 Foods: 50 foods for healthier people and a healthier planet |last=Drewnowski |first=Adam |date=February 2019 |website=World Wide Fund for Nature |access-date=4 April 2019 |archive-date=25 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190325002921/https://www.wwf.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-02/Knorr_Future_50_Report_FINAL_Online.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2018, WWF, TRAFFIC and IFAW launched the Coalition to End Wildlife Trafficking Online with 21 tech companies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=End Wildlife Trafficking Online |url=https://www.endwildlifetraffickingonline.org/2021-progress-update |access-date=30 December 2022 |archive-date=30 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221230180625/https://www.endwildlifetraffickingonline.org/2021-progress-update |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2017, Instagram accounts, Sal Lavallo and Jessica Nabongo ate a trafficked, endangered pangolin at a hotel in Gabon.<ref>{{cite web |title=Instagram influencers eat pangolin in Gabon - call it 'armadillo' |url=https://africageographic.com/stories/video-instagram-influencer-eats-pangolin-gabon-calls-armadillo/ |website=africageographic.com |access-date=23 March 2023 |date=6 June 2019 |archive-date=13 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230213095831/https://africageographic.com/stories/video-instagram-influencer-eats-pangolin-gabon-calls-armadillo/ |url-status=live }}</ref> There is often no penalty to social media accounts for cruelty to animals on social media platforms.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Shrivastava |first1=Rashi |author1-link=Forbes |title=Hundreds Of Social Media Videos With Billions Of Views Show Wild Animals Being Tortured, Report Finds |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/rashishrivastava/2022/11/22/hundreds-of-social-media-videos-with-billions-of-views-show-wild-animals-being-tortured-report-finds/?sh=43079376fa5d |website=Forbes |access-date=23 March 2023 |date=22 November 2022 |archive-date=21 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230521110846/https://www.forbes.com/sites/rashishrivastava/2022/11/22/hundreds-of-social-media-videos-with-billions-of-views-show-wild-animals-being-tortured-report-finds/?sh=43079376fa5d |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Dalton |first1=Jane |title=Anger as Instagram refuses to remove 'vile' videos of animal cruelty |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/tech/instagram-animal-cruelty-abuse-video-pet-dog-fight-tiger-alan-mcelligott-a9692446.html |website=The Independent |access-date=23 March 2023 |date=28 August 2020 |archive-date=13 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230213094802/https://www.independent.co.uk/tech/instagram-animal-cruelty-abuse-video-pet-dog-fight-tiger-alan-mcelligott-a9692446.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The organization also regularly publishes reports, fact sheets, and other documents on issues related to its work to raise awareness and provide information to policy and decision makers.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.panda.org/about_our_earth/all_publications/ |title=Publication & Resources |access-date=28 March 2010 |archive-date=25 April 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100425162427/http://www.panda.org/about_our_earth/all_publications/ |url-status=dead}}</ref>
