Several conservatives and Republicans have criticized the plan for its stances on climate change and trade.<ref name="Friedman 2023" /><ref name="The Economist-2023" /> [[Ron DeSantis]] embraced Project 2025 in August 2023.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Slattery |first=Gram |date=August 18, 2023 |title=Insight: Conservative think tank emerges as force behind DeSantis campaign |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/conservative-think-tank-emerges-force-behind-desantis-campaign-2023-08-18/ |publisher=[[Reuters]] |quote=The Florida governor has also embraced Heritage's 'Project 2025.' |access-date=August 12, 2024 |archive-date=September 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240903172237/https://www.reuters.com/world/us/conservative-think-tank-emerges-force-behind-desantis-campaign-2023-08-18/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

After Trump won the [[2024 United States presidential election]], left-leaning media sources highlighted how right-wing commentators began saying on social media that Project 2025 was the official plan. Former White House advisor [[Steve Bannon]] and Texas official [[Bo French]] supported transparency about implementing Project 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Saric |first=Ivana |date=November 7, 2024 |title=Trump's MAGA allies gloat Project 2025 "is the agenda" |url=https://www.axios.com/2024/11/07/trump-project-2025-second-term-agenda |access-date=November 7, 2024 |website=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |archive-date=November 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241108225044/https://www.axios.com/2024/11/07/trump-project-2025-second-term-agenda |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Oamek |first=Paige |date=November 7, 2024 |title=Steve Bannon's Project 2025 Joke Says What We Knew All Along |url=https://newrepublic.com/post/188097/steve-bannon-donald-trump-project-2025 |access-date=2024-12-09 |magazine=[[The New Republic]] |issn=0028-6583}}</ref>

=== Other reactions and responses ===

In April 2024, responding to criticism of the project, Heritage released a document titled "5 Reasons Leftists {{smallcaps|HATE}} Project 2025".<ref name="heritage.org-2024" /> Restating many of its previously published objectives, the document said that "the radical Left hates families" and "wants to eliminate the family and replace it with the state"; that leftist "elites use the 'climate crisis' as a tool for scaring Americans into giving up their freedom"; that the "radical Left wants our country to travel down [the] same dark path" toward becoming the [[Soviet Union]], [[North Korea]], or [[Cuba]]; and that "woke propaganda" should be eliminated at every level of government.<ref name="heritage.org-2024" />
{{external media| float = right| video1 = [https://www.c-span.org/program/book-tv/after-words-with-david-graham/658768 ''After Words'' interview with David Graham on ''The Project'', May 2, 2025], [[C-SPAN]]}}
In July 2024, [[Oren Cass]], contributing author of Mandate's chapter on the Department of Labor, criticized the project's leadership: "Gaining productive power requires focusing on people's problems and explaining how you are going to solve them, not pounding the table for Christian nationalism or a second American revolution."<ref name="Ward-2024a" /> In April 2025, journalist David Graham published a book-length study, ''The Project: How Project 2025 Is Reshaping America''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Graham |first=David A. |title=The Project: How Project 2025 Is Reshaping America |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/the-project-explores-project-2025s-origins-and-goals-to-reshape-american-culture |location=New York |publisher=Random House |year=2025 |isbn=979-8217153725}}</ref>
==Implementation (2025–present)==
{{See also|Second presidency of Donald Trump}}
[[File:Donald Trump Signs One Big Beautiful Bill into Law.png|thumb|By signing the [[One Big Beautiful Bill Act]] into law on July 4, 2025, Trump effectively implemented many policies akin to Project 2025.]]

Trump's actions during his second term as president have reignited scrutiny of Project 2025, with critics warning that his administration is actively implementing its agenda across multiple sectors.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Crowley |first=Kinsey |title=What is Project 2025? Trump policy moves bring conservative agenda into spotlight (again) |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2025/01/29/what-is-project-2025/78020165007/ |access-date=2025-02-03 |website=[[USA Today]] |language=en-US |archive-date=February 3, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250203210300/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2025/01/29/what-is-project-2025/78020165007/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Paul Dans has expressed satisfaction that Trump's early executive orders align with the project's ''Mandate for Leadership''.<ref name="cnnTolan" /> Trump's early executive actions closely mirrored Project 2025's outline. This may indicate that his administration was rapidly enacting a pre-planned playbook.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trump and Project 2025: President's early moves mirror conservative playbook – National {{!}} Globalnews.ca |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/10989366/donald-trump-project-2025-executive-orders-comparison/ |access-date=2025-02-03 |website=[[Global News]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Warnock: We're seeing Project 2025 play out 'before our very eyes' |url=https://www.msnbc.com/all-in/watch/warnock-we-re-seeing-project-2025-play-out-before-our-very-eyes-230735941882 |access-date=2025-02-03 |website=[[MSNBC]] |language=en |archive-date=February 3, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250203051520/https://www.msnbc.com/all-in/watch/warnock-we-re-seeing-project-2025-play-out-before-our-very-eyes-230735941882 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":8" /> His executive orders on gender policies, federal hiring, and foreign aid reflected the project's policies, signaling a shift toward more autocratic governance.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mansfield |first=Erin |title=Gender, hiring, foreign aid: 3 ways Project 2025 is turning up in Trump's actions |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2025/01/31/project-2025-trump-executive-orders/77977234007/ |access-date=2025-02-03 |website=[[USA Today]] |language=en-US |archive-date=February 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250202235802/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2025/01/31/project-2025-trump-executive-orders/77977234007/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Trump's nominations were confirmed faster than in his first term and faster than Biden's cabinet nominations.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kim |first1=June |last2=Yourish |first2=Karen |last3=Lee |first3=Jasmine C. |last4=Cahalan |first4=Sarah |title=Tracking Trump's Cabinet Confirmations |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/01/29/us/politics/trump-cabinet-confirmations-tracker.html |website=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=27 March 2025 |date=29 January 2025}}</ref>

Several groups track the implementation of Project 2025, including the Center for Progressive Reform and Governing for Impact<ref name="reform">{{Cite web|author=Center for Progressive Reform and Governing for Impact|title=Project 2025 Executive Action Tracker|website=progressivereform.org |url=https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1n0xtOFS-7vRfUU-sr4ZNURrSNJO-fNlG/edit?gid=232350695#gid=232350695|access-date=January 4, 2026 |year=2026}}</ref> and the Project 2025 Tracker.<ref name="tracker">{{Cite web|author1=rusticgorilla|author2=mollynaquafina|title=Project 2025 Tracker|website=project2025.observer/en |url=https://www.project2025.observer/en |access-date=January 4, 2026 |year=2026}}</ref>

=== Roles in the second Trump administration ===
{{See also|Second cabinet of Donald Trump}}
After Trump won the 2024 election, he nominated several Project 2025 contributors to positions in his second administration.<ref name="Kanno-Youngs 2024">{{Cite news |last1=Kanno-Youngs |first1=Zolan |last2=Green |first2=Erica L. |date=November 29, 2024 |title=Trump Disavowed Project 2025 During the Campaign. Not Anymore. |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/29/us/politics/trump-project-2025.html |url-access=subscription |access-date=January 19, 2025 |issn=0362-4331 }}</ref> His choice to lead the FCC, [[Brendan Carr (lawyer)|Brendan Carr]], wrote the manifesto's chapter about the agency.<ref name="nyt-kang-nov-24-fcc">{{cite news |last1=Kang |first1=Cecilia |title=Trump Picks Brendan Carr to Lead F.C.C. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/17/technology/fcc-nominee-brendan-carr-trump.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 17, 2024 |archive-date=December 8, 2024 |access-date=November 18, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241208001144/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/17/technology/fcc-nominee-brendan-carr-trump.html |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Tom Homan]], picked by Trump to act as a [[border czar]], also contributed to the Project 2025 document.<ref name="npr-treisman-24">{{cite news |last1=Treisman |first1=Rachel |title=What to know about Tom Homan, the former ICE head returning as Trump's 'border czar' |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/11/11/nx-s1-5186522/tom-homan-border-czar-trump |work=[[NPR]] |date=November 11, 2024}}</ref> Trump nominated [[Russell Vought]] to direct the [[Office of Management and Budget]]. After these selections, [[Karoline Leavitt]] issued a statement saying "President Trump never had anything to do with Project 2025."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barrow |first=Bill |date=2024-11-23 |title=After Trump's Project 2025 denials, he is tapping its authors and influencers for key roles |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-project-2025-administration-nominees-843f5ff20131ccba5f056e7ccc5baf23 |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=[[Associated Press]] |language=en |archive-date=November 24, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241124002204/https://apnews.com/article/trump-project-2025-administration-nominees-843f5ff20131ccba5f056e7ccc5baf23 |url-status=live }}</ref> Leavitt herself is an instructor for Project 2025's "Conservative Governance 101" training program<ref name="con-gov-101">{{cite web |title=Conservative Governance 101 |url=https://www.project2025.org/training/conservative-governance-101/ |website=Project 2025 |date=July 26, 2023 |publisher=Heritage Foundation |access-date=4 December 2024|archive-date=January 20, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250120042033/https://www.project2025.org/training/conservative-governance-101/|url-status=live}}</ref> and was chosen by Trump as [[White House Press Secretary]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-leavitt-white-house-first-press-briefing-5ba5ff116e18c29b04c934a24a8983d1 | title=Karoline Leavitt, the youngest White House press secretary, makes her debut in the briefing room | website=[[Associated Press News]] | date=January 28, 2025 | access-date=February 5, 2025 | archive-date=February 5, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250205125744/https://apnews.com/article/trump-leavitt-white-house-first-press-briefing-5ba5ff116e18c29b04c934a24a8983d1 | url-status=live }}</ref>

Other authors or contributors to Project 2025<ref name="Dans & Groves 2023" /> who have been nominated or appointed to roles in the second Trump administration include [[Michael Anton]] (contributor, appointed Director of Policy Planning);<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/statement-president-elect-donald-j-trump-announcing-the-nomination-michael-anton-director | title=Statement by President-elect Donald J. Trump Announcing the Nomination of Michael Anton as Director of Policy Planning at the State Department &#124; the American Presidency Project | access-date=February 4, 2025 | archive-date=February 17, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250217175025/https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/statement-president-elect-donald-j-trump-announcing-the-nomination-michael-anton-director | url-status=live }}</ref> [[Paul S. Atkins]] (contributor, nominated for Chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission);<ref>{{cite web | url=https://natlawreview.com/article/sec-lives-under-new-leadership-what-expect | title=Paul Atkins Nominated as Securities and Exchange Commission Chair }}</ref> [[Steven G. Bradbury]] (contributor, nominated for Deputy Secretary of Transportation);<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.heritage.org/press/heritage-applauds-steve-bradburys-nomination-deputy-secretary-transportation | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250112010216/https://www.heritage.org/press/heritage-applauds-steve-bradburys-nomination-deputy-secretary-transportation | url-status=unfit | archive-date=January 12, 2025 | title=Heritage Applauds Steve Bradbury's Nomination for Deputy Secretary of Transportation }}</ref> [[Troy Edgar]] (contributor, nominated for Deputy Secretary of Homeland Security);<ref>{{cite web | url=https://executivegov.com/2024/12/trump-taps-troy-edgar-dhs-deputy-secretary/ | title=President-Elect Trump Chooses Troy Edgar as DHS Deputy Secretary | date=December 20, 2024 }}</ref> Jon Feere (contributor, appointed Chief of Staff at ICE);<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.ice.gov/leadership | title=ICE Leadership &#124; ICE | date=February 8, 2025 | access-date=February 8, 2025 | archive-date=March 16, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150316202302/https://www.ice.gov/leadership | url-status=live }}</ref> [[Pete Hoekstra]] (contributor, nominated for ambassador to Canada);<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/trump-hoekstra-ambassador-canada-nominee-1.7389147 |title=Trump nominates former Michigan congressman Pete Hoekstra to be ambassador to Canada |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250217175025/https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/trump-hoekstra-ambassador-canada-nominee-1.7389147 |access-date=February 8, 2025 |archive-date=February 17, 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Roman Jankowski (contributor, appointed Chief Privacy Officer and Chief Freedom of Information Act Officer for the Department of Homeland Security); and Peter Navarro (author, appointed Senior Counselor for Trade and Manufacturing).<ref name="navarroAppoint1" /><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.dhs.gov/person/roman-jankowski | title=Roman Jankowski &#124; Homeland Security | access-date=February 8, 2025 | archive-date=February 7, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250207110906/https://www.dhs.gov/person/roman-jankowski | url-status=live }}</ref> After writing some of the education policy proposals in ''Mandate'', Lindsey Burke became the deputy chief of staff for policy and programs for the department of education.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schultz |first1=Brooke |title=Trump Admin. Adds Project 2025 Author to Education Department Staff |url=https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/trump-admin-adds-project-2025-author-to-education-department-staff/2025/06 |work=Education Week |date=9 June 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Environmental regulation ===
{{See also|Second presidency of Donald Trump#Environmental and energy policy}}
Aspects of the project implemented in the first days of Trump's second term include executive orders to reopen large areas of Alaska, including the [[Arctic National Wildlife Refuge]], to oil drilling,<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/oil-industry-unlikely-rush-alaska-despite-trumps-call-drill-2025-01-23/ | title=Oil industry unlikely to rush to Alaska despite Trump's call to drill | work=[[Reuters]] | date=January 23, 2025 | last1=Dang | first1=Sheila | last2=Volcovici | first2=Valerie | last3=Volcovici | first3=Valerie }}</ref> and the withdrawal of a pending Biden administration ban on [[Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances|PFAS]] in industrial discharge.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.wect.com/2025/01/31/trump-administration-withdraws-proposal-limit-pfas-discharge-amounts/ | title=Trump Administration withdraws proposal to limit PFAS discharge amounts | date=January 31, 2025 | access-date=February 5, 2025 | archive-date=February 11, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250211152601/https://www.wect.com/2025/01/31/trump-administration-withdraws-proposal-limit-pfas-discharge-amounts/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Federal workers ===
{{See also|2025 United States federal mass layoffs|2025 United States federal government shutdown#Mass layoffs}}
Metadata show that [[United States Office of Personnel Management]] memos sent to federal workers were written by Peter Noah and James Sherk, both associated with the Heritage Foundation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cole |first=Samantha |date=2025-01-28 |title=Memos to Federal Employees Were Written By People With Ties to Project 2025, Metadata Shows |url=https://www.404media.co/opm-memos-to-federal-employees-metadata/ |access-date=2025-01-28 |website=404 Media |language=en |archive-date=January 28, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250128075205/https://www.404media.co/opm-memos-to-federal-employees-metadata/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Executive power ===
{{See also|Targeting of political opponents and civil society under the second Trump administration#Mass firings and expansion of presidential power|Unitary executive theory#Since 2025}}
According to [[Media Matters for America]], Trump's early budget freezes and spending cuts reflected Project 2025's aggressive push to downsize government programs and shift power to conservative institutions. In addition, his push to weaken FEMA is part of a broader Project 2025 strategy to reduce the federal government's role in disaster relief and shift responsibility to state and private entities.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fisher |first=Allison |date=2025-01-29 |title=Trump is signaling he wants to shutter or gut FEMA — another Project 2025 scheme |url=https://www.mediamatters.org/donald-trump/trump-signaling-he-wants-shutter-or-gut-fema-another-project-2025-scheme |access-date=2025-02-03 |website=Media Matters for America |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":4" />

On February 7, 2025, the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) announced that it would change its maximum [[indirect cost rate]] for university [[research grant]]s from 50% in some cases to 15%, as recommended by Project 2025.<ref name="nyt-jewett-uni-25">{{cite news |last1=Jewett |first1=Christina |title=A Trump policy change will restrict billions in funding for medical research programs at universities |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/07/us/politics/medical-research-funding-cuts-university-budgets.html?smid=url-share |access-date=8 February 2025 |date=2025-02-07 |archive-date=February 8, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250208041818/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/07/us/politics/medical-research-funding-cuts-university-budgets.html?smid=url-share |url-status=live }}</ref>

Trump's policy on TikTok diverged from Project 2025's call to ban the app.<ref name="cnnTolan">{{Cite web |first1=Steve |last1=Contorno |first2=Casey |last2=Tolan |date=2025-01-31 |title=Trump said he hadn't read Project 2025 – but most of his early executive orders overlap with its proposals {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/01/31/politics/trump-policy-project-2025-executive-orders-invs/index.html?utm_medium=social&utm_source=blueskyCNN&utm_content=2025-01-31T09:28:27 |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=[[CNN]] |language=en |archive-date=February 10, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250210132439/https://www.cnn.com/2025/01/31/politics/trump-policy-project-2025-executive-orders-invs/index.html?utm_medium=social&utm_source=blueskyCNN&utm_content=2025-01-31T09%3A28%3A27 |url-status=live }}</ref> (See: [[Donald Trump–TikTok controversy|Donald Trump and TikTok]])

[[Executive Order 14191]]—titled "Expanding Educational Freedom and Opportunity for Families—diverted funding from public schools to private school vouchers, a move directly aligned with Project 2025's goal to reshape the education system.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Maiers |first=Staci |title=Trump's latest executive order overreaches to steal money from public school students to fund private school vouchers {{!}} NEA |url=https://www.nea.org/about-nea/media-center/press-releases/trumps-latest-executive-order-overreaches-steal-money-public-school-students-fund-private-school |access-date=2025-02-03 |website=www.nea.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=7 April 2025 |title=Federal register, EO14191 |url=https://www.federalregister.gov/presidential-documents/executive-orders/donald-trump/2025 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250407172154/https://www.federalregister.gov/presidential-documents/executive-orders/donald-trump/2025 |archive-date=7 April 2025 |access-date=7 April 2025 |website=[[federal register]]}}</ref> Project 2025 advocated changes to foreign aid, including a foreign aid freeze; in January 2025, Trump initially signed an executive order freezing new foreign aid for 90 days, and later in January the administration sent a notice requiring that stop-work orders be issued for all existing foreign aid.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.kff.org/policy-watch/the-status-of-president-trumps-pause-of-foreign-aid-and-implications-for-pepfar-and-other-global-health-programs/ | title=The Status of President Trump's Pause of Foreign Aid and Implications for PEPFAR and other Global Health Programs | date=February 3, 2025 }}</ref>

The executive order [[Restoring the Death Penalty and Protecting Public Safety]] was a step toward Project 2025's goal of expanding capital punishment. It directs the Attorney General to seek the death penalty in cases of murder of a police officer and capital crimes by illegal aliens. It also directs the DOJ to ensure that states that wish to apply the death penalty have a sufficient supply of lethal injection materials.<ref>{{cite web |title=Restoring The Death Penalty And Protecting Public Safety |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/restoring-the-death-penalty-and-protecting-public-safety/ |website=The White House |access-date=24 March 2025 |date=21 January 2025}}</ref>

{{See also|Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration#Executive Orders}}
At the beginning of his second term, Trump signed [[Executive Order 14168]], [[Executive Order 14187]], and [[Executive Order 14183]], which revoked the federal government's recognition of transgender people.<ref name="guard14168">{{cite news |last1=Pengelly |first1=Martin |title=Trump rolls back trans and gender-identity rights and takes aim at DEI |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/jan/20/trump-executive-order-gender-sex |access-date=3 April 2025 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=21 January 2025}}</ref><ref name="eo14187">{{cite web |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/protecting-children-from-chemical-and-surgical-mutilation/ |title=Executive Order: Protecting Children for Chemical and Surgical Mutilation |publisher=US White House |date=January 28, 2025 |access-date=January 29, 2025 |archive-date=January 29, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250129224724/https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/protecting-children-from-chemical-and-surgical-mutilation/ |url-status=live}}{{source-attribution}}</ref><ref name="transmilban1">{{Cite web |date=2025-01-28 |title=Trump signs executive orders prioritizing military 'excellence and readiness'|work=[[Washington Examiner]] |url=https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/3302523/trump-executive-orders-military-excellence/ |access-date=2025-01-29 |archive-date=January 28, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250128214519/https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/3302523/trump-executive-orders-military-excellence/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In practice, this means the federal government will use ''sex'' in lieu of ''gender'' in documents. Additionally, only male and female options will be given on forms, and transgender inmates will be imprisoned according to their biological sex. The federal government also ceased to financially support [[gender-affirming surgery]]<ref name="guard14168"/><ref name="wh14168">{{cite web |title=Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/defending-women-from-gender-ideology-extremism-and-restoring-biological-truth-to-the-federal-government/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250121214116/https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/defending-women-from-gender-ideology-extremism-and-restoring-biological-truth-to-the-federal-government/ |archive-date=21 January 2025 |website=[[White House]]|date=January 21, 2025 }}</ref> and attempted to ban transgender people from the military.<ref name="transmilban1"/><ref name="guard-18mar2025">{{cite news |title=US judge blocks Trump's ban on trans people serving in the military |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/mar/18/judge-blocks-trump-executive-order-trans-military-ban |access-date=March 18, 2025 |work=[[The Guardian]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=March 18, 2025}}</ref>

'''''Seaspiracy''''' ({{IPAc-en|s|i:|ˈ|s|p|ɪ|r|ə|s|i}}) is a 2021 [[documentary film]] about the [[environmental impact of fishing]] directed by and starring Ali Tabrizi, a British filmmaker.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web|date=March 31, 2021|title=Meet the 27-year-old filmmaker behind Netflix's controversial documentary, Seaspiracy|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/news/seaspiracy-ali-tabrizi-age-married-netflix-b1824931.html|access-date=April 4, 2021|website=The Independent|archive-date=March 31, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210331105324/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/news/seaspiracy-ali-tabrizi-age-married-netflix-b1824931.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The film examines [[Human impact on marine life|human impacts on marine life]] and advocates for ending [[Fish as food|fish consumption]].

The film explores environmental issues affecting oceans, including [[Marine plastic pollution|plastic pollution]], [[ghost net]]s and [[overfishing]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Seaspiracy: what is Ali and Lucy Tabrizi's shocking Netflix fishing industry documentary about?|url=https://www.scotsman.com/whats-on/arts-and-entertainment/seaspiracy-what-is-ali-and-lucy-tabrizis-shocking-netflix-fishing-industry-documentary-about-3180441|access-date=March 26, 2021|website=[[The Scotsman]]|date=March 26, 2021|archive-date=May 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210526143645/https://www.scotsman.com/whats-on/arts-and-entertainment/seaspiracy-what-is-ali-and-lucy-tabrizis-shocking-netflix-fishing-industry-documentary-about-3180441|url-status=live}}</ref> and argues that [[Commercial fishing|commercial fisheries]] are the main driver of [[marine ecosystem]] destruction.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Faut-il cesser de manger du poisson?|url=https://www.ledevoir.com/societe/environnement/597750/faut-il-cesser-de-manger-du-poisson|access-date=March 28, 2021|website=[[Le Devoir]]|date=March 27, 2021|language=fr|quote=Avec ce documentaire, tourné dans plusieurs régions maritimes du globe, le réalisateur Ali Tabrizi cherche donc à mettre en lumière ce qu'il considère comme un aveuglement collectif face à la dégradation des écosystèmes marins. Et pour lui, il ne fait aucun doute que les pêcheries commerciales sont le principal moteur de destruction de ces milieux naturels, qui sont le fruit de centaines de millions d'années d'évolution.|archive-date=March 3, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240303183839/https://www.ledevoir.com/piano/auth|url-status=live}}</ref> The film rejects the concept of [[Sustainable fishery|sustainable fishing]] and criticises several [[marine conservation]] organisations, including the [[Earth Island Institute]] and its [[dolphin safe label]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|last=Winkelman|first=Natalia|date=March 24, 2021|title='Seaspiracy' Review: Got Any Scandals? Go Fish.|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/24/movies/seaspiracy-review.html|access-date=March 26, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=March 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210325013159/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/24/movies/seaspiracy-review.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and the [[sustainable seafood]] certifications of the [[Marine Stewardship Council]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Our Seaspiracy response {{!}} Marine Stewardship Council|url=https://www.msc.org/media-centre/news-opinion/news|access-date=March 26, 2021|website=[[Marine Stewardship Council]]|archive-date=March 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210326191544/https://www.msc.org/media-centre/news-opinion/news|url-status=live}}</ref> It also criticises efforts by organisations to reduce household plastic, contrasting their impact with that of ghost nets.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gopesh |first=Sushrut |date=April 11, 2021|title='Seaspiracy' Summary & Analysis - Big Lie Of The Fishing Industry |url=https://dmtalkies.com/seaspiracy-documentary-film-2021/|access-date=April 11, 2021|website=Digital Mafia Talkies|archive-date=April 11, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210411061244/https://dmtalkies.com/seaspiracy-documentary-film-2021/|url-status=live}}</ref> It accuses these initiatives of being a [[cover-up]] for the [[environmental impact of fishing]] and corruption in the fishing industry.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web|last=Back|first=Grace|title=Netflix's New Documentary 'Seaspiracy' Is As Eye-Opening As It Is Terrifying|url=https://www.elle.com.au/culture/netflix-seaspiracy-plot-cast-details-release-date-24916|access-date=March 26, 2021|website=ELLE|date=March 26, 2021|archive-date=March 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210326070303/https://www.elle.com.au/culture/netflix-seaspiracy-plot-cast-details-release-date-24916|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":19" /> ''Seaspiracy'' concludes by supporting [[marine reserve]]s and for ending fish consumption.<ref>{{Cite web|date=March 26, 2021|title=Seaspiracy, il lato oscuro della pesca|url=https://www.lastampa.it/mare/2021/03/26/news/seaspiracy-il-lato-oscuro-e-nefasto-della-pesca-1.40077069|access-date=March 28, 2021|website=[[La Stampa]]|language=it-IT|quote=La tesi di "Seaspiracy è che non c'è grigio e bianco, appunto, ma solo riserve marine e smettere di mangiare pesce, di tutti i tipi.|archive-date=March 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210326224127/https://www.lastampa.it/mare/2021/03/26/news/seaspiracy-il-lato-oscuro-e-nefasto-della-pesca-1.40077069|url-status=live}}</ref>

The film was produced by [[Kip Andersen]], director of the documentary ''[[Cowspiracy]],<ref name=":5" />'' and used the same production team as this previous film. Initial financial support was provided by British entrepreneur [[Dale Vince]], and it was acquired by [[Netflix]] in 2020.

The film premiered on Netflix globally in March 2021 and garnered immediate attention in several countries.<ref name=":4" /> The film received mixed reviews; reviewers praised it for bringing attention to its subject matter, but it was accused of scientific inaccuracy<ref name=":5">{{Cite news|last=Gatten|first=Emma|date=April 1, 2021|title=Seaspiracy fact vs fiction: The truth behind Netflix's controversial new documentary|work=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/environment/2021/03/31/seaspiracy-fact-v-fiction-truth-behind-netflixs-controversial/|access-date=April 1, 2021|issn=0307-1235|quote=The film's producer, Kip Andersen, is a prominent vegan who made the earlier documentary Cowspiracy, and has set up a vegan meal planning subscription service that is linked from the Seaspiracy website.|archive-url= https://archive.today/20210409090108/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/environment/2021/03/31/seaspiracy-fact-v-fiction-truth-behind-netflixs-controversial/
 | archive-date = April 9, 2021}}</ref> and was criticised by some ocean experts.<ref name=":18" /><ref name=":11" /><ref name=":21">{{Cite web|last=Allen|first=Liz|title=Seaspiracy: A Call To Action Or A Vehicle Of Misinformation?|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/allenelizabeth/2021/04/10/seaspiracy-a-call-to-action-or-a-vehicle-of-misinformation/|access-date=May 22, 2021|website=Forbes|archive-date=May 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210522152703/https://www.forbes.com/sites/allenelizabeth/2021/04/10/seaspiracy-a-call-to-action-or-a-vehicle-of-misinformation/|url-status=live}}</ref> Organisations and individuals interviewed or negatively portrayed in the film disputed its assertions and accused the film of misrepresenting them.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|date=March 31, 2021|title=Seaspiracy: Netflix documentary accused of misrepresentation by participants|url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/mar/31/seaspiracy-netflix-documentary-accused-of-misrepresentation-by-participants|access-date=March 31, 2021|website=The Guardian|archive-date=March 31, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210331103709/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/mar/31/seaspiracy-netflix-documentary-accused-of-misrepresentation-by-participants|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web|title=Seaspiracy film assails fishing and aquaculture sectors that seem ready for a good fight|url=https://www.aquaculturealliance.org/advocate/seaspiracy-film-assails-fishing-and-aquaculture-sectors-that-seem-ready-for-a-good-fight/|access-date=March 29, 2021|website=Global Aquaculture Alliance|date=March 26, 2021|archive-date=March 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210326175635/https://www.aquaculturealliance.org/advocate/seaspiracy-film-assails-fishing-and-aquaculture-sectors-that-seem-ready-for-a-good-fight/|url-status=live}}</ref> ''Seaspiracy'' also prompted responses from other environmental organisations, academics and seafood industry groups, and several media outlets [[fact-checking|fact-checked]] certain statements in the film.

== Synopsis ==
[[File:Marine organisms entangled in a ghost net within the Maldives (Olive Ridley Project).jpg|alt=Underwater photo of marine organisms intertwined in a ghost net within the Maldives|thumb|Marine organisms entangled in a ghost net within the Maldives]]
Tabrizi acts as both the narrator and protagonist of the film, discovering key pieces of information at the same moment as the viewer. This [[framing device]] serves to provide narrative momentum and suspense.<ref name=":1"/> The film centers early on the collapse of [[whale]], [[shark]], [[dolphin]] and [[sea turtle]] populations. The film asserts that the focus of [[List of environmental organizations|environmental groups]] on comparatively small consumer plastics like [[Drinking straw|straws]] has obfuscated the larger problem of [[plastic waste]] from fishing gear, or [[ghost net]]s, as well as the devastation of [[bycatch]]. The film also suggests environmental organizations have been unable to define or effectively implement [[Sustainable fishery|sustainable fishing]], [[sustainable seafood]] or [[dolphin-safe]] products. These criticisms are particularly focused on the [[Marine Stewardship Council]], the [[Earth Island Institute]] and the [[Plastic Pollution Coalition]].<ref name=misrepresent/>

The film's settings are global, including the [[Taiji dolphin drive hunt]] in southern Japan, [[whaling in the Faroe Islands]], [[Thailand|Thai]] and [[China|Chinese]] fish markets, coastal [[West Africa]], and [[Aquaculture of salmonids|salmon aquaculture]] farms in [[Aquaculture in the United Kingdom|Scotland]]. At various moments, Tabrizi and his crew appear to face imminent peril from local authorities or corrupt fishing industry players; some of the action is presented through [[hidden camera]] techniques, and animation is used to depict scenes of violence. Activities of the [[Sea Shepherd Conservation Society]]—an American conservation group focused on direct action at sea—feature prominently in the film, including an extended section documenting [[Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing|illegal fishing]] practices and worker exploitation in [[Liberia]]n waters. The film also includes an investigation into [[Slavery in the 21st century|modern slavery]] conditions on [[Human trafficking in Thailand#Fishing industry trafficking|Thai fishing vessels]], and interviews several survivors.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Berlatsky|first=Noah|date=March 23, 2021|title='Seaspiracy' Explores the Need for Systemic Change to Save Our Oceans|url=https://progressive.org/api/content/157fd806-8be1-11eb-af94-1244d5f7c7c6/|access-date=March 26, 2021|website=[[The Progressive]]|archive-date=March 3, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240303183655/https://progressive.org/latest/seaspiracy-systemic-change-save-oceans-berlatsky-210323/|url-status=live}}</ref>

That the cessation of fish consumption is the solution to collapsing fish stocks and human exploitation remains a consistent message throughout the film. Statistics repeatedly buttress this point, including various fish species listed at >90% wild population loss, and the claim that global oceans could be essentially devoid of fish by 2048.<ref name=":12" /> The possibility of fish farming [[aquaculture]] is introduced, only to be dismissed after a trip to Scotland. The film suggests that aquaculture is untenable due to the problem of feed for farmed fish and the prevalence of disease and coastal degradation.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.sundaypost.com/fp/seaspiracy/ |title=Seaspiracy facts challenged by Scottish fish farming organisations as documentary controversy continues |last=McEachern |first=Megan |date=20 April 2021 |publisher=The Sunday Post |quote= |archive-date=January 28, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220128014222/https://www.sundaypost.com/fp/seaspiracy/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Production and release ==
''Seaspiracy'' received production support and initial funding by British renewable energy entrepreneur [[Dale Vince]] after meeting ''[[Cowspiracy]]'' director Kip Anderson in 2016.<ref name=":20">{{Cite web|last=Norris|first=Phil|date=March 4, 2021|title=Netflix releases trailer for Dale Vince's new documentary|url=https://www.gloucestershirelive.co.uk/news/gloucester-news/netflix-releases-trailer-dale-vinces-5074191|access-date=May 22, 2021|website=GloucestershireLive|archive-date=May 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210522152713/https://www.gloucestershirelive.co.uk/news/gloucester-news/netflix-releases-trailer-dale-vinces-5074191|url-status=live}}</ref> The same production team was used as this previous film.<ref name=":14" /> Ali Tabrizi had previously directed a film called ''Vegan'' in 2018.<ref name=":15" /> ''Seaspiracy'' was acquired by Netflix in 2020<ref name=":20" /> and released on the platform on March 24, 2021.<ref>{{Citation|last=Tabrizi|first=Ali|title=Seaspiracy|date=March 24, 2021|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt14152756/|type=Documentary|others=Ali Tabrizi, Richard O'Barry, Lucy Tabrizi, Lori Marino|access-date=March 28, 2021|archive-date=March 28, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210328143636/https://www.imdb.com/title/tt14152756/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=March 23, 2021|title=Facebook|url=https://www.facebook.com/seaspiracy/photos/a.301982896952178/1118949791922147/|access-date=March 29, 2021|website=[[Facebook]]|publisher=Seaspiracy|archive-date=May 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210526143645/https://www.facebook.com/seaspiracy/photos/a.301982896952178/1118949791922147/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Reception ==
The documentary was one of the top ten most watched films on Netflix in several countries in the week of its release and generated significant traction on social media.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|last=Korban (d_korban)|first=Demi|date=March 29, 2021|title='Seaspiracy' leaps into Netflix top 10 as social media frenzy hits seafood industry |url=https://www.intrafish.com/analysis/seaspiracy-leaps-into-netflix-top-10-as-social-media-frenzy-hits-seafood-industry/2-1-989318|access-date=March 30, 2021|work=Intrafish |archive-date=March 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210329210639/https://www.intrafish.com/analysis/seaspiracy-leaps-into-netflix-top-10-as-social-media-frenzy-hits-seafood-industry/2-1-989318|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Critical response ===

On [[review aggregator]] website [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film holds an approval rating of 75% based on 8 critic reviews, and an average rating of 7.7/10.<ref>{{cite web|title=Seaspiracy (2021)|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/seaspiracy|access-date=April 18, 2021|website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|archive-date=April 12, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412201223/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/seaspiracy|url-status=live}}</ref>

Natalia Winkelman of ''[[The New York Times]]'' gave a mixed-to-negative review, concluding that the film "does present some pieces of reporting — including an inquiry into dolphin-safe tuna can labels — that are surprising and memorable. But even the film's notable points seem to emerge only briefly before sinking beneath the surface, lost in a sea of murky [[Conspiracy theory|conspiratorial thinking]]."<ref name=":1" />

Aswathi Pacha also reviewed the film negatively in ''[[The Hindu]]'', citing concerns over its scientific veracity and accusations of misrepresentation from participants.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Pacha|first=Aswathi|date=2021-04-03|title='Seaspiracy' review: Fact and fiction meet fish in controversial Netflix documentary|work=The Hindu|url=https://www.thehindu.com/entertainment/movies/seaspiracy-review-fact-and-fiction-meet-fish-in-controversial-netflix-documentary/article34229848.ece|access-date=2021-12-13|issn=0971-751X|archive-date=April 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210403131823/https://www.thehindu.com/entertainment/movies/seaspiracy-review-fact-and-fiction-meet-fish-in-controversial-netflix-documentary/article34229848.ece|url-status=live}}</ref>

Liz Allen of ''[[Forbes]]'' was also critical of the film, writing "While perhaps produced with good intentions, Seaspiracy fails to provide a critical lens to the problems it unveils".<ref name=":21" /><ref name=":22" />

John Serba of [[Decider.com|''Decider'']] said, "''Seaspiracy'' isn't the purest form of documentary journalism, but Tabrizi makes his point with enough principled persuasion to make it worth your time," while also questioning its tone, saying "some of the fishing industry's troublesome ethical quandaries occur in the shadows, but to call its corrupt elements conspiratorial is almost pointlessly sensational".<ref name=":19">{{Cite web|date=March 24, 2021|title=Stream It Or Skip It: 'Seaspiracy' on Netflix, a Revealing Documentary Targeting the Corruption of the Commercial Fishing Industry|url=https://decider.com/2021/03/24/seaspiracy-on-netflix-stream-it-or-skip-it/|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=Decider|archive-date=March 28, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210328140309/https://decider.com/2021/03/24/seaspiracy-on-netflix-stream-it-or-skip-it/|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[The Independent]]'' rated it 4 out of 5 stars and called it a "shocking indictment of the commercial fishing industry".<ref>{{Cite web|date=March 30, 2021|title=Seaspiracy is a shocking indictment of the fishing industry – review|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/reviews/seaspiracy-review-netflix-documentary-fishing-b1824324.html|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=The Independent|archive-date=April 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210403180830/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/reviews/seaspiracy-review-netflix-documentary-fishing-b1824324.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Emma Stefanski of ''[[Thrillist]]'' said, "If shock and awe are what it takes to get the message across, then ''Seaspiracy'' is effective, if not particularly multifaceted."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Stefansky|first=Emma|title=Netflix's 'Seaspiracy' Documentary Unearths the Fishing Industry's Dark Secrets|url=https://www.thrillist.com/entertainment/nation/seaspiracy-netflix-documentary-review|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=Thrillist|date=March 25, 2021|archive-date=March 27, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210327205343/https://www.thrillist.com/entertainment/nation/seaspiracy-netflix-documentary-review|url-status=live}}</ref>

''[[Common Sense Media]]'' gave the film a 4 out of 5 stars and 15+ rating, calling it "tough but necessary viewing" and "backed with evidence from journalists, authors, marine biologists, oceanographers, frontline activists, and industry insiders". It questions the use of director Ali Tabrizi as protagonist to be followed around.<ref>{{Cite web|date=March 24, 2021|title=Seaspiracy - Movie Review|url=https://www.commonsensemedia.org/movie-reviews/seaspiracy|access-date=April 1, 2021|website=[[Common Sense Media]]|archive-date=April 28, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428020511/https://www.commonsensemedia.org/movie-reviews/seaspiracy|url-status=live}}</ref>

Writing for the [[American socialist]] publication ''[[Jacobin (magazine)|Jacobin]]'', Spencer Roberts says that the film "is not without its faults. Its interview style is abrasive. It has excessive animation. It makes a couple of statistical misinterpretations and several oversimplifications. Yet the film is mainly accurate and devastatingly detailed."<ref name="Spencer">{{cite news |last=Roberts |first=Spencer |date=April 14, 2021 |title=What Seaspiracy Gets Right About the Exploitative Fishing Industry |url=https://jacobinmag.com/2021/04/seaspiracy-marine-science-fishing-industry-netflix |work=[[Jacobin (magazine)|Jacobin]] |location= |access-date=April 16, 2021 |archive-date=April 15, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210415185017/https://www.jacobinmag.com/2021/04/seaspiracy-marine-science-fishing-industry-netflix |url-status=live }}</ref> Addressing the disputes over its scientific accuracy, he says "[i]t's fair to say that ''Seaspiracy'' cited some studies that can be considered dated or disputed, but it also left out some of the most harrowing statistics published in recent years", including the bycatch of 8.5 million sea turtles from 1990 to 2008,<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Wallace |first1= Bryan P.|last2=Lewison|first2= Rebecca L.|display-authors=etal. |date=2010 |title=Global patterns of marine turtle bycatch |journal=[[Conservation Letters]] |volume=3|issue=3 |pages=131–142 |doi=10.1111/j.1755-263X.2010.00105.x |s2cid= 2639284|doi-access=free |bibcode= 2010ConL....3..131W}}</ref> total fish hauls peaking in 1996,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pauly |first1=Daniel |last2=Zeller |first2=Dirk |date=2016 |title=Catch reconstructions reveal that global marine fisheries catches are higher than reported and declining |journal=[[Nature Communications]] |volume=7 |article-number=10244 |doi=10.1038/ncomms10244  |doi-access=free|pmid=26784963 |pmc=4735634 |bibcode=2016NatCo...710244P }}</ref> and perhaps 25% of all fishing ships using forced labor.<ref name="Spencer"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=McDonald|first1=Gavin G.|last2=Costello |first2=Christopher |display-authors=etal. |date=2021 |title=Satellites can reveal global extent of forced labor in the world's fishing fleet |journal=[[PNAS]] |volume=118 |issue=3 |article-number= e2016238117|doi=10.1073/pnas.2016238117 |pmid=33431679|pmc=7826370 |bibcode=2021PNAS..11820162M|s2cid=231586627|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Responses from animal rights groups ===
[[People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals|PETA]] wrote the movie "is not to be missed"<ref>{{cite web|last=Sullivan|first=Katherine|date=March 26, 2021|title='Seaspiracy' Dives Deep Into 'Bycatch' and 'Dolphin-Safe' Tuna Scandals|url=https://www.peta.org/blog/seaspiracy-what-is-bycatch-is-dolphin-safe-tuna-really-safe/|access-date=March 30, 2021|work=[[People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals|PETA]]|publisher=|quote=|archive-date=March 27, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210327114104/https://www.peta.org/blog/seaspiracy-what-is-bycatch-is-dolphin-safe-tuna-really-safe/|url-status=live}}</ref> and encouraged readers to host watch parties.<ref>{{Cite web|date=March 24, 2021|title=How to Host a Watch Party for Netflix's 'Seaspiracy'|url=https://www.peta.org/action/host-seaspiracy-watch-party/|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=PETA|archive-date=March 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210324223340/https://www.peta.org/action/host-seaspiracy-watch-party/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2022, the film won PETA's Oscat award for best picture.<ref name=Oscat>{{cite web |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/zendaya-lost-daughter-candyman-peta-oscat-winners-2022-1235113667/ |title=Zendaya, 'The Lost Daughter,' 'Candyman' Among PETA Oscat Winners |first=Etan |last=Vlessing |publisher=The Hollywood Reporter |date=March 17, 2022 |access-date=March 22, 2022 |quote=The best picture Oscat went to Seaspiracy, Netflix's documentary by director Ali Tabrizi about the devastation the fishing industry has brought to marine animals and ecosystems. |archive-date=March 22, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220322144437/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/zendaya-lost-daughter-candyman-peta-oscat-winners-2022-1235113667/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Responses from environmental groups ===
[[Greenpeace]] commended the film for promoting various marine issues, but challenged the conclusion of abstaining from fish consumption, distinguishing between industrial fishing and traditional harvesting. Greenpeace instead suggested alternate solutions.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Protecting the Oceans: why turning vegan can't be the only answer|url=https://www.greenpeace.org/international/story/46985/protect-the-oceans-why-vegan-cant-only-answer|access-date=April 10, 2021|website=Greenpeace International|archive-date=April 11, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210411020743/https://www.greenpeace.org/international/story/46985/protect-the-oceans-why-vegan-cant-only-answer/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Seaspiracy the movie was chilling but what can I do now?|url=https://www.greenpeace.org/aotearoa/story/seaspiracy-netflix-movie-take-action|access-date=April 3, 2021|website=Greenpeace Aotearoa|date=April 2021|archive-date=April 2, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210402020152/https://www.greenpeace.org/aotearoa/story/seaspiracy-netflix-movie-take-action/|url-status=live}}</ref> A representative of [[Fauna and Flora International]] wrote that the film has "bitterly divided the environmental community" and described its interpretation of scientific studies as "highly problematic and often woefully misleading." Although also questioning its "western-centric and absolutist perspective", it accepted that it was "broadly right on some central issues... with significant caveats".<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |last=Steadman |first=Daniel |title=Seaspiracy - the urgent messages behind the flawed argument|url=https://www.fauna-flora.org/news/seaspiracy-lets-not-lose-sight-of-the-urgent-message-behind-the-flawed-arguments|access-date=April 7, 2021|work=[[Fauna and Flora International]] |date=April 6, 2021|archive-date=April 12, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412221849/https://www.fauna-flora.org/news/seaspiracy-lets-not-lose-sight-of-the-urgent-message-behind-the-flawed-arguments|url-status=live}}</ref>

Charles Clover of [[Blue Marine Foundation]] and author of the book [[The End of the Line (book)|''The End of the Line'']] criticised the film's scientific accuracy, saying "there are a few jaw-dropping factual errors" such as its framing of [[Cetacean stranding|whale strandings]]. He said such strandings have a variety of causes other than plastic pollution alone, and accused ''Seaspiracy'' of deriving its narrative from previous documentaries, such as the film adaptation of his book. Nonetheless, he praised its communication of marine fisheries and conservation issues to a new audience, stating "[t]he problem of overfishing is immense, global, remote, horrifying and it is really hard to get people to focus on. Until now, Tabrizi's generation thought banning plastic straws was more important. But it isn't. Overfishing is." Although he found a "lot to admire" in the film's criticisms of the fishing industry and sustainable seafood certification organisations, he called the film's conclusion of not eating fish "thoroughly unsatisfactory".<ref name=":10">{{Cite web|date=March 31, 2021|title=Seaspiracy: should we stop eating fish?|url=https://www.bluemarinefoundation.com/2021/03/31/seaspiracy-should-we-stop-eating-fish/|access-date=April 1, 2021|website=Blue Marine Foundation|archive-date=April 1, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210401064502/https://www.bluemarinefoundation.com/2021/03/31/seaspiracy-should-we-stop-eating-fish/|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Environmental journalism]] outlets ''[[Earther]]'' (a publication of ''[[Gizmodo]]'') and ''[[Hakai Magazine]]'' both gave negative reviews. They both criticised the film for suggesting that previous media had not covered the facts discussed in the film, and questioned its tone and accuracy.<ref name=":18" /><ref name=":15">{{Cite web|title=Don't Watch Netflix's Seaspiracy|url=https://earther.gizmodo.com/dont-watch-netflixs-seaspiracy-1846630338|access-date=April 7, 2021|website=Earther|date=April 7, 2021|archive-date=April 7, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210407140508/https://earther.gizmodo.com/dont-watch-netflixs-seaspiracy-1846630338|url-status=live}}</ref> A reviewer in ''Hakai Magazine'' wrote, "had Tabrizi looked at any of these issues in greater depth, he'd have found that journalists have been covering these sorts of stories for years and have not glossed over the nuance."<ref name=":18">{{Cite web|title=Seaspiracy Harms More Than It Educates|url=https://www.hakaimagazine.com/article-short/seaspiracy-harms-more-than-it-educates/|access-date=April 7, 2021|website=Hakai Magazine|archive-date=April 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210406115450/https://www.hakaimagazine.com/article-short/seaspiracy-harms-more-than-it-educates/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Responses from seafood industry groups ===
Internal documents leaked before the film's release authored by the [[National Fisheries Institute]], a trade group representing the US seafood industry, revealed a new media strategy to protect the fishing industry and to characterize the then-unreleased documentary as a "dishonest attack".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://plantbasednews.org/culture/film/fishing-industry-leaked-documents-expose-plan-to-attack-seaspiracy/|title=Leaked Documents From Fishing Industry Expose Plan To Attack Seaspiracy Netflix Release|website=Plant Based News|last=Baker|first=Emily|date=March 16, 2021|access-date=April 3, 2021|archive-date=March 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210330051602/https://plantbasednews.org/culture/film/fishing-industry-leaked-documents-expose-plan-to-attack-seaspiracy/|url-status=live}}</ref> The National Fisheries Institute appealed to Netflix ahead of the film's release to "distinguish between legitimate documentaries and propaganda", stating "audiences will not recognize the film's true agenda [as] a [[Veganism|vegan]] indoctrination movie".<ref name=":8" />

After the movie was released, a spokesperson for Scottish Salmon Producers Organisation (SSPO) said the film's coverage of [[Aquaculture in the United Kingdom#Salmon|Scottish salmon aquaculture]] was "wrong, misleading and inaccurate".<ref name="Independent2021-03-30" /> The [[Global Aquaculture Alliance]] also criticised the film, saying "reputable NGOs have worked tirelessly with industry over the past 20-plus years to continually improve the lives of the people working in aquaculture and fisheries as well as the ecosystems in which aquaculture and fisheries are practiced", and suggested abandoning fisheries and aquaculture would "abandon the approximately 250 million people employed by the industry and rob billions of people of a healthful source of protein".<ref name=":8" />

=== Responses from academics ===
Bryce Stewart, a [[University of York]] marine ecologist and fisheries biologist, criticised the film's scientific accuracy and neutrality, calling it "the worst kind of journalism" and questioning its lack of coverage of the [[Effects of climate change on oceans|impacts of climate change on oceans]]. He said that "the biggest error is to say that [[Sustainable fishery|sustainable fisheries]] don't exist. This is like saying that [[sustainable agriculture]] doesn't exist. All food production systems have an impact on the natural world, but obviously some more than others." He acknowledged "the movie was right to highlight overfishing as the biggest current threat to marine biodiversity. This is widely accepted by scientists and the evidence for this is very strong".<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web|date=March 30, 2021|title=Everything you need to know about Seaspiracy, the controversial new Netflix documentary|url=https://inews.co.uk/culture/film/seaspiracy-fact-check-netflix-documentary-what-about-accuracy-explained-935761|access-date=March 31, 2021|website=inews.co.uk|archive-date=March 31, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210331000444/https://inews.co.uk/culture/film/seaspiracy-fact-check-netflix-documentary-what-about-accuracy-explained-935761|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Kleinman|first=Jake|title='Seaspiracy' fact check: An expert debunks the controversial Netflix doc|url=https://www.inverse.com/science/seaspiracy-fact-check-debunked-interview|access-date=April 10, 2021|website=Inverse|date=April 9, 2021|archive-date=April 9, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210409213934/https://www.inverse.com/science/seaspiracy-fact-check-debunked-interview|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Daniel Pauly]], project leader of the [[Sea Around Us (organization)|Sea Around Us]] project at the [[UBC Institute for the Oceans and Fisheries|Institute for the Oceans and Fisheries]] at the [[University of British Columbia]], wrote in [[Vox (website)|''Vox'']] that the documentary "make[s] the important point that industrial fishing is... a too often out-of-control, sometimes criminal enterprise that needs to be reined in and regulated." However, he said it also "undermines [its message] with an avalanche of falsehoods", citing its coverage of [[marine debris]], [[bycatch]] and [[Sustainable fishery|sustainable fishing]], as well as "blames the ocean conservation community, i.e., the very NGOs trying to fix things, rather than the industrial companies actually causing the problem".<ref name=":11">{{Cite web|last=Pauly|first=Daniel|date=April 13, 2021|title=What Netflix's Seaspiracy gets wrong about fishing, explained by a marine biologist|url=https://www.vox.com/2021/4/13/22380637/seaspiracy-netflix-fact-check-fishing-ocean-plastic-veganism-vegetarianism|access-date=April 13, 2021|website=Vox|archive-date=April 13, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210413125055/https://www.vox.com/2021/4/13/22380637/seaspiracy-netflix-fact-check-fishing-ocean-plastic-veganism-vegetarianism|url-status=live}}</ref>

In an article in ''[[Nature Ecology and Evolution]]'', [[Dyhia Belhabib]] criticised the film's conclusion of ending fish consumption, calling this "embedded in white privilege and colonialism" and "[ignoring] that more than 90% of the global fishing effort is small-scale and coastal in nature". She proposed management solutions and [[Decolonization of knowledge|decolonisation]] of ocean science and advocacy.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Belhabib|first=Dyhia|date=May 12, 2021|title=Ocean science and advocacy work better when decolonized|journal=Nature Ecology & Evolution|volume=5|issue=6|pages=709–710|doi=10.1038/s41559-021-01477-1|pmid=33981027|issn=2397-334X|doi-access=|bibcode=2021NatEE...5..709B |s2cid=234485402 }}</ref>

=== Responses from those featured ===
The [[Marine Stewardship Council]], [[Earth Island Institute]] and [[Plastic Pollution Coalition]] disputed their negative portrayal in the documentary, and suggested that their representatives' comments were cherry-picked.<ref name=misrepresent>{{cite news |last1=McVeigh |first1=Karen |title=Seaspiracy: Netflix documentary accused of misrepresentation by participants |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/mar/31/seaspiracy-netflix-documentary-accused-of-misrepresentation-by-participants |access-date=April 7, 2021 |work=The Guardian |date=March 31, 2021 |archive-date=April 7, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210407025546/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/mar/31/seaspiracy-netflix-documentary-accused-of-misrepresentation-by-participants |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|date=March 29, 2021|title=Marine organisations and experts react to hit Netflix documentary 'Seaspiracy'|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/seaspiracy-netflix-marines-true-story-b1824038.html|access-date=March 29, 2021|website=The Independent|archive-date=March 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210329173228/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/seaspiracy-netflix-marines-true-story-b1824038.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> [[Oceana (non-profit group)|Oceana]] disputed the statement that they receive funding from the seafood industry.<ref>{{Cite news|title=A statement from Oceana on Netflix's Seaspiracy|url=https://oceana.org/statement-oceana-netflixs-seaspiracy|access-date=March 29, 2021|website=Oceana|archive-date=April 1, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210401040435/https://oceana.org/statement-oceana-netflixs-seaspiracy|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Christina Hicks]], an academic at [[Lancaster University]] and [[James Cook University]] who appeared in the film, did not endorse it. She said she committed her career to the fishing industry, in which "there are issues but also progress and fish remain critical to food and nutrition security in many vulnerable geographies".<ref name=":9" /><ref name="Independent2021-03-30">{{Cite web|date=March 30, 2021|title=Viewers react to controversial new Netflix documentary, Seaspiracy|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/news/seaspiracy-netflix-fishing-environment-reaction-b1823860.html|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=The Independent|archive-date=March 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210329205832/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/news/seaspiracy-netflix-fishing-environment-reaction-b1823860.html|url-status=live}}</ref> However, ''[[The Guardian]]'' columnist [[George Monbiot]] expressed his support for the film and its message. While acknowledging some inaccuracies, Monbiot says that the main point of the film is correct: the fishing industry is the greatest cause of the ecological destruction of the oceans, and cites the 2019 [[Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services|IPBES]] [[Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services|report]] as evidence to back this assertion.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Monbiot |first=George |author-link=George Monbiot |date=April 7, 2021|title=Seaspiracy shows why we must treat fish not as seafood, but as wildlife |url=http://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2021/apr/07/seaspiracy-earth-oceans-destruction-industrial-fishing|access-date=April 7, 2021|website=The Guardian|archive-date=April 9, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210409171534/https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2021/apr/07/seaspiracy-earth-oceans-destruction-industrial-fishing|url-status=live}}</ref> The marine conservation biologist [[Callum Roberts (biologist)|Callum Roberts]] from the [[University of Exeter]] also argued against criticism. He said "my colleagues may rue the statistics, but the basic thrust of it is we are doing a huge amount of damage to the ocean and that's true. At some point you run out. Whether it's 2048 or 2079, the question is: 'Is the trajectory in the wrong direction or the right direction?'"<ref name=":9"/>

== Scientific accuracy ==
The scientific accuracy of several statements in ''Seaspiracy'' has been questioned by several [[Fisheries science|fisheries scientists]]<ref name=":11" /><ref name=":9" /><ref name=":16">{{Cite news|last=Horton|first=Helena|date=March 31, 2021|title=Netflix documentary Seaspiracy under fire from scientists|work=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03/31/netflix-documentary-seaspiracy-fire-scientists/ |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/03/31/netflix-documentary-seaspiracy-fire-scientists/ |archive-date=January 12, 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|access-date=April 7, 2021|issn=0307-1235}}{{cbignore}}</ref> and [[marine conservation]]ists.<ref name=":18" /><ref name=":10" /> ''[[BBC News]],'' ''[[Newsweek]]'' and ''[[Radio Times]]'' have each written a [[Fact-checking|fact check]] article about the film.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Henry |first1=Grace |last2=Berry |first2=Jo |title=Seaspiracy fact checker: Truth behind the Netflix documentary|url=https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/documentaries/seaspiracy-fact-check-netflix-truth/|access-date=April 16, 2021|website=Radio Times|archive-date=April 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210415202720/https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/documentaries/seaspiracy-fact-check-netflix-truth/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Fishing nets versus plastic straws as marine debris ===
[[File:Turtle entangled in marine debris (ghost net).jpg|alt=A turtle entangled in a ghost net|thumb|A turtle entangled in a ghost net]]
[[File:Great Pacific Garbage Patch-Map-2017.jpg|alt=Map showing the extent of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch and the US West Coast|thumb|The Great Pacific Garbage Patch in 2017]]
In ''Seaspiracy'', narrator Tabrizi criticises a public focus on plastic straws, stating that they only account for 0.03% of ocean plastic. He contrasts this with [[Ghost net|fishing nets]], saying they make up 46% of the [[Great Pacific Garbage Patch]]. The fishing net statement derives from a 2018 study, which examines floating marine debris by weight. The study found that at least 46% of floating plastic in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch came from fishing nets.<ref name="Transcript" /><ref>{{Cite web|title='Seaspiracy': 8 Major Takeaways From the New Netflix Doc|url=https://www.greenmatters.com/p/seaspiracy-facts|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=Green Matters|date=March 29, 2021|archive-date=April 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210410151237/https://www.greenmatters.com/p/seaspiracy-facts|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lebreton|first1=L.|last2=Slat|first2=B.|last3=Ferrari|first3=F.|last4=Sainte-Rose|first4=B.|last5=Aitken|first5=J.|last6=Marthouse|first6=R.|last7=Hajbane|first7=S.|last8=Cunsolo|first8=S.|last9=Schwarz|first9=A.|last10=Levivier|first10=A.|last11=Noble|first11=K.|date=March 22, 2018|title=Evidence that the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is rapidly accumulating plastic|journal=Scientific Reports|volume=8|issue=1|page=4666|doi=10.1038/s41598-018-22939-w|pmid=29568057|pmc=5864935|bibcode=2018NatSR...8.4666L|issn=2045-2322|quote=Over three-quarters of the GPGP mass was carried by debris larger than 5 cm and at least 46% was {{sic|comprised |hide=y|of}} fishing nets.|doi-access=free}}</ref>

According to the ''BBC News'' fact check, the share of plastic straws in ocean plastic (0.03%) seems to be calculated using numbers from two studies. One study is on plastic straws on coastlines, the other on floating marine plastic in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. The fact check cites [[Jenna Jambeck]], the author of the coastline study, saying "no-one really knows how much of it is straws, but experts agree that it is certainly a lot less than dumped fishing gear." The author of the latter study on the Great Pacific garbage patch, is quoted as saying "[fishing gear] fragments much more slowly and is also very buoyant; prime candidates to hang around in the GPGP", as opposed to thinner plastics like straws and bags, which disintegrate and sink.<ref name=":12">{{Cite news|date=April 8, 2021|title=Is Netflix's Seaspiracy film right about fishing damaging oceans?|work=[[BBC News]]|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/56660823|access-date=April 9, 2021|archive-date=April 9, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210409001600/https://www.bbc.com/news/56660823|url-status=live}}</ref>

An article in ''[[Forbes]]'' concluded that the film's focus on the Great Pacific Garbage Patch was "misleading", as this region of the ocean accumulates buoyant plastics and therefore "does not provide a particularly accurate depiction of the marine plastic in the entire ocean overall".<ref name=":22">{{Cite web|last=Allen|first=Liz|title=Why Seaspiracy's Focus On The Great Pacific Garbage Patch Is Misleading|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/allenelizabeth/2021/04/13/why-seaspiracys-focus-on-the-great-pacific-garbage-patch-is-misleading/|access-date=June 2, 2021|website=Forbes|archive-date=June 2, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602220318/https://www.forbes.com/sites/allenelizabeth/2021/04/13/why-seaspiracys-focus-on-the-great-pacific-garbage-patch-is-misleading/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Empty oceans by 2048 statement ===
The film says that a leading fisheries expert found "that if current fishing trends continue, we will see virtually empty oceans by the year 2048."<ref name="Transcript">{{Cite web|date=March 30, 2021|title=Seaspiracy (2021) - Transcript|url=https://scrapsfromtheloft.com/2021/03/30/seaspiracy-2021-transcript/|url-status=live|access-date=March 31, 2021|website=Scraps from the loft|quote=Well, the latest study actually showed that 46% of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is fishing nets alone(...)But perhaps one of the most shocking facts of all came from one of the world's leading fisheries experts estimating that if current fishing trends continue, we will see virtually empty oceans by the year 2048.(...)I couldn't believe what I was hearing. The internationally recognized seafood label was a complete fabrication since it guaranteed nothing. At this point, I began to wonder what else was being covered up| archive-url= https://archive.today/20210410202532/https://scrapsfromtheloft.com/2021/03/30/seaspiracy-2021-transcript/
 | archive-date = April 10, 2021 }}</ref>

This prediction originates from the conclusion section of a 2006 study by a team of [[Marine biology|marine ecologists]] led by [[Boris Worm|Dr. Boris Worm]] published in [[Science (journal)|''Science'']].<ref name="Worn 2006">{{cite journal |title=Impacts of Biodiversity Loss on Ocean Ecosystem Services |journal=Science |date=2006 |last=Worm |first=Boris |volume=314 |issue=5800 |pages=787–790 |doi=10.1126/science.1132294 |pmid=17082450 |bibcode=2006Sci...314..787W |s2cid=37235806 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281257970 |access-date=April 9, 2021 |quote=Conclusions. Positive relationships between diversity and ecosystem functions and services were found using experimental (Fig. 1) and correlative approaches along trajectories of diversity loss (Figs. 2 and 3) and recovery (Fig. 4). Our data highlight the societal consequences of an ongoing erosion of diversity that appears to be accelerating on a global scale (Fig. 3A). This trend is of serious concern because it projects the global collapse of all taxa currently fished by the mid–21st century (based on the extrapolation of regression in Fig. 3A to 100% in the year 2048). |archive-date=March 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240303183721/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281257970_Impacts_of_Biodiversity_Loss_on_Ocean_Ecosystem_Ser_vices |url-status=live }} {{Free access}}</ref> In the final paragraphs of the study, the authors extrapolated from the percentage of fisheries that have already collapsed and predicted that 32 years later, no more fish would be caught in the ocean.<ref name="Worn 2006"/><ref name="Seaspiracy Facts Website">{{cite web |url=https://www.seaspiracy.org/facts |title=Seaspiracy Facts |access-date=April 15, 2021 |archive-date=April 16, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416001614/https://www.seaspiracy.org/facts |url-status=live }}</ref> When interviewed for the BBC fact-check article about ''Seaspiracy'' in 2021, Worm said, "the 2006 paper is now 15 years old and most of the data in it is almost 20 years old. Since then, we have seen increasing efforts in many regions to rebuild depleted fish populations". The BBC also noted that other experts had taken issue with the original 2006 study.<ref name=":12" />

=== Dolphin-safe tuna labels ===
[[File:Eilat Dolphin Reef (3).jpg|alt=Photo of a dolphin underwater|thumb|A dolphin underwater]]
The film criticises [[dolphin safe label]]s on [[tuna]] and says that "the internationally recognized seafood label was a complete fabrication since it guaranteed nothing".<ref name="Transcript" /> This is in response to Mark Palmer, associate director of the International Marine Mammal Project of the Earth Island Institute, who says on camera that "dolphin safe" tuna cannot be guaranteed, and that observers can be bribed. Palmer has accused the documentary of taking him out of context.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite web|date=April 1, 2021|title=Fact checking dolphin-safe label claims made by Netflix doc 'Seaspiracy'|url=https://www.newsweek.com/fact-check-seaspiricy-dolphin-safe-labels-guaranteed-1579804|access-date=April 3, 2021|website=Newsweek|archive-date=April 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210403180838/https://www.newsweek.com/fact-check-seaspiricy-dolphin-safe-labels-guaranteed-1579804|url-status=live}}</ref>

Senior fisheries scientist Sara McDonald of the [[Monterey Bay Aquarium]] was quoted by ''Newsweek'' in a ''Seaspiracy'' fact check article: "The U.S. dolphin-safe program has been very effective. Dolphin mortality in the 1980s was 130,000. In 2018, there were 819 documented deaths." However, a representative of the [[Natural Resources Defense Council]] stated that although "the U.S. laws are good if everyone is being honest, that doesn't mean nothing ever gets in. [Law enforcement] can't catch it all." ''Newsweek's'' fact-check article concluded that dolphin safe labels cannot guarantee that no dolphins are harmed during fishing.<ref name=":7" />
